In William Faulkner's "The Sound and the Fury," time emerges as a central motif, juxtaposing the despair of Quentin Compson against the enduring hope of Dilsey Gibson. Quentin's tragic descent into hopelessness underscores his inability to reconcile his rigid code of honor with the inexorable passage of time. His fixation on the past, symbolized by the futile attempt to destroy his watch, encapsulates his struggle to control change, which ultimately leads to his demise. In stark contrast, Dilsey embraces a worldview grounded in faith, hope, and love, drawing strength from her Christian beliefs to navigate the currents of time with resilience and optimism.

Quentin's internal conflict is steeped in a sense of lost honor, compounded by his obsessive concern with his sister Caddy's perceived tarnishing of their family's reputation. This rigidity binds him to a past that offers neither solace nor redemption. Time, for Quentin, is a relentless adversary, wholly unforgiving of his inability to liberate himself and his sister from the constraints of tradition. His suicide represents both an escape from and a culmination of his tortured existence, wherein he fails to accept the inevitability of social change—the very essence that Caddy personifies in her defiance of societal norms.

In contrast, Dilsey's optimistic outlook arises from her embrace of change and her faith in a future beyond the material constraints of time. Her existence is rooted in a love that transcends temporal bounds, facilitating a healthy acceptance of the evolving world around her. Unlike Quentin, who perceives time as an oppressive force, Dilsey embodies a symbolic rebirth for the South, seeing potential in the new societal paradigms taking shape. Her faith signifies a bridge to a future imbued with hope, a narrative of renewal that starkly contrasts with Quentin's perception of inevitability and despair.

This dichotomy between Quentin's entrapment in the past and Dilsey's openness to the future is poignantly illustrated through their differing experiences of time. For Quentin, the ceaseless ticking of his watch serves as a haunting reminder of his futile battle against change. In destroying the watch, he attempts to halt the flow of time and assert control over his fate—an endeavor ultimately rendered meaningless by his self-imposed end. Dilsey, on the other hand, experiences time as a gentle, coherent stream, imparting resolution and hope. Her section of the narrative, infused with tranquility and acceptance, highlights the triumph of faith over despair.

Through vivid imagery, Faulkner encapsulates the central tragedy of the novel—that of Quentin's refusal to adapt in a world that is progressively moving forward. The southern landscapes, with their languid motions and lingering beauty, mirror Quentin's stagnation, while the burgeoning life vibrant in Dilsey's presence symbolizes a positive transformation. Dilsey's unwavering faith serves as a counterpoint to Quentin's despair, emphasizing the novel's thematic exploration of the futility of resisting change and the potential for redemption through acceptance.

In essence, the contrasting perspectives on time and change underscore a narrative shift that embodies the resolution and hope embodied by Dilsey. Where Quentin sees only the tragic weight of history, Dilsey perceives opportunity for rebirth, thereby illustrating the profound impact that internal conflict and acceptance—or lack thereof—have on human experience. Through these characters, Faulkner poignantly portrays the complexities of time, honor, and social evolution, capturing the enduring tension between despair and hope within the human condition.

Manipulation, a profound and pervasive theme in classical literature, emerges in diverse forms across various narrative landscapes, revealed through symbolism, characterization, and intricate plot developments. Nathaniel Hawthorne expertly utilizes symbolism in "The Scarlet Letter," particularly with the letter "A," initially intended by society as a mark of shame for Hester Prynne's adultery. Yet, beneath this overt meaning, the letter embodies deeper, subtler forces of manipulation at work. The initial "A" in Arthur Dimmesdale's name notably symbolizes not only a direct connection to Hester's shame but also alludes to dualities—beginning and ending, aspiration and agony, authority and abasement. Pearl's relationship with the scarlet letter reinforces this symbolic weight; for her, the scarlet "A" becomes a familiar, even comforting emblem integral to her identity, unintentionally challenging the community's intended manipulation of her mother's sin and subverting societal condemnation. Thus, Hawthorne expands the narrative beyond Hester’s personal adversity, splintering the manipulative intent behind the emblematic letter and transforming it into an intricate exploration of identity, interpretation, and morality.

The complex dimensions of literary manipulation receive insightful illumination from Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's observation that, "We judge ourselves by what we feel capable of doing, while others judge us by what we have already done." This remark underscores the dual nature of manipulation—societal judgment seeks to control through perceptions of past actions, while self-interpretation hinges on internal potential. Such dualities saturate Shakespeare's "Hamlet," wherein manipulation manifests prominently through an array of characters driven by motives ranging from raw ambition to political survival. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern exemplify the archetypal manipulators certainly motivated by a desire for acceptance, status, and influence within the royal court. Yet their ambition renders them susceptible to exploitation, used ultimately as pawns by King Claudius. Their initial intention to control Hamlet’s fate through deceit backfires spectacularly, emphasizing the complexities inherent in acts of manipulation. Their ultimate demise represents the inevitable consequences awaiting those who surrender moral autonomy in pursuit of manipulative ends, emphasizing a critical difference outlined profoundly by literary figures who grapple consistently with the ethical implications of power and influence.

Ultimately, Shakespeare exemplifies the destructive potential of manipulation not merely as a personal failing but as a pervasive societal disease. Hamlet's cunning and strategic maneuvering demonstrate the motif's broader thematic significance; he deftly replaces the incriminating letter intended for his demise with one orchestrating Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's deaths instead. This act underscores Hamlet's meaningful engagement with manipulation not merely as victim but as a careful architect, reversing roles to serve self-preservation and justice. Simultaneously, this event demonstrates the destructive spiral manipulation inevitably invites—revealing a complex interplay between power dynamics, consequence, and ethical choice. Juxtaposed with Hawthorne’s multilayered symbolism, Shakespeare’s exploration highlights literary manipulation's profound thematic resonance, illustrating the human capacity to weaponize both language and intent. Literature, through authors such as Hawthorne and Shakespeare, thus presents manipulation as a multifaceted force capable of defining or decimating characters, revealing deeper truths about humanity's nature to control, deceive, and ultimately influence destiny itself.

Edna's journey is a testament to her rebellion against the societal norms that suffocate her. As she separates from her husband, she signifies her rejection of the expectations placed upon her as a wife and a mother. This act of defiance is further emphasized by her attempt to crush her wedding ring, a symbol of her struggle against the constraints of marriage and convention. The ring, once a symbol of love and commitment, now represents the shackles that bind her to a life she no longer desires. As she tries to destroy it, she is, in effect, trying to break free from the societal norms that dictate her role as a woman.

The character of the doctor serves as a parallel to Edna's husband, dismissing female individualism and suggesting conventional solutions for Edna's behavior. He advises her to return to her community, to resume her duties as a wife and mother, and to suppress her desires for independence and self-discovery. This highlights the patriarchal double standards that dictate men's and women's roles differently, allowing men to pursue their desires while expecting women to conform to societal expectations. As Edna's husband remarks, "I give you as much money as you want...What more can a woman want?" This quote underscores the societal commentary on the limited roles and desires attributed to women.

Edna's relationship with Arobin further illustrates the societal view of her as a failed mother and woman. Arobin's treatment of Edna as a mistress, rather than a partner, emphasizes the societal perception of women who prioritize their own desires over their duties as wives and mothers. In contrast, Robert's abandonment of Edna highlights her inability to find a non-conventional partner who accepts her for who she is. As Edna navigates these relationships, she is met with characters who embody the societal roles and critiques that she is trying to escape.

Edna's positive reaction to Mariequita's wildness signifies her psychic transformation, as she begins to embrace her own desires and individuality. Mariequita's carefree nature and disregard for societal norms inspire Edna to question her own constraints and seek a more authentic life. Edna's secret engagement with taboo literature also symbolizes her awakening and independence, as she seeks knowledge and understanding of her own desires and aspirations. As she delves into these forbidden texts, she feels a sense of liberation, as if she is uncovering secrets that have been hidden from her.

As Edna visits the island, she feels a sense of freedom she has never experienced before. The island, with its vast expanse of sea and sand, represents a space where she can break free from the societal constraints that have defined her life. The warm sun on her skin and the sound of the waves crashing against the shore evoke a sense of joy and liberation, as if she is finally able to breathe. In this moment, Edna is transformed, her eyes opened to the possibilities of a life beyond the conventions of society. As she stands on the island, she is, in effect, standing at the threshold of a new life, one that is hers alone to create.

There are three main aspects of the gun control controversy: sociological, ethical, and legal. The sociological aspect is the effectiveness or lack of effectiveness that gun control laws have on reducing violent crimes. The ethical aspect is the protection of the United States citizens and protecting them from crime. The legal issues revolve mainly around the Second Amendment and how it is interpreted, and the laws and regulations associated with it (Lee).

Gun control activists blame the wide use and availability of lethal weapons for the United States’ high murder and crime rates. There are over 30,000 deaths resulting from gunfire every year. More than half are murders, a little less than half are suicides and the rest are fatal accidents. Several hundred of these victims are children (Ballaro). Gunfire deaths from 1980 to 1997 equaled close to four hundred thousand. That is more than the casualties from WWI and WWII combined, and would equal the death toll of nearly eight Vietnams (Harwood). The United States has some of the highest gun-related violence rates in the developed world. This is due to the number of guns Americans own, the availability of extremely powerful and lethal guns, and the lack of comprehensive, uniform laws. If gun control laws limited the availability of guns, it would lower homicide rates. Just as the now regular use of bicycle helmets has greatly reduced the amount of head trauma injuries (Ballaro).

One of the biggest reasons for the United States’ shockingly high gun-related violence rates is the sheer amount of firearms owned. One in three homes has guns. The total amount of arms in the United States is close to two hundred and forty million (Ballaro). American citizens own between fifty and seventy million handguns. Handguns escalate disputes into fatal incidents because they are easy to conceal and transport (Harwood). Supporters of gun control state that the formation of the National Guard over a hundred years ago nullified any need for militias, and the all-out legality of guns should be questioned (Bowman).

The police force in the United States is in danger from the large arsenal of weapons and the overwhelming lack of gun control legislation. In 1997 the Los Angeles police were authorized to carry assault rifles after a shootout with gunmen armed with AK-47s. In September of 2007 the Miami police chief John Timoney made the same decision. He said the decision was undesirable, but mandatory due to fact that the criminals his men faced wielded extremely high caliber weapons. In the previous year fifteen of the seventy-nine gun related homicides involved assault weapons (Ballaro). Criminologist Franklin Zimring and Gordon Hawkins of the University of California conducted a large-scale study on gun related violence and homicide in the United States compared to other countries. They discovered that the United States have similar crime rates as other developed countries, but much higher homicide rates (Harwood). The gun violence seemed to correlate to the stringency of gun control laws of each of the countries.

During the Portuguese colonial period in Angola, a system of racial hierarchies was entrenched that significantly influenced the region's social, political, and economic dynamics. The Portuguese colonial administration established a rigid classification where Europeans occupied the highest social tier. Beneath them were the Afro-Portuguese or mestiços, a group that emerged from unions between Portuguese settlers and indigenous women. At the lowest tier were the indigenous African populations, who were often subject to exploitation and marginalization. Despite having initially small numbers and being concentrated along the coast, the European settlers were able to maintain dominance partly through the imposition of these hierarchies. The interior of Angola resisted Portuguese settlement due to logistical challenges and hostile conditions that resulted in high mortality rates, thereby discouraging free immigration. Instead, Portugal's strategy of penal colonization involved utilizing convicts, known as degradados, to establish settlements within Angola. However, this system was fraught with difficulties, leading to more complex social stratifications and ethnic tensions.

Portuguese colonial policies heightened existing ethnic tensions, contributing to later strife and conflict within Angola. The colonial powers often favored certain ethnic groups over others, exacerbating divisions that would later become catalysts for nationalist movements and civil wars following Angola's independence in 1975. The Mbundu and the Kimbundu ethnic groups, for instance, maneuvered within these divisive structures to gain leverage over trade and political activities, while others were marginalized. This fracturing of ethnic unity during colonial rule laid the groundwork for regional and ethnic factions that competed for power in the post-colonial era. These tensions were evident in the protracted civil wars that ensued, as various factions, often aligned along ethnic lines, vied for control of the nation's political future.

From an economic standpoint, the Afro-Portuguese emerged as a dominant force, crucial in shaping Angola’s economic landscape. Their role as intermediaries in the slave trade was pivotal, as they expanded trade networks from the Kongo kingdom to the central highlands. Key ports such as Luanda and Benguela became vital nodes in the transatlantic slave trade, connecting Angola with Brazil and other Portuguese colonies. The surge in trade bypassed traditional centers like São Salvador, which declined in prominence. Luanda, bolstered by the burgeoning Afro-Portuguese class, became the epicenter of economic activity, overshadowing traditional African trade hubs. As the Afro-Portuguese consolidated economic and political power, they also negotiated their position within the colonial society, further perpetuating colonial frameworks and racial hierarchies. The economic transformations instigated by the slave trade would indelibly impact Angola's societal structure, with enduring ramifications felt even after the abolition of the slave trade and the eventual decolonization of the nation.

As I delve into the realm of church history and war narratives, I find myself drawn to the thematic similarities between Edgar Allan Poe's 'Dream-Land' and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's 'The King of Thule'. Both works evoke a sense of longing and loss, a yearning for a utopian world that is forever elusive. I see parallels between this nostalgia and the way World War II films portray bravery and fearless resolve, showcasing war heroes and villains in a stark, black-and-white dichotomy. I often imagine myself playing the role of a war hero, with an impersonal view of the enemy, and it is this detachment that allows me to navigate the complexities of war and church history. The two are intertwined, with the church thriving under persecution and conflict, its growth and resilience a testament to the human spirit. My own fascination with the Pentecostal movement is marked by a critical view, acknowledging both its merits and flaws, and I am reminded of the need for nuance and balance in my understanding of historical events. As I trace the origins of the modern church back to Martin Luther's separation from the Roman Catholic Church, I am struck by the ways in which the Church's political entanglement before Luther was critiqued, with church power being influenced by societal marriages and alliances.

I reflect on Martin Luther's actions, including nailing his 95 Theses, which led to his excommunication from the Church, and I am struck by the irony and tragedy of the Church's rejection of his attempts to reform. It is a narrative that explores the cyclical nature of history, suggesting that historical awareness can shape the future. As I consider the contemporary cultural references that shape my understanding of these events, I am reminded of the power of storytelling and the ways in which it can both unite and divide us. I think of the World War II films that I grew up watching, with their heroic narratives and simplistic morality, and I realize that my own understanding of war and church history is filtered through these cultural lenses. And yet, as I look back on the history of the church, I am aware of the need to move beyond simplistic narratives and to engage with the complexities and nuances of the past. The church's rejection of Martin Luther, despite his attempts to reform, is a stark reminder of the dangers of dogma and the importance of critical thinking. As I navigate the interplay of church history and war narratives, I am drawn to the idea that it is only through a deep understanding of the past that we can hope to shape a more just and compassionate future. Through this journey, I am constantly reminded of the importance of empathy, self-reflection, and historical awareness in shaping my understanding of the world and my place within it.

Due to its smaller size, it was jokingly known as Bundesdorf during that period, which literally meant “Federal Village.” (Time Magazine, 1964) 

The core areas of the country would be the city-states of Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen as well as Bavaria for its unique foods, dress (such as the Lederhosen and Dirndl), interesting dialects, music, and culture which attracts millions to its area, and to events such as Oktoberfest.

The German language itself is an art-form, and quite well established within the world. Germanic languages form the basis of English itself and it doesn't take long for one to notice the similarities between the two languages if you study them both. The most widely used and proper form of German is called Hochdeutsch, or “High German” though once you travel outside of the major cities, you'll start to encounter several different forms. Estimates vary, but it is believed that between 50 and 250 different dialects of the German language exist. (About.com, 2011)

Part of this reason is the fact that Germany was not united until the 1870's, and thus the border cultures tended to take in similarities to their neighbors, and their neighbors took in parts of German. Such as The Elsace-Lorraine region of France where one can find a dialect known as Elsässich. (About.com, 2011) Everything from greetings “Hallo”, “Grüß Gott!”, “Moin!” change depending on which part of Germany you are in.

As stated in (About.com, 2011), there are 6 dialect families. They include Friesich, or Frisian which is spoken in small areas around the North Sea coastal region and is the smallest of them all. Niederdeutsch, also known as Plattdeutsch is low-German, and is named after the low lands of the area (Nieder is the same basis for the name of the The Netherlands, or Niederlande in German.)

Next we have Mitteldeutsch (Middle German) through the middle of the country, with the Fränkisch dialect within its borders, that follows the Main river. Alemannisch in Switzerland and the Bavarian-Austrian dialect.

This can cause some minor problems, though this is mainly a problem for tourists or inexperienced German as a second language, speakers. Germans usually have little problem understanding a German from another dialect other than a few key words which may cause confusion (similar to jelly/jam/jello, or college/high school/university confusions that we see in American vs British English.) Though a certain Austrian had no trouble speaking publicly to the masses of Germany, and they understood him just fine.

Adolf Hitler attempted to turn Germany into a nation-state. Though historically and currently, Germany has been a conglomerate of different tribes, races, religions, and people. After World War II, there was a great urge to get people to immigrate to Germany, and that they did! Especially from the country of Turkey.

Emergence results from internal reflection. It is the construction of new ideas or theories based on a synthesis of existing knowledge, and it is the primary source of originality.

Piaget’s theory of cognitive development answers the question of “when” we learn. According to Piaget, children develop according to stages. The rate of development depends on the fulfillment of intellectual and emotional milestones, each stage building on the successful completion of previous stages. The specifics of Piaget’s theory have been improved by further research, but Piaget’s stage-oriented view of development remains the most prominent theory of when learning occurs.

Why do we learn? Many people have never asked this question. Lev Vygotsky’s theory of Social Cognition offers interesting insight into the reasons behind learning. According to Vygotsky, learning occurs primarily because of cultural influence. The social cognition learning model posits that children learn because culture teaches them both what to think and how to think.

How we learn has been a widely studied and, at times, a hotly debated topic. The earliest modern model of learning is B.F. Skinner’s behaviorist theory. Behaviorism is the theory that positive and negative reinforcement influences and controls learning. According to Skinner, negative reinforcement, also known as punishment, will discourage behavior, while positive reinforcement, like praise, will encourage it. Animal studies strongly support the behaviorist model. Animals learn very quickly to avoid the button or lever that delivers a shock while pressing the button that delivers the food. Many psychologists dispute behaviorism’s ability to tell the whole story. After all, human beings respond to more than just rewards and punishments. Many cognitive scientists have dismissed behaviorism because of its perceived inability to explain the intricate methods of learning and cognition in which the human brain engages. Additionally, it fails to explain how the social environment affects learning. The idea that behavior can be explained without referencing sociocultural influences is a tenet of behaviorism, leading to a theory that most scientists dismiss as too narrow. A person’s behavior depends on more than just the rewards and punishments that they have experienced throughout their life. Noam Chomsky, a famous linguist, dismissed behaviorism for its inability to explain language acquisition in children. Language seems to be learned without being explicitly taught.

All of these theories can co-exist because they attempt to explain different methods or types of learning. Each answers a different question, and together, they provide a broad understanding of the brain and learning.

The Montessori method of teaching is a modern educational movement that encourages teachers to view children and classroom education differently than the common teacher-student relationship. Instead of focusing on academic education, the Montessori method focuses on respecting and encouraging each child’s individual differences, providing a nurturing environment to teach social interaction and emotional skills. The Montessori method is most often applied at the pre-school level due to its focus on early child development.

In Lackner v. North, the plaintiff brought suit for punitive damages following reckless skiing that resulted in significant injuries. The court determined that while North’s actions were undeniably reckless, they did not rise to the level of despicability required for punitive measures. The court emphasized that despicable conduct must embody an element of evil or criminal intent—a concept well established in punitive damages jurisprudence (see, e.g., Burns v. People, 89 A.D.2d 555, 561 (1994)). In its analysis, the court contrasted the behavior at issue with conduct that would shock societal norms, noting that although North’s actions demonstrated gross negligence through a blatant disregard for safety, they lacked the malice necessary to be branded as despicable. This distinction underlined the principle that while recklessness may warrant punitive actions, such punishment is reserved for instances where a defendant’s conduct transcends mere imprudence and displays a conscious disregard for the well-being of others. The decision in Lackner v. North thus contributed to a growing body of case law that differentiates between high-risk negligence and conduct that is inherently evil in nature.

Meanwhile, in Angie M. v. The Super. Crt. of San Diego Co, a different facet of punitive damages was examined under circumstances involving unequivocally despicable actions. In that case, Hiemstra was found to have manipulated Angie, an act that constituted a deliberate and conscious disregard for her welfare. The court concluded that Hiemstra’s conduct was outrageous and violated multiple statutory provisions—a determination that underscored the necessity of exhibiting evil intent for conduct to be classified as despicable. This case was contrasted with that of Martin, where the defendant’s intent was limited to the benign goal of finishing dinner. Although Martin’s conduct was argued by the plaintiff as despicable due to a prioritization of personal interests over customer safety, the court found that without clear evidence of evil or criminal intent, his actions could not be equated with the egregious misconduct seen in Angie M. The judicial reasoning in these cases reiterated that for punitive damages to be appropriate, the defendant’s behavior must not only be reckless but must possess an element of malicious or conscious disregard—an element that shocks the collective conscience of society. Furthermore, in contexts where multiple customer injuries were involved, the strength of the plaintiff’s argument in cases resembling Martin’s was enhanced, though still requiring clear demonstrable malice to meet the elevated standard. Collectively, these decisions provided a balanced legal framework by comparing and contrasting instances of reckless versus despicable conduct. They reaffirmed that while punitive damages remain a potent legal remedy, their application hinges on a rigorous examination of intent and the extent to which a defendant’s actions depart from accepted societal and statutory norms.

One particular type of Duty-based Theory is Kantian Deontology, where a perfect duty is one that a person is required to carry out, an example of which is keeping a promise. Keeping the promise may have a good or bad result, but according to Kantian Deontology the result of keeping the promise should not influence the decision to carry out the duty. This theory applies in the case of an institution that does not uphold its promise as stated in its mission statement. Duties are related to individuals.

Another example that can be applied in the case of an organization breaching its mission statement is Rights Based Theory. Basically, “a right is a morally or legally justified claim on someone else.” When dealing with a situation from a Rights Based Theory, it is important to consider the rights of those within the context of the circumstances. In particular, an action can be judged as correct only if the individual’s rights are upheld. Clearly, Rights based Theory dictates that the institution make a correction out of commitment to upholding the rights of the students.

Lastly, the “being” category of ethics relates to virtue. According to the presentation, Dr. Aultman states that virtue can include “justice, benevolence, loyalty, friendliness and courage.” In this case, one needs to concentrate on having the right motivation for action (justice, benevolence, etc.) and not adhering to rules at the expense of people. Also, virtues can be flexible and allow those following this “being” category to make assessments on each situation that one encounters.

Most institutions have a mission statement, regardless if the organization is a university, business, or other entity. However, there are times when this mission statement is not followed – whether due to lack of man-power, will-power or circumstances preventing the organization from meeting its obligations. In the case that I would like to present, a university did not maintain its mission statement.

As a child growing up, my mother worked as an administrator in a hospital in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit. She would explain interesting cases to us at the dinner table, much to my father’s disgust. One case in particular that has stayed with me was that of a child who was diagnosed with appendicitis. A concern in this case was that the child’s family was Christian Science and therefore the child was not receiving what my mother deemed proper medical care. As children ourselves, we asked our mom about why parents would not give their child the care that was needed?

As a child myself, I believed without questioning what I was told and thought along the lines that my mother had taught us – that this family’s beliefs were jeopardizing their child’s life. I do not recall what the outcome of the case was, but the idea that Christian Science was dangerous and an unhealthy religion did stick. How could simple thought and praying fix a physical ailment? The child needed surgery and quickly!
