John Ingerfield, oil and tallow refiner, of Lavender Wharf, Limehouse, comes of a hard-headed, hard-fisted stock. The first of the race that the eye of Record, piercing the deepening mists upon the centuries behind her, is able to discern with any clearness is a long-haired, sea-bronzed personage, whom men call variously Inge or Unger. Out of the wild North Sea he has come. Record observes him, one of a small, fierce group, standing on the sands of desolate Northumbria, staring landward, his worldly wealth upon his back. This consists of a two-handed battle-axe, value perhaps some forty stycas in the currency of the time. A careful man, with business capabilities, may, however, manipulate a small capital to great advantage. In what would appear, to those accustomed to our slow modern methods, an incredibly short space of time, Inge's two-handed battle-axe has developed into wide lands and many head of cattle; which latter continue to multiply with a rapidity beyond the dreams of present- day breeders. Inge's descendants would seem to have inherited the genius of their ancestor, for they prosper and their worldly goods increase. They are a money-making race. In all times, out of all things, by all means, they make money. They fight for money, marry for money, live for money, are ready to die for money.

In the days when the most saleable and the highest priced article in the markets of Europe was a strong arm and a cool head, then each Ingerfield (as "Inge," long rooted in Yorkshire soil, had grown or been corrupted to) was a soldier of fortune, and offered his strong arm and his cool head to the highest bidder. They fought for their price, and they took good care that they obtained their price; but, the price settled, they fought well, for they were staunch men and true, according to their lights, though these lights may have been placed somewhat low down, near the earth.

Then followed the days when the chief riches of the world lay tossed for daring hands to grasp upon the bosom of the sea, and the sleeping spirit of the old Norse Rover stirred in their veins, and the lilt of a wild sea- song they had never heard kept ringing in their ears; and they built them ships and sailed for the Spanish Main, and won much wealth, as was their wont.

Later on, when Civilisation began to lay down and enforce sterner rules for the game of life, and peaceful methods promised to prove more profitable than violent, the Ingerfields became traders and merchants of grave mien and sober life; for their ambition from generation to generation remains ever the same, their various callings being but means to an end.

A hard, stern race of men they would seem to have been, but just--so far as they understood justice. They have the reputation of having been good husbands, fathers, and masters; but one cannot help thinking of them as more respected than loved.

They were men to exact the uttermost farthing due to them, yet not without a sense of the thing due from them, their own duty and responsibility--nay, not altogether without their moments of heroism, which is the duty of great men. History relates how a certain Captain Ingerfield, returning with much treasure from the West Indies--how acquired it were, perhaps, best not to inquire too closely--is overhauled upon the high seas by King's frigate. Captain of King's frigate sends polite message to Captain Ingerfield requesting him to be so kind as to promptly hand over a certain member of his ship's company, who, by some means or another, has made himself objectionable to King's friends, in order that he (the said objectionable person) may be forthwith hanged from the yard-arm.

Presently Mrs. Watts returned, candle in hand, smelling more aromatically of something hot and strong than ever.

"Simes says it's brass, and worth eightpence, and here's the money. Strike me dead, if he said more than eightpence, there!--strike him blind, if he'll get a farden out of it!"

"Where's the money?"

"Here's fippence--tuppence for to-night, and a penny you owe me, that makes eightpence; and as for supper, why, I'll keep my word--no one can ever say of Mother Watts that she didn't keep her word in anythink she undertooked."

"I--I don't care so much about supper as I did--ain't I just husky? No singing to-morrow, mother."

"Only singing small," was the rejoinder with a grunt at her own wit; "you'd do better picking up brooches--you was allers clever with your fingers, mind you. I only wish I'd been 'arf as sharp when I was young."

"I--I only wish I hadn't--found the thing," commented the girl, sorrowfully.

"Well, I'm blest!"

Mrs. Watts was taking off the lid of her saucepan, and probing the contents with a fork.

"Fippence isn't a fortun, and the young chap gave me a ha-penny once when I was singing in Suffolk Street--I didn't mean it, somehow--I said I never would again! Don't you remember when mother died here, how she went on just at the last as to what was to become o' me; and didn't I say I'd grow up good, and stick to singing and begging, and all that fun--or go to the workus--or anythink?"

"Ah! your mother was a fine 'un to go on sometimes."

"And then I----"

"Now, I don't want to hear anythink about your goings on--I don't know where you found that brassy brooch--I don't want to know--Simes don't want to know! We takes your word for it, that it was come by proper, and the less you say about it, the better; and the sooner you turns into bed, if you don't want no supper, the better too."

"I don't see a good twopen'orth over there," commented Mattie; "they're as full as ever they can stick."

"Take the rug, gal, and have it all to yourself, here by the fire."

"Well, it's not so bad. I say--you know old Wesden?"

"What, in Suffolk Street?--well."

"He's got a party to-night--I have been a listening to the music--they've been dancing and all manner. And laughing--my eye! they just have been a-laughing, Mother Watts--I've been laughing myself to hear 'em."

"Um," was the unsympathetic response.

"It's a buff-day--Wesden's gal's buff-day. You know Wesden's gal--proud of herself rather, and holds her head up in furst-rate style, as well she may with such a shop as her father's got in Suffolk Street, and good and pretty as she is, Lor bless her! I s'pose old Wesden's worth pounds and pounds now?"

"Hundreds."

"Hundreds and hundreds of pounds," commented Mattie, coiling herself in the rug upon the floor; "ah! I s'pose so. I often thinks, do you know, I should like to be Wesden's little gal--what a lucky thing it'd be to be turned somehow into Wesden's little gal, just at Christmas time, when fairies are about."

"What!"

"Real fairies, on course--not the gals with the legs in the pantermines. If there was any real fairies on course too, but I'm too knowing to b'lieve that. But if there was, I'd say, please turn me into Wesden's little gal, and give me the big doll by the parler door, and dress me like a lady in a blue meriner."

"Well, you are going on nicely about Wesden's gal. That was allus your fault, Mattie--such a gal to jaw, jaw, jaw--such a clapper, clapper, clapper about everythink and everybody."

"I was just a-thinking that I was going it rather, but I ain't a bit sleepy, and I thought you wouldn't mind me while you was having your supper, and my throat's so awful sore, and you ain't so sharp quite, as you are sometimes. Do you know what I'd do, if I was a boy?"

The drawing-room of the Bruton Street house was bathed in a soft golden hue, the lamplight filtered through delicate silk shades casting gentle patterns upon the walls. An ornate clock chimed the quarter hour with a sweet, melodious note that resonated faintly through the polished air.

Seated by the fireplace, Lady Henry reclined in her favorite armchair, upholstered in a faded tapestry of greens and crimsons. Her face bore the noble gravitas of age, tempered by a subtle wistfulness. Mademoiselle Le Breton sat at her side, holding the hand of her charge with a protective tenderness.

A short distance away, Sir Wilfrid and young Delafield were engaged in quiet conversation, their voices harmonious with the room's composure. Their presence lent an air of vitality to the evening, their figures silhouetted against the curtained windows where the glow of gas lamps outside held back the night.

"It is gratifying to see you, Jacob," remarked Sir Wilfrid, his gaze drifting from his young companion to the ember dance in the hearth. "I scarce anticipated such a reunion upon my return from the Continent. Do you find much satisfaction in your new duties?"

Jacob, with an air of gentle contemplation, nodded. "It is a change, Sir Wilfrid, and one that suits me well. The land holds a steadfast charm, unhurried and perennial. Each task seems but a natural extension of the seasons."

"Indeed," replied Sir Wilfrid, with a hint of longing in his tone. "The city, with its relentless pursuits, often obscures the simpler beauties of the countryside. Were it not for our necessities, I would oft trade these cobblestones for green pastures."

Their conversation lulled into a companionable silence, punctuated only by the soft rustle of the embers. Lady Henry stirred, her voice tremulous yet imbued with authority. "Sir Wilfrid," she called, her tone as commanding as ever despite her frailties. "Pray tell of your voyage. I yearn for tales that whisk me beyond these walls."

Sir Wilfrid, sensing the innate curiosity that still burned within Lady Henry, positioned himself comfortably upon a nearby settee. He recounted his travels with passion, his descriptions vivid and colorful, his language weaving a tapestry of foreign lands and distant cultures.

Jacob listened intently, his own imagination carried abroad by Sir Wilfrid's eloquence. He saw the chiseled mountains of the Alps, the azure Mediterranean lapsing upon ancient shores, and the vibrant marketplaces thrumming with life's endless desires and despairs.

Mademoiselle Le Breton occasionally interjected, her voice soft yet probing for details that might amuse Lady Henry. Her presence seemed to compose an ethereal bridge between the infirmity of age and the vigor of youth, her quiet dignity a balm to the household.

The evening drifted on, time measured not by the ticking clock but by the leisurely cadence of conversation. The lamplight dimmed just slightly, hinting at the world beyond the windows where clouds scudded across a trespassing moon.

"A remarkable journey, indeed," mused Lady Henry, finally breaking the lingering spell of Sir Wilfrid's narratives. "Yet I remain content in my modest dominion here. For within these walls, blessedly, I find loyalty and trust, rare treasures in an ever-shifting world."

Her words resonated in the quiet room, offering solace against the night. In response, Sir Wilfrid bowed his head, a gesture of profound respect wrapped in understanding.

Jacob's gaze turned towards the solitary figure of Mademoiselle Le Breton, who captured his attention more compellingly than his imagination of distant lands. Her steadfast care for Lady Henry was unwavering, an enduring testament to her character.

As the fire softened into a gentle glow, the guests fell into pleasant contemplation. Lady Henry's countenance, though shadowed by frailty, held a hint of satisfaction, her heart lightened by the camaraderie of the evening.

The clock chimed once more, and the conversation shifted. Jacob and Sir Wilfrid spoke of more practical matters, of schemes and ambitions, of family and fortune, their words a tapestry of hope and aspiration.

Lady Henry listened, her mind wandering to memories of her own youth, when she, too, held the world in the palm of her hand. Time had wrought many changes, but the essence of life remained mesmerizing in its unpredictable dance.

Sir Wilfrid eventually rose to depart, bidding Lady Henry a gracious farewell while expressing heartfelt gratitude to Mademoiselle Le Breton. Jacob followed suit, his departure lingering with an unspoken promise of return.

As the door closed softly behind them, Lady Henry reclined further, her heart warmed by the evening's encounters. Mademoiselle Le Breton, attending to her needs with practiced serenity, sensed the peace that now settled over the room.

Outside, the city lay cloaked in night's embrace, the carriage wheels echoing softly through deserted streets. The world beyond Bruton Street seemed distant, a mere whisper in the vast expanse of time, as within the house, the enduring presence of friendship and memory held steadfast against the night.

A tapping on the door with a stick diverted the general attention.

The door was opened, and enter a policeman, a man in private clothes, with a billycock hat and a walking-stick, accompanied by a pale-faced, long-haired youth, of fourteen years of age.

"Nothing particular the matter--only something lost as usual, Mrs. Watts," said the man in private dress, politely. "Where's Mattie to-night?"

"There she is. She's been in all the evening with a bad throat."

"Poor girl--throats is bad at this time of the year."

The speaker looked at the lad at his side, after giving the first turn backward to the rug.

"Is this the girl?"

The policeman took the candle from the table, and held the light close to the girl's face--white, pinched, and haggard, with black eyes full of horror.

"Don't say it's me, please," she gasped, in a low voice; "I'm the gal that sings in Suffolk Street on a Saturday night, and they gives wittles to at Wesden's. It isn't me."

Mattie had intended to brave it out at first, to have remained stolid, sullen, and defiant, after the manners of her class; but she felt ill and nervous, and the shadow of the prison-house loomed before her and made her heart sink. If it had been a policeman, or old Wesden, or anybody but this boy three years her senior in age, many years her junior in knowledge of the world, she would have been phlegmatic to the last; but this boy had been kind to her twice in life--once on Christmas-eve, and once on a Saturday night before that, and she gave way somewhat, partly from her new and unaccountable weakness, partly because it was not a very stern face that looked down into hers.

Policeman, detective, and Master Hinchford went down the stairs to the court, out of the court into Kent Street, black and noisome--a turgid current, that wore only a semblance of stillness at hours more late than that.

As we sat in the coach, rattling along the dusty road to Worcester, I could not help but think of the kind stranger who had escorted me home so kindly only a few days before. His story of the sick child, and the cruel woman who had brought suffering into their quiet lives, had made a deep impression on my mind. It was a picture that would not be easily erased – one of a poor man, worn and weary, but with a heart full of hope and a spirit unbroken.

My companion, Tod, seemed engrossed in his own thoughts, staring out of the window at the rolling hills and verdant woods that began to stretch out before us. His brow was furrowed in a frown, and I could sense a heaviness in the air around him. I turned to his stepmother, Mrs. Todhetley, and saw that she was watching us both with a wise and gentle eye.

"I daresay you are troubled, Tod?" I asked, my voice low so as not to startle him.

He turned to me, his eyes clouding over, and I could see the turmoil in their depths. "Troubled?" he repeated, his voice a little rough. "I was, until my parents told me it was all over - that you were safe, and that mother was pleased you were home."

I nodded, though I knew it was not the answer he sought. "It was very kind of you to think of me, Tod," I said, trying to change the subject. "I was grateful for the carriage ride, and the gentleman's kindness."

He shook his head, as if in disagreement with himself. "It was not kindness, exactly," he said. "It was a duty, or a sense of fairness. My father would have done the same, if he had been there."

I nodded, understanding what he meant. His father, the Squire, was a man of principle and justice, and I had a great respect for him. Even his presence seemed to command a certain authority, and his face was etched with lines that spoke of years of honest toil. But in spite of his stern appearance, I knew he was a kind and fair man, and that his heart was heavy with the burden of his duties.

We rode in silence for a while, the only sound the creaking of the coach and the rattle of the wheels on the road. But as we approached the outskirts of the town, a sense of excitement began to stir in me. I had never been to Worcester before, and I was eager to see the great buildings and the bustling streets. The Assizes were assembling, and the town was full of people come to hear the trials. I had heard that the Squire was to serve on the grand jury, and I wondered if I would be able to watch him at work.

As the coach drew near the Squire's lodgings, I could see that preparations were already in full swing. The family was busy with the packing and the unpacking, and the air was filled with the clatter of luggage and the sound of voices calling out orders. I felt a surge of excitement, knowing that we were about to embark on a new adventure together.

The Squire, resplendent in his formal suit, strode towards us, his face stern and his eyes shining with a sense of duty. "Ah, my dear family," he said, his voice deep and commanding. "I am glad to see you. We have a busy few days ahead of us, but I trust we shall make the most of it."

Tod and his stepmother nodded, and I felt a sense of awe at the thought of the great work that lay before us. I, too, tried to look brave and composed, but my heart was racing with excitement and anticipation. Little did I know what the coming days would bring, or the trials we would face together as a family.

As the Squire handed us each a small, delicate box containing some of his finest gloves and a crisp new handkerchief, I could not help but feel a sense of pride and connection to this man who was now our guardian and guide. His love for us, and his desire to do what was right, shone brightly in his eyes, and I felt a deep gratitude towards him.

Tod's stepmother smiled at me warmly, her eyes twinkling with a hint of mischief. "We shall have a wonderful time, I am sure," she said, as she folded her arms around her son's waist. "And who knows? Perhaps we shall see some truly remarkable cases at the Assizes."

As she spoke, I saw the Squire's eyes light up with a sense of interest, and I could sense the excitement building in him. He was a man of justice, and the thought of hearing the pleas of the accused and the condemned must have been almost too much for him to bear.

The coach door creaked open, and a liveried footman stood waiting, bowing low. The Squire handed us each a rug, and we stepped down into the bright sunlight, our eyes blinking against the glare.

"And so, he locked himself in," declared Trubie, pacing before the hearth with the nervous energy of a caged lion. The firelight cast dancing shadows upon his anxious face.

"Locked himself in, you say?" queried Dr. Thornton, his brow furrowed in concern. "But why? And for how long?"

"Since last night, Doctor. Since Roath departed. I have knocked repeatedly, but receive no answer. Not a sound. It is most unsettling."

Dr. Thornton stroked his chin thoughtfully. "Roath was the last to see him, then? What was the nature of their discourse, do you know?"

"They were discussing... mathematics, I believe. A particularly thorny problem that had occupied Arling's mind these past weeks. Roath, as ever, possessed the keener intellect, and supposedly unravelled the conundrum before Arling's very eyes."

"Ah, yes, Roath and his figures. A formidable mind, that. Yet, a formidable mind does not always a sound constitution make," Dr. Thornton mused. "Did Arling appear distressed or unwell last evening?"

"Distressed, perhaps. Unwell, not outwardly so. But he was certainly vexed by his inability to grasp the solution as readily as Roath. You know how sensitive he can be to such perceived shortcomings."

Dr. Thornton sighed. "Indeed. A sensitive soul, Arling. One who feels deeply. It is both his strength and his weakness. Have you attempted to force the door, Trubie?"

"I have, Doctor. But it is a stout door, and locked fast from within. I fear to damage it unduly without knowing the extent of the emergency."

"Prudence is wise," Dr. Thornton conceded. "But we cannot stand idly by while Arling remains locked away, potentially in distress. We must attempt to gain entry. Trubie, fetch me a strong crowbar. We shall see if we can persuade the door to yield."

Trubie hastened to comply, his face a mask of apprehension. Dr. Thornton, meanwhile, stood before the locked door, listening intently for any sound from within. But only silence greeted his ears. A silence so profound that it chilled him to the bone.

When Trubie returned, breathless, with the requested tool, Dr. Thornton took it with a grim nod. "Stand back, Trubie," he instructed. "This may require some force."

He positioned the crowbar carefully, taking a deep breath before applying leverage. The wood groaned in protest, but held fast. He tried again, exerting more pressure. This time, there was a splintering sound, and the lock began to give way.

With a final heave, the door burst open, revealing a scene that sent a wave of shock through both men.

Arling lay upon his bed, pale and still. His eyes were closed, and his breathing was shallow and labored. A half-empty vial lay on the bedside table, its contents emitting a faint, acrid odor.

"Good heavens!" exclaimed Dr. Thornton, rushing to Arling's side. He felt for a pulse, his brow furrowing with concern. "He is alive, but barely. Trubie, quickly! Fetch me some water and a clean cloth. And send for Mrs. Miggins. We shall need her assistance."

Trubie, his face ashen, obeyed without question, hurrying to fulfill the doctor's commands. Dr. Thornton, meanwhile, worked feverishly to revive Arling, dabbing his forehead with cool water and attempting to rouse him from his slumber.

"Arling! Arling, can you hear me?" he called out, his voice filled with urgency. "Wake up, my boy! Wake up!"

At the same moment that Arminell came out on the terrace, the rector’s wife, Mrs. Cribbage, drove up in her wickerwork pony-carriage, and entered the house to pay a visit to Lady Lamerton.

Giles ran off to see his rabbits, and Jingles was left alone walking with Arminell.

“I suppose you are not burdening Giles with many lessons, now that he is convalescent?” said the girl.

“No, her ladyship does not wish him to be pressed. He is still heavy in his head with cold.”

“Well,” said Arminell, “I did not come here to talk about Giles, so we will dismiss him from our conversation. I have been considering this miserable matter, and I want to know what action you purpose taking on it.”

“I also,” said the tutor, “have been revolving the matter in my head, and I have resolved to leave Orleigh as soon as possible, and to ask my uncle, Mr. James Welsh, my mother’s brother, to assist me to enter a literary career.”

“Literary career! in what branch?”

“I intend to write for the press, I mean for the papers. Mr. Welsh lives by his profession, and I will do the same.”

“That must be more interesting than teaching little boys Mensa—mensæ, Dominus—domini.”

“The press is the sceptre that now rules the world, and I will wield it.”

“Oh, how I envy you!” said Arminell. “You are about to do something, something worth the labour, something the thought of which kindles ambition. You will escape out of this wearisome round of hum-drum into the world of heroic action. Here is my lord spending his life in petty duties as he regards them and has no result at the end to show; my lady thinking, planning, executing, and also with no result appearing; and I, wasting my time practising at the piano, running my voice over scales, doing a little sketching, reading odds and ends, picking flowers—and nothing can come of it all. We are made for more serious work.”

Within a week of Tom Bristow's first visit to Pincote, and his introduction to the Copes, father and son, Mr. Cope, junior, found himself, much to his disgust, fairly on his way to New York. He would gladly have rebelled against the parental dictum in this matter, if he had dared to do so; but he knew of old how worse than useless it would be for him to offer the slightest opposition to his father's wishes.

"You will go and say goodbye to Miss Culpepper as a matter of course," said Mr. Cope to him. "But don't grow too sentimental over the parting. Do it in an easy, smiling way, as if you were merely going out of town for a few days. Don't make any promises--don't talk about the future--and, above all, don't say a word about marriage. Of course, you will have to write to her occasionally while you are away. Just a few lines, you know, to say how you are, and all that. No mawkish silly love-nonsense, but a sensible, manly letter; and be wisely reticent as to the date of your return. Very sorry, but you don't know how much longer your business may detain you--you know the sort of thing I mean."

When the idea had first entered Mr. Cope's mind that it would be an excellent thing if he could only succeed in getting his son engaged to Squire Culpepper's only child, it had not been without an ulterior eye to the fortune which that young lady would one day call her own that he had been induced to press forward the scheme to a successful issue. By marrying Miss Culpepper, his son would be enabled to take up a position in county society such as he could never hope to attain either by his own merits, which were of the most moderate kind, or from his father's money bags alone. But dearly as Mr. Cope loved position, he loved money still better; and it was no part of his programme that his son should marry a pauper, even though that pauper could trace back her pedigree to the Conqueror. And yet, if the squire went on speculating as madly as he was evidently doing now, it seemed only too probable that pauperism, or something very much like it, would be the result, as far as Miss Culpepper was concerned. Instead of having a fortune of at least twenty thousand pounds, as she ought to have, would she come in for as many pence when the old man died? Mr. Cope groaned in spirit as he asked himself the question, and he became more determined than ever to carry out his policy of waiting and watching, before allowing the engagement of the young people to reach a point that would render a subsequent rupture impossible without open scandal--and scandal was a bugbear of which the banker stood in extreme dread.

Fortunately, perhaps, for Mr. Cope's view, the feelings of neither of the people chiefly concerned were very deeply interested. Edward had obeyed his father in this as in everything else. He had known Jane from a child, and he liked her because she was clever and good-tempered. But she by no means realized his ideal of feminine beauty. She was too slender, too slightly formed to meet with his approval. "There's not enough of her," was the way he put it to himself. Miss Moggs, the confectioner's daughter, with her ample proportions and beaming smile, was far more to his taste. Equally to his taste was the pastry dispensed by Miss Moggs's plump fingers, of which he used to devour enormous quantities, seated on a three-legged stool in front of the counter, while chatting in a free and easy way about his horses and dogs, and the number of pigeons he had slaughtered of late. And then it was so much easier to talk to Miss Moggs than it was to talk to Jane. Miss Moggs looked up to him as to a young magnifico, and listened to his oracular utterances with becoming reverence and attention; but Jane, somehow, didn't seem to appreciate him as he wished to be appreciated, and he never felt, quite sure that she was not laughing at him in her sleeve.

After the tempest in a teapot (or, more accurately, the shillings in a hotel bill) had subsided, a welcome peace settled upon our little London lodgings. Francesca, darling, bewildering creature that she was, declared the entire episode "perfectly thrilling," her eyes sparkling with an enthusiasm that belied any true understanding of the financial intricacies that had just transpired. Salemina, ever practical, merely arched a perfectly sculpted eyebrow and murmured something about the merits of a sound finishing school education. As for myself, the whole affair had provided ample material for my sketchbook, for truly, the contortions of Francesca's face as she grappled with the complexities of pounds, shillings, and pence were a sight to behold, worthy of Hogarth himself.

Our days fell into a familiar pattern, a comfortable rhythm of sightseeing and social calls interspersed with leisurely afternoons spent in Hyde Park or browsing the bookshops of Charing Cross Road. Francesca, possessed of an unflagging energy that could only belong to the very young and very rich, dragged us from one social engagement to the next, her dance card perpetually full. Salemina, ever the dutiful chaperone, navigated these social waters with her usual aplomb, dispensing witty observations and sage advice in equal measure. And I, content to observe the world from the comfortable vantage point of my sketchbook, found myself increasingly drawn to the quieter corners of London life, the bustling street markets, the flower sellers hawking their wares, the children playing hopscotch on cobblestone streets.

It was on one such solitary afternoon ramble that I stumbled upon a curious little shop tucked away on a quiet side street, its dusty windows overflowing with a jumble of books, maps, and faded prints. The air inside was thick with the smell of old paper and leather, and a hush lay over the place, broken only by the gentle ticking of a grandfather clock in the corner. Behind a mountain of books sat a man, his face as lined and worn as the volumes that surrounded him. He peered at me over the top of his spectacles, his gaze sharp and appraising. I felt a strange sense of recognition, as if I had met him before, though I knew that to be impossible.

Hesitantly, I inquired about a particular volume on English watercolours, a book I had been searching for in vain for weeks. To my surprise, the old man's face broke into a smile, and he disappeared into the labyrinthine stacks, emerging moments later with the very book in hand. As I reached for my purse, he waved away my money with a dismissive gesture. "A gift, madam," he said, his voice a raspy whisper. "For a fellow lover of beauty."

I left the shop feeling strangely exhilarated, the weight of the old man's gift heavy in my hands. As I made my way back to our hotel, I couldn't shake the feeling that something significant had occurred, though I couldn't quite put my finger on what it was. The encounter had left me with a sense of disquiet, a feeling that my carefully ordered world was about to be upended.

That evening, as we dressed for a particularly grand ball, Francesca flitting about our room like a hummingbird in a cloud of silk and scent, I shared the story of my encounter with the old bookseller. To my surprise, both Salemina and Francesca listened with rapt attention, their usual banter stilled. When I finished, Francesca surprised me by commenting, "How perfectly romantic! It's like something out of a novel, isn't it?"

Salemina, however, remained silent for a moment, her brow furrowed in thought. "It is rather odd, isn't it?" she mused. "Giving away a valuable book like that." Her gaze met mine, and I saw a flicker of something unreadable in her eyes. "Perhaps, my dear," she said slowly, "you should be careful."

But though I admired her ceaselessly for this, she was no less in admiration of my daring strength and prowess. I felt myself a perfect Paladin in her defense. I remember that the chip-yard which we used to cross, on our way to the barn, was tyrannized over by a most loud-mouthed and arrogant old turkey-cock, that used to strut and swell and gobble and chitter greatly to her terror. She told me of different times when she had tried to cross the yard alone, how he had jumped upon her and flapped his wings, and thrown her down, to her great distress and horror. The first time he tried the game on me, I marched up to him, and by a dexterous pass, seized his red neck in my hand, and confining his wings down with my arm, walked him ingloriously out of the yard.

How triumphant Susie was, and how I swelled and exulted to her, telling her what I would do to protect her under every supposable variety of circumstances! Susie had confessed to me of being dreadfully afraid of "bears," and I took this occasion to tell her what I would do if a bear should actually attack her. I assured her that I would get father's gun and shoot him without mercy--and she listened and believed. I also dilated on what I would do if robbers should get into the house; I would, I informed her, immediately get up and pour shovelfuls of hot coal down their backs--and wouldn't they have to run? What comfort and security this view of matters gave us both! What bears and robbers were, we had no very precise idea, but it was a comfort to think how strong and adequate to meet them in any event I was.

Sometimes, of a Saturday afternoon, Susie was permitted to come and play with me. I always went after her, and solicited the favor humbly at the hands of her mother, who, after many washings and dressings and cautions as to her clothes, delivered her up to me, with the condition that she was to start for home when the sun was half an hour high. Susie was very conscientious in watching, but for my part I never agreed with her. I was always sure that the sun was an hour high, when she set her little face dutifully homeward. My sisters used to pet her greatly during these visits. They delighted to twine her curls over their fingers, and try the effects of different articles of costume on her fair complexion. They would ask her, laughing, would she be my little wife, to which she always answered with a grave affirmative.

"Early marriages?" said my mother, stopping her knitting looking at me, while a smile flashed over her thin cheeks: "what's the child thinking of?"]

Yes, she was to be my wife; it was all settled between us. But when? I didn't see why we must wait till we grew up. She was lonesome when I was gone, and I was lonesome when she was gone. Why not marry her now, and take her home to live with me? I asked her and she said she was willing, but mamma never would spare her. I said I would get my mamma to ask her, and I knew she couldn't refuse, because my papa was the minister.

I turned the matter over and over in my mind, and thought sometime when I could find my mother alone, I would introduce the subject. So one evening, as I sat on my little stool at my mother's knees, I thought I would open the subject, and began:

"Mamma, why do people object to early marriages?"

"Early marriages?" said my mother, stopping her knitting, looking at me, while a smile flashed over her thin cheeks: "what's the child thinking of?"

"I mean, why can't Susie and I be married now? I want her here. I'm lonesome without her. Nobody wants to play with me in this house, and if she were here we should be together all the time."

As the hand of the merchant rested upon his own door, he almost dreaded to enter. He shrank from meeting that clouded visage. The shadows were dark when he left in the morning, and experience told him that he need scarcely hope to find them dispelled. Happily, though still in the sky, the clouds were broken, and gleams of sunshine came breaking through. Ah! if they had only possessed sufficient power to disperse the shadows that all day long had been gathering around the heart of Mr. Abercrombie! But that was impossible. Self-respect had been forfeited; and a consciousness of having, in his impatient haste, acted unjustly, haunted his thoughts. And so, the shadows that were not to be dispersed by the feeble sun-rays from the countenance of his wife, gradually diffused themselves, until the light that struggled with them grew pale.

"Did you know," said Mrs. Abercrombie, breaking in upon the oppressive silence that succeeded, after all had retired for the night but herself and husband, "that the mother of Edward Wilson is very poor and in a decline?"

"I was not aware of it," was the brief response.

"It is so. Mrs. Archer was here this afternoon, and was telling me about them. Mrs. Wilson, who, until within a few weeks past, has been able to earn something, is now so weak that she cannot leave her bed, and is solely dependent on the earnings of her son. How much do you pay him?"

"Only three dollars a week," answered Mr. Abercrombie, shading his face with his hand.

"Only three dollars! How can they live on that? Mrs. Archer says that Edward is one of the best of lads--that he nurses his mother, and cares for her with unfailing tenderness; indeed, he is her only attendant. They are too poor to pay for the services of a domestic. Could you not afford to increase his wages?"

"I might, perhaps," said Mr. Abercrombie, abstractedly, still shading his face.

"I wish you could," was the earnest reply. "It will be a real charity."

Mr. Abercrombie made no response; and his wife pursued the subject no further. But the former lay awake for hours after retiring to bed, pondering the events of the day which had just closed.

The sun had gone down amid clouds and shadows; but the morrow dawned brightly. The brow of Mrs. Abercrombie was undimmed as she met her family at the breakfast-table on the next morning, and every countenance reflected its cheerful light. Even Mr. Abercrombie, who had something on his conscience that troubled him, gave back his portion of the general good feeling. Lighter far was his step as he went forth and took his way to his store. His first act on his arriving there, was, to ease his conscience of the pressure thereon, by sending for Edward Wilson, and restoring him to his place under new and better auspices.

And thus the shadows passed; yet, not wholly were they expelled. The remembrance of pain abides long after the smarting wound has healed, and the heart which has once been enveloped in shadows, never loses entirely its sense of gloomy oppression. How guarded all should be lest clouds gather upon the brow, for we know not on whose hearts may fall their shadows.

GENTLE HAND.

I DID not hear the maiden's name; but in my thought I have ever since called her "Gentle Hand." What a magic lay in her touch! It was wonderful.

When and where, it matters not now to relate--but once upon a time as I was passing through a thinly peopled district of country, night came down upon me, almost unawares. Being on foot, I could not hope to gain the village toward which my steps were directed, until a late hour; and I therefore preferred seeking shelter and a night's lodging at the first humble dwelling that presented itself.

As autumn leaves began to flutter and dance upon the lawn, the atmosphere at the Rectory underwent a subtle yet palpable transformation. Mr. Underwood found himself ensnared within a web of intricate circumstances, woven with threads of both reservation and resignation.

The new mistress of the household, Lady Price - now Mrs. Bevan - had proven to be a staunch guardian of her husband's health, much to the dismay of those who had once flourished under his predecessor's regime. Her prudence extended to the purse strings as vigilantly as it did to Mr. Bevan's wellbeing, a chivalrous concern that unwittingly stifled the flow of resources to the parish activities.

Underwood, now burdened with the dual challenges of dwindling finances and Lady Price's critical disposition, found his spirits persistently dampened. It seemed each sermon his rector delivered, though devoid of the spirit that once animated them, now echoed against walls cold and unforgiving. The senior curate wrestled daily with the daunting task of maintaining order amidst chaos, his own health perilously on par with the beleaguered coffers.

Mrs. Bevan, meanwhile, harbored within her bosom a begrudging animosity towards Mr. Underwood and his kin. Their lineage, steeped in nobility, stood in stark contrast to her own origins, a specter that loomed ominously over her interactions with the curate. She endeavored to mask her reservations behind a facade of civility, a manoeuvre that, while preserving appearances, only served to deepen the rift between them.

Amidst these tribulations, an unexpected glimmer of hope emerged. There arose whispers among the parishioners of a proposed restoration project for the crumbling church walls, a venture that could not only revitalize the sacred edifice but also infuse new life into the Rectory's troubled affairs. Mr. Underwood, ever the pragmatist, recognized in this endeavor a potential reprieve from the confines of fiscal austerity that had besieged him.

As the winds of change swept through the Rectory, the question lingered in the air: Would this noble venture serve as a panacea for their woes, or would the seeds of discontent continue to bear bitter fruit? Only time would reveal the outcome of this struggle between preservation and progress, as the Rectory stood poised on the precipice of its new era.

"Why so?" replied his booby lordship, with a stare of awkward astonishment.

"Why so!" echoed his friend; "because, if the young lady has a proper sense of her own dignity, she will not accept an offer of marriage from one who has made her an offer of another description; and if she has not that sense of dignity, but merely makes a profitable market of your passion for her, she will despise you for a fond fool, and you, when your fondness is over, will look upon her as a cunning, artful baggage. I know nothing about Miss Primrose; but I am very sure that no woman is fit to be a wife who could ever forgive a proposal of a different description."

The sagacious hereditary legislator could not understand this logic, and he stared at his friend as if he thought that he was crazy. "Bless my soul, Erpingham," at length he said, "what nonsense you are talking. I really cannot understand you. What can be more natural and regular than to offer her marriage, if she will not accept me on any other terms. You talk about hating sentimentality; I am sure you are now talking as much sentimentality as any one need wish to hear."

Erpingham had exerted himself so much by the two last speeches which he had made, as not to wish to continue the discussion, or to undergo any more blundering interrogations from his noble friend; he therefore began to resume his indolent attitude, and said, "Well, do as you like best, Spoonbill, only remember I did not refuse my advice when you asked it. Will you stop now and take your dinner with me?"

Lord Spoonbill was not any more disposed than his friend to carry on the discourse, and therefore declined the invitation to dine, and made the best of his way home again. As he rode homewards he attempted to think, but he found no small difficulty in that mental operation. There are some advertising schoolmasters who profess to teach their pupils to think; but as we were not educated in one of these thought-mongering seminaries, we cannot think how thinking can be taught. It may be possible, for the only impossibility in these days is to decide à priori that anything is impossible. But we do verily believe that, had Lord Spoonbill been at one of these establishments, he would have puzzled his preceptor as much as his preceptor would have puzzled him.

By the time that his lordship had arrived at home he had come to the conclusion of his thinking, and the result was, that he thought Erpingham to be quite an altered man; and he also thought that he would not follow the ridiculous advice which his friend had given him.

Penelope made her appearance at dinner, and looked, as Lord Spoonbill said, most divinely. How Lord Spoonbill should know what divine looks are, we cannot tell: perhaps he meant that Penelope looked like a parson. However Penelope might look at dinner, it is very certain that Lord Spoonbill looked very much at Penelope. But the young lady's thoughts were so pleasingly and agreeably engaged, and her anticipations were so delightful, that everybody and everything appeared agreeable to her. It was very different with the Countess of Smatterton. Her anticipations were not very pleasant: her ladyship apprehended that the return of Mr Primrose to England would be the destruction of her prospects, as far as they related to Miss Primrose. Having already observed that the young lady had manifested some reluctance to the public exhibition of her musical talents, the Countess very naturally supposed that Mr Primrose would indulge an only child in whatever fancy she might take up.

It was a mild morning, and while the sun’s gentle rays crept over the rolling hills of Riverton Park, Mr. Edward Fairweather and Miss Cecilia Merton found themselves engaged in a contemplative conversation near the conservatory. “My dear Miss Merton,” said Mr. Fairweather with a courteous inclination, “I have long been of the opinion that those who labor not for their own renown but solely for the glory of our Heavenly Father are indeed scarce in this oft self-serving world.” His tone, earnest and warmly inquisitive, lent an air of noble purpose to his inquiry.

Miss Merton, with a delicate hesitancy that only enhanced her sincerity, replied, “Sir, your words are like gentle bells awakening a slumbering heart. I should be delighted to observe and perhaps point out to you some souls who, in their quiet labors, mirror the unselfish charity of our Lord.” For in that moment, as in many others past, both their minds had danced upon the idea of discovering faithful and unpretentious workers in a society too frequently beguiled by ambition.

Meanwhile, in the very grounds of Riverton Park, preparations were vigorously underway. The great edifice known as Park House was receiving careful restoration; stones that had borne the wear of many seasons were being polished anew, and the gardens, once overgrown and neglected, were now being remade as a tapestry of blooming shrubs and carefully clipped hedges. The transformation of this stately estate stirred much conversation among the local gentry, who whispered eagerly of the imminent arrival of its noble new proprietor.

As the laborers toiled under the tender guidance of experienced architects and gardeners, it became increasingly clear that the coming change in household management would also mark a renewal in the spirit of the place. Rumors had abounded in recent days about the character and domestic arrangements of the incoming lord, Colonel Dawson; moreover, it was confirmed by certain reliable sources that a distinguished lady was to take up residence within Park House as well—an arrangement that promised both elegance and mystery in equal measure.

It was in the midst of this bustling scene that the carriage, drawn by two dignified horses, was seen approaching the ancient drive. Colonel Dawson, tall and resolute in manner, stepped gracefully from the vehicle accompanied by his refined sister, Miss Dawson, and a gentleman of considerable promise, Mr. Horace Jackson, who happened to be his young nephew. Their entrance resounded more than merely as the arrival of new occupants—it signified the dawning of fresh hopes for the continued prosperity and virtuous habitation of Riverton Park.

Those assembled around the entrance of the estate could scarce contain their curiosity. Miss Merton, in quiet awe, remarked to Mr. Fairweather with reflective admiration, “I daresay, sir, one perceives that not only are unselfish deeds to be found in the humble labors of the gardeners and carpenters, but also in the noble bearings of these arrivals. Their countenances whisper of a sincere commitment to the welfare of others, and might well be inferred to be followers of that divine example set by our Saviour.” Mr. Fairweather, with a soft smile, acknowledged her opinion, further enriching the discourse.

As the new colonel exchanged cordial greetings with those on hand, his voice carried assurances of benevolence and a desire to unite the revived estate with the best traditions of social and moral responsibility. “Gentlefolk,” he declared in a tone both firm and compassionate, “I am well aware that the strength of any household lies not solely in wealth or lineage, but in the hearts of those who serve and who live in unassuming unity for the wider good.” Such words, imbued with the soft power of conviction, elicited murmurs of approval from many present.

The conversation afterwards turned once more to the nature of virtuous service, as Mr. Fairweather and Miss Merton strode slowly along a newly laid stone path in the gardens. “Perhaps,” ventured Mr. Fairweather, “we might, in due time, partake in a further discourse on the subtle art of leading lives devoted to that higher purpose.” Miss Merton, her eyes sparkling with the promise of a shared quest for truth, readily concurred with gentle enthusiasm.

Though the day’s proceedings were marked by the orchestration of a grand new beginning, the gentle dialogue between kindred spirits continued to explore the purity of service and the remarkable power of unselfish love. In their conversation, as in the labors restoring the venerable house, there was a conscious, almost sacred, intention to weave a thread of goodness through all that was tender and true.

Leaving behind the newly installed fountains and blossoming mazes, both Mr. Fairweather and Miss Merton resolved that future meetings would nurture their shared reflections on duty and divine charity. In such moments of earnest discussion and quiet admiration, it could be discerned that the true restoration of Riverton Park was not solely a matter of brick and mortar, but one that stirred the very essence of courtesy, faith, and community.

Night had descended upon the ancient manor-house, its solemn timbers whispering of secrets best left unspoken, while beneath the pale gleam of a crescent moon a silent contrivance of brass and iron lay half-concealed in the shadowed recesses of the neglected garden. The contrivance, with its interlocking gears and spiraling rods, seemed, as if by some uncanny design, to mirror the intricate workings of the human soul—a dark, mysterious mechanism driven by passions too profound for mortal reckoning.

The subtle speech of the autumn wind, laden with the scent of decaying leaves and distant rain, lent a forlorn quality to the night, evoking the modern ponderings of a man whose spirit might—were it in the grip of fevered invention—at once marvel at nature's quiet machinery and recoil from its daunting impersonation of artifice. In such moments, amidst the interplay of analytical reason and dreamy fancy, the unfathomable powers of life and death merged into a single, spectral vision.

Against the backdrop of a vast, starless sky, the manor’s solitary windows glowed like the watchful eyes of ancient deities. Within one of these dim lit chambers, an erudite scholar, long fascinated by the interplay of art and science, perused a collection of manuscripts that revealed the inner workings of both man and the mysterious contrivance hidden amid the overgrown hedges. His mind, employing a delicate balance of classical poise and imaginative frenzy, was soon captivated by the enigmatic contraption that whispered to him in the silent tongue of machinery.

His thoughts turned incessantly to the nature of that contrivance, its every cog and wheel arranged with a precision that defied the common limits of human artifice, as though it had been wrought by both a divine hand and a demonic craft. He recalled the words of an esteemed contemporary, who had once likened the phenomenon of nature’s design to that of an elaborate mechanism, wherein every pulsation in the heart mirrored the ticking of an unseen clock. Thus, with an eye both serene and searching, he endeavored to unravel the mystery.

In the dim light of his study, the interplay of sober logic and fevered imagination stirred his convictions. He commenced a detailed inquiry into the contrivance’s origin, poring over ancient ledger pages and yellowed blueprints that hinted at its mechanical purpose yet veiled its true, perhaps ghostly, intent. The evidence he gathered was perplexing—a synthesis of scientific precision and something ineffably poetic, as if the instrument itself were an invocation of a spectral, long-forgotten art.

On that dismal eve, the subtle murmur of gears and piston-rods in the quiet recesses of the garden struck a chord deep within his breast—a resonance that spoke of an unknown force, a mechanism of life itself that pulsed, almost imperceptibly, with the same rhythmic cadence as the eternal march of time. The disclosure unsettled him. The fine line between rational discovery and eerie superstition began to blur as each new detail added depth to the intangible horror that crept upon his heart.

He resolved to venture forth, despite the gnawing apprehension that the hidden machinery might awaken some unholy phantasm of the past. Clad in a worn greatcoat and armed with only a lantern and his unquenchable curiosity, he stepped outside, where the spectral apparatus lay in waiting under the vigilant stars. His every step was measured and deliberate, as if he were an automaton himself, moved by inexorable forces and strangulated by the profound gravity of his own contemplations.

As he neared the contrivance, its details became ever more discernible: delicate filigree interlaced with robust iron bars, and rivets that shone with a grim luster under the feeble lamp-light. Here, in this remote corner of the estate, the convergence of natural decay and mechanical intricacy evoked both revulsion and rapture—a dichotomy reminiscent of the fabled duality of the heart that can harbor both deepest sorrow and sublime truth.

In the still air, punctuated only by the soft tick of the distant clock-tower and the rustle of ancient elm leaves, the scholar’s mind turned to the forces that had set this apparatus in motion. Was it a relic of a bygone age, a mere curiosity wrought by the hands of a forgotten artisan? Or was it, rather, the physical embodiment of the inscrutable laws that govern the interplay of human fate and the inevitable, mechanized march of progress?

With a mixture of dread and inexorable resolve, he began to disentangle the labyrinth of parts, each delicate segment a testament to an artistry that rivaled nature’s own design. In that moment, under the spectral gleam of the moon and as the nocturnal murmur of the estate swelled to a somber symphony, he felt a stirring—a revelation perhaps—that the secrets of the contrivance might well unlock truths not only about the machinations of metal and clockwork, but also about the very essence of life and its cyclical descent into mystery.

I suffered this martyrdom in silence. I would not tell my mother, as all cowards did. What the effect on me would have been if circumstances had allowed Jane Painter to continue her persecution I am afraid to think; but fortunately for me the event occurred which she was waiting for. My grandmother died very suddenly. The last words she was heard to utter were, Poor Anthony!' I was not sorry when she died. I tried to look sad, as everybody else looked, but I knew that I was a dreadful hypocrite.

There was a friend of the family of whose name I have no remembrance, and whom, from a certain personal peculiarity, I must denominate Snaggletooth. He was a large man--very tall, and round in proportion--with a glistening bald head, a smooth full-fleshed face, and clear gray eyes. In repose, and when he was not speaking, he was by no means an unpleasant-looking man; his face was benignant, and his clear gray eyes beamed kindly upon you. But directly he smiled he became transformed, and his features were made to assume an almost fiendish expression by reason of a hideous snaggle-tooth which thrust itself forward immediately he opened his mouth. It stuck out like a horn, and the change it effected in his appearance was something marvellous.

As the friend of the family, Snaggletooth came forward and offered his assistance. My father being confined to his bed by sickness, there was no man in the house to look after the funeral of my grandmother, and Snaggletooth's services were gladly accepted. I fancy that he was fond of funerals, from the zealous manner in which he attended to the details of this and a sadder one which followed not long afterwards. Setting this fancy aside, he proved himself a genuine and disinterested friend. We had no near relatives; my mother was an only daughter, and my father had but one brother, older than he, whom I had never seen, and who had disappeared from the place many years ago. He was supposed to be dead; and from certain chance words which I must have heard, I had gained a vague impression that he was not a credit to the family.

It was a strange experience for me to sit in my grandmother's room after her death, gazing at her empty armchair. I could not keep away from the room; I crept into it at all hours of the day, and sat there trembling. I mentally asked the stone monkey-figure what it thought of my grandmother's death, and I put my fingers in my ears lest I should hear an answer. Jane Painter found me there in the evening when she came to put me to bed, and stated that my grandmother's spirit was present, and that she was in communication with it. She held imaginary conversations with my grandmother's ghost in the dusk, speaking very softly and waiting for the answers. The effect was ghastly and terrifying. These conversations related to nothing but poor me, and the exquisite pain Jane Painter inflicted upon me by these means may be easily imagined.

The first thing Snaggletooth did after my grandmother's funeral was to search for her long stocking and the treasures it was supposed to contain. Taking the words in their literal sense, I really thought that the long stocking would be found hidden somewhere--under the bed perhaps, or among the feathers, or up the chimney--stuffed with money, in shape resembling my grandmother's leg, which I knew from actual observation to be a substantial one.

'Perhaps she made a will,' observed Snaggletooth to my mother. Jane Painter was present, hovering about us with hungry jealous eyes, lest she should be cheated.

Now it came to pass that, during the many years of their residence beneath the same roof, there grew up a strong feeling of friendship between Peter Steinmarc and the widow Staubach, so strong that in most worldly matters the widow would be content to follow her friend Peter's counsels without hesitation. And this was the case although Peter by no means lived in accordance with the widow's tenets as to matters of religion. It is not to be understood that Peter was a godless man,--not so especially, or that he lived a life in any way scandalous, or open to special animadversion from the converted; but he was a man of the world, very fond of money, very fond of business, doing no more in the matter of worship than is done ordinarily by men of the world,--one who would not scruple to earn a few gulden on the Sunday if such earning came in his way, who liked his beer and his pipe, and, above all things, liked the fees and perquisites of office on which he lived and made his little wealth. But though thus worldly he was esteemed much by Madame Staubach, who rarely, on his behalf, put forth that voice of warning which was so frequently heard by her niece.

But there are women of the class to which Madame Staubach belonged who think that the acerbities of religion are intended altogether for their own sex. That men ought to be grateful to them who will deny? Such women seem to think that Heaven will pardon that hardness of heart which it has created in man, and which the affairs of the world seem almost to require; but that it will extend no such forgiveness to the feminine creation. It may be necessary that a man should be stiff-necked, self-willed, eager on the world, perhaps even covetous and given to worldly lusts. But for a woman, it behoves her to crush herself, so that she may be at all points submissive, self-denying, and much-suffering. She should be used to thorns in the flesh, and to thorns in the spirit too. Whatever may be the thing she wants, that thing she should not have. And if it be so that, in her feminine weakness, she be not able to deny herself, there should be those around her to do the denial for her. Let her crush herself as it becomes a poor female to do, or let there be some other female to crush her if she lack the strength, the purity, and the religious fervour which such self-crushing requires. Poor Linda Tressel had not much taste for crushing herself, but Providence had supplied her with one who had always been willing to do that work for her. And yet the aunt had ever dearly loved her niece, and dearly loved her now in these days of our story. If your eye offend you, shall you not pluck it out? After a sort Madame Staubach was plucking out her own eye when she led her niece such a life of torment as will be described in these pages.

When Linda was told one day by Tetchen the old servant that there was a marriage on foot between Herr Steinmarc and aunt Charlotte, Linda expressed her disbelief in very strong terms. When Tetchen produced many arguments to show why it should be so, and put aside as of no avail all the reasons given by Linda to show that such a marriage could hardly be intended, Linda was still incredulous. "You do not know aunt Charlotte, Tetchen;--not as I do." said Linda.

"I've lived in the same house with her for fourteen years," said Tetchen, angrily.

"And yet you do not know her. I am sure she will not marry Peter Steinmarc. She will never marry anybody. She does not think of such things."

"Pooh!" said Tetchen; "all women think of them. Their heads are always together, and Peter talks as though he meant to be master of the house, and he tells her everything about Ludovic. I heard them talking about Ludovic for the hour together the other night."

"You're perfectly ridiculous," murmured Juliet, turning away with an expression of deep displeasure. "As if she wouldn't bring all sorts of elegant stuff with her, and make your cheap things look insignificant."

"I don't think she will," returned Anthony with conviction. "She'll bring nothing out of keeping with the house."

"I thought you told me she was of a wealthy family."

"She is. But if she marries me she leaves all that behind. I'll have no wife on any other basis."

"Well--for a son of the Robesons of Kentucky you are absolutely the most absurd boy anybody ever heard of," declared the girl hotly under her breath. Then she walked over and ordered a certain inexpensive rug for the living-room with the air of a princess and the cheeks of a poppy.

IV.--THE COST OF FROCKS

It may have been that Miss Marcy was piqued into trying to see how little she could spend, but certain it was that from the time she left the carpet shop she begged for no exceptions to Mr. Robeson's rule of strict economy. She selected simple, delicate muslins for the windows, one and all, without a glance at finer draperies; bought denims and printed stuffs as if she had never heard of costlier upholsteries; and turned away from seductive pieces of Turkish and Indian embroideries offered for her inspection with a demure, "No, I don't care to look at those now," which more than once brought a covert smile to Anthony's lips and a twinkle to the eyes of the salesman. It was so very evident that the fair buyer did not pass them by for lack of interest.

Altogether, it was an interesting week these three people spent--for a week it took. Anthony began to protest after the first two days, and said he could not ask so much of his friends. But Juliet would not be hindered from taking infinite pains, and Mrs. Dingley good humouredly lent the two her chaperonage and her occasional counsel, such as only the gray-haired matron of long housewifely experience can furnish.

The selection of the furniture took perhaps the most time, and was the hardest, because of the difficulty of finding good styles in keeping with the limited purse. Anthony possessed a number of good pieces of antique character, but beyond these everything was to be purchased. Juliet turned in despair from one shop after another, and when it came to the fitting of the dining-room she grew distinctly indignant.

"It's a perfect shame," she said, "that they can't offer really good designs in the cheap things. Did you ever see anything so hideous? Tony, if I were you I'd rather eat my breakfast off one of those white kitchen tables--or----"

She broke off suddenly, rushed away down the long room to a group of chastely elegant dining-room furniture and came back after a little with a face of great eagerness to drag her companions away with her. She took them to survey a set of the costliest of all.

"Have you gone crazy?" Anthony inquired.

"Not at all. Tony, just study that table. It's massive, but it's simple--simple as beauty always is. Look at those perfectly straight legs--what clever cabinet maker couldn't copy that in--in ash, Tony? Then there are stains--I've heard of them--that rub into wood and then finish in some way so it's smooth and satiny. You could do that--I'm sure you could. Then you'd get the lovely big top you want. And the chairs--do you see the plain, solid-looking things? I know they could be made this way. Then the dining-room would be simply dear!"

"Juliet, you're coming on," declared Anthony with satisfaction that evening as the two, back at the Marcy country place, strolled slowly over the lawn toward the river edge. "At this rate you'll do for a poor man's wife yourself some day. That frock you have on now--isn't that a sort of concession to the humble company you're in?"

As the conversation with the Baron continued, Otto's mind wandered, struggling to keep up with the intricacies of art and society that his brother Gerard seemed to effortlessly navigate. He felt a familiar sense of inadequacy creeping in, a shift in the conversation that pointed out his own lack of passion for the finer things in life. It was in moments like these that Otto found himself yearning for simpler, more straightforward discussions, a world where wealth and status held less weight.

The Baron, always one to speak his mind freely, turned his attention back to Otto, a shrewd glint in his eye. "Ah, my dear Otto, you mustn't waste your years in Java any longer," he remarked, his tone slightly teasing. "You are not getting any younger, my boy. It's time to consider a suitable match, someone with a bit of money to her name. You can't rely on your brother's fortunes forever, you know."

Otto bristled slightly at the suggestion, feeling the weight of expectation pressing down on him. While he understood the practicality of the Baron's advice, marrying for wealth seemed a cold and calculating endeavor. He longed for a love that transcended the trappings of money and status, a connection based on genuine affection and shared values.

The Baron, sensing Otto's hesitation, leaned back in his chair and let out a hearty laugh. "Ah, Otto, always the idealist," he chuckled. "But remember, my boy, duty often trumps sentimentality. A good marriage can bring stability and security, something you may find lacking in your current pursuits. Think of it as a business arrangement, if you must."

Otto felt a pang of disquiet at the Baron's words, his sense of duty warring with his desire for autonomy. He knew the importance of securing his future, of fulfilling his familial obligations, but at what cost? Was he doomed to a life of practicality and compromise, forever bound by the expectations of others?

As the conversation turned to lighter topics, the Baron's jovial demeanor returned, his easy-going nature once again taking center stage. "Ah, Otto, my boy, you take life too seriously," he mused, a twinkle in his eye. "You must learn to enjoy the simple pleasures, to embrace the whims of fate with a light heart. It is the Van Helmont way, after all, to face life's challenges with a smile and a shrug."

Reflecting on his family's history, the Baron recounted tales of generations past, each marked by a similar philosophy of carefree living. He spoke of ancestors who had faced adversity with grace, who had weathered storms of change with a steadfast sense of self. The Van Helmonts were a resilient lot, their legacy one of resilience in the face of uncertainty.

And as Otto listened to the Baron's stories, a newfound appreciation for his heritage blossomed within him. Perhaps there was wisdom in the Baron's words, a lesson to be learned about the balance between duty and joy, between tradition and innovation. In that moment, Otto felt a sense of peace settle over him, a quiet resolve to chart his own course, guided by both his heart and his head.

As Sir Wilfrid descended the staircase later that evening, the memory of Mademoiselle Le Breton's enigmatic presence lingered in his thoughts. The Duchess of Rochford's carriage had been announced, and Sir Wilfrid, having paid his respects to his hostess, found himself caught in the departing throng. He paused on the landing, observing the graceful descent of shimmering gowns and the murmur of polite farewells.

And then he saw her again. Mademoiselle Le Breton stood at the foot of the stairs, a serene figure amidst the flurry of departures. She wore a gown of deep crimson, its simple lines accentuating her statuesque figure. A strand of pearls, their soft glow echoing the creamy perfection of her skin, adorned her neck. Her dark hair, swept back from her face, revealed the delicate curve of her cheekbones and the quiet intelligence in her eyes.

She turned slightly, her gaze sweeping over the departing guests. For a fleeting moment, their eyes met, and Sir Wilfrid felt an unexpected jolt, a recognition that both intrigued and unsettled him. Had he encountered this striking woman before? The question, like a half-remembered melody, danced elusively at the edge of his consciousness.

Her features, he mused, hinted at a French lineage, perhaps a touch of the exotic in their delicate symmetry. Yet, there was a quiet reserve about her, a subtle air of — dare he say it — melancholy that belied a simple Parisian upbringing. He recalled Delafield's words: "Mademoiselle arranges it." What precisely did that arrangement entail? And what lay beneath the composed façade of Lady Henry's enigmatic companion?

As if summoned by his thoughts, Mademoiselle Le Breton excused herself from a group of departing matrons and moved towards a small, elegantly appointed drawing-room that branched off the main hallway. The door stood slightly ajar, and Sir Wilfrid, unable to resist the allure of the unknown, found himself drawn towards the muffled voices emanating from within.

"—most trying, my dear," a voice tinged with fatigue reached him. The Duchess of Rochford, wrapped in an ermine-trimmed cloak, stood facing Mademoiselle Le Breton. "Poor Lady Henry! To be so afflicted, and at such a relatively young age."

"Indeed, Your Grace," came the quiet reply. "Lady Henry bears her trials with remarkable fortitude."

"But to be so dependent on — on others," the Duchess continued, her voice lowered conspiratorially. "One does so hope that her — her companion is all that she should be."

"Mademoiselle Le Breton is utterly devoted to Lady Henry," came the steady reply. But to Sir Wilfrid's keen ear, a note of strain, a hint of tightly controlled emotion, underscored the words.

"Of course, of course," the Duchess murmured, adjusting her shawl with a distracted air. "Well, my dear, you have been most kind. Please convey my fondest regards to Lady Henry. Until next week, then?"

"Until next week, Your Grace," Mademoiselle Le Breton echoed, a faint smile touching her lips.

The Duchess, with a final flurry of silk and a waft of expensive perfume, swept past Sir Wilfrid. He hesitated, momentarily caught between the impropriety of eavesdropping and the undeniable allure of the unfolding scene. Mademoiselle Le Breton, her back to him, stood motionless, her gaze fixed on the closed door.

The rustle of his coat, however, betrayed his presence. She turned, her eyes widening slightly in surprise. A flicker of — what? Apprehension? Relief? — crossed her features before her composure returned, swift and seamless as the fall of a theater curtain.

"Yes; I see."

Camelia leaned back in her end of the little sofa, her arms folded, her head bent in a light scrutiny of her companion's face. The warm quiet of the summer day pervaded the peaceful room, a room with so many associations for both of them. They had studied, read there together for years; laughed, quarrelled, been the best of friends and the fondest of enemies. Perior, as he looked about it, could call up a long vista of Camelias, all gay, all attaching, all evasive, all culminating and fulfilling themselves with an almost mathematical inevitableness, as was now so apparent to him, in the long, slim "personage" beside him, her eyes, as he knew, studying him, her mind amused with conjectures as to what he really thought of her, she herself quite ready to display the utmost sincerity in the attempt to elicit that thought. Oh no, Camelia would keep up very few pretences with him. Perior, gazing placidly enough at the sunlit green outside the morning-room, knew very well what he thought of her.

"Are you estimating the full extent of my folly," she asked presently, "tempering your verdict by the consideration of extenuations?"

This was so apt an exposition of his mental process that Perior smiled rather helplessly.

"See," she said, rising and going to the writing-table, "I'll help you to leniency; show you some very evident extenuations." From a large bundle of letters she selected two. "Weigh the extent of my influence, and find it funny, if you like, as I do."

"I wonder if you quite realize the ludicrous aspect of our conversation," said Perior, taking a thick sheaf of paper from the first letter.

"Quite--quite. Only you push me to extremes. I must make you own my importance--my individuality."

"Ah, from Henge," said Perior, looking at the end of the letter. "He was my fag at Eton, you know; dear old Arthur!"

"Yes, and you quarrelled with him five years ago, about politics."

"We didn't quarrel," said Perior, with a touch of asperity; "he was quite big enough not to misunderstand my opposition. Must I read all this, Camelia? It looks rather dry."

"Well, I should like you to. He is one of the strongest men in the government, you know."

"Quite. He is the man for me, despite past differences of opinion. The man for you, too, perhaps," he added, glancing sharply up at her from the letter; "his devotion is public property, you know."

"But my reception of his devotion isn't," laughed Camelia.

"I am snubbed," said Perior, returning to the letter, and flushing a little. Camelia noted the flush. Dear old Alceste! Shielding so ineffectually, under his sharp blunt bearing, that quivering sensitiveness.

She put her hand through his arm, sinking down beside him, her eyes over his shoulder following his, while he read her--certificate. Perior quite understood the smooth making of amends.

"Well, what do you say to that?" she asked when he had obediently read to the very end.

"I should say that he was a man very much in love," said Perior, folding the letter.

"You are subtle if you can trace an amorous influence in that letter."

"It doesn't call for subtlety. Samson only abandons himself so completely under amorous circumstances. I hope you are not going to shear the poor fellow."

"For shame," said Camelia, while Perior, looking at her reflectively, softly slapped the palm of his hand with Arthur Henge's letter. "I am his comrade. I help him; I am on his side, if you please, and against the Philistines."

"Oh, are you? And this? Ah! this is from the leader of the Philistines, Rodrigg. Yes, I heard that Rodrigg was in the toils." Perior examined the small, compact handwriting without much apparent curiosity.

As the warm sunlight began to wane on that languid summer evening, casting a gentle glow over the sleepy town of Teignmouth, the twins, Henrietta and Frederick, found themselves ensconced in their favourite arbour, surrounded by the vibrant blooms of their mother's meticulously tended garden. The air was alive with the soft hum of insects and the sweet fragrance of blooming flowers, creating a sense of serenity that seemed to envelop the young pair in its soothing embrace. The open carriage, which had earlier borne Frederick from the railway station, now stood empty, its fine bay horses having been led away to their well-deserved rest, after a day spent patiently enduring the relentless attacks of the summer sun.

The gentle rustle of leaves and the soft creaking of the arbour's wooden latticework served as a calming background melody, as the twins sat together, their faces aglow with the warm light of the setting sun. Henrietta, her countenance a picture of serene contentment, listened intently as Frederick regaled her with tales of his academic exploits, his eyes sparkling with a mixture of pride and mischief. The warmth of the evening, combined with the comforting presence of her twin brother, had served to dispel the faint sense of melancholy that had settled over Henrietta, following their earlier discussion regarding their mother's decision not to join them.

As the stars began to twinkle in the evening sky, like diamonds scattered across the velvet expanse, Frederick's conversation turned to the subject of his future plans, his voice filled with a sense of purpose and determination. He spoke of his desire to secure a place at the prestigious Oakwood Academy, an institution renowned for its rigorous academic standards and esteemed faculty. Henrietta listened with rapt attention, her eyes shining with a mixture of admiration and concern, as her brother outlined his aspirations, his words painting a vivid picture of a future filled with promise and possibility.

The sound of footsteps, crunching on the gravel path, served to interrupt the twins' conversation, as their cousin, Alex Langford, emerged from the gathering dusk, a look of quiet confidence etched upon his features. His eyes, a deep shade of blue, sparkled with a sense of warmth and friendly regard, as he approached the arbour, his movements economical and assured. Henrietta's face broke into a radiant smile, as she extended a hand in greeting, her manner gracious and welcoming. Frederick, too, rose to his feet, his eyes narrowing slightly, as he regarded his cousin, a faint sense of competitiveness flickering in their depths.

As the three young people sat together, the conversation turned to the subject of Alex's academic achievements, his name having been mentioned earlier in the context of Frederick's aspirations. Henrietta, her eyes sparkling with interest, asked her cousin to enlighten her regarding his studies, her tone encouraging and sincere. Alex, his countenance a picture of modesty, spoke of his love for the classical authors, his words weaving a spell of enchantment, as he discussed the works of the great masters.
