Mrs Croft was, in addition, connected locally; Mr Shepherd, prompt to display any agreeable circumstance, did not allow this to pass unnoticed. "A respectable family alliance, sir," he remarked, nodding significantly, "must ever be considered a source of satisfaction."

Anne, who sat near her father, inclined to listen quietly, heard Mr Shepherd’s comment and, recollecting herself, cautiously enquired of Mrs Croft after that lady’s brother, Mr Wentworth.

Mrs Croft responded warmly, with unaffected cheerfulness. "My brother? Ah, yes, Frederick Wentworth; he has always spoken highly of his visit here, during his stay at Monkford. The neighbourhood pleased him mightily, but his profession afforded little leave or leisure to renew acquaintances."

Anne’s heart quickened slightly at this discourse, though no one else seemed particularly moved; for Sir Walter quickly found himself weary of Wentworths and Monkfords, his attention again returning to Admiral Croft’s appearance and the fitness of these guests. "A familial tie to a curate," he silently reasoned, "must indeed be quite immaterial; one cannot erect connexions with every obscure clergyman in the county. It must be enough that he has none of those distressing children." This thought satisfied him sufficiently, enough at least for him to decide the Crofts to be worthy prospective occupants of Kellynch.

Mrs Clay, who attended discreetly to all conversation likely to interest Sir Walter, met his observant eye with a practised smile of concurrence. "One could hardly find a more agreeable couple," said she quietly, noticing well the turn of her patron's countenance.

"Perhaps not," returned Sir Walter, thoughtfully. "Certainly their discretion and habits seem commendable, and they have none of those unmanageable encumbrances; without children, a house is likely to be tolerably preserved."

Elizabeth Elliot, who had been silently observing her father's reactions, interposed briefly to remark that though childlessness might guarantee the house’s preservation, she could not consider it a recommendation towards pleasant sociability. "There is something depressing," she declared with a faint sigh, "in the prospect of an old hall like Kellynch entirely lacking the existence of youthful liveliness."

Anne softly disagreed, though neither heard nor regarded; for her father had heard sufficient to feel assured of his own decision. Having arrived at this favourable estimation, he consented, with no further hesitation, to place the details of lease and arrangement fully into Mr Shepherd’s capable hands.

And so, at last, the plan was made certain; Kellynch was to be occupied, the Crofts established. Sir Walter, reconciled by conviction of their suitability, soon consoled himself in contemplation of Bath as offering more congenial society, whilst Anne, in silence, began to dwell upon a changed existence, the absence of Kellynch Hall, and unexpectedly, the stirring remembrance of Frederick Wentworth.

“I say, my father’s past,” said Charlie. “Won’t he be pleased to find you two girls out? What do you wander about so late for? it’s getting dark. I call that foolish, when you might be out, if you pleased, all the day.”

“My boy, you do not know anything about it,” said the elder sister with dignity; “and you shall go by yourself if you do not walk quietly. There! people are looking at us; they never looked at us till you came.”

“Charlie is so handsome,” said Marian laughing, as they all turned a corner, and, emancipated from the public observation, ran along the quiet street, a straggling group, one now pressing before, and now lagging behind. This big boy, however, so far from being handsome, was strikingly the opposite. He had large, loose, ill-compacted limbs, like most young animals of a large growth, and a face which might be called clever, powerful, or good-humoured, but certainly was, without any dispute, ugly. He was of dark complexion, had natural furrows in his brow, and a mouth, wide with fun and happy temper at the present moment, which could close with indomitable obstinacy when occasion served. No fashion could have made Charlie Atheling fashionable; but his plain apparel looked so much plainer and coarser than his sisters’, that it had neither neatness nor grace to redeem its homeliness. He was seventeen, tall, big, and somewhat clumsy, as unlike as possible to the girls, who had a degree of natural and simple gracefulness not very common in their sphere. Charlie’s masculine development was unequivocal; he was a thorough boy now, and would be a manful man.

“Charlie, boy, have you been thinking?” asked Agnes suddenly, as the three once more relapsed into a sober pace, and pursued their homeward way together. There was the faintest quiver of ridicule in the elder sister’s voice, and Marian looked up for the answer with a smile. The young gentleman gave some portentous hitches of his broad shoulders, twisted his brow into ominous puckers, set his teeth--and at last burst out with indignation and unrestrained vehemence--

“Have I been thinking?--to be sure! but I can’t make anything of it, if I think for ever.”

“You are worse than a woman, Charlie,” said the pretty Marian; “you never can make up your mind.”

“Stuff!” cried the big boy loudly; “it isn’t making up my mind, it’s thinking what will do. You girls know nothing about it. I can’t see that one thing’s better than another, for my part. One man succeeds and another man’s a failure, and yet the one’s as good a fellow and as clever to work as the other. I don’t know what it means.”

“So I suppose you will end with being misanthropical and doing nothing,” said Agnes; “and all Charlie Atheling’s big intentions will burst, like Beau’s soap-bubbles. I would not have that.”

“I won’t have that, and so you know very well,” said Charlie, who was by no means indisposed for a quarrel. “You are always aggravating, you girls--as if you knew anything about it! I’ll tell you what; I don’t mind how it is, but I’m a man to be something, as sure as I live.”

“You are not a man at all, poor little Charlie--you are only a boy,” said Marian.

“And we are none of us so sure to live that we should swear by it,” said Agnes. “If you are to be something, you should speak better sense than that.”

“Oh, a nice pair of tutors you are!” cried Master Charlie. “I’m bigger than the two of you put together--and I’m a man. You may be as envious as you like, but you cannot alter that.”

Now, though the girls laughed, and with great contempt scouted the idea of being envious, it is not to be denied that some small morsel of envy concerning masculine privileges lay in the elder sister’s heart. It was said at home that Agnes was clever--this was her distinction in the family; and Agnes, having a far-away perception of the fact, greatly longed for some share of those wonderful imaginary advantages which “opened all the world,” as she herself said, to a man’s ambition; she coloured a little with involuntary excitement, while Marian’s sweet and merry laughter still rang in her ear. Marian could afford to laugh--for this beautiful child was neither clever nor ambitious, and had, in all circumstances, the sweetest faculty of content.

"Ye have called me, Sir Daniel," he said. "Was it to laugh at my poor plight?"

"Nay, now, let laugh," said the knight. "Good shrew, let laugh, I pray you. An ye could see yourself, I warrant ye would laugh the first."

"Well," cried the lad, flushing, "ye shall answer this when ye answer for the other. Laugh while yet ye may!"

"Nay, now, good cousin," replied Sir Daniel, with some earnestness, "think not that I mock at you, except in mirth, as between kinsfolk and singular friends. I will make you a marriage of a thousand pounds, go to! and cherish you exceedingly. I took you, indeed, roughly, as the time demanded; but from henceforth I shall ungrudgingly maintain and cheerfully serve you. Ye shall be Mrs. Shelton--Lady Shelton, by my troth! for the lad promiseth bravely. Tut! ye will not shy for honest laughter; it purgeth melancholy. They are no rogues who laugh, good cousin.--Good mine host, lay me a meal now for my cousin, Master John.--Sit ye down, sweetheart, and eat."

"Nay," said Master John, "I will break no bread. Since ye force me to this sin, I will fast for my soul's interest.--But, good mine host, I pray you of courtesy give me a cup of fair water; I shall be much beholden to your courtesy indeed."

"Ye shall have a dispensation, go to!" cried the knight. "Shalt be well shriven, by my faith! Content you, then, and eat."

But the lad was obstinate, drank a cup of water, and, once more wrapping himself closely in his mantle, sat in a far corner, brooding.

In an hour or two there rose a stir in the village of sentries challenging and the clatter of arms and horses; and then a troop drew up by the inn-door, and Richard Shelton, splashed with mud, presented himself upon the threshold.

"Save you, Sir Daniel," he said.

"How! Dickie Shelton!" cried the knight; and at the mention of Dick's name the other lad looked curiously across. "What maketh Bennet Hatch?"

"Please you, sir knight, to take cognisance of this packet from Sir Oliver, wherein are all things fully stated," answered Richard, presenting the priest's letter. "And please you farther, ye were best make all speed to Risingham; for on the way hither we encountered one riding furiously with letters, and by his report, my Lord of Risingham was sore bestead, and lacked exceedingly your presence."

"How say you? Sore bestead?" returned the knight. "Nay, then, we will make speed sitting down, good Richard. As the world goes in this poor realm of England, he that rides softliest rides surest. Delay, they say, begetteth peril; but it is rather this itch of doing that undoes men; mark it, Dick. But let me see, first, what cattle ye have brought.--Selden, a link here at the door!"

And Sir Daniel strode forth into the village street, and, by the red glow of a torch, inspected his new troops. He was an unpopular neighbour and an unpopular master; but as a leader in war he was well beloved by those who rode behind his pennant. His dash, his proved courage, his forethought for the soldiers' comfort, even his rough gibes, were all to the taste of the bold blades in jack and salet.

"Nay, by the rood!" he cried, "what poor dogs are these? Here be some as crooked as a bow, and some as lean as a spear. Friends, ye shall ride in the front of the battle; I can spare you, friends. Mark me this old villain on the piebald! A two-year mutton riding on a hog would look more soldierly! Ha! Clipsby, are ye there, old rat? Y' are a man I could lose with a good heart; ye shall go in front of all, with a bull's-eye painted on your jack, to be the better butt for archery; sirrah, ye shall show me the way."

The day was waning in that peculiar manner in which one may observe the inevitable decay of some long-held certainty, and as I once more approached the quiet habitation where Brooksmith now resided, I could not but feel that the quietude itself bore the fainter echoes of former drollery—a sound now all too muffled by the insidious intrusion of commerce and necessity. With a hesitance borne of a mixture of pity and a forlorn desire to have salvaged from his fate something remotely akin to propriety, I found him poised by the window, looking out at the hastening twilight with an air of grave resignation. He confessed, in a tone that was both self-deprecating and defiantly candid, that the exigencies of the state had compelled him to abandon the abode permanently this very night; he had received, from Mr. Offord’s departing legacy, a sum of eighty pounds—hardly the largesse one might expect to provide a new beginning in these uncertain times. Though his words were measured, there was an undeniable tremor beneath their calm surface, as if that modest fortune had been robbed of all its promise by the crushing realities of a life that had long forsaken the accumulation of modest savings in favor of urgent necessities and merciful compromises. And now, with the impending darkness as his silent confidante, he murmured of a need to look about for opportunities yet unseen, and, not without a certain hesitancy mingled with hope, he ventured that perhaps I might be of some assistance in this most delicate of affairs.

There ensued a lingering pause, full of unspoken regrets and the heavy burden of acceptances long made, during which Brooksmith’s gaze seemed fixed upon an unseen bride of destiny, each word of his confession laden with the intricate burden of past sacrifices and the bitter fruit of experience. I perceived in his account not merely the pragmatic tally of a sum, but rather the sorrowful arithmetic that must have accompanied every gesture, every instinctual act of choice to survive at the price of parting with one’s hopes. It was, in truth, a delicate misfortune—I confess a certain disappointment in the paltry seventy-six plus four additional pounds—that had conjured in me an abiding sense of rue and, in a way, the melancholic recognition that fate, in its often indifferent governance, would rarely allow the virtuous to escape the clutches of industry and despair unscathed. In the glimmer of that transient hour, while the shadows lengthened, Brooksmith delineated a life now recalibrated to the merciless terms set by fortune—a recalibration in which the promise of his future seemed to be measured not in the abundance of coin but in the audacity of his aspiration, tempered, nonetheless, by the gravity of his prudent recollections.

Thus, as the night strove to assert its ephemeral dominion over the remnants of a troubled day, and as our discourse turned from the arithmetic of legacy to the more inscrutable computations of personal salvation, it became manifest that the inherent uncertainties of his chosen path were to be navigated with deliberate care. In the subdued luminescence of the lamp by which Brooksmith now reluctantly presided over his meager estate, every whispered hope, every clandestine ambition was weighed against the relentless logic of necessity. A certain resolve, not entirely his own perhaps but shared in the quiet intimacy of our conversation, passed between us—a silent consent that aid, if it could be rendered, would be rendered in the spirit of solidarity among those who, though vanquished by circumstance, still harboured a rewarding defiance against the ruin of their lives. And so, with an accord unadorned by grand gestures but sincere in its modest commitment, I prepared to set forth into the uncertain night, driven by the poignant conviction that even a legacy as scant as eighty pounds might serve, however precariously, as a stepping-stone toward a gentler, if no less challenging, reformation of a life that had known too many sacrifices.

A certain official personage or two, perhaps deputies from the coroner, or from the parish, or from the undertaker furnishing the coffin and the two sets of bearers--who can tell?--whose mission it was to see the appointed proceedings carried out, cleared by their hands and gestures a space around the grave. The people fell back obediently. They pressed and elbowed each other no doubt, and grumbled at others crushing them; but they kept themselves back in their places. A small knot, gentlemen evidently, and probably friends of the deceased, were allowed to approach the grave. The grave-diggers stood near, holding the torches. But for those flaring torches, the crowd would have seen better: they saw well enough, however, in the bright moonlight.

In the churchyard, having taken up his station there behind an upright tombstone, where tombstones were thick, stood an officer connected with the police. He was in plain clothes--in fact, nobody remembered to have seen him in other ones--and had come out tonight not officially but to gratify himself personally. Ensconced behind the stone, away from everybody, he could look on at leisure through its upper fretwork and take his own observations, not only of the ceremony about to be performed, but of those who were attending it. He was a middle-sized, spare man, with a pale face, deeply sunk green eyes, that had a habit of looking steadily at people, and a small, sharp, turned-up nose. Silent by nature and by habit, he imparted the idea of possessing a vast amount of astute keenness as a detector of crime: in his own opinion he had not in that respect an equal. Nobody could discern him, and he did not intend they should.

Amidst a dead silence, save for the creaking of the cords, amidst a shiver of sympathy, of pity, of awful thoughts from a great many of the spectators, the black covering was thrown aside and the coffin was lowered. There was a general lifting off of hats; a pause; and then a rush. One in the front rank--a fat woman, who had fought for her place--stepped forward in her irrepressible curiosity to take a last look inside the grave; another followed her; the movement was contagious, and there was a commotion. Upon which the men holding the torches swept them round; it threw out the flame rather dangerously, and the rushers drew back again with half a cry. Not quite all. A few, more adventurous than the rest, slipped round to the safer side, and were in time to read the inscription on the lid:

"JOHN OLLIVERA. Aged 28."

Short enough, and simple enough, for the sad death. Only a moment after the cords were drawn away did it remain visible; for the grave-diggers, flinging their torches aside, threw in the earth, spadeful upon spadeful, and covered it up from sight.

The shallow grave was soon filled in; the grave-diggers flattened it down level with spades and feet: no ceremony accorded, you see, to such an end as this poor man had made. Before it was quite accomplished, those officially connected with the burial, or with the buried, left the ground and departed. Not so the mob of people: they stayed to see the last; and would have stayed had it been until morning light. And they talked freely now, one with another, but were orderly and subdued still.

Mr. Jones stayed. He had not mixed with the people, but stood apart in the churchyard, under the shade of the great yew-tree. Soon he began to move away, and came unexpectedly upon the detective officer standing yet behind the gravestone. Mr. Jones halted in surprise.

It was a morning of peculiar tranquility at Barton Cottage, where a gentle breeze, barely lifting the lace curtains, ushered in a day that seemed pregnant with possibilities. Mrs. Dashwood, having set aside her mourning garb for less austere attire, sat by the window with an air of contemplative contentment. Her thoughts, accustomed to flit like a ruffled bird from one concern to another, now hovered over the subject of Elinor's future—most particularly in the form of a certain Mr. Edward Ferrars, whose visits had become notably frequent of late.

Elinor, ever engaged with her embroidery, seemed the picture of serene industriousness, though her needle threaded lighter and less purposeful than usual. So incipient was the tenderness she had developed for Edward, it appeared with the translucence of new bloom, yet shimmered with the promise of an enduring attachment. And although no formal proposal had yet been made, Mrs. Dashwood sensed a mutual understanding blooming between them, one that revealed itself in shared glances and shades of unspoken affection, perceptible only to those observers with the most discerning eyes.

Marianne, meanwhile, reclined in the sunlight near her sister, an anthology of poetry languidly held in her lap but largely unread. Her mind wandered through the verdant lanes of her youthful imagination, dreaming up a vision of love much more fiery and tempestuous than the gentle affection unfolding before her. That she held a genuine fondness for Edward, Marianne would not dispute; yet his presence stirred neither intense admiration nor serious critique in her heart. For Marianne, love had always been an affair tempestuous and grand, sung with fervent abandon across the windswept cliffs and groves that she often wandered.

Yet Marianne's effervescence had a quiet acceptance for Edward's growing place in their lives, astutely recognizing that his qualities spoke deeply to her sister's own tastes and temperament. She observed Edward's willingness to listen, truly listen, when Elinor spoke of art or philosophy, even if his responses were measured in comparison to her own enthusiasms. Understandably, his lack of profound intimacy with the arts left Marianne somewhat cold, but she could not deny the sincerity of his character and the gentle steadiness of his affection for Elinor.

Edward, for his part, seemed to find an uncommon solace within the walls of Barton Cottage. He deftly tailored his sensibilities to fit the patterns of its domesticity, far removed from the oppressive expectations imposed upon him by his family. Here, in the company of those unswayed by vanity and moneyed ambition, Edward felt more himself, his spirit unburdened by the fear of disappointing others. His shyness, which elsewhere might have confined his thoughts and feelings to the inner recesses of his heart, gradually dissolved in Elinor's presence, revealing a man of depth and empathy beneath his unremarkable exterior.

Mrs. Dashwood spoke little of her observations, yet her maternal instincts compelled her to pave an unobtrusive way towards Elinor's happiness. She took pleasure in arranging opportunities for the young couple to indulge in private discourse, advocating subtly through the practicalities of everyday life. Whether suggesting Edward join them for their outdoor walks or encouraging him to linger over dinner, her actions were rife with an almost unnoticeable intention.

Any reservations present in Elinor's heart, however slight, could be traced back to a cautiousness engrained by experience. Her profound sense of duty, shaped by the spectres of past disappointments, gently tempered the ebullience of her affection. She weighed the consequences and the responsibilities that might accompany such an attachment, mindful of her family's financial constraints and Edward's own familial obligations.

Thus, in fits and starts, Elinor plucked the petals of her burgeoning love, counting each as either a blessing or a burden until she reached a decision known only to herself. To an outside observer, she appeared self-possessed and tranquil, her outward calm belying the inner confusions of her heart. The cares of prudence whispered in her ear even as her heart beat a fervent melody of its own.

Within this interplay of emotions, there emerged in Elinor's heart a conviction that Edward's earnest affection, albeit quiet, was strong enough to bridge the gulf between their hopes and constraints. Yet, as in all matters of great consequence, the path ahead remained fraught with the inherent uncertainties of life, each step requiring a deliberation and courage uniquely her own.

Meanwhile, the sun, now climbing higher in the azure sky, marked the arrival of a new visitor—an arrival that would punctuate the Dashwood household with yet another shift in their evolving narrative. The gentleman entered the drawing-room with a briskness that suggested both purpose and amiability. He was Charles Brandon, an acquaintance from the neighborhood, possessing manners that were courteous, if not slightly officious, but entirely congenial.

Charles's presence served to break the introspective quietude of the morning, his conversation reaching out with polite inquiries and genial observations upon the weather and local happenings. Although his visits were infrequent, they were no less welcomed, as Charles had—through good humour and impeccable decorum—endeared himself to the family's sensibilities. His admiration for Elinor was evident in his regard, though tempered by an awareness of a certain disparity in their affections.

In undertaking the complexities of their delicate quadrille, the Dashwoods and their visitors found themselves navigating the shifting currents of propriety, affection, and irretrievable circumstance, all the while maintaining a fragile dance between personal obligation and the heart's ineffable inclinations. Thus, the morning drew itself into afternoon, drawing gently—as if on invisible threads—the lives of our characters ever further into the richly interwoven tapestry of love and life at Barton Cottage.

Well, the evening had been set in motion with such high hopes, and yet it all seemed to unravel before our very eyes. The air in the grand hall was thick with anticipation, and the murmur of a thousand eager souls filled the room. The chandeliers blazed with an intensity that seemed to reflect the collective hope pinned on the young pianist, Mr. Decker, whose star was poised to rise that very night. I found myself standing near the edge of the stage, a vantage point that granted me a view of the crowd and thecomings and goings behind the scenes. It was a scene of controlled chaos, with musicians tuning their instruments, ushers directing latecomers, and the occasional flash of a nervous smile exchanged between those who had worked tirelessly to bring this night to fruition.

Mr. Decker’s entrance had been anticlimactic, to say the least. He had appeared from the wings, his face pale and drawn, his eyes darting about as though searching for an escape. His hands, which had trembled unsteadily in mine earlier, now fiddled with the buttons of his coat, his movements a nervous tic that did little to disguise his growing panic. I had congratulated him, of course, my words meant to bolster his spirits as much as they were an attempt to convince myself of the evening’s success. But even as I spoke, I sensed his unease, a tension that hung about him like a shroud.

The arrival of Herr H---- from Leipzig and Mr. J---- of New York had been meant as a comfort, a reassurance that this was not merely a local affair but a moment of national, even international, significance. The two men, both pillars of the musical world, had been wheeled in with all the ceremony of conquering heroes, their presence a guarantee of the evening’s importance. Yet, as I watched Mr. Decker’s reaction to their arrivals, I could see that such grand gestures did little to ease his growing panic. If anything, the weight of their expectations seemed to crush him further, his steps faltering as he withdrew once more behind the curtain, leaving me to wonder if he would ever return.

And then, as the first notes of the overture drifted through the air, a hush fell over the crowd, a silence that was almost palpable. It was the kind of silence that precedes a great moment, a moment that would define the course of a career, of a life. But as the minutes dragged on, the silence began to feel less like anticipation and more like apprehension. I glanced toward the wings, my heart sinking as I realized that Mr. Decker was nowhere to be seen. The moments ticked by, each one stretching into an eternity, until finally, the conductor turned toward the audience, his face a mask of strained politeness.

“It seems Mr. Decker is unavoidably delayed,” he announced, his voice carrying the faintest edge of exasperation. A ripple of disappointment and confusion swept through the crowd, and for a moment, it seemed as though the entire evening might dissolve into chaos. I caught the eye of my brother-in-law, who was seated several rows ahead, and nodded toward the door. He rose with a quiet determination, his movements a testament to the years of refined etiquette that had shaped him into the man who could navigate such crises with grace.

Behind the scenes, the scramble to salvage the evening was underway. The Nice Boy, a young ingenue whose name I had forgotten, was brought forward with little more than a moment’s notice. Her performance, though competent, lacked the fire and passion that might have saved the evening, and the audience’s initial enthusiasm began to wane. I found myself glancing repeatedly toward the exit, half expecting Mr. Decker to appear at any moment, his presence a redemption of sorts for the debacle that had unfolded. But the minutes turned into hours, and though the evening eventually came to a close, the memory of what might have been lingered like a ghost in the air.

In the aftermath, the crowd dispersal was slower than usual, the conversations less animated, the laughter less frequent. I overheard snippets of disappointment and sympathy, the latter directed as much at Mr. Decker as at the evening’s failure. “Poor fellow,” one gentleman remarked, his tone heavy with commiseration, “he clearly had the weight of the world upon his shoulders.” Another nodded in agreement, though I detected a faint undercurrent of judgment in his gaze. The evening had not gone as planned, and while some chose to see it as a moment of human frailty, others saw it as a failure of nerve, a shortfall that would likely define Mr. Decker’s career in the minds of many.

As the last of the guests filtered out, I lingered for a moment, the echo of the evening’s events still hanging in the air. The grand piano, once the centerpiece of the room, now seemed diminished, its polished surface reflecting the dimming lights of the hall like a mirror to the disappointment that had filled the space. I thought of Mr. Decker, of the cold, trembling hands that had shaken mine earlier, and wondered what had become of him. Had he found his way to a hotel, as I had heard some whisper, or had he succumbed to the very same demons that had driven him to seek solace in drink? The answer, I supposed, would come in time, but for now, the night belonged to the echoes of failure and the faint hope that tomorrow might bring a different story.

Six months passed—six long, delightful months of sun, and summer, and smiles, without a cloud to darken, without a care to trouble them. No thought of dividing us crossed my mother's mind; the doctor's advice was too seriously considered, his authority too implicitly obeyed, to admit of the idea of my going to school being so much as entertained. And, on my side, to whom were my thoughts given, but to Mary?

We lived for each other—we breathed for each other—we thought for each other. If I was away from her for more than five minutes together, I began to be fretful and uneasy; and if she was away from me, she came back with her sweet little face all flushed and excited, and threw her arms round my neck in a quiet, pretty, tantalizing way, which was perfectly irresistible. "Oh, George, I am so happy to see you again! It is so long since I saw you last. I thought you were never coming back!" That is what she said to me, with her plump, youthful arms round my neck, and her warm, young breath on my cheek—and how, I should like to know, was a fellow of thirteen to resist such a sister as that?

For I was a fellow of thirteen, please to remember; and Mary was a child of ten; and we were both, as I have already said, without father or mother to care for us, and without brother or sister to come between us. Is it wonderful, then, I ask—is it not, on the contrary, quite natural and likely—that our childish thoughts of each other should have taken the form of sweetheart and lover?

The summer holidays were over; and still I did not go back to school. No; the doctor said it was of no use my going back to school yet awhile. My mother opened her eyes wider than usual at this, and said she thought it very strange. The doctor only shook his head, and told her she would see, if she would only wait; and that was all. So I, of course, saw nothing at all, and waited accordingly.

My time being so very much at my own disposal, I determined to improve it by beginning to teach Mary everything I knew myself. The idea no sooner occurred to me than I put it into execution.

Our studies—if studies they could be called—were carried on entirely in the open air. My class-room was a little green slope in the garden, at the back of the bailiff's cottage; my pupils' seat was a root of an elm tree, which grew at the bottom of the slope; the sky above, and the fresh air all about us, was my class-room ceiling and walls; and the only teaching implement I employed was my own voice. It is useless to inquire how long these lessons lasted, or what they were about. Sometimes I invented stories for Mary, and related them with the most wonderful energy and feeling; sometimes I acted whole plays—tragedy, comedy, and opera—all by myself; sometimes I was a school-master, and Mary was a class, and I asked her dreadful sums, and she answered them all right, directly; sometimes we were gipsies in the wood, and I taught Mary to tell fortunes by the lines in her hand—oh, what a soft little hand it was! I used to think I could have gone on holding it, and looking at the pretty pink palm of it, for the rest of my life!

One day—it was just at the time when my lessons to Mary were in the most flourishing condition—I was sitting, as usual, on the grass by the elm-tree root, waiting for my pupil to come to me. She was later than usual that morning; and I began to wonder very much what it was that kept her away from me so long. My wondering, however, was put an end to, though not very satisfactorily, in a minute or two more. I heard footsteps behind me; and, looking round, saw a servant-girl, who immediately dropped a very elaborate curtsey, and said,

"If you please, sir, my mistress's compliments, and would I be so kind as to step round to the house, as she wished to speak to me particularly."

For some moments they watched him breathlessly as he frowned in indecision, then--

“You’ll have to look out for the steward,” he said, and the girl sank to a stool while two great tears rolled down her cheeks. The captain’s eyes softened and his voice was gentle as he laid his hand on her head.

“Don’t feel hurt over what I said, miss. You see, appearances don’t tell much, hereabouts--most of the pretty ones are no good. They’ve fooled me many a time, and I made a mistake. These men will help you through; I can’t. Then when you get to Nome, make your sweetheart marry you the day you land. You are too far north to be alone.”

He stepped out into the passage and closed the door carefully.

“Well, bein’ as me an’ Glenister is gougin’ into the bowels of Anvil Creek all last summer, we don’t really get the fresh-grub habit fastened on us none. You see, the gamblers down-town cop out the few aigs an’ green vegetables that stray off the ships, so they never get out as far as the Creek none; except, maybe, in the shape of anecdotes.

“We don’t get intimate with no nutriments except hog-boosum an’ brown beans, of which luxuries we have unstinted measure, an’ bein’ as this is our third year in the country we hanker for bony fido grub, somethin’ scan’lous. Yes, ma’am--three years without a taste of fresh fruit nor meat nor nuthin’--except pork an’ beans. Why, I’ve et bacon till my immortal soul has growed a rind.

“When it comes time to close down the claim, the boy is sick with the fever an’ the only ship in port is a Point Barrow whaler, bound for Seattle. After I book our passage, I find they have nothin’ aboard to eat except canned salmon, it bein’ the end of a two years’ cruise, so when I land in the States after seventeen days of a fish diet, I am what you might call sated with canned grub, and have added salmon to the list of things concernin’ which I am goin’ to economize.

“Soon’s ever I get the boy into a hospital, I gallop up to the best restarawnt in town an’ prepare for the huge pot-latch. This here, I determine, is to be a gormandizin’ jag which shall live in hist’ry, an’ wharof in later years the natives of Puget Sound shall speak with bated breath.

“First, I call for five dollars’ worth of pork an’ beans an’ then a full-grown platter of canned salmon. When the waiter lays ’em out in front of me, I look them vittles coldly in their disgustin’ visages, an’ say in sarcastic accents:

“‘Set there, damn you! an’ watch me eat real grub,’ which I proceed to do, cleanin’ the menu from soda to hock. When I have done my worst, I pile bones an’ olive seeds an’ peelin’s all over them articles of nourishment, stick toothpicks into ’em, an’ havin’ offered ’em what other indignities occur to me, I leave the place.”

Dextry and the girl were leaning over the stern-rail, chatting idly in the darkness. It was the second night out and the ship lay dead in the ice-pack. All about them was a flat, floe-clogged sea, leprous and mottled in the deep twilight that midnight brought in this latitude. They had threaded into the ice-field as long as the light lasted, following the lanes of blue water till they closed, then drifting idly till others appeared; worming out into leagues of open sea, again creeping into the shifting labyrinth till darkness rendered progress perilous.

Occasionally they had passed herds of walrus huddled sociably upon ice-pans, their wet hides glistening in the sunlight. The air had been clear and pleasant, while away on all quarters they had seen the smoke of other ships toiling through the barrier. The spring fleet was knocking at the door of the Golden North.

The night was thick with the obscure plotting of shadows that danced along the cobbled streets, each lurking corner echoing with the rustle of imminent treachery. Joe, sturdy in his resolve yet wary of Murdock's clandestine intentions, walked briskly, his heart drumming an anxious tune deep within his breast. Trust was a fleeting wraith, elusive and haunting in its absence.

A chill wind howled mournfully through the narrow alleyways, a spectral whisper of caution to those who would disregard its ominous counsel. Murdock, eyes narrowing with a malevolent glint, cast a sidelong glance at Joe, who strode beside him with a determined stride. A sardonic smile twisted Murdock’s lips, the mark of a man trapped within his own vile stratagems.

"Joe," Murdock began, his voice a silken snare bedecked in mock sincerity, "this night promises a conclusion to our shared history. The lawyer awaits with papers to settle our affairs."

"Make sure your intentions align with your words, Murdock," Joe replied, his gaze unwavering, penetrating the shroud of deceit that cloaked Murdock’s every syllable. He had not forgotten the insinuations that had marred their recent confrontation, nor the creeping doubt that shadowed Murdock's every gesture.

An ominous laugh bubbled from the depths of Murdock’s being. "Fear not," he retorted, masking contempt with feigned affability. "All shall be resolved in due course."

Their path took them toward the station, where flickering gas lamps cast dappled pools of light amidst the encroaching dusk. Unbeknownst to them, another figure pursued them from a judicious distance. Detective Graves, seasoned in the art of deception and the farce of innocence, followed with a stealth born of duty and suspicion.

The railway platform buzzed with the electric hum of concealed anticipation, the air thick with the untold stories of those who journeyed under the cloak of night. Murdock procured their tickets, his eyes darting to the shadows in which Graves concealed himself. The detective observed, a silent sentinel, his mind a cauldron of calculated schemes and ethical resolve.

As the train exhaled great clouds of steam, belching heat into the frigid air, Murdock and Joe boarded. The detective, attuned to their every movement, slipped unnoticed into the car behind them. The journey began, a nocturnal odyssey wrought with peril and unvoiced intentions.

A flicker of doubt crossed Joe's mind as the train wove a path through the darkness. He felt the gaze of destiny upon him, a destiny wrought with deception, but he could not yet untangle the threads of fate that intertwined around him.

The rhythmic churning of wheels beat an insistent tempo, one that echoed in the hollows of Joe's consciousness. Across from him, Murdock feigned disinterest, his thoughts an elaborate tapestry of betrayal. Each mile carried them further from the safety of the well-traveled, deeper into the treacherous realm of the unknown.

Within the confines of the adjacent car, Detective Graves remained alert, the embodiment of vigilance and resolve. He thought of the web that Murdock spun with insidious precision, and his resolve hardened. No innocent would fall prey under his watchful gaze.

Joe, though uncertain, found comfort in the silent companionship of the stars that blinked across the firmament outside the window. He would meet whatever fate awaited with courage, unwilling to cower beneath the shadows cast by deceit.

The train slowed, a mournful whistle cutting through the stillness as they approached a modest station cloaked in secrecy and foreboding. Murdock rose with feigned cheer, gesturing for Joe to follow.

"Come, Joe," Murdock beckoned with oily assurance. "Our destination is near."

Dread coiled in Joe's gut, constricting with every step. Yet, resilience stemmed the tide of fear.

The detective lingered, slipping like a shadow from the train, unobserved by the cunning eyes of his quarry. Drifting amidst anonymity, Graves resolved to unveil the malice that circled around Joe like a deadly vulture.

Into the night's embrace, they ventured, the plangent call of owls echoing from the thicket, a harmony of forewarning. The path they trod was slick with possibility, danger lying in wait like vipers in the underbrush.

Joe's mind churned with thoughts of escape and justice, of unseen allies in his fight against the pernicious intent that hovered at his shoulder.

Thus, the night pulled its veil tighter around the trio, each unawares of the role they were destined to play in the looming crescendo of the tale, shadows and truths vying for victory in the dawn's pale light.

The fire crackles low in the grate, casting long shadows that dance and flicker upon the worn spines of the countless volumes lining my study walls. It is an evening much like countless others that have preceded it; an evening steeped in the comforting silence of solitude, broken only by the gentle ticking of Master Humphrey's Clock, which stands sentinel upon the mantle.

The clock, with its ornate carvings and mellow chime, is more than a mere timepiece. It is the heart of our little society, a silent witness to the tales we have shared and the dreams we have dared to dream. Within its sturdy frame, nestled amongst the intricate workings of gears and springs, rests a hidden compartment. There, we deposit our written offerings, stories and sketches and musings, bound together by a common thread of romanticism and a shared belief in the power of imagination.

We are an unlikely quartet, united by circumstance and drawn together by a mutual yearning for something beyond the mundane. There's the deaf gentleman, his keen eyes sparkling with an almost childlike wonder as he observes the world around him, deciphering its secrets through observation and intuition. And then there's dearest Amelia, her gentle spirit and quiet strength a soothing balm to the occasional melancholic pronouncements of our esteemed poet, Mr. Willoughby. His words, often tinged with a wistful longing for days gone by, possess a rare beauty, a lyrical tapestry woven from threads of memory and imagination.

At each gathering, we observe a peculiar custom. Two chairs, their seats unoccupied, remain a constant fixture around the roaring fireplace. They are a poignant reminder, both of what might be, and of what has been. A symbol of open arms, welcoming the possibility of new kindred spirits who might one day share in our unique fellowship. But they are also a solemn tribute, a silent acknowledgment of those dear friends, now departed, whose absence is felt keenly in the spaces they once filled with laughter and lively debate.

It is my hope, dear reader, that in sharing the chronicles of Master Humphrey's Clock, I might impart some small measure of the wisdom gleaned from our humble gatherings. Perhaps within these pages, you too shall discover the profound beauty of simple pleasures, the enduring power of shared stories, and the solace that comes from embracing the mysteries of the human heart.

For within these walls, within the warm glow cast by the crackling fire and the steady ticking of Master Humphrey's Clock, we have found something truly extraordinary: a sanctuary for the soul, a place where imagination reigns supreme, and where the bonds of friendship, forged in shared passions, prove stronger than the relentless march of time.

Amid the pale gleam of the waning moon, the desolate graveyard lay enshrouded in a silvered hush, as though Heaven itself had taken leave from earthly troubles to bestow a benediction upon those whose lives were numbered and unnamed. The ancient headstones—each one a silent testament to lost souls—stood in haphazard rows upon frost-kissed ground, their weathered inscriptions muted by time and neglect. Along the edge of this somber necropolis, a lonely cross, etched against the ink-blue vault of night, received the lunar beams like a precious relic of faith amid despair. In that spectral glimmer, the markers seemed to whisper of hopes once kindled and now consigned to quiet eternity, their secrets mingling with the brisk sigh of the wind, and casting a reflective pall over the silent land as if urging enshrined memories to awaken amidst the woody shadows.

Beyond the border of that solemn repository, where the trail of light yields to an ever-lengthening darkness, the sea itself assumed a mournful role in the nightly pageant. Fishermen, their hearts as burdened as the nets they cast, navigated in vessels worn and forlorn across the glassy expanse, their eyes briefly lingering upon the cross that shone in sanctified isolation. To them, the shoreline was a hymn of remembrance—a consecrated space where the elements of earth, water, and sky converged in mourning harmony. Such quiet observation lent dignity to the nameless dead, as if the gentle tide, in its perpetual caress of the rugged bluff, sought to cleanse the scars of bygone sorrows and offer solace to those who had come to rest without the soft murmur of loved ones near.

Not far removed from these celestial and maritime musings lay the grim reality of Scrabble Alley, where young Skippy made his humble abode within the cavernous gloom of a neglected basement apartment. In a decrepit tenement that had long surrendered to the ravages of poverty and despair, Skippy's life unfolded with the quiet inevitability of a chapter written in sorrow. The scant light that filtered through the narrow, grimy window fell upon meager furnishings and the etchings of hope scratched upon cold walls, as if the very space around him, although ravaged by misfortune, yearned to shelter remnants of innocence. Here, in the paradox of the nocturne and the narrow quarters, the dissonance between the celestial radiance and the dim confines of urban desolation played out nightly—a grim ballet choreographed by the indifferent hand of fate.

In the course of his meandering existence, Skippy had often been counseled to “skip” the path of idle musing and frivolous ambition, a summons to urgency delivered by stern faces and weary tones alike. One such recollection—evident in the haze of his memory like a fleeting shadow—was of a near-collision with an imposing carriage whose wheels clattered over the cobbles of Scrabble Alley, its occupant, a gentleman of no small hauteur, decrying the youth's seeming impertinence with a cascade of rebukes. Chased by the echoes of that reprimand, Skippy had fled into the murk, his small form swallowed by the labyrinthine alleyways, leaving behind only the fluttering whispers of admonishment. Such episodes, embedded in the fabric of his daily routine, underscored a life perpetually wedged between the relentless demands of an unsympathetic society and the nascent dreams that dared to bloom in shadowed corners.

Yet as the moon journeyed across the vaulted heavens, its light continued unabated, weaving an unspoken connection between realms of the living and the departed. In the gentle interplay of nocturnal radiance upon ancient stone and in the quiet defiance of a boy enduring his lot amid urban decay, there stirred a singular beauty—a tender recognition that even in the obscurity of life’s unremitting hardships, there remained fragments of grace. Skippy, though confined within the meager bounds of his deteriorating shelter, could not help but be enchanted by the distant hymn of the night, its cadence echoing with promises of redemption found, perhaps, in the silent communion between the forsaken graves and the shimmering cross. And so it was that the contrasting worlds of ephemeral human worry and eternal celestial serenity converged, beckoning the wandering soul toward a destiny yet uncharted, whispering that in even the bleakest of corners, light and solace might be found.

That evening, Philip sat alone in the dimly lit parlour, the silence broken only by the crackling of the fire in the hearth. The weight of his recent loss pressed heavily upon him, yet beneath the grief lay a steely resolve. He must be strong; he must face the future with courage.

He rose from his seat and crossed to the old oak desk, its surface worn smooth by years of use. It had been his father's, and now, it was his. Within its drawers lay the remnants of a life well-lived, papers and documents that held the key to his father's affairs.

With trembling hands, Philip began to sort through the pile. Bills, receipts, letters - a tangled web of financial obligations that he must now unravel. He worked late into the night, his brow furrowed in concentration, the flickering candlelight casting long, dancing shadows on the walls.

The task was daunting, but Philip was determined to understand the full extent of his father's debts. He knew that the auction on Thursday would be crucial, and he prayed that it would yield enough to cover the outstanding expenses.

As the first rays of dawn crept through the window, Philip leaned back in his chair, his eyes heavy with fatigue. He had made some progress, but much remained to be done.

He resolved to continue his work after breakfast, which he would take at Frank Dunbar's house. The thought of spending a few hours in the company of his friend brought a measure of comfort to his weary soul.

Later that morning, Philip walked along the familiar village street towards the Dunbar residence. The air was crisp and cool, and the birds sang merrily in the trees, their cheerful melodies a stark contrast to the sadness in his heart.

He was greeted warmly by Mrs. Dunbar, a kind and matronly woman who had always shown him great affection. Frank, too, was pleased to see him, and the two friends sat down to a hearty breakfast of eggs, bacon, and toast.

"I'm so glad you came, Philip," said Frank, his voice filled with genuine concern. "It must be dreadfully lonely for you at home."

"It is, Frank," replied Philip. "But I must make the best of it. I have much to do before the auction."

"Is there anything I can do to help?" asked Frank. "I wish I could do more, but you know my circumstances."

"Your friendship is help enough, Frank," said Philip, smiling gratefully. "That is more valuable than money."

After breakfast, Philip returned to his home and resumed his work on his father's papers. He discovered a number of unpaid bills, but he also found a few assets that he had not been aware of.

Among them was a small portfolio of stocks, which his father had purchased some years ago. Philip examined the certificates carefully, his heart pounding with excitement. If these stocks had any value, they could make a significant difference in his financial situation.

He decided to seek the advice of Mr. Grimshaw, the local banker, a man known for his honesty and integrity. Philip packed the certificates into his satchel and set off towards the village bank.

Mr. Grimshaw greeted him with a friendly smile and invited him into his office. Philip explained his situation and presented the stock certificates for his inspection.

The banker examined the documents with a practiced eye, his expression unreadable. Philip waited anxiously, his hopes hanging in the balance.

Finally, Mr. Grimshaw looked up, a twinkle in his eye. "Well, Philip," he said, "it appears that your father was a shrewd investor. These stocks have appreciated considerably over the years."

"Do you mean they're worth something?" asked Philip, his voice trembling with excitement.

"Indeed, they are," replied Mr. Grimshaw. "I would estimate their current value to be several hundred dollars."

Philip's heart leaped with joy. This was more than he had dared to hope for. With the proceeds from the stocks, he would be able to pay off his father's debts and still have something left over to start his own life.

"Thank you, Mr. Grimshaw," he said, his voice filled with gratitude. "You have given me hope for the future."

Oscar Dalrymple drew down the corners of his mouth; it gave an unpleasing expression to his face, which was naturally cold. At that moment a bird rose within range; Oscar raised his piece, fired and brought it down. "That," said he, "is how I like to waste good powder and shot."

"All right, Mr. Oscar," was the Rector's hearty answer. "To use it is better than to waste it, but to waste it is better than to run risks. Most of the accidents that happen with guns are caused by want of precaution."

"Shall I draw your charge, Mr. Robert?" asked Hardy; who, as a good church-going man, had a reverence for all the Rector said, in the church and out of it.

"Draw the charge from my gun!" retorted Hardy's young master; not, however, speaking within ear-shot of Mr. Cleveland. "No. I can take care of my playthings, if others can't, Hardy," he added, with all the self-sufficiency of a young and vain man.

Presently there came up a substantial farmer, winding across the stubble towards his own house, which they were passing. He rented under Mr. Dalrymple.

"Famous good sport today, hasn't it been, Squire?" cried he, saluting his landlord.

"Famous. Never better. Will you accept a pair, Lee?" continued Mr. Dalrymple. "We have bagged plenty."

The farmer gladly took the pheasants. "I shall tell my daughters you shot them on purpose, Squire," said he, jestingly.

"Do," interposed Robert, with a laugh. "Tell Miss Judith I shot them for her: in return for her sewing up that rent in my coat, the other day, and making me decent to go home. Is the fence, where I fell, mended yet?"

"Mended yet?" echoed Mr. Lee. "It was up again in an hour after you left, Mr. Robert."

"Ah! I know you are the essence of order and punctuality," returned Robert. "You must let me have the cost."

"Time enough for that," said the farmer. "'Twasn't much. Good-afternoon, gentlemen; your servant, Squire."

"Oh--I say--Lee," called out Robert, as the farmer was turning homewards, while the rest of the party pursued their way, "about the mud in that weir? Hardy says it will hurt the fish to do it now."

"That's just what I told you, Mr. Robert."

"Well, then---- But I'll come down tomorrow, and talk it over with you: I can't stop now."

"As you please, sir. I shall be somewhere about."

Robert Dalrymple turned too hastily. His foot caught against something sticking out of the stubble, and in saving himself he nearly dropped his gun. He recovered the gun with a jerk, but the trigger was touched, he never knew how, or with what, and the piece went off. A cry in front, a confusion, one man down, and the others gathered round him, was all Robert Dalrymple saw, as through a mist. He dropped the gun, started forward, and gave vent to a cry of anguish. For it was his father who had fallen.

The most collected was Oscar Dalrymple. He always was collected; his nature was essentially cool and calm. Holding up Mr. Dalrymple's head and shoulders, he strove to ascertain where the injury lay. Though very pale, and lying with closed eyes, Mr. Dalrymple had not fainted.

"Oh, father," cried Robert, as he throw himself on his knees beside him in a passion of grief, "I did not do it purposely--I don't know how it happened."

"Purposely--no, my boy," answered his father, in a kind tone, as he opened his eyes. "Cheer up, Charley." For, in fond moments, and at other odd times, they would call the boy by his second name, Charles. Robert often clashed with his father's.

"I do not believe there's much harm done," said the sufferer. "I think the damage is in my left leg."

"Dodo talked to me a good deal about her marriage. I am sorry about it, for I think that Chesterford will be terribly disillusioned. You know he doesn't take things lightly, and he is much too hopelessly fond of Dodo ever to be content with what she will grant him as a wife. But we cannot do anything. I told her what I thought, not because I hoped to make any change in the matter, but because I wished her to know that for once in her life she has made a failure--a bad, hopeless mistake. That has been my revenge. Come, it's after one, I must go home. I shall go there this evening; shall I see you?"

Jack went home meditating rather bitterly on things in general. He had a sense that Fate was not behaving very prettily to him. She had dealt him rather a severe blow in April last, which had knocked him down, and, having knocked him down, she now proceeded in a most unsportsmanlike way to kick him. Jack had a great idea of fair play, and Fate certainly was not playing fair. He would have liked to have a few words with her on the subject. The world had been very kind on the whole to him. He had always been popular, and his life, though perhaps rather aimless, was at least enjoyable. And since the world had been kind to him, he was generous to the world in general, and to his friends in particular. It had always held a high opinion of him, as a thoroughly healthy-minded and pleasant companion, and he was disposed to hold a similar opinion of it. Consequently, when Dodo had refused him that spring, he had not thought badly of her. He did not blame her, or get bitter about it; but though he had flattered himself that he was used to Dodo's ways, and had always recognised her capabilities in the way of surprising her friends, he had not been quite prepared for the news of her engagement. In fact, he was surprised, and also rather resentful, chiefly against the general management of mundane affairs, but partly also against Dodo herself. Dodo had not told him of her engagement; he had been left to find it out for himself. Then, again, she was engaged to a man who was hopelessly and entirely in love with her, and for whom, apart from a quiet, unemotional liking, she did not care two straws, except in so far as he was immensely rich and had a title, two golden keys which unlocked the most secret doors of that well-furnished apartment known as Society, which constituted Dodo's world. Hitherto her position had been precarious: she had felt that she was on trial. Her personality, her great attractiveness and talents, had secured for herself a certain footing on the very daïs of that room; but she had always known that unless she married brilliantly she would not be sure of her position. If she married a man who would not be always certain of commanding whatever money and position--for she would never have married a wealthy brewer--could command, or, worst of all, if in her unwillingness to accept anything but the best she could get, she did not marry at all, Dodo knew that she never would have that unquestioned position that she felt was indispensable to her. Jack knew all this perfectly well--in fact Dodo had referred to it that morning--and he accepted it philosophically as being inevitable. But what he did not like was being told that he would not have done on general grounds, that he was too fond of his own way, that he would not have given Dodo rein enough. He had known Dodo too long and too well, when he proposed to her, to have any of a lover's traditional blindness to the faults of his love. He knew that she was, above all things, strongly dramatic, that she moved with a view to effect, that she was unscrupulous in what she did, that her behaviour was sometimes in questionable taste; but this he swallowed whole, so to speak. He was genuinely attached to her, and felt that she possessed the qualities that he would most like to have in his wife. Bertie had said to him that morning that she was stimulating, and would not wear well. Stimulating she certainly was--what lovable woman is not?--and personally he had known her long, and she did wear well. The hidden depths and unsuspected shallows were exactly what he loved her for; no one ever fell in love with a canal; and though the shallows were commoner than the depths, and their presence was sometimes indicated by a rather harsh jarring of the keel, yet he believed, fully and sincerely, in the dark, mysterious depths for love to lose itself in. Besides, a wife, whose actions and thoughts were as perfectly calculable and as accurately calculated as the trains in a Bradshaw, was possessed of sterling qualities which, however estimable, were more suited to a housekeeper than a mistress.

Mrs. Cusworth turned deadly pale, and a look of fear came into her eyes. Salome hastily turned to Philip, and her appealing glance told him he must not touch on a subject that would alarm and agitate her mother.

’I mean,’ said Philip hastily, ’that a man, inexperienced like myself, entering a large house in which there are domestics, of whose freaks and vagaries he knows nothing, and desires to know less, is like a colonist in Papua, of the natives of which nothing certain has been revealed. They may be cannibals; they may, on the other hand, be inoffensive. Of landladies in lodging-houses I have had a long and bitter experience. I have run the gamut of them, from the reduced gentlewoman to the wife of an artisan, and I believe it is one of those professions which, like vivisection, dries up the springs of moral worth. It will be essential to my happiness, I may say to my success in the business, to have a responsible person to manage the house for me. You, madam, will relieve me from grave embarrassments if you will consent to remain here on the same terms as heretofore. It will indeed be conferring on me a lasting favour, which I know I am not justified in asking.’

’It is very good of you to suggest this,’ began the widow.

’On the contrary,’ interrupted Philip, ’it is selfish of me to propose it—to wish to retain you in a place where you must be surrounded by sorrowful reminiscences, and tie you to work when you ought to be free from every care.’

’I thank you,’ said Mrs. Cusworth. ’It so happens that I am distressed by pecuniary losses, and I am therefore glad to accept your offer.’

’I am sorry, madam, that you have met with losses. But I do not wish to force you to accept obligations for which you do not feel yourself equal without understanding exactly how matters stand. Mrs. Sidebottom and I have consulted together about the probable wishes of my deceased uncle, and we unite in thinking that he never intended to leave Miss Cusworth unprovided for. The will he had drawn out perhaps erred on the side of excessive liberality to her and disregard of the claims of his own relations. That was cancelled—how, we cannot say. Suffice it to say, it was cancelled, but without cancelling the obligation to do something for Miss Cusworth. We are quite sure that Mr. Pennycomequick intended to provide for her, and Mrs. Sidebottom and I agree in proposing for her acceptance such a sum as was invested by my late uncle for the benefit of Mrs. Baynes on her marriage a twelve month ago.’

He was the lawyer—formal, cold, stiff—as he spoke, measuring his sentences and weighing his words. Even when he endeavoured to be courteous, as when inviting the widow to stay on in his house, he spoke without ease of manner, graciousness, and softness of tone.

’Of course,’ said Mrs. Cusworth, ’it has been a great disappointment to us that we received nothing from Mr. Pennycomequick——’

’Mother!’ interrupted Salome, quivering, flushing to the roots of her hair, then turning white. Mrs. Cusworth was one of those ordinary women who think it becomes them not to receive a favour as a favour, but as a due. Salome at once felt the grace and kindness of the arrangement proposed for her advantage by Philip, and had little hesitation in attributing it to him, and freeing Mrs. Sidebottom from the initiative, at least, in it. But her mother supposed it due to her dignity to receive it as a concession to a legitimate claim.
