It had been a happy thought of Mary's to get her two younger sisters, girls of eleven and sixteen, to be present, to enhance the venerable appearance of the party by the contrast of their bloom and freshness.

“Are these your little granddaughters?” inquired Henry, benevolently inspecting them over the tops of his spectacles as he patted the elder of the two on the head, a liberty she would by no means have allowed him in his proper character, but which she now seemed puzzled whether to resent or not.

“Yes,” replied Mary, with an indulgent smile. “They wanted to see what an old folks' party was like, though I told them they wouldn't enjoy it much. I remember I thought old people rather dull when I was their age.”

Henry made a little conversation with the girls, asking them the list of fatuous questions by which adults seem fated to illustrate the gulf between them and childhood in the effort to bridge it.

“Annie, dear, just put that ottoman at Mrs. Hyde's feet,” said Mary to one of the little girls. “I 'm so glad you felt able to come out this evening, Mrs. Hyde! I understood you had not enjoyed good health this summer.”

“I have scarcely been out of my room since spring, until recently,” replied Jessie. “Thank you, my dear” (to the little girl); “but Dr. Sanford has done wonders for me. How is your health now, Mrs. Fellows?”

“I have not been so well an entire summer in ten years. My daughter, Mrs. Tarbox, was saying the other day that she wished she had my strength. You know she is quite delicate,” said Mary.

“Speaking of Dr. Sanford,” said Henry, looking at Jessie, “he is really a remarkable man. My son has such confidence in him that he seemed quite relieved when I had passed my grand climacteric and could get on his list. You know he takes no one under sixty-three. By the way, governor,” he added, turning around with some ado, so as to face George, “I heard he had been treating your rheumatism lately. Has he seemed to reach the difficulty?”

“Remarkably,” replied George, tenderly stroking his right knee in an absent manner. “Why, don't you think I walked half the way home from my office the other day when my carriage was late?”

“I wonder you dared venture it,” said Jessie, with a shocked air. “What if you had met with some accident!”

“That's what my son said,” answered George. “He made me promise never to try such a thing again; but I like to show them occasionally that I'm good for something yet.”

He said this with a “he, he,” of senile complacency, ending in an asthmatic cough, which caused some commotion in the company. Frank got up and slapped him on the back, and Mary sent Annie for a glass of water.

George being relieved, and quiet once more restored, Henry said to Frank:--

“By the way, doctor, I want to congratulate you on your son's last book. You must have helped him to the material for so truthful a picture of American manners in the days when we were young. I fear we have not improved much since then. There was a simplicity, a naturalness in society fifty years ago, that one looks in vain for now. There was, it seems to me, much less regard paid to money, and less of morbid social ambition. Don't you think so, Mrs. Tyrrell?”

“It's just what I was saying only the other day,” replied Nellie. “I'm sure I don't know what we 're coming to nowadays. Girls had some modesty when I was young,” and she shook her head with its rows of white curls with an air of mingled reprobation and despair.

“Did you attend Professor Merryweather's lecture last evening, Mrs. Hyde?” asked Frank, adjusting his eye-glasses and fixing Jessie with that intensity of look by which old persons have to make up for their failing eyesight. “The hall was so near your house, I did n't know but you would feel like venturing out.”

Edith hesitated for a moment before entering the room, an intuition stirring within her that she had ventured into a space where secrets were weighed, and confidences exchanged. She had approached with the innocence of youth, believing herself privy to all the affairs within the grand halls of Tinto, but now she found herself an unexpected spectator to a tableau of intrigue.

"Edith, my dear," said Torrance, rising awkwardly from his seat, his brow furrowed with an expression of disquiet that did not entirely mask his pride. "I hope you did not find the sound of our conversation distressing."

"My dear," stammered Beaufort, his gaze darting between Edith and Lady Caroline, his voice laced with an uncharacteristic vulnerability, "I assure you, my intentions were entirely above board."

Lady Caroline, a woman whose intellect was as sharp as her eyes were piercing, addressed Edith with a gentle firmness. "You catch us at a rare moment of reflection, my child. Let us not alarm you. Mr. Beaufort was merely sharing his thoughts on a matter of import."

"A matter of some import, indeed," Torrance interjected, crossing his arms as if to shield himself from the cool air that seemed to penetrate the very walls of the room. "It is a matter of bringing forth the truth, and untangling the knots that bind us unexpectedly."

Edith, her mind racing to piece together the fragments of this sudden drama, perceived an undercurrent of dissension. It was clear that the gathering, once intended to be a small, intimate affair, had been transformed into a forum for conjecture and confrontation. The arrival of Dr. Stirling and his wife had surely tipped the scales, introducing a new dynamic with their unexpected presence.

It was in this charged atmosphere that Torrance recounted his earlier disappointments, his frustration palpable as he spoke of his desire to draw forth the confidences of John Erskine. "I had envisioned a close circle of confidants, not an assembly grown to six. Dr. Stirling's inclusion, though well-intentioned, has complicated our purpose."

"Complicated, indeed," murmured Mrs. Stirling, her voice a soft counterpoint to the room's tension, her gaze lingering over the dinner table, which bore the marks of Torrance's eccentric taste - old-fashioned silverware glinted under the candles' flicker, a testament to his pride in the past.

Edith observed her companions, noting the guarded exchanges and the subtle signals exchanged among them. The weight of unspoken words hung heavily in the air, and she felt the press of many stories untold. As a silent observer, she became a participant, albeit unwilling, in the complex web of deceit and revelation that wove its way through the evening.

The revelation of Mrs. Stirling's genuine admiration for the silverware seemed a small victory amidst the larger struggle for clarity and understanding. It was a moment of connection, a crumb of normalcy in the midst of turmoil, reminding Edith that beneath the masks of propriety and artifice, individuals were bound by shared experiences and simple pleasures.

As the evening wore on, the room seemed to close in, the walls seeming to narrow around the small group, each member ensnared in their own thoughts and expectations. Edith, ever observant, prepared herself for the unveiling of truths, for the fragile bonds of trust were on the brink of fracture, and the night promised to be one of disclosures, both painful and enlightening.

The company was entirely of the softer sex,--an epithet not perhaps in the strictest accordance with an array of faces that really might have shamed witchcraft. Bronzed, blear-eyed, and weather-beaten, seamed with age and scarred with sickness, shrewd-looking, suspicious, and crafty in every lineament, there was yet one characteristic predominant over all,--an intense and abject submission, an almost slavish deference to every observation addressed to them. Their dress bespoke the very greatest poverty; not only were they clothed in rags of every hue and shape, but all were barefooted, and some of the very oldest wore no other covering to their heads than their own blanched and grizzled locks.

Nor would a follower of Lavater have argued too favorably of the prosperity of Irish regeneration, in beholding that array of faces,--low-browed, treacherous-looking, and almost savagely cruel, as many of them were in expression. There was not, indeed, as often is to be remarked amongst the peasant class of many countries, a look of stupid, stolid indifference; on the contrary, their faces were intensely, powerfully significant, and there was stamped upon them that strange mixture of malignant drollery and sycophancy that no amount of either good or adverse fortune ever entirely subdues in their complex natures.

The expediency of misery had begotten the expediency of morals, and in all the turnings and windings of their shifty natures you could see the suggestions of that abject destitution which had eaten into their very hearts. It would have puzzled a moralist to analyze these “gnarled natures,” wherein some of the best and some of the worst features of humanity warred and struggled together. Who could dare to call them kind-hearted or malevolent, grateful or ungrateful, free-giving or covetous, faithful or capricious, as a people? Why, they were all these, and fifty other things just as opposite besides, every twenty-four hours of their lives! Their moods of mind ranged from one extreme to the other; nothing had any permanency amongst them but their wretchedness. Of all their qualities, however, that which most obstructed their improvement, ate deepest into their natures, and suggested the worst fears for the future, was suspicion. They trusted nothing,--none,--so that every benefit bestowed on them came alloyed with its own share of doubt; and all the ingenuity of their crafty minds found congenial occupation in ascribing this or that motive to every attempt to better their condition.

Mary Martin knew them--understood them--as well as most people; few, indeed, out of their own actual station of life had seen so much of their domesticity. From her very childhood she had been conversant with their habits and their ways. She had seen them patient under the most trying afflictions, manfully braving every ill of life, and submitting with a noble self-devotion to inevitable calamity; and she had also beheld them, with ignorant impatience, resenting the slightest interference when they deemed it uncalled for, and rejecting kindness when it came coupled with the suggestion of a duty.

By considerable skill, and no little patience, she had insinuated a certain small amount of discipline into this disorderly mass. She could not succeed in persuading them to approach her one by one, or wait with any semblance of order while she was yet occupied; but she enforced conformity with at least one rule, which was, that none should speak save in answer to some question put by herself. This may seem a very small matter, and yet to any one who knows the Irish peasant it will appear little short of miraculous. The passion for discursiveness, the tendency to make an effective theme of their misery, whatever particular shape it may assume, is essentially national; and to curb this vent to native eloquence was to oppose at once the strongest impulse of their natures.

As the days lengthened and the sun's warmth increased in intensity, young Emily and her brother Theodore found themselves drawn to the meadow in a manner most peculiar. It was as if an unseen hand beckoned them, whispering secrets through the rustling leaves and the hum of the meadow's denizens. The tall, golden grasses swayed in the breeze, casting shadows that danced around them like ancient spirits, beckoning them to step further within the secluded realm.

One sunny afternoon, as they ventured deeper into the heart of the meadow, they stumbled upon a sight that filled them with wonder. In the midst of the tall grass, a wondrous creature stirred, its iridescent feathers shimmering like precious jewels. A bird, unlike any they had seen before, perched upon the branch of a nearby oak. Its eyes were a brilliant shade of emerald, and its tail feathers fanned out like a royal banner, quivering slightly in the wind. The creature observed them with an air of regal indifference, yet Theodore could not help but feel a sense of kinship with this majestic creature.

"It's a peacock," Emily whispered, her eyes wide with wonder. "I've only ever seen them in illustrations, but I didn't know they existed here." She reached out a tentative hand, and to her astonishment, the creature did not fly away. Instead, it bent its neck gracefully and allowed Emily to gently stroke its tail feathers. Theodore watched in awe as the feathers shimmered and shifted colors in response to his sister's touch.

As they marveled at the remarkable sight, Emily's eyes fell upon a small, hidden glade just beyond the tall grass. The ground was carpeted with small, sweet-smelling wildflowers that danced in the breeze, and at its center stood a trio of tall, slender lilies, their golden petals swaying gently. The sight was so enchanting that Theodore could not resist the temptation to pluck one of the flowers, only to recall his sister's earlier words about their secret spots. He hesitated, his fingers tightening around the stem, and then, with a sigh, let go. "We should leave it," he said, his voice barely above a whisper. "It's like our own secret treasure."

They wandered away from the glade, leaving the peacock to its solitude. As they neared the edge of the meadow, a soft, rhythmic sound caught their attention. They followed the sound, and to their delight, found themselves standing before a gentle waterfall, the likes of which they had only ever heard of in the great tapestries at the grand estate of their neighbor. The water cascaded over smooth, pebbled rocks, gleaming in the sun, and Theodore felt a familiar sense of ownership over their secret discovery. It was their waterfall, their treasure hidden beneath the tall grass and far away from the bustling world.

As they sat beside the water's edge, Emily's fingers brushed against the cool, smooth pebbles. She leaned back, closing her eyes and allowing the sun to warm her face. "I feel like we've discovered something magical, Theodore," she said, her voice soft and dreamy. "It's like this meadow is our own enchanted kingdom, hidden away from the world." Theodore smiled, his eyes fixed on the peacock, now perched upon a branch above them, its tail feathers shimmering like liquid gold. "And we're the rulers of this kingdom, Emily," he said, his voice filled with conviction. "We'll protect our enchantments and keep our secrets until the end of time."

The gardens of Court Netherleigh lay bathed in the golden hues of the declining sun, their formality softened by the gentle sway of the evening breeze. Entwined in the shadows of the ancient oaks, Adela found herself once more ensnared in her preoccupied musings. Her heart danced to the rhythm of thoughts unbidden, each step echoing the distant murmurs of Captain Stanley's name. As the last light of day faded, she stood at the bay window, peering through the dusty glass at the horizon, her thoughts adrift on the same endless sea.

"Ah, there you are, Adela!" Miss Margery's voice broke the silence, a sliver of reality punctuating the fragile confines of her reverie. "I've found the opera-glasses; they were tucked away in the drawer where we keep the maps—quite as it should be." Miss Margery's tone held a note of mild reproof, her eyes twinkling with the merriment of a secret discovery. "You might remember to attend to such trifles, my dear, else you'll have the whole household running on errands for you."

Adela offered a wan smile, her musings momentarily displaced by the unexpected turn of events. "Thank you, Margery. I must confess, my thoughts were elsewhere." Her glance held a touch of wistfulness, a longing veiled but palpable. "I was contemplating the beauty of this very garden, how it would look when the sun had risen again."

Miss Margery raised an eyebrow, her curiosity piqued. "A fine exercise in imagination, to be sure. However, the truth of it is often found in the ordinary, don't you agree?" With that, she pointed the opera-glasses towards the distant pathway, where Frances Chenevix had just vanished.

As Adela took the glasses, the world before her sharpened, revealing the industrious figures of road laborers, their tasklines displacing the romantic visions that had enchanted Frances Chenevix. The disappointment etched across her features was evident; the velvet opera house filled with aristocracy she had imagined was instead a stage for peasants tilling the land.

The evening deepened, and with it, the quiet of Court Netherleigh seemed to cloak the estate in a mantle of anticipation. Sir Francis Netherleigh, whose footsteps across the estate were as silent as his life, had almost managed to restore the family fortunes through the parsimony of his living. Yet, the future of Court Netherleigh teetered on the brink of uncertainty. The title, set to lapse, could be restored only through the masculine line of descent—a son who would bear his name and carry the legacy forward.

The denizens of Court Netherleigh whispered amongst themselves, their conjectures spinning like gossamer coursing through the estate. The three distant female cousins, heirs to the estate only by default, were seldom at Court. They moved like shadows on the periphery, their presence felt more by absence.

In the drawing room, Adela's thoughts wove intricate patterns, each thread tied to the fates of those she held dear. The image of Captain Stanley, his countenance framed by the opera-glasses, lingered in her mind—a specter of longing and apprehension. She had seen him but once in the mirror of reflection, a fleeting glimpse amidst the mundane realities of daily life.

Sir Francis, in his study, pored over ledgers and accounts with a quiet diligence. His life was an ode to restraint, his countenance a study in stoic endurance. He was a portrait of resilience in the face of adversity, determined to salvage his ancestral home from the ruins wrought by extravagance and folly.

The evening wore on, and as the moon rose, casting long, ethereal shadows across the manicured lawns, the inhabitants of Court Netherleigh retreated to their chambers, their dreams peopled with the echoes of the day. Adela, lost in contemplation, found solace in the quiet of her room—a refuge from the whispers of the world outside.

In the stillness of the night, Adela's thoughts drifted, painting dreams of a future where concern for Captain Stanley mingled with visions of life at Court Netherleigh. The opera-glasses rested on her nightstand, silent witnesses to her reverie, their lenses reflecting the complexities of a heart suspended between longing and loyalty. And as the night deepened, and the estate lay cradled in the arms of slumber, Adela's dreams were filled with the quiet dignity of Sir Francis Netherleigh and the tantalizing specter of Captain Stanley—a duo of destinies entwined within the tapestry of her heart.

The young gentleman apologized, whined, protesting his sorrow. Three weeks later, M. Gaussine, professor of the Sumarian language at the Sorbonne, who was walking behind them.

"Come along, child," murmured M. Raindal, trying to lead his daughter away. "Yes, they are to be married. I only heard of it yesterday!... But she had stood still, unable to move, although she could hardly keep from screaming aloud in her pain. She had been on the verge of fainting. What an outrageous memory! Then came the ghastly days in her room, still impregnated with the rogue's perfume,--the long hours of day dreams, when she had taken her vows of renunciation, swearing henceforth to devote herself to a life of study as others are driven by despair into religion!

In spite of her work, however, and of the long years that had passed since then, she had been unable to dismiss from her mind, no matter how much learning she had crowded it with, the tenacious image of the charming Albârt, who, notwithstanding the offices of his father-in-law, was said to be buried miles away from Paris, in an obscure Lycée of Provence.

Thérèse was still dazzled by the memory of his caresses, as were those mortals of antiquity whom a god had loved. He remained her mourned husband, the masterful lord of her secret life; and when they wanted to marry her, to give her to another man, it was always he who came between, who took her back, resurrecting in her austere frame his Theresoun of old, his captivated Theresoun. Invisible to all others, but present to her, he would seem to be there, hand on hip, his knee bent in that swaggering attitude of bravado, murmuring with sneering lips, "But look, ma chato, look, compare us!... Is it possible ... after me?" It was true; how could she stoop--betray him! And so in a few brusque words the new suitor was always dismissed.

"So you don't want him, child?" M. Raindal would ask pitifully, only to be met with a refusal so sharp and angry, and like a blow that it left him dazed, reduced him to silence, and effectively prevented any further argument.

"Well, dear, are we ready?... I was delayed by a newspaper man, a reporter who interviewed me on Cleopatra, the English in Egypt ... and I don't know what.... Tell me, you did not feel too impatient?"

Thérèse started on hearing the jovial voice of her father.

"No, no, I was thinking; I was working, walking up and down."

"Good! I am glad of it...." And as one does to a friend or a colleague, he took her arm and rapidly led her towards the Boulevard St. Michel.

Some attempted a guess; some instinctively smiled, moved by vague sympathetic ideas. Sometimes students who knew the master by sight purposely stared at him to win a glance for themselves, or even, moved by respect, saluted him.

But this medical report of Dr. Guyon’s--bringing facts and arguments to confirm his opinion, that there was no physical reason why the Cagots should not be received on terms of social equality by the rest of the world--did no more for his clients than the legal decrees promulgated two centuries before had done. The French proved the truth of the saying in Hudibras,

He that’s convinced against his will Is of the same opinion still.

And, indeed, the being convinced by Dr. Guyon that they ought to receive Cagots as fellow-creatures, only made them more rabid in declaring that they would not. One or two little occurrences which are recorded, show that the bitterness of the repugnance to the Cagots was in full force at the time just preceding the first French revolution. There was a M. d’Abedos, the curate of Lourbes, and brother to the seigneur of the neighbouring castle, who was living in seventeen hundred and eighty; he was well-educated for the time, a travelled man, and sensible and moderate in all respects but that of his abhorrence of the Cagots: he would insult them from the very altar, calling out to them, as they stood afar off, “Oh! ye Cagots, damned for evermore!” One day, a half-blind Cagot stumbled and touched the censer borne before this Abbé de Lourbes. He was immediately turned out of the church, and forbidden ever to re-enter it. One does not know how to account for the fact, that the very brother of this bigoted abbé, the seigneur of the village, went and married a Cagot girl; but so it was, and the abbé brought a legal process against him, and had his estates taken from him, solely on account of his marriage, which reduced him to the condition of a Cagot, against whom the old law was still in force. The descendants of this Seigneur de Lourbes are simple peasants at this very day, working on the lands which belonged to their grandfather.

This prejudice against mixed marriages remained prevalent until very lately. The tradition of the Cagot descent lingered among the people, long after the laws against the accursed race were abolished. A Breton girl, within the last few years, having two lovers each of reputed Cagot descent, employed a notary to examine their pedigrees, and see which of the two had least Cagot in him; and to that one she gave her hand. In Brittany the prejudice seems to have been more virulent than anywhere else. M. Emile Souvestre records proofs of the hatred borne to them in Brittany so recently as in eighteen hundred and thirty-five. Just lately a baker at Hennebon, having married a girl of Cagot descent, lost all his custom. The godfather and godmother of a Cagot child became Cagots themselves by the Breton laws, unless, indeed, the poor little baby died before attaining a certain number of days. They had to eat the butchers’ meat condemned as unhealthy; but, for some unknown reason, they were considered to have a right to every cut loaf turned upside down, with its cut side towards the door, and might enter any house in which they saw a loaf in this position, and carry it away with them. About thirty years ago, there was the skeleton of a hand hanging up as an offering in a Breton Church near Quimperle, and the tradition was, that it was the hand of a rich Cagot who had dared to take holy water out of the usual bénitier, some time at the beginning of the reign of Louis the Sixteenth; which an old soldier witnessing, he lay in wait, and the next time the offender approached the bénitier he cut off his hand, and hung it up, dripping with blood, as an offering to the patron saint of the church. The poor Cagots in Brittany petitioned against their opprobrious name, and begged to be distinguished by the appellation of Malandrins. To English ears one is much the same as the other, as neither conveys any meaning; but, to this day, the descendants of the Cagots do not like to have this name applied to them, preferring that of Malandrin.

Mrs. Baske was introduced to Mr. Mallard by Mrs. Spence, whose manner, though buoyant, conveyed an air of restrained authority that seemed to govern the very atmosphere of the gathering. The two stood clad in congeniality, their speech tinged with the inflections of a shared understanding, as if each word exchanged was a careful stitch in the fabric of their acquaintance.

“Ah, Mr. Mallard,” Mrs. Baske said, her tone neither too assertive nor too timid, “Mrs. Spence recounts a journey imbued with much introspection. I daresay it has its particular charms, does it not?”

Mallard, leaning just slightly forward, nodded with grave acknowledgment. “Indeed, it does. Yet, it often appears to one that what charms lie therein are themselves a distraction from the stark realities awaiting us upon our arrival. Miss Doran, for instance, bore the burden of two discordant desires: the pull towards Naples, that siren of antiquity, and an ungainly melancholy for the sights we must forfeit along the way.”

“Ah, yes,” Mrs. Baske interjected, raising a delicate hand as if to invoke the image of distant vistas. “How curious it is that one might long for the very experience that is just beyond reach yet find solace in fleeting glimpses of the world unravelling on the horizon.”

“Precisely,” Mallard concurred, his brow furrowing slightly, revealing an innate restless spirit. “She resorted to a novel for distraction, though I observed her focus wane as the story waned—a complex brocade whose meaning slipped through her fingers like sand.”

A silence enveloped them momentarily, punctuated only by the distant echo of revelry in the courtyard. The sun’s glowing finale cast a golden hue over their faces, bringing forth an ephemeral connection that spoke of shared burdens and untold stories.

“In point of fact,” Mallard continued, “Miss Doran will not receive visitors until her energies are fully restored. We shall, as I instructed, hold our morning visits to Mrs. Lessingham and the rest until she is fit to welcome us. I seek not to disturb her repose.”

Mrs. Baske’s eyes twinkled with latent curiosity. “You remain ever the diligent guardian, Mr. Mallard. One would not mistaken your thoroughness for mere restraint. But one might wonder, do you not pine for more of the company to grant your work a semblance of companionship?”

Mallard’s countenance softened, yet was not devoid of a certain austerity. “Companionship holds little allure against a litany of tasks that beckon me from every corner of the world. I intend to withdraw briefly to Naples, to refresh my mind in foreign dealings before I set my sights on Amalfi and Paestum.”

“Ah, the ruins of Paestum,” Mrs. Baske breathed, her admiration evident. “One feels the history stir within the stones themselves! How fortunate is your calling, Mr. Mallard, to delve into the depths of such remnants.”

A solemnity descended upon him. “Yet, is there not something tragic amidst these remnants, dear lady? Take, for instance, our acquaintance with Mr. Elgar. His downfall—spurred on by drink—is a reminder that the allure of ruin is often shrouded in a more personal despair.”

“Such a lamentable fate,” said Mrs. Baske, lowering her voice as though to shield the topic from the exuberance of onlookers. “Mere absence of strength bids ruin to dreams once noble. Do you truly believe there lies no redemption for him?”

“I fear,” Mallard replied, his gaze drifting momentarily to the lively throng beyond, “that some spirits are permanently dimmed by the shadows they invite. Elgar could have traversed the heights of achievement; yet, he spiraled into those dark waters, leaving behind only aspirations unfulfilled.”

“An overwhelming sorrow indeed,” breathed Mrs. Baske. “One cannot help but consider how narrowly such fates may veer from our own. What say you, Mr. Mallard, does the world weigh heavier upon you for such reflections?”

“Easier to ponder in the silence of one’s own heart than on the bustling paths of society, Mrs. Baske. For every man who grapples with despair, there stands a challenge. Will he rise or sink? Thus, we are bound to our futures, our destinies forged upon choices made in the recesses of the mind.”

Speculation, however, thrives upon doubt and intrigue, and the talk persisted, winding its way through the crowded thoroughfares of Mayfair and Knightsbridge, until finally reaching the ear of the fair Miss Durrant.

Marion Durrant, now twenty-three winters young, lived a tranquil existence with her aged aunt, Mrs. Fothergill, in a small but elegantly appointed house on the west side of Hyde Park. By the benign provision of a deceased uncle, Miss Durrant had inherited a modest but steady income, sufficient to support herself and her aunt in comfort, though not, perhaps, in luxury. Yet, despite the undeniable advantages of her financial situation, the young woman's prospects remained uncertain, and her connection to the prominent Cheyne family, through her lover, Charles Cheyne, afforded her a connection to the upper echelons of society. Though their relationship may have been one of discretion, it afforded her a cherished sense of belonging to a world beyond her own narrow orbit.

In this singular manner, on the day of the fateful accident in Piccadilly, the trifling concerns of her own domestic life were submerged, for the instant, beneath the pressing realities of a more public incident. A light brougham, speeding along the narrow strip of asphalt, was bearing down upon a larger, slower moving bus, its bumper travelling at an alarming velocity. They drove through Lyndhurst, where the twinkling little lights in the shop-windows were being extinguished by envious shutters, and where the shop-keepers paused in their work of extinction to stare amazedly at the passing carriage; not that a carriage was a strange apparition in Lyndhurst, but because the inhabitants had so little to do except stare.

Violet sat looking steadily out of the window, watching every bit of the road. How could she tell when she would see it again--or if ever, save in sad regretful dreams?

They mounted the hill, from whose crest Vixen took one last backwards look at the wide wild land that lay behind them--a look of ineffable love and longing.
