For the rest her brown hair grew low over her broad white forehead, and was topped by a neat little lace cap with ribbons of a violet color. A plain collar and plain cuffs encircled her smooth, round neck, and her plump dimpled hands. Her merino dress, covering but not hiding the charming outline of her bosom, matched the color of the cap-ribbons, and was brightened by a white muslin apron coquettishly trimmed about the pockets, a gift from Lady Lydiard. Blushing and smiling, she let the door fall to behind her, and, shyly approaching the stranger, said to him, in her small, clear voice, “If you please, sir, are you Mr. Hardyman?”

It has often been remarked, that the sins of the father are visited upon the children, even to the third and fourth generation; and though I am far from presuming to arraign the decrees of a just and merciful Providence, I must confess, that in my own case, the consequences of my respected progenitor's peculiar notions of benevolence were painfully exemplified. For whilst his ample fortune, amassed by habits of industry and frugality--virtues he held in especial esteem, as forming the very cornerstone of national prosperity--secured to me all the external advantages that wealth can bestow, it had been gathered at a cost which cast a shadow upon my spirit, and tinged even the bright hues of early youth with a certain melancholy gravity.

My father, imbued with the conviction that the possession of riches brought with it an increased responsibility for their judicious employment--an opinion, I may add, by no means uncommon amongst those who have acquired wealth by their own exertions--was ever foremost in subscribing to public institutions, and in contributing to the support of those charitable undertakings which then, as now, abounded in our land. Yet, I must confess, that his liberality in these particulars, however commendable in the eyes of the world, did not altogether spring from that pure and disinterested philanthropy which should ever be the mainspring of true beneficence. There was, if I may so express myself, a certain air of self-complacency, a sort of unconscious assumption of superiority in his acts of charity, as though he were dispensing, not merely his superfluous wealth, but also a portion of that wisdom and prudence which he deemed himself to possess in an eminent degree. And indeed, it must be acknowledged, that his judgment in matters of business was seldom at fault, and his advice, especially on financial affairs, was eagerly sought after and implicitly relied upon by a large circle of acquaintances. But alas! in the more delicate and intricate concerns of the heart, in those secret springs of human action which defy the cold calculations of worldly wisdom, he was but an indifferent guide; and it was perhaps this very deficiency, this want of sympathy with the finer feelings of our nature, which had gradually estranged him from the generality of mankind, and led him to seek his chief enjoyment in the solitary contemplation of his own wealth and importance.

"You will be fatigued after your long journey, Mr. Ainsworth," said Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, arranging a stray lock of hair that had escaped her elaborate coiffure. "I trust the accommodations at the Swan were to your liking? Though, to be sure, a rural inn cannot boast the comforts of your London residence. Still, one must sometimes endure a minor discomfort for the sake of the country air. My Amelia, when she visits her aunt in Bath--" and Mrs. Featherstonehaugh paused, casting a benevolent eye upon her daughter, who was diligently embroidering a particularly vivid rose upon a tapestry frame--"finds the air most beneficial, though she is quite accustomed to all the modern conveniences, are you not, my love?"

Mr. Ainsworth sighed inwardly, a habit he had cultivated to mask the more cynical observations that frequently occupied his mind. "The Swan, madam, proved... adequate," he replied, choosing his words with care. "Though I confess, I would have welcomed a letter upon my arrival. One feels a certain desolation, you see, when venturing into a new parish, uncertain of one's welcome, and finding no familiar hand to offer greeting. My own mother, bless her soul, is not given to correspondence, and my siblings are, alas, too consumed with their own affairs to spare a thought for their brother languishing in the wilds of Hertfordshire. They have such different temperaments to me. Indeed, they scarcely approve of my ambition to serve the church, deeming it, I suspect, a somewhat... unambitious pursuit for a man of my education." He directed a pointed glance towards Miss Featherstonehaugh, as though she might possess some hidden understanding of the burdens he bore. "Miss Featherstonehaugh, I dare say, is fortunate to have such solicitous family, eager to provide news and assurances."

He cleared his throat, suddenly feeling a warmth creeping into his cheeks. "Indeed," he continued, "it is a rare thing in these times to find such devotion to good works as that which Miss Featherstonehaugh displays. One hears tales of young ladies dedicating themselves to fashionable pursuits, to balls and flirtations, but it is a testament to her character that she chooses instead to visit the sick and comfort the afflicted. Though, to be sure," Mr. Ainsworth added hastily, as if to retract the compliment, "one must be careful not to allow such zeal to overwhelm one's constitution. Too much dedication, however admirable, can lead to... well, to an imbalance of humours, as the old physicians used to say. One must cultivate moderation in all things, even in the pursuit of virtue."

At that moment, Miss Featherstonehaugh rose from her chair, a delicate blush mantling her fair cheeks. "If you will excuse me, Mama," she said, her voice barely above a whisper, "I promised Mrs. Higgins that I would call upon her this afternoon. She has been suffering terribly with the rheumatism, and I fear she lacks proper sustenance. I shall return before tea, I trust." With a curtsey to Mr. Ainsworth, she gathered her shawl and bonnet, and departed, leaving a faint fragrance of lavender in her wake. Mr. Ainsworth watched her go, a peculiar sensation fluttering in his breast, a mixture of admiration and, dare he admit it, a touch of envy. It was not merely her beauty, though she was undeniably fair; it was the unwavering purpose that shone in her eyes, the quiet determination that seemed to emanate from her very being. He wondered, not for the first time, if he possessed such conviction himself.

As Van Berg briskly made his way out of the concert hall, he could feel the weight of disappointment settling upon him like a heavy cloak. The frivolity and shallowness of the girl and her attendant had stirred within him a deep sense of unease, reminding him of the emptiness that often lurked behind the facade of beauty and charm. As he stepped out into the cool night air, the echoes of the symphony still lingered in his mind, haunting him with their fading melodies.

Lost in his thoughts, Van Berg wandered aimlessly through the dimly lit streets, seeking solace in the quiet solitude of the night. His footsteps echoed against the cobblestones, a steady rhythm that seemed to punctuate the emptiness that gnawed at his soul. The events of the evening had left him feeling adrift, as if he were a ship tossed upon a turbulent sea, with no land in sight to anchor him.

As he walked, Van Berg found himself drawn to a secluded park that lay bathed in the soft glow of the moonlight. The shadows danced among the trees, casting strange and eerie shapes upon the ground, adding to the sense of unease that gripped him. He wandered deeper into the park, his footsteps muffled by the thick carpet of fallen leaves that covered the ground, creating a hushed and eerie atmosphere.

Suddenly, he was startled by a soft sound that seemed to emanate from the darkness ahead. His heart quickened in his chest as he strained to catch the source of the sound, his senses heightened by the eerie stillness of the night. As he crept closer, he saw a figure standing beneath a spreading oak tree, their form shrouded in shadow. A sense of foreboding washed over him, his instincts warning him of impending danger.

Van Berg hesitated for a moment, unsure whether to approach or retreat. But something within him urged him forward, drawn by a curiosity that bordered on recklessness. As he drew nearer, the figure stepped into the moonlight, revealing a face that bore a striking resemblance to the girl he had seen at the concert hall. But there was something different in her eyes, a depth and intensity that seemed to pierce through his soul, leaving him transfixed in her gaze.

In the heart of the teeming metropolis, the hum of Bishopsgate Street swelled with an unusual fervour. The cobblestones, slick with a thin sheen of rain, echoed the eager whispers of an expectant crowd, jostling for vantage points to witness the spectacle unfolding. Above the din rises a formidable structure, a grand edifice of stone and glass, where the United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking and Punctual Delivery Company held sway. The authorities, in their blue and white regalia, wove through the throng, bearing lanterns and banners that unfurled in the biting wind, heralding the imminent arrival of the gathering's principals. The air was thick with the aroma of fresh baked goods, mingling with the ever-present fog, a sinister reminder of the crisp autumn air that nipped at the heels of winter.

As the clock atop St. Mary Axe struck twelve with a mournful toll, Sir Matthew Pupker emerged from his carriage, a portly figure attired in a bemedalled coat, his face a ruddy hue that bespoke of health and prosperity. He was flanked by two Members of Parliament, Mr. Berks and Mr. Sanner, notable for their smart black frock coats and the silverhafts of their mudah rounds. The crowd erupted in a chorus of applause, even as the policemen, like a phalanx of husky appliances, formed a barrier to maintain order. Among them, Mr. Bonney, navigating through the crush with an agile grace, winked at his companion, Nicholas Nickleby, a young man of uncertain origins but undeniable charm.

The duo slipped into the grand entrance, greeted by a herald who announced their arrival with a voice that boomed through the cavernous lobby. The room, a hybrid of opulence and function, bore testament to the company's wealth and the indulgence of its executives. The walls were adorned with portraits of its founding fathers, their eyes following the congregants with an almost accusatory gaze. Gas lamps hissed and flickered, casting elongated shadows that danced macabrely upon the polished marble floor. Mr. Bonney, ever the vivacious spark, took the initiative, mounting a stage adorned with a tiered platform and a table of well-polished mahogany. He brandished a gavel, a resplendent piece of ebony inlaid with gold, its head gleaming like a polished daisy. He raised it high, and with a swift, vigorous blow, banged it down, the sound resonating like a thunderclap. The hum of conversation ceased, and all eyes turned to the impromptu platform.

As Sir Matthew ascended the stage, the air was thick with anticipation. He delivered a speech, his voice resonant yet measured, laying out the company's achievements, its relentless pursuit of excellence, and its unwavering commitment to the well-being of its fellow citizens. He gestured expansively, his fingers tracing the air as though painting a picture with words. Mr. Nickleby, standing alongside him, watched as the crowd was engulfed by Sir Matthew's oratory. Yet, amidst the overwhelming support, there was a whispering undercurrent. The discontented murmurs grew louder, untenable, as some attendees expressed their dissatisfaction with the air of pomposity and impenetrable jargon that had descended like a shroud. The murmurs swelled into protests, clamours of dissent echoing through the grand hall. The atmosphere was soon charged with a palpable electricity, much like the Statute of Liberty's torch, flickering precariously in the distance. The police, readying their truncheons like medieval warriors, stared sternly at the mass of humanity before them. In their midst, a lone figure, disguised as Mr. Punch, juggled his comical weapons, anointing the tense atmosphere with a clownish levity. The crowd, initially fueled by indignation, began to chuckle, the tension easing as the absurdity of the situation dawned on them. The stage was set for a dramatic turn, the plot thick with intrigue, and the stage play, the people's bread and butter, was about to be served.

“Did you say you lived in Chelsea?” at length asked Billy, in a stupid self-convicting sort of way.

“No,” replied the fair lady with a smile; “I never mentioned Chelsea.”

“Oh, no; no more you did,” replied Billy, taken aback, especially as the lady led up to no other place.

“Did she like the country?” at length asked he, thinking to try and fix her locality there, if he could not earth her in London.

“Yes, she liked the country, at least out of the season—there was no place like London in the season,” she thought.

Billy thought so too; it was the best place in summer, and the only place in winter.

Well, the lady didn’t know, but if she had to choose either place for a permanency, she would choose London.

This sent the Billy funds up a little. He forgot his intention of following her into the country, and began to expatiate upon the luxuries of London, the capital fish they got, the cod and hoyster sauce (for when excited, he knocked his h’s about a little), the cod and hoyster sauce, the turbot, the mackerel, the mullet, that woodcock of the sea, as he exultingly called it, thinking what a tuck-out he would have in revenge for his country inn abstinence. He then got upon the splendour of his own house in Doughty Street—the most agreeable in London. Its spacious entrance, its elegant stone staircase; his beautiful drawing-room, with its maroon and rose-coloured brocaded satin damask curtains, and rich Tournay carpet, its beautiful chandelier of eighteen lights, and Piccolo pianoforte, and was describing a most magnificent mirror—we don’t know what size, but most beautiful and becoming—when the pace of the vehicle was sensibly felt to relax; and before they had time to speculate on the cause, it had come to a stand-still.

“Stopped,” observed Billy, lowering the window to look out for squalls.

No sooner was the window down, than a head at the door proclaimed mischief. The tête-à-tête was at an end. The guard was going to put Pheasant-feather bonnet inside. Open sesame —W-h-i-s-h. In came the cutting wind—oh dear what a day!

“Rum for a leddy?” asked the guard, raising a great half-frozen, grog-blossomy face out of the blue and white coil of a shawl-cravat in which it was enveloped,—“Git in” continued he, shouldering the leddy up the steps, without waiting for an answer, and in popped Pheasant-feathers; when, slamming-to the door, he cried “right!” to the coachman, and on went the vehicle, leaving the enterer to settle into a seat by its shaking, after the manner of the omnibus cads, who seem to think all they have to do is to see people past the door. As it was, the new-comer alighted upon Billy, who cannoned her off against the opposite door, and then made himself as big as he could, the better to incommode her. Pheasant-feathers, however, having effected an entrance, seemed to regard herself as good as her neighbours, and forthwith proceeded to adjust the window to her liking, despite the eyeing and staring of Miss Willing. Billy was indignant at the nasty peppermint-drop-smelling woman intruding between the wind and his beauty, and inwardly resolved he would dock the guard’s fee for his presumption in putting her there. Miss Willing gathered herself together as if afraid of contamination; and, forgetting her role, declared, after a jolt received in one of her seat-shiftings, that it was just the “smallest coach she had ever been in.” She then began to scrutinise her female companion’s attire.

"I have worked it out at last. You were right about its being less than the other."

"Is Dr. Macpherson not here?"

He turned sharply at the words, a pencil in his hand, surprise on his face. A good face; for its old gay careless look had departed for ever, and the dark blue eyes--darker even than of yore--wore a serious gravity that never left them, a gravity born of remorse. The face was older than the figure, and not in the least like Cyril Thornycroft's; it looked fully its seven-and-twenty years--nay, looked nearer thirty; but all its expression was merged in surprise. No wonder; to see a beautiful girl in blue silk, with blue ribbons in her fair hair, standing there; when he had only expected the professor, in his old threadbare coat and spectacles. It was Robert Hunter.

"I beg your pardon," he said, coming forward. "Can I do anything for you?"

"I thought Dr. Macpherson was here. I came to see him."

Never losing her calm self-possession on any occasion, as so many young ladies do on no occasion at all, Miss Thornycroft stepped up to the side glass cases to examine the curiosities, talking as easily to him as though she had known him all her life. Without being in the least free, there was an openness of manner about her, an utter absence of tricks and affectation, a straightforward independence, rather remarkable in a young lady. For Robert Hunter it possessed a singular charm.

Before the professor came in, who had forgotten himself down in his cellar, where he had gone after a cherished specimen in the frog line; before Mr. Hunter had pointed out to her a quarter of the new acquisitions in the glass cases--animal, vegetable, and mineral--they knew all about each other: that he was Susan Hunter's brother, and that she was Miss Thornycroft of Coastdown. At mention of her name, a brief vision connected with the past floated across Robert Hunter's brain--of a certain summer evening when he was returning to Guild with his poor young wife, and saw the back of a high open carriage bowling away from his sister's gate, which he was told contained Mr. and Miss Thornycroft. Never since that had he heard the name or thought of the people.

"Do you know, when I came into the room just now, and you were standing with your back to me, I nearly took you for one of my brothers. At the back you are just like him."

Robert Hunter smiled slightly. "And not in the face?"

"Not at all--except, perhaps, a little in the forehead. Cyril has hazel eyes and small features. The hair is exactly like his, the same colour, and grows just as his does in front, leaving the forehead square. If you were to hide your face, showing only the top of the forehead and the hair, I should say you were Cyril."

The professor appeared, and they went into the more habitable part of the house. Robert had not seen his sister since she was a little girl; he had not seen Anna since they parted at Guild. It was altogether an acceptable meeting; but he looked at Anna's face somewhat anxiously.

"Have you been working very much, Anna?" he took occasion to ask, drawing her for a moment aside.

"I am always working very hard," she answered, with her sweet smile of patient endurance. "There is a great deal to be done in schools, you know; but I am well off at Miss Jupp's compared to what I was at the other place. They are very kind to me."

"You have a look upon you as if you felt tired always. It is a curious impression to draw though, perhaps, considering I have seen you but for ten minutes."

"I do feel tired nearly always," acknowledged Anna. "The Miss Jupps think London does not agree with me. I am going to Coastdown for a change for the holidays; I shall get better there."

Of these young women, one had an olive complexion, with the red blood mantling under it, and black hair, and glorious black eyebrows.

The other was fair, with a massive but shapely throat, as white as milk; glossy brown hair, the loose threads of which glittered like gold, and a blue eye, which, being contrasted with dark eyebrows and lashes, took the luminous effect peculiar to that rare beauty.

Their short petticoats revealed a neat ankle, and a leg with a noble swell; for Nature, when she is in earnest, builds beauty on the ideas of ancient sculptors and poets, not of modern poetasters, who, with their airy-like sylphs and their smoke-like verses, fight for want of flesh in woman and want of fact in poetry as parallel beauties.

They are, my lads.--Continuez!

These women had a grand corporeal trait; they had never known a corset! so they were straight as javelins; they could lift their hands above their heads!--actually! Their supple persons moved as Nature intended; every gesture was ease, grace and freedom.

What with their own radiance, and the snowy cleanliness and brightness of their costume, they came like meteors into the apartment.

Lord Ipsden, rising gently from his seat, with the same quiet politeness with which he would have received two princes of the blood, said, “How do you do?” and smiled a welcome.

“Fine! hoow's yoursel?” answered the dark lass, whose name was Jean Carnie, and whose voice was not so sweet as her face.

“What'n lord are ye?” continued she; “are you a juke? I wad like fine to hae a crack wi' a juke.”

Saunders, who knew himself the cause of this question, replied, sotto voce, “His lordship is a viscount.”

“I didna ken't,” was Jean's remark. “But it has a bonny soond.”

“What mair would ye hae?” said the fair beauty, whose name was Christie Johnstone. Then, appealing to his lordship as the likeliest to know, she added, “Nobeelity is jist a soond itsel, I'm tauld.”

The viscount, finding himself expected to say something on a topic he had not attended much to, answered dryly: “We must ask the republicans, they are the people that give their minds to such subjects.”

“And yon man,” asked Jean Carnie, “is he a lord, too?”

“I am his lordship's servant,” replied Saunders, gravely, not without a secret misgiving whether fate had been just.

“Na!” replied she, not to be imposed upon, “ye are statelier and prooder than this ane.”

“I will explain,” said his master. “Saunders knows his value; a servant like Saunders is rarer than an idle viscount.”

“My lord, my lord!” remonstrated Saunders, with a shocked and most disclamatory tone. “Rather!” was his inward reflection.

“Jean,” said Christie, “ye hae muckle to laern. Are ye for herrin' the day, vile count?”

“No! are you for this sort of thing?”

At this, Saunders, with a world of empressement, offered the Carnie some cake that was on the table.

She took a piece, instantly spat it out into her hand, and with more energy than delicacy flung it into the fire.

“Augh!” cried she, “just a sugar and saut butter thegither; buy nae mair at yon shoep, vile count.”

“Try this, out of Nature's shop,” laughed their entertainer; and he offered them, himself, some peaches and things.

“Hech! a medi--cine!” said Christie.

“Nature, my lad,” said Miss Carnie, making her ivory teeth meet in their first nectarine, “I didna ken whaur ye stoep, but ye beat the other confectioners, that div ye.”

The fair lass, who had watched the viscount all this time as demurely as a cat cream, now approached him.

This young woman was the thinker; her voice was also rich, full, and melodious, and her manner very engaging; it was half advancing, half retiring, not easy to resist or to describe.

It was a period, ere the inexorable march of time had softened the harsh contours of remembrance, that Ireland stood witness to a tumultuous dance of upheaval and aspiration. Upon this canvas of transition, my tale unfolds, lingering, as it must, upon the canvas of a land whose spirit defies the desolation which threatens its very existence.

For amidst the rugged west, where Oughterard's borders meet the vast expanse of untamed nature, lay an area whose beauty was veiled beneath layers of neglect and sorrow. A desolation so profound it seemed the very earth itself had turned its back upon its own creation. But as one traverses the terrain, gradually, the land unveils her charms—her bosom swells with verdant grasslands, her eyes reveal serene lakes, her embrace enfolds the shadow of ancient forests.

Yet, amidst this patchwork of renewal, there rises the imposing silhouette of Cro' Martin Castle, a monument to the fortitude of a people who, through centuries of trial, have inscribed their legacy upon its weathered stones. A structure of such antiquity that its very existence stands as a testament to the endurance of a lineage, the Martins, whose story, intertwined with the fate of Ireland itself, now commands our attention.

The castle, with its blend of architectural styles, tells a tale of opulence and modesty in equal measure. Within its walls, one finds not only the remnants of age but also a sanctuary of comfort and elegance that rivals any palatial grandeur of the continent. Yet, it stands aloof, overlooking the landscape much like the Martins themselves—a family deeply rooted in their homeland, observing the world with a cautious eye and a heart full of hope.

Upon this backdrop, my narrative must venture forth, for the story of the Martins is not merely a chronicle of generations but a mirror reflecting the essence of Ireland's enduring spirit. As I proceed, I must remind myself of the task at hand—to weave together a tapestry of tales that speaks not only of the family's trials but also of their triumphs, their resilience, and their unwavering commitment to their homeland.

So it is that, with a heart heavy with the weight of this responsibility, I continue, ever mindful of the fair land that has borne witness to so much. For Ireland, in her temporal plight, has shown a strength that outmatches her afflictions, a will that remains undaunted despite the odds. And in the annals of time, it is my fervent hope that her future will be one of prosperity, where her sons and daughters may walk in peace, under skies unmarred by strife.

Thus, we journey with the Martins through moments of despair and elation, each event echoing the broader narrative of a nation's reclamation of its rightful place in the sun. And as the pages turn, the labyrinth of the past begins to reveal the contours of a future where Ireland blooms, not in spite of her history, but because of it—a beacon of hope and resilience to all who gaze upon her shores.

MATHERS.--Eight pieces of shortbread, five slabs of toffee, seven sausage-rolls. (The rolls were cut in half to be eaten first thing before they went bad. But Bradwell said Mathers had made the selection of a fool, and so Mathers was rather vexed with Bradwell.)

NEWNES.--Ten loaves (five brown), one packet of beef tabloids. (Trelawny congratulated Newnes.)

MCINNES.--A lot of spring onions and lettuces, costing one-and-sixpence. (McInnes had been reading a book about chaps getting scurvy on a raft, and he thought a siege would be just the place for scurvy, so he bought all green stuff; and Bradwell said it was good.)

CORKEY MINIMUS.--Three pounds of mixed sweets. (Bradwell smacked his head when he heard what Corkey minimus had got; but Trelawny pointed out that a few sweets served out from time to time might distract the mind.)

DERBYSHIRE.--A pigeon-pie and thirteen currant buns with saffron in them.

FORREST.--Four pots Bovril, one bottle cider. (Bovril can be taken on bread like treacle, and once saved the lives of several shipwrecked sailors.)

WATSON MINOR.--Two pounds dog-biscuits, one pound dried figs, one box of dates. (Asked why he took dog-biscuits, he explained it was because he had seen an advertisement about the goodness of them. It said they had dried buffalo meat in them, which was a thing you could live for an immense duration of time on. Trelawny said that was pretty fair sense for a kid.)

All this splendid food was brought out of boxes where it had been hidden and placed in the hands of Bradwell; and that night he sat up with a candle and drew out bills of fare and made calculations. We were rather surprised in the morning to hear the rations would not last more than a fortnight, but Trelawny said the siege must be over long before that. Nobody slept much, and many had dressed before the first bell rang. When the second bell rang Trelawny and Bradwell went to the door to listen.

Presently Thompson, of all people, came up and tried to get in and couldn’t. He shook the door, then saw the envelope addressed to the Doctor, and said:

“What’s the meaning of this, you fellows? Let me in at once!”

But nobody answered. Then he cleared off. At 8.30 the string was lowered from the window, and Trelawny went and stood by it to pull up any letter that might be fastened to it. But none was. Some of the chaps were prowling about outside looking at the Wing Dormitory, but Trelawny wouldn’t let anybody go to the windows except himself.

Then, as nothing happened, we had breakfast. McInnes and Forrest were told off to help Bradwell, and each chap’s rations were put on his bed after he had made it. We all got the same except Gideon--a slice of bread, two sardines, half one of Mathers’s sausage-rolls, and half a tumbler of water. So we began at once to see what a jolly serious thing a siege is. And Gideon saw it more than we did, because he had no sardines and no sausage-roll. He offered Trelawny money for a little more food, but Trelawny said he shouldn’t have as much as one mixed sweet, though he might pay gold for it. He said, “You will have barely enough to keep you alive.” And Gideon turned awfully white when he heard it.

Breakfast didn’t take more than about five minutes, then there was a tremendous knocking at the iron door, and Bradwell said the trouble had begun, but Trelawny said it was the summons to a parley. Anyway, we heard the Doctor’s voice, and it wasn’t much of a parley, strictly speaking, because he spoke first, and merely gave us two minutes to be in our places down-stairs.

Suddenly a young man riding a valuable horse came out from behind the clump of poplars and flowering briar-rose.

“It is an Englishman,” remarked the Colonel.

“Lord bless you, yes, General,” said the post-boy; “he belongs to the race of fellows who have a mind to gobble up France, they say.”

The stranger was one of the foreigners traveling in France at the time when Napoleon detained all British subjects within the limits of the Empire, by way of reprisals for the violation of the Treaty of Amiens, an outrage of international law perpetrated by the Court of St. James. These prisoners, compelled to submit to the Emperor’s pleasure, were not all suffered to remain in the houses where they were arrested, nor yet in the places of residence which at first they were permitted to choose. Most of the English colony in Touraine had been transplanted thither from different places where their presence was supposed to be inimical to the interests of the Continental Policy.

The young man, who was taking the tedium of the early morning hours on horseback, was one of these victims of bureaucratic tyranny. Two years previously, a sudden order from the Foreign Office had dragged him from Montpellier, whither he had gone on account of consumptive tendencies. He glanced at the Comte d’Aiglemont, saw that he was a military man, and deliberately looked away, turning his head somewhat abruptly towards the meadows by the Cise.

“The English are all as insolent as if the globe belonged to them,” muttered the Colonel. “Luckily, Soult will give them a thrashing directly.”

The prisoner gave a glance to the caleche as he rode by. Brief though that glance was, he had yet time to notice the sad expression which lent an indefinable charm to the Countess’ pensive face. Many men are deeply moved by the mere semblance of suffering in a woman; they take the look of pain for a sign of constancy or of love. Julie herself was so much absorbed in the contemplation of the opposite cushion that she saw neither the horse nor the rider. The damaged trace meanwhile had been quickly and strongly repaired; the Count stepped into his place again; and the post-boy, doing his best to make up for lost time, drove the carriage rapidly along the embankment. On they drove under the overhanging cliffs, with their picturesque vine-dressers’ huts and stores of wine maturing in their dark sides, till in the distance uprose the spire of the famous Abbey of Marmoutiers, the retreat of St. Martin.

“What can that diaphanous milord want with us?” exclaimed the Colonel, turning to assure himself that the horseman who had followed them from the bridge was the young Englishman.

After all, the stranger committed no breach of good manners by riding along on the footway, and Colonel d’Aiglemont was fain to lie back in his corner after sending a scowl in the Englishman’s direction. But in spite of his hostile instincts, he could not help noticing the beauty of the animal and the graceful horsemanship of the rider. The young man’s face was of that pale, fair-complexioned, insular type, which is almost girlish in the softness and delicacy of its color and texture. He was tall, thin, and fair-haired, dressed with the extreme and elaborate neatness characteristic of a man of fashion in prudish England. Any one might have thought that bashfulness rather than pleasure at the sight of the Countess had called up that flush into his face. Once only Julie raised her eyes and looked at the stranger, and then only because she was in a manner compelled to do so, for her husband called upon her to admire the action of the thoroughbred. It so happened that their glances clashed; and the shy Englishman, instead of riding abreast of the carriage, fell behind on this, and followed them at a distance of a few paces.

High noon at Talbot's Cross-roads, with the mercury standing at ninety-eight in the shade--though there was not much shade worth mentioning in the immediate vicinity of the Cross-roads post-office, about which, upon the occasion referred to, the few human beings within sight and sound were congregated. There were trees enough a few hundred yards away, but the post-office stood boldly and unflinchingly in the blazing sun. The roads crossing each other stretched themselves as far as the eye could follow them, the red clay transformed into red dust which even an ordinarily lively imagination might have fancied was red hot. The shrill, rattling cry of the grasshoppers, hidden in the long yellow sedge-grass and drouth-smitten corn, pierced the stillness now and then with a suddenness startling each time it broke forth, because the interval between each of the pipings was given by the hearers to drowsiness or heated unconscious naps.

In such napping and drowsiness the present occupants of the post-office were indulging. Upon two empty goods boxes two men in copperas-coloured jean garments reclined in easy attitudes, their hats tilted over their eyes, while several others balanced their split-seated chairs against the house or the post-porch and dozed.

Inside the store the postmaster and proprietor tilted his chair against the counter and dozed also, though fitfully, and with occasional restless changes of position and smothered maledictions against the heat. He was scarcely the build of man to sleep comfortably at high noon in midsummer. His huge, heavy body was rather too much for him at any time, but during the hot weather he succumbed beneath the weight of his own flesh. Hamlin County knew him as "Big Tom D'Willerby," and, indeed, rather prided itself upon him as a creditable possession. It noted any increase in his weight, repeated his jokes, and bore itself patiently under his satire. His indolence it regarded with leniency not entirely untinged with secret exultation.

"The derndest, laziest critter," his acquaintances would remark to each other; "the derndest I do reckon that ever the Lord made. Nigh unto three hundred he weighs, and never done a lick o' work in his life. Not one! Lord, no! Tom D'Willerby work? I guess not. He gits on fine without any o' that in his'n. Work ain't his kind. It's a pleasin' sight to see him lyin' round thar to the post-office an' the boys a-waitin' on to him, doin' his tradin' for him, an' sortin' the mail when it comes in. They're ready enough to do it jest to hear him gas."

And so they were. About eight years before the time the present story commences, he had appeared upon the scene apparently having no object in view but to make himself as comfortable as possible. He took up his quarters at one of the farm-houses among the mountains, paid his hostess regularly for the simple accommodations she could afford him, and, before three months passed, had established his reputation and, without making the slightest apparent effort, had gathered about him a large circle of friends and admirers.

"His name's D'Willerby," Mrs. Pike would drawl when questioned about him, "an' he's kin to them D'Willerbys that's sich big bugs down to D'Lileville. I guess they ain't much friendly, though. He don't seem to like to have nothin' much to say about 'em. Seems like he has money a-plenty to carry him along, an' he talks some o' settin' up a store somewhars."

In the course of a month or so he carried out the plan, selecting Talbot's Cross-roads as the site for the store in question. He engaged hands to erect a frame building, collected by the assistance of some mysterious agency a heterogeneous stock consisting of calicoes, tinware, coffee, sugar, tobacco, and various waif and stray commodities, and, having done so, took his seat on the porch one morning and announced the establishment open.

In the respite following his harrowing escape, Gilead P. Beck found solace in contemplation. The campfire crackled, casting dancing shadows on the log walls of Patrick's Camp, where he and his savior, the young man named Hector, tended to their wounds and the dying embers of chaos. The air was filled with an unusual tension, a silent arousal that seemed to weigh heavily upon the very trunks of the ancient, gnarled pines.

Beck stood, grimacing as he leaned forward to add another log to the fire. The snap of dry kindling echoed through the quiet camp like a distant gunshot. He felt the weight of his thoughts pressing down upon him, a palpable force that threatened to overwhelm him. He had seen death today, had stared it in the eye and emerged unscathed, and here he stood, alive and breathing. It was a rude awakening, a stark reminder of the fleeting nature of life in these wild and untamed lands.

"Yer too good a shot, Hector," Beck mused, turning to face the young man, his eyes reflecting the flickering light. "I reckon we'd be suited to a partnership, if you're aimin' to stick around these parts."

Hector looked up from his bandaged arm, a wry smile gracing his lips. "I reckon I am, Gilead. These here woods hold secrets, don't they? And secrets are worth more than gold, if you know what to look for."

Beck nodded, his eyes scanning the shadows that receded with each snap of fire. He had seen the gold dust, the remnants of dreams and ambitions that lay scattered like petals at the feet of pioneers. He had seen the futility of their efforts, the harsh reality that would see so many of these men, these families, die poor despite their labor. It was a harsh lesson, one he had learned the hard way.

"The world's changin', Hector," Beck said, his voice barely above a whisper. "Patrick's Camp is a shadow of its former self. I've heard tell that Empire City is on the rise, that it'll be comin' up to eclipse this here camp in no time."

Hector leaned back, his eyes narrowing as he considered this revelation. "Empire City, eh? I've heard speak of it. The riches, the progress, the chance for something better. It's a siren, Beck, callin' out to those who would listen."

Beck looked away, his gaze drifting towards the distant horizon. "It's a mirage, Hector. A promise held out just beyond the last bend of the trail, never to be caught. But we can dream, can't we? We can dream of a better life, of honor and respect."

The conversation drifted like the smoke from the dying fire, each word hanging heavy in the air. Beck found his mind wandering back to the bear, to Grisly's lifeless form lying in the woods. He still felt a twinge of respect for the creature, a killer that had met its match today. Yet he mourned for his rifle, that old companion that had seen him through thick and thin, that had met its end at the bear's cruel paws.

Hector must have sensed his discomfort, for he shifted his gaze towards the trees where the bear's body lay. "We'll return it to the woods, Beck. Let it meat the earth, let it fertilize the ground that gave birth to it."

Beck nodded, a sudden chill gripping him. "It's a strange world, Hector. A world where a man's fate can be sealed by a single, foolish decision. I was reckless, Hector. I took the risk without thought, without understanding the danger that lay in wait."

Hector sighed, his eyes reflecting the fire's dance. "We all take risks, Beck. We all dance with danger. It's in our blood, in our very bones. We're pioneers, after all. It's what we do."

Beck laughed softly, a bitter sound, "Yes, we are. Pioneers, searching for fortune, for a better life. But the woods are vast, the wilderness unforgiving. And some of us, many, pay the price before the dream is fulfilled."

The conversation lapsed into silence, a heavy weight hanging in the air. Beck's mind wandered back to the old days, to the glory of Patrick's Camp in its heyday. Gold dust had shone bright, dreams had danced in the eyes of men and women alike. The Trade had been a symphony of pleasure and pain, of hope and despair. It was a world long past, a world that Beck knew was unforgiving.

Yet here he was, standing at the threshold of a new age, a new dawn. Empire City loomed, a beacon of hope or a grim specter, Beck knew not. But he knew one thing for certain - change was coming. The wind whispered secrets, the trees sighed with ancient wisdom, and the fire burned with the souls of those who had come before.

Beck turned away from Hector, his gaze fixed on the dark expanse of night. The world was a vast and unyielding force, a tapestry woven with the threads of dreams and nightmares.

The morning light filtered through the lace curtains, casting a soft glow on the room where Mrs. Caldwell lay, exhausted but content. She cradled her newborn daughter in her arms, marveling at the miracle of life that had taken place in the darkness of the night. Beth, they had decided to call her, a name that felt right to both parents in the end.

As she gazed down at the delicate features of her child, Mrs. Caldwell's heart swelled with a love so fierce and powerful that it almost took her breath away. Despite the pain and uncertainty of the past few hours, she could not help but feel a deep sense of gratitude for the new life that now lay in her arms. Everything seemed to fade away in that moment, leaving only the warmth of her daughter's tiny body against her own.

Outside, the summer sun had begun to rise, casting a golden light over the rooftops of the houses opposite. The world was waking up to a new day, but for Mrs. Caldwell, it felt as though time had stood still. She was lost in the moment, caught between the past and the future, with only the present and the fragile bond between mother and child to guide her.

In the distance, she could hear the sound of church bells ringing, calling the faithful to morning prayer. The familiar sound brought a sense of peace to her troubled mind, a reminder that amidst all the chaos and uncertainty of life, there was still a spark of hope and goodness to hold onto. She closed her eyes, letting the sound wash over her like a balm, soothing her weary soul and filling her with a renewed sense of purpose and determination.

He approached the Angel with a nervous cough.

"Those," said the Vicar, "were ladies."

"How grotesque," said the Angel, smiling and smelling the sweet briar. "And such quaint shapes!"

"Possibly," said the Vicar. "Did you, ahem, notice how they behaved?"

"They went away. Seemed, indeed, to run away. Frightened? I, of course, was frightened at things without wings. I hope---- they were not frightened at my wings?"

"At your appearance generally," said the Vicar, glancing involuntarily at the pink feet.

"Dear me! It never occurred to me. I suppose I seemed as odd to them as you did to me." He glanced down. "And my feet. You have hoofs like a hippogriff."

"Boots," corrected the Vicar.

"Boots, you call them! But anyhow, I am sorry I alarmed----"

"You see," said the Vicar, stroking his chin, "our ladies, ahem, have peculiar views--rather inartistic views--about, ahem, clothing. Dressed as you are, I am afraid, I am really afraid that--beautiful as your costume certainly is--you will find yourself somewhat, ahem, somewhat isolated in society. We have a little proverb, 'When in Rome, ahem, one must do as the Romans do.' I can assure you that, assuming you are desirous to, ahem, associate with us--during your involuntary stay----"

The Angel retreated a step or so as the Vicar came nearer and nearer in his attempt to be diplomatic and confidential. The beautiful face grew perplexed. "I don't quite understand. Why do you keep making these noises in your throat? Is it Die or Eat, or any of those...."

"As your host," interrupted the Vicar, and stopped.

"As my host," said the Angel.

"Would you object, pending more permanent arrangements, to invest yourself, ahem, in a suit, an entirely new suit I may say, like this I have on?"

"Oh!" said the Angel. He retreated so as to take in the Vicar from top to toe. "Wear clothes like yours!" he said. He was puzzled but amused. His eyes grew round and bright, his mouth puckered at the corners.

"Delightful!" he said, clapping his hands together. "What a mad, quaint dream this is! Where are they?" He caught at the neck of the saffron robe.

"Indoors!" said the Vicar. "This way. We will change--indoors!"

So the Angel was invested in a pair of nether garments of the Vicar's, a shirt, ripped down the back (to accommodate the wings), socks, shoes--the Vicar's dress shoes--collar, tie, and light overcoat. But putting on the latter was painful, and reminded the Vicar that the bandaging was temporary. "I will ring for tea at once, and send Grummet down for Crump," said the Vicar. "And dinner shall be earlier." While the Vicar shouted his orders on the landing rails, the Angel surveyed himself in the cheval glass with immense delight. If he was a stranger to pain, he was evidently no stranger--thanks perhaps to dreaming--to the pleasure of incongruity.

They had tea in the drawing-room. The Angel sat on the music stool (music stool because of his wings). At first he wanted to lie on the hearthrug. He looked much less radiant in the Vicar's clothes, than he had done upon the moor when dressed in saffron. His face shone still, the colour of his hair and cheeks was strangely bright, and there was a superhuman light in his eyes, but his wings under the overcoat gave him the appearance of a hunchback. The garments, indeed, made quite a terrestrial thing of him, the trousers were puckered transversely, and the shoes a size or so too large.

He was charmingly affable and quite ignorant of the most elementary facts of civilization. Eating came without much difficulty, and the Vicar had an entertaining time teaching him how to take tea. "What a mess it is! What a dear grotesque ugly world you live in!" said the Angel. "Fancy stuffing things into your mouth! We use our mouths just to talk and sing with. Our world, you know, is almost incurably beautiful. We get so very little ugliness, that I find all this ... delightful."

The morning sun filtered through the lattice blinds of the breakfast parlour at Bexley, casting a soft, golden hue upon the polished mahogany table. The air was redolent with the scent of fresh bread and the faint aroma of coffee, though the latter was a luxury that had come to Bexley only in recent years. Miss Anna Vere, sitting at her ease in a gracefully carved chair, looked absently out of the window, her thoughts wandering to the days when such refinements were unknown, and the household had contented itself with simpler pleasures.

Beside her, Gerald Vere leaned back in his chair, his plate barely touched, though his eyes were bright with the vigour of a man who had weathered many a storm and emerged all the wiser for it. He turned his head slightly, his gaze meeting Anna’s, and a knowing smile played upon his lips. “You are far away, my dear,” he said, his voice a deep, resonant baritone, “but I know the path of your thoughts.”

Anna gave a little start, as though roused from a daydream, and her eyes met his with a playful reproach. “Guilty, Gerald,” she replied, her tone light and airy, “I was but remembering the days when this house was seldom stirred save by the comings and goings of the farmhands, and now behold us sitting here like landed gentry, with coffee to_our_ cups.”

“And what is amiss in that?” Gerald inquired, folding his arms across his chest. “Is not prosperity a blessing? Or do you pine for the days when our table was bare, and our walls hung with nothing but the memories of hard work?”

Anna laughed, a sound as clear as the ringing of a bell, and shook her head. “Prosperity is no ill, Gerald, but it has its own burdens. The simplicity of our past was a comfort, a reassurance that life, however toilsome, was true and real. Now, with wealth and ease, one begins to wonder if the soul itself does not grow restless.”

Gerald considered this for a moment, his brow furrowing slightly. “True enough,” he murmured, “but restlessness is the lot of man, and wealth or want, it will always find a way to make its presence known.”

At that moment, the door to the parlour opened with a gentle creak, and Sibby entered, her usual bustling manner tempered by the years. She carried a tray laden with fresh bread and butter, and behind her, with a step that was still surprisingly spry for his years, came Mr. Clement vere, his face alight with a childlike eagerness that belied his failing health.

“Ah, Sibby!” Lance cried, rising from his seat with a warmth that was as familiar as the morning sun. “You see your baby has begun to run alone.”

“Clem, Clem!” Anna exclaimed, her voice filled with concern. “You should be abed. It is too early for you to be up.”

“Nonsense, Anna,” Gerald interjected, though there was a soft edge to his tone that belied his words. “Let the boy enjoy his moment. He has earned it.”

Clement smiled, a weak but genuine smile, and took a seat at the table, his hands trembling slightly as he reached for a slice of bread. “It is good to be up,” he said, his voice a thread of sound, barely audible. “It is good to see you all.”

Lance, ever the sentinel, took a seat beside his brother, his arm resting lightly upon Clem’s shoulder. “You rest, old friend,” he said softly. “We will attend to you.”

The conversation turned to lighter matters, though the spectre of Clem’s frailty hung in the air like the faintest of mists. Lance sang a simple melody, his voice a deep, rich baritone that filled the room with a warmth that was both nostalgic and comforting. It was a song from their youth, one that had been sung around the fire on winter nights, and as Lance’s voice rose and fell, the others listened in silence, their hearts stirred by the memories it evoked.

When the song had ended, Clem leaned back in his chair, his eyes closed, a faint smile upon his lips. “That was good,” he murmured. “That was very good.”

Lance rose, his movements deliberate and careful, and took his brother’s arm. “Come,” he said. “It is time for you to rest.”

Clem made no protest, his strength evidently spent, and with Lance’s steadying arm about him, he rose slowly, his thin frame trembling slightly. Together, they moved towards the door, their figures a poignant study in contrasts: the robust, vigorous Lance; the frail, declining Clem.

As they left the room, Sibby lingered a moment longer, her eyes lingering upon the departing figures. “The long boy did it all by himself,” she muttered, though whether to herself or to the others, none could say.

Gerald and Anna exchanged a knowing glance, their minds turning to the changes that had come to Bexley, and to the enduring truth that some things, no matter how much the world might change, remained forever constant.

As Mr. Brimmington settled into his new abode, he found himself surrounded by an eerie silence that seemed to seep through the very walls of the old farmhouse. The creaking floorboards and howling wind outside served as a constant reminder of his solitude in this remote corner of the world. Yet, despite the initial sense of disappointment that had washed over him upon his arrival, he couldn't deny the strange allure that the desolate landscape held for him.

Venturing out into the overgrown garden, Mr. Brimmington discovered a neglected maze of twisted paths and wild vegetation that seemed to have a life of its own. As he wandered through the tangled undergrowth, he couldn't shake the feeling that there was something lurking just beyond his line of sight, watching his every move with unseen eyes. The rustling of the leaves and distant cry of a lone bird only added to the eerie atmosphere that enveloped the farm.

Back inside the house, Mr. Brimmington found himself drawn to a winding staircase that led up to a dusty attic filled with forgotten relics of the past. As he rummaged through old trunks and yellowed manuscripts, he uncovered a hidden treasure trove of historical documents and artifacts that piqued his curiosity. The history of the farmhouse seemed to come alive before his very eyes, each piece telling a story of its own.

Intrigued by the mysterious past of his new home, Mr. Brimmington delved deeper into the archives, piecing together the fragments of information he gathered along the way. From faded photographs to cryptic diaries, he uncovered a tale of love, loss, and betrayal that had unfolded within the walls of the farmhouse centuries ago. As he immersed himself in the rich tapestry of history that surrounded him, Mr. Brimmington felt a newfound sense of purpose wash over him.

With each passing day, the farmhouse revealed more of its secrets to Mr. Brimmington, drawing him further into its enigmatic embrace. The once desolate surroundings now felt alive with the whispers of ancient spirits, guiding him on a journey of discovery that would forever change the course of his life. And as he continued to unravel the mysteries of the past, Mr. Brimmington realized that his decision to purchase the isolated farm-house sight unseen was perhaps the best choice he had ever made.

The air in Crimsworth Hall, though thick with the scent of beeswax and old damask, did little to sweeten my humor. Indeed, the very grandeur of the place, its silent testament to generations of Crimsworths who had lived and died within its stone embrace, seemed only to amplify the gnawing discontent that had taken root in my breast. I had hoped, upon discovering those portraits of my parents, to feel a sense of belonging, a connection to this place that was, by right of birth, partially mine. Instead, I felt like an interloper, a distant cousin who had arrived uninvited to a family gathering, dressed in clothes too plain and bearing gifts too meager.

My aunt, Miss Crimsworth, remained an enigma. She treated me with a politeness so studied, so meticulously measured, that it felt more like a performance than genuine affection. Her questions were precise and carefully chosen, her answers, when she deigned to offer them, were similarly guarded. I suspected she knew far more about my circumstances, about my past, than she let on, and this suspicion only deepened the sense of unease that pervaded my days. The servants, too, were a source of perpetual observation, their glances darting and furtive, their whispers hushed and conspiratorial. I was, without a doubt, an object of intense scrutiny, a puzzle they were all attempting to solve.

Yesterday, I had attempted to break through the icy reserve that surrounded my aunt, to engage her in a more personal conversation. I had spoken of my father, of his kindness and his untimely death, hoping to evoke some shared memory, some flicker of familial warmth. But her response was chillingly detached. She acknowledged my father’s existence, of course, but spoke of him as one might speak of a distant acquaintance, with a cool, impersonal objectivity that bordered on indifference. I was left with the distinct impression that she regarded my father’s choice to marry outside the Crimsworth family, to embrace a life beyond the confines of Crimsworth Hall, as a betrayal, a stain upon the family name.

And then there was the matter of the letter. I had written to Charles, my oldest and dearest friend, detailing my arrival at Crimsworth Hall, my encounters with my aunt and cousin, my impressions of the surrounding landscape. I had poured out my heart to him, as I had done a hundred times before, seeking his counsel, his reassurance, his unwavering support. But days had turned into weeks, and still no reply. I could only assume, with a sinking heart, that he was still ensconced in his new colonial post, the distance and demands of his new station having already begun to erode the bonds of our long-standing friendship.

I spent much of my time wandering the grounds of Crimsworth Hall, seeking solace in the solitude of the surrounding woods. The ancient trees, their gnarled branches reaching skyward like supplicating arms, seemed to offer a silent understanding, a comforting presence in the midst of my growing isolation. I would sit for hours beneath their leafy canopy, lost in thought, attempting to make sense of my present circumstances, to chart a course for my future.

The town of X-, with its belching chimneys and grimy streets, held little appeal. The factories, with their ceaseless din and suffocating atmosphere, were a constant reminder of the trade I had so reluctantly embraced. I felt suffocated by the predictability of my existence, by the relentless pursuit of profit that seemed to be the sole driving force behind the lives of those around me.

I yearned for something more, something beyond the accumulation of wealth, something that would ignite my passion and give purpose to my days. Perhaps, I thought, I could dedicate myself to some noble cause, some work of public benefit that would alleviate the suffering of others. Or perhaps I could devote myself to the pursuit of knowledge, to the study of literature and philosophy, to the exploration of the human condition.

Such thoughts occupied my mind as I strolled through the gardens late one afternoon, the air fragrant with the scent of roses and honeysuckle. I paused before a sundial, its bronze face tarnished with age, and watched as the shadow slowly crept across its surface. Time, I reflected, was a precious commodity, and I could not afford to waste it on idle discontent. I must find a way to make my mark upon the world, to leave behind something of lasting value.

The drawing-room of the Jareds was a place where the hum of conversation often took on the air of a well-choreographed dance, each person stepping in perfectly timed measure with the next. On this particular afternoon, the atmosphere was particularly vibrant, as the ladies gathered with an eagerness that hinted at the approach of some small excitement. Mrs. Franklin, with her usual vivacity, sat at the piano, her fingers idly playing a tune that seemed to echo the restless energy of the room. Dolly, her youngest daughter, perched on a nearby chair, listened with a mischievous glint in her eye, while Ruth, ever the orchestrator of affairs, moved about the room with purposeful strides, arranging parcels and adjusting draperies as though preparing for a ball.

"Mother," Dolly began, her voice tinged with playful impudence, "do you truly believe that Genevieve is but nineteen? She seems to me as ancient as Methuselah!"

Mrs. Franklin chuckled, her eyes crinkling with amusement. "Dear, Genevieve is nineteen in years, but in spirit, she is closer to Methuselah's age. However, you must remember, it is society's wont to inflate the years of some and deflate the years of others, depending on who is holding the scissors."

Ruth, overhearing this, paused in her ministrations and turned with a knowing smile. "Ah, but Genevieve is never older than the age of her last beau," she quipped, earning herself a playful swat from Mrs. Franklin.

The mention of beaus brought a flush to Dolly's cheeks, and for a moment, the room seemed to hold its breath. But before the silence could grow awkward, Ruth's sharp ears caught the sound of laughter from the hall. "They come!" she announced, her tone brimming with anticipation. "And, mark my words, this will be an event worth remembering."

The door swung open, and in stepped Mrs. Jared, her bejeweled fan clutched tightly in hand, followed closely by Miss Billy, her prim demeanor contrasting sharply with the lively chatter already swirling in the room. Miss Billy's entrance was marked by a faint sniff of disapproval, as though she had stepped into a room of ill repute rather than a gathering of her closest friends.

"Mrs. Jared," Ruth greeted, her voice sweet as honey, "how I longed for your arrival! I have news that would set even your most jaded heart abuzz."

Mrs. Jared raised an eyebrow, clearly intrigued. "Indeed? Do tell, and spare me no detail."

Ruth leaned forward conspiratorially, her eyes twinkling with mischief. "There is to be a fancy-dress procession at the rink this very evening, all in aid of the Mission. The ladies are to be queens and princesses, and the gentlemen—why, they are to be everything from shepherds to sea captains!"

Miss Billy's lips tightened into a thin line, and she sniffed again, louder this time. "A fine use of one's time, I must say. What next? Will the reverend gentlemen of the town take to the ice in their cassocks?"

Ruth's laughter rang out, rich and infectious. "Why, Miss Billy, I believe I have struck a chord! For indeed, the reverend gentlemen are not the only ones taking to the ice in costumes. Mr. Hill, the former insurance agent turned clergyman, is to appear as a bishop in full regalia—though rumor has it, he will be more at home on the ice than in the pulpit."

Miss Billy's cheeks flushed with indignation. "Mr. Hill! That hoyden! To dress as a bishop—goodness gracious! What will the congregation think when they see him gliding about like a peacock in someone else's feathers?"

Ruth, undeterred by Miss Billy's outrage, clapped her hands together in delight. "Oh, Miss Billy, you must come! The occasion calls for your discriminating eye. Besides, what fun is a procession without its fair share of scandal?"

Mrs. Franklin, who had been listening with growing amusement, interjected. "Indeed, Miss Billy, the thought of Mr. Hill in his episcopal robes is worth the price of admission. And what of the ladies? Have we any particularly splendid attire in store?"

Dolly, ever eager to contribute, bounced excitedly in her chair. "Genevieve is to be a Spanish duchess, with a train so long it will require an entire contingent of footmen to manage it. And Miss Clara—oh, Miss Clara! She is to appear as a gypsy, with jewels and all!"

Miss Billy harrumphed, her disapproval clear. "Gypsies! What on earth possesses the young to adopt such absurd notions? It is unbecoming, to say the least."

Ruth, undaunted, waved a dismissive hand. "Nonsense, Miss Billy. Gypsies are as much a part of our society as bishops in cassocks. Besides, Clara's gypsy costume is assemblage of the most exquisite silks and embroidery—nothing to cause offense, I assure you."

As the conversation continued, the room filled with laughter and ribaldry, each person contributing their own二分之一 to the growing anticipation of the evening's event. Even Miss Billy, though still reserving her judgment, found herself drawn into the mirth, her stern expression softening as the infectious joy of the moment swept her up.

Meanwhile, in a corner of the room, Mrs. Franklin subtly observed her guests, her mind turning over the subtle currents of their interactions. She noted the way Dolly's eyes sparkled with suppressed excitement, Ruth's hand gestures growing more expansive with each tale, and Miss Billy's slowly softening resistance. It was a tapestry of human nature, each thread woven with the care and precision of a master artisan.

As the afternoon wore on, the preparations for the evening began to take shape, each person contributing their part with varying degrees of enthusiasm. Miss Billy, though still doubtful, found herself drawn into the fray, her sharp wit providing a counterpoint to the general frivolity. Ruth, ever the organizer, ensured that every detail was attended to, her mind racing with plans and possibilities. And Mrs. Franklin, always the observer, sat back with a contented smile, her fingers still idly plucking at the piano keys, as though the music of the room itself were her greatest accompaniment.

The evening promised to be one of those rare occasions where the boundaries of society were gently pushed, and even the most strait-laced among them allowed themselves a moment of abandon. For in the end, was not life itself a grand procession, with each of us playing our part in the grand theater of existence?

"With a great many soldiers, Uncle Wal?" queried little Ned.

"No; with what in these days would be considered a very small army; only 180 soldiers, of whom 27 were cavalry."

"Cavalry?" repeated Ned, in a tone of enquiry.

"Yes, soldiers on horseback. The Peruvians, having never before seen a horse, took each mounted man and the steed he rode to be but one animal, and were much afraid of them. The firearms, too, inspired great terror, as they knew nothing of gunpowder and its uses.

"At that time there was war among the natives of Peru and Quito. Huano Capac, the former Inca of Peru, had died some years previous, leaving Peru to his son Huascar, and Quito, which he had conquered shortly before, to another son--half-brother to Huascar. The two had quarrelled and had been fighting each other for about two years, and just before the arrival of the Spaniards Atahualpa had defeated his brother Huascar, taken him prisoner, and confined him in a strong fortress."

"Perhaps," remarked Evelyn, "if they had not been so busy fighting each other they might have discovered the approach of Pizarro, their common enemy, in season to prevent the mischief he was prepared to do them."

"Very possibly," returned Walter. "As it was, the Spaniards drew near Atahualpa's victorious camp, where they found fifty thousand men assembled. Pizarro had at the most only two hundred; a mere handful in comparison with the numbers of the Peruvians, but by a most daring and diabolical stratagem he got possession of the unsuspecting Inca.

"Atahualpa came to visit him in a friendly spirit. A priest began explaining to him the Christian, or rather the papal religion; told him that the Pope had power over all the kingdoms of the earth and that he had presented Peru to the King of Spain; also that they had come to take possession in the name of that king.

"Naturally that made Atahualpa very angry; so angry that he indignantly interrupted the priest, saying that the Pope--whoever he was--must be a crazy fool to talk of giving away countries which did not belong to him. Then he asked on what authority such claims were made.

"The priest pointed to a Bible. Atahualpa dashed it angrily to the ground, and the fields began to fill with Indians. Then Pizarro waved a white scarf--the signal he had agreed upon with his men--and his artillery poured sudden death into the terrified masses of Indians, while the Spanish cavalry rode them down in a furious, merciless way. The ranks of the poor, unarmed Peruvians were thrown into confusion; their foes were butchering them without mercy; they could do little to save themselves; they used every effort to defend and save the sacred Inca, but in vain; and after hours of that fiendish murdering of the poor, defenceless creatures, the Spaniards got full possession of him.

"At first they pretended to be very kind to him, especially when he offered, as his ransom, to fill the room in which he stood with gold as high as he could reach.

"Huascar, in his prison, heard of this and offered a still larger ransom for himself, and to prevent it Atahualpa had him secretly murdered.

"Soon after that the gold for Atahualpa's ransom began to pour in, and when there was as much as he had promised he demanded his freedom. But Pizarro refused to let him go--though he took the gold--accusing him of plotting against him; and after much base treachery the Spaniards held a mock trial and condemned Atahualpa to be burned. But when they led him out to the stake he consented to be baptized, and for that they were so very merciful as to strangle before burning him."

Oke took me out of his study, and into the dining room, where luncheon awaited us. A long, oak table stood beneath a chandelier of branching antlers, laden with silver dishes. It seemed a place more suited for a baronial feast than a simple midday meal. The walls, like the hall, were lined with portraits, grim-faced ancestors staring down upon us with an air of faint disapproval, as if we were somehow failing to live up to their standards of consequence.

As we sat, Oke regaled me with anecdotes about the house and its previous occupants; tales of reckless squires, love affairs gone awry, and fortunes won and lost in the space of a single evening at cards. He spoke with a certain detached amusement, as if the weight of history were something he could observe from a safe distance, rather than a force that shaped his very existence. I couldn't help but feel a pang of sympathy for Mrs. Oke, trapped in this place of echoes and shadows, with a husband who seemed to have settled so comfortably into his role as caretaker of a bygone era.

After luncheon, Oke suggested a stroll about the grounds. The October air was crisp and invigorating, and the leaves crunched satisfyingly beneath our feet as we walked. The gardens were a marvel of manicured perfection, stretching away from the house in a series of terraces and parterres. Ancient yew hedges formed intricate mazes, and marble statues gleamed palely in the dappled sunlight.

"The gardens are Mrs. Oke's domain, you know," Oke remarked, pausing before a particularly impressive rose bush. "She spends hours out here, tending to them. It's her escape, I suppose." He paused, a flicker of something that might have been concern crossing his otherwise placid features. "She has such a delicate constitution, you see. The quiet, the beauty…they soothe her nerves."

I found myself growing increasingly curious about this Mrs. Oke. Was she truly as fragile as her husband suggested? Or was there something more to her reclusive nature, something hidden beneath the surface of her delicate constitution? I resolved to learn more.

As we rounded a corner, we came upon a small, secluded gazebo, draped with ivy. It was nestled amidst a grove of ancient oak trees, its roof barely visible through the foliage. Oke hesitated, then turned to me with a slightly apologetic smile.

"I believe Mrs. Oke is resting there," he said. "Perhaps we should not disturb her."

But my curiosity was piqued. I could sense that he was trying to shield me from something, and the impulse to uncover the truth became irresistible.

"Surely, we could just take a quick peek?" I suggested, my voice perhaps a shade too eager. "I would be loath to intrude, of course, but I'm simply eager to express my gratitude."

Oke hesitated again, his brow furrowed in a way that suggested inner conflict. "Very well," he said at last, with a sigh. "But please, be quiet. We mustn't startle her."

He led the way through the grove, his footsteps muffled by the thick carpet of leaves. As we approached the gazebo, I could hear a faint sound, a low, rhythmic humming that seemed to vibrate in the very air around us. Oke stopped at the entrance, and with a trembling hand, pushed aside the ivy that concealed it.

"Why, what is it?" asked Clytie. "Don't you think we ought to try to understand modern social conditions and do what we can to improve them? If you would only go through some of those streets in the river wards and into some of the houses--oh, dear me, dear me!"

But Abner would none of this. "Do you think your river wards, as you call them, are any worse than our barn-yard in the early days of March? Do you imagine your cheap vawdyville theatres are any more tiresome than our Main Street through the winter months?"

No, Abner's thoughts had been focused too long on the wrongs of the rural regions to be able to transfer themselves to the sufferings and injustices of the town. He saw the city collectively as the oppressor of the country, and Leverett Whyland, by reason of Clytie's innocent prattle, became the city incarnate in a single figure.

"I know your Mr. Whyland," he said. "I've met him; I know all about him. He lives on his rents. His property came to him by inheritance, and half its value to-day is due to the general rise brought about by the exertions of others. He is indebted for food, clothing and shelter to the unearned increment."

"Lives on his rents? Is there anything wrong in that? So do I, too--when they can be collected. And if you talk about the unearned increment, let me tell you there is such a thing as the unearned decrement."

"Nonsense. That's merely a backward swirl in a rushing stream."

"Not at all!" cried Clytie, now in the full heat of controversy. "If you were used to a big growing city, with all its sudden shifts and changes, you would understand. Even the new neighbourhoods get spoiled before they are half put together--builders treat one another so unfairly; while, as for the old ones--why, my poor dear father is coming to have row after row that he can't find tenants for at all, unless he were to let them to--to objectionable characters."

Clytie threw this out with all boldness. The matter was purely economic, sociological; they were talking quite as man to man. Abner brought every woman to this point sooner or later.

As for the troubles of landlords, he had no sympathy with them. And to him the most objectionable of all "objectionable characters" was the man who had a strong box stuffed with farm mortgages--town-dwellers, the great bulk of them. "Oh, the cities, the cities!" he groaned. Then, more cheerfully: "But never mind: they are passing."

"Passing? I like that! Do you know that eighteen and two-thirds per cent of the population of the United States lives in towns of one hundred thousand inhabitants and above, and that the number is increasing at the rate of----"

"They are disintegrating," pursued Abner stolidly. "By their own bulk--like a big snowball. And by their own badness. People are rolling back to the country--the country they came from. Improved transportation will do it." The troubles of the town were ephemeral--he waved them aside. But his face was set in a frown--doubtless at the thought of the perdurable afflictions of the country.

"Don't worry over these passing difficulties that arise from a mere temporary congestion of population. They will take care of themselves. Meanwhile, don't sport with them; don't encourage your young friends to make them a vehicle of their own selfish pleasures; don't----"

Clytie caught her breath. So she was a mere frivolous, inconsequential butterfly, after all. Why try longer to lend the Helping Hand--why not cut things short and be satisfied with the Social Triumph and let it go at that? "I was meaning to ask you to dine with me some evening next week at a settlement I know, but now...."

The old servant spoke less to Beaufort than to himself; but the visitor was not accustomed to hold such colloquies with a family butler. He stared, then grew impatient, and disposed to resent the old fellow's familiarity. The next moment the bell rang, and Rolls hurried away. Beaufort followed him out into the hall, where a man was standing evidently on guard. John was at the door of the drawing-room, pale, but perfectly composed. "The dogcart immediately," he said to Rolls, and beckoned to Beaufort to come in. "I am going before the sheriff-substitute about this matter," he said. "Beaufort, you will come with me. Mr Granger, this is my friend Mr Beaufort, an English barrister. He may go with me, I suppose, to watch over my interests? You see that what we were threatened with yesterday has come to pass."

"I see, indeed," said Beaufort, "with sorrow and surprise. What is it that has to be done now?"

"The sheriff will make no objection," said the head of the county police, a plain, grave man, with regret in his face. "It's my duty to take Mr Erskine before the sheriff. The result of the examination will be, let us hope, that he'll come cannily home again, when all has been inquired into in due form. There is no reason to take a gloomy view. The sheriff will maybe find there's no case: and I'm sure I wish so with all my heart."

They all sat round with the utmost gravity to listen to this little speech. It was not a moment for light-heartedness. John sat between the table and the door, in perfect self-command, yet very pale. Notwithstanding all the respect shown to him, and the good feeling from which he had everything to hope, the most innocent of men may be excused a feeling of dismay when he is, to all intents and purposes, arrested on a criminal charge, with issues to his good fame and social estimation, even if nothing more, which it is impossible to calculate. They sat in silence while the dogcart was getting ready, a strange little company. After a while, the officer, to lessen the embarrassment of the moment, and make everything pleasant, began to address various little remarks about the weather and other commonplace topics to the two gentlemen, such as, "This is a very agreeable change from all the wet we've been having;" or, "The news this morning is more satisfactory about that Afghan business." The responses made, as may be supposed, were not very effusive. It was a relief when the dogcart came to the door. Old Rolls stood and watched it go down the avenue, with his countenance firmly set, and a stern resolution gathering about his mouth. Bauby stole out and stood by his side in the morning light, with her apron to her eyes, and her capacious bosom convulsed with sobs.
