'What have you to say for the poor man, then!' exclaimed Ermine, rousing to the contest. 'If there is a tragedy at the sulphur-house, it belongs to the sulphur-man, not to the sulphur-woman.'

'He is not a sulphur-man, he is a coal-man; keep to your bearings, Ermine.'

'I tell you,' pursued my cousin, earnestly, 'that I pitied that unknown man with inward tears all the while I sat by that trap door. Depend upon it, he had his dream, his ideal; and this country girl with her great eyes and wealth of hair represented the beautiful to his hungry soul. He gave his whole life and hope into her hands, and woke to find his goddess a common wooden image.'

'Waste sympathy upon a coal-miner!' I said, imitating my cousin's former tone.

'If any one is blind, it is you,' she answered, with gleaming eyes. 'That man's whole history stood revealed in the selfish complainings of that creature. He had been in the Community from boyhood, therefore of course he had no chance to learn life, to see its art-treasures. He has been shipwrecked, poor soul; hopelessly shipwrecked.'

And Mr Easy threw himself back in his chair, imagining, like all philosophers, that he had said something very clever.

Dr Middleton knew his man, and therefore patiently waited until he had exhausted his oratory.

"I will grant," said the doctor at last, "that all you say may have great truth in it; but, Mr Easy, do you not think that by not permitting a boy to be educated, you allow him to remain more open to that very error of which you speak? It is only education which will conquer prejudice, and enable a man to break through the trammels of custom. Now, allowing that the birch is used, yet it is at a period when the young mind is so elastic as to soon become indifferent; and after he has attained the usual rudiments of education, you will then find him prepared to receive those lessons which you can yourself instil."

"I will teach him everything myself," replied Mr Easy, folding his arms consequentially and determinedly.

"I do not doubt your capability, Mr Easy; but unfortunately you will always have a difficulty which you never can get over. Excuse me, I know what you are capable of, and the boy would indeed be happy with such a preceptor, but--if I must speak plain--you must be aware as well as I am, that the maternal fondness of Mrs Easy will always be a bar to your intention. He is already so spoiled by her, that he will not obey; and without obedience you cannot inculcate."

"I grant, my dear sir, that there is a difficulty on that point; but maternal weakness must then be overcome by paternal severity."

"May I ask how, Mr Easy, for it appears to be impossible?"

"Impossible! By heavens, I'll make him obey, or I'll--" Here Mr Easy stopped before the word "flog" was fairly out of his mouth--"I'll know the reason why, Dr Middleton."

Dr Middleton checked his inclination to laugh, and replied, "That you would hit upon some scheme, by which you would obtain the necessary power over him, I have no doubt; but what will be the consequence? The boy will consider his mother as a protector, and you as a tyrant. He will have an aversion to you, and with that aversion he will never pay respect and attention to your valuable precepts when he arrives at an age to understand them. Now it appears to me that this difficulty which you have raised may be got over. I know a very worthy clergyman who does not use the birch; but I will write, and put the direct question to him; and then if your boy is removed from the danger arising from Mrs Easy's over-indulgence, in a short time he will be ready for your more important tuition."

"I think," replied Mr Easy, after a pause, "that what you say merits consideration. I acknowledge that in consequence of Mrs Easy's nonsensical indulgence, the boy is unruly, and will not obey me at present; and if your friend does not apply the rod, I will think seriously of sending my son John to him to learn the elements."

The doctor had gained his point by flattering the philosopher.

In a day he returned with a letter from the pedagogue in answer to one supposed to be sent to him, in which the use of the birch was indignantly disclaimed, and Mr Easy announced to his wife, when they met that day at tea-time, his intentions with regard to his son John.

"To school, Mr Easy? what, send Johnny to school! a mere infant to school!"

"Surely, my dear, you must be aware that at nine years it is high time that he learned to read."

"Why he almost reads already, Mr Easy; surely I can teach him that. Does he not, Sarah?"

"Lord bless him, yes, ma'am, he was saying his letters yesterday."

"Heaven knows how weak I might be if he were to talk to me again as he talked last night!" she said to herself. "I might not be able to bear it a second time. Oh Rorie, if you knew what it cost me to counsel you wisely, to bid you do your duty; when the vision of a happy life with you was smiling at me all the time, when the warm grasp of your dear hand made my heart thrill with joy, what a heroine you would think me! And yet nobody will ever give me credit for heroism; and I shall be remembered only as a self-willed young woman, who was troublesome to her relations, and had to be sent away from home."

She was thinking this while she sat in her father's chair, deliberating upon the Captain's last speech. She decided presently to yield, and obey her mother and stepfather. After all, what did it matter where she went? That scheme of being happy in Sweden with Miss McCroke was but an idle fancy. In the depths of her inner consciousness Violet Tempest knew that she could be happy nowhere away from Rorie and the Forest. What did it matter, then, whether she went to Jersey or Kamtchatka, the sandy desert of Gobi or the Mountains of the Moon? In either case exile meant moral death, the complete renunciation of all that had been sweet and precious in her uneventful young life--the shadowy beech-groves; the wandering streams; the heathery upland plains; the deep ferny hollows, where the footsteps of humanity were almost unknown; the cluster of tall trees on the hill tops, where the herons came sailing home from their flight across Southampton Water; her childhood's companion; her horse; her old servants. Banishment meant a long farewell to all these.

"I suppose I may take my dog with me?" she asked, after a long pause, during which she had wavered between submission and revolt, "and my maid?"

"I see no objection to your taking your dog; though I doubt whether my aunt will care to have a dog of that size prowling about her house. He can have a kennel somewhere, I daresay. You must learn to do without a maid. Feminine helplessness is going out of fashion; and one would expect an Amazon like you to be independent of lady's-maids and milliners."

"Why don't you state the case in plain English?" cried Vixen scornfully. "If I took Phoebe with me she would cost money. There would be her wages and maintenance to be provided. If I leave her behind, you can dismiss her. You have a fancy for dismissing old servants."

"Had you not better see to the packing of your trunks?" asked Captain Winstanley, ignoring this shaft.

"What is to become of my horse?"

"I think you must resign yourself to leave him to fate and me," replied the Captain coolly; "my aunt may submit to the infliction of your dog, but that she should tolerate a young lady's roaming about the island on a thoroughbred horse would be rather too much to expect from her old-fashioned notions of propriety."

"Besides, even Arion would cost something to keep," retorted Vixen, "and strict economy is the rule of your life. If you sell him--and, of course, you will do so--please let Lord Mallow have the refusal of him. I think he would buy him and treat him kindly, for my sake."

"Wouldn't you rather Mr. Vawdrey had him?"

"Yes, if I were free to give him away; but I suppose you would deny my right of property even in the horse my father gave me."

"Well, as the horse was not specified in your father's will, and as all his horses and carriages were left to your mother, I think there cannot be any doubt that Arion is my wife's property."

"Ruined my constitution, you did!" cried Nestley, striking the table with his clenched fist. "And for what? For your own amusement, I suppose."

Beaumont watched him through a haze of cigarette smoke, a supercilious smile playing upon his lips. "My dear fellow," he drawled, "you do exaggerate so. A few nights on the town never hurt anyone."

"A few nights!" Nestley sprang to his feet, his voice shaking with barely suppressed fury. "It was every night, for months on end! You, with your endless thirst for brandy and late hours, dragging me along with you like a damned puppet!"

He paced the room, his hands clenching and unclenching at his sides. The other occupants, sensing a scene, had discreetly withdrawn to the furthest corners, leaving the two men in a tense bubble of isolation.

"You knew I couldn't handle it," Nestley continued, his voice thick with emotion. "You knew my health was delicate. But did you care? Not you! You were having too much fun, leading me down the primrose path to ruin."

Beaumont flicked a speck of ash from his impeccably tailored waistcoat, his expression one of languid amusement. "Come now, Doctor," he purred, "don't tell me you've gone and turned into a teetotaler. Why, I remember the nights you could outdrink even me, and I flatter myself I have a rather strong head for liquor."

"That was before," Nestley spat, his voice raw. "Before I realized the hold it had on me, before I woke up one morning staring into the abyss. It took me five years, five long years to climb out of that hole you helped dig for me."

He stopped his pacing and stood before Beaumont, his chest heaving. "Five years of discipline, of denying myself every indulgence, to rebuild what you so carelessly destroyed."

Beaumont raised an eyebrow, a flicker of something akin to admiration flitting across his features. "Well, well, Doctor," he murmured, "it seems you possess a stronger will than I gave you credit for. Most commendable."

But the compliment, if indeed it was one, rang hollow in Nestley's ears. It did nothing to erase the bitterness, the resentment that festered within him.

"You find it amusing, do you?" he asked, his voice low and dangerous.

Beaumont shrugged, his indifference like a slap in the face. "Life is rather amusing, don't you think? All these twists and turns, these little dramas we create for ourselves. Keeps things interesting, wouldn't you say?"

Nestley stared at him, his anger warring with a profound weariness. Beaumont would never understand, never comprehend the true cost of his actions. He was like a child playing with fire, oblivious to the potential for destruction.

"I suppose it is," Nestley said finally, his voice devoid of inflection. "For some."

The fact appeared to cause Mr. Davis no slight dissatisfaction. His bearing, his looks, his voice, all betrayed it.

'I want some money,' he observed.

'Then you'll have to want,' returned his wife.

'Ain't you got none?'

'No, nor shan't have, not till I've took these two coats in.'

'Then what'll it be?'

'You know very well what it'll be--three-and-six--one-and-nine apiece--if there ain't no fines.'

'And this is what they call the land of liberty, the 'ome of the free, where people slave and slave--for one-and-nine.'

Mr. Davis seemed conscious that the conclusion of his sentence was slightly impotent, and spat on the floor as if to signify his regret.

''Tain't much slaving you do, anyhow.'

'No, nor it ain't much I'm likely to do; I'm no servile wretch; I'm free-born.'

'Prefers to make your living off me, you do.'

'Well, and why not? Ain't woman the inferior animal? Didn't Nature mean it to be her pride to minister to man? Ain't it only the false veneer of a rotten civilization what's upset all that? If I gives my talents for the good of the species, as I do do, as is well known I do do, ain't it only right that you should give me something in return, if it's only a crust and water? Ain't that law and justice-- natural law, mind you, and natural justice?'

'I don't know nothing about law, natural or otherwise, but I do know it ain't justice.'

Mr. Davis looked at his wife, more in sorrow than in anger. He was silent for some seconds, as if meditating on the peculiar baseness of human nature. When he spoke there was a whine in his raucous voice, which was, perhaps, meant to denote his consciousness of how much he stood in need of sympathy.

'I'm sorry, Matilda, to hear you talk to me like that, because it forces me to do something what I shouldn't otherwise have done. Give me them coats.'

She had just finished packing up the coats in the linen wrapper, and was pinning up one end. Snatching up the parcel, she clasped it to her bosom as if it had been some precious thing.

'No, Tommy, not the coats!'

'Matilda, once more I ask you to give me them coats.'

'What do you want them for?'

'Once more, Matilda, I ask you to give me them coats.'

'No, Tommy, that I won't--never! not if you was to kill me! You know what happened the last time, and all I had to go through; and you promised you'd never do it again, and you shan't, not while I can help it--no, that you shan't!'

Clasping the parcel tightly to her, she drew back towards a corner of the room, like some wild creature standing at bay. Mr. Davis, advancing towards the table, leaned on it, addressing her as if he desired to impress her with the fact that he was endeavouring not to allow his feelings to get the better of his judgment.

'Listen to me, Matilda. I'm soft and tender, as well you know, and should therefore regret having to start knocking you about; but want is want, and I want 'arf a sovereign this day, and have it I must.'

'What do you want it for?'

Mr. Davis brought his clenched fist sharply down upon the table--possibly by way of a hint.

'Never you mind what I want it for. I do want it, and that's enough for you. You trouble yourself with your own affairs, and don't poke your nose into mine, my girl; you'll find it safest.'

'I'll try to get it for you, Tommy.'

Mr. Davis was scornful.

'Oh, you will, will you! How are you going to set about getting 'arf a sovereign? Perhaps you'll be so good as to let me know. Because if you can lay hands on 'arf a sovereign whenever one's wanted, it's a trick worth knowing. You're such a clever one at getting 'old of the pieces, you are, and always have been.'

"Well, good riddance, I say!" grumbled the old man, watching Dete's figure shrink into the distance, a dark speck against the vibrant green of the mountainside. He turned his gaze then, sharp and scrutinizing, upon the child. "So, you are what she left behind, are you? A handful of sorrow, no doubt."

Heidi, quite unperturbed by his gruff pronouncements, continued to observe a particularly industrious beetle making its slow and steady progress across the rough-hewn planks of the cabin porch. She followed its journey with an intentness that seemed to exclude all else from her world.

The old man scowled. "And have you nothing to say for yourself, girl? Not a 'good day' or a 'how do you do'? Are you struck dumb, perhaps?" He poked at her with the gnarled end of his walking stick, not unkindly, but with a certain testiness that betrayed his discomfort.

Heidi, startled by the sudden intrusion, looked up, her eyes wide and innocent. "The beetle," she said, her voice small but clear, "is going somewhere important."

The old man stared at her, his face a study in bewilderment. "Important? A beetle? What nonsense is this? Are you daft, child?" He sighed, a sound like wind whistling through the crags. "Dete has foisted upon me a simpleton, it seems. Just what I needed." He turned and stumped into the cabin, leaving Heidi alone on the porch.

She watched him disappear into the dim interior, then turned her attention back to the beetle, which had now reached the edge of the plank and was poised to venture into the tall grass below. She watched it disappear from view, then, with a sigh of her own, stood up and followed the old man into the cabin.

The cabin was small and sparsely furnished. A rough table stood in the center of the room, surrounded by three-legged stools. A fire crackled merrily in the hearth, casting dancing shadows on the walls. The air was thick with the scent of wood smoke and something else… something earthy and unfamiliar.

The old man was rummaging in a wooden chest, muttering to himself. Heidi stood quietly by the door, observing him with a mixture of curiosity and apprehension.

"Now, where is it?" he grumbled, pulling out a tangle of old clothes. "That blasted woman never could leave things where they belonged." He finally unearthed a small, wooden bowl and a spoon. "There, that will have to do." He turned to Heidi, holding out the bowl. "Are you hungry, girl?"

Heidi nodded, her eyes fixed on the bowl.

"Well, come then," he said, leading her to the table. "There's goat's milk and some hard bread. It's not much, but it will have to suffice." He poured the milk into the bowl and placed it before her, along with a chunk of the bread. "Eat up now. A body can't think on an empty stomach."

Heidi hesitated, then picked up the spoon and began to eat. The milk was rich and creamy, and the bread, though hard, had a satisfying chew. She ate slowly and deliberately, savoring each mouthful. The old man watched her, his eyes softening slightly. Perhaps, he thought, this child wouldn't be such a burden after all. Perhaps, just perhaps, she would bring a little light into this lonely place. Only time would tell.

The gentle warmth of the afternoon sun filtered through the sprawling windows of the countess's chambers, casting a golden hue on the polished wooden floor. Mavra, with her nimble fingers already stained with the hues of rose and emerald from the tapestry she was working on, paused for a moment to pass her hand across her brow. She was not accustomed to the quiet monotony of this labor, which was so different from the bustling life of her village home.

Mavra's thoughts drifted back to a time when her mother would wake her before the sun had breached the hills, her mother's voice a comforting lullaby to the dawn. She would then sit beside her, following her mother's precise stitches as she embroidered a tiny flower blossom, each stitch told a tale of patience and love. Her mother had been a skilled embroiderer herself, having served the family of a neighboring duke before falling on hard times. It was her mother's knowledge and skill that had secured Mavra's position in the countess's service, a stroke of fortune that Mavra could never forget.

The life at the grand estate was not as glamorous as it first appeared. The grand halls echoed with a silence that felt foreign to Mavra's ears, accustomed to the hum of livestock and the lively chatter of the market. The staff, despite the warmth of their smiles, seemed to carry an air of secretiveness, as if whispering too loudly would shatter the delicate balance of their world.

The countess, on the other hand, was a woman of contradictions. She was as warm as the sun's reflux during winter, her kindness as sharp as a blade. She would often find Mavra in the gardens, her head bent over her work, and would stop to offer words of praise, mixing them with gentle reminders of her duties. One day, after observing Mavra's approximation of a bird, the countess had smiled and said, "You have a remarkable eye, Mavra. It is as if the very essence of nature is captured in your stitches."

Mavra felt a deep affection for the countess, a bond that was not entirely one-sided. The countess often asked about Mavra's village, her eyes lighting up with curiosity. Yet, there was a sadness that lingered in her gaze, a longing for the simpler life that Mavra still carried with her.

As the sun began to set, painting the sky with hues of orange and purple, Mavra's thoughts turned to her health. The air in the countess's chambers grew stifling, the scent of beeswax and perfume increasingly oppressive. She felt a familiar ache in her chest, a restlessness that she had not experienced in the village. The countess noticed it too, her brow furrowing as she watched Mavra's cheeks lose their rosy glow.

"Mavra," she called out one evening, her voice echoing in the quiet rooms, "you have been spending too much time indoors. Spring has scarcely begun, yet you seem to have forgotten the joy of the outdoors."

Mavra looked up, her voice barely a whisper. "It is just the scarcity of the world beyond these walls that I find challenging, Countess. The quietude is so different from the village life."

The countess leaned in, her eyes filled with understanding. "I understand, Mavra. You are a creature of the open fields, the whispering winds, and the rustling leaves. The castle walls, no matter how beautiful, cannot replace the simplicity and freshness of the countryside."

She shook her head, a gentle smile playing on her lips. "I neglected to assign you duties that require outdoor activity. I have been remiss in my responsibilities. Your stay here should be beneficial, not confining. I shall have a word with the gardener, he will need an extra pair of hands."

Mavra looked at her with uncertainty. "But Countess, I am yet inexperienced in gardening. I fear I may not be of much help."

The countess waved her hand dismissively. "Nonsense, you have the touch of an artist. The plants will thrive under your care. Besides, it is good for the soul, the nurturing of life. It is one of the reasons I keep a garden, Mavra. The green and growing things bring a certain peace to my spirits."

As the days passed, the countess kept her word. Mavra found herself spending more time outdoors, her hands now stained not just with the colors of her embroidery, but with the earth itself. The castle gardens were now her domain, a world of vibrant colors and sweet scents. She found joy in the simple task of weeding, of nurturing the small flowers that blossomed under her care.

As evening drew its velvet cloak over the rugged contours of the storied land, the fog began to steal across the restless sea like a phantom bride. Aros, or Aros Jay, cradled in this embrace of ephemeral mystery, appeared a sanctuary enshrined in mist. To the casual gaze, it was still the southern bastion of the mainland, but to those who navigated these treacherous waters, Aros Jay was a sovereign realm, the House of God whispering cautionary tales to the mariners of yore.

The promontory, with its guardian granite sentinels plunging into the depths below, had long been blessed with a name that echoed with the dread of its reputation. The sailors spoke in hushed tones of the Roost, a seething beast of the deep whose appetite was slaked in the ebb and swell. It was here that the Merry Men, those fickle jesters of the sea, reveled in their dance, the waves rearing their heads skyward before crashing in a discordant melody of thunderous exile. The very thought of these terpsichorean titans was enough to send the stoutest mariner scrambling for the cloak of safety.

Yet, the hearts of the islanders, though stirred by tales of tumult, burned with a spark of defiance. Their tenacity was the stuff of legend, for they sought no safe haven but rather to tame the wild Roost with the gentle touch of human ingenuity. In defiance of the capricious whims of nature, they labored tirelessly, erecting beacons of light and buoys to shepherd the path around the lethal embrace of the Merry Men. It was said that these sentinels would guide the lost, steer them clear of the perilous eddies where the green waters of the sea met the somber frown of the granite cliffs.

The night, with its cloak of clouds, bore witness to their industrious vigil, for even as the Stars whirled overhead in their eternal dance, the islanders hummed a song of endeavor, their voices as harmonious as the crackling of the bonfires that illuminated their clandestine efforts. The waves, though they howled their nocturnal dirge, seemed for a fleeting moment to pause, as if sensing the quiet resolve of those who would reclaim the land from the grip of the Roost.

As the dawn broke, bathing the coast of Aros in a soft, golden light, the fruits of their labor stood as a testament not only to their resilience but to their unyielding spirit. The lights, now steadfast against the morning mist, whispered promises of safer passage, their silent glow a beacon of hope amidst the tumult of the sea. And it was here, at the confluence of land and sea, that the legend of Aros Jay would continue to unfold, a tale of fortitude and pride in the face of nature's most implacable foes.

The sun had not yet set upon the bustling streets of the theatre district, but the shadows were beginning to lengthen, casting a golden hue over the cobblestones. Inside the modest office of Mr. Wattles, the theatre manager, a sense of unease lingered in the air. The room, though small, was filled with the clutter of his professional life—scripts, playbills, and ledgers scattered across his desk, a testament to the chaotic world of theatrical management.

Mr. Wattles sat behind his desk, his fingers steepled in a gesture of deep thought. His brow was furrowed, and his eyes darted nervously toward the door, as if expecting someone to burst in at any moment. The decision he had made earlier that day still weighed heavily upon his mind, a decision that had beenExtracted by none other than Al Allston, the ambitious young man who had taken it upon himself to shake things up at the theatre.

"Mr. Wattles," Al had said, his voice brimming with confidence, "if we are to succeed, we must take risks. Miss Hendricks may be an amateur, but she has the makings of something extraordinary. Give her a chance, and I assure you, the audience will be abuzz with excitement. And with the silver spoons—"

At the mention of the silver spoons, Mr. Wattles had almost laughed aloud. The idea had seemed, at first, preposterous. Silver spoons distributed to female attendees? It sounded more like a scheme to lining one's pockets than a legitimate marketing ploy. But Al had pressed on, his eyes gleaming with the fire of a man who believed in his own genius.

"My good sir," Al had continued, "I have already secured a batch of these spoons from a supplier in the city. They are of the finest quality, and when engraved with the theatre's crest, they will serve as a delightful keepsake for the ladies. It is a unique gesture, something the public will talk about long after the curtain falls."

Mr. Wattles had hesitated, his mind torn between the promise of success and the very real possibility of failure. The theatre was Already struggling to turn a profit, and any misstep could spell disaster. But Al's enthusiasm was contagious, and before he knew it, Mr. Wattles had found himself nodding in agreement.

Now, as the clock struck five, Mr. Wattles was preparing to approach the mayoress, the very woman who had inspired this daring plan. Her name was Mrs. Margaret Worthington, a woman of considerable influence in the town, though her husband's position as mayor was what had earned her the title. She was known for her love of the theatre, though her forays into amateur dramatics were the subject of much whispering in the corridors of the local social circles.

As Mr. Wattles stepped out of his office and into the bustling hallway, he was met by the familiar sight of Al, leaning casually against the wall, a mischievous grin spreading across his face. "一切进展顺利吗？" Al inquired, his tone brimming with the confidence that never seemed to wane.

"Not a moment too soon, I assure you," Mr. Wattles replied, his voice tinged with the weight of his decision. "The mayoress is waiting in her parlour. I trust you have arranged for the spoons to be delivered promptly?"

"Of course," Al replied, his grin widening. "They will be waiting at the theatre by tonight's performance. The ladies will be most delighted."

With a nod, Mr. Wattles set off toward the mayoress's residence, his mind a whirlwind of doubt and hope. The Mayoress's parlour was a room of grand proportions, filled with the scent of freshly baked pastries and the soft murmur of her parrot, perched atop its cage. Mrs. Worthington herself was seated at her desk, a pen in hand, her hair neatly coiffed, and her dress of the finest silk.

"Mr. Wattles," she greeted, her voice smooth and commanding, "what brings you to my parlour this evening?"

Mr. Wattles took a deep breath, his hands trembling slightly as he approached the desk. "Madam, I come with an offer—an opportunity that I believe you would find most intriguing."

The mayoress raised an eyebrow, her eyes narrowing in curiosity. "An opportunity, you say?"

"Yes, madam," Mr. Wattles replied, his voice steady despite his racing heart. "There is a small part in our upcoming performance that we believe would suit you most admirably. It is a role of some consequence, though not overly demanding. If I may be so bold, I believe your talents could bring it to life in a most captivating manner."

The mayoress sat back in her chair, her lips pursed in thoughtful consideration. "A part in your theatre? Mr. Wattles, I must confess, I have been ratherinactive of late. But I am intrigued by your suggestion."

"There is more, madam," Mr. Wattles continued, his voice gaining confidence with each word. "My associate, Mr. Allston, has conceived a most ingenious plan to attract a larger audience. We propose to distribute silver souvenir spoons to female attendees, engraved with the theatre's crest. It is a gesture of goodwill, something to be cherished long after the performance."

The mayoress's eyes lit up, her interest piqued. "Silver spoons? That is indeed a novel idea. And you believe this will encourage attendance?"

"Absolutely, madam," Mr. Wattles replied, his confidence now unshaken. "The spoons are of the finest quality, and the engraving adds a touch of elegance. I assure you, it will be a talking point among the ladies."

The mayoress leaned forward, her curiosity now fully awakened. "And what is the role you have in mind for me?"

"It is a role of some importance, madam," Mr. Wattles replied, his voice. "A lady of influence, much like yourself. It is a part that requires grace and poise, and I believe you would excel in it."

The mayoress nodded, her mind racing with the possibilities. "Very well, Mr. Wattles. I shall accept your offer. But I must warn you, I expect the role to be precisely as you have described. Anything less, and I shall hold you accountable."

Mr. Wattles bowed slightly, relief washing over him. "I assure you, madam, you will not be disappointed."

As Mr. Wattles exited the mayoress's parlour, his heart lighter than it had been in weeks, he could not help but feel a sense of anticipation. The plan was coming together, and with the mayoress on board, the stage was set for a performance unlike any other. But as he walked back to the theatre, his mind could not help but dwell on the uncertainties that lay ahead. The Mayoress was a formidable woman, and while her influence could be a boon, it could also be a double-edged sword.

Meanwhile, back at the theatre, Al Allston was busily making preparations, his mind already racing ahead to the possibilities of success. The silver spoons had been delivered, and he had arranged for their distribution with meticulous care. The audience would be dazzled, he was certain of it, and the Mayoress's performance would be the talk of the town.

But as the night drew closer, the anxiety within Mr. Wattles grew. The stakes were higher than ever, and the slightest misstep could undo all his efforts. The Mayoress's performance was not the only thing at risk; the future of the theatre itself hung in the balance.

Fanny paced back and forth in the parlor, wringing her hands in agitation. “Tom, it's dire! Not a soul else to fetch Polly, and you won't move from that armchair.”

Tom barely glanced up from his newspaper, a scowl playing on his lips. “You cannot dress up like a boy while I'm the one to do all the fetching,” he retorted, folding the page with decisive finality. “Besides, it's a fool's errand, fetching a stranger, and it's raining cats and dogs out there.”

“I'm not going to ruin my new bonnet and you know it,” Fanny insisted, her eyes flashing stormily. “And it's not a stranger, it's my finest school chum. Polly has been ever so eager to return home, and who else will take care of her? I know you'd rather stay cozied up with your paper, but someone must do the doing.”

Tom sighed deeply, feeling less inclined to argue. He knew his sister's fancy for Polly Sampson, who was as fair and dreamlike as the heroines of her romances. “I shan't be late,” he said, standing up with a groan. “But I must warn you, she'd best be as described, for else I shall not recognize her.”

With a satisfied smile, Fanny leaned over to kiss his cheek. “Polly will recognize you, Tom. She's very particular, she is, and always takes care with her appearance. Besides, she'll be carrying that ribbon sash I gave her. You'll see her.”

Polly Sampson was to arrive from a distant town to visit Fanny, having heard of his sister's beauty and charm through letters. Tom's distaste for the entire arrangement was evident; he found the idea of fetching a girl who had not yet once crossed his path highly Objecting to it as an intrusion on his quiet life, he was yet prevailed upon by Fanny's appeals and the promise of an afternoon respite in Ned Miller's company.

As he stepped out, Tom was not accustomed to such weather. The rain poured down relentlessly, soaking his cloak and forming puddles beneath his feet. The coachman drove him through the slick streets, his horse's hooves splashing in the water. Tom shivered, pulling his collar tighter around his neck, and could not help but wonder what manner of girl Fanny had dragged him to the effort.

He arrived at the station, the clock tower's cheerful chimes dinging out the hour while he waited. The carriage lurched to a halt as a knot of young women descended from the train, chatting animatedly and laughing at some shared joke. Tom noted with consternation that none bore the hint of a ribbon sash, and his anxiety grew with every passing moment. Did he know their faces? Did they recognize him? The uncertainty sat sourly in his stomach.

As the crowd dispersed, one girl approached him, her eyes bright and eager. “Are you...Tom?” she asked, her voice like a fall of bells. “I'm Polly. I've heard so much about you.”

Tom stumbled backward, his cheeks flushing. “Indeed? But how could you recognize me?” he asked, his gaze sweeping over her from head to toe.

Polly laughed, a sound so bright and warm that it banished his remaining doubts. “Of course I recognized you, Tom. You have Fanny's eyes.”

Tom's brow furrowed in surprise, but he offered a hand to facilitate Polly's descent from the crates they had climbed out of. “A good thing Fanny warned me to seek you,” he murmured, helping her upright.

Polly smiled, taking his offered arm. “It's good to see you, Tom. I trust Fanny's letters described you well.”

As they walked to the carriage, the rain continued to pour down. Tom could not help but think of Fanny's assurances that Polly would recognize him without any trouble. Indeed, Polly seemed to have taken quite to him, her chatter filling the silence between them. She asked about the family, the town, and all manners of trivial things that Tom did not think worth mentioning, but he answered dutifully, finding her indistinctive charm disarming.

Once they were safely inside the carriage, Polly leaned forward to touch Tom's sleeve. “Do you know why I wanted to visit?” she asked, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “To see you, of course. I've felt as if I know you well from Fanny's writing.”

Tom raised an eyebrow, giving her an indulgent smile. “Fanny's writing? But you seemed to be acquainted with half the town when I first met you.”

“Ah, well, that's another matter altogether,” Polly said with a laugh. “But it's you who interests me. I wanted to see how you got along and if you shared her warmth and humor."

Tom chuckled, shaking his head. “I fear you'll find me lacking, Polly. I'm a simple man, I am.”

Polly patted his hand, a reassuring smile on her lips.

The next morning dawned with a soft glow filtering through the cracks in the worn shutters of Judith's modest bedroom. She stirred from her sleep, the remnants of a dream still clinging to her mind like a fine mist. Rubbing her eyes, she sat up in bed and gazed out the window, watching as the first rays of sunlight painted the landscape in hues of gold and pink.

As she dressed and made her way downstairs, Judith's thoughts drifted back to the events of the previous day. The encounter with John Storms had left her feeling both exhilarated and anxious. There was something about him, a spark of intelligence and intensity that drew her in despite her best efforts to remain aloof. She could still hear the timbre of his voice, the way he spoke of books and ideas with a passion that matched her own.

Descending the creaking staircase, Judith found her father already awake and seated at the small kitchen table, a cup of steaming tea in hand. His weathered face lit up with a smile as she entered the room, and he motioned for her to join him. She took a seat opposite him, pouring herself a cup of tea and savoring the warmth that spread through her chilled fingers.

"Good morning, my dear," her father said, his voice soft and gravelly with age. "Did you sleep well?"

Judith nodded, a small smile playing on her lips. "Yes, father, I did. Thank you."

They sat in companionable silence for a few moments, the only sound the gentle ticking of the old grandfather clock in the corner. Judith's father reached for a worn leather-bound book on the table, his eyes lighting up with enthusiasm as he opened it to a marked page.

"I came across this passage last night," he began, his voice taking on a reverent tone. "It reminded me of you, my dear. Listen."

As he began to read aloud, Judith felt a swell of emotion rise within her. The words resonated with her in a way she couldn't quite explain, touching something deep within her soul. Her father's love of literature had always been a source of comfort for her, a shared bond that transcended the hardships of their daily life.

After breakfast, Judith decided to take a walk along the edge of the fields, seeking solace in the familiar landscape. The sun was high in the sky now, casting long shadows across the rolling hills and meadows. She wandered aimlessly, lost in thought, until a familiar figure caught her eye.

John Storms was approaching from the distance, his stride purposeful and determined. Judith's heart quickened at the sight of him, a mixture of excitement and uncertainty churning in her stomach. Would he acknowledge her presence, or would he pass by as though she were a mere shadow in the landscape?

As he drew closer, Judith could see a look of concern etched on his handsome features. His eyes met hers, and for a moment, time seemed to stand still. There was an unspoken connection between them, a silent understanding that transcended words.

"Miss Judith," he said, his voice low and urgent. "I must speak with you."

"George, George, come here," exclaimed Lady Raleigh; "you must not leave this spot all day long, as Master Jack may be here at any minute. Do you understand? So go into the field at once and get the pony in, and you had better have him harnessed, all ready to go to the station. And will you go now to the post-office and see if there is a telegram? You might wait there on the chance, or at all events be in readiness. But don't go beyond the grounds, whatever you do. Dear boy, how I love him!"

And perfectly happy in the certainty of everything being properly arranged now that she had given her own orders, Lady Raleigh swept away to arrange a royal feast for the prodigal.

"Please, Mr. Digby, be I to stop here till Master Jack comes?" asked the bewildered George.

Digby laughed quietly, and re-lighted his cigarette.

"If you take my advice, George, do your work as usual, and don't bother about Master Jack. When he does come he won't dream of sending a telegram to say so. That is not Jack's way."

"Will he walk from the station?" asked Lady Joan, carelessly. The others had all strolled away; and, in the presence of the maid who was clearing away the breakfast things, she felt it incumbent upon her to say something commonplace. Digby, who, being a man, felt no such necessity, looked at the pretty little foot that was swinging backwards and forwards, and wondered why she wanted to know.

"Not he! That is not Jack's way either. He will drive up in a coach and four when we have given up expecting him, and want to know why we did not all go down to the station in a body to meet him. Then there will be a hubbub, and Jack will be king of the house again."

"And you will be dethroned?" she asked maliciously.

He heard the question, and did not notice the malice in it.

"Only until he begins to say why he has come, and the rain has spoiled the hay," he said, with another laugh.

With the peculiar good fortune which has attended the oracle of all ages, Digby's prediction came true, and Jack did come home that evening when every one had stopped talking about him, and there was a universal tendency among his brothers and sisters to avoid the topic of his arrival. It was tea-time, and the Squire was standing in the middle of the drawing-room and allowing himself to be coaxed on to his favorite subjects by certain methods known only to his children; though Lady Joan, with her accustomed shrewdness, and partly from a desire to fall into the spirit of her surroundings, however dull they might be, also lent her aid in drawing him out, and Sir Marcus became a willing and unconscious victim.

"Interested in duck-breeding, did you say?" he exclaimed eagerly; "then you shall see something you can't see in Pont Street or any of your swell West End places," forgetting for the moment his envy of Lady Joan's charming house in town. "You shall come over one of our famous duckeries, and see what you've been eating with green peas all the season, and learn how we breed ducks in Murville. It isn't every one who gets the opportunity of coming to the very centre of the most important village industry in the home counties, and it is quite time you saw how the laboring man is kept from starvation by a little help and a little encouragement. Why, let me tell you, though I am a modest man, God knows, and it is not I who should say it, that if it had not been for my letters to the papers, the duck interest would have completely died out in Murville long ago. And where would the working-man have been then? Do you know, my dear young lady, that I, that is, Murville, or rather, I should say, my letter to the county paper has been quoted in the 'Daily Liberal'? There's fame for you! You didn't know you had come to such a world-renowned place, eh? Ah, we are not so hidden in Murville, after all; that is, the--the cause of the elevation of the laborer has its opportunities even in a small village like this."

Zoe, having seen to the household business with her customary diligence that morn, returned to her quiet boudoir where the promise of studies awaited her renewed attention. The room, filled with the soft morning light that filtered through the lace curtains, afforded her a gentle solitude in which the neglect of her books might be redressed, notwithstanding the recent bustle caused by familial departures.

Aunt Dicey, ever the steadfast guardian of domestic order, had already secured the necessary linens and measures from pantry and storeroom earlier in the day, thereby relieving her mistress of any undue interruption in her scholarly pursuits. It was a duty which, though not overtly grand, nonetheless bestowed upon both mistress and servant a quiet pleasure in the seamless management of their humble abode.

It was about this time that the door to the boudoir, with little more than a soft knock, swung open to admit Ella Conly, whose arrival was as unexpected as it was welcome. With her arms already brimming with parcels and her eyes alit with a familiar warmth, she traversed the room as if to declare that no hour was too late for the union of kindred spirits.

Without delay or formality, Ella took her place by Zoe’s side, her presence stirring the quiet air into a congenial conversation. “I had but a fleeting thought,” she remarked in a tone replete with the earnest simplicity so characteristic of our small community, “that you might, in solitude, benefit from the company of one who knows well both the weight and the solace which such moments can bestow.”

As the two settled by the window, soft beams of light dancing upon their hands, Ella began to recount news of her brother, Art, whose labors as a devoted physician had increasingly drawn attention from both the sick and the hopeful. In articulate phrases, she conveyed her deep admiration for his ceaseless dedication to alleviating human suffering, a quality which endeared him to patients as much as his own kin.

Her reminiscence soon took on a tender melancholy as she recalled the times when Art had been a constant pillar of support during her more vulnerable hours. “I remember,” she confided quietly, “how, in my earliest days, his care and gentle reassurances dispelled the gloomiest of my fears, and I am ever grateful for that nurturing presence despite the many demands that now occupy his time.”

Zoe listened with a measured, empathetic gaze, her own thoughts turning toward the delicate balance between duty and desire for intellectual quietude. The tranquility of the room was punctuated by small, occasional sounds of the household—Aunt Dicey bustling about with her customary efficiency, the steady ticking of the old clock upon the mantel—a reminder of the simple rhythms that governed their lives.

In that gentle interlude, Ella revealed further intentions for the day. With a modest air of industrious determination, she spoke of her plan to set about the delicate task of embroidering Christmas gifts for her brothers. “Let not the season of goodwill pass us unobservant,” she declared, “for in the making of these small tokens we may capture the spirit of care that binds our family even as we endure the distance.”

There was, in her tone, a quiet insistence on the virtues of self-reliance and the finer arts of domestic craft. The suggestion, though made without fanfare, imbued the room with an air of purpose that Huiinitiative and familial affection alike would soon share. It was a sentiment that, in the best traditions of our genteel society, transformed an ordinary afternoon into a chapter of shared solace and communal endeavour.

Thus did the hours drift on, with Zoe slowly setting aside her studies to engage in the thoughtful discourse fostered by her guest, both of them enveloped in the prosperous quietude of a day that promised a melding of heart and home. Ideas, kindly and reflective, passed between them as naturally as the light across the patterned rug.

Outside, the winter wind, though distant, hinted at the approach of colder days, and the thought of a forthcoming winter at Viamede lent an added urgency to their idle promises. Yet within, beneath the shelter of familiar walls, the warmth of conversation and the gentle spirit of shared craft stood in firm opposition to the harshness of nature beyond.

Even as the day advanced, a calm determination prevailed that neither solitude nor departure would ever diminish the quiet joys of companionship and the relentless pursuit of domestic artistry. In the soft murmur of their voices and the subtle motions of their hands, there was found a testament to the enduring bonds of family and friendship, celebrated in every modest endeavor of the heart.

It was, perhaps, in such moments that one might discern the true nature of life—a composition wrought of small kindnesses and steadfast traditions, in which each small act of care contributed to a larger tapestry of enduring love and dutiful commitment.

The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word.

The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth.

At last the children reached the summit in front of the hut. When Deta saw the little party of climbers she cried out shrilly: "Heidi, what have you done? What a sight you are! Where are your dresses and your shawl? Are the new shoes gone that I just bought for you, and the new stockings that I made myself? Where are they all, Heidi?"

The child quietly pointed down and said "There."

The aunt followed the direction of her finger and descried a little heap with a small red dot in the middle, which she recognized as the shawl.

"Unlucky child!" Deta said excitedly. "What does all this mean? Why have you taken your things all off?"

"Because I do not need them," said the child, not seeming in the least repentant of her deed.

"How can you be so stupid, Heidi? Have you lost your senses?" the aunt went on, in a tone of mingled vexation and reproach. "Who do you think will go way down there to fetch those things up again? It is half-an-hour's walk. Please, Peter, run down and get them. Do not stand and stare at me as if you were glued to the spot."

"I am late already," replied Peter, and stood without moving from the place where, with his hands in his trousers' pockets, he had witnessed the violent outbreak of Heidi's aunt.

"There you are, standing and staring, but that won't get you further," said Deta. "I'll give you this if you go down." With that she held a five-penny-piece under his eyes. That made Peter start and in a great hurry he ran down the straightest path. He arrived again in so short a time that Deta had to praise him and gave him her little coin without delay. He did not often get such a treasure, and therefore his face was beaming and he laughingly dropped the money deep into his pocket.

"If you are going up to the uncle, as we are, you can carry the pack till we get there," said Deta. They still had to climb a steep ascent that lay behind Peter's hut. The boy readily took the things and followed Deta, his left arm holding the bundle and his right swinging the stick. Heidi jumped along gaily by his side with the goats.

'You must take care what you say to Lizzie about the Hazlebys,' said Lady Merton; 'a very little might make it appear that we wished to set her against her step-mother's relations.'

'Oh! that would never do,' said Anne, 'but I am afraid it will be very difficult to keep from shewing what we think, if Mrs. Hazleby is all that Lizzie says.'

'Your Papa was pleased with what he saw of Major Hazleby last year,' said Lady Merton.

'Oh yes, Lizzie likes him very much,' said Anne; 'it is the lady of whom she has such a horror.'

'I should fancy,' said Lady Merton, 'that Mrs. Woodbourne's horror of her was almost equal to Lizzie's.'

'Kind gentle Aunt Mildred,' said Anne, 'do you think she ever had a horror of anyone?'

'It is certainly rather a strong word,' said Lady Merton, 'but you will allow me to say that she has a great dread of her; I think Mrs. Hazleby scolds and frightens her.'

'What a fury she must be,' said Anne, laughing, 'to be able to scold and frighten such a gentle Desdomona as Mrs. Woodbourne.'

'Do not say too much on that subject,' said Lady Merton, 'or we shall be forced to call your beloved Lizzie a fury.'

'O Mamma!' cried Anne, 'you cannot say that she is impetuous and violent now. She used, I allow, to be rather overbearing to Mrs. Woodbourne; but that was before she was old enough fully to feel and love her gentleness. Then she did take advantage of it, and argue, and dispute, but now--'

'She has her own way without disputing,' said Lady Merton.

'O Mamma, do you think so?' said Anne, as if she thought it a terrible accusation. 'Yes, I really think that she has, but then her way is generally right.'

'Yes,' said Lady Merton, 'she is in some respects more fit to govern herself than most girls of sixteen. Her good sense will keep her from going very far wrong.'

'Very far, Mamma?' repeated Anne.

'Yes, for such an excitable impetuous creature is not likely to escape going wrong, without steady control from herself or from someone else,' said Lady Merton.

'But I can hardly imagine Lizzie's actually doing wrong,' said Anne; 'we were certainly both naughty children, but I think the worst we did, was rather what makes nurses scold, than what would seriously displease you or Papa.'

'Oh! she was always an upright, noble-spirited child,' said Lady Merton.

'And now,' continued Anne, 'when she is much interested in anything, when her brilliant dark eyes are lighted up, and her beautiful smile is on her lips, and her whole face is full of brightness, and she looks slight and airy enough to be a spirit, and when she is talking about some things--I could fancy her some higher kind of creature.'

Lady Merton smiled. 'I think I know what you mean,' said she; 'I used to feel something of the kind with her mother.'

'What a wonderful person Aunt Katherine must have been!' cried Anne. She paused, and presently added, 'Mamma, I do not know whether I ought to say so, but much as I like Mrs. Woodbourne, I do rather wonder that Uncle Woodbourne married again.'

'So did your Papa and I,' said Lady Merton; 'but you must excuse him, when you think of his three little girls, Elizabeth especially, requiring such anxious care of body and mind.'

'But you do not think Mrs. Woodbourne could manage Lizzie?' said Anne.

'No,' said Lady Merton, 'she could not manage her in the least, but her mild influence has, I think, been of great service to her. Lizzie has certainly grown more gentle of late, and I think it is from consideration for her and the little children.'

'And I suppose,' said Anne, 'that Mrs. Woodbourne has done as much for Kate as anyone could.'

One April day the heat was almost insupportable; but the sun's rays were not those brazen beams that sometimes in Northern cities burn the air and scorch the pavements to a white heat; rather were they soft and still; the moist earth exhaled her richness, not a leaf stirred, and the whole level country seemed sitting in a hot vapor-bath. In the early dawn the keeper had performed his outdoor tasks, but all day he remained almost without stirring in his chair between two windows, striving to exist. At high noon out came a little black bringing his supplies from the town, whistling and shuffling along, gay as a lark. The keeper watched him coming slowly down the white road, loitering by the way in the hot blaze, stopping to turn a somersault or two, to dangle over a bridge rail, to execute various impromptu capers all by himself. He reached the gate at last, entered, and, having come all the way up the path in a hornpipe step, he set down his basket at the door to indulge in one long and final double-shuffle before knocking. "Stop that!" said the keeper through the closed blinds. The little darkey darted back; but as nothing further came out of the window--a boot, for instance, or some other stray missile--he took courage, showed his ivories, and drew near again. "Do you suppose I am going to have you stirring up the heat in that way?" demanded the keeper.

The little black grinned, but made no reply, unless smoothing the hot white sand with his black toes could be construed as such; he now removed his rimless hat and made a bow.

"Is it, or is it not warm?" asked the keeper, as a naturalist might inquire of a salamander, not referring to his own so much as to the salamander's ideas on the subject.

"Dunno, mars'," replied the little black.

"How do you feel?"

"'Spects I feel all right, mars'."

The keeper gave up the investigation, and presented to the salamander a nickel cent. "I suppose there is no such thing as a cool spring in all this melting country," he said.

But the salamander indicated with his thumb a clump of trees on the green plain north of the cemetery. "Ole Mars' Ward's place--cole spring dah." He then departed, breaking into a run after he had passed the gate, his ample mouth watering at the thought of a certain chunk of taffy at the mercantile establishment kept by Aunt Dinah in a corner of her one-roomed cabin. At sunset the keeper went thirstily out with a tin pail on his arm, in search of the cold spring. "If it could only be like the spring down under the rocks where I used to drink when I was a boy!" he thought. He had never walked in that direction before. Indeed, now that he had abandoned the town, he seldom went beyond the walls of the cemetery. An old road led across to the clump of trees, through fields run to waste, and following it he came to the place, a deserted house with tumble-down fences and overgrown garden, the out-buildings indicating that once upon a time there were many servants and a prosperous master. The house was of wood, large on the ground, with encircling piazzas; across the front door rough bars had been nailed, and the closed blinds were protected in the same manner; from long want of paint the clapboards were gray and mossy, and the floor of the piazza had fallen in here and there from decay. The keeper decided that his cemetery was a much more cheerful place than this, and then he looked around for the spring. Behind the house the ground sloped down; it must be there. He went around and came suddenly upon a man lying on an old rug outside of a back door. "Excuse me. I thought nobody lived here," he said.

Half a dozen Chicago newsboys, varying in age from ten to sixteen years, with piles of papers in their hands, joined in the chorus.

They were standing in front and at the sides of the Sherman House, on the corner of Clark and Randolph Streets, one of the noted buildings in the Lake City. On the opposite side of Randolph Street stands a gloomy stone structure, the Court House and City Hall. In the shadow of these buildings, at the corner, Luke Walton, one of the largest newsboys, had posted himself. There was something about his bearing and appearance which distinguished him in a noticeable way from his companions.

To begin with, he looked out of place. He was well grown, with a frank, handsome face, and was better dressed than the average newsboy. That was one reason, perhaps, why he preferred to be by himself, rather than to engage in the scramble for customers which was the habit of the boys around him.

It was half-past five. The numerous cars that passed were full of business men, clerks, and boys, returning to their homes after a busy day.

Luke had but two papers left, but these two for some unaccountable reason remained on his hands an unusual length of time. But at length a comfortable-looking gentleman of middle age, coming from the direction of La Salle Street, paused and said, "You may give me a News, my boy."

"Here you are, sir," he said, briskly.

The gentleman took the paper, and thrusting his hand into his pocket, began to feel for a penny, but apparently without success.

"I declare," he said, smiling, "I believe I am penniless. I have nothing but a five-dollar bill."

"Never mind, sir! Take the paper and pay me to morrow."

"But I may not see you."

"I am generally here about this time."

"And if I shouldn't see you, you will lose the penny."

"I will risk it, sir," said Luke, smiling.

"You appear to have confidence in me."

"Yes, sir."

"Then it is only fair that I should have confidence in you."

Luke looked puzzled, for he didn't quite understand what was in the gentleman's mind.

"I will take both of your papers. Here is a five-dollar bill. You may bring me the change to-morrow, at my office, No. 155 La Salle Street. My name is Benjamin Afton."

"But, sir," objected Luke, "there is no occasion for this. It is much better that I should trust you for two cents than that you should trust me with five dollars."

"Probably the two cents are as important to you as five dollars to me. At any rate, it is a matter of confidence, and I am quite willing to trust you."

"Thank you, sir, but----"

"I shall have to leave you, or I shall be home late to dinner."

Before Luke had a chance to protest further, he found himself alone, his stock of papers exhausted, and a five-dollar bill in his hand.

While he stood on the corner in some perplexity, a newsboy crossed Randolph Street, and accosted him.

"My eyes, if you ain't in luck, Luke Walton," he said. "Where did you get that bill? Is it a one?"

"No, it's a five."

"Where'd you get it?"

"A gentleman just bought two papers of me."

"And gave you five dollars! You don't expect me to swaller all that, do you?"

"I'm to bring him the change to-morrow," continued Luke.

The other boy nearly doubled up with merriment.

"Wasn't he jolly green, though?" he ejaculated.

"Why was he?" asked Luke, who by this time felt considerably annoyed.

"He'll have to whistle for his money."

"Why will he?"

"Cause he will."

"He won't do anything of the sort. I shall take him his change to-morrow morning."

"What?" ejaculated Tom Brooks.

"I shall carry him his change in the morning--four dollars and ninety-eight cents. Can't you understand that?"

Their acquisitions were distributed through the various rooms. A crib filled with hay and a cork cathedral decorated the museum.

On Pécuchet's chimney-piece there was a St. John the Baptist in wax; along the corridor were ranged the portraits of episcopal dignitaries; and at the bottom of the staircase, under a chained lamp, stood a Blessed Virgin in an azure mantle and a crown of stars. What a pity that the St. Peter was broken, and how nicely it would have done in the vestibule!

Pécuchet stopped sometimes before the old pit for composts, where he discovered the tiara, one sandal, and the tip of an ear; allowed sighs to escape him, then went on gardening, for now he combined manual labour with religious exercises, and dug the soil attired in the monk's habit, comparing himself to Bruno. This disguise might be a sacrilege. He gave it up.

But he assumed the ecclesiastical style, no doubt owing to his intimacy with the curé. He had the same smile, the same tone of voice, and, like the priest too, he slipped both hands with a chilly air into his sleeves up to the wrists. A day came when he was pestered by the crowing of the cock and disgusted with the roses; he no longer went out, or only cast sullen glances over the fields.

Bouvard suffered himself to be led to the May devotions. The children singing hymns, the gorgeous display of lilacs, the festoons of verdure, had imparted to him, so to speak, a feeling of imperishable youth. God manifested Himself to his heart through the fashioning of nests, the transparency of fountains, the bounty of the sun; and his friend's devotion appeared to him extravagant, fastidious.

"Why do you groan during mealtime?"

"We ought to eat with groans," returned Pécuchet, "for it was in that way that man lost his innocence"--a phrase which he had read in the Seminarist's Manual, two duodecimo volumes he had borrowed from M. Jeufroy: and he drank some of the water of La Salette, gave himself up with closed doors to ejaculatory prayers, and aspired to join the confraternity of St. Francis.

The early morning sun rose gently over the rugged peaks, casting long shadows down the slopes of Cader Idris. The village of Aber-Aydyr stirred awake slowly, with the smoke from the hearths curling lazily into the crisp, invigorating air. George Bowring, with a determination peculiar to his character, had already shaken off the last vestiges of sleep and was bustling about with great energy, tightening straps and checking the provisions for our next leg of adventure. His vigour was infectious, and I found myself soon ready despite the reluctance of my limbs, weary from days of hearty travel. We stood for a moment in silence, surveying the green pastures and the sheep that grazed contentedly below.

As we prepared to leave the quaint village, we were met by Glyn Owen, a sturdy young farmer, whose broad shoulders and ruby cheeks betokened a life lived in harmony with the land. "Morning's come fair and bright for your climb, sirs," said Owen, with a jovial nod. "But mind you, the weather here can turn like a maiden's mood. Best make haste up the ridge if you mean to avoid the clouds." This counsel, delivered with simple sincerity, gave George cause to clap the fellow on the back in appreciation, and we ventured on with renewed enthusiasm, our spirits buoyed by both the kindness of the stranger and the gleam of adventure ahead.

Once on the path, our conversation turned to the craggy landscape unfolding before us, stark and imposing. The earth here was untouched by city hands, with nature asserting her unyielding dominion over hill and hollow. We marveled at the beauty, peculiar in its wildness, and a world apart from the grey smog of London. George spoke with admiration, "Here, where the land is uncompromising and pure, one gains a truer perspective of existence, stripped to fundamentals." His statement, profound in its simplicity, lingered on the air as we continued our ascent amid the sporadic cry of a hawk cutting through the morning calm.

As the path looped ever upward, a veil of mist began to envelop the mountain, bringing with it an uncanny stillness. It was as though the peaks themselves were holding their breath, watching and waiting for some ancient and unseen cue from the elements. George, unperturbed, pressed on, his pace steady and unyielding, while my thoughts drifted towards an older world where men told tales by firelight of mountain spirits and fateful encounters. The clouds around us thickened, and the air grew chill, the sense of otherworldliness deepening with each step we took into the heights.

All at once, the mist parted, revealing a panorama so grand it commanded silence. The land stretched limitless and vast; valleys swooped down into the shadowed embrace of distant hills, kissed by streams that glinted like quicksilver. I pondered over this great expanse, breathing in the majesty and the mystery of the place. George turned to me with a peculiar gleam in his eye, "The world holds uncountable wonders beyond title and rank—a humbling thought in our present epoch, is it not?" I nodded, sharing the sentiment that amidst such grandeur, our own affairs seemed fleeting and insubstantial as a wandering breeze.

Our reflections were cut short by a shift in the wind, and the reticent sun found the courage to shine full upon us again. We were fools to think the mist the mountain's last defense, as a gust now carried with it a fine spray of rain. Laughing, we drew close, hoods pulled over our heads, aware that for all our plans and preparations, we were merely guests of this ancient sovereignty. Pressing onward towards the summit, we embraced the elements—an exhilarating, fleeting triumph of man against the mountain's ever-watchful eye. Here, in this unforgettable theater of stone and sky, we found ourselves anew, and I knew, with certainty, that whatever awaited us next would be met with the full measure of our courage and friendship.

Jenn–ell, there is really not much to describe about Jenny, beyond that she was sweetly little, had a winning old-fashioned air about her, was very good, that is, very kind, and was adored by the school-children, whom she taught first for love and then for dress and pocket-money. She was but nineteen, and all unminted woman as yet. No lover had yet come to stamp her features with his masterful superscription. Was she pretty? Heroines ought to be either very pretty or very plain. Well, the beauty that was going to be was as yet only beginning at the eyes. They were already beautiful. No, she wasn't pretty yet, but she wasn't plain.

Jenny's face slept as yet. When the fairy prince came and kissed it, there was no telling to what beauty it would awake. The fairy prince! That was going to be our friend Theophil, of course. Well, of course, though it's a little early on to admit it. However, I am unequal to the task of concealing from the hawk-eyed reader through a succession of chapters that Jenny and Theophil were to be each other's "fates." Of course, he hadn't been there a month before Jenny's face was beginning to wear that superscription of his passionate intelligence, to grow merry from his laughter, and still sweeter by his kisses.

Of course, Theophil and Jenny fell in love. Do you think it was merely to save New Zion and to bring the Renaissance to Coalchester that Theophilus Londonderry was sent to live in Zion Plac–r for any other purpose less important than to love Jenny? Yes, we may as well take that for granted as we begin the next chapter.
