To Franz Liszt

In a Spanish city on an island in the Mediterranean, there stands a convent of the Order of Barefoot Carmelites, where the rule instituted by St. Theresa is still preserved with all the first rigor of the reformation brought about by that illustrious woman. Extraordinary as this may seem, it is none the less true. Almost every religious house in the Peninsula, or in Europe for that matter, was either destroyed or disorganized by the outbreak of the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars; but as this island was protected through those times by the English fleet, its wealthy convent and peaceable inhabitants were secure from the general trouble and spoliation. The storms of many kinds which shook the first fifteen years of the nineteenth century spent their force before they reached those cliffs at so short a distance from the coast of Andalusia.

If the rumour of the Emperor’s name so much as reached the shore of the island, it is doubtful whether the holy women kneeling in the cloisters grasped the reality of his dream-like progress of glory, or the majesty that blazed in flame across kingdom after kingdom during his meteor life.

In the minds of the Roman Catholic world, the convent stood out pre-eminent for a stern discipline which nothing had changed; the purity of its rule had attracted unhappy women from the furthest parts of Europe, women deprived of all human ties, sighing after the long suicide accomplished in the breast of God. No convent, indeed, was so well fitted for that complete detachment of the soul from all earthly things, which is demanded by the religious life, albeit on the continent of Europe there are many convents magnificently adapted to the purpose of their existence. Buried away in the loneliest valleys, hanging in mid-air on the steepest mountainsides, set down on the brink of precipices, in every place man has sought for the poetry of the Infinite, the solemn awe of Silence; in every place man has striven to draw closer to God, seeking Him on mountain peaks, in the depths below the crags, at the cliff’s edge; and everywhere man has found God. But nowhere, save on this half-European, half-African ledge of rock could you find so many different harmonies, combining so to raise the soul, that the sharpest pain comes to be like other memories; the strongest impressions are dulled, till the sorrows of life are laid to rest in the depths.

The convent stands on the highest point of the crags at the uttermost end of the island. On the side towards the sea the rock was once rent sheer away in some globe-cataclysm; it rises up a straight wall from the base where the waves gnaw at the stone below high-water mark. Any assault is made impossible by the dangerous reefs that stretch far out to sea, with the sparkling waves of the Mediterranean playing over them. So, only from the sea can you discern the square mass of the convent built conformably to the minute rules laid down as to the shape, height, doors, and windows of monastic buildings. From the side of the town, the church completely hides the solid structure of the cloisters and their roofs, covered with broad slabs of stone impervious to sun or storm or gales of wind.

The church itself, built by the munificence of a Spanish family, is the crowning edifice of the town. Its fine, bold front gives an imposing and picturesque look to the little city in the sea. The sight of such a city, with its close-huddled roofs, arranged for the most part amphitheatre-wise above a picturesque harbour, and crowned by a glorious cathedral front with triple-arched Gothic doorways, belfry towers, and filigree spires, is a spectacle surely in every way the sublimest on earth. Religion towering above daily life, to put men continually in mind of the End and the way, is in truth a thoroughly Spanish conception. But now surround this picture by the Mediterranean, and a burning sky, imagine a few palms here and there, a few stunted evergreen trees mingling their waving leaves with the motionless flowers and foliage of carved stone; look out over the reef with its white fringes of foam in contrast to the sapphire sea; and then turn to the city, with its galleries and terraces whither the townsfolk come to take the air among their flowers of an evening, above the houses and the tops of the trees in their little gardens; add a few sails down in the harbour; and lastly, in the stillness of falling night, listen to the organ music, the chanting of the services, the wonderful sound of bells pealing out over the open sea. There is sound and silence everywhere; oftener still there is silence over all.

The streets of Paris echoed with the heavy footsteps of tired and weary artists, their faces etched with the burdens of their craft. The air was thick with a sense of desperation, as if every passing moment was a battle against time itself. In the dimly lit alleys, one could hear the whispers of broken dreams and the cries of those who had given everything to their art, only to be left empty-handed.

Among this sea of struggling souls was a young painter named Emile, his once bright eyes now dulled by the weight of his ambitions. He had come to Paris with dreams of fame and fortune, but now found himself drowning in debt and despair. His days were spent toiling away in a cramped studio, his nights haunted by the specter of his creditors.

Despite the hardships he faced, Emile held on to a flicker of hope that burned deep within his heart. He believed that through his art, he could transcend the boundaries of his reality and touch the lives of others in ways he never thought possible. But as the days turned into weeks and the weeks into months, that hope began to wane, replaced by a sense of resignation to his fate.

The city itself seemed to conspire against him, its polluted air seeping into his lungs and clouding his thoughts. The once grand boulevards were now filled with the stench of decay, a stark reminder of the moral degradation that permeated every corner of Paris. The upper class reveled in their lavish parties and extravagant lifestyles, while the lower and middle classes struggled to make ends meet, their existence a constant battle against poverty and neglect.

Emile, like many of his fellow artists, found solace in the arms of pleasure, seeking refuge from the harsh realities of his life in the fleeting embrace of temporary distractions. But even in the midst of his hedonistic pursuits, he could not escape the overwhelming sense of emptiness that gnawed at his soul.

One fateful night, as he wandered the streets in search of inspiration, Emile stumbled upon a hidden alleyway that seemed to beckon to him with a whisper of mystery. Intrigued, he followed the winding path until he came upon a small, unassuming shop tucked away in the shadows.

As he stepped inside, the air was heavy with the scent of incense and ancient tomes, the shelves lined with curious artifacts and strange trinkets. At the center of the room sat a figure cloaked in darkness, their eyes gleaming with an otherworldly light.

"You seek answers, young artist?" the figure spoke, their voice a low, melodious hum that seemed to reverberate through Emile's very being.

Emile nodded, his heart pounding with a mixture of fear and excitement. "I seek truth, wisdom, a way to transcend this world of illusion and find my place among the stars."

The figure smiled, a knowing glint in their eyes. "You have come to the right place, my dear Emile. For I am the keeper of secrets, the guardian of mysteries. I can show you the path to enlightenment, but be warned, the journey will not be easy."

Without hesitation, Emile accepted the figure's offer, his curiosity outweighing any sense of caution. And so began his descent into a world beyond his wildest imagination, where reality blurred with fantasy and the boundaries of his existence were tested in ways he could never have imagined.

The sun hung low in the sky, casting a golden hue over the rough-hewn stockade that stood as a silent sentinel against the wilderness. The air was thick with the scent of pine and the distant chirping of birds, their songs carrying a sense of calm that contrasted with the restless energy Leonidas felt within him. He had not expected to encounter anyone upon his return to the stockade, least of all a woman of such delicate and refined appearance.

She was lean and tall, her form slight and graceful, though her eyes betrayed a kind of quiet strength that belied her gentle demeanor. Her attire was of a finer sort, the fabric soft and flowing, with lace adorning her sleeves and neckline. Her hair, dark and glossy, was piled high upon her head, though a few strands had escaped and framed her face, giving her an air of both sophistication and vulnerability. It was her eyes, however, that drew his attention the most—they were a deep, warm brown, flecked with hints of gold, and they bore a look of earnestness that made him feel as though he were being studied with a keen and discerning gaze.

“Come here—please—won’t you?” she repeated, her voice soft yet clear, with a lilt that suggested she was accustomed to being obeyed. There was a kindness in her tone that soothed him, though he could not help but wonder what a woman of her station and apparent delicacy was doing at a place as rough and isolated as this stockade.

Leonidas hesitated only for a moment before stepping closer, his boots crunching softly against the gravel beneath his feet. “Ma’am,” he began, tipping his hat in a gentlemanly manner, “I’m at your service.”

She smiled, a small, delicate curve of her lips that seemed to lighten the entire area. “Thank you,” she said, her voice warm and inviting. “I’m in need of a favor, and I was hoping you might be able to assist me.”

Her request was simple enough, though it carried a weight that made Leonidas pause. She asked him to post a letter for her, the address written in a neat, precise hand upon the envelope. She made him swear not to read the address or to speak of the task to anyone, her eyes never leaving his face as she imparted this condition. There was something about the way she spoke that made him feel as though he were being trusted with a secret of great importance, and he found himself nodding in agreement without a second thought.

“It’s not much to ask,” she said, her tone apologetic. “But it means a great deal to me.”

Leonidas shook his head. “Not at all, ma’am. I’m honored to be of service.”

She hesitated, her fingers intertwining as though she were nervous, and then she produced a small coin from her purse—a half-dollar, gleaming in the sunlight. “For your trouble,” she said, offering it to him with a slight bow of her head.

But Leonidas found himself stepping back, his pride swelling within him. “I couldn’t accept payment for such a small favor,” he said, his voice firm. “It would be my pleasure to see to it that your letter is delivered.”

She frowned, her brow furrowing in a way that made him wonder if he had done the right thing. “Are you sure?” she asked, her voice tinged with a hint of doubt. “You know, there could be questions asked… at home.”

Leonidas felt a pang of guilt, though he refused to let it show. “I assure you, ma’am, I’ll say nothing of this. Your trust means a great deal to me.”

She studied him for a moment longer, as though weighing his words, and then she nodded, a small smile returning to her lips. “Thank you,” she said softly. “You have my gratitude.”

Leonidas watched as she turned and walked away, her skirts rustling softly as she moved. She did not look back, and though he tried to convince himself that he was merely curious, he found himself following her with his eyes until she was out of sight. There was something about her that intrigued him, a sense of mystery that clung to her like a shroud, and he couldn’t help but wonder what lay behind her quiet, unassuming exterior.

As the days passed, Leonidas found himself thinking often of the woman he had encountered at the stockade. He had gone about his business as usual, posting the letter without so much as glancing at the address, just as she had requested. But the memory of her smile, her demeanor, and the way she had placed such trust in him lingered in his mind, refusing to be dispelled.

He had hoped to see her again, to learn more about the woman who had sought him out in such an unlikely place. But the days turned into weeks, and though he passed by the stockade many times, he never once encountered her. It was as though she had vanished into the ether, leaving behind only the faintest trace of her presence.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon and the stars began to sprinkle the sky, Leonidas found himself walking along the same path that had led him to the stockade all those weeks ago. The air was cool, carrying with it the scent of the approaching autumn, and the leaves crunched beneath his feet as he walked. He had no particular destination in mind, but the walk itself was soothing, a chance to clear his mind of the constant chatter of his thoughts.

As he rounded a bend in the path, he was startled to see a figure ahead of him, walking in the opposite direction. At first, he thought it was just another traveler, someone making their way through the wilderness. But as he drew closer, he realized with a start that it was her—the woman from the stockade.

She was walking quickly, her hands clenched at her sides, her expression one of urgency. There was a tension about her that he had never noticed before, a stiffness in her posture that spoke of hidden worries. She did not see him at first, her gaze fixed on the path ahead, and Leonidas found himself pausing, unsure of what to do.

“Ma’am,” he called out, his voice hesitant. “Is everything all right?”

She stopped in her tracks, turning to face him with a start. For a moment, her expression was one of surprise, and then she seemed to relax, her features softening into a look of recognition.

“Leonidas,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper. “I wasn’t expecting to see you here.”

He stepped closer, his heart pounding in his chest. “I could say the same,” he replied, his voice steady despite the turmoil within him. “What brings you out this way?”

She hesitated, her eyes darting around as though she were searching for something—or someone. “I… I’m just taking a walk,” she said, her voice trembling slightly. “I needed some air.”

Leonidas studied her closely, his instincts telling him that there was more to her story than she was letting on. “If you don’t mind my asking, ma’am, are you in some sort of trouble?”

She seemed to consider him for a moment, her eyes narrowing as though she were weighing her options. “No,” she said finally, her tone firm. “I’m fine. Thank you for your concern.”

Leonidas was not convinced, but he knew better than to press the issue. Instead, he offered her a polite smile. “Well, if you ever find yourself in need of assistance again, you know where to find me.”

She nodded, her expression softening once more. “Thank you,” she said. “I appreciate it.”

With that, she turned and continued on her way, her步伐 quick and purposeful, as though she were eager to put as much distance between herself and Leonidas as possible. He watched her go, his mind racing with questions and suspicions. There was something about her that insisted she was not just a simple woman taking a walk in the evening air. But no matter how hard he tried, he could not quite put his finger on what it was.

As the days turned into weeks, Leonidas found himself returning to the stockade more often, his mind constantly drawn back to the encounter with the mysterious woman. He had sworn to her that he would not speak of the letter, and though part of him wondered why she had been so insistent on secrecy, he had no intention of breaking his word. Still, the mystery of it all gnawed at him, refusing to be ignored.

One evening, as he stood at the stockade, the setting sun casting long, shadowy fingers across the landscape, Leonidas was startled by the sound of approaching footsteps. He turned, expecting to see a traveler or perhaps a local, but what he found instead was the woman—again.

This time, she did not seem surprised to see him. In fact, she appeared almost as though she had been expecting him. “Leonidas,” she said, her voice calm and steady, “I need your help again.”

Leonidas frowned, his heart sinking. “Ma’am,” he began, “I thought I made it clear—”

She held up a hand, silencing him. “No, no,” she said, her tone apologetic. “It’s nothing like that. I’m not asking you to post another letter. I… I need someone to look after something for me.”

He crossed his arms, his skepticism evident. “And why would you come to me for such a thing?”

She hesitated, her eyes darting around once more, as though she were searching for an escape. “Because… because I trust you,” she said at last, her voice barely audible.

Leonidas was taken aback by the sincerity in her tone. “You trust me?” he repeated, his voice tinged with disbelief.

“Yes,” she said, her gaze meeting his once more. “I trust you.”

And with that, she reached into her purse and pulled out a small, ornately carved box, its surface光滑 and polished. She placed it in his hands, her fingers brushing against his for a moment before withdrawing. “Please,” she said, her voice urgent. “Keep this safe for me. And whatever you do, don’t open it.”

Leonidas felt a strange mixture of emotions: curiosity, apprehension, and a growing sense of unease. “Ma’am,” he said, his voice firm, “I don’t know what you’re involved in, but—”

“Leonidas,” she interrupted, her tone sharp but softened by a hint of desperation. “Please. Just this once, trust me.”

He looked at the box in his hands, its weight a tangible reminder of the mystery that surrounded her. “Why can’t you keep it yourself?”

She shook her head, her expression one of quiet frustration. “It’s not safe for me to have it. I need someone I can trust to look after it.”

Leonidas studied her for a long moment, his mind racing. Part of him wanted to refuse outright, to tell her that he had no interest in being involved in whatever shady dealings she might be up to. But then he thought of the way she had looked at him when she had asked him to post the letter, the trust in her eyes, and he found himself nodding in agreement.

“All right,” he said, his voice heavy with reluctance. “I’ll keep it safe. But if anything happens because of this—”

“Nothing will happen,” she interrupted, her tone firm. “I promise.”

With that, she turned and walked away, leaving Leonidas alone with the mysterious box. He examined it for a moment, running his fingers over its surface, before tucking it away in his pocket. Whatever secrets it held, he knew that he was now irrevocably tied to the woman who had placed it in his care. And as much as he tried to convince himself otherwise, he couldn’t help but feel a growing sense of unease in the pit of his stomach.

DECEMBER 28th, 1764.—It is a curious sensation, this feeling of being adrift upon the sea of memory. One searches the depths, not always for treasure, but often merely to assure oneself that the ship of one's life has, indeed, sailed the courses one believes it has. I find myself, in these latter years, increasingly drawn to the shadows of the past, to the dim-lit chambers where the echoes of long-dead voices linger. Perhaps it is a comfort, a way of warding off the chill of the encroaching night. Whatever the cause, my mind returns, with an almost painful clarity, to events that transpired long before my own humble existence became intertwined with the matter I am now compelled to relate. It is a history, in truth, that hinges upon the actions of men and women I never knew, yet whose choices shaped the very fabric of my life, no less than the lives of those closest to me. To tell the tale of the strange happenings at Oakhaven Grange, I must first delve into the history of the family who dwelt there, a history steeped in secrets, shrouded in whispers, and marked by a peculiar isolation from the wider world. Oakhaven Grange, nestled deep within the folds of the Derbyshire hills, stood as a testament to a bygone era. Originally a small hunting lodge, it had gradually expanded over the centuries, each generation adding their own imprint to the structure. Its grey stone walls, weathered by countless seasons, spoke of resilience and endurance. The roof, a patchwork of slate tiles, sloped steeply, protecting the inhabitants from the harsh winds that swept across the moor. The windows, small and leaded, cast an amber glow upon the interior, creating an atmosphere of perpetual twilight. The Grange was surrounded by ancient oak trees, their gnarled branches reaching skyward like supplicating arms. These trees, silent sentinels, had witnessed generations of the Ashworth family come and go. They had seen births and deaths, joys and sorrows, loves and betrayals. They held within their rings the secrets of Oakhaven Grange, secrets that time had not yet erased. To approach the Grange, one had to traverse a narrow, winding lane, bordered by overgrown hedges and shadowed by looming trees. The lane was often muddy, churned up by the hooves of horses and the wheels of carriages. It was a lonely place, far removed from the bustle of towns and villages. Few travellers ventured down this path, and those who did were often met with suspicion by the inhabitants of the Grange. The Ashworths had always been a reclusive family, preferring the solitude of their estate to the company of outsiders. They were a proud family, descended from a long line of landowners and merchants. In the early years of the 18th century, Oakhaven Grange was owned by Mr. Silas Ashworth, a man of austere habits and unwavering convictions. He was a descendant of staunch Puritans, and his life was governed by a strict moral code. Mr. Ashworth was a man of few words, but his pronouncements carried considerable weight within the household. He held strong opinions on matters of religion and politics, and he was not afraid to express them, regardless of the consequences. His wife, Mrs. Eliza Ashworth, was a woman of gentler disposition. She was a devout woman, but her faith was tempered with compassion and understanding. Mrs. Ashworth was a skilled herbalist and healer, and she was often called upon to tend to the sick and injured in the surrounding villages. She was beloved by the local people, who saw her as a source of comfort and solace. Mr. and Mrs. Ashworth had one child, a daughter named Miss Clara Ashworth. She was a beautiful young woman, with raven hair, piercing blue eyes, and a graceful demeanor. Miss Ashworth was a voracious reader, and she spent much of her time immersed in books. She was fascinated by history, literature, and philosophy. She possessed a keen intellect and a thirst for knowledge. However, her intellectual curiosity was often at odds with the limited opportunities available to women in that era. She yearned for a life beyond the confines of Oakhaven Grange, but she knew that her duty lay in fulfilling her parents' expectations.The Ashworths were not entirely isolated from the outside world. They maintained a small circle of acquaintances, consisting mainly of other landowners and clergymen. They attended church regularly, and they participated in local social events. However, they always kept a certain distance from their neighbors. They were viewed with a mixture of respect and suspicion by the local community.

In the weary light of dawn, the landscape lay still, as though holding its breath in anticipation of what was to come. The air was crisp with the chill of the morning, setting a stark contrast against the smoldering remnants of the campfire around which the sentries huddled. Major Dewes stood apart from his men, a solitary figure under the waning moon, mulling over the fragments of Linforth’s last letter. The paper, now creased and worn from handling, bore the whispered farewell of a life abruptly severed.

"Love is a quiet vigil," Linforth had penned, “a keeper of promises yet to be fulfilled.” The words echoed in Dewes' mind as he looked towards the distant hills, their shadows stretching long into the waking day. He could feel the weight of Linforth's resolve heavy upon his shoulders, a mantle passed without ceremony or even intention. And yet, amidst the hardship and danger, there was a purpose resilient enough to bridge the void left by his comrade's fall.

Dewes turned to Luffe, who approached with a brisk stride that belied the heaviness of his heart. Luffe’s eyes were set with a flinty determination, his mind already ticking over the details of their next move. Though Linforth’s absence was like a wound, raw and insistent, the mission's momentum surged onward, unperturbed by individual loss.

"These paths we tread are lined with shadows," said Luffe as he joined Dewes, his voice a mere rumour in the chill air. “Yet with each step forward, we diminish their reach. Linforth knew this. It’s what kept him going.”

Dewes nodded, his thoughts momentarily disengaging from the present to wander back to Linforth's tales—of nights spent under a sky peppered with stars, of fireside stories shared with men bonded by a shared quest. There was a warmth in those memories, a shared understanding that defied the overarching darkness they faced.

As they canvassed the fort's mud-bricked bounds, their attention stayed on the distant horizon where their foe lingered unseen but near. The tribes, emboldened by Linforth's demise, poised themselves as an unyielding barricade upon the path of their undertaking. Wafadar Nazim, their leader, was a man wreathed in his own legend—cunning and nerve bound in sinew and will.

"What do we know of Wafadar Nazim’s intentions?" Dewes asked, breaking the brooding silence.

Luffe paused, considering the question. "Only what he wants us to know," he replied, eyes narrowing as he scanned the horizon. "But that’s the theatre of it, Dewes. There's a dance to every negotiation, and Wafadar plays with a flair. It's the bluster and posturing we must see through."

A distant bugle call announced the changing of the guard, its clear notes slicing through the air’s tension. Dewes watched the routine unfold—a necessary ritual to steady the nerves and kindle a semblance of normalcy within these walls of uncertainty.

Beyond the fort’s gates, a sea of humanity milled about, a mingling of adversaries and allies alike. And amidst them, unknowable intentions flitted like whispered secrets on the wind. This turbulent frontier, silent yet screaming with historical echoes, held its breath for the dance to begin.

Dewes and Luffe exchanged a knowing glance. “To open the gates,” Luffe said, “to parlay—a gamble, but one grounded in holding a belief in something more substantial than the solidity of stone and iron.”

"Then we have little choice," Dewes replied. "These stones are but a vessel. It is the pulse of the road that beats within our chests, the rhythm of our forebears that guides our hands."

As if lending its consent, the sun broke free from its morning tether, casting a golden hue over the fort's walls and the determined faces of the men within. It was time. Time to rise beyond the mourning hues and step onto the pathway chiseled by hope and history.

Gates creaked open, inviting fate to make its entrance. Shadows of past and present intermingled, drawing shapes of uncertainty and fortitude. The road stretched out before them, as if inscribed by the thoughts and dreams of those who had come before, compelling them forward into the unknown.

The sun hung low in the sky, casting a warm glow over the ancient stone buildings that lined the path to the river. Tom and Markham continued their leisurely stroll, the gentle sound of their footsteps mingling with the distant lapping of the water.

As they walked, a comfortable silence settled between them, broken only by the occasional rustle of leaves in the breeze. Markham glanced at his friend, noting the thoughtful furrow in his brow. Tom's eyes were fixed on the horizon, a distant look of contemplation in their depths.

"I can't shake the feeling that we are merely players in a grand theatrical production," Tom mused, breaking the silence at last. "But the roles we play are not of our choosing, and the script seems to have been written by someone else entirely."

Markham nodded in agreement, understanding the sentiment all too well. "It's as if we are trapped in a narrative that we did not write, forced to act out scenes that we never auditioned for."

They both chuckled at the absurdity of the situation, finding solace in the shared understanding of their predicament. The weight of expectation, both internal and external, hung heavy in the air, like a thick fog obscuring the path ahead.

"I often wonder," Markham began, his voice low and contemplative, "if this is all there is to life. Endless days of study, rigid expectations, and the relentless pursuit of success. Is this truly living, or are we merely existing?"

Tom sighed, a heavy breath that seemed to carry the weight of the world on its wings. "I fear that many of us have lost sight of what it means to truly live. We are so consumed by our ambitions and obligations that we forget to pause and savor the simple joys that make life worth living."

Their conversation continued long into the evening, the setting sun casting long shadows across the cobblestone path. They discussed their hopes and fears, their dreams and disappointments, laying bare their souls in the fading light.

As they reached the riverbank, the last remnants of daylight fading into dusk, Tom turned to Markham with a determined glint in his eye. "We cannot change the roles we have been given, my friend. But we can choose how we play them. Let us not be mere actors on a stage, but authors of our own destinies."

Markham nodded in silent agreement, a newfound resolve shining in his eyes. Together, they stood at the water's edge, the river flowing gently past them, carrying their hopes and dreams on its shimmering surface.

And as the first stars began to twinkle in the evening sky, a sense of peace settled over them, a shared understanding that they were not alone in their journey. For in each other, they had found kindred spirits, fellow travelers on the winding road of life.

When I had finished reading this note I sat for a long while thinking hard. Then I examined the two jars. They were labelled "Cythyl." One was full, the other nearly full. "The rest must be on the corpse of the Red Admiral," I thought, "no matter if it is in a corked bottle----"

I took all the things back to the chest, laid them carefully on the straw, and closed the lid. The gendarme sentinel at the gate saluted me respectfully as I crossed over to the Groix Inn. The Inn was surrounded by an excited crowd, and the hallway was choked with gendarmes and peasants. On every side they greeted me cordially, announcing that the real murderer was caught; but I pushed by them without a word and ran upstairs to find Lys. She opened her door when I knocked and threw both arms about my neck. I took her to my breast and kissed her. After a moment I asked her if she would obey me no matter what I commanded, and she said she would, with a proud humility that touched me.

"Then go at once to Yvette in St. Julien," I said. "Ask her to harness the dog-cart and drive you to the convent in Quimperlé. Wait for me there. Will you do this without questioning me, my darling?"

She raised her face to mine. "Kiss me," she said innocently; the next moment she had vanished.

I walked deliberately into the Purple Emperor's room and peered into the gauze-covered box which had held the chrysalis of Apatura Iris. It was as I expected. The chrysalis was empty and transparent, and a great crack ran down the middle of its back, but, on the netting inside the box, a magnificent butterfly slowly waved its burnished purple wings; for the chrysalis had given up its silent tenant, the butterfly symbol of immortality. Then a great fear fell upon me. I know now that it was the fear of the Black Priest, but neither then nor for years after did I know that the Black Priest had ever lived on earth. As I bent over the box I heard a confused murmur outside the house which ended in a furious shout of "Parricide!" and I heard the gendarmes ride away behind a wagon which rattled sharply on the flinty highway. I went to the window. In the wagon sat Yves Terrec, bound and wild-eyed, two gendarmes at either side of him, and all around the wagon rode mounted gendarmes whose bared sabres scarcely kept the crowd away.

"Parricide!" they howled. "Let him die!"

I stepped back and opened the gauze-covered box. Very gently but firmly I took the splendid butterfly by its closed fore wings and lifted it unharmed between my thumb and forefinger. Then, holding it concealed behind my back, I went down into the café.

Of all the crowd that had filled it, shouting for the death of Yves Terrec, only three persons remained seated in front of the huge empty fireplace. They were the Brigadier Durand, Max Fortin, the chemist of Quimperlé, and the Purple Emperor. The latter looked abashed when I entered, but I paid no attention to him and walked straight to the chemist.

"Monsieur Fortin," I said, "do you know much about hydrocarbons?"

"They are my specialty," he said astonished.

"Have you ever heard of such a thing as cythyl?"

"Schweineri's cythyl? Oh, yes! We use it in perfumery."

"Good!" I said. "Has it an odour?"

"No--and, yes. One is always aware of its presence, but really nobody can affirm it has an odour. It is curious," he continued, looking at me, "it is very curious you should have asked me that, for all day I have been imagining I detected the presence of cythyl."

"Do you imagine so now?" I asked.

"Yes, more than ever."

You do very well, my friends, to treat me with some little reverence, for in honouring me you are honouring both France and yourselves. It is not merely an old, grey-moustached officer whom you see eating his omelette or draining his glass, but it is a fragment of history. In me you see one of the last of those wonderful men, the men who were veterans when they were yet boys, who learned to use a sword earlier than a razor, and who during a hundred battles had never once let the enemy see the colour of their knapsacks. For twenty years we were teaching Europe how to fight, and even when they had learned their lesson it was only the thermometer, and never the bayonet, which could break the Grand Army down. Berlin, Naples, Vienna, Madrid, Lisbon, Mosco–e stabled our horses in them all. Yes, my friends, I say again that you do well to send your children to me with flowers, for these ears have heard the trumpet calls of France, and these eyes have seen her standards in lands where they may never be seen again.

Even now, when I doze in my arm-chair, I can see those great warriors stream before m–he green-jacketed chasseurs, the giant cuirassiers, Poniatowsky's lancers, the white-mantled dragoons, the nodding bearskins of the horse grenadiers. And then there comes the thick, low rattle of the drums, and through wreaths of dust and smoke I see the line of high bonnets, the row of brown faces, the swing and toss of the long, red plumes amid the sloping lines of steel. And there rides Ney with his red head, and Lefebvre with his bulldog jaw, and Lannes with his Gascon swagger; and then amidst the gleam of brass and the flaunting feathers I catch a glimpse of him, the man with the pale smile, the rounded shoulders, and the far-off eyes. There is an end of my sleep, my friends, for up I spring from my chair, with a cracked voice calling and a silly hand outstretched, so that Madame Titaux has one more laugh at the old fellow who lives among the shadows.

Although I was a full Chief of Brigade when the wars came to an end, and had every hope of soon being made a General of Division, it is still rather to my earlier days that I turn when I wish to talk of the glories and the trials of a soldier's life. For you will understand that when an officer has so many men and horses under him, he has his mind full of recruits and remounts, fodder and farriers, and quarters, so that even when he is not in the face of the enemy, life is a very serious matter for him. But when he is only a lieutenant or a captain he has nothing heavier than his epaulettes upon his shoulders, so that he can clink his spurs and swing his dolman, drain his glass and kiss his girl, thinking of nothing save of enjoying a gallant life. That is the time when he is likely to have adventures, and it is often to that time that I shall turn in the stories which I may have for you. So it will be tonight when I tell you of my visit to the Castle of Gloom; of the strange mission of Sub-Lieutenant Duroc, and of the horrible affair of the man who was once known as Jean Carabin, and afterwards as the Baron Straubenthal.

You must know, then, that in the February of 1807, immediately after the taking of Danzig, Major Legendre and I were commissioned to bring four hundred remounts from Prussia into Eastern Poland.

The hard weather, and especially the great battle at Eylau, had killed so many of the horses that there was some danger of our beautiful Tenth of Hussars becoming a battalion of light infantry. We knew, therefore, both the Major and I, that we should be very welcome at the front. We did not advance very rapidly, however, for the snow was deep, the roads detestable, and we had but twenty returning invalids to assist us. Besides, it is impossible, when you have a daily change of forage, and sometimes none at all, to move horses faster than a walk. I am aware that in the story-books the cavalry whirls past at the maddest of gallops; but for my own part, after twelve campaigns, I should be very satisfied to know that my brigade could always walk upon the march and trot in the presence of the enemy. This I say of the hussars and chasseurs, mark you, so that it is far more the case with cuirassiers or dragoons.

We made the run to Silver-Store in fine time, the tropic sun beatin' down on the deck and the salt spray stingin' me face. Twenty-four marines we had aboard, all primed and ready to face whatever devilment might be waitin' on that speck o' land. Not that there was much to see, mind you. Silver-Store, from a distance, was nothin' more than a hump o' green risin' outta the turquoise water, a few palm trees wavin' lazy-like in the breeze.

But don't let the peaceful scene fool ya, for Silver-Store held a bellyful o' treasure. The silver mines o' Honduras, they poured their bounty onto her shores. Mules, laden down with more wealth than a king's ransom, would trek down from the mountains, their hooves kickin' up dust on the jungle trails. And it was our duty, see, to make sure not a single ounce of that silver fell into the wrong hands.

Pirates, they say, had been sniffin' around these waters, their ships like hungry sharks circlin' a school o' fish. But I ain't seen a single black flag since we left Port Royal. The mere threat of our presence, the sloop bristlin' with cannons and the marines itchin' for a fight, seemed to keep 'em at bay.

The island itself, once we finally set foot on her sandy shores, was a riot o' sights and smells. The air hung heavy and sweet, thick with the scent o' unknown blooms and the tang o' salt. Strange birds with feathers brighter than any jewel squawked from the treetops, their calls echoin' through the thick, green foliage.

But all this, the beauty and the danger o' the place, faded to the back o' me mind as we approached the fort. It was a crude affair, cobbled together from stone and timber, its walls patrolled by men wearin' the strained look o' those who've stared too long into the face o' uncertainty.

The commander, a man by the name o' Captain Hawthorne, greeted us with a curt nod, his face as weathered and hard as the coral reefs that ringed the island. He wasted no time on pleasantries, his voice, when he spoke, was rough as gravel, his words clipped and urgent.

"Glad you're here," he rasped, his eyes dartin' towards the dense jungle that pressed close to the fort's walls. "Situation's worse than we thought."

"Pirates?" I asked, feelin' a chill run down me spine despite the heat.

He shook his head, his expression grim. "Not pirates, lad. Something far stranger, far more fearsome."

He leaned closer, his voice little more than a whisper. "It's the silver, see. It's gone missin'."

His words struck me like a blow. Silver gone? From Silver-Store? Impossible! This island was a fortress, its every inch guarded, its every route watched.

"But how?" I stammered, my mind strugglin' to grasp the enormity o' it. "The island's secure. The mules, they just arrived yesterday-"

"And the silver," Hawthorne interrupted, his voice low and laced with a fear I'd never heard before, "vanished without a trace."

Wilfrid Athel went down invalided a few days after the beginning of Trinity term. The event was not unanticipated. At Christmas it had been clear enough that he was overtaxing himself; his father remarked on the fact with anxiety, and urged moderation, his own peculiar virtue. Wilfrid, whose battle with circumstances was all before him, declined to believe that the body was anything but the very humble servant of the will. So the body took its revenge.

He had been delicate in childhood, and the stage of hardy naturalism which interposes itself between tender juvenility and the birth of self-consciousness did not in his case last long enough to establish his frame in the vigour to which it was tending. There was nothing sickly about him; it was only an excess of nervous vitality that would not allow body to keep pace with mind. He was a boy to be, intellectually, held in leash, said the doctors. But that was easier said than done. What system of sedatives could one apply to a youngster whose imagination wrought him to a fever during a simple walk by the seashore, who if books were forcibly withheld consoled himself with the composition of five-act tragedies, interspersed with lyrics to which he supplied original strains? Mr. Athel conceived a theory that such exuberance of emotionality might be counterbalanced by studies of a strictly positive nature; a tutor was engaged to ground young Wilfrid in mathematics and the physical sciences. The result was that the tutor's enthusiasm for these pursuits communicated itself after a brief repugnance to the versatile pupil; instincts of mastery became as vivid in the study of Euclid and the chemical elements as formerly in the humaner paths of learning; the plan had failed. In the upshot Wilfrid was sent to school; if that did not develop the animal in him, nothing would.

He was not quite three-and-twenty when the break-down removed him from Oxford. Going to Balliol with a scholarship, he had from the first been marked for great things, at all events by the measure of the schools. Removal from the system of home education had in truth seemed to answer in some degree the ends aimed at; the lad took his fair share of cricket and football, and kept clear of nervous crises. At the same time he made extraordinary progress with his books. He acquired with extreme facility, and his ambition never allowed him to find content in a second place; conquest became his habit; he grew to deem it the order of nature that Wilfrid Athel's name should come first in the list. Hence a reputation to support. During his early terms at Balliol he fagged as hard as the mere dullard whose dear life depended upon a first class and a subsequent tutorship. What he would make of himself in the end was uncertain; university distinctions would probably be of small moment to him as soon as they were achieved, for already he spent the greater portion of his strength in lines of study quite apart from the curriculum, and fate had blessed him with exemption from sordid cares. He led in a set devoted to what were called advanced ideas; without flattering himself that he was on the way to solve the problem of the universe, he had satisfaction in reviewing the milestones which removed him from the unconscious man, and already clutched at a measure of positive wisdom in the suspicion that lie might shortly have to lay aside his school-books and recommence his education under other teachers. As yet he was whole-hearted in the pursuit of learning. The intellectual audacity which was wont to be the key-note of his conversation did not, as his detractors held, indicate mere bumptiousness and defect of self-measurement; it was simply the florid redundancy of a young mind which glories in its strength, and plays at victory in anticipation. It was true that he could not brook the semblance of inferiority; if it were only five minutes' chat in the Quad, he must come off with a phrase or an epigram; so those duller heads who called Athel affected were not wholly without their justification. Those who shrugged their shoulders with the remark that he was overdoing it, and would not last out to the end of the race, enjoyed a more indisputable triumph. One evening, when Athel was taking the brilliant lead in an argument on 'Fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute,' his brain began to whirl, tobacco-smoke seemed to have dulled all the lights before his eyes, and he fell from his chair in a fainting-fit.

“Young sir,” said the stranger, “what place is this? Am I near Forest Lea?”

A flash of joy crossed Walter. “Edmund! are you Edmund?” he exclaimed, colouring deeply, and looking up in his face with one quick glance, then casting down his eyes.

“And you are little Walter,” returned the cavalier, instantly dismounting, and flinging his arm around his brother; “why, what a fine fellow you are grown! How are my mother and all?”

“Well, quite well!” cried Walter, in a transport of joy. “Oh! how happy she will be! Come, make haste home!”

“Alas! I dare not as yet. I must not enter the house till nightfall, or I should bring danger on you all. Are there any troopers near?”

“Yes, the village is full of the rascals. But what has happened? It is not true that—” He could not bear to say the rest.

“Too true!” said Edmund, leading his tired horse within the shelter of the bushes. “It is all over with us!”

“The battle lost!” said Walter, in a stifled tone; and in all the bitterness of the first disappointment of his youth, he turned away, overcome by a gush of tears and sobs, stamping as he walked up and down, partly with the intensity of his grief, partly with shame at being seen by his brother, in tears.

“Had you set your heart on it so much?” said Edmund, kindly, pleased to see his young brother so ardent a loyalist. “Poor fellow! But at least the King was safe when I parted from him. Come, cheer up, Walter, the right will be uppermost some day or other.”

“But, oh, that battle! I had so longed to see old Noll get his deserts,” said Walter, “I made so sure. But how did it happen, Edmund?”

“I cannot tell you all now, Walter. You must find me some covert where I can be till night fall. The rebels are hot in pursuit of all the fugitives. I have ridden from Worcester by byroads day and night, and I am fairly spent. I must be off to France or Holland as soon as may be, for my life is not safe a moment here. Cromwell is bitterer than ever against all honest men, but I could not help coming this way, I so much longed to see my mother and all of you.”

“You are not wounded?” said Walter, anxiously.

“Nothing to speak of, only a sword-cut on my shoulder, by which I have lost more blood than convenient for such a journey.”

“Here, I’ll lead your horse; lean on me,” said Walter, alarmed at the faint, weary voice in which his brother spoke after the first excitement of the recognition. “I’ll show you what Lucy and I call our bower, where no one ever comes but ourselves. There you can rest till night.”

“And poor Bayard?” said Edmund.

“I think I could put him into the out-house in the field next to the copse, hide his trappings here, and get him provender from Ewins’s farm. Will that do?”

“Excellently. Poor Ewins!—that is a sad story. He fell, fighting bravely by my side, cut down in Sidbury Street in the last charge. Alas! these are evil days!”

“And Diggory Stokes, our own knave?”

“I know nothing of him after the first onset. Rogues and cowards enough were there. “Oh, had I but been there, to turn them all to shame!”

“There were a few, Walter; Lord Cleveland, Hamilton, Careless, Giffard, and a few more of us, charged down Sidbury Street, and broke into the ranks of the rebels, while the King had time to make off by S. Martin’s Gate. Oh, how I longed for a few more! But the King was saved so far; Careless, Giffard, and I came up with him again, and we parted at nightfall. Now, although Harroll had been refused a dozen times--not by Miss Delancy, but by her father--the young man's naturally optimistic spirits suffered only temporary depression; and a few evenings later he asked for her again, making it a bakers' dozen--an uncanny record.

"Really, Jim, I don't see what way," said Mr. Delancy, without emotion. "I don't want you for a son-in-law, and I'm not going to have you. That's one of the reasons I allow you the run of the house. My daughter sees too much of you to care for you. It's a theory of my own, and a good one, too."

"Why don't you want me for a son-in-law?" asked the young man, for the hundredth time.

"Can you give me one single reason why I should want you?" asked Mr. Delancy wearily.

Harroll stood buried in meditation for a few moments. "No," he said, "I can't recall any important reasons at the moment."

The farmer finished his supper and then went out to see that everything was all right around the farm for the night. A little later he took a lamp and went upstairs. Tiptoeing his way through an upper hall he came to a pause in front of Nat's room.

"Asleep, jest as I thought," he told himself, after listening to the boy's breathing. Then he peeped into the room, to behold Nat lying under the cover of the bed, with his face turned to the wall.

"I'll give him another talkin' to in the mornin'," the farmer told himself; and then retired, with no thought of what was going to happen before the sun arose upon another day.

NAT LEAVES THE FARM

Farmer Balberry was mistaken; Nat was not asleep, nor was there any thought of sleep in the boy's mind.

The youth had not even gone to bed. He had been sitting on a chair by the open window when he had heard his uncle coming upstairs, and to deceive his relative had jumped into bed and pulled the blanket up over him.

When Nat was thrust up the stairs his mind was in a tumult. He felt that his uncle was not treating him fairly--and he wanted his supper very much.

It is bad enough to have a real grievance of any kind--it is worse when one must bear it on an empty stomach. As he made his way to his room the boy was in a savage humor and fit to do almost any deed.

"Uncle Abner is getting worse every day!" he muttered to himself. "He treats me worse than I would treat a dog!"

Sitting by the open window Nat thought of many things--of the death of his parents, and of the taking off of his aunt--and of how his miserly uncle had treated him ever since.

"It's not fair!" he told himself, over and over again. "Uncle Abner doesn't believe in giving a boy a fair show. I wish I lived with somebody else."

The more he thought over the situation the more he felt that he ought not to stand such treatment. He felt that he was entitled to his supper, and also to some spending money if not to regular wages. At the present time he had not a cent in the world.

"If I had a few dollars I might strike out for myself," he reasoned. "But I haven't even a few cents. Wonder how I could raise a few dollars?"

As said before Nat's worldly possessions were few. In his room he had some trinkets from home and also an old silver watch which had belonged to his father.

"I might sell the watch," he thought, but then decided that it would be best to keep the heirloom.

Then he thought of Jennie, the white and brown cow. As a calf she had been given to Nat by his mother, and she was now a part of the herd on the Balberry farm.

"Jennie ought to be worth twenty or twenty-five dollars," he said to himself. "That's a pile of money, for a start. Wonder how I could manage to sell her?"

Thus speculating, Nat gradually drifted around to the point where he decided that he would leave the farm at once. He had told his uncle that he wanted his supper or he would not work for the man any more, and he meant to keep his word.

By the time all was quiet around the house and he was certain both the housekeeper and his uncle had retired, Nat had settled just what he was going to do.

Making no noise, he slipped off his working clothes and put on his best suit--something just a trifle better than the others. He also donned a clean shirt and collar and necktie and got out his best hat and shoes. Then, with his other possessions wrapped in a small bundle, and with his shoes under his arm, he tiptoed his way out of the bedchamber, along the hall, and down to the lower floor of the farmhouse.

"A penny a bunch; only a penny, sweet violets," cried a soft little voice, just outside the Bank of England, one morning in early spring; "only a penny a bunch!"

But the throng of busy clerks hurrying on to their various places of business heard not that childish voice amidst the confused din of omnibus and cabs, and so she stood, timidly uttering her cry--"Sweet violets!"--unheeded by the passers-by.

She was a fragile little creature of about ten years old, small for her age, with shy yet trustful eyes, and soft, brown, curly hair; and as she stood there, clad in a black frock and a straw hat, well worn, it is true, but free from tatters, with a piece of crape neatly fastened around it, had any one amidst that busy multitude paused to look at the little flower-seller, they would have wondered why so young a child was trusted alone in that noisy, bustling place.

"I say, Pollie, how many have yer sold, eh?" exclaimed another girl, coming up to he–uite a different type of girlhood, a regular London arab, one who from her very cradle (if ever she possessed such a luxury) had battled through life heedless of all rubs and bruises, ready to hold her own against the entire world, and yet with much of hidden goodness beneath the rugged surface.

"Only two bunches," replied little Pollie, somewhat sadly.

"Only two!" repeated the other. "My eye! yer won't make a fortin, that's sartin!"

"The people don't seem to see me, not even hear me," said the child.

"'Cos why, you don't shout loud enuff," explained the bigger girl. "If yer wants to get on in the world, yer must make a noise somehow. Make the folks hear; never minds if yer deafens 'em, they'll pay 'tention to yer then. See how I does it."

At that moment four smart youths came strolling leisurely along arm-in-arm, trying to appear as though merely out on pleasure, though they knew full well they must be in their office and at their desks before the clock struck ten.

These were just the customers for Sally Grimes, and away she rushed full upon them, her thin ragged shawl flying in the wind, and her rough hair, from which the net had fallen, following the example of the shawl; and as she reached the somewhat startled youths, who almost stumbled over her, she held her only remaining posy right in their faces, screaming out in a harsh grating voice, rendered harsh by her street training--

"Now, then, gents, this last bunc–nly a penny!"

Polly looked on in utter amazement. It is true she did not understand Sally's logic, but she saw plainly that the sweet violets were sold, for presently back came the girl, crying out--

"That's the way to do it. I've sold all mine; now let's see what you've got left. Why, ten more bunches! Come, give us two or three, I'll get rid of 'em for yer; I'll bring yer back the money. Look sharp, I see some folks a-comin'."

And without further parley she snatched up several of the dainty little bunches tied up so neatly by Pollie's mother, and rushed off in pursuit of purchasers.

She was certainly very fortunate, for in spite of a stern-looking policeman who was watching her movements, she sold them, speedily returning with the money to little Pollie, who by this time was getting almost bewildered with the noise around.

"There, my gal," said the kind girl, "there's the money for yer; look, six pennies. My! ain't yer rich. Now I'm off to Covent Garding to the old 'ooma–other, I means, yer know. There St. Poll's a-strikin' ten; good-bye."

So saying, the friendly Sally Grimes darted off amidst the crowd, leaving the child to manage for herself, and very lonely she felt after her good-natured ally was gone.

As to making Susan angry, that simply was impossible. When things went desperately wrong with her in any way she would just come right to me and cry a little on my shoulder. Then, when I had comforted her, she would chipper up and be all right again in no time. Gregory Wilkinson happened to come in one day while a performance of this sort was going on, and for fear that he should think it odd Susan explained to him that it was a habit of hers when things very much worried her and she felt like being ugly to people. (The trouble that day was that the colored girl, who had a wonderful faculty for stirring up tribulation, had broken an India china teacup that had belonged to Susan's grandmother, and that Susan had thought the world of.) That evening, while we were sitting on the veranda smoking, and before Susan, who was helping clear the supper-table, had joined us, Gregory Wilkinson said to me, with oven, more emphasis than usual, that Susan was the finest woman he had ever known; and he added that he was very sorry that when he was my ago he had not met and married just such another.

He and I talked a good deal at odd times about the money that our great-great-great-uncle the pirate had buried, and that through all these years had stayed buried so persistently. He did not take much interest in the matter personally, but for my sake, and still more for Susan's sake, he was beginning to be quite anxious that the money should be found. He even suggested that we should take Old Jacob over to the bay-side and let him try again to find the Martha Ann's anchorage; but a little talk convinced us that this would be useless. The old man had been given every opportunity, during the two days that we had cruised about with him, to refresh his memory; and we both had been the pained witnesses of the curious psychological fact that the more he refreshed it, the more utterly unmanageable it had become. The prospect, we agreed, was a disheartening one, for it was quite evident that for our purposes Old Jacob was, as it were, but an elderly, broken reed.

About this time I noticed that Gregory Wilkinson was unusually silent, and seemed to be thinking a great deal about something. At first we were afraid that he was not quite well, and Susan offered him both her prepared mustard plasters and her headache powders. But he said that he was all right, though he was very much obliged to her. Still, he kept on thinking, and he was so silent and preoccupied that Susan and I were very uncomfortable. To have him around that way, and to be always wondering what he could possibly be thinking about, Susan said, made her feel as though she were trying to eavesdrop when nobody was talking.

One afternoon while we were sitting on the veranda--Susan and I trying to keep up some sort of a conversation, and Gregory Wilkinson thinking away as hard as ever he could think--a thin man in a buggy drove down the road and stopped at our hitch-ing-post. When he had hitched his horse he took out from the after-part of the buggy a largo tin vessel standing on light iron legs, and came up to the house with it. He made us all a sort of comprehensive bow, but stopped in front of Susan, set the tin vessel upon its legs, and said:

"Madam, you behold before you the most economical device and the greatest labor-saving invention of this extraordinarily devicious and richly inventive age. This article, madam"--and he placed his hand upon the tin vessel affectionately--"is Stowe's patent combination interchangeable churn and wash-boiler."

In the waning light of the parlor, where the shadows danced with the embers of the encroaching fire, Madison found himself face to face with Safie, her eyes sparkling like polished stones. The room was filled with an air of unspoken tension, a taut string ready to snap at the slightest touch. Safie's laughter, a vibrant melody from their shared past, echoed through the rarified atmosphere. "Madison, dear, you look as if you've seen a ghost," she said, her voice a sweet poison, "Let us put away the formality, for we both know we've dealt with ghosts before. Have a seat, do. I insist." She swept her hand towards an empty chair as if it were a throne.

Madison, his heart a heavy drum in his chest, complied, taking his seat. The room seemed to shift under his feet, the very furniture seemed to whisper his name, mocking him. "Safie," he began, his voice a rough sympathy for the familiar, "I must talk to you about... our past."

"Our past," she echoed, her voice dripping with sarcasm, "Yes, those distant shores where our ghosts reside. You were a steady oar in my boat, Madison, until the storm came. Now you wish to set sail on the open sea again?" She laughed, a sharp echo that stung like salt on a wound.

"It's not laughter, Safie," Madison persisted, "It's... it's a matter of faith. Of... of the spirit."

"Oh, the spirit," she sniffed, "You mean that faint echo of your convictions, like the last strains of a forgotten melody. You're a man of the cloth now, are you not? Yet you stand before me, the adept and the condemned." She leaned forward, her eyes burning into him, "Why the blazing desire to preach your sermon, when I offered you no invitation?"

Madison shifted uneasily in his seat, his hands wringing like wet clothes. "I am not here to preach, Safie. I'm here to... to implore. To remind you of the path you once were on."

"And your reminder is?" She arched an eyebrow in mock curiosity, her smile a slash of irony.

"It's... it's love," Madison said, his voice barely above a whisper. "Love, and the spirit that guides us to it. Love, and the divine that binds us all."

She threw her head back and laughed, a long, guttural roll that seemed to shake the very foundations of the house. "Love? Madison, you, of all people, should know better than to invoke that word so carelessly. You of all people, who has watched my spirit crumble like a house of cards."

Madison recoiled as if struck, his face turning a mottled red. "I did not... I did not mean to hurt you, Safie. You must believe that."

"Believe," she repeated, her eyes narrowing, "Is that what you call believing when you've lost faith in yourself? When you've set aside your love for the altar of your new god?"

Madison solitude, his voice a ragged breath. "I... I have not lost faith, Safie. I have gained it, in the truest sense. I've found something profound, something that I... I believe you can find again."

"And what," she asked, her voice a dangerous purr, "is this profound thing that you've found?"

Madison looked down at his hands, wrested under the scrutiny of her gaze. "It's... it's a revelation. I've come to... to realize that I've wasted time, Safie. I've spent years running from the truth, from the love that I felt for you. I've been a fool."

Safie's smile was a cruel twist of her lips. "A fool in love. How quaint. And what of this revelation? How does it manifest?"

Madison raised his head, his eyes meeting hers, steady and certain. "It manifests in... in my confession. I've told... I've told her, Safie. I've told your current partner, about my feelings for you."

Safie's eyes widened slightly, the color draining from her face. "You did what?" she whispered.

"I confessed," Madison said, his voice a grim determination, "I confessed everything. And... and she seemed satisfied. Understandable. She knew."

Safie's laughter was harsh, a savage bark that ended in a choked sob. "She knew? How wonderful. She knew, and she still accepted you? How romantic."

Madison reached out a hand, his voice pleading, "Safie, you must understand. I didn't mean to cause pain. I... I love you. I always have. And I will not stop loving you."

Safie stood up, her chair scraping against the floor like fingernails on a chalkboard. "Love? You speak of love, yet you've caused me nothing but pain. You're a plague, Madison, a disease that I cannot shake.
