On the saw-mill brig the minister quickly organised a search party, the brig that Rob had floored anew but the week before, rising daily with the sun to do it, because the child's little boot had caught in a worn board. From it she had often crooned to watch the dank mill-wheel climbing the bouncing burn. Ah, Rob, the rotten old planks would have served your turn.

'The Whunny road' were the words passed from mouth to mouth, and the driblet of men fell into line.

Impetuous is youth, and the minister was not perhaps greatly to blame for starting at once. But Lang Tammas, his chief elder, paused on the threshold.

'The Lord giveth,' he said solemnly, taking off his hat and letting the night air cut through his white hair, 'and the Lord taketh away: blessed be the name of the Lord.'

The saw-miller opened his mouth, but no words came.

The little search party took the cold Whunny road. The day had been bright and fine, and still there was a smell of flowers in the air. The fickle flowers! They had clustered round Davy and nestled on her neck when she drew the half-ashamed saw-miller through the bleating meadows, and now they could smile on him when he came alone--all except the daisies. The daisies, that cannot play a child false, had craned their necks to call Davy back as she tripped over them, and bowed their heavy little heads as she toddled on. It was from them that the bairn's track was learned after she wandered from the Whunny road.

By and by the hills ceased to echo their wailing response to Hobart's bell.

Far in the rear of the more eager searchers, the bellman and the joiner had found a seat on a mossy bank, and others, footsore and weary, had fallen elsewhere from the ranks. The minister and half a dozen others scattered over the fields and on the hillsides, despondent, but not daring to lag. Tinkers cowered round their kettles under threatening banks, and the squirrels were shadows gliding from tree to tree.

At a distant smithy a fitful light still winked to the wind, but the farm lamps were out and all the land was hushed. It was now long past midnight in country parts.

Rob Angus was young and strong, but the heaven-sent gift of tears was not for him. Blessed the moaning mother by the cradle of her eldest-born, and the maid in tears for the lover who went out so brave in the morning and was not at evenfall, and the weeping sister who can pray for her soldier brother, and the wife on her husband's bosom.

Some of his neighbours had thought it unmanly when Rob, at the rumble of a cart, hurried from the saw-mill to snatch the child in his arms, and bear her to a bed of shavings. At such a time Davy would lift a saw to within an inch of her baby face, and then, letting it fall with a wicked chuckle, run to the saw-miller's arms, as sure of her lover as ever maiden was of man.

A bashful lover he had been, shy, not of Davy but of what men would say, and now the time had come when he looked wistfully back to a fevered child tossing in a dark bed, the time when a light burned all night in Rob's kitchen, and a trembling, heavy-eyed man sat motionless on a high-backed chair. How noiselessly he approached the bonny mite and replaced the arm that had wandered from beneath the coverlet! Ah, for the old time when a sick imperious child told her uncle to lie down beside her, and Rob sat on the bed, looking shamefacedly at the minister. Mr. Dishart had turned away his head. Such things are not to be told. They are between a man and his God.

The Squire, crimson with indignation, rose hastily from his chair. His hand trembled as he reached for his hat and gloves, lying upon the table beside him.

"I had not expected this from you, Cope," he said, his voice shaking with suppressed anger. "I came to you as a friend—as an old friend—believing that in my hour of need you would stand by me. It seems I was mistaken."

Mr. Cope, still seated calmly at his desk, regarded the Squire with an unreadable expression in his keen, grey eyes. He made no attempt to rise, nor did he offer any word of apology or explanation.

"I have never, in all my born days," continued the Squire, his voice rising with each word, "been so insulted—so slighted! To think that you, Cope, of all people, would treat me with such—such—"

Words failed him. He choked back a torrent of angry exclamations, his face now a mottled purple. The silence in the room stretched, heavy and suffocating, broken only by the ticking of the grandfather clock in the corner.

Finally, Mr. Cope spoke, his voice measured and calm in stark contrast to the Squire's agitation. "My dear fellow," he began, "let us not allow a momentary misunderstanding to cloud our judgment. I am a man of business, as you well know. And in matters of business, sentiment must, of necessity, take a back seat."

"Sentiment!" The Squire spat the word out as if it were poison. "Is that what you call it? Sentiment! When I am faced with ruin, with the loss of my ancestral home, the very roof over my head—you offer me sentiment!"

He strode towards the door, each step echoing his mounting fury. Pausing on the threshold, he turned back to face Mr. Cope, his figure silhouetted against the dim light of the hallway.

"I came to you for help, Cope," he said, his voice now low and dangerous, "not for a lesson in financial pragmatism. I had thought better of you. I had thought ours was a friendship that transcended such—such cold-hearted calculations."

With a final, disdainful glance at the impassive figure seated behind the desk, the Squire turned on his heel and strode out of the room, slamming the door behind him with a resounding crash that echoed through the silent house.

Mr. Cope, still seated at his desk, remained unmoved by the Squire's outburst. He picked up a silver letter opener and began meticulously cleaning his fingernails, a faint smile playing about his lips. The Squire, he mused, was a fool. A sentimental fool who allowed his heart to rule his head.

He, Cope, was made of sterner stuff. He had learned long ago that in this world, sentiment was a luxury that only the wealthy could afford. And the Squire, alas, was no longer among their number. He, Cope, had seen to that.

"Hearken, dear reader," I begin, "to the whispers of that mountainside, where the very air seemed to pulse with a mysterious energy; a force that only those attuned to nature could perceive. Amidst the cacophony of machinery, a solitary figure stood at the threshold of this rugged edifice—a building of rough-hewn timber, claiming kinship with the wildness that surrounded it.

The newcomer was but a stranger in these parts, yet his eyes were sharp as a hawk's, accustomed to the vast panoramas of the high country. He had received word of a Bradley—a name that bore the weight of a legend among the locals—and sought him out with the determination of one who had traversed countless miles in pursuit of a singular purpose.

"Much obliged, there!" came a call from within the dim interior, as if the mountain itself were speaking through mortal lips. The voice carried the resonance of honest toil and weathered age; it was as if the very essence of the land had found form in the person of Bradley.

"You seek Bradley, eh?" the old man queried, his eyes twinkling with a knowing glance. “You'll find him at the edge of the world, where heaven meets earth. Follow yon faint trail, but do it now ere the light to guide your way is lost."

The stranger, faithful to his charge, set forth on this obscure path. His mind, seasoned by the rigors of the terrain, quickly divined the tracks of animal or man beneath the scattered leaves and loose stones of the earth. The journey was one of keen observation, a dance with shadows and light, where every step forward was a testament to his mountaineering prowess.

As the day waned, the trail twisted and turned, leading him ever deeper into the heart of wilderness. The canopy of foliage, once a comforting shelter, now grew dense and foreboding, whispering secrets long withheld from the uninitiated. Just when the path seemed to falter and fade like a memory, a sudden glint of sunlight caught his eye—a clear indication that perseverance had not been in vain.

Following this beacon, the stranger found himself paused at the very edge of a precipice that dropped away into the depths of the Great Canyon. The sight was a thing of both awe and terror: a vast chasm that seemed to yawn into eternity, its silent depths a mirror reflecting the grandeur of creation.

For a moment, the stranger stood motionless, lost in the contemplation of this mighty spectacle—a vision that stirred within him a profound sense of insignificance yet a stirring of reverence for the indomitable spirit that could carve such majesty from the very core of the earth.

At last, gathering his faculties, he descended, his heart heavy with the weight of celestial contemplation, only to meet the Bradley abode. There, in a humble dwelling that bore the marks of generations past, Mrs. Bradley awaited his arrival, her eyes as vast and unassailable as the canyon behind him.

“Well met,” she said, her voice carrying the same mountain air that had led him here. "Your delivery is precious, and your journey has not been in vain. Let us partake of solitude and hearth whilst the world outside roars on undisturbed.”

And so they conversed, their voices melding with the eternal hum of the wilderness, each word carrying the weight of untold stories and the promise of undiscovered adventures that lay just beyond the bend of the trail.

'We've got over the difficulty of a doctor,' said my father.

'How?' I answered.

'Burke has consented to engage one. I told him if he would carry a surgeon, by which I mean feed and accommodate him in the ship, I would bear the other charges. He has a month before him, and may find a man who wants a change of air and who'll give his services for a cabin and food. Or, which is more likely, he'll meet with some intelligent young gentleman who wants to try his 'prentice hand on sailors before starting in practice ashore. Doctors find sailors useful as subjects; they can experiment on them without professional anxiety as to the result.'

Now that it was as good as settled I was to sail in the 'Lady Emma,' I looked forward to meeting Mr. Moore next day with dread and misery. I was going away alone. All the risks of the sea lay before me. I was low and poor in health. Who could be sure that the ocean would do for me all that the doctors had promised? Who was to say it would let me return alive? I might never meet my love again. When I said good-bye to the man who by this time should have been my husband, it might be for ever, and the thought made the prospect of meeting him next day almost insupportable.

He found me alone in the drawing-room. The servant admitted him and closed the door. I stood up very white and crying; he took me in his arms and kissed me, led me to a chair and sat beside me, holding my hand and nursing it, and looking into my face for a little while, scarcely able to speak. How shall I describe him, whose love for me, as you shall presently read, was such as to make my love for him, when I think of him as he sat beside me that day, as I follow him in memory afterwards, too deep for human expression? He was tall, fair, eyes of a dark blue, deep but gentle, and easily impassioned. He wore a large yellow moustache, and was as perfectly the model of an English gentleman in appearance as Captain Burke was a merchant skipper.

He began immediately on the subject of my voyage.

'It's hard we should be parted; but I like your little ship, Marie. I've not met your old nurse, but I judge from what your father tells me you could not be in better and safer hands. Captain Burke seems a fine fellow--a thorough, practical seaman. I wish I could accompany you.'

'Oh, Archie, I shall be so long alone!'

'Ay, but you're to get well, dearest. I've thought the scheme over thoroughly. If there's nothing for it but a voyage as the doctors insist, your father's plans, your old nurse's suggestion, could not be bettered. Who would look after you on board a big steamer? There is nobody to accompany you--no relative, nobody we know, no party of people I can hear of to entrust you to--making, I mean, such a voyage as the doctors advise. I should be distracted when you were gone in thinking of you as alone on a steamship at sea, with not a soul to take the least interest in you saving the captain; and captains, I believe, do not very much love these obligations. Civility, of course, everybody expects, but a big ship to look after is a big business to attend to.'

'It will be a terribly long voyage.'

'To Valparaiso, and then to Sydney and Algoa Bay, and home. About fourteen months. So Burke calculates it. A long time, Marie; but if it is to make you strong, it will not be too long.'

In this wise we talked; then, there being two hours of daylight left, I put on my hat and jacket and, taking my lover's arm, went with him slowly down the great gap in the cliffs to the seashore. It was sheltered down here. The yellow sunshine lay upon the brown sand, and flashed in the lifting lengths of seaweed writhing amidst the surf, and had a sense of April warmth, though it was a keen wind that then blew--a northerly wind, strong, with a hurry of white clouds like endless flocks of sheep, scampering southwards. The sands made a noble promenade, surf-furrowed and hard as wood; the breakers tumbled close beside us with a loud roar of thunder, and exquisite was the picture of the trending cliffs, snowclad, gleaming with a delicate moonlike light in the pale airy blue distance. All sights and sounds of sky and sea appealed to me now with a meaning I had never before found in them. I would stop my lover as we walked, to observe the swift and beautiful miracle of the moulding of a breaker as it arched out of the troubled brine, soaring, into a snowstorm, arching headlong to the sands with the foam flying from its rushing peak like white feathers streaming from a dazzling line of helmets; and once or twice as we talked, I would pause to mark the flight of the gulls stemming the wind aslant in curves of beauty, or sailing seawards on level, tremorless wings, and flinging a salt ocean song with their short raw cries through the harsh bass and storming accompaniment of the surf.

Our quaint village of Netherwood lay shrouded in an aura of mystery, its old stone church standing as a sentinel amidst the whispering woods. The wind, as it swept through the trees, carried the faint whispers of ancient tales, drawing in the curious and the brave. On certain evenings, when the moon cast its silvery glow upon the landscape, the village girls would steal away to the churchyard, their hearts aflutter with anticipation, to watch for the "shadows" that danced upon the walls on St. John's Eve. It was a tradition passed down through generations, a ritual that wove a spell of enchantment around the village, and one that the owls, with their wise, knowing eyes, seemed to sanction with their nocturnal flights from the belfry.

In the distance, yet within sight of the church, stood the sturdy, stone-built homestead of Oakhurst Farm, its slate roof a deep, foreboding grey that seemed to absorb the sunlight. The farm, with its rolling fields and wooded copses, was the domain of the kindly Mr. Ryder, a widower of gentle disposition, whose years were beginning to tell upon his frame. His two sons, William and James, were the mainstays of the farm, their rugged, sun-browned faces a testament to their tireless labors, while their sister, Emily, with her delicate features and gentle hands, moved quietly about the house, a soft, golden light seeming to attend her every step. It was a peaceful, serene household, one that seemed to embody the very essence of rural life, and yet, as with all things, the seeds of change were already sown, waiting to sprout and alter the course of their lives forever.

It was on a crisp, autumnal morning, the air alive with the scent of woodsmoke and damp earth, that a stranger arrived in Netherwood. His name was Thomas Blackwood, a young man of strong, handsome features, with eyes that seemed to hold a deep, unspoken sadness. He came with a letter of introduction from a distant relation, and was warmly received by Mr. Ryder, who, in his kindness, offered Thomas a position on the farm, to assist with the outdoor work and help his sons with the management of the land. As Thomas settled into his new role, he found himself drawn to Emily, with her quiet, gentle ways, and the two began to spend many an hour together, walking the rolling hills and wooded glades of Oakhurst Farm, their conversation flowing easily, like a softly babbling brook.

As the days turned into weeks, Thomas and Emily's friendship deepened, and the villagers, with their keen eyes and quick tongues, began to notice the blossoming romance. William and James, however, were not so sure, their rugged, practical natures making them wary of this stranger, who seemed to have captured their sister's heart with such ease. They would often watch him, their eyes narrowed, as he worked in the fields, his strong, capable hands moving with a quiet confidence that belied the hint of melancholy that clung to him like a shadow. And yet, despite their reservations, they could not deny the change that had come over Emily, her face aglow with a soft, radiant light, her laughter echoing through the house, like the sweet, tinkling sound of a bell.

But as the seasons passed, a new presence came to Oakhurst Farm, one that would shatter the peaceful tranquility of their lives. Her name was Lucy, a cousin of the Ryders, with a beauty that was as striking as it was volatile. She arrived unexpectedly, her eyes flashing with a fierce, inner light, and her presence seemed to stir up the very air around her, like a whirlwind that left a trail of chaos in its wake. Thomas, with his sensitive, emotional nature, was immediately drawn to her, his eyes locking onto hers, like a moth to a flame, and Emily, with her gentle heart, felt the first pangs of jealousy, a quiet, gnawing sense of unease that threatened to undermine the very foundations of her happiness.

As the winter months drew in, with their cold, dark nights, and icy mornings, the atmosphere at Oakhurst Farm grew increasingly tense. Thomas, torn between his feelings for Emily and his fascination with Lucy, found himself walking a precarious tightrope, his emotions seesawing wildly, like a ship in a storm. Emily, sensing the shift in his affections, felt her heart slowly breaking, like the gentle, insistent dripping of water onto stone, while Lucy, with her mercurial temper, seemed to delight in the chaos she had unleashed, her eyes glinting with a mischievous, otherworldly light. And in the midst of this turmoil, the old stone church stood watch, its stone walls bearing silent witness to the drama that was unfolding, like a patience, unspoken chronicler of the human heart.

For many days after the women took possession of the previously desolate half of his mother's house, Stephen found little peace within himself. The sound of voices—the light, hopeful murmurs of feminine companionship—drifting through dividing walls became an unfamiliar intrusion upon his solitude, a detection of humanity which strangely disturbed and provoked him to a restless consideration he had not hitherto known. He would sit alone, conscious of each cheerful note rising upward in the corridors, and a bitterly curious impatience would seize upon him, as if the newly arrived inmates mocked him with the simplicity of their gentle endurance and unfading cheer. He had supposed their coming would quiet that grim, relentless ghost of poverty which haunted his mother's cares and shadowed his own ambitious pride, but instead, he found his spirit burdened by a deeper dissatisfaction, one that no payment of silver, however timely or generous, might easily heal.

Indeed, Stephen had yet to comprehend the truth—not one blazoned by mere charity, nor branded with the strong fire of reproof, but quietly whispered under every roof beam sheltering startled hopes—that human souls must lean one upon another, the weakest and the strongest mingling in life's arduous journey towards the same unseen goal. It was a truth which he stubbornly resisted beneath the armor of a too-rigid pride, deeming himself above the gentle hardships, patient sacrifices, and humble joys that graced the days of commoner hearts. He was a proud man, and pride carried for him the illusion of virtue, the delusion of strength; pride built a deceptive fortress around him, isolating him beneath the false banner of superiority. So, even in the silent stillness of private nights, troubled sleep, and uneasy dreams, he did not yet dare the poignant humility to ask what the cheerfulness of these widowed women might imply for the troubled gloom of his own spirit.

With the brightening warmth of spring came visible alterations in the little household which had been so long oppressed by shadows. The elder widow, gentle and determined, took tender command of their modest territory, arranging her few belongings with neat economy and appealing grace. It seemed to Stephen, who watched secretly from shadowed windows and shaded porches, as though the women brightened their small dwelling merely by inhabiting it, lending a richer beauty to each familiar corner through the patient dignity of their carefully adjusted poverty. More puzzling still was the younger widow, whose animated face, despite heavy grief clouding once-laughing eyes, retained the heroic cheer of unstifled gratitude. She moved lightly, always smiling, her slender figure straightened bravely against whispers of sorrow. Her voice had a mellow sweetness that reached Stephen through doors kept discreetly ajar, melting briefly his rigid composure and disturbing the proud quietude upon which he jealously insisted.

At length it came to Stephen's knowledge that the aching cheerfulness—that indefatigable courage which irritated and perplexed him in turns—hid behind itself a story of loss and sorrow so profound that even his proud heart softened momentarily beneath its touch. He learned it from his mother, whose quiet affection had already drawn the younger widow into delicate confidences over afternoon tea. What she revealed of the woman's misfortune forced an unfamiliar pang of remorseful shame into his unwilling heart, wrenching from his proud disdain a glimmering acknowledgment that strength often dwelt where he saw only weakness, and courage flourished even as grief laid waste life's fairest landscapes. It was strange to him to recognize suddenly, by contrast and reflection, the narrowness and poverty of spirit underlying his own carefully guarded superiority. Strange, and discomfiting; for pride does not relinquish its false strength easily nor without painful convulsions of resistance and denial.

Yet Stephen, though outwardly unchanged, felt within himself the subtle stirrings of something new and humbling, an uncertain reverence for that beauty of soul which endured unnoticed beneath life's tragedies and commonplace trials. Gradually, stealthily, and with painful resistance he began to see that human worth could not be measured by wealth, nor dignity defined by isolation; that a smiling woman bravely facing grief might be of greater stature than the proudest, most self-sufficient soul who ever scorned the sacred bond that joined human beings in affectionate brotherhood. In the anxious silence of his private consciousness, Stephen was beginning—slowly, imperfectly, yet inevitably—to approach that bitter yet liberating admission of folly, that confession which might alone save him from the loneliness and impoverished sterility of his long-nurtured pride.

Under the vast, cerulean dome of the Manhattan sky, amidst the ceaseless hum of bustling life, Major paused, his footsteps echoing faintly against the asphalt paths. His mind, however, was engrossed in distant memories, where the sultry whisper of Southern pines mingled with the clamor of crowded streets, a spectral orchestra playing in the void of his thoughts.

He sought Jack Hardy, his old confidant, whose name was whispered with reverence among the members of the Ducking Club on Crab Island. Yet here he was, misguided, lurking near the esteemed doors of Delmonico's, a bastion of opulent dining where the elite gathered under chandeliers that looked down with the hauteur of highborn angels. Alas, Major's quarry was not to be found amidst the clinking of fine cutlery and the discreet hum of witty conversations.

Recalling the tales told by Jefferson, Hardy's loyal servant, a man who had risen from the ashes of the Old South like a Phoenix from ashes, Major's heart swelled with admiration for this embodiment of progress. Jefferson, with a nod that spoke volumes, had informed him that Jack, his master and friend, had ventured forth to the rugged coastlines of Maine, seeking solace in the chill embrace of the North. Major chuckled at the thought, reminiscing on the times they'd shared, the camaraderie born of shared hardship and the peculiar comforts of life on Crab Island.

Jack Hardy, this mocking bird of Major's affections, had always been a wanderer, a spirit free, untethered by the mundane. Major couldn't help but admire his friend's audacity, his willingness to flutter from one corner of the world to another. Yet, Major's loyalty knew no bounds—it stretched across oceans, spanned continents, and embraced the unseen threads of their shared bond.

As the city lights dimmed and the moon cast a silvery pallor over the urban jungle, Major made his way to the docks, a plan forming in his restless mind. He would find Jack Hardy, not in the gilded chambers of Delmonico's, nor in the suffocating confines of New York's urban sprawl, but where the true spirit of freedom resided—on the unpredictable currents of the Atlantic, where the horizon beckoned with the promise of adventure.

His resolve fortified by the setting sun, Major hailed a skiff, whispering to the oarsman the coordinates of Crab Island. There, he would await his friend, the tempest of his soul, knowing that Jack, like a true vagabond, would eventually return to the haven they had created together.

Meanwhile, Jefferson, with the grace of a man who had seen the world transform, prepared the Major's quarters with a meticulous care that spoke of both service and friendship. His presence was a silent testament to the complexities of their shared history—a history that had seen slavery's cruel reign crumble, yielding to a new dawn of freedom and equality, yet one that still bore the scars of the past.

Major, lost in contemplation, pondered the irony of his situation. Here he was, a Major without a war, a title inherited not from valor or conquest, but from the affectionate jest of his late wife, who had cherished the memory of her previous husband's designation. The world, it seemed, had its strange ways of bestowing honor, and Major found himself honored by fate, bound by affection to a friend whose spirit was as elusive as the northern lights.

As the skiff sliced through the inky waters, Major steeled himself for the journey ahead, embracing the unknown with the fervor that had once led him to espouse the peculiar beliefs of his Southern kin, a zeal that had waned but left him with a soul sated with memories of a time and place that would forever hold a piece of his heart.

And as the lights of New York dwindled into the horizon, Major found solace in the thought that his quest was not merely for Jack Hardy, but for the pieces of himself that he had left scattered along the journey—fragments of loyalty, of friendship, and of a world that was forever changing, yet somehow remained the same.

It will be observed by the literary and commercial world that, in this transaction, the name of the really responsible party does not show on the title-page. I--George Robinson--am that party. When our Mr. Jones objected to the publication of these memoirs unless they appeared as coming from the firm itself, I at once gave way. I had no wish to offend the firm, and, perhaps, encounter a lawsuit for the empty honour of seeing my name advertised as that of an author. We had talked the matter over with our Mr. Brown, who, however, was at that time in affliction, and not able to offer much that was available. One thing he did say; "As we are partners," said Mr. Brown, "let's be partners to the end." "Well," said I, "if you say so, Mr. Brown, so it shall be." I never supposed that Mr. Brown would set the Thames on fire, and soon learnt that he was not the man to amass a fortune by British commerce. He was not made for the guild of Merchant Princes. But he was the senior member of our firm, and I always respected the old-fashioned doctrine of capital in the person of our Mr. Brown.

When Mr. Brown said, "Let's be partners to the end; it won't be for long, Mr. Robinson," I never said another word. "No," said I, "Mr. Brown; you're not what you was--and you're down a peg; I'm not the man to take advantage and go against your last wishes. Whether for long or whether for short, we'll pull through in the same boat to the end. It shall be put on the title-page--'By One of the Firm.'" "God bless you, Mr. Robinson," said he; "God bless you."

And then Mr. Jones started another objection. The reader will soon realize that anything I do is sure to be wrong with Mr. Jones. It wouldn't be him else. He next declares that I can't write English, and that the book must be corrected, and put out by an editor? Now, when I inform the discerning British Public that every advertisement that has been posted by Brown, Jones, and Robinson, during the last three years has come from my own unaided pen, I think few will doubt my capacity to write the "Memoirs of Brown, Jones, and Robinson," without any editor whatsoever.

On this head I was determined to be firm. What! after preparing, and correcting, and publishing such thousands of advertisements in prose and verse and in every form of which the language is susceptible, to be told that I couldn't write English! It was Jones all over. If there is a party envious of the genius of another party in this sublunary world that party is our Mr. Jones.

But I was again softened by a touching appeal from our senior partner. Mr. Brown, though prosaic enough in his general ideas, was still sometimes given to the Muses; and now, with a melancholy and tender cadence, he quoted the following lines;--

"Let dogs delight to bark and bite, For 'tis their nature to. But 'tis a shameful sight to see, when partners of one firm like we, Fall out, and chide, and fight!"

So I gave in again.

It was then arranged that one of Smith and Elder's young men should look through the manuscript, and make any few alterations which the taste of the public might require. It might be that the sonorous, and, if I may so express myself, magniloquent phraseology in which I was accustomed to invite the attention of the nobility and gentry to our last importations was not suited for the purposes of light literature, such as this. "In fiction, Mr. Robinson, your own unaided talents would doubtless make you great," said to me the editor of this Magazine; "but if I may be allowed an opinion, I do think that in the delicate task of composing memoirs a little assistance may perhaps be not inexpedient."

In the dim light of the dining room, the ambiance was charged with an unspoken tension. The supper had been served with a silk-smooth grace, yet the air was thick with whispers and exchanged glances—whispers of a comparative age and whispers of a heavy history. The butler had retired, leaving the family to their meager conversation. Robert Morville, the elder Mr. Edmonstone, sat at the head of the table, his eyes reflecting the flickering candle flame. His wife, the graceful Mrs. Edmonstone, her face a blend of sorrow and curiosity, folded her napkin as if to hide her trembling hands. The sound of silverware quietly clinking against fine china was the only accompaniment to their hushed words.

'The boy is as unpredictable as a wild beast,' muttered Mr. Edmonstone, stirring his wine with a distracted fork. 'Eager to run, eager to rebel—impossible to guide.' His voice was a low rumble, like distant thunder threatening a summer storm. Amabel, the eldest, lifted her head with a start, a mischievous twinkle in her eyes. She was playing with her fork, absentmindedly stabbing at a piece of roast chicken. 'You would not catch me in a tussle, sir,' she quipped, a playful lilt in her voice that belied the seriousness of the matter. Her sister, Charlotte, sitting beside her, snickered quietly, her eyes sparkling with amusement. Mr. Edmonstone's stern gaze did not falter.

'You, Amabel, are not the one who bears the burden of his charge. And you, Charlotte,' he said, his voice softening, 'should not carry the weight of his actions on your shoulders.' His glance flickered to Charlotte, her head bowed over her plate, a shadow of embarrassment flitting across her face. She stole a glance at Amabel, her expression mirroring her sister's mischief, and despite the gravity of the conversation, a smirk tugged at the corners of their mouths. Amabel's shoulder shook with suppressed laughter, and she quickly hid her face behind a napkin.

But Charlotte was not so astute. She let out a small laugh, a bubbling sound that was quickly echoed by Amabel. Their father, a stern expression fixed on his face, raised an eyebrow. 'What has amused you so?' he inquired, and Charlotte, realizing her folly, clamped her mouth shut, her eyes wide with sudden realization of her mistake. Mrs. Edmonstone, noticing the turmoil, looked at her daughter with a mix of concern and exasperation. 'Charlotte, my dear, whatever is the matter?' she asked softly.

Charlotte, guilt-ridden, lowered her head. 'Nothing, mother,' she mumbled. She stole a glance at her father, who was studying her intently, his eyes unyielding. She felt a familiar heat rise to her cheeks and turned to her plate, her appetite lost. Amabel, oblivious to Charlotte's mortification, was struggling to keep her composure. She was sitting with her back to her mother, but the suppressed laughter made her shoulder jerk and her entire body Shak with barely contained mirth.

'Robert,' Mrs. Edmonstone said, her voice a calm anchor in the storm of amusement, 'Something seems to have bothered the girls. Perhaps they need a change of atmosphere.' Her voice was steady and firm, a clear indication that she was not pleased with her daughters' behavior, yet it held the threat of a lenient punishment underscored heavily by a soothing tone. Mr. Edmonstone nodded, his face making a stern mask of resolution. 'Very well. Perhaps a walk in the gardens before we retire might serve as a distraction.'

The girls, understanding the playful reprimand, straightened their backs and agreed. As they moved to clear away, Mrs. Edmonstone's voice followed them, a soft admonition, 'Remember, Amabel, to mind the rose garden; it's not a place for your fiery antics.' Amabel, keeping a straight face, gave a mocking salute before turning to leave. Charlotte, however, said nothing, her eyes still cast downwards in contrition.

As they stepped outside into the cool night, the house seemed to sigh around them, the weight of Redclyffe's history settling on their shoulders like a tangible cloak. The gardens were bathed in the soft glow of the moonlight, casting eerie shadows from the ancient oaks and moss-covered paving stones. Amabel, unfazed by the ghostly atmosphere, laughed softly, 'Charlotte, I believe the fireplace in Sir Hugh's chamber may be more sinister than the ghosts of this garden.' Charlotte, her face pale even in the moon's soft light, whispered back, 'I believe it is you, Amabel, who bring the fire and darkness to our family.'

Back of Ridgewood village was a forest of large extent, bordering on a narrow stream. This woods was owned by an Eastern capitalist and he had as yet permitted no woodman's ax to resound in its depths.

Game abounded, and the woods was the frequent resort for amateur hunters, among them the young civil engineer, August Bordine.

It was his frequent visits to Eastman's woods with gun and game-bag that brought him in frequent contact with the Vanes, and especially Victoria, who, during the short space of a few months, had become violently smitten with the handsome face and gentlemanly bearing of the young engineer.

It was this fact that determined Bordine to shorten his stay at the cottage on the day in question.

"There isn't the least danger," assured August, as he lifted his gun to the hollow of his arm and prepared to depart from the Vane cottage.

"Then you will not stay?"

Tears actually stood in the blue eyes of Miss Vane.

"Good gracious! Vic, what a baby," and he laughed aloud.

He stepped to her side, however, and as her face pale, pretty, even though babyish, was upturned to his he could not resist the temptation, and he bent and kissed her full upon the pouting lips.

Then a pair of soft arms were wound quickly about his neck, and a voice whispered softly:

"Why can't you stay with me always, August?"

He tore himself loose instantly, a guilty feeling entering his heart. He was acting the hypocrite with a vengeance, and it did not agree with his honorable nature.

"Confound it, Miss Vane, what a tease you are. There comes your brother now, and I must away."

"You will call when you return from your hunt?"

"Perhaps."

He then passed outside.

A single horseman was riding slowly down the forest road toward the village.

He must needs pass the cottage.

August Bordine had called the traveler Victoria's brother. He saw his mistake as he passed out, but did not deem it necessary to rectify it.

He swung his rifle to his shoulder, and moved, with a long stride, toward the nearest point of woods.

Vaulting a fence, he crossed a bit of clearing and entered a clump of trees.

Here he paused and looked back.

The strange horseman had halted at the cottage, and was conversing with Victoria.

Bordine saw him lift his hat politely, and knew that it was no tramp this time who craved favor at the cottage.

"I don't think the girl will require my presence this time," muttered the young engineer.

She did, however, as the sequel proved.

Bordine, whistling softly, turned away and plunged deeply into the forest.

For several hours August Bordine scoured the woods in search of game. His hunt proved unsuccessful, however, and with weary limbs and anything but pleasant mood he retraced his steps.

At length he stood in the road within sight of the Vane cottage.

Everything looked quiet and peaceful about the place.

No smoke curled up from the kitchen chimney, although the sun was low in the western heavens.

"Vic hasn't begun to prepare supper it seems," muttered Bordine. "Wonder if I had best go up that way and call. Of course Ransom has returned. I believe I will and inquire who the gentleman was who called just as I was entering the woods."

And so Bordine turned his steps in the direction of the Vane cottage. The front door was closed, and a dead silence reigned over the place as he came up.

"Wonder if the folks are gone."

Bordine rapped.

No answer was vouchsafed.

He rapped again.

Silence profound as the grave.

"Well, there seems nobody at home. Vic sometimes occupies the back porch with the cat and her book; I will see."

The morning sun filtered through the lace curtains of the Poynsett drawing-room, casting delicate patterns on the Persian rug below. It was a day full to bursting with the gaieties of country house socializing—a garden fête was planned that afternoon, followed by an evening of music and conviviality. With society swarming, Mrs. Poynsett observed these preparations with a practiced eye for detail, a touch of mischief dancing in her gentle gaze.

"There, Rosamond," she remarked, with her usual briskness, "I do hope that canopy will not tumble upon the good squire of Harthfield. He has a disposition as volatile as his horses."

Rosamond, lightly arranging the pianoforte sheet music, responded with a carefree lilt, "Fear not, Mother, if the tent gives way, perhaps we shall entertain the party with a further spectacle. The esteemed squire, beneath the canvas, provided he has his wits about him, would make quite the scene."

At this, Cecil, glancing over a rendering of the guest list, replied with her characteristic precision, "Were he to fall, no doubt his opinions would be aired as virulently as his politics."

Aware of Cecil's tastes, never far from the decorum she held dear, Mrs. Poynsett shifted to another topic, "You are aware, of course, that the Duncombes are to join us? Their newest discussions on reform must promise quite the captivation."

"They reform only what needs no change," countered Rosamond with a skew of her head, her tresses catching the sunlight mischievously. A look crossed her features as if a thought unbidden had taken its hold, but she said no more on it.

Before the room could sink back into silence, Frank, ever the bringer of vitality, bounded in with the intrepid spirit of one whose plans seldom hewed to the straight and narrow. "Well then, my dears," began he, knuckles whitening upon a newspaper more crumpled than orderly, "have you heard of the latest at Harthfield—they've installed nothing less than a racing course amid their oak fields."

"A racing course? Truly, Frank, have they?" Mrs. Poynsett responded in a tone mingling surprise and tolerance, the corners of her mouth curving in her perennial amusement at the folly of men. "What comes next? Perhaps one’s garden shall outstretch the House of Lords."

Cecil, for all her reserve, toppled her composure with a sigh, "If Lady Amelia supposes she may remodel the estate, I am certain it will not stay contained to mere gallops."

An uncomfortable quietude lent upon them then, one Rosamond valiantly strove to dispel by a change of subject, "I heard Miss Duncombe speaks this evening upon the education of women—did you not think her last address the cause of much consideration?"

"Consideration? Controversy, rather," remarked Frank. "You shall speak yourself plainly in this: not every heart takes kindly to such ideas."

"And yet," Mrs. Poynsett interposed gently, "the world was made not of stone alone but must be molded from many hands."

As if on cue, the door opened with a soft exhale, releasing Julius to their midst. He was ever a blend of his mother's calm previsions and his own lively ambitions. "I come as emissary from Rockpier with tidings and tales," he jested, a gentle quirk at his lips.

At his advent, Frank seized the opportunity to inquire, "And how went the service? Did the good Mr. Bindon stump and thunder with his usual vigor?"

"The congregation seemed much pleased," Julius reported, falling into an easy seat. "Herbert Bowater's readings added a clear and confident note, Mrs. Hornblower says he draws more each Sunday."

"Young Bowater's family bears a strong influence, no doubt," Cecil supplied, with raised brow to match her tone.

Rosamond, curious as ever, added, "Does his sister accompany him still? Such spirit in one so young!"

Having seen enough of the room's pace, Julius offered his peculiarly acquiring nod, "Yes, indeed, Miss Lavinia Bowater stays with the Hornblowers as well. Her ministrations to the children promise quite the invigorating spirit."

"One hopes such exertion is appreciated," muttered Frank, not immune from the occasional barb of society's sting.

Yet it was then Mrs. Poynsett, smoothing the wrinkles from her morning dress with soft resolve, restored the moment's equilibrium with her singular prowess, "Come now, we must all bend ourselves to readiness. This fête shall not receive itself."

And so, as the appointed hour to gather swept near, the household, each with their particular manner of hope and resolve, drifted to their stations, in perfect concert with the life that made Poynsett manor a mosaic of industry and intention.
