She changed her sentence. ‘It makes one think, and want to be good.’

‘It is what all truly beautiful things should do’ said John.

‘Oh! I am glad you say so,’ exclaimed Violet. ‘It is like what Annette and I have wondered about--I mean why fine statues or pictures, or anything of that kind, should make one feel half sad and half thoughtful when one looks at them long.’

‘Perhaps because it is a straining after the only true beauty.’

‘I must tell Annette that. It was she that said it was so,’ said Violet; ‘and we wondered Greek statues gave one that feeling, but I see it must be the reason.’

‘What statues have you seen?’

‘Those at Wrangerton House. Lord St. Erme is always sending cases home, and it is such a festival day to go up and see them unpacked, and Caroline and Annette go and take drawings, and I like to wander about the rooms, and look at everything,’ said Violet, growing talkative on the theme of home. ‘There is one picture I like above all, but that is a sacred subject, so no wonder it should have that feeling in it.’

‘What is it?’

‘It is a Madonna,’ she said, lowering her voice. ‘A stiff old-fashioned one, in beautiful, bright, clear colouring. The Child is reaching out to embrace a little cross, and his Mother holds him towards it with such a sad but such a holy face, as if she foreboded all, and was ready to bear it.’

‘Ah! that Ghirlandajo?’

‘That is the name!’ cried Violet, enchanted. ‘Have you seen it?’

‘I saw Lord St. Erme buy it.’

‘Do you know Lord St. Erme?’ said Violet, rather awe-struck.

‘I used to meet him in Italy.’

‘We wish so much that he would come home. We do so want to see a poet.’

John smiled. ‘Is he never at home?’

‘O, no, he has never been at Wrangerton since his father died, twelve years ago. He does not like the place, so he only comes to London when he is in England, and papa goes up to meet him on business, but he is too poetical to attend to it.’

‘I should guess that.’

‘I have done wrong, said Violet, checking herself; ‘I should not have said that. Mamma told us that we ought never to chatter about his concerns. Will you, please, not remember that I said it?’

As far as the outer world is concerned, I certainly will not,’ said John kindly. ‘You cannot too early learn discretion. So that picture is at Wrangerton?’

‘I am so glad you liked it.’

‘I liked it well enough to wish for a few spare hundreds, but it seems to have afforded no more pleasure to him than it has given to me. I am glad it is gone where there is some one who can appreciate it.’

‘Oh, said Violet,’ Matilda knows all about the best pictures. We don’t appreciate, you know, we only like.’

‘And your chief liking is for that one?’

‘It is more than liking,’ said Violet; ‘I could call it loving. It is almost the same to me as Helvellyn. Annette and I went to the house for one look more my last evening at home. I must tell her that you have seen it!’ and the springing steps grew so rapid, that her companion had to say, ‘Don’t let me detain you, I am obliged to go gently up-hill.’ She checked her steps, abashed, and presently, with a shy but very pretty action, held out her arm, saying timidly, ‘Would it help you to lean on me? I ought not to have brought you this steep way. Matilda says I skurry like a school-girl.’

He saw it would console her to let her think herself of service and accepted of the slender prop for the few steps that remained. He then went up-stairs to write letters, but finding no ink, came to the drawing-room to ask her for some. She had only her own inkstand, which was supplying her letter to Annette, and he sat down at the opposite side of the table to share it. Her pen went much faster than his. ‘Clifton Terrace, Winchester,’ and ‘My dear father--I came here yesterday, and was most agreeably surprised,’ was all that he had indited, when he paused to weigh what was his real view of the merits of the case, and ponder whether his present feeling was sober judgment, or the novelty of the bewitching prettiness of this innocent and gracious creature. There he rested, musing, while from her pen flowed a description of her walk and of Mr. Martindale’s brother. ‘If they are all like him, I shall be perfectly happy,’ she wrote. ‘I never saw any one so kind and considerate, and so gentle; only now and then he frightens me, with his politeness, or perhaps polish is the right word, it makes me feel myself rude and uncourteous and awkward. You said nothing gave you so much the notion of high-breeding as Mr. Martindale’s ease, especially when he pretended to be rough and talk slang, it was like playing at it. Now, his brother has the same, without the funny roughness, but the greatest gentleness, and a good deal of quiet sadness. I suppose it is from his health, though he is much better now: he still coughs, and he moves slowly and leans languidly, as if he was not strong. He is not so tall as his brother, and much slighter in make, and fairer complexioned, with gray eyes and brown hair, and he looks sallow and worn and thin, with such white long hands.’

"Dost thou know any fault or crime in this man that should prevent God's blessing from resting on thy marriage with him? Dost thou feel aversion or repugnance to him in any way?"

And to all this what could I say? I could only stammer out that I did not think I loved him enough; and my poor old father saw in this reluctance only the fancy of a silly girl who did not know her own mind, but who had now gone too far to recede.

So we were married, in the Court chapel, a privilege which Madame Rupprecht had used no end of efforts to obtain for us, and which she must have thought was to secure us all possible happiness, both at the time and in recollection afterwards.

We were married; and after two days spent in festivity at Carlsruhe, among all our new fashionable friends there, I bade good-by for ever to my dear old father. I had begged my husband to take me by way of Heidelberg to his old castle in the Vosges; but I found an amount of determination, under that effeminate appearance and manner, for which I was not prepared, and he refused my first request so decidedly that I dared not urge it. "Henceforth, Anna," said he, "you will move in a different sphere of life; and though it is possible that you may have the power of showing favour to your relations from time to time, yet much or familiar intercourse will be undesirable, and is what I cannot allow." I felt almost afraid, after this formal speech, of asking my father and Fritz to come and see me; but, when the agony of bidding them farewell overcame all my prudence, I did beg them to pay me a visit ere long. But they shook their heads, and spoke of business at home, of different kinds of life, of my being a Frenchwoman now. Only my father broke out at last with a blessing, and said, "If my child is unhappy--which God forbid--let her remember that her father's house is ever open to her." I was on the point of crying out, "Oh! take me back then now, my father! oh, my father!" when I felt, rather than saw, my husband present near me. He looked on with a slightly contemptuous air; and, taking my hand in his, he led me weeping away, saying that short farewells were always the best when they were inevitable.

It took us two days to reach his château in the Vosges, for the roads were bad and the way difficult to ascertain. Nothing could be more devoted than he was all the time of the journey. It seemed as if he were trying in every way to make up for the separation which every hour made me feel the more complete between my present and my former life. I seemed as if I were only now wakening up to a full sense of what marriage was, and I dare say I was not a cheerful companion on the tedious journey. At length, jealousy of my regret for my father and brother got the better of M. de la Tourelle, and he became so much displeased with me that I thought my heart would break with the sense of desolation. So it was in no cheerful frame of mind that we approached Les Rochers, and I thought that perhaps it was because I was so unhappy that the place looked so dreary. On one side, the château looked like a raw new building, hastily run up for some immediate purpose, without any growth of trees or underwood near it, only the remains of the stone used for building, not yet cleared away from the immediate neighbourhood, although weeds and lichens had been suffered to grow near and over the heaps of rubbish; on the other, were the great rocks from which the place took its name, and rising close against them, as if almost a natural formation, was the old castle, whose building dated many centuries back.

“Is she sleeping?” whispered one gentle, anxious voice.

“Not now,” replied the other, a soft, melodious tone. “She’s been lying awake, and thinking, I fancy. Her eyes have been open this half-hour past.”

“Does she show signs of remembering?” The inquiry was made with bated breath, as if the speaker feared to awaken some dormant pang.

“Not yet, I think. Though, once or twice, I’ve seen a look of trouble pass across her face, like the shadow of a cloud on a summer’s day.” The nurse’s words were spoken with a quiet, soothing emphasis, as if to calm the listener’s fears.

“Poor child! How her eyes looked, when she first came round! So dull, so vacant! I thought, for a moment, we had lost her.” The voice trembled, and the speaker’s words were barely audible.

“Hush! Don’t fret, now. She’s on the mend, thank God! And, with care, she’ll come round, and be as bright as ever.” The nurse’s tone was reassuring, but her eyes betrayed a lurking anxiety, a fear that she dared not express.

The two women stood, side by side, in the dimly-lit chamber, watching the pale, wan face, that lay on the pillow. The stillness was oppressive, broken only by the soft, regular breathing of the sleeper.

As they stood, a footstep, outside the door, made them turn, simultaneously. It was a heavy, clumsy tread, and the nurses exchanged a glance of dismay. “It’s Willie,” whispered one, “come to see his sister.”

The door creaked, and a tall, lanky figure, with a vacant, foolish face, and a shambling gait, entered the room. His eyes, once bright, and full of intelligence, now stared, with a dull, lack-lustre gaze, and his smile, was a weak, meaningless thing.

“Willie, my boy,” said the nurse, advancing to meet him, “you shouldn’t have come in, just now. Your sister’s not well enough, yet, to see visitors.” But Willie merely stared, uncomprehending, his eyes fixed on the bed, where his sister lay.

“Susan,” he muttered, in a thick, drawling voice, “Susan’s ill. Father said—” He paused, and his eyes wandered, aimlessly, round the room. The nurses exchanged a sorrowful glance, and one of them took Willie’s arm, and led him, gently, from the room.

As they disappeared, the other nurse returned to the bedside, and gazed, anxiously, at the patient. Susan’s eyes were open, now, and she was staring, wistfully, into space. The nurse’s heart ached, as she looked at the frail, fragile form, and the pale, sorrowful face.

“Susan, dear, how are you, now?” she asked, softly, trying to rouse the girl from her reverie. But Susan merely turned, listlessly, and murmured, “Michael?” The nurse’s eyes dropped, and she hesitated, before replying.

“Michael’s well, dear. He’s out, just now, attending to the farm.” The words were spoken, with a studied care, a deliberate evasion, and the nurse’s conscience smote her, as she looked at the trusting, childlike face, that lay on the pillow.

Susan’s eyes lingered, wistfully, on the nurse’s face, as if seeking something, that was not there. Then, they dropped, and she lay, silent, and still, her thoughts, a mystery, that no one could divine.

The sun, outside, was shining, brightly, casting a warm, golden light, over the landscape. But, in the sick-room, all was dim, and shadowy, and the only sound, was the soft, regular breathing, of the patient.

As the nurse stood, watching, a faint, troubled look, passed across Susan’s face, and she murmured, incoherently, “Father?” The nurse’s heart sank, and she knew, that the moment of revelation, was at hand. But, for now, she merely bent, and whispered, softly, “Hush, dear, don’t think of that, now. You must rest, and get well.”

The door, outside, creaked, again, and the nurse’s head turned, expectantly. It was Michael, come to inquire, after his sister. His face was grave, and anxious, and his eyes, scanned the room, with a keen, searching gaze. The nurse met him, with a whispered, “She’s awake, now, and seems a little better.” But Michael’s eyes, were fixed, on the bed, where Susan lay, and his face, was sombre, and foreboding.

As he approached, the bed, Susan’s eyes, lifted, and met his, with a faint, questioning glance. But Michael’s face, was impassive, and his voice, was low, and guarded, as he asked, “How is she, nurse?”

As the carriage rumbled on its way to Overton Manor, Mr. Clarence Pomfret indulged in a reverie, his gaze wandering out the window to the lush expanse of countryside beyond. He felt a sense of satisfaction wash over him, a pleasant warmth that began in his chest and seeped outward through his very being. It was a feeling that had been growing in him of late, a feeling that was as hard to shake as a summer fog drifting off the Avon.

He had not yet risen with the family that morning, as he had been feeling particularly inclined for a quiet moment to himself. In the solitude of his dressing room, he had read a few lines from the Psalms, felt the stillness of the morning settle within him, and then stepped out into the garden for a brief stroll. And now, as he rode in the carriage, he felt refreshed and invigorated, his mind alert and clear.

The carriage door swung open and he stepped down onto the gravel drive, the crunching of the stones beneath his feet a gentle accompaniment to his thoughts. Mrs. Jenkins, his housekeeper, greeted him warmly as he dismounted, her kind eyes shining with a welcome. "Good morning, sir. I do hope you slept well."

As he handed his hat and stick to a waiting footman, he replied, "Indeed I did, Jenkins. And I must confess, I feel quite refreshed. The morning air agrees with me." He smiled, and she nodded, her eyes twinkling with understanding.

Following Jenkins into the manor, Mr. Pomfret made his way to the morning room, where the family was already gathered about the breakfast table. His daughter, Fanny, looked up from her seat, a smile spreading across her face as he entered. "Father!" she exclaimed, stretching out a hand.

He took it, bending to kiss her forehead. "Good morning, Fanny. I see you're already up and about." His son, Harry, looked up from his breakfast, a look of mild interest on his face. "Good morning, Father."

As they took their seats at the table, Mr. Pomfret's thoughts turned to the day ahead. There were matters of business to attend to, correspondence to answer, and perhaps a visit to the estate's farms, if the weather held fair. But for now, he was content to sit with his family, enjoying the quiet morning moments.

After breakfast, he excused himself, feeling a sudden impulse to take the air. Jenkins anticipated his desire and handed him his hat and stick. "Shall I have the carriage brought round, sir?" she asked.

Mr. Pomfret nodded, smiling. "No, I think not, Jenkins. I shall walk. The morning is far from over, and the air is still pleasant." He stepped out into the driveway, feeling the sun on his face, the breeze rustling the leaves in the trees.

As he walked, he found his mind beginning to wander, his thoughts straying from the concerns of the day to more pleasant matters. It was a fine morning, after all, and he felt grateful for the simple joys in life. The sound of birdsong, the scent of the blooming flowers, the warmth of the sun on his skin – all these things combined to create a sense of contentment that was hard to shake.

He had not gone far when he heard the distant chime of a church bell. He smiled, feeling a sense of satisfaction. It was a reminder that, despite the distractions of the world, there were still moments of peace and calm to be found. And as he walked, he found his heart growing lighter, his spirit lifted by the simple goodness of the day.

The sound of the bell grew louder, and he quickened his pace, his feet carrying him towards the church at Littlehill. He had not been there in some time, but he felt drawn to the quiet reverence of the place. And as he approached the manor gates, he noticed something that caused him to frown – fresh horse hoof marks on the gravel.

To this end I sketched the character of Mary Martin. By making the opening of my story date from the time of the Relief Bill, I intended to picture the state of the country at one of the most memorable eras in its history, and when an act of the Legislature assumed to redress inequalities, compose differences, and allay jealousies of centuries' growth, and make of two widely differing races one contented people.

I had not, I own, any implicit faith in Acts of Parliament, and I had a fervent belief in what kindness--when combined with knowledge of Ireland--could do with Irishmen. I have never heard of a people with whom sympathy could do so much, nor the want of it be so fatal. I have never heard of any other people to whom the actual amount of a benefit was of less moment than the mode it was bestowed. I have never read of a race who, in great poverty and many privations, attach a higher value to the consideration that is bestowed on them than to the actual material boons, and feel such a seemingly disproportioned gratitude for kind words and generous actions.

What might not be anticipated from a revulsion of sentiment in a people like this, to what violence might not this passion for vengeance be carried, if the notion possessed them that they, whom she called her betters, only traded on the weakness of their poverty and the imbecility of their good faith? It was in a fruitful soil of this kind that the agitation now sowed the seeds of distrust and disorder; and with what fatal rapidity the poison reproduced itself and spread, the history of late years is the testimony.

If such traits as I have endeavored to picture in Mary Martin were engaged in the work of benevolence tomorrow, they would be met on every side by discouragement and defeat. The priest would denounce them as a propaganda artfully intended to sap the ancient faith of the people; the agitators would denounce them as the cunning flatteries of political solicitation; the people themselves would distrust them as covering some secret object; and the National Press would be certain to utter its warnings against whatever promised to establish peace or contentment to the land.

I have said already, and I repeat it here, that this character of Mary Martin is purely fictitious; and there is the more need I should say it, since there was once a young lady of this very name,--many traits of whose affection for the people and efforts for their well being might be supposed to have been my original. To my great regret I never had the happiness to have met her; however, I have heard much of her devotion and her goodness.

I am not sure that some of my subordinate characters were not drawn from life. Mrs. Nelligan, I remember, had her type in a little Galway town I once stopped at, and Dan Nelligan had much in common with one who has since held a distinguished place on the Bench.

Of the terrible epidemic which devastated Ireland, there was much for which I drew on my own experience. Of its fearful ravages in the west, in the wilds of Clare, and that lonely promontory that stretches at the mouth of the Shannon into the Atlantic, I had been the daily witness; and even to recall some of the incidents passingly was an effort of great pain.

Of one feature of the people at this disastrous time, I could not say enough; nor could any words of mine do justice to the splendid heroism with which they bore up, and the noble generosity they showed each other in misfortune. It is but too often remarked how selfish men are made by misery, and how fatal is a common affliction to that charity that cares for others. There was none of this here; I never in any condition or class recognized more traits of thoughtful kindness and self-denial than I did amongst these poor, famished, and forgotten people. I never witnessed in the same perfection, how a widespread affliction could call up a humanity great as itself, and make very commonplace natures something actually heroic and glorious.

The atmosphere at Kellynch Hall grew increasingly strained as the days passed. Sir Walter's pride, though chafed by the necessities of their changed circumstances, remained unyielding, while Lady Russell, ever the voice of reason, sought to navigate the tempest of their financial ruin with the utmost delicacy. The weight of their debts pressed heavily upon her, and her mind was constantly occupied with plans of retrenchment, each more ingenious than the last, designed to spare Sir Walter and Elizabeth the full brunt of their reduced fortunes. Yet, despite her efforts, the spectre of debt loomed ever larger, casting its shadow over the once-proud estate.

It was a circumstance most peculiar, and not without a touch of irony, that Anne, the youngest and most overlooked of the Elliot daughters, had become the unexpected confidante in this matter of retrenchment. Lady Russell, in her wisdom, had discerned in Anne a singular acumen, a quiet strength of character that the others, in their preoccupation with airs and trifles, had long since neglected. Anne's suggestions, though modestly offered, carried a weight that none could ignore. She spoke not of the superficial trims and tweaks that Lady Russell had initially proposed, but of a more rigorous approach, one that embraced honesty andseverity, to restore the family's finances to a state of stability. Her words, though spoken softly, carried the force of conviction, and Lady Russell, to her credit, listened.

But Sir Walter, when presented with the proposed measures, was little inclined to entertain them. His dignity, already bruised by the necessity of such changes, rebelled at the mere suggestion of further deprivation. To him, the idea of retrenchment was akin to a degradation, a compromising of the Elliot name and the splendour that had been their birthright. Seven years, Lady Russell had declared, was the time required to clear the debts, a period he deemed insupportable. “Seven years!” he had exclaimed, his voice rang with the force of his wounded vanity. “Seven years of such ignominy and discomfort is a sentence worse than any fate I could imagine.” And so, with a vehemence that brooked no argument, he declared his preference to abandon Kellynch Hall rather than endure the proposed reductions.

In the wake of this decision, Mr. Shepherd, the family solicitor, arrived at Kellynch Hall to offer his counsel. His presence was a stark reminder of their precarious situation, and his advice was plain: if the Elliots were to secure any measure of financial solvency, a change of residence was not merely advisable but imperative. “A removal,” he declared, with the matter-of-fact tone of one accustomed to brokering difficult truths, “would afford the necessary opportunity for a substantial adjustment in Sir Walter’s way of living. Kellynch Hall, with all its grandeur, is no longer a tenable proposition, given the constraints of your present circumstances.”

Though Lady Russell had anticipated such a recommendation, the weight of Mr. Shepherd’s words landed with a force that was difficult to ignore. The decision to leave Kellynch, a place that had been the Elliot family’s home for generations, was a bitter pill to swallow. Yet, as she conversed with Mr. Shepherd, Lady Russell could not help but acknowledge the wisdom of his counsel. Kellynch, with its opulent expenses and inescapable associations with their former splendour, was indeed an obstacle to any meaningful retrenchment. It was, she realised, a symbol of the past, and the past, however dear, must give way to the needs of the present.

As the solicitor took his leave, Lady Russell turned her thoughts to Anne, her youngest daughter, whose wisdom and foresight had been so instrumental in shaping their plans. She determined to seek Anne’s counsel once more, for in her, she had found a steadfast ally, a daughter whose quiet strength and unwavering integrity offered a beacon of hope in these dark times. Together, they would navigate the stormy seas of their financial ruin, guided by a steadfast resolve to restore their family’s fortunes, even as they sought to preserve the dignity of their name.

Here Mr. Anderson, his face a mask of forced resignation, interrupted.

Mr. Anderson merely grunted, turning his gaze towards Al.

"Mr. Allston, I trust this… arrangement is entirely above board?" he asked, his tone laced with suspicion. "I have a profound unease regarding these theatrical ventures. I insist upon a meeting, at your earliest convenience, to discuss your… motives."

Al, though privately amused by the mayor's gruff demeanor, maintained a respectful countenance.

"Certainly, Mr. Anderson," he replied. "I shall be pleased to address any concerns you may have. But time presses, as I mentioned. Mrs. Anderson's swift departure is paramount."

As Al spoke, a commotion erupted from the darkened hallway beyond the parlor. Raised voices, punctuated by the clatter of what sounded like falling furniture, echoed through the house.

"What in tarnation is that ruckus?" Mr. Anderson muttered, his brow furrowed in annoyance.

Before anyone could answer, a figure stumbled into the room, propelled forward by a force unseen. It was Mr. Wattles, his face flushed with anger, his cravat askew. Behind him, a disheveled man, clearly the worse for drink, brandished a gleaming knife.

"I'll get you for this, Wattles!" the man snarled, his words slurred. "You think you can cast me aside like an old boot? I'll show you! I'll show you all!"

Al recognized the man immediately. It was Farley, Mr. Wattles's erstwhile advance agent, now clearly a man consumed by bitterness and drink.

Mr. Wattles stood his ground, though a flicker of fear danced in his eyes.

"Farley, put that thing away!" he commanded, his voice trembling slightly. "You're drunk and making a fool of yourself."

"A fool, am I?" Farley roared, taking a step closer, the knife glinting menacingly in the dim light. "You'll see who the fool is when I've… when I've…"

His words trailed off into incoherent mumbling, his drunken rage momentarily deflated. He swayed precariously on his feet, the knife wavering in his grasp.

Suddenly, the fight seemed to drain out of him. The menacing snarl dissolved into a pathetic whimper.

"Oh, Mr. Wattles," he sobbed, dropping to his knees. "Forgive me! I didn't mean it! I'm just… lost. Lost and alone. Please, don't turn me in to the authorities!"

Mr. Wattles, his anger seemingly evaporated by Farley's sudden collapse, sighed heavily.

"Get up, Farley," he said, his voice now weary. "You're a disgrace to yourself."

He extended a hand to help the fallen man to his feet.

"I won't have you arrested," he continued, "But you must leave this house immediately. And never darken my door again."

Farley, still weeping, clung to Mr. Wattles's hand.

"Thank you, Mr. Wattles," he choked out. "Thank you. I… I don't know what I would have done."

Mr. Wattles gently disengaged his hand.

"There's something else you should know, Farley," he said, his voice regaining its firmness. "I've already engaged a new advance agent. A Mr. Al Allston. He is far more capable than you ever were."

Farley’s bloodshot eyes widened in disbelief. He turned his gaze upon Al, who had watched the entire scene with a detached curiosity.

"That boy?" he scoffed, a sneer twisting his lips. "He’s barely old enough to shave! What does he know about advance work? This is preposterous!"

As I stood there, grappling with the enigma that was the Aristocrat of the Imperishables, I felt the burden of my own mortal coil weighing upon me. His words still echoed in my mind, a mocking refrain that stirred a sense of discomfort and bewilderment. This was not the first time I had encountered the like of him, but his words had a way of gnawing at my very being, like a worm eating away at the tender shoots of a delicate flower.

The scene had shifted, and the motley assembly was now gathered around a roaring fire, the flames casting flickering shadows on the faces of the gathered youth. His voice, like a gentle breeze on a summer's day, had lulled us back into a semblance of comfort. Yet, I, for one, could not shake off the feeling of discomfort that had settled within me.

His eyes gleamed with a knowing light, as if he held some secret that we, mere mortals, could hardly begin to grasp. And yet, there was a hint of playfulness in his mien, a droll glint that told of a deeper humor lurking beneath the surface. He was a master of sorts, a conjurer of words, weaving a spell of words that both entranced and unsettled us.

"I shall tell you a tale, my young friends," he said, his voice weaving a gentle spell. "A tale of Samson, the strong and the weak, who fell to a snare, a rope to the will of another, a leaf to the gust of the wind." He leaned forward, his eyes aglow with mischief, and commenced to speak. "In days of yore, when the sun beat down upon the parched earth, Samson, that great and mighty one, walked among us. He was a wonder, a man of unyielding strength, with muscles like the trunks of ancient trees and a heart of gold."

As he spoke, his voice dripped with a honeyed sweetness, drawing us in, entrancing us with his words. We, the young and the wistful, hung on his every phrase, drinking in the tale like thirsty plants drink in the morning dew. And when he finished, we were all but giddy with the joy of it, our faces aglow with the warmth of the fire and the warmth of the tale itself.

But, as the laughter and the oohs and ahhs subsided, a stillness fell upon the assembly, a stillness of anticipation, for we knew that he was but in the mood for more. He smiled, a slow and wicked smile, and leaned back in his chair, his eyes glinting like stars on a clear night. "And now, my young friends," he said, his voice dripping with a queasy sweetness, "I shall show you a sight that will leave you all but agog with wonder."

Raising his hands, he conjured a bubble, a great soap-bubble that swelled and floated before us, reflecting the firelight like a mirror reflecting the moon. It grew, and grew, until it seemed a mirage, wondrous and whimsical, before our very eyes. And then, with a suddenness that left us gasping, it burst, dissolving into nothingness, leaving naught but a faint smell of soap and a hint of that je ne sais quoi that seems to cling to all things strange and wonderful.

As the bubble vanished, he vanished too, like a spirit departing the earthly realm. The fire crackled and spat, casting a golden glow upon the assembly, and in the center of that glow, we stood, frozen, like rabbits caught in the sights of a hunter. We looked at one another, and at the spot where he had stood, and then, like a summer's breeze, a murmur began to spread among us.

The determination once made, she adhered to it. She had felt a vague annoyance at the constancy and the persistency with which regret for the lost society of Sabran recurred to her. She had attributed it to the solitude in which she lived: that solitude which is the begetter and the nurse of thought may also be the hotbed of unwise fancies. It was indeed a solitude filled with grave duties, careful labours, high desires and endeavours; but perhaps, she thought, the world for a while, even in its folly, might be healthier, might preserve her from the undue share which the memory of a stranger had in her musings.

Her people, her lands, her animals, would none of them suffer by a brief absence; and perhaps there were duties due as well to her position as to her order. She was the only representative of the great Counts of Szalras. With the whimsical ingratitude to fate common to human nature, she thought she would sooner have been obscure, unnoticed, free. Her rank began to drag on her with something like the sense of a chain. She felt that she was growing irritable, fanciful, thankless; so she ordered the huge old palace in the Herrengasse to be got ready, and sought the world as others sought the cloister.

In a week's time she was installed in Vienna, with a score of horses, two score of servants, and all the stir and pomp that attend a great establishment in the most aristocratic city of Europe, and she made her first appearance at a ball at the Residenz covered with jewels from head to foot; the wonderful old jewels that for many seasons had lain unseen in their iron coffers--opals given by Rurik, sapphires taken from Kara Mustafa, pearls worn by her people at the wedding of Mary of Burgundy, diamonds that had been old when Maria Theresa had been young.

She had three months of continual homage, of continual flattery, of what others called pleasure, and what none could have denied was splendour. Great nobles laid their heart and homage before her feet, and all the city looked after her for her beauty as she drove her horses round the Ringstrasse. It left her all very cold and unamused and indifferent.

She was impatient to be back at Hohenszalras, amidst the stillness of the woods, the sound of the waters.

'You cannot say now that I do not care for the world, because I have forgotten what it was like,' she observed to her aunt.

'I wish you cared more,' said the Princess. 'Position has its duties.'

'I never dispute that; only I do not see that being wearied by society constitutes one of them. I cannot understand why people are so afraid of solitude; the routine of the world is quite as monotonous.'

'If you only appreciated the homage that you receive----'

'Surely one's mind is something like one's conscience: if one can be not too utterly discontented with what it says one does not need the verdict of others.'

'That is only a more sublime form of vanity. Really, my love, with your extraordinary and unnecessary humility in some things, and your overweening arrogance in others, you would perplex wiser heads than the one I possess.'

In the midst of these stratagems, wherein Ormond found his most potent ally, lurked the seeds of unforeseen consequences. As he delved deeper into the labyrinth of human duplicity, the lines that delineated right from wrong became increasingly blurred. His methods, though successful, were not without their own unique challenges. The tangled web he wove ensnared not only those whom he sought to deceive, but occasionally ensnared him as well.

Indeed, it was in the quiet moments, away from the shadows of his machinations, when Ormond would often find himself reflecting upon the nature of trust and the ethics of subterfuge. Yet, these reflections were mere epiphenomena in the grand theatre of his pursuits. His mind, once engaged in the plot of stratagem, seldom returned to ponder the morality of the game he played. The thrill of the chase, the thrill of the victory—these were the spurs that urged him forward, ever onward in his quest for mastery.

It was during such a moment of reflection that he espied a veiled figure across the candle-lit room. It was a visage he had hoped to avoid, yet its presence was a testament to the interconnectedness of all things. This stranger, unlike others, bore the mark of shared experience, a kindred spirit in the art of duplicity. Their encounter was one of mutual understanding, a silent acknowledgment of the burdens they bore. From this collaboration, a new chapter unfolded, one marked by schemes that were as intricate as the antique clocks Ormond favored, each tick and tock echoing with the potential for profound consequences.

In the wake of these affairs, Miss Dudley found herself at a crossroads, her fate as interwoven with Ormond’s as the threads of a tapestry. The events that transpired were veiled in secrecy, known only to those closest to the game. Ormond, the master of shadows, remained an enigma to all but a chosen few. His plans, so broad and deep, were akin to the vast ocean, its surface calm but for the hidden currents that shaped its depths. To the observer, Ormond was a cipher, his every move calculated and concealed, his true intentions obscured by the mist of conjecture and rumor.

Yet, despite his disciplined facade, Ormond was not immune to the lures of passion. The very excesses that had once defined his youth found modern expressions, albeit with a refined patina. He engaged in dalliances that society whispered about in hushed tones, affairs that were as controversial as they were clandestine. These liaisons, while frowned upon by the sanctimonious, were to Ormond a release, a means to temper the rigors of his clandestine endeavors. Thus, the man of stratagems lived a life as complex and multifaceted as the plots he devised, a figure whose darkness danced with a flickering light of hedonistic pleasure, forever in the balance.

“But that's just where you misunderstand them, Drummond,” said Courtland, smiling. “They have no reason to keep up an attitude towards their neighbors, who still know them as 'Squire' so-and-so, 'Colonel' this and that, and the 'Judge,'--owners of their vast but crippled estates. They are not ashamed of being poor, which is an accident.”

“But they are of working, which is DELIBERATION,” interrupted Drummond. “They are ashamed to mend their fences themselves, now that they have no slaves to do it for them.”

“I doubt very much if some of them know how to drive a nail, for the matter of that,” said Courtland, still good-humoredly, “but that's the fault of a system older than themselves, which the founders of the Republic retained. We cannot give them experience in their new condition in one day, and in fact, Drummond, I am very much afraid that for our purposes--and I honestly believe for THEIR good--we must help to keep them for the present as they are.”

“Perhaps,” said Drummond sarcastically, “you would like to reinstate slavery?”

“No. But I should like to reinstate the MASTER. And not for HIS sake alone, but for freedom's sake and OURS. To be plain: since I have taken up this matter for the company, I have satisfied myself from personal observation that the negro--even more than his master--cannot handle his new condition. He is accustomed to his old traditional task-master, and I doubt if he will work fairly for any other--particularly for those who don't understand him. Don't mistake me: I don't propose to go back to the whip; to that brutal institution, the irresponsible overseer; to the buying and selling, and separation of the family, nor any of the old wrongs; but I propose to make the old master OUR OVERSEER, and responsible to US. He is not a fool, and has already learned that it is more profitable to pay wages to his old slaves and have the power of dismissal, like any other employer, than be obliged, under the old system of enforced labor and life servitude, to undergo the cost of maintaining incompetence and idleness. The old sentiment of slave-owning has disappeared before natural common-sense and selfishness. I am satisfied that by some such process as this utilizing of the old master and the new freedom we will be better able to cultivate our lands than by buying up their estates, and setting the old owners adrift, with a little money in their pockets, as an idle, discontented class to revive old political dogmas, and foment new issues, or perhaps set up a dangerous opposition to us.

“You don't mean to say that those infernal niggers would give the preference to their old oppressors?”

“Dollar for dollar in wages--yes! And why shouldn't they? Their old masters understand them better--and treat them generally better. They know our interest in them is only an abstract sentiment, not a real liking. We show it at every turn. But we are nearing Redlands, and Major Reed will, I have no doubt, corroborate my impressions. He insists upon our staying at his house, although the poor old fellow, I imagine, can ill afford to entertain company. But he will be offended if we refuse.”

“He is a friend of yours, then?” asked Drummond.

“I fought against his division at Stony Creek,” said Courtland grimly. “He never tires of talking of it to me--so I suppose I am.”

A few moments later the train glided beside the Redlands platform. As the two travelers descended a hand was laid on Courtland's shoulder, and a stout figure in the blackest and shiniest of alpaca jackets, and the whitest and broadest of Panama hats, welcomed him. “Glad to see yo', cun'nel. I reckoned I'd waltz over and bring along the boy,” pointing to a grizzled negro servant of sixty who was bowing before them, “to tote yo'r things over instead of using a hack. I haven't run much on horseflesh since the wah--ha! ha! What I didn't use up for remounts I reckon yo'r commissary gobbled up with the other live stock, eh?” He laughed heartily, as if the recollections were purely humorous, and again clapped Courtland on the back.

The dim light of the dawn found Mr. Sawyer already astride his spirited steed, a little grey horse that now seemed but an extension of his own confident form. Like Sir Launcelot himself, he cleaved through the early mists with an ease and grace that bespoke a seasoned rider, masterful in every sense of the word. His thoughts flitted back to the previous day's exploits, reliving the moment when he had found himself at the fore of the galloping throng, navigating treacherous ditches and formidable fences with a sureness one might attribute to divine providence. More than once had he caught an admiring glance from fellow sportsmen, both humble and noble, as they witnessed his unrivaled prowess upon the field.

As the tranquil countryside gradually roused from its slumber, Mr. Sawyer's mind wandered towards considerations far removed from the thrill of the chase. Within him simmered a restlessness that refused to be quenched by the humdrum of provincial life, alluring as the call of the horn might be. He possessed a spirit that yearned for greater challenges, for the broader canvases offered by distant lands and more illustrious hunting grounds. In quiet moments, these desires would spill forth in dreams vivid and irresistible, visions of foreign plains where wild creatures ran free, tantalizingly elusive as any mythic beast.

Yet even as he envisioned himself amidst crack regiments and regal assemblies, his sober judgment intervened, suppressing those flights of fancy with a practicality born of years traversing not just the fields, but the equally challenging terrain of life's own uncertainties. The prospect of tearing oneself from the familiar warmth of recognized faces and cherished customs was no small undertaking. Friends, foolish as they sometimes seemed with their provincial concerns, nonetheless spoke a language he understood—a comfort not easily cast aside. The dream of emigration was thus shaded with the grey hues of reality, transforming what seemed but a simple dream into a formidable expedition fraught with doubt.

Thus, Mr. Sawyer rode on, accompanied by the song of awakening morning larks, reconciling the ache of untapped potential with the reassuring solidity of the world he knew. The crisp air that filled his lungs, the rhythmic beat of hooves beneath him, felt grounding in its consistency. Still, his imagination roamed ever ahead, mapping unknown territories where his skills might truly shine. As the sun finally broke through the veil of clouds, a fiery orb in the autumn sky, its light beckoned not just a new day, but a fresh chapter, unwritten and full of possibility. Even in the quietude of provincial life, it seemed, the heart of an adventurer kept its own relentless pace.

Sir John was silent for some moments, as if his thoughts and feelings were too powerful to produce utterance. Sir John at length rose, and, with great solemnity of tone and manner, addressed his youngest daughter, who was seated a silent spectator of the whole scene.

"Chrystal, it is time for me to take some steps towards removing you from such examples. I shall accompany you to Brierly to-morrow, and place you, for the present, under Boscawen's care. He will take charge of you till I can claim you in peace. When I have deposited you in safety, I shall remove from Wetheral for ever. Your mother and sister will accompany me into Scotland, as I shall reside in future at Fairlee."

Nothing could exceed Lady Wetheral's terror at these words, spoken so calmly and so decidedly. She rushed towards her husband, and seized his arm with nervous trepidation.

"Don't go into Scotland, John! oh, don't go there, to horrid Fairlee! I shall die there--no, no; say you will not take me from Wetheral, and I will promise any thing, John!" Her ladyship's alarm became very powerful, and she sank to the ground. Christobelle would have flown to the bell to summon Thompson, but her father forbade the action; he begged that such scenes might never be disclosed to the eyes of the household. He raised her, and laid her on a sofa, but it was some time ere her senses returned. She wandered evidently for some hours in her conversation, and was at length placed in bed, under the influence of a powerful narcotic. Christobelle watched by her as she slept.

Sir John Wetheral felt all this most painfully; but he was now awake to the weakness of his conduct in placing such implicit confidence in his lady's system of education; he felt too late how indolently he had succumbed to her tears and reproaches against his own better judgment, even to the sacrifice of Julia; and now he was resolved to save Clara, at the risk of sacrificing for ever all future hopes of domestic felicity. Her ladyship's fearful apprehensions of Fairlee threatened an illness: but Sir John was firmly resolved to quit Shropshire; to leave at once the scene of deception which irritated his mind; to save, if possible, the fate which awaited Clara, should her evil genius give her into the power of Sir Foster Kerrison.

Christobelle was still watching in her mother's room, when she opened her eyes, and faintly called for Thompson. Christobelle did not reply, but walked softly to the side of her bed, to inquire how she felt after her long sleep. Her eyes were heavy, for she closed them as she spoke.

"Is that you, Thompson? I have had such horrible dreams: your master is going into Scotland, and poor Miss Clara will be taken away from Sir Foster, after all my trouble."

"It is me, mamma," whispered Christobelle.

"Well, well," replied her mother, petulantly, "never mind who it is, you are equally included in this dreadful Fairlee business. I shall never live to reach Scotland: the dullness of the place--no neighbourhood--all old married men--not a match there fit for Clara--altogether it will kill me."

A silence of some moments ensued, and she spoke again in low complaining tones.

"Your poor father's violence has made me seriously ill, Bell, and he must lay my death at his own door. The other girls wondered, but Lina Maynard's freaks always set the fashion, and Amy, to her astonishment and boundless delight, found herself the pet of the Seminary. The little blonde, Lina's sweetheart, alone rebelled against the new order of things and was furiously jealous, for which she was promptly snubbed by Lina, and Amy taken into her place. And meanwhile Lina caught herself several times wondering whether Arthur Steele was satisfied with the way she was keeping her pledge.

Although he had walked the street every afternoon and had met nearly all the other girls at the Seminary, he had not seen Lina again. His mother, whom he took about a good deal on pleasure drives, seriously wondered if the eagerness of city life was really spoiling his faculty for leisurely pleasures. He always seemed to be looking out ahead for something, instead of quietly enjoying the passing sights and scenery. He had consented to accompany Amy to a little church sociable on the evening before his departure. It was a species of entertainment which he detested, but he thought he might possibly meet Lina there, as Amy had said some of the Seminary girls would be present.
