This little tale was written between two and three years ago, in the hope that it might help to call the attention of wiser and better men than I am, to the questions which are now agitating the minds of the rising generation, and to the absolute necessity of solving them at once and earnestly, unless we would see the faith of our forefathers crumble away beneath the combined influence of new truths which are fancied to be incompatible with it, and new mistakes as to its real essence. That this can be done I believe and know: if I had not believed it, I would never have put pen to paper on the subject.

I believe that the ancient Creed, the Eternal Gospel, will stand, and conquer, and prove its might in this age, as it has in every other for eighteen hundred years, by claiming, and subduing, and organising those young anarchic forces, which now, unconscious of their parentage, rebel against Him to whom they owe their being.

But for the time being, the young men and women of our day are fast parting from their parents and each other; the more thoughtful are wandering either towards Rome, towards sheer materialism, or towards an unchristian and unphilosophic spiritualism. Epicurism which, in my eyes, is the worst evil spirit of the three, precisely because it looks at first sight most like an angel of light. The mass, again, are fancying that they are still adhering to the old creeds, the old church, to the honoured patriarchs of English Protestantism. I wish I could agree with them in their belief about themselves. To me they see–ith a small sprinkling of those noble and cheering exceptions to popular error which are to be found in every age of Christ's churc–o be losing most fearfully and rapidly the living spirit of Christianity, and to be, for that very reason, clinging all the more convulsivel–nd who can blame them?--to the outward letter of it, whether High Church or Evangelical; unconscious, all the while, that they are sinking out of real living belief, into that dead self-deceiving belief-in-believing, which has been always heretofore, and is becoming in England now, the parent of the most blind, dishonest, and pitiless bigotry.

The dust, stirred up by the devil’s dance, settled slowly, leaving a haze in the afternoon sun. Orme, dismounted now and brushing down the beast with a familiarity that bordered on impertinence, looked up at me with a peculiar glint in his eye. It was not a look of triumph, precisely, but something more knowing, more considered.

“A fine animal,” he remarked, his voice level, betraying no hint of the exertion he had just expended. “A noble spirit, misunderstood, perhaps.”

I grunted in reply. Noble spirit indeed! I had seen that beast throw grown men clear over the stable door. Misunderstood? More like actively malicious. Yet, there was no denying the man’s skill. He had handled Satan as though he were a kitten, a lamb even.

"You have a way with horses, Mr. Orme," I conceded, grudgingly.

He merely inclined his head. "Horses," he said, "and men… often require the same approach. Firmness tempered with understanding. A hand that guides, not forces."

I considered this pronouncement, chewing on it as a farmer might chew on a particularly tough piece of beef. There was a kernel of truth there, certainly, but also a certain… loftiness that rubbed me the wrong way.

"And you find Fairfax County… in need of such an approach, do you, sir?" I asked, the edge in my voice sharper than I intended.

He met my gaze directly, his blue eyes unwavering. "Everywhere needs such an approach, my friend. But some places, perhaps, more than others."

A chill ran down my spine, despite the lingering warmth of the afternoon sun. His words hung in the air, heavy with unspoken implications. The matter of slavery, so delicately avoided in polite conversation, seemed to press itself upon us, an invisible presence in the stable yard.

“Indeed,” I said, noncommittal. “Well, Mr. Orme, I believe you have earned yourself a supper. The least I can do is offer you a plate, after such a display.”

He smiled, a genuine smile this time, that reached his eyes. "I accept with pleasure. A good ride always sharpens the appetite."

We walked in silence back towards the inn, the sounds of clanking harnesses and the gentle nicker of horses filling the void. Inside, the common room was beginning to fill with travelers and locals alike, their voices a low hum of conversation. Mistress Higgins, bustling behind the bar, greeted us with a nod and a knowing look in her eye.

"That horse of yours gave 'im a proper workout, did he?" she asked, jerking her thumb towards Orme.

"He did," I replied. "But Mr. Orme seems to be equal to the task."

“Hm,” she said, pouring a tankard of ale. "There's more to that one than meets the eye, if you ask me."

I could not disagree. There was something unsettling about the man, something that went beyond his smooth words and his effortless horsemanship. He moved with an air of self-assurance that seemed almost… inappropriate, given the circumstances. A man who spoke in churches about the peculiar institution of slavery and then rode wild horses with equal aplomb.

Later, over a hearty supper of roasted chicken and potatoes, I found myself drawn into conversation with Orme once more. He spoke of his travels, of the vast expanses of the West, of the untamed spirit of the frontier. His words painted vivid pictures of sprawling landscapes and rugged individuals, a world far removed from the genteel society of Fairfax County.

“The West is a different breed of cat altogether,” he said, taking a sip of wine. “Out there, a man is judged only by his actions, not by his lineage or his opinions. A man can be free to be himself, to make his own destiny.”

"And you find yourself stifled here, in Fairfax?" I asked, unable to resist the bait.

He paused, his gaze drifting towards the window. "Stifled? Perhaps that is too strong a word. But there is a certain… rigidity here, a resistance to change. A clinging to the past that threatens to suffocate the future."

"Ridiculous!" exclaimed Miss Penelope, tossing a discarded length of shimmering silk onto the growing pile. "All this frippery for a stay of but a few weeks! One would think she planned to conquer the entire University!"

The object of her scorn, a fair-haired young woman of perhaps nineteen summers, merely sighed, turning away from the overflowing wardrobe. "It is Mama's wish, Penelope. You know she has always indulged my… whims."

Penelope snorted. "Whims indeed! More like a blatant disregard for sensible expenditures. Here, in this bastion of learning! Who will appreciate such finery? The Dons? I think not!"

A small, wizened woman, Martha, the lady's maid, bustled forward, carefully gathering up the offending silk. "Madam requires certain… accoutrements, Miss Penelope. It is only proper."

"Proper!" Penelope’s voice rose an octave. "Proper for what? Leading young men astray with her Parisian fripperies? She is here to learn, not to ensnare!"

The fair-haired girl, whose name was Eleanor, sank onto a nearby chaise lounge, a weary expression clouding her delicate features. "Oh, Penelope, must we argue so early? My head aches dreadfully."

Martha cast a warning glance at Penelope. "Miss Eleanor is not feeling quite the thing this morning. Perhaps a cup of tea, Madam?"

Eleanor nodded gratefully. "Yes, Martha, that would be most welcome." She closed her eyes, momentarily shutting out her cousin’s incessant harangue. Oxford! It was all so different from what she had imagined. She had envisioned scholarly discussions, dusty books, and the hushed reverence of ancient halls. Instead, she found herself surrounded by mountains of silk and satin, the subject of endless debate and, it seemed, her cousin's deep disapproval.

Later that day, dressed in a simple gown of dove-grey wool, Eleanor ventured out into the bustling streets of Oxford. She longed to escape the suffocating atmosphere of her cousin’s house and breathe in the bracing air of intellectual freedom. She wandered aimlessly, her eyes drawn to the grandeur of the colleges, the quiet dignity of the chapels, and the throng of students hurrying to and fro.

Lost in her contemplation, she almost collided with a young man laden with books.

"Forgive me, Madam!" he exclaimed, his face flushing crimson as he struggled to maintain his precarious balance.

Eleanor smiled. "No harm done, Sir. I was not paying attention."

He bowed awkwardly, scattering a few pamphlets in the process. "Permit me…" he stammered, fumbling to gather the scattered papers.

Eleanor knelt to assist him, their hands brushing as they reached for the same offending leaflet. She glanced up at him, and for a fleeting moment, their eyes met. His were a striking shade of blue, filled with an earnest intelligence that captivated her.

"Thank you," he murmured, his voice barely audible. "I am… rather clumsy, I fear."

"Not at all," Eleanor replied, feeling a strange flutter in her chest. "Perhaps you are simply preoccupied with weighty matters."

He smiled, a genuine smile that transformed his features. "Indeed. The pursuit of knowledge can be a rather… absorbing endeavor."

"I can well imagine," Eleanor said. "I am here to… observe."

"Observe?" He tilted his head, his brow furrowed in curiosity. "Pray tell, what is it that you observe?"

Eleanor hesitated. She could hardly admit that she was merely trying to escape the suffocating confines of her cousin’s expectations. "The… the vibrancy of university life," she offered lamely. "The… the pursuit of learning."

He seemed unconvinced, but he merely nodded politely. "A worthy pursuit indeed. I am Charles, by the way. Charles Ashworth, of Oriel College."

"Eleanor," she replied, offering her hand. "Eleanor Fairchild."

Charles Ashworth. The name resonated within her, a small spark of something new and unexpected igniting in the depths of her heart.

As Miriam sat with her back to the unvarnished walls of their drab, dingy lodgings in the City, her dark tresses cascading down her back like a waterfall of obsidian, her thoughts strayed far from the desolate scene before her. Her countenance, though worn from the trials of her daily existence, shone with a fire that seemed to burn brighter with each passing day, and Gerald, with his quick perceptions and keen eye for beauty, could not help but be struck by the dramatic presence she presented in her violet velvet dress, an opulent garment that, in its richness, served as a stark contrast to the bleak surroundings.

"Your father has been prophesying a rara avis, a bird of uncommon plumage," he began, a smile dancing in the corners of his mouth, as he spoke in a low, measured tone, and though his words seemed to be a jest, they contained a thread of truth. "Alas, I fear that the bird he has envisioned may prove to be nothing more wonderful than a humble dove." He bowed his head, his eyes roving across the room, as if searching for some hidden meaning in the stark simplicity of their quarters. Miriam listened, her ears tuned to the gentle cadence of his voice, and though she smiled at his words, there was a fleeting shadow in her eyes, a hint of a sorrow that he had glimpsed before, but could not quite grasp.

The air was heavy with the scent of damp earth and coal smoke, a noxious odor that seemed to cling to every surface, and Miriam's delicate nostrils flared in distaste. For her, the City, with its drab, grey sky and drizzly atmosphere, held little charm; the soil seemed stagnant, the air thick with the stench of decay. Her heart yearned for the open spaces, the rolling hills and sparkling waters of the West End, where sunflowers bloomed in profusion and wildflowers sprouted from every vacant lot. She longed to shed the restrictive confines of this squalid district, to breathe the fresh air of the countryside, to leave behind the mercantile's cluttered, thronging streets.

Gerald watched her countenance, saw the unshed tears that trembled on the edge of her eyelids, and his heart ached with compassion. He felt a fleeting pang of doubt, wondering if he had truly understood her, if he had been justified in his first impressions. Her eyes, like almonds set in a mask of pale, clear skin, shone with a light that seemed almost otherworldly, a glimmer of a spirit that hinted at a depth, a complexity he had not yet begun to fathom. And her lips, a debutante's bow, curved upwards in a gentle, eager smile, inviting him to partake of her thoughts, to share in her joys and sorrows.

Miriam's ears, her fingers sparkling with imitation gems – diamonds, rubies, and emeralds that shone like glinting dew on the petal of an orchid – shone brightly in the diffused light of the room. Her father, a man of some influence, though not fortune, insisted that she wear the trappings of elegance, for the sake of appearances, for the sake of appearances alone. Yet, despite these false accoutrements, her eyes shone with a sincerity, a genuineness that seemed at odds with the artificial finery that adorned her person.

"You, at least, are a creature of familiar acquaintance," he continued, his voice tinged with a hint of wistfulness, a shadow of longing that seemed to flicker across his eyes. "The dove, with its soft, gray plumage, its tranquil cooing cry, is a bird I know well. It flutters about the purlieus of city squares, gathering crumbs, searching for sustenance in the labyrinthine streets." He studied her face, hoping to unravel the tangled threads of her thoughts, and as he looked, a minute crack in his veneer of nonchalance widened into a faint furrow, a small, almost imperceptible sign that her presence had begun to pierce the armor of his reserve.

"You, Miriam Byrne, a creature of mystique, of Eastern lineage, of velvety tresses and eyes that dance like pools of starlight, are far removed from any bird of familiar acquaintance," he declared, his voice tinged with wonder, his eyes never leaving the captivating features of her face. And for an instant, a ray of ordinary self-awareness faltered in his chest, leaving him momentarily tongue-tied, as if he had stumbled upon a secret he had not known existed, a secret that threatened to alter the direction of his life forever.

Another general feature seemed to be the strange character of a large part of the population. Puddleford was filled with bankrupts, who had fled from their eastern creditors, anxious for peace of mind and bread enough to eat. Like decayed vessels, that had been tempest-tossed and finally condemned, these hulks seemed to be lying up in ordinary in the wilderness. Puddleford was to that class a kind of hospital. This man, upon inquiry, I found had rolled in luxury, but a turn in flour one day blew him sky-high. Another failed on a land speculation. Another bought more goods than he paid for. Another had been mixed up in a fraud. Another had been actually guilty of crime. The farming community were generally free from these charges; but Puddleford proper was not.

The "Colonel," as we called him, was a fair specimen of the bankrupt class. He was one of those unfortunate beings who was well enough started in the world; but after having been tossed and buffeted around by his own extravagance, he was finally driven into the forest. He was educated, polished, proud, and poor. He had sunk two or three fortunes, earned by somebody else, chasing pleasure around the world. His reputation having become soiled, and his pockets emptied, he concluded--to use his own language--to "hide himself from his enemies and die a kind of civil death." "Men," said the Colonel, "are naturally robbers, and it is safer to run than fight with them." I have heard him declare, in a jocose way, that he was the most "injured man living; for the whole human family," he said, "set to and picked his pockets, and now the public ought to support him." He said, "he couldn't see why the government didn't pass laws for the relief of cases like his; for a government is good for nothing that fails to support its people. Starvation in a republic would be a disgrace, and ought not to be permitted." The Colonel said "there was no use in fighting destiny--no one man can do it--and it was his destiny to be poor." He said he "had no place to remove to, and that he couldn't get there if he had;" that he was "like an old pump that needs a pail of water thrown in every time it is used to set it a-going."

The Colonel resided in the village of Puddleford. His family was composed of a wife and two daughters, a couple of dashing girls, who looked like birds of fine plumage that had been driven by a storm beyond their latitude. His household furniture was made up of the fag-ends of this and that, which had somehow escaped a half a dozen sheriff's sales. His family wardrobe had been rescued in the same way, and contained all the fashions of the last twenty-five years. Here and there were scattered some plain articles of western manufacture, by way of contrast. Three shilling chairs stood on a faded Brussels carpet; an unpainted white-wood table supported a silver tea-set; thus, the faded splendor of the past contrasted with the rustic simplicity of the present. One thing I must not overlook: the Colonel had an old tattered carriage that had followed him through good and evil report, his ups and downs of life. I have often been amused to see it roll along with a melancholy air of superiority, putting on the face of a good man in affliction. It was drawn by two diminutive Indian ponies, who would turn and look wildly at the antiquated thing, as if apprehensive of danger.

The Colonel kept an office, and pretended to act as a kind of land agent, and agent for insurance companies, and so on. He was never known to pay a debt; it being against his principles, as he used to say: besides, he said "his note would last a man ten times as long as the money; and they were not very uncurrent neither; for the justice of the peace at Puddleford had taken a very great many of them, and passed his judgment upon them for their full face."

I must confess, the old lady's words had quite flustered me. To hear her speak of the Hoggarty diamond as though it were some celebrated relic, and to connect me, however distantly, to her cousin Mick and his sisters, was quite overwhelming. Mr. Polonius, however, seemed unfazed by the revelation, his professional demeanour never faltering.

"Indeed, madam," he said, with a polite inclination of his head, "a most remarkable jewel, to be sure. And one that has seen its share of history, if the stories are to be believed."

He glanced at me, a knowing twinkle in his eye. "Rest assured, sir," he continued, "your aunt's jewel shall be treated with the utmost care and discretion. Our finest craftsmen shall see to its resetting, and the design will be both elegant and secure."

I mumbled my thanks, still rather dazed by the encounter. The old lady, meanwhile, was off on another tangent, regaling us with tales of her cousin Mick's escapades in the Indies, his penchant for exotic finery, and the rumour of a Rajah's ransom lost at sea.

Mr. Polonius listened patiently, interjecting the occasional "Indeed, madam" or "How fascinating," whilst discreetly signalling to an assistant to fetch refreshments. The two younger ladies, who had hitherto been occupied with their own baubles, now turned their attention to the old lady, their eyes wide with a mixture of amusement and awe.

I, however, was beginning to feel rather out of my depth. This chance encounter, this unexpected glimpse into the Hoggarty family history, had left me feeling strangely adrift. What was I, a humble clerk, doing in this gilded cage, surrounded by jewels and whispers of fortunes made and lost?

As if sensing my unease, Mr. Polonius smoothly steered the conversation back to the matter at hand. "Now then, sir," he said, consulting a small notebook he produced from his waistcoat pocket. "Regarding the design for your aunt's jewel..."

He proceeded to sketch out several options, his pencil moving with deft precision across the page. There were delicate floral motifs, intricate scrolls, and geometric patterns inspired by the ancients. Each design was more exquisite than the last, and I found myself completely at a loss.

"Perhaps," suggested Mr. Polonius, observing my hesitation, "a simple, elegant setting would be most appropriate. Something that allows the brilliance of the stone to speak for itself."

He sketched a final design, a classic bezel setting with subtle detailing that managed to be both understated and refined. It was perfect.

"Yes," I breathed, "that is precisely what I had in mind."

Mr. Polonius smiled, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Excellent choice, sir. A timeless design for a timeless treasure."

He made a few notations in his book, then tore out the page and handed it to me. "A pleasure doing business with you, sir. Your aunt will be most pleased, I am sure."

I thanked him, and with a final nod to the old lady and her companions, made my exit. As I stepped back out onto the bustling street, the weight of the jewel in my pocket seemed heavier than before. It was no longer just a piece of jewellery, but a tangible link to the past, a symbol of the Hoggarty legacy, and, perhaps, a harbinger of things to come.

The morning after the incident, Pablito awoke with a heavy heart, the echoes of Valentina’s fury still reverberating in his mind. The shadows of the room seemed to mock him, casting long, accusatory fingers across the floor. His hand trembled as he reached for the glass of water on his nightstand, his thoughts spiraling into the chaos of the previous night. Nieves’s face, pale and drawn, flashed before his eyes, her wide, imploring gaze a testament to the turmoil she must have felt. And Valentina—her eyes, glowing with a fire that could reduce the boldest soul to ash. He shuddered, the memory of her blows still fresh upon his skin.

Swearing softly, he rose from his bed and dressed in haste, the weight of his actions pressing down upon him like a shroud. The air outside was thick with the scent of damp earth and the distant murmur of the city beginning to stir. Pablito walked aimlessly, his boots sinking slightly into the cobblestones, each step a reminder of the path he had chosen. Love, he had once believed, was a noble quest, a journey worth any sacrifice. But now, with his heart tangled in the threads of two women’s affections, he could not escape the feeling that he had become a pawn in a game far beyond his control.

As he wandered, his mind inevitably drifted back to Nieves. Her laughter, like the soft chiming of bells, had once filled his days with joy. But now, her presence seemed to bring only pain, a bittersweet reminder of what he had lost. He clenched his fists, his knuckles whitening as he struggled to banish her image. Yet, as he turned a corner, he found himself standing before the very house where she resided, the door creaking softly in the breeze. Before he could retreat, it opened, and Nieves stepped out, her eyes widening in surprise.

“Pablito,” she murmured, her voice trembling. “I—I was not expecting you.”

Before he could finish, a shrill cry pierced the air, and Valentina emerged from the shadows, her face a storm of anger. “How dare you stand there, you reckless fool!” she shouted, her voice echoing down the street. “Do you think I will allow you to toy with her heart again? I warned you, Pablito—I warned you!”

Nieves gasped, stepping back in fear, but Pablito stood firm, though his resolve faltered under the intensity of Valentina’s glare. “I am no longer the man you think I am,” he declared, his voice steadier than he felt. “I have made mistakes, but I am determined to atone for them.”

New Zion, despite its name, was, as I have hinted, no longer new. The fiery zeal which had once made it a living schism had long since died out of it. Carried years before, a little blazing ember of faith, from a flourishing hearth of Nonconformity some streets away, it had puffed and gleamed a little space in the eloquence of the offended zealots who carried it hotfoot that Sunday morning, but its central fire had been poor, and for a long time no evangelistic bellows had awakened in it even a spark.

Its original elders had long since lost heart and passed away. A dwindling remnant of their children, from old association, just kept its doors from actually closing, and made a mournful interruption in its musty silence on Sundays. Life was too low to support a Wednesday prayer-meeting, and Sunday by Sunday that life ebbed lower. New life from the outside must come, and speedily, or it must die.

But new life was already on the way. On the town side the sad streets round New Zion led one into a more prosperous High Street, and indeed Zion Street itself, as it turned the corner, flamed into quite a jovial and ruddy sho– provision merchant's, and kept by Eli Moggridge. The name did its owner considerable wrong, for its suggestion of puritanical sanctimoniousness was a flat contradiction of the jovial and ruddy personality, the huge red-whiskered laugher, for whom it stood, and of whom the shop, with its healthy smell of cheese and its air of exuberant prosperity, was a much more truthful expression. Well, the business was growing with such gusto that Mr. Moggridge felt he might afford a home away from his shop, and thus he came to take the biggish empty house which presently put on new paint and once more seemed quite proud of being "Zion View."

Till this time, Mr. Moggridge. had "attended" elsewhere, but he was not so young as he had been and somewhat stouter, and the stealthy approach of comfortable habits had suggested to him that his old chapel was rather at an unnecessary distance. Then, too, the fact of his house being called after New Zion seemed to impose a sort of obligation towards the sad old chapel. Besides, Mr. Moggridge was not inhumanly above the pleasures of self-importance, and though he did not express it in just those words, or indeed in any words at all, the idea of his being the Maecenas of New Zion was suddenly born within him.

Now, quick was even the word with Mr. Moggridge, as became a successful man of business, and for him to conceive an idea was to carry it out, as goods were always delivered from Mr. Moggridge's shop, with despatch. Also in some dim far-off way Mr. Moggridge's mind had, all unconsciously, been stirred by vibrations of what we call the New Spirit. The new spirit of any age works its way even into its businesses, and though Mr. Moggridge wouldn't have so described it, it was the "New Spirit" that had made the success of his provision shop. Speaking of the need of New Zion, Mr. Moggridge called it "new blood." He meant the "New Spirit;" and it was in reply to his advertisement for a new pastor, that the "New Spirit" in the person of Theophilus Londonderry came one Sunday to preach at New Zion.

ENDS QUITE ROMANTICALLY

Eli Moggridge was a judge of men, and he liked Theophilus Londonderry at a glance. Theophilus Londonderry was also a judge of men, and he liked Eli Moggridge. In fact, two men that needed each other had met.

You couldn't help laughing a little at Mr. Moggridge at first, soon you couldn't help respecting him,--Theophilus Londonderry was almost to know what it was to love him. Indeed, that Mr. Moggridge was just the man he was was a matter of no small importance to the young minister. A chief deacon is nothing less than a fate, and it is in his power to be no little of a tyrant. Had Mr. Moggridge's interest in New Zion been of a different character, he would inevitably have been as great a hindrance as he was to prove a help. Fortunately that interest was recreative rather than severely religious. It was to be for him a sort of Sunday-business to which he was to devote his vast spare energies. He wanted to see it a "going concern," and, hating stagnation in his neighbourhood, he looked about for a specialist whom he could trust to make it move and hum and whizz.

In the quietude of a discernibly restless room, where the light of day filtered in through the half-drawn curtains with a slant that played tricks upon the walls, Mr. Neal stood in contemplation, his brow furrowed with the weight of unvoiced emotions. The clattering of wheels and the clamour of voices from the street below rendered the air outside festive, competing markedly with the austere silence that enveloped him. Wildbad, with its lively throngs sauntering unaware of the struggles that burdened him, seemed like a world apart, pulsing with joyous life that he could scarcely touch.

“Mrs. Armadale requires a clearer understanding,” he murmured to himself, his voice scarcely rising beyond the threshold of thought. Yet the thoughts he uttered possessed a gravity that was lost on him alone, for there was no one whispering counsel to ease the tempest within him. His mind raced with considerations, yet each time he drew near to an answer, uncertainty bore him away from it with the swiftness of a crisp autumn wind.

“It is absurd to tarry here during such a moment. I ought to have ventured to her at once,” he said, reflexively brushing back a strand of hair that had wandered loose over his forehead. The words echoed only in the confines of his unease, swallowed by the weighty atmosphere, pregnant with unresolved tension. All the while, he wrestled with the unwelcome knowledge that he required more than mere good intentions to confront Mrs. Armadale about her husband’s condition.

Peering out into the bustling street, a wave of envy washed over him. He saw couples strolling, their hands linked, laughter spilling forth—a stark contrast to the grim narrative he was tethered to. “To be so unencumbered,” he sighed, “is there not something desirable in that?” Yet the question was hollow to him, as he knew well that inside that carefree façade, many held burdens just as heavy, couched in silence as oppressive as his own.

At that moment, a soft knock resounded at his door—tentative, yet somehow instilling a quiver of hope. “Enter,” he called, and the door creaked open to unveil a slight figure swathed in a shawl. It was Ruth, the maid, whose face bore the weariness of one who served beneath the shadow of trouble. Her eyes were bright with something akin to urgency. “Mr. Neal?” she inquired, hesitating on the threshold, her voice a blend of deference and expectation.

“What is it, Ruth?” he answered, tightening the collar of his coat as if it might shield him from the turmoil to come. There was an air of expectation as she shifted her weight from one foot to the other, regarding him with a mixture of sympathy and concern that set his pulse racing in unexpected rhythm.

“It is about Mrs. Armadale, sir. She is in the garden—she’s asking for you,” the maid replied, her voice a tremor in the hushed room. The very mention of her name struck a spark in him, igniting feelings he had sought to suppress. “But she—she may not be in a fit state—”

“Release no words of caution, my dear Ruth,” he interjected sharply, surprising himself with the fervour of his response. “To see Mrs. Armadale is not just necessary, it is essential.” And with that, he felt the gale of resolve sweep through him, chafing against his earlier hesitance.

As he stepped into the garden, its vibrant hues enveloping him like a shawl of vivid warmth, the contrast was stark—the splendor of flowers offering a riot of colour in the very face of his grave pursuit. Yet, amid the blooming flora, there was Mrs. Armadale, seated upon a wooden bench, her countenance the embodiment of sorrowful abstraction as she gazed toward the cerulean sky, unaware of the suffusion of life swirling around her.

“Mrs. Armadale,” he ventured softly, his heart carrying an unfamiliar tenderness as he approached her. But her awareness remained tantalizingly out of reach, as though she dwelled in a realm far removed from their immediate reality, a ghost animated only by the memory of what once was, or might yet be. With an urgency borne from the depths of newfound resolve, he took a breath and resolved to breach the gap that separated them, standing resolute before the embodiment of his own turmoil.

Linton was the only boy who had a pair of skates equal to Randolph's. He, too, was a contestant, but, being three years younger than Luke and Randolph, had no expectation of rivaling them.

Randolph had his friends near him, administering the adulation he so much enjoyed.

"I have no doubt you'll get the watch, Randolph," said Sam Noble. "You're a better skater any day than Luke Larkin."

"Of course you are!" chimed in Tom Harper.

"The young janitor doesn't think so," said Randolph, his lips curling.

"Oh, he's conceited enough to think he can beat you, I make no doubt," said Sam.

"On those old skates, too! They look as if Adam might have used them when he was a boy!"

This sally of Tom's created a laugh.

"His skates are old ones, to be sure," said Randolph, who was quick-sighted enough to understand that any remark of this kind might dim the luster of his expected victory. "His skates are old enough, but they are just as good for skating as mine."

"They won't win him the watch, though," said Sam.

"I don't care for the watch myself," said Randolph, loftily. "I've got a silver one now, and am to have a gold one when I'm eighteen. But I want to show that I am the best skater. Besides, father has promised me ten dollars if I win."

"I wish I had ten dollars," said Sam, enviously.

He was the son of the storekeeper, and his father allowed him only ten cents a week pocket-money, so that ten dollars in his eyes was a colossal fortune.

"I have no doubt you would, Sam," said Tom, joyously; "but you couldn't be trusted with so much money. You'd go down to New York and try to buy out A. T. Stewart."

"Are you ready, boys?" asked Mr. Hooper.

Most of the boys responded promptly in the affirmative; but Luke, who had been tightening his straps, said quickly: "I am not ready, Mr. Hooper. My strap has broken!"

"Indeed, Luke, I am sorry to hear it," said the teacher, approaching and examining the fracture. "As matters stand, you can't skate."

Randolph's eyes brightened. Confident as he professed to feel, he knew that his chances of success would be greatly increased by Luke's withdrawal from the list.

"The prize is yours now," whispered Tom.

"It was before," answered Randolph, conceitedly.

Poor Luke looked disappointed. He knew that he had at least an even chance of winning, and he wanted the watch. Several of his friends of his own age had watches, either silver or Waterbury, and this seemed, in his circumstances, the only chance of securing one. Now he was apparently barred out.

"It's a pity you shouldn't skate, Luke," said Mr. Hooper, in a tone of sympathy. "You are one of the best skaters, and had an excellent chance of winning the prize. Is there any boy willing to lend Luke his skates?"

"I will," said Frank Acken.

"My dear boy," said the teacher, "you forget that your feet are several sizes smaller than Luke's."

"I didn't think of that," replied Frank, who was only twelve years old.

"You may use my skates, Luke," said Linton Tomkins. "I think they will fit you."

Linton was only thirteen, but he was unusually large for his age.

"You are very kind, Linton," said Luke, "but that will keep you out of the race."

"I stand no chance of winning," said Linton, "and I will do my skating afterward."

"I don't think that fair," said Randolph, with a frown. "Each boy ought to use his own skates."

"There is nothing unfair about it," said the teacher, "except that Luke is placed at disadvantage in using a pair of skates he is unaccustomed to."

Randolph did not dare gainsay the teacher, but he looked sullen.

The air hung heavy with the scent of whiskey as Larry O'Leary led the officers through the dense undergrowth of the forest. The sun was setting, casting long shadows across the trees and creating an eerie atmosphere. Larry walked with purpose, his gaze fixed ahead as if he could already see the hidden still in the distance.

The officers followed closely behind, their footsteps muffled by the thick carpet of leaves on the forest floor. The tension between them was palpable, a silent understanding that they were about to uncover something illicit and dangerous.

Finally, they reached a clearing where a small shack stood, smoke rising lazily from the chimney. Larry stopped in front of the door, his hand hesitating over the latch.

"I must warn you, gentlemen," he said, his voice low and grave. "The owner of this still is the best friend I have in the world. But duty calls, and I cannot turn a blind eye to the law."

The officers exchanged a glance before one of them stepped forward, pushing the door open with a creak. The interior of the shack was dimly lit, the smell of alcohol overpowering. Barrels lined the walls, and copper pipes snaked across the floor, leading to a large copper still in the corner.

"The evidence is damning," the officer declared, a mix of satisfaction and regret in his voice.

Larry hung his head, a heavy weight settling on his shoulders. "I'll never be able to look at him straight in the face after this, and that's the truth," he said, his voice barely a whisper.

As they made their way back through the forest, the officers couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. The betrayal of a friend weighed heavily on their minds, a reminder of the thin line between loyalty and duty.

Back in town, rumors swirled about Larry's betrayal, his newfound reputation as an informer spreading like wildfire. Some whispered in hushed tones about his treachery, while others praised his bravery for upholding the law.

But Larry's actions did not go unnoticed by the criminal underworld. His once loyal friends now eyed him with suspicion, unsure of where his loyalties truly lay. And as the rewards for his information grew, so too did the danger that lurked in the shadows.

Meanwhile, in a cozy parlor across town, two gentlemen sat in deep conversation. Edmund and Harold, men of letters and intellect, debated the effects of education on women's emotions and ideals. The crackling fire cast a warm glow over the room, illuminating the stacks of books that lined the walls.

"It is a great folly to believe that education will only serve to enlighten the minds of women," Harold argued, his voice firm.

But Edmund shook his head, a thoughtful expression on his face. "I believe that women possess an innate femininity that cannot be extinguished by mere learning. It is this very essence that sets them apart and gives them strength."

Their discussion continued long into the night, touching on topics of love, duty, and the complexities of the human heart. And as they delved deeper into the mysteries of womanhood, a sense of hope blossomed in their hearts, a belief that despite the challenges they faced, the future held promise for all.

There, in the deepening dusk of the garden, stood Captain Carroll, his gaze fixed upon the threshold of the summer-house, a figure of suspense and expectancy. The faded hues of the day lingered, dappling the air with their last reluctant caress. The pear-tree, a relic of forgotten summers, stood with bent boughs as if whispering to the wind of bygone days. Its gnarled form, draped in moss and ivy, bore testament to a lifetime’s story, and its branches, heavy with the weight of leaves that had turned amber before the season's end, seemed to rustle with secrets known only to it.

At his feet, the rose-leaves lay strewn, a tapestry of crimson and gold that mocked the fading light with their fervent display. They lay scattered as if the very fingers of the night had plucked them, and yet, they spoke of a grave—a grave of lost love or departed dreams, whose scent lingered despite the encroaching chill.

Carroll, still as a sentinel, awaited the arrival of the woman who had claimed his thoughts. The murmur of the evening breeze through the foliage was his only company, and yet, it seemed to him a chorus of whispers, urging him to hasten, to anticipate the arrival of the enigmatic figure whose passage through the garden would forever alter the course of his life.

In her presence, he felt a strange mixture of trepidation and elation. She had the power to captivate, to draw forth the innermost yearnings of any man fortunate enough to find her glance, and yet, she was elusive, as fleeting as the petals that adorned her hair. Each movement suggested a dance, a performance that held him entranced, uncertain if it were real or but a figment of his longing.

Through the myriad of leaves, a soft voice called out, "Captain Carroll?" Startled, he turned to see Brianna, her form illuminated by the last rays of the setting sun. She held out a hand, adorned with a single rose, its petals reflecting the twilight sky.

"I see you have not abandoned your vigil," she said, her voice a melody that matched the cadence of the wind. "The night grows colder, and yet, you remain."

His heart quickened at the sight of her, the simple gesture of offering a rose a bold declaration of intent. He took her hand and drew her closer, under the canopy of ancient branches that seemed to approve their union.

"Brianna," he began, his words spilling forth like a dam breaking, "I have been waiting for you, not just here, but in my dreams each night. You are the reason the stars shine, the perfume that lingers long after the rose has faded."

She smiled, a tender, knowing smile that spoke volumes of their shared understanding. "And what would Captain Carroll have me do with my stars and my rose, if I were to grace him with my presence?"

The question hung between them, a delicate proclamation of their mutual attraction. He leaned in, his breath mingling with hers, the anticipation building as they stood there, suspended in the twilight.

"Captain Carroll," she whispered, her eyes shimmering with unspoken promises, "perhaps it is time to write another chapter, one where we are not merely actors in someone else's tale, but creators of our own destiny."

We do not keep Christmas now as we used to do in old Hanover. We have not time for it, and it does not seem like the same thing. Christmas, however, always brings up to me my cousin Fanny; I suppose because she always was so foolish about Christmas.

My cousin Fanny was an old maid; indeed, to follow St. Paul’s turn of phrase, she was an old maid of the old maids. No one who saw her a moment could have doubted it. Old maids have from most people a feeling rather akin to pity--a hard heritage. They very often have this feeling from the young. This must be the hardest part of all--to see around them friends, each “a happy mother of children,” little ones responding to affection with the sweet caresses of childhood, whilst any advances that they, their aunts or cousins, may make are met with indifference or condescension. My cousin Fanny was no exception. She was as proud as Lucifer; yet she went through life--the part that I knew of--bearing the pity of the great majority of the people who knew her.

She lived at an old place called “Woodside”, which had been in the family for a great many years; indeed, ever since before the Revolution. The neighborhood dated back to the time of the colony, and Woodside was one of the old places. My cousin Fanny’s grandmother had stood in the door of her chamber with her large scissors in her hand, and defied Tarleton’s red-coated troopers to touch the basket of old communion-plate which she had hung on her arm.

The house was a large brick edifice, with a pyramidal roof, covered with moss, small windows, porticos with pillars somewhat out of repair, a big, high hall, and a staircase wide enough to drive a gig up it if it could have turned the corners. A grove of great forest oaks and poplars densely shaded it, and made it look rather gloomy; and the garden, with the old graveyard covered with periwinkle at one end, was almost in front, while the side of the wood--a primeval forest, from which the place took its name--came up so close as to form a strong, dark background. During the war the place, like most others in that neighborhood, suffered greatly, and only a sudden exhibition of spirit on Cousin Fanny’s part saved it from a worse fate. After the war it went down; the fields were poor, and grew up in briers and sassafras, and the house was too large and out of repair to keep from decay, the ownership of it being divided between Cousin Fanny and other members of the family. Cousin Fanny had no means whatever, so that it soon was in a bad condition. The rest of the family, as they grew up, went off, compelled by necessity to seek some means of livelihood, and would have taken Cousin Fanny too if she would have gone; but she would not go. They did all they could for her, but she preferred to hang around the old place, and to do what she could with her “mammy”, and “old Stephen”, her mammy’s husband, who alone remained in the quarters. She lived in a part of the house, locking up the rest, and from time to time visited among her friends and relatives, who always received her hospitably. She had an old piece of a mare (which I think she had bought from Stephen), with one eye, three legs, and no mane or tail to speak of, and on which she lavished, without the least perceptible result, care enough to have kept a stable in condition. In a freak of humor she named this animal “Fashion”, after a noted racer of the old times, which had been raised in the county, and had beaten the famous Boston in a great race. She always spoke of “Fash” with a tone of real tenderness in her voice, and looked after her, and discussed her ailments, which were always numerous, as if she had been a delicate child. Mounted on this beast, with her bags and bundles, and shawls and umbrella, and a long stick or pole, she used occasionally to make the tour of the neighborhood, and was always really welcomed; because, notwithstanding the trouble she gave, she always stirred things up. As was said once, you could no more have remained dull where she was than you could have dozed with a chinkapin-burr down your back. Her retort was that a chinkapin-burr might be used to rouse people from a lethargy (she had an old maid’s tongue). By the younger members of the family she was always welcomed, because she furnished so much fun. She nearly always fetched some little thing to her host--not her hostess--a fowl, or a pat of butter from her one old cow, or something of the kind, because, she said, “Abigail had established the precedent, and she was ‘a woman of good understanding’--she understood that feeding and flattery were the way to win men.” She would sometimes have a chicken in a basket hung on the off pummel of her old saddle, because at times she fancied she could not eat anything but chicken soup, and she did “not wish to give trouble.” She used to give trouble enough; for it generally turned out that she had heard some one was sick in the neighborhood, and she wanted the soup carried to her. I remember how mad Joe got because she made him go with her to carry a bucket of soup to old Mrs. Ronquist.

He leant upon his gun, with his eyes fixed in the direction where Byres had fallen.

Joey stood by him--for nearly ten minutes not a word was spoken. At last Rushbrook said--

"Joey, my boy, I've killed many a man in my time, and I have thought nothing of it; I slept as sound as ever the next night. But then, you see, I was a soldier, and it was my trade, and I could look on the man I had killed without feeling sorrow or shame; but I can't look upon this man, Joey. He was my enemy; but--I've murdered him--I feel it now. Go up to him, boy--you are not afraid to meet him--and see if he be dead."

Joey, although generally speaking fear was a stranger to him, did, however, feel afraid; his hands had often been dyed with the blood of a hare or of a bird, but he had not yet seen death in his fellow-creatures. He advanced slowly and tremulously through the dark towards the furze-bush in which the body laid; Mum followed, raising first one paw and pausing, then the other, and as they came to the body, the dog raised his head and gave such a mournful howl, that it induced our hero to start back again. After a time Joey recovered himself; and again advanced to the body. He leant over it, he could distinguish but the form; he listened, and not the slightest breathing was to be heard; he whispered the pedlar's name, but there was no reply; he put his hand upon his breast, and removed it reeking with warm blood.

"Father, he must be dead, quite dead," whispered Joey, who returned trembling. "What shall we do?"

"We must go home," replied Rushbrook; "this is a bad night's work;" and, without exchanging another word until their arrival, Rushbrook and Joey proceeded back to the cottage, followed by Mum.

Jane had remained in a state of great anxiety during her husband's absence, watching and listening to every sound; every five minutes raising the latch of the door, and looking out, hoping to see him return. As the time went on, her alarm increased; she laid her head down on the table and wept; she could find no consolation, no alleviation of her anxiety; she dropped down on her knees and prayed.

She was still appealing to the Most High, when a blow on the door announced her husband's return. There was a sulken gloom over his countenance as he entered: he threw his gun carelessly on one side, so that it fell, and rattled against the paved floor; and this one act was to her ominous of evil. He sat down without speaking; falling back in the chair, and lifting his eyes up to the rafters above, he appeared to be in deep thought, and unconscious of her presence.

"What has happened?" inquired his wife, trembling as she laid her hand on his shoulder.

"Don't speak to me now," was the reply.

"Joey," said the frightened woman in a whisper, "what has he done?"

Joey answered not, but raised his hand, red with the blood which was now dried upon it.

Jane uttered a faint cry, dropped on her knees, and covered her face, while Joey walked into the back kitchen, and busied himself in removing the traces of the dark deed.

A quarter of an hour had elapsed--Joey had returned, and taken his seat upon his low stool, and not a word had been exchanged.

"Smell anything?" he whispered.

I gave a sniff and raised my eyebrows inquiringly.

"Sheep?" said I, softly.

My companion nodded.

"They must be somewhere close by," said he, in a voice hardly audible. "Go very carefully and keep your eyes wide open. If you see anything, stop instantly."

We were lying side by side upon the rocks, Dick considerately waiting a moment while I got my breath again, and were just about to crawl forward, when there came the sound of a sudden rush of hoofs and a clatter of stones from some invisible point ahead of us, and then dead silence again.

"They've winded us and gone off," whispered Dick. But the next moment he added eagerly, "There they are! Look! There they are! Up there! See? My! What a chance!"

Immediately on our left was a deep gorge, so narrow and precipitous that we could not see the bottom of it from where we lay. The sheep, having seemingly got wind of us, with that agility which is always so astonishing in such heavy animals, had rushed down one side of the precipitous gorge and up the other, and now, there they were, all standing in a row--eleven of them--on the opposite summit, looking down, not at us, but at something immediately below them.

"What do you suppose it is, Dick?" I whispered.

"Don't know," my companion replied. "Mountain-lion, perhaps: they are very partial to mutton. Anyhow," he continued, "if we want to get a shot we must shoot from here: we can't move without the sheep seeing us, and they'd be off like a flash if they did. You take a shot, Frank. Take the nearest one. Sight for two hundred yards."

"No," I replied. "You shoot. I shall miss: I'm too unsteady for want of breath."

"All right."

Raising himself a fraction of an inch at a time until he had come to a kneeling position, Dick pushed his rifle-barrel through a crevice in the rocks, took aim and fired. The nearest sheep, a fine fellow with a handsome pair of horns, pitched forward, fell headlong from the ledge upon which he had been standing and vanished from our sight among the broken rocks below; while the others turned tail and fled up the mountain, disappearing also in a minute or less.

"Come on!" cried Dick, springing to his feet. "Let's go across and get him. Round this way. Don't trust to that slope of ice: you may slip and break your neck."

"But the mountain-lion, Dick," I protested. "Suppose there's a mountain-lion down there."

"Oh, never mind him!" Dick exclaimed. "If there was one, he's gone by this time. And even if he should be there yet, he'd skip the moment he saw us. We needn't mind him. Come on!"

Away we went, therefore, Dick in the lead, and scrambling quickly though carefully down the rocky wall, we made our way up the bed of the ravine until we found ourselves opposite the ledge upon which the sheep had been standing. Here we discovered that the wall of the gorge was split from top to bottom by a narrow cleft--previously invisible to us--filled with hard snow, and whether the sheep had been standing on the right side or the left of this crevice, and therefore on which side the big ram had fallen, we could not tell; for the wall of the gorge, besides being exceedingly rough, was littered with great masses of rock against any of which the body of the sheep might have lodged.

"I'll tell you what, Frank," said my companion. "It might take us an hour or two to search all the cracks and crannies here. The best plan will be to climb straight up to the ledge where the sheep stood and look down. Then, if he is lodged against the upper side of any of these rocks, we shall be able to see him. But as we can't tell whether he was standing on the right or the left of this crevice, suppose you climb up one side while I go up the other."

"The fish is burning," he said, "and the oat cakes too; for I am smelling them ben the house;" and Janet ran to her fireside, and hastily turned her herring and cakes.

"I'm feared you won't think much of your meat to-night," she said regretfully; "the tea is fairly ruined."

"Never mind the meat, Mother," said Andrew. "We don't live to eat."

"Never mind the meat, indeed! What perfect nonsense! There is something wrong with folk that don't mind their meat."

"Well then, you shouldn't be so vain of yourself, Mother. You were preening like a young girl when I first got sight of you--and the meat taking care of itself."

"Me, vain! No! No! Nobody that knows Janet Binnie can ever say she is vain. I wot well that I am a frail, miserable creature, with little need of being vain, either for myself or my children. You are a great hand at arguing, Andrew, but you are always in the wrong. But draw to the table and eat. I'll warrant the fish will prove better than it is bonnie."

They sat down with a pleasant content that soon broadened into mirth and laughter, as Jamie Logan began to tell and to show how the peddler lad had fleeched and flethered the fisher wives out of their bawbees; adding at the last "that he could not come within sight of their fine words, they were that civil to him."

"Senselessly civil, no doubt of it," answered Janet. "A peddler aye gives the whole village a fit of the liberalities. The like of Jean Robertson spending a crown on him! Foolish woman, the words are not to seek that she'll get from me in the morning."

Then Jamie took a letter from his pocket, and showed it to Andrew Binnie. "Robert Toddy brought it this morning," he said, "and, as you may see, it is from the firm of Henderson Brothers, Glasgow; and they say there will be a berth for me very soon now in one of their ships. And their boats are good, and their captains good, and there is chances for a fine sailor on that line. I may be a captain myself one of these days!" and he laughed so gayly, and looked so bravely into the face of such a bold idea, that he persuaded every one else to expect it for him. Janet pulled her new shawl a little closer and smiled, and her thought was: "After all, Christina may wait longer, and fare worse; for she is turned twenty." Yet she showed a little reserve as she asked:--

"Are you then Glasgow-born, Jamie?"

"Me! Glasgow-born! What are you thinking of? I am from the auld East Neuk; and I am glad and proud of being a Fifer. All my common sense comes from Fife. There is none loves the 'Kingdom' more than I, Jamie Logan. We are all Fife together. I thought you knew it."

At these words there was a momentary shadow across the door, and a little lassie slipped in; and when she did so, all put down their cups to welcome her. Andrew reddened to the roots of his hair, his eyes filled with light, a tender smile softened his firm mouth, and he put out his hand and drew the girl to the chair which Christina had pushed close to his own.

"You are welcome, and more than welcome, Sophy," said the Mistress; but for all that, she gave Sophy a glance in which there was much speculation not unmixed, with fear and disapproval. For it was easy to see that Andrew Binnie loved her, and that she was not at all like him, nor yet like any of the fisher-girls of Pittendurie. Sophy, however, was not responsible for this difference; for early orphanage had placed her in the care of an aunt who carried on a dress and bonnet making business in Largo, and she had turned the little fisher-maid into a girl after her own heart and wishes.

John Barty drew deeply upon his pipe, the pungent smoke curling about his grizzled face in a most distracting fashion. He regarded his son, Barnaby, with eyes narrowed almost to slits, as if trying to pierce the very soul of him.

"Seven hundred thousand pounds, ye say?" he rumbled at length, the words seeming to rumble up from some deep cavern within his chest.

Barnaby, standing straighter now, though still a flicker of uncertainty danced in his gaze, inclined his head. "Aye, Father. Uncle Thomas… he left it all to me."

Natty Bell, who had been shifting from one foot to the other like a restless colt, suddenly smacked his thigh with a resounding thwack.

"Why, blast me if the lad ain't set for life!" he exclaimed, his eyes wide with a mixture of awe and disbelief. "Seven hundred thousand! Enough to buy half of Kent, I reckon!"

John Barty, however, remained unimpressed. He took another long pull on his pipe, the bowl glowing a fierce red in the dim light of the cottage.

"And what, pray tell," he said, his voice thick with suspicion, "do ye intend to do with all this… this coin?"

Barnaby cleared his throat, his gaze drifting towards the worn, wooden floor. "I… I wish to travel, Father. To see the world, perhaps. To learn… to improve myself."

John Barty snorted, a sound like the bellows of a forge. "Improve yourself? Ye're already stronger than any man in these parts! What more improvement do ye need?"

Natty Bell, eager to avert a brewing argument, chimed in. "Why, John, a bit of travel never hurt nobody! Broadens the mind, it does!"

John Barty shot him a withering glance. "Broadens the pockets of those what prey on innocents, more like. London is a den of vipers, Barnaby. Ye'll be fleeced before ye can say Jack Robinson."

Barnaby, however, stood his ground. "I shall be careful, Father. I am not a fool."

John Barty puffed furiously on his pipe, his silence heavy with disapproval. He knew his son. He knew the stubborn streak that ran through him, as deep and unyielding as the granite hills of their homeland.

At length, he spoke, his voice softer now, tinged with a reluctant resignation. "And what of… what of the fighting, Barnaby? Will ye abandon the ring?"

Barnaby hesitated, a shadow of regret passing over his face. "I… I do not know, Father. I have not yet decided."

Natty Bell, ever the optimist, clapped Barnaby on the back. "Why, lad, ye can do both! Be a gentleman by day, and a bruiser by night! A regular Corinthian, ye'll be!"

John Barty glared at Natty, his eyes flashing with a spark of the old fire. "A Corinthian, is it? More like a fool! A fancy waistcoat and a silver-handled cane won't save him from a broken nose."

Barnaby sighed, running a hand through his thick, dark hair. "I understand your concerns, Father. But I must follow my own path. I must see what lies beyond these hills."

John Barty fell silent again, his gaze fixed on the swirling smoke rising from his pipe. He knew he could not stop his son. Barnaby had a will of his own, and a fortune besides.

He only hoped that the world would treat him kindly, that it would not break the spirit of the boy he had raised. He finished his pipe, and a long silence descended upon the small cottage.

“Whereabouts is the fiddle, Phil?”

“It isn't here,” answered our hero.

“Ain't it goin' to be sold?”

“Of course not! It's mine. I told you that once already.”

“We'll see!” said Nicholas angrily.

And going up to Squire Pope, he held a brief conversation with that gentleman.

The squire nodded vigorously, and walked over to Philip.

“Philip,” said he, “go and bring your violin.”

“What will I do that for!” asked our hero quietly.

“So that it may be sold.”

“It is not to be sold,” returned Philip quietly. “It belongs to me.”

“Nothing belongs to you except your clothes!” said the squire angrily. “I require you to go and fetch the instrument.”

“And I decline to do it,” said Philip.

“Do you know who I am,” demanded the squire, with ruffled dignity.

“I know you perfectly well,” answered Philip “but I am the owner of the violin, and I don't mean to have it sold.”

“YOU will repent this!” said Squire Pope, who felt that his lawful authority and official dignity were set at naught.

Philip bowed and left the house. He did not know what steps the squire might take, but he was resolved not to give up his cherished violin.

Squire Pope was not a bad man, nor was he by nature a tyrant, but he was so fully convinced of his own superior judgment that he was in all things obstinately bent on having his own way. He had persuaded himself that our young hero, Philip, would be better off in the poorhouse than in a place where he could earn his own living, and no one could convince him to the contrary.

As to the boy's feelings on the subject, he considered those of no importance. He had good reason to know that Philip would object to being an inmate of the almshouse, but he was determined that he should go there.

In like manner, before the auction was over, he saw clearly that it would realize a sum more than sufficient to pay the funeral expenses of the late Mr. Gray and the few small bills outstanding against his estate, and that there was no necessity that Philip's violin should be sold, but none the less he resolved that it should be sold.

“Shall I allow a young lad to dictate to me?” Squire Pope asked himself, in irritation. “Certainly not! I know better what is right than he. It is ridiculous that a town pauper should own a violin. Why, the next thing, we shall have to buy pianos for our almshouses, for the use of the gentlemen and ladies who occupy them. A violin, indeed!”

This Squire Pope regarded as irresistible logic and withering sarcasm combined.

He saw Philip go out of the cottage, but, as the sale was not over, he was unable to follow him.

“Never mind, I'll fix him as soon as I have time,” he said to himself.

“Back so soon? Is the auction over!” asked his friend, Frank Dunbar, who was engaged in splitting wood in the rear of the house.

“No, Frank, not quite; but it's almost over..Who do you think bid on father's gold watch?”

“I don't know.”

“Nick Holden.”

“He didn't get it, did he?”

“I am glad to say not. Your father bought it.”

“Did he! Why, he's got one watch already.”

“I am glad he's got it. I couldn't bear to think of Nick Holden carrying my father's watch. He was disappointed about one thing besides.”

“What was that?”

“The violin. He went to Squire Pope, and complained that it was not in the sale.”

“That's just like his impudence. What did the squire say?”

“He came to me and ordered me to get it, so that it might be sold.”

“Shall I get it for you, then?”

“Not much!” answered Philip emphatically. “It is mine, as I have already told you. If the auction doesn't bring in enough to settle up everything, I may agree to sell it for a fair price; but I am sure, from the prices, that it won't be necessary.”

She agreed to go to the ghat, though, and went back into the hut to wait for the ox-cart while Abdul cooked a meal on the powder-blackened ground with the last of the millet, and gave thanks to Allah.

There was no room for Tooni to ride when they started. She walked alongside carrying the baby and its little bundle of clothes. There was nothing else to carry, and that was fortunate, for the cart in which the memsahib lay was too full of sick and wounded to hold anything more. In Tooni's pocket a little black book swung to and fro; it was the memsahib's book; and in the beginning of the firing, before the fever came, Tooni had seen the memsahib reading it long and often. They had not been killed in consequence, Tooni thought; there must be a protecting charm in the little black book; so she slipped it into her pocket. They left the looking-glass behind.

The ox-cart passed out creaking, in its turn, beyond the earthworks of the English encampment into the city, where the mutinous natives stood in sullen curious groups to watch the train go by. A hundred yards through the narrow streets, choked with the smell of gunpowder and populous with vultures, and Abdul heard a quick voice in his ear. When he turned, none were speaking, but he recognised in the crowd the lowering indifferent face of a sepoy he knew--one of the Nana Sahib's servants. Saying nothing, he fell back for Tooni and laid his hand upon her arm. And when the cart creaked out of the town into the crowded, dusty road that led down to the ghat, neither Abdul nor Tooni were in the riotous crowd that pressed along with it. They had taken refuge in the outer bazar, and Sonny Sahib, sound asleep and well hidden, had taken refuge with them.

As to Sonny Sahib's mother, she was neither shot in the boats with the soldiers that believed the written word of the Nana Sahib, nor stabbed with the women and children who went back to the palace afterwards. She died quietly in the oxcart before it reached the ghat, and the pity of it was that Sonny Sahib's father, the captain, himself in hospital four hundred miles from Cawnpore, never knew.

There is a marble angel in Cawnpore now, standing in a very quiet garden, and shut off even from the trees and the flowers by an enclosing wall. The angel looks always down, down, and such an awful, pitiful sorrow stands there with her that nobody cares to try to touch it with words. People only come and look and go silently away, wondering what time can have for the healing of such a wound as this. There is an inscription--

SACRED TO THE PERPETUAL MEMORY OF A LARGE COMPANY OF CHRISTIAN PEOPLE, CHIEFLY WOMEN AND CHILDREN, WHO NEAR THIS SPOT WERE CRUELLY MURDERED BY THE FOLLOWERS OF THE REBEL NANA DHUNDU PANT OF BITHUR, AND CAST, THE DYING WITH THE DEAD, INTO THE WELL BELOW, ON THE XVTH DAY OF JULY MDCCCLVII.'

And afterward Sonny Sahib's father believed that all he could learn while he lived about the fate of his wife and his little son was written there. But he never knew.

Tooni and Abdul heard the terrible news of Cawnpore six months later. They had gone back to their own country, and it was far from Cawnpore--hundreds and hundreds of miles across a white sandy desert, grown with prickles and studded with rocks--high up in the north of Rajputana. In the State of Chita and the town of Rubbulgurh there was no fighting, because there were no Sahibs. The English had not yet come to teach the Maharajah how to govern his estate and spend his revenues. That is to say, there was no justice to speak of, and a great deal of cholera, and by no means three meals a day for everybody, or even two. But nobody was discontented with troubles that came from the gods and the Maharajah, and talk of greased cartridges would not have been understood. Thinking of this, Abdul often said to Tooni, his wife; 'The service of the sahib is good and profitable, but in old age peace is better, even though we are compelled to pay many rupees to the tax-gatherers of the Maharajah.' Tooni always agreed, and when the khaber came that all the memsahibs and the children had been killed by the sepoys, she agreed weeping. They were always so kind and gentle, the memsahibs, and the little ones, the babalok--the babalok! Surely the sepoys had become like the tiger-folk. Then she picked up Sonny Sahib and held him tighter than he liked. She had crooned with patient smiles over many of the babalok in her day, but from beginning to end, never a baba like this. So strong he was, he could make old Abdul cry out, pulling at his beard, so sweet-tempered and healthy that he would sleep just where he was put down, like other babies of Rubbulgurh. Tooni grieved deeply that she could not give him a bottle, and a coral, and a perambulator, and often wondered that he consented to thrive without these things, but the fact remains that he did. The man and woman, their breaths still ragged from the hasty flight along the cobbled streets, shuffled into the dimly lit tavern. The patrons, a motley crew of lost souls, barely glanced up from their drinks and cards as the newcomers entered. The man's hand, a tested sailor's hands with callouses and blisters, unclasped thewatch from his vest pocket, the silver glinting faintly in the poor light. The woman's eyes, tired and wary, scanned the room, taking note of the smoke-stained walls and the rag-tag furniture. They'd heard tales of this place, the Ship's Black Breath, where one could lose their soul as quickly as their coin. But they had little choice.

The patrons,Amos, the former scholar with his beard unkempt and his mind lost to whiskey, and Martha, a cosseted spinster turned into a harlot, barely acknowledged the pair. Only Jack, the veteran of many a war, his face etched with lines of pain and laughter, raised his glass in greeting. "New blood, eh?" he said, his voice gritty with years of tobacco and hard living. The man, Thomas, nodded, his fingers tracing the watch's engravings. It was a fine piece, the farmer's pride and joy, now their used coin.

Thomas approached Jack, leaning in close as if afraid the entire room wasn't yet theirs. "We've been on the run," he confessed, his voice barely a whisper. "The law's after us." His eyes flickered towards the woman, Elizabeth, who stood by the door, her heart pounding in her chest. "Our last mark was a drunken farmer. His watch..." Thomas's fingers paused on the timepiece, his smile a cruel edge. "A bit of justice, you might say."

Jack chuckled, a sound like distant thunder. "And what of your child? The one left behind?"

Thomas's face darkened. "A half-grown boy. Not our proudest moment." He leaned back, the watch disappearing again into the folds of his shirt. "We'll find him, make him right. Can't let him starve." His gaze hardened, "But if anyone asks, you've never seen us."

Amos, roused from his stupor by some nameless instinct, looked up. "And the watch? What's it worth on this side of the law?"

Thomas shrugged, a nonchalant gesture. "Pretty coin, pretty prisoners. We've got a fella waiting. He'll take care of it, quiet as the night."

Martha, her bonnet askew, fluffed her skirts with a weary hand. "You're a clever pair, aren't you? Evading the law while piling up the plunder."

Elizabeth bristled, her hands clutching the woolen shawl around her shoulders. "We ain't thieves. Just... survivors."

Thomas's gaze softened for a moment. "We are survivors, Elizabeth. That's all we are. And we'll stay that way." He looked back at Jack, his voice hard. "You know the games played here, old man. The exchange, the debt, the fate of us all."

Jack nodded, his expression grave. "And what of your child? You heard the town's talk. The tale of the kid left behind, the watch gone, and the farmer's daughter missing."

Thomas's grip tightened, his knuckles white. "We'll find him. We'll right what's wrong." He looked away, his gaze falling on the door. "But for now, we need rest, and then... then we'll see if there's a way out of this."

Amos, back to his drink, mumbled something about coincidence and fate. Thomas ignored him, walking over to Elizabeth. "It'll be alright," he murmured, his hand on her arm. "We'll find our way through this."

Elizabeth looked up at him, her eyes haunted. "And if we can't?"

Thomas was silent for a moment, then reached into his pocket, drawing out a small, smooth stone. He placed it in her hand, closing her fingers around it. "A promise of better days. This stone belongs to my mother. She used to say it was a token of hope, a reminder that even in the darkest night, there's a dawn to come."

Martha, with a laugh that held little humor, said, "You're a romantic, Thomas. But hope won't save us from the law or the debt that follows us."

Thomas's hand tightened around Elizabeth's, his eyes filled with an intensity that made the room fade away. "Hope is all we have, Martha. It's all any of us have. That, and each other."

As the room fell silent, the smoke hanging heavy in the air like a pall, the patrons of the Ship's Black Breath watched the new arrivals in a mix of pity and envy. For they knew, as well as Thomas and Elizabeth, that in this place, hope was a dangerous commodity.
