And he felt, with a force that startled him, an overwhelming desire to help her, to shelter her from the cruel realities of the world, to restore to her the bloom of youth and happiness that had so clearly been stolen away.

It was a curious sensation for a young man of Harris’s background and temperament. He was not, by nature, sentimental; indeed, he prided himself on his clear-headedness, his rational approach to problems, his freedom from the emotional excesses that he saw as a weakness in others. He was well-connected, possessed of a comfortable fortune, and had enjoyed the advantages of a first-rate education. His interests lay primarily in intellectual and political pursuits; he frequented the debates at the Oxford Union, wrote occasionally for the more serious periodicals, and had even entertained, fleetingly, the notion of entering Parliament. Love and marriage were matters that he had, hitherto, regarded with a certain detachment, as topics best left to the novelists and poets. He had observed the matrimonial pursuits of his contemporaries with amusement, if not a little disdain, and had often declared his intention of remaining a bachelor, at least until he had achieved some measure of distinction in the world. He moved in circles where eligible young ladies were plentiful, and he had been exposed to their charms and blandishments from an early age. He found them agreeable enough companions, capable of stimulating conversation and graceful dancing partners, but none had ever succeeded in capturing his imagination or stirring his heart. They were, he supposed, perfectly fine women, but they were, somehow, all of a piece – predictable in their opinions, conventional in their manners, and utterly lacking in that indefinable something that could spark a genuine connection.

And yet, this girl – a complete stranger, encountered only for a fleeting moment – had achieved what all the carefully cultivated graces of London society had failed to do. She had pierced his armor of indifference, touched a chord within him that he had not known existed, and left him utterly bewildered by the strength of his reaction. He found himself dwelling upon her image with a persistence that bordered on obsession. He replayed their brief encounter in his mind, analyzing every word, every gesture, every fleeting expression that crossed her face. He wondered about her circumstances, her history, her hopes and fears. He pictured her alone and vulnerable in the vast, indifferent city, struggling to survive against forces that were far beyond her control. And he felt a surge of protectiveness so powerful that it almost overwhelmed him. He knew, of course, that such feelings were absurd. He was a rational man, a man of the world; he could not allow himself to be governed by sentimentality. He had a duty to himself, to his family, to the causes that he had espoused. He could not allow himself to be distracted by a passing fancy, by a quixotic impulse to rescue a damsel in distress.

Mr. Ness had an occasional pupil; that is to say, he never put himself out of the way to obtain pupils, but did not refuse the entreaties sometimes made to him that he would prepare a young man for college, by allowing the said young man to reside and read with him. "Ness's men" took rather high honours, for the tutor, too indolent to find out work for himself, had a certain pride in doing well the work that was found for him.

When Ellinor was somewhere about fourteen, a young Mr. Corbet came to be pupil to Mr. Ness. Her father always called on the young men reading with the clergyman, and asked them to his house. His hospitality had in course of time lost its recherche and elegant character, but was always generous, and often profuse. Besides, it was in his character to like the joyous, thoughtless company of the young better than that of the old--given the same amount of refinement and education in both.

Mr. Corbet was a young man of very good family, from a distant county. If his character had not been so grave and deliberate, his years would only have entitled him to be called a boy, for he was but eighteen at the time when he came to read with Mr. Ness. But many men of five-and-twenty have not reflected so deeply as this young Mr. Corbet already had. He had considered and almost matured his plan for life; had ascertained what objects he desired most to accomplish in the dim future, which is to many at his age only a shapeless mist; and had resolved on certain steady courses of action by which such objects were most likely to be secured. A younger son, his family connections and family interest pre-arranged a legal career for him; and it was in accordance with his own tastes and talents. All, however, which his father hoped for him was, that he might be able to make an income sufficient for a gentleman to live on. Old Mr. Corbet was hardly to be called ambitious, or, if he were, his ambition was limited to views for the eldest son. But Ralph intended to be a distinguished lawyer, not so much for the vision of the woolsack, which I suppose dances before the imagination of every young lawyer, as for the grand intellectual exercise, and consequent power over mankind, that distinguished lawyers may always possess if they choose. A seat in Parliament, statesmanship, and all the great scope for a powerful and active mind that lay on each side of such a career--these were the objects which Ralph Corbet set before himself. To take high honours at college was the first step to be accomplished; and in order to achieve this Ralph had, not persuaded--persuasion was a weak instrument which he despised--but gravely reasoned his father into consenting to pay the large sum which Mr. Ness expected with a pupil. The good-natured old squire was rather pressed for ready money, but sooner than listen to an argument instead of taking his nap after dinner he would have yielded anything. But this did not satisfy Ralph; his father's reason must be convinced of the desirability of the step, as well as his weak will give way. The squire listened, looked wise, sighed; spoke of Edward's extravagance and the girls' expenses, grew sleepy, and said, "Very true," "That is but reasonable, certainly," glanced at the door, and wondered when his son would have ended his talking and go into the drawing-room; and at length found himself writing the desired letter to Mr. Ness, consenting to everything, terms and all. Mr. Ness never had a more satisfactory pupil; one whom he could treat more as an intellectual equal.

The days grew shorter, and the chill of autumn crept into the Virginia air. The leaves painted the landscape in hues of red and gold, a stark contrast to the looming specter of war that hung over the land. As the Grand Army prepared to advance, the anticipation was palpable, with rumors swirling like fallen leaves in the wind.

John Bladburn remained an enigmatic figure, his past shrouded in mystery. Though he had assured the narrator of his clean record and lack of family ties, there was a lingering sense of unease that surrounded him. Strong, ever the jovial companion, continued to jest about Bladburn, his sharp wit cutting through the tension like a knife.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon in a blaze of fiery orange, Bladburn approached the narrator with a solemn expression on his face. He spoke of his time as a wanderer, drifting from place to place with no clear purpose or destination. The narrator listened intently, captivated by the tale of a man searching for something he could not name.

As the days passed, the Grand Army remained stationary, their cannons silent and their troops restless. The rumors of impending battle grew louder, but still, no orders came for the advance. Bladburn, always the observer, noted the anxiety that gripped the camp like a vice, his keen eyes missing nothing.

One night, under the canopy of stars that stretched endlessly above them, Bladburn revealed a secret that he had guarded closely for years. He spoke of a love lost, a betrayal suffered, and a wound that had never fully healed. The narrator, touched by his vulnerability, offered a silent companionship that spoke louder than words ever could.

As the Virginia nights grew colder, Bladburn's past began to unravel like a delicate tapestry. The threads of his life were woven together with lies and half-truths, creating a portrait of a man haunted by his own demons. Strong, ever the optimist, tried to lighten the mood with his jests, but even he could sense the weight of the secrets that lay heavy on Bladburn's shoulders.

One fateful morning, as the sun rose over the horizon in a symphony of colors, the orders finally came for the Grand Army to advance. The camp erupted into a frenzy of activity, the tension that had been building for weeks finally finding release. Bladburn, his face a mask of resignation, prepared himself for the battle that lay ahead.

As the first shots rang out in the distance, echoing through the hills like a mournful symphony, Bladburn turned to the narrator with a steely glint in his eye. He spoke of redemption, of atonement, of finding peace in the midst of chaos. The narrator, his heart heavy with the weight of what was to come, nodded in silent understanding.

And so, as the Virginia landscape was bathed in the crimson light of dawn, Bladburn led the Grand Army into battle, his past finally laid to rest and his future uncertain. Strong, ever the loyal friend, stood by his side, ready to face whatever fate had in store. And as the echoes of war faded into the distance, leaving only silence in their wake, the narrator knew that the tale of John Bladburn would be forever etched in his memory, a testament to the resilience of the human spirit.

A few stars came out hesitatingly above Deadwood Slope. A cold wind that had sprung up with the going down of the sun fanned them into momentary brightness, swept the heated flanks of the mountain, and ruffled the river. Where the fallen man lay there was a sharp curve in the stream, so that in the gathering shadows the rushing water seemed to leap out of the darkness and to vanish again. Decayed drift-wood, trunks of trees, fragments of broken sluicing,--the wash and waste of many a mile,--swept into sight a moment, and were gone. All of decay, wreck, and foulness gathered in the long circuit of mining-camp and settlement, all the dregs and refuse of a crude and wanton civilization, reappeared for an instant, and then were hurried away in the darkness and lost. No wonder that as the wind ruffled the yellow waters the waves seemed to lift their unclean hands toward the rock whereon the fallen man lay, as if eager to snatch him from it, too, and hurry him toward the sea.

It was very still. In the clear air a horn blown a mile away was heard distinctly. The jingling of a spur and a laugh on the highway over Payne's Ridge sounded clearly across the river. The rattling of harness and hoofs foretold for many minutes the approach of the Wingdam coach, that at last, with flashing lights, passed within a few feet of the rock. Then for an hour all again was quiet. Presently the moon, round and full, lifted herself above the serried ridge and looked down upon the river. At first the bared peak of Deadwood Hill gleamed white and skull-like. Then the shadows of Payne's Ridge cast on the slope slowly sank away, leaving the unshapely stumps, the dusty fissures, and clinging outcrop of Deadwood Slope to stand out in black and silver. Still stealing softly downward, the moonlight touched the bank and the rock, and then glittered brightly on the river. The rock was bare and the man was gone, but the river still hurried swiftly to the sea.

“Is there anything for me?” asked Tommy Islington, as, a week after, the stage drew up at the Mansion House, and Bill slowly entered the bar-room. Bill did not reply, but, turning to a stranger who had entered with him, indicated with a jerk of his finger the boy. The stranger turned with an air half of business, half of curiosity, and looked critically at Tommy. “Is there anything for me?” repeated Tommy, a little confused at the silence and scrutiny. Bill walked deliberately to the bar, and, placing his back against it, faced Tommy with a look of demure enjoyment.

“Ef,” he remarked slowly,--“ef a hundred thousand dollars down and half a million in perspektive is ennything, Major, THERE IS!”

MRS. SKAGGS'S HUSBANDS.

It was characteristic of Angel's that the disappearance of Johnson, and the fact that he had left his entire property to Tommy, thrilled the community but slightly in comparison with the astounding discovery that he had anything to leave. The finding of a cinnabar lode at Angel's absorbed all collateral facts or subsequent details. Prospectors from adjoining camps thronged the settlement; the hillside for a mile on either side of Johnson's claim was staked out and pre-empted; trade received a sudden stimulus; and, in the excited rhetoric of the “Weekly Record,” “a new era had broken upon Angel's.” “On Thursday last,” added that paper, “over five hundred dollars was taken in over the bar of the Mansion House.”

Of the fate of Johnson there was little doubt. He had been last seen lying on a boulder on the river-bank by outside passengers of the Wingdam night coach, and when Finn of Robinson's Ferry admitted to have fired three shots from a revolver at a dark object struggling in the water near the ferry, which he “suspicioned” to be a bear, the question seemed to be settled. Whatever might have been the fallibility of his judgment, of the accuracy of his aim there could be no doubt. The general belief that Johnson, after possessing himself of the muleteer's pistol, could have run amuck, gave a certain retributive justice to this story, which rendered it acceptable to the camp.

The early light of a fog-bound morning stirred the humble adjoining rooms where Angus and Lottie sat in quiet contemplation, their hearts heavy with the recollection of recent days. Outside, the wind whispered of change, as though it carried with it the lullabies of both death and hope. The memory of that gentle soul’s peaceful departure lingered in Angus’s mind like a benediction, a token of nature’s rare compassion for mortals in their hour of distress.

Angus, having witnessed the serene final moments of a kindred spirit, now regarded the transient nature of existence with a newfound reverence. “Lottie, did you not see in her countenance the calm resignation of a soul departing earthly bonds?” he murmured, voice imbued with both sorrow and gratitude. His words echoed in the modest chamber, where each beam of light revealed the tender interplay of hope and despair.

Lottie, whose tender heart had long borne the burden of deprivation, answered with a tremulous sigh, her eyes reflecting the weariness of uncounted troubled nights. “Indeed, Angus, her departure was as a soft benediction, yet it wakes a fear within me for those still bound to life’s harsh necessities,” she replied. In her voice there shimmered not only regret but an unspoken dread for the fate of those she held dear.

Her thoughts swiftly turned to their ailing babe, whose recent hardships now seemed tempered by the promise of recovery after his troublesome tooth had finally passed. “Our little one grows stronger, and yet, how shall the bitter draft of our cold rooms fail to chill his tender form?” she lamented, the sorrow of poverty spilling into every quivering syllable. Her delicate countenance betrayed the conflict between gratitude for small mercies and the ever-looming spectre of want.

A pause ensued, during which the gentle ticking of the clock carried the weight of every lost hope. Angus, ever the sentinel of reason amidst despair, clasped Lottie’s hand and observed, “Our fortunes may be as fleeting as the light that now wanes, yet there is solace to be found in our humble perseverance.” His words, simple in sentiment, evoked a quiet resilience that steadied their wavering hearts.

Lottie’s eyes glistened as the confessions of her past, long shrouded in sorrowful secrecy, began to emerge. With trembling resolve, she recounted a secret held close by her dear departed mother—a truth regarding their family’s dire circumstances and a modest ruse committed in a desperate bid for extra coin. “Angus, forgive me if my voice falters, but I must confess that I once took a small measure of cunning to secure an extra morsel of sustenance for our dying hearth,” she whispered, as if the very admission might shatter the fragile stillness of their world.

Her revelation did not bring reproach from him, but rather, a solemn nod of understanding entwined with unconditional compassion. “Lottie, in such times, when fortune’s gaze seems unyielding, every modest act borne of love for one’s kin must be forgiven by the law of necessity,” replied Angus, echoing the venerable truths that had oft been recited by weary souls in similar straits.

In that moment, as the ghostly remnants of twilight clung to the edges of their chamber, a subtle yet unmistakable shift in the air was perceived—a silent herald of new beginnings. Lottie, her grief mingling with tentative hope, revealed another of her secret endeavors: the acceptance of a position as an amanuensis, spurred by an advertisement placed by the enigmatic Miss Harman. “I received word, dear husband, from Miss Harman’s advertisement; an opportunity, though hidden in modesty, to earn the means to comfort our aching hearts and cold hearth,” she declared softly, her tone at once both apologetic and resolute.

Thus commenced a new chapter in their humble existence—one tinged with uncertainty yet brimming with the audacity of self-redemption. As the day advanced and the heavens painted their quiet hues, Angus and Lottie resolved to embrace this opportunity, however modest it might be, as a salve for the wounds inflicted by relentless poverty. Their conversation, though tentative, sparked within them the poise necessary to face a future wrought with both promise and peril.

The hearth in their small parlour, though offering but a weak and flickering flame, became the emblem of their nascent hopes. Each spark was a silent prayer for warmth, a testament to the indomitable spirit of a family that dared to dream amidst adversity. “Let us then cherish these small fortunes,” Angus murmured, “for even the slightest glow may guide us through the darkness.” His words, imbued with the gravity of their plight, resonated deeply in the quiet confines of their home.

Outside, the narrow streets of their modest neighbourhood bore witness to countless other souls yet burdened by similar misfortunes, a silent chorus of shared despair and unyielding hope in a world that seemed all too indifferent. The couple’s plight was but a single melody in the greater symphony of life’s trials—a melody that, if only played with sufficient tenderness, might inspire revival even in the most barren of hearts.

In these early hours, as the mist slowly receded, the couple endeavoured to restore warmth not only to their frozen abodes but also to their weary spirits. Lottie, with eyes now both resolute and wistful, regarded her husband with a profound tenderness. “Angus, though life’s bitter winds may yet howl about us, let us ever stand together as one, and may the gentle art of writing bear the promise of a new dawn,” she entreated softly.

The prospect of her budding employment as an amanuensis shone as a slender beam of hope, illuminating darker recesses of despair. “Miss Harman’s trust, though modest in measure, is a rare grace bestowed upon us; it shall not only enrich our coffers but restore dignity to the family name,” Lottie continued, her voice a blend of pride and earnest apprehension. In that moment of vulnerability, the past and future converged as she recounted the sacrifices of her lineage and the silent struggles of her mother.

Angus, whose countenance was stern yet touched by soft compassion, recalled days gone by when virtue was its own reward. “We are but humble servants to fate, my dear, and every small step, every modest gift, must be embraced as though it were providence incarnate,” he affirmed, his words a quiet rallying cry against the indomitable march of misfortune. His faith was a beacon in the oppressive gloom of poverty.

With each shared confession and each tender word, the couple wove together a tapestry of resilience and shared destiny. The room, scant as it was in material comforts, brimmed with an ethos of mutual redemption and the promise of better days. Their conversation was neither flamboyant nor elaborate; it was a simple affirming of life’s intrinsic dignity amidst the starkest trials.

As diminishing night gave way to the reluctant embrace of day, Angus and Lottie resolved to count every blessing, however slight, and to seize upon each opportunity as a stepping stone toward a brighter morrow. Thus, with a quiet determination, they gathered their scant belongings and prepared themselves for the tasks and challenges that awaited beyond their modest threshold.

In the gentle unfolding of a new day, the whispers of hardship were counterbalanced by a promise—a promise that even in the bleakest hours, the human spirit, when united in love and purpose, could prevail against the harsh vicissitudes of fate. Their modest triumphs, woven together by shared tears and tender ambitions, heralded the nascent stirrings of change that might, in time, transform their fortunes forever.

The sun, already high in the heavens, cast long, dancing shadows through the trees, dappling the dusty road with shifting patterns of light and shade. The rhythmic swaying of the litter, borne upon the shoulders of two stalwart Indians, lulled Padre Jose into a fitful slumber. Yet, even in the hazy realm between wakefulness and dreams, the memory of the encounter clung to him like a shroud.

He recalled the sneering countenance of the stranger, the glint of avarice in his eyes as he proffered the heavy bag of gold. “Turn back, Padre,” the stranger had hissed, his voice a silken whisper that belied the venom in his words. “Embrace the comfort these coins can bring. Why waste your waning years in this godforsaken wilderness?”

But Padre Jose had seen the cunning trap laid bare before him. “Begone, tempter!” he had thundered, brandishing his crucifix like a flaming sword. “Your gold holds no allure for a servant of God. My soul is not for sale, nor is the salvation of these poor souls entrusted to my care!”

The stranger’s features twisted in a rictus of rage. With a guttural roar, he lunged, his hands reaching for the holy symbol that dared to defy him. Padre Jose felt a searing pain as the crucifix was wrenched from his grasp, a numbness spreading through his limbs like a paralyzing chill. Then, only darkness.

Now, as consciousness slowly returned, he felt the gentle rocking of the litter and heard the murmur of voices around him. He opened his eyes, his vision blurred and unfocused. Gradually, the shapes around him sharpened, resolving themselves into the concerned faces of his flock.

Ignacio, his face etched with worry, knelt beside him. “Padre, Padre, can you hear me?” he implored, his voice trembling with relief.

Padre Jose blinked, trying to gather his scattered senses. “Ignacio? What… what happened?”

“You are safe now, Padre,” Ignacio assured him, gently wiping the sweat from the priest’s brow. “We found you lying on the mountainside, a short distance from where… from where he attacked you.”

“The stranger… the Devil…” Padre Jose stammered, his voice hoarse with exertion.

Ignacio’s eyes widened in alarm. “Do not speak of him, Padre. He is gone, banished by your unwavering faith. But tell me, how did you escape his clutches?”

Padre Jose struggled to sit up, his body protesting with a dull ache. “I… I do not know,” he confessed, his brow furrowed in thought. “The last thing I remember is the crucifix being torn from my grasp. Then, nothing. Only a swirling void.”

“It is a miracle, Padre!” Ignacio exclaimed, his eyes shining with awe. “The Devil intended to silence your voice, to extinguish the light of faith you bring to these mountains. But God, in His infinite mercy, protected you. He lifted you from harm’s way and delivered you safely into our hands.”

In the waning light of a summer’s eve—when the sky blushed as though in timid confession of its follies—and amidst the vast, whispering environs of the Moors, it came to pass that our erstwhile foundling, Jesse Cliffe, now unshackled from the petty concerns of apprenticeship and the trammels of civil society, ventured into a realm of solitude so wide and uncharted that even the most daring souls of the neighbouring hamlets might have deemed it a kind of wild, unbridled liberty. No longer the errant, much-maligned waif whom the rural authorities, with their bureaucratic indifference and abundant superstitions, had seen as naught but a bothersome byword to be lost, recovered, and lost yet again, Jesse had assumed the austere mantle of one who, by his own stray design, had embraced a fate far removed from the lachrymose histories of foundlings and errants. His departure from the employ of that irascible cattle-dealer Samuel Goddard—a man who, in his own fusty manner, had deemed it fit to mould the delicate spirit of youth into the hard-edged apparatus of commerce—was celebrated, if indeed one might speak of such a solitary victory, by the very elements of nature itself. For it was under a vault of deepening purples and dusky blues, with the wind sauntering across the heathered slopes as if in conspiratorial mirth, that Jesse, with a wild gleam kindred to that of the feral creatures which roamed these barren lands, resolved to fashion a life in which survival was a careful art, and convention a despised chain. He set about his new existence with a combination of adroit improvisation and an innate knowledge of the rhythm by which the Moors and their denizens—both beast and bumbling human—must abide; gathering the remnant fruits offered by a barren earth, fashioning shelters from the unyielding bracken, and tracking the denizens of the wilderness with an ease that belied his tender years, he was at once a student of nature’s unspoken laws and a reluctant emissary of its stern populism. Even as the local sportsmen, who once scoffed at the notion of a neglected child becoming more than a mere trifle in the annals of their quotidian amusement, began to whisper his name with a note of grudging admiration—acknowledging, perhaps, that in the art of field-sporting and the quiet lore of the hunt there lay a subtle grace—a certain rough nobility in the boy who neither burgled strictly nor clung wholly to the conventions of society, but instead trod the fine line between necessity and moral rectitude with the balance of a seasoned acrobat, our Jesse pursued his freedom with the unerring determination of one who has long been abandoned to destiny’s whims.

Thus it was that, amid the swirling mists and the echoing calls of the far-off curlews, Jesse Cliffe, now self-proclaimed and unburdened by the petty griefs of neglect and the vexations of unworthy masters, navigated the treacherous interplay between isolation and communion. In his modest lean-to, constructed from the fallen limbs of ancient oaks and the scattered stones of forgotten homesteads, he had, over a scarce period yet measured in the slow rhythm of nature’s pulse, instituted a peculiar order—a veritable code of conduct which shunned both wanton avarice and despair, and rather embraced a conscientious moderation wherein neither plenty nor hunger might reign supreme. His days were marked by the exigencies of the hunt and the careful, almost ritualistic tending to the small plots of wild grains and herbs which he coaxed from the untamed soil; his nights were lit by the flickering dance of a modest fire, whose fleeting light bore witness to whispered soliloquies on duty and desire that he dared not confess to any eavesdropping ear. And though societal reproach and the usual disapproving glances of his erstwhile employers had long receded into the sullen sepia of memory, a community of solitary wanderers—comprising both weathered sportsmen and even the occasional itinerant poet, whose soul found kinship in the lullabies of the heath—would sometimes, in moments of unguarded reverie, acknowledge his modest triumph through nods and murmurs as though he were a figure of myth reawakened. In his careful stewardship of his newfound liberty, there dwelt an ineffable concord between the rugged austerity of the Moors and the tender, unyielding spirit that had once been so neglectfully cast adrift; and thereby, as the wind sighed among the heather and small, cunning animals skittered to and fro in the twilight, the legacy of the forsaken child acquired a gentle, enduring resonance—a testament not only to the sterner elements of nature but also, indeed, to that innate human desire to overmaster even the wildest fortunes in pursuit of a truth that lay hidden, yet persistently beckoning, beyond the confines of polite society.

This, then, was the phantom death! Yonder venomous reptile it was, then, that, creeping out of some secret hiding-place, and visiting the unhappy men one after another, had stung them in their sleep, in the darkness of the cabin, and vanished before they had struck a light and realized indeed that something desperate had come to them!

Whilst I stood looking at the snake, whose horror seemed to gain fresh accentuation from the very beauty of its snow-white speckled skin and diamond-bright eyes, the boatswain, armed with a long handspike, and followed by a number of the crew, came headlong to the cabin. He thrust the end of the handspike under the belly of the creature, and hove it into the middle of the berth.

“Stand clear!” he roared, and with a blow or two smashed the reptile’s head into a pulp. “Open that cabin window,” said he. One of the men did so, and the boatswain with his boot scraped the mess of mashed snake on to the handspike and shook it overboard.

“I told you they was poisoned,” he cried, breathing deep; “and, oh my God, Mr. West—and I humbly ask your pardon again for having suspected ye—do you know, sir, whilst I was a-talking to you just now I was actually thinking of taking up my quarters in this here cabin this very night.”

Thus much: and now to end this singular experience in a sentence or two. Three days after the discovery of the snake we sighted and signalled a large English merchantman bound to London from the Rio de la Plata. Her chief officer came aboard, and we related our story. He asked to see the snake. We told him we had thrown it overboard. On my describing it, he informed me that he guessed it was the little poisonous reptile known in certain districts of South America as the Ibiboboko. He returned to his ship, and shortly afterwards the commander sent us his third officer, with instructions to keep in company as long as possible.

BROKERS’ BAY.

Brokers’ Bay is situated on the West Coast of England. You may search the map for it in vain, and the reason why I call it by any other name than that it bears will, when you have read this story, be as clear as the mud in the water that brims to the base of Brokers’ cliffs. Brokers’ Bay is a fine, curving sweep of land. For how many centuries the sea has been sneakingly ebbing from it who can imagine? The time has been when the galleon and the carack strained at their hempen ground tackle at anchors six fathoms deep where the white windmill now stands within musket-shot of the Crown and Anchor, and where the church spire darts the gleam of its weathercock above the green thickness of a huddle of dwarf trees near the little vicarage.

About fifty years ago a company of enterprising souls took it into their heads to reclaim some of the land which the subtly and ceaselessly ebbing sea, rising and falling with moon-like regularity, yet receding ever, though noticeably only in spans of half-centuries, was leaving behind it. They armed themselves with the necessary legal powers, they subscribed all the capital they considered needful, and by processes of embanking, draining, manuring, and the like, they succeeded in raising wheat and grass, vegetables and flowers, where, since and long before the days of the painted Briton, shuddering in the November blast, or perspiring away his small clothes under the July sun, nothing had flourished but the dab and the crab.

Yet the speculation on the whole was a failure. It was a patriotic achievement in its way, and those concerned in it deserved well of the nation; for if it be a fine thing to bleed for one’s country, how much finer must it be to add to its dimensions, to enlarge its latitude and longitude, and extend the home-sovereignty of the monarch? Yet, though a pretty considerable village stood hard by the reclaimed land, houses did not increase. The builder, whose Christian name is Jerry, came down to Brokers’ Bay, and took a look around, and went home again, and did nothing. He was not to be decoyed, he said. Brokers’ Bay was not the right sort of place to start a town in, he thought. There was too much mud, Mr. Jerry considered. He calculated that when the water was out there was a full mile and three-quarters of slime. Oh yes, whilst the slime was still slimy it reflected the sky just the same as if it had been water, and it took a noble blood-red countenance of a hot sunset evening, when the sea was a pink gleaming streak just under the horizon, and it was very pleasing in that sort of way. But what were the doctors going to say about all that mud, and what opportunities would a waste of slush, extending one and three-quarter miles at ebb tide, provide the local historian with when he came to write a guide-book and invent Roman and Early English names for the immediate district, and deal with the salubriousness of the climate, and give an analysis of the drinking water? And what about the bathing? There was none. And what length of pier would be wanted if the seaward end of it was to be permanently water-washed?

Fortunately I was too well acquainted with the peculiar variations of etiquette and manners exhibited by the different peoples of the East and West to betray my astonishment at this exposure. I poured him the bath for which he seemed so eager, and politely excused myself with the explanation that I must provide him with refreshments.

As I had my own private larder in the second stateroom, I had no need to call upon the steward for a luncheon, having on hand various sweets, potted meats, English biscuits, and Chinese conserves, in addition to my wines. When I returned with a well-stocked tray, I found my guest struggling to don his linen over his coat. His relief was unmistakable when I signed him to lay aside everything and slip on a loose lounging-robe.

Following my example, he seated himself at the little folding table. When served, he waited, seemingly reluctant to eat alone. Accordingly I served myself, and fell to without delay. At my first mouthful he also caught up knife and fork and began to eat with undisguised heartiness yet with a nicety and correctness of manners that astonished me. When I expressed my surprise that our table etiquette should be so similar, he explained with charming candor that he was but copying my actions.

I could not repress my admiration. “Here’s to our friendship!” I said, raising my glass to him. “May it soon ripen to the mellowness of this wine.”

I doubt if he sensed the meaning of the words, but he raised his glass, and his face glowed with responsive pleasure as together we drank the toast. The act of good-fellowship seemed to bring him still nearer to me, and as I gazed across into his glowing face I could almost forget our differences of race. In my robe and smoking-cap his color and the obliqueness of his eyes appeared less pronounced, and I realized that in all other respects his features differed little from my own. True, my eyes were dark blue and his jet black, and though my nose was rather low between the eyes, his was still flatter. But below their bridges our noses rose in the same softly aristocratic curve. The outlines of our faces were of a like oval contour, there was a close similarity about our mouths and chins, and even our eyebrows curved with an identical high and even arch.

“My friend,” I said, “do not answer unless you feel free to explain,--but I wonder that you, a relative of the Emperor, should be compelled to start your travels in this secret manner.”

“Shogun, not Emperor,” he corrected. “Law over Shogun, too. I travel naibun--incognito. Shimadzu Satsuma-no-kami my friend. I teach Raugaku--the Dutch learning,--war ways, history, engineering. No man know real me at Kagoshima. Daimio of Satsuma gone Yedo. I steal aboard. No man know. Shogunate no punish daimio, my friend.”

“They would punish even the Prince of Satsuma if they found you had escaped from his province?”

My guest nodded. “Very old law.”

“Yet you would leave the country at the risk of death?”

His smile deepened into a look of solemn joy. I give his broken Dutch a fair translation.

“My soul is in the eyes of Woroto Sama. There is trust between us. I speak without concealment. The tojin peoples of the west have dealt harshly with the Chinese. The black ships have destroyed many forts and bombarded great cities. I fear the black ships may come to devastate Dai Nippon; yet my people know even less of your people than did the Chinese. The Dutch of Deshima warn us to heed the demands of the tojin to open our ports. The officials in control of the Shogunate shut their ears.”

“She ain't here now.”

Mr. Brice's face displayed his disappointment. But the true lover holds a talisman potent with old and young. Mrs. Tarbox felt a sneaking maternal pity for this suddenly stricken Strephon.

“She's gone home,” she added more gently--“went at sun-up this mornin'.”

“Home,” repeated Brice. “Where's that?”

Mrs. Tarbox looked at her husband and hesitated. Then she said--a little in her old manner--“Her uncle's.”

“Can you direct me the way there?” asked Brice simply.

The astonishment in their faces presently darkened into suspicion again. “Ef that's your little game,” began Hiram, with a lowering brow--

“I have no little game but to see her and speak with her,” said Brice boldly. “I am alone and unarmed, as you see,” he continued, pointing to his empty belt and small dispatch bag slung on his shoulder, “and certainly unable to do any one any harm. I am willing to take what risks there are. And as no one knows of my intention, nor of my coming here, whatever might happen to me, no one need know it. You would be safe from questioning.”

There was that hopeful determination in his manner that overrode their resigned doggedness. “Ef we knew how to direct you thar,” said the old woman cautiously, “ye'd be killed outer hand afore ye even set eyes on the girl. The house is in a holler with hills kept by spies; ye'd be a dead man as soon as ye crossed its boundary.”

“Wot do YOU know about it?” interrupted her husband quickly, in querulous warning. “Wot are ye talkin' about?”

“You leave me alone, Hiram! I ain't goin' to let that young feller get popped off without a show, or without knowin' jest wot he's got to tackle, nohow ye kin fix it! And can't ye see he's bound to go, whatever ye says?”

Mr. Tarbox saw this fact plainly in Brice's eyes, and hesitated.

“The most that I kin tell ye,” he said gloomily, “is the way the gal takes when she goes from here, but how far it is, or if it ain't a blind, I can't swar, for I hevn't bin thar myself, and Harry never comes here but on an off night, when the coach ain't runnin' and thar's no travel.” He stopped suddenly and uneasily, as if he had said too much.

“Thar ye go, Hiram, and ye talk of others gabblin'! So ye might as well tell the young feller how that thar ain't but one way, and that's the way Harry takes, too, when he comes yer oncet in an age to talk to his own flesh and blood, and see a Christian face that ain't agin him!”

Mr. Tarbox was silent. “Ye know whar the tree was thrown down on the road,” he said at last.

“Yes.”

“The mountain rises straight up on the right side of the road, all hazel brush and thorn--whar a goat couldn't climb.”

“Yes.”

“But that's a lie! for thar's a little trail, not a foot wide, runs up from the road for a mile, keepin' it in view all the while, but bein' hidden by the brush. Ye kin see everything from thar, and hear a teamster spit on the road.”

“Go on,” said Brice impatiently.

“Then it goes up and over the ridge, and down the other side into a little gulch until it comes to the canyon of the North Fork, where the stage road crosses over the bridge high up. The trail winds round the bank of the Fork and comes out on the LEFT side of the stage road about a thousand feet below it. That's the valley and hollow whar Harry lives, and that's the only way it can be found. For all along the LEFT of the stage road is a sheer pitch down that thousand feet, whar no one kin git up or down.”

“I understand,” said Brice, with sparkling eyes. “I'll find my way all right.”

“And when ye git thar, look out for yourself!” put in the woman earnestly. “Ye may have regular greenhorn's luck and pick up Flo afore ye cross the boundary, for she's that bold that when she gets lonesome o' stayin' thar she goes wanderin' out o' bounds.”

But Prue had a New England village to answer; she had the family's belongings to take care of--no great task in itself; she had little Miss Prue to oversee. Grave men who were professors of astronomy, or Greek antiquities, or Hebrew, and who, therefore, knew all about it, told her, in language of whose correctness Addison would have been proud, that the aborigines of the American plains were bloodthirsty in the extreme. Fluttering women detailed anecdotes of sudden death at the hands of Indians. One and all bade her good-by with the firm conviction, openly expressed, that she would never return; upon which all whom weeping became wept, while others displayed their best handkerchiefs as a sort of defiant substitute for more open emotion. Prue saw the little town fade into distance with mingled feelings, of which terror was the predominant, until her husband explained to her, by the aid of an airy little octavo which he had stuffed into an inadequate bag, that Professor Nincomb's theory of glacial action was not only false, but would be conclusively proved to be so by the new theory of erosion. At this she brightened. Prue owned to a vague impression that glacial action had something to do with the North Pole, so the argument per se had little weight with her. But Prue was a New Englander, and devout in the New England fashion, and she settled back on Divine Providence with great thankfulness. She argued that no scheme of things could dispense ruthlessly with so wonderful an affair as the theory of erosions. Therefore the scheme of things would take care of the only possessor of the theory. Indians lost their terrors, she and little Miss Prue fell asleep together, leaving the doctor still poring excitedly over the octavo of Professor Nincomb.

Their first serious difficulties were encountered at Three Rivers. Of course, in the circumstances, the mild little doctor quite failed in his attempts to secure transportation. How should he, a scientist, know or care anything about gold excitements? The hustle confused him, the crowd stunned him, the fierce self-reliance and lack of consideration of these rough men alarmed him.

He came back to the board hotel very much discouraged. "There is not a conveyance of any sort to be found," he informed Mrs. Prue, "and there is great difficulty in estimating the precise duration of the present state of affairs. It may continue into next summer; or so, at least, I was informed by a very estimable person."

That was unbearable. Think of little Miss Prue being required, in the third year of her diminutive life, to face the heat of the plains in midsummer! Think of the cost of living a twelvemonth in such a place as Three Rivers! Prue put on her hat and went out into the turbulent camp. Until that moment she had deemed it wisest to remain in her room.

She was greeted only with respect. Men paused and looked after her. You see, Prue had such grave, calm eyes, that looked straight at you with so much confidence; and such a sensitive, serious mouth, that argued such a capacity for making up quiet opinions of people--and acting on them--that you were always very much inclined to take off your hat, even if you were Tony Quinn and middling drunk. It was not ten minutes before she had corroborated the doctor's bad news; but she had also heard incidentally of Billy Knapp, Alfred, and Buckley. The hotel-keeper pointed out the latter--that quiet man with the brown beard. Prue went straight to him and stated her case.

In the statement she laid great stress on the importance of the dip of strata. If the doctor did not get to work before long, he would be unable to finish his explorations before his means had become exhausted. Prue waxed quite technical. She used a number of long words and a few long phrases, hoping thus to awe the calm and contemplative individual in front of her.

"Come, Ermengarde," he whispered, gently urging his younger sister towards the schoolroom door.

"But what will Aunt say?" fretted Ermengarde, her brow furrowed with worry. "We are already tardy, and she expressly warned us..."

"Never you mind Aunt Elizabeth," interrupted Basil with a confident air. "It was my doing entirely. I was delayed, you see, with Father in the library, discussing... well, discussing important matters of the estate." He puffed out his chest a bit, hoping the vague explanation would suffice. Ermengarde, bless her trusting heart, never doubted him for a moment.

The schoolroom buzzed with the joyful chaos of a high tea, made all the more exuberant by the return of the elder Wilton boys from their respective schools. The younger children, freed from the constraints of their afternoon lessons, were a whirlwind of excited chatter and laughter. Even the normally unflappable Miss Nelson, her usually severe features softened by a rare smile, seemed caught up in the celebratory atmosphere.

"There you are at last, Basil, my dear boy!" she exclaimed as the two siblings entered. Her gaze then fell upon Ermengarde, and the hint of a frown flickered across her face. "And Ermengarde, late as usual. I trust there is a perfectly good reason for this tardiness?"

Basil, ever the dutiful protector of his beloved sister, stepped forward. "The fault lies entirely with me, Miss Nelson," he declared, his voice ringing with sincerity. "I fear I detained Ermengarde with my own dawdling."

Miss Nelson regarded him with a knowing look. She saw through his little charade, of course, but chose to indulge him. Basil, with his kind heart and gentlemanly manners, was undeniably her favorite amongst the Wilton brood.

"Very well, Basil. See that it doesn't happen again." Her tone, though firm, held a distinct lack of its usual reprimand.

Relieved, Basil steered Ermengarde towards the tea table, already laden with an assortment of tempting treats. As they took their places amongst their siblings, Miss Nelson allowed herself a small sigh. While she shared in the general merriment of the occasion, a shadow of unease lingered at the back of her mind.

The summer stretched before them, long and, she feared, potentially fraught with the usual childish squabbles and misadventures. Eric, with his boundless energy and penchant for mischief, was sure to be at the heart of most of them. The thought of navigating the next few months, attempting to maintain some semblance of order amidst the chaos, filled her with a distinct sense of foreboding. Still, she reminded herself, it was summertime, a time for children to be children. With a deep breath and a silent prayer for patience, she turned her attention back to her charges, determined to enjoy the festivities, however fleeting they might be.

The sun hung low in the west, casting long shadows across the cobblestone streets of Aldersbury, now bathed in the soft, golden light of departure. Market day had waned, leaving in its wake a hum of satisfied transactions and a lingering air of festivities. The streets, once a swirling vortex of activity, were tranquil, save for the occasional rustle of passersby and the distant tolling of St. Juliana's, marking the transition from afternoon to evening.

Amidst this quietude, Mr. Bourdillon, resplendent in his blue coat adorned with gilt buttons, found himself at a crossroads, his mind aflutter with the events of the day. His departure to London was imminent, and he paused on the edge of Bride Hill, reflecting on the encounter with the Holyhead Mail coach, a vessel that had once carried whispers of battles won and peace secured, and tales of noble nuptials. His thoughts, however, were momentarily disrupted by the lively chatter of the village cobbler, whose enthusiasm for the latest shipment of leather had the infectious quality of a lively market jester.

"Ah, Mr. Bourdillon, just in time! You'll not miss the post, eh? Finest leather from London, I say," the cobbler's voice rang out, tinged with the accents of Aldshire's rich soil and the spirit of its hardworking folk.

Mr. Bourdillon, ever courteous, returned the cobbler's smile, though his gaze remained fixed on the horizon, where the early stars were beginning their celestial dance. "A pleasure, Mr. Turner. I must avail myself of the mail, as important matters await me in the city. Good luck with your new stock," he replied, his voice carrying an undertone of finality.

With a nod, Mr. Bourdillon stepped onto the road leading out of Aldersbury, his pace deliberate yet brisk, a solitary figure against the backdrop of dusk. The air, thick with the aromatic scent of blooming gillyflowers and the tang of distant hayfields, seemed to offer a mournful parting as he passed the threshold of the town. The ancient oaks lining the path whispered secrets to the wind, a farewell to the young man who carried with him the hopes and dreams of a community that held a special place in his heart.

As Mr. Bourdillon descended the gentle incline leading to the outskirts, his thoughts veered towards the letter he was to deliver. A missive from a dear friend, it contained news of a scientific breakthrough that promised to unravel the mysteries of the natural world. The weight of such an important task made him pause, causing him to reflect on the interconnectedness of the world, the threads that bound Aldersbury to London, London to the farthest reaches of the globe. Each step carried him closer to his destiny, a journey that was as much about the destination as the path traversed.

Just as the twilight sky was kissed by the first sliver of moon, Mr. Bourdillon reached the point where Aldersbury's embrace waned, and the open road lay before him. In that moment, he felt a profound sense of gratitude for the life that had led him to this juncture, where the past and future intertwined, and where the bustling market place of Aldersbury gave way to the limitless expanse of adventure. And as he set foot upon the uncertain terrain of the unknown, the echoes of the town's daily life faded into the gentle rhythm of the road beneath his feet, a symphony of solitude and anticipation.

"Hast thou seen him?" quoth I, with a gaze as piercing as the northern star.

"Nay, but I've had him itemized to me by the wife o' Samson Slumber, a teller of tales as fervent as a hermit's prayer. A chin as sharp as a blade, a brow as creased as the earth after a tempest, he hath the visage of one who hath known both triumph and tribulation."

"Methinks," spake I, my voice a melody somber and deep, "that man's visage doth bear the stamp of his own mettle; a chin carved by determination, a brow furrowed by the weight of mankind's follies."

"Indeed, Master Sharrow," retorted she, her voice brimming with the fervor of a bard recounting an age-old saga, "this Lord Silex stands as a relic of a time forgotten, a demon from the tales 'neath the moonlight."

"Yet," mused I, a twinkle in my eye as subtle as the flicker of a candle's flame, "there is within me a something that doth stir on his behalf, as if the mere mention of his name weaves a tale of redemption amidst the shroud of scandal."

"By my troth!" exclaimed my spouse, her countenance one of disbelief, "I do believe, Master Sharrow, that thou'dst offer solace to a ghost in the gloaming."

Just then, there came a knock at our chamber door, and forth stepped Lady Adella Trenyon, her gaze as keen as a falcon's and her silhouette as regal as a queen's. She had overheard our discourse and was plied by the tales of Lord Silex.

"Do tell me more, dear Marian," beseeched Lady Trenyon, her countenance alight with curiosity, "for I have long held disdain for tales of gossip, yet this Lord Silex intrigues me as does a riddle wrapped in enigma."

Marian, with a nod, continued her narration, her voice a tapestry of vivid descriptions and hushed whispers. She painted Lord Silex as a phantom of vengeance, his wrath eternal, his spirit as restless as a ghost in the night, driven by a betrayal so profound it had turned his very soul to stone.

"Yet," mused Lady Trenyon, her wisdom as timeless as the echoes of ancient ballads, "we often judge men by the stories spun around them, much like we perceive a forest by the single tree we gaze upon. One act can cast a long shadow, but let us not forget that a man's life is a book, not a mere chapter."

As if summoned by the very mention of his name, Sir John Trenyon, Lady Trenyon's venerable uncle, entered the room, a figure straight out of history's pages. His presence was commanding, his stories as rich as the tales told by the ancient bards.

"Ah, Lady Trenyon," greeted Sir John, his voice a deep baritone as resonant as a cathedral's bell, "I've heard whispers of Lord Silex, a man shaped by the very currents of fate. Let me share with you a slice from the tapestry of his story, for in the annals of our family, his name is woven like a thread of gold."

And so, as the twilight bled into night, Lady Trenyon listened, her heart a vessel of both skepticism and longing for tales of yore, tales intertwined with the threads of loyalty and betrayal. The room filled with the murmurs of the past, a past where Lord Silex, the demon of Denbeigh, loomed large, yet within the shadows, a flicker of compassion dared to dance.

"So, dear Marian, tell me," implored Lady Trenyon, her voice a melody as delicate as a dancer’s step, "was Lord Silex, in his bleakest hour, a man deserving of mercy, or merely a specter of his own making?"

And thus, the tale unfolded, a narrative as intricate as the web spun by a spider, as enigmatic as the whisper of the wind. Each syllable, a step further into the labyrinth of Lord Silex's life, where the lines between villain and victim blurred amidst the tapestry of human frailty and ambition.

Lord Silex, the epitome of a man whose past was as dark as the deepest abyss, whose future as uncertain as a vagabond's journey, stood at the crossroads of redemption, a figure as captivating as the moon beholds the stars.

"And so," mused Lady Trenyon, her eyes reflective pools of contemplation, "might not the very essence of Lord Silex's being be the embodiment of hope, concealed within the guise of villainy, waiting for the moment when truth shall unveil his hidden visage?"

As the embers of the fire danced in the hearth, Lady Trenyon’s mind was a canvas upon which the story of Lord Silex was painted anew, each stroke of her imagination bringing the figure of the infamous lord closer to a semblance of humanity, a being entwined with the very fabric of existence.

The days following our encounter on the frozen pond had passed with a strange tranquility. I found myself consumed by thoughts of Florence, her voice echoing in my mind with every turn of the page. I wrestled with conflicting emotions, torn between the rational understanding that I could never claim her affections and the inexplicable yearning that burned within.

"Henry," I confided one evening, seeking solace in the familiar presence of my friend. "I find myself in a quandary that none can comprehend but that which troubles my heart."

He regarded me with a mixture of curiosity and concern. "What troubles thee, old friend?"

"Florence...she has revealed to me a secret that has shaken the very foundations of my resolve."

Henry listened with an attentiveness that I had grown to appreciate over the months we'd spent together. When I finished, he sighed deeply, his eyes reflecting a contemplative gaze.

"Now I see," he said softly. "Yet, my dear Damon, know that Florence speaks highly of thee to me. Despite her own affections, she knows the depth of thy character."

Encouraged by his words, I pressed on, eager to unburden my troubled soul further. "And what of Ralph Buckstone, Henry? What have you seen in him that Florence, in her honest heart, has overlooked?"

Henry's expression darkened ever so slightly. "Ralph Buckstone is a man of ambition, no doubt, but his pursuit of success is marred by a reckless disregard for those around him. He dismisses the efforts of others with a cavalier indifference that Florence, with her keen heart, ought not to ignore."

His words, though delivered with restraint, struck a chord within me. It was as if a veil had been lifted, revealing the shadow that Ralph cast over their relationship.

Days turned to weeks, and the crisp air of winter gave way to the gentle embrace of spring. The town buzzed with life, as our scholarly pursuits resumed with fervor. Yet, amidst the bustling classrooms and lively discussions, my heart remained entwined in the delicate dance of unrequited love.

One afternoon, as I sat poring over tomes of literature, a knock came at my door. Florence stood before me, her cheeks flushed with the exertion of walking through the brisk breeze.

"Damon," she began hesitantly, "I hope you will not hold my previous words against me. I have been wrestling with my own conscience, and I must admit that your character has left an indelible impression upon me. Ralph and I...we are not suited, as I once believed."

Her confession took me by surprise, yet a sense of relief washed over me, delicate and serene.

"Florence," I replied, my voice steady despite the tumult of emotion, "I would not wish to burden you with my own longings. You have my word—our confidences shall remain as they were."

She smiled, a genuine warmth that seemed to brighten the very walls of my study. "Thank you, Damon. Your kindness is a beacon in these tumultuous times."

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the campus, I realized that my journey was far from over. The road ahead was uncertain, fraught with challenges and adversity. Yet, with Florence's newfound clarity and my steadfast resolve, I found a renewed sense of purpose.

The tale of "The Turning of Griggsby" was but a prelude to the adventures that lay ahead. Together with Florence, Henry, and our mutual friend Ralph Buckstone, we would navigate the complexities of love, ambition, and the fleeting nature of youth. And as I embarked on this grand voyage, unwavering in my determination, I carried with me the knowledge that true growth often lies within the labyrinth of the heart.

"Dear me!" said Van Bibber. He made a mental note to get a live one in the morning, and then he said: "That's very sad. But dead dolls do come to life."

The little girl looked up at him, and surveyed him intently and critically, and then smiled, with the dimples showing, as much as to say that she understood him and approved of him entirely. Van Bibber answered this sign language by taking Madeline's hand in his and asking her how she liked being a great actress, and how soon she would begin to storm because that photographer hadn't sent the proofs. The young woman understood this, and deigned to smile at it, but Madeline yawned a very polite and sleepy yawn, and closed her eyes. Van Bibber moved up closer, and she leaned over until her bare shoulder touched his arm, and while the woman buttoned on her absurdly small shoes, she let her curly head fall on his elbow and rest there. Any number of people had shown confidence in Van Bibber--not in that form exactly, but in the same spirit--and though he was used to being trusted, he felt a sharp thrill of pleasure at the touch of the child's head on his arm, and in the warm clasp of her fingers around his. And he was conscious of a keen sense of pity and sorrow for her rising in him, which he crushed by thinking that it was entirely wasted, and that the child was probably perfectly and ignorantly happy.

"Look at that, now," said the wardrobe woman, catching sight of the child's closed eyelids; "just look at the rest of the little dears, all that excited they can't stand still to get their hats on, and she just as unconcerned as you please, and after making the hit of the piece, too."

"She's not used to it, you see," said the young woman, knowingly; "she don't know what it means. It's just that much play to her."

This last was said with a questioning glance at Van Bibber, in whom she still feared to find the disguised agent of a Children's Aid Society. Van Bibber only nodded in reply, and did not answer her, because he found he could not very well, for he was looking a long way ahead at what the future was to bring to the confiding little being at his side, and of the evil knowledge and temptations that would mar the beauty of her quaintly sweet face, and its strange mark of gentleness and refinement. Outside he could bear his friend Lester shouting the refrain of his new topical song, and the laughter and the hand-clapping came in through the wings and open door, broken but tumultuous.

"Does she come of professional people?" Van Bibber asked, dropping into the vernacular. He spoke softly, not so much that he might not disturb the child, but that she might not understand what he said.

"Yes," the woman answered, shortly, and bent her head to smooth out the child's stage dress across her knees.

Van Bibber touched the little girl's head with his hand and found that she was asleep, and so let his hand rest there, with the curls between his fingers. "Ar–re you her mother?" he asked, with a slight inclination of his head. He felt quite confident she was not; at least, he hoped not.

The woman shook her head. "No," she said.

"Who is her mother?"

The woman looked at the sleeping child and then up at him almost defiantly. "Ida Clare was her mother," she said.

Van Bibber's protecting hand left the child as suddenly as though something had burned it, and he drew back so quickly that her head slipped from his arm, and she awoke and raised her eyes and looked up at him questioningly. He looked back at her with a glance of the strangest concern and of the deepest pity. Then he stooped and drew her towards him very tenderly, put her head back in the corner of his arm, and watched her in silence while she smiled drowsily and went to sleep again.

The moon had waned to a silver crescent, casting a faint light upon the prairie, which, in the stillness of the night, seemed to slumber beneath its gaze, like a dark and somnolent giant. My own eyelids had grown heavy, weighed down by the fatigue of the day's exploits, and I had sought a secluded spot near an arroyo, where I might rest awhile, and escape the din and turmoil of the encampment.

As I settled myself, I called out to Hibbets, that amiable and somnolent companion, now tasked with watching over our slumbering party. "Hibbets, Sleepy-head," I whispered, "keep thy wits about thee, good friend. The hour is dark, and the prairie a place of peril, even to the most wakeful of men."

But the soothing tones of my voice proved of little avail, for Hibbets, despite his sobriquet, was no sooner bedded down than he gave himself over to the allurements of Morpheus. I smiled to myself, for I knew that his slumber would be undisturbed by the direst of alarms, and that he would remain steadfast in his vigilance, when the urgency of the hour demanded it most.

And I, too, succumbed to the enticements of sleep, feeling the soft grasses of the prairie cradle my weary form, and the cool night air whisper sweet melodies in my ear. My eyelids drooped, my breathing grew slow, and I descended into the realm of dreams, where the cares and troubles of the world were lost in the endless vastness of the prairie.

But my repose was short-lived, for a strange and ominous noise rent the stillness of the night, a low, distant rumble, like the muttering of thunder on a summer's day. The ground beneath me seemed to tremble and shake, as if the very foundations of the earth were rent asunder. I sat up with a start, my heart racing, and my senses alert.

As I listened, the noise grew louder, and the trembling of the ground more pronounced. I could feel the earth itself vibrating beneath my feet, like the resonance of a harp string struck by an unseen hand. My mind was filled with a sense of foreboding, for I knew that such sounds were often portents of great danger, and that the prairie, in all its vast expanse, was a place of mystery and terror.

And then, in the distance, I saw it - a dark, seemingly endless mass, rapidly expanding and growing more distinct, like a living thing taking form and substance. My heart leapt with a thrill of alarm, for I knew that we were in the presence of something elemental and wild, a force beyond the control of human will.

In a single, hasty glance, I took in the chaotic scene before me. The herd, a vast and terrifying mass of buffalo, was racing towards us, their shaggy forms looming large, their eyes red-rimmed and blazing with a fierce, primitive light. The air was filled with the cries of the beasts, a deafening tumult that threatened to shake the very foundations of the earth.

My senses reeled, as I realized that our camp was directly in the path of the stampede. I sprang to my feet, my rifle grasping hand, my mind racing with the desperate need to escape the approaching danger. But time was short, and the herd drawing closer with every passing moment.

I turned to make a frantic appeal to Hibbets, now roused from his slumber by the commotion. But he, too, was paralyzed with fear, his eyes wide with a mixture of terror and confusion. I knew, in that instant, that we were lost, that our only hope lay in a swift and desperate bid for escape.

With a swift glance around me, I spotted a trail leading east, a narrow path through the scrub and the rocks, which might afford us some protection from the stampede. Without hesitation, I sprang towards it, my rifle at the ready, my heart pounding in my chest.

Hibbets, roused from his frozen state, joined me in a stumbling, panic-stricken dash. But we were too late, the herd already upon us, its fiery eyes blazing with a fierce and savage light. In a last, desperate bid for escape, I seized the shoulder of a massive bull, grasping its shaggy neck and hair in a fierce, cocked grip.

The world around me grew mad, a whirlwind of hooves, horns, and dust, a chaos of sound and fury that threatened to consume us all. I closed my eyes, bracing myself for the worst, as the buffalo beneath me bucked and twisted, its powerful muscles straining against my grasp. And in that instant, I knew that our fate, and the fate of our party, hung precariously in the balance.

It was a morning of unlooked-for felicity. The warm sun, shining brightly in a sky of the purest azure, cast its golden rays upon the happy faces of the inmates of Cleeve. The anxiety which had, of late, beset the countenance of Mrs. Cusworth, had, to Salome's delighted observation, materially lessened; her eyes, those bright and expressive orbs, sparkled with a renewed luster, and her step, though still slightly languid, betokened a growing strength. It was a day that well nigh seemed to justify the oft-repeated augury of a kindly fate.

As Salome descended to the morning room, her eyes met those of her mother, and a tender smile rewarded her. "Mama, you are looking better, I do declare!" she exclaimed, her voice, like the gentle music of a silver brook, flowing with joy and relief. Mrs. Cusworth's countenance flushed with pleased gratification, and she extended her hand, which Salome, with expressions of affection, took and pressed against her cheek. It was a tender moment, a moment pregnant with sweet and tender feeling, and Salome felt her heart overflowing with love and tenderness for this dear, delicate, and suffering mother of hers.

In this happy frame of mind, Salome refrained from communicating the singular circumstance which had occurred during the previous night. She knew that an unnecessary alarm might prove hurtful to her mother, and so, she wisely suppressed the knowledge of the mysterious nocturnal visitor, to whose footsteps she had been witness. A fleeting thought, however, crossed her mind, a thought which she was at no loss to interpret. She suspected that the careless neglect of one of the domestics had led to the open door, and that the midnight prowler, with feet so silent as a ghost, had availed himself of the opportunity thus offered.

Her suspicions, however, were not directed towards any one in particular, and she could not bring herself to accuse any of the household servants. She had indeed some reason to believe that the maid, Emily, who was responsible for locking the doors and windows, might have overlooked her duty in some measure, though she flatly denied any such negligence, with a vehemence that seemed almost ill-concealed. Salome, however, was not convinced by the maid's assertion, and her thoughts were busy with a plan of investigation which, she hoped, would elicit the truth, and bring the careless culprit to a sense of shame.

She therefore decided upon a course of action, one which would render it impossible for the miscreant to escape detection. The walls surrounding the garden were high and substantial, and the short side of the enclosure was divided into separate sections by a low palisade, with a convenient gate in the centre. Salome thought of placing one of her brother's traps near this gate, which, when sprung, would leave no doubt as to the escape route taken by the midnight visitor. But, alas! in her haste to effect this end, she overlooked the importance of securing the other side, the long side, where a bough of the ancient casement tree, a tree of gnarled and twisted limbs, stretched far and near, forming a useful ladder to the top of the wall, and thus a secret passage for escape. This grave oversight did not escape her thoughts, though, for a short time, she was not aware of the extent of the consequences that might ensue.

Her mother's improvement served as a timely distraction, a gentle breeze that swept away the clouds of anxiety, and, as they sat together in the morning room, Mrs. Cusworth, with an air of quiet satisfaction, announced that a change, a pleasing and unexpected change, had occurred in their fortunes. A legacy, received from a distant relative, which had been assumed to be of a trifling nature, turned out to be of considerable value, a sum sufficient to render any financial uncertainty quite impossible. "We shall not, dear Salome," she said with a gentle smile, "be compelled to leave Cleeve after all. The idea of moving to Redstone is, therefore, quite abandoned. We shall remain here, and I have determined to devote myself to the pleasures of our quiet country life."

Salome's countenance remained unaltered, though her inward amazement at her mother's decision was not to be gainsaid. She had taken measures for securing lodgings at Redstone, and was already satisfied that the prospect of that quiet, rural life, far removed from the bustling world, would be a charm to them both. "But, dear mother," she said, after a moment's consideration, "what is the reason for this change of purpose? I had, as you know, already secured lodgings at Redstone, and I was beginning to feel that the transition would be a welcome one."

He knew that it must be done sooner or later, and to-day was best, for his heart could be no sorer.... Yes, here they were, the ungiven gifts.
