When you are a young housekeeper with infants and only a nurse-maid besides the cook, a day’s company means the revolutionizing of the entire domestic machinery. In the city people carelessly come and go, and the household of the entertainer is put to no special preparation for them, but it is an unwritten law in the country that before the advent of the seldom guest “to spend the day” the entire domicile must be swept and garnished from top to bottom.

As Ethel Waring rubbed and polished and dusted she could but remember that she had gone through the process of cleaning three times before for Henry’s mother, who had always hitherto disappointed her. She prided herself on being really fond of her mother-in-law, and his sister Nan had been her particular friend, but Aunt Eliza and Mary Appleton were the kind of people—well, the kind of people that belonged to her husband’s family, and they always saw everything around the house. She cleaned now for the fourth time magnanimously. Since she had moved into the country, and went to and from the city two or three times a week, it had seemed odd to have her friends and relatives look upon the half-hour’s journey in train and ferry-boat as a mighty undertaking, to be planned for weeks ahead; and although she had been in her cottage over a year, she had not yet become used to this point of view, and still expected people to come after they had promised to.

There was something grimly sacrificial in her preparations now that upheld her in her disappointment; her husband could not remember her pleasure, but she was working her fingers off for his people. Yes, she had nothing to look forward to but neglect—and the worst of it was that he would not even know that he was neglecting her.

Perhaps, however, he did remember after all. She watched every word and gesture of his up to the very morning of their anniversary. He was so happy and merry and affectionate in his efforts to win her to smiles that she could hardly withstand the infectiousness of it. But she felt after his cheerful good-by as if the tragedy of her future years had begun.

There was, indeed, no time for the luxury of quiet wretchedness. The two children had to be bathed and put to bed for the morning nap, which both she and Beesy prayed might be a long one, so that the last clearing up might be done, and the table set, and the salad-dressing made, and the cream whipped for the jelly, and she herself dressed and in the drawing-room before twelve o’clock.

There was the usual panic when the butcher was late with the chickens, and the discovery was made that the green grocer had not brought what was ordered, and the usual hurried sending forth of Beesy to the village at the last moment for the missing lettuce, only to be told that “there was none in town this day”—a fact that smites the suburban housekeeper like a blow. But finally everything was ready, the table set to perfection, the drawing-room curtains drawn at their most effective angle, the logs burning on the andirons, the chairs set most cozily, and the vase of jonquils with their long, green stalks showing through the clear glass, giving a lovely brightness to the room in their hint of approaching spring. The babies, sweet and fresh, in the whitest of frocks, and hair curled in little damp rings, ran up and down and prattled beside the charmingly dressed, pretty mother, who sat with her embroidery in hand and who could not help feeling somewhat of a glow of satisfaction through her sadness. But after Harry had peeped out from the curtains some twenty times to see if grandmamma was coming, and little Marjorie had fallen down and raised a large bump on her forehead, and the one-o’clock train had come in, there was a certain change in the situation. The cook sent up word should she put on the oysters, and Mrs. Waring answered no, to wait until the next train, although that did not arrive until two o’clock. She pretended that her guests had missed the earlier train, but in her soul she felt the cold chill of certainty that they would not come.

Six months from the point at which we left our story, a party of gentlemen, who on their way to the Highland Moors, had stopped in Edinburgh for the night, strolled together in the public gardens of the place.

They found little company there besides children and nurse-maids at that time, so that a young lady of quiet, but distinguished appearance, who came towards them and turned down one of the shady walks, with a group of little companions followed by their attendant, more particularly attracted the attention of the strangers.

"What a remarkably pretty, lady-like looking girl, that is; how well she walks," said one.

"So Trevor seems to think," said another, for their friend had lingered behind, and now stood apparently half irresolute, looking in the direction where the young lady had disappeared.

"Come on, don't let us be in his way," and then laughing, they pursued their walk.

Trevor seemed not disinclined to profit by their consideration--he hesitated no longer, but disappeared at once within the shaded path.

Need we say, whose footsteps he followed--or whose the startled countenance, which turned towards him, when having reached the spot where the object of his pursuit had arrived, he in a low tone pronounced the name of "Mary," or how in an opposite direction to that taken by the nurse and children, they were soon walking on slowly, side by side, together.

"But Eugene, is not this wrong?" Mary said, after the first tearful joy of this most unexpected meeting had a little subsided, and her heart rather sunk, to find by her lover's hasty explanation, that no new turn of events, touching favourably on their mutual happiness, had brought him to her side. "Is not this wrong after the agreement we had made?"

"What Mary!" with tender reproach, "are you so little glad to see me as thus to speak? However, as you are so much more scrupulous than affectionate, I am not afraid to tell you that I had not counted upon this pleasure, though I did not think myself bound quite to avoid the place which contained you; but when, by mere accident, I saw you a few yards distant, I think not the most punctilious of your friends, would expect it to be in the nature of man, to look after you and turn coolly the other way."

Mary smiled upon him, as if she needed no other excuse.

"How well you look, Mary!" Eugene continued, gazing on the countenance of his companion, lit up, as it was, by the glow of animated pleasure, "happier, better, than when I saw you last--too well, I am almost tempted to think, and too happy, considering the circumstances of our case. I--you must allow, look far less so."

Mary gazed with tender anxiety into her lover's face. Was she then really to suppose that the change she remarked upon his handsome countenance, since the happy Silverton days, was caused by his love for her?

The haggard cheek--the restless, unhealthful fire which burnt in those dark eyes! A thrill of womanly pleasure was mixed with the tender pain the idea inspired.

"You certainly do not look as well as when at Silverton," she answered with a gentle sigh, as the many associations those words conjured up, rose before her; "but your expedition to the Moors will do you so much good. If you have been in London all this time, I do not wonder at your feeling ill. As for my looks," she added, "no doubt at this moment they are bright and happy--you must not judge of them in general from their appearance now, not that I mean to say I am not happier, and perhaps therefore looking better than when you saw me last--for then--all was doubt, and dread, and uncertainty, and I was very miserable--but now since all that was removed, I have been happy--yes, truly happy in comparison; though at times I fear I am inclined to be sad and impatient-hearted. I was spoilt at first by too much unalloyed happiness, and it is hard to resign oneself to the long and unbroken separation, I had thought ours must be, but there is the happy prospect at the end--and this year, long and weary as it may seem--must pass away like any other."

"Come, Barbara, sit beside me under this ancient oak, and listen well," said Deta softly, though a tremor of earnestness lay in her tone. "For it is time I divulge that which we have long concealed in secret. The man whom you know as the Alm-Uncle, though oft spoken of in fearful whispers, bears a past of triumph and lament we dare not speak aloud elsewhere."

Barbara leaned forward, her eyes aglow with a mixture of curiosity and apprehension. "Tell me, dear Deta, what is it that ties our kin to this solitary soul? My mind conjures images of a man shrouded in disgrace and haunted by harsh retribution, yet I sense that there is more hidden beneath the villagers’ tales."

Deta nodded, her gaze drifting momentarily to the distant mountains. "Long ago, he was a man of great fortune, bestowed with a vast and verdant farm that flourished under his care. However, pride and folly ensnared him. He sought solace in goblets of wine and the lure of gambling rather than in the honest sweat of his brow. In that pursuit, he lost not only his wealth, but also the affections of his kin, who found his ways intolerable and forsook him."

As a cool breeze swept over the hillside, Barbara interjected with gentle urgency, "But what of his duty now? How is it that he bears responsibility for the care of the child? I had thought his heart hardened by bitter regrets, his soul closed against the world. How does he come to safeguard the well-being of another?"

A faint, sardonic smile touched Deta's lips. "Ah, dear Barbara, it is not merely duty that binds him to that little one. An unspoken bond—a remnant of unacknowledged kinship—ties us all together. Though the path he trod led him astray, circumstances now demand he subsume his past misdeeds beneath a mantle of care. His apparent severity belies a tenderness reserved for those who depend upon him, a truth overlooked by quick judgments."

Just then, Deta’s gaze shifted, and she noted the goatherd Peter guiding the child within a safe range of the hillside. "See there," she whispered, "where young Peter wheels the child to the pasture? Thus does providence allow me to recount these matters without fear that our innocent charge may be led into the entanglements of our lore."

Barbara folded her hands, her countenance reflecting concern intermingled with wonder. "Yet, Deta, a secret such as this weighs heavy upon my conscience. How might I, a simple listener, bear such a truth without tarnishing the love I hold for this child and for the land that nurtures our spirits?"

"Promise me, then, that you shall hold this confession as sacred as your heart's own desires," Deta answered, her voice rising in a tone both firm and imploring. "Let not the idle prattle of the village or the prejudices of the unknowing contaminate our shared past. The Alm-Uncle, though barred from our commonplace discourse, remains a man ensnared by fate. While his fortunes crumbled in a haze of iniquity, a spark of redemption yet flickers within him, a spark that now guides his every act towards earning forgiveness."

Barbara’s eyes glistened with those unspoken secrets of sorrow and hope. "I pledge, dear Deta, that I shall keep your words within my bosom, as one carries a cherished relic from a bygone age. For though the tale be marred by missteps of the past, I sense the promise of eventual atonement—an unfolding drama written by destiny itself."

Deta’s countenance softened with relief and resolve as she resumed her narrative. "Upon losing all that was dear to him, the Alm-Uncle withdrew into isolation upon a solitary peak, far from the bustling hamlets below. In this silent refuge, amid the echoing whispers of winds and the gentle murmur of the valley, he began to rebuild not his fortune, but his honor. No longer shall the remnants of his past transgressions dictate his future, for each day he labors in quiet penitence."

Thus, as the dusk deepened into the serene embrace of twilight, the two friends remained vested in a covenant of trust. Deta’s confession, imbued with both regret and hope, mingled with the rustling of mountain leaves. And while distant echoes of the village tales persisted, there now shone a fragile light of understanding—a light that promised to guide not only the solitary Alm-Uncle in his journey towards redemption but also those who, like Barbara and Deta, dared to see beyond the veil of scandal into the heart of human fallibility.

The winter winds swept through the village, carrying with it a chill that seeped into the bones of those who dared to venture outside. But within the cozy confines of Anthony Croft's workshop, there was a warmth that emanated from the crackling fireplace and the passion that burned within the young man's heart. As he stood before his workbench, surrounded by tools and scraps of wood, he felt a sense of purpose unlike any he had ever known.

The ancient maple wood from the Bean Maple at Pleasant Point lay before him, its rich history and potential for greatness beckoning him to bring it to life once more. With a steady hand and a keen eye, Anthony began the meticulous process of crafting a new violin, each stroke of his blade guided by a deep reverence for the craft and the legacy of the instrument makers who had come before him.

As the days turned into weeks, Anthony's workshop became a sanctuary of sound and creativity, the melodious notes of his violin filling the air with a haunting beauty that seemed to transcend time itself. The villagers who passed by would pause to listen, their hearts stirred by the soulful music that poured forth from the humble abode of the young artisan.

But amidst the harmony that echoed through the village, there were whispers of doubt and skepticism that lingered in the air like a discordant note in an otherwise perfect melody. Some questioned Anthony's choice to pursue a path so unconventional, while others simply could not understand the depth of his commitment to the craft. Yet, despite the naysayers and skeptics, Anthony remained steadfast in his determination to follow his passion and fulfill his destiny as a master violin maker.

As the final touches were put in place and the last strings were strung, Anthony knew that his creation was more than just a violin – it was a testament to his unwavering faith in the power of music to move the soul and transform lives. With a sense of fulfillment that transcended words, he lifted the instrument to his chin, closed his eyes, and began to play.

The music that flowed forth was like nothing the villagers had ever heard before – a symphony of emotion and artistry that spoke to the very core of their beings. It was as if the ancient maple wood had infused the notes with a magic that could only be felt, not explained. And as Anthony's bow danced across the strings, weaving a tapestry of sound that seemed to touch the very heavens, the villagers knew that they were witnessing something truly extraordinary.

Ah, Bohemia! Where the spirit of romance dances amidst the shadows of indifference and want. Here, in this land that is as elusive as a dream, we behold the visage of our heroes—the artists, the dreamers, souls who would rather roam the realms of imagination than tread the mundane paths of necessity. Yet, for all their fiery hearts and restless souls, these bohemians are often destined to fade into the silent annals of history, their names whispered only in the murmurs of forgotten tales.

Stoicism, you say? A mockery it is, when faced with the stark reality of a world that offers neither charity nor understanding to those who have dedicated their existence to the ethereal pursuit of art. You see, dear observer of the human condition, these beings are not spared by our common sense—it only feeds their fire, urging them to rise against the iron chains of practicality. To them, the promise of a five-franc piece is but a fleeting shadow, while the notion of ready-made, shiny boots descending from the heavens is a cruel jest.

Our bohemians reject the tradecraft of survival, for to them, it would be sacrilege against the altar of their souls. They stand, a collective testament to the paradox of existence, balancing precariously between the rapture of creation and the yawning abyss of destitution. Pride swells in their chests, a fortress against the siren calls of compromise, a shield that ultimately becomes their downfall.

War, some call it, this ceaseless battle for recognition and sustenance. But it is a war where triumph is elusive, and victory a distant dream. The leaders bask in fleeting fame, their names echoing through grand halls, while the true soldiers of the battlefield, the artists who labor in obscurity, vanish into the mists of time, leaving naught but echoes of their genius.

And yet, new stars are born from the ashes of the old. There exists a romanticism, a scandalous allure to the notion of suffering for art—a myth woven from the tales of past poets and artists who, like martyrs, offered their lives in exchange for immortality. This myth, this romantic masquerade, draws forth fresh legions to the cause, eager to write their own legends amidst the squalor and splendor of Bohemia.

Indeed, our earth is a cruel stage, where the finest actors are often doomed to the darkest corners, their performances unappreciated by the lukewarm audience that prefers the warmth of the mainstream. And so, here we stand, in the ever-dimming twilight of Bohemia, a witness to the perpetual duel between aspiration and despair, where every glance at the horizon is a prayer for a softer world, a world that understands and cherishes the unfathomable contributions of art.

Yet, let us not forsake hope entirely. For within the very walls that confine these artists, there exists a silent camaraderie, a shared understanding that binds them together in their solitude. They are legion, these souls of Bohemia, a brotherhood of dreamers who, despite the odds, continue to pen their verses and paint their visions, ever striving to leave a mark upon the indifferent canvas of time.

So, let us raise a silent toast to them—to these valiant spirits who dare to live beyond the reach of comfort, whose hearts are the truest of all, for they beat for ideals that transcend the material. And as we watch them tread this perilous path, let us remember that in the end, it is not the triumph over adversity that defines them, but their unwavering dedication to the fire within—a fire that shall continue to flicker, casting long shadows across the annals of history, until the final curtain falls upon this earthly stage.

In the chamber above lay the pale, almost pulseless form of Edith. A young girl, who had been as her sister for many years, sat holding her thin white hand. The face of the invalid was turned to the wall. Her eyes were closed; and she breathed so quietly that the motions of respiration could hardly be seen. Nearly ten minutes had elapsed from the time a servant whispered to the aunt that there was some one in the parlor, when Edith turned, and said to her companion, in a low, calm voice--

"Mr. Florence has come."

The girl started, and a flush of surprise went over her face.

"He is in the parlor now. Won't you ask him to come up?" added the dying maiden, still speaking with the utmost composure.

Her friend stood surprised and hesitating for some moments, and then turning away, glided from the chamber. She found the aunt and Mr. Florence in the passage below, the latter pleading with the former for the privilege of seeing Edith, which was resolutely denied.

"Edith wants to see Mr. Florence," said the girl, as she joined them.

"Who told her that he was here?" quickly asked the aunt.

"No one. I did not know it myself."

"Her heart told her that I was here," exclaimed Mr. Florence--and, as he spoke, he glided past the aunt, and, with hurried steps, ascended to the chamber where the dying one lay. The eyes of Edith were turned towards the door as he entered; but no sign of emotion passed over her countenance. Overcome by his feelings, at the sight of the shadowy remnant of one so loved and so wronged, the young man sunk into a chair by her side, as nerveless as a child; and, as his lips were pressed upon her lips and cheeks, her face was wet with his tears.

Coming in quickly after, the aunt took firmly hold of his arm and sought to draw him away, but, in a steady voice, the invalid said--

"No--no. I was waiting for him. I have expected him for days. I knew he would come; and he is here now."

All was silence for many minutes; and during this time Edwin Florence sat with his face covered, struggling to command his feelings. At a motion from the dying girl, the aunt and friend retired, and she was alone with the lover who had been false to his vows. As the door closed behind them, Edwin looked up. He had grown calm. With a voice of inexpressible tenderness, he said--

"Live for me, Edith."

"Not here," was answered. "The silver chord will soon be loosened and the golden bowl broken."

"Oh, say not that! Let me call you back to life. Turn to me again as I have turned to you with my whole heart. The world is still beautiful; and in it we will be happy together."

"No, Edwin," replied the dying maiden. "The history of my days here is written, and the angel is about sealing the record. I am going where the heart will never feel the touch of sorrow. I wished to see you once more before I died; and you are here. I have, once more, felt your breath upon my cheek; once more held your hand in mine. For this my heart is grateful. You had become the sun of my life, and when your face was turned away, the flower that spread itself joyfully in the light, drooped and faded. And now, the light has come back again; but it cannot warm into freshness and beauty the withered blossom."

In the dim glow of a retiring sun, I find myself seated in this humble chamber, the walls of which bear the faint stains of past endeavour and the fainter marks of failure. My thoughts, like the shadows cast by the waning light, stretch long and contemplative, tracing the labyrinth of experiences that have led me to this pass. It is not without a certain degree of melancholic reflection that I consider the events that have unfolded since our last interaction—events that, though fraught with disappointment, have yet yielded a harvest of wisdom, however bitter the taste.

For, as I have come to understand in the fullness of time, there is a certain art to advertising that transcends the mere act of informing. It is a craft that demands ingenuity, a touch of panache, and an ability to foresee the whims of a fickle public. In days of yore, it sufficed to erect a plain board or distribute a printed pamphlet, but now the world moves with a swifter foot, and the advertiser must needs keep pace. It is not enough to declare the arrival of a shipment of goods; one must conjure a narrative, a spectacle, a reason for the public to pause and take notice. That is the essence of the trade, and it is a lesson I have learned at some cost.

But let me not weary you with mere pontificating, for there is a story to be told, and it is a story of trials and triumphs, of error and enlightenment. Let us journey back to the days when I first sought to apply my principles to the practical world of commerce, when I partnered with a man whose name is now a byword for obstinacy, and another whose vanity was as vast as the ocean itself. Together, we embarked upon a venture that was doomed from its inception, not because of any lack of effort on my part, but because of the blind obstinacy of one and the preening conceit of the other.

Mr. Thomas Brown, of whom I speak, was a man of no mean repute in the circles of finance, though his reputation was built upon a foundation of greed rather than judgment. He was a man who believed that success was a matter of capital alone, that with enough coin one could command the world. It was this belief that led him to reject my more imaginative suggestions, to scoff at the notion of innovation, and to insist upon the old, tried-and-true methods that had served him well in his earlier days. “Advertising,” he would say, with a tone of authority that bespoke his limited understanding, “is a matter of repetition. You print your message, and you print it again, and again, until the public takes notice.” To this, I could only shake my head and wonder at the narrowness of his vision.

And then there was Mr. Samuel Jones, a man of prodigious vanity and little else. Where Mr. Brown was all business, Mr. Jones was all_self-importance, a man who believed that his mere presence in a room was sufficient to elevate the spirits of all who were present. He was a dandy, a man who prided himself on his appearance, his wit, and his ability to charm the most recalcitrant of souls. It was this last quality that had initially recommended him to me, for I believed that charm could be a powerful tool in the world of commerce. However, I soon discovered that his charm was the weapon of a man who cared little for the substance of a matter, who preferred flattery to facts, and whose vanity was such that he could not abide the notion of learning from others.

Thus, our partnership was a curious blend of avarice and arrogance, of Mr. Brown’s narrow-mindedness and Mr. Jones’s insufferable self-regard. It was a combination that was as combustible as gunpowder, and it was not long before the sparks began to fly. I, for my part, sought to guide the enterprise with a steady hand, to introduce new ideas, to break free from the stifling constraints of tradition, and to embrace the possibilities that modern advertising offered. But my efforts were met with resistance at every turn, with Mr. Brown dismissing my suggestions as “fancy notions” and Mr. Jones deriding them as “unnecessary frills.”

And so, the business floundered, its progress hampered by the very same forces that had been its foundation. There were moments when I despaired, when I questioned my own judgment, when I wondered if my faith in innovation was misplaced. But then, in the quiet of the night, I would return to my thoughts, to my principles, and I would remind myself that failure is but a stepping-stone to success, that every misstep is a lesson in disguise.

Now, as I sit here in this dimly lit room, I find myself filled with a renewed sense of purpose, a determination to see my ideas realized, to prove that creativity and innovation are not mere whimsies but the very lifeblood of commerce. I have learned much in my time, and I am resolved to apply that knowledge with a fresh perspective, to build anew, to rise from the ashes of defeat and fashion a future that is both brighter and more prosperous.

Even the later citizens in Atherly felt an equal resentment against her, but from different motives. That her drinking habits and her powerful vocabulary were all the effect of her aristocratic alliance they never doubted. And, although it brought the virtues of their own superior republican sobriety into greater contrast, they felt a scandal at having been tricked into attending this gilded funeral of dissipated rank. Peter Atherly found himself unpopular in his own town. The sober who drank from his free “Waterworks,” and the giddy ones who imbibed at his “Gin Mill,” equally criticised him. He could not understand it; his peculiar predilections had been accepted before, when they were mere presumptions; why should they not NOW, when they were admitted facts? He was conscious of no change in himself since the funeral! Yet the criticism went on. Presently it took the milder but more contagious form of ridicule. In his own hotel, built with his own money, and in his own presence, he had heard a reckless frequenter of the bar-room decline some proffered refreshment on the ground that “he only drank with his titled relatives.” A local humorist, amidst the applause of an admiring crowd at the post-office window, had openly accused the postmaster of withholding letters to him from his only surviving brother, “the Dook of Doncherknow.” “The ole dooky never onct missed the mail to let me know wot's goin' on in me childhood's home,” remarked the humorist plaintively; “and yer's this dod-blasted gov'ment mule of a postmaster keepin' me letters back!” Letters with pretentious and gilded coats of arms, taken from the decorated inner lining of cigar-boxes, were posted to prominent citizens. The neighboring and unregenerated settlement of Red Dog was more outrageous in its contribution. The Red Dog “Sentinel,” in commenting on the death of “Haulbowline Tom,” a drunken English man-o'-war's man, said: “It may not be generally known that our regretted fellow citizen, while serving on H. M. S. Boxer, was secretly married to Queen Kikalu of the Friendly Group; but, unlike some of our prosperous neighbors, he never boasted of his royal alliance, and resisted with steady British pluck any invitation to share the throne. Indeed, any allusion to the subject affected him deeply. There are those among us who will remember the beautiful portrait of his royal bride tattooed upon his left arm with the royal crest and the crossed flags of the two nations.” Only Peter Atherly and his sister understood the sting inflicted either by accident or design in the latter sentence. Both he and his sister had some singular hieroglyphic branded on their arms,--probably a reminiscence of their life on the plains in their infant Indian captivity. But there was no mistaking the general sentiment. The criticisms of a small town may become inevasible. Atherly determined to take the first opportunity to leave Rough and Ready. He was rich; his property was secure; there was no reason why he should stay where his family pretensions were a drawback. And a further circumstance determined his resolution.

He was awaiting his sister in his new house on a little crest above the town. She had been at the time of her mother's death, and since, a private boarder in the Sacred Heart Convent at Santa Clara, whence she had been summoned to the funeral, but had returned the next day. Few people had noticed in her brother's carriage the veiled figure which might have belonged to one of the religious orders; still less did they remember the dark, lank, heavy-browed girl who had sometimes been seen about Rough and Ready. For she had her brother's melancholy, and greater reticence, and had continued of her own free will, long after her girlish pupilage at the convent, to live secluded under its maternal roof without taking orders. A general suspicion that she was either a religious “crank,” or considered herself too good to live in a mountain mining town, had not contributed to her brother's popularity. In her abstraction from worldly ambitions she had, naturally, taken no part in her brother's family pretensions. He had given her an independent allowance, and she was supposed to be equally a sharer in his good fortune. Yet she had suddenly declared her intention of returning to Atherly, to consult him on affairs of importance. Peter was both surprised and eager; there was but little affection between them, but, preoccupied with his one idea, he was satisfied that she wanted to talk about the family.

From a nail in the closet Tom took down a pair of old wooden-framed skates, on which, however, he could beat many who were provided with club-skates of the most approved styles.

A walk of a quarter of a mile brought the boys to Round Pond, which was situated near the center of the village. It was small, not more than three-quarters of a mile in circumference; but it was frozen clear as glass, and looked tempting to the young skaters as they descended the bank, and sat down by the margin to put on their skates.

Many boys and a few girls were already on the ice. When Tom and Harry arrived some of them came to greet the new-comers. It was evident that both were general favorites.

Among the boys who came up was Rupert Simpson.

“What made you so late, Harry?” he asked, impatiently.

“I called for Tom, and he had some wood to saw and split before he could come.”

“I suppose you helped him,” suggested Rupert, with a sneer.

“I did.”

Rupert looked astonished and disgusted.

“I didn’t know you hired out to saw and split wood,” he said, with another sneer.

“Now you do know it, I suppose you will cut my acquaintance,” said Harry, pleasantly.

“I suppose you have a right to suit yourself. You wouldn’t catch me sawing and splitting wood. We leave that to the servants.”

“You couldn’t give me a job, could you? However, it would be of no use. I only work for Tom.”

Rupert shrugged his shoulders, and his attention was drawn to Tom’s old skates.

“Those skates look as if they dated back to the ark,” said he, rudely.

“I don’t think they are quite so old as that,” returned Tom, coolly.

“They are a curiosity, anyway.”

“They can do good service, Rupert, that is, when Tom wears them,” said Harry. “In spite of our fine club-skates, I believe we should find it hard work to keep up with him.”

“Speak for yourself!” said Rupert, haughtily.

“No, I speak for you, too.”

“Try it! A race! a race!” exclaimed the boys in chorus.

“I will race with Harry,” said Rupert, hastily.

“No; you can beat me; I admit that in advance. Race with Tom.”

Tom said nothing. By this time his skates were on, and he was quite ready to enter upon a trial of speed with Rupert, or any boy on the pond; but he did not care to betray any anxiety on the subject.

Rupert was rather conceited on the subject of his skating. With the exception of Tom Thatcher, he was probably the best skater in the village--that is, among the boys--and felt pretty confident that he could beat Tom himself. His reluctance was due only to his not liking to place himself on an equality with the boy who pegged shoes for his father at fifty cents per day. The clamor of the boys, however, and the anticipation of a triumph over his rival overruled his objections, and he said:

"Yes," said Mrs. Sandford, "it's quite likely we shall have a rainy day to-morrow, and, when it once begins, I shouldn't wonder if we had two or three days of it, after such a dry time!"

"Well, we won't believe anything quite so dreadful just now," said Kate. "We'll go to sleep now, and hope for the best."

Mrs. Sandford was somewhat triumphant in the justification of her weather wisdom, when they heard, next morning, the sound of the rain pattering down on the veranda without. The morning did, indeed, look gray, dull, unpromising, as even a July day can sometimes look. May was rather mournful over the loss of the light and color, and the general change that had come over the landscape. But Kate persisted in her optimistic declaration that she believed it would soon clear up, and then everything would be even more lovely than before. Meantime they would have the chance of seeing how the Falls looked in bad weather!

And, indeed, they were by no means without beauty, even now. The purity of the central green was gone, but the soft gray tones melting away into gray mist, under a gray sky, gave the effect of a sketch rather than a finished picture, with suggestions of sublimity far beyond the visible.

As they wistfully scanned the sky after breakfast, watching for a promising gleam of blue, Kate proposed a programme to be carried out as soon as it should clear.

"You see it will be too wet for much walking and scrambling about, which would never do for Hugh, at any rate. Now, let us order a carriage and take a nice leisurely drive all about the country. We've seen the Falls pretty well now, and we can do the battle-grounds--Lundy's Lane and Queenston Heights, and take the Whirlpool on the way."

"Well, we'll see," said Mrs. Sandford resignedly, "if it does clear." So she settled down to her knitting. Hugh Macnab sat scribbling in his note-book; Flora amused herself at the piano, and May hovered about the veranda, still enthralled by the spell of the "Thunder of Waters," even in a washed-out sketch, as Kate styled it. But by and by, a warm, soft gleam stole through the mist-laden atmosphere, small patches of blue sky appeared, and, in a very short time, the color had, as if by magic, come back to the scene; the foliage stood out greener than before, and the emerald once more gemmed the center of the Horse-shoe Falls, though somewhat less than it had previously appeared.

The carriage was quickly summoned, and they were soon rolling smoothly along the road that led away from the river, through the quiet little village of Drummondville--back to Lundy's Lane.

"You see we are really beginning at the end," said Kate. "Lundy's Lane came at the close of the war, in 1814, and it began in October, 1812, at Queenston Heights, which we are going to see this afternoon. For, you see, the American troops kept harassing this border for a couple of years."

"Just as your English forefathers used to harass my Scotch ones long ago," said Hugh.

"Oh, and I suppose the Scotch never did likewise! Indeed, I rather think they were a good deal the worst," laughed Kate. "But, at any rate, this sort of thing had been going on for nearly two years, keeping the poor people in a state of constant dread, and I think Sir Gordon Drummond and his sixteen hundred men, part of them British troops and part Canadian volunteers, must have been pretty tired of it. He made up his mind, however, that, come what might, he wouldn't retire before even five thousand Americans. That hill there was where he stationed his troops, and, as the guidebook says, they stayed there, though the Americans did their best to drive them off. At last they tired out the American general, who fell off with his defeated army to their camp, away up there beyond Chippewa--in the direction we walked the first afternoon--and I believe they never halted till they got back to Fort Erie, from whence they had come."

"Oh ... tut!" said Doddie.

Van Oudijck appeared on the threshold of his office, which always had the door open, but which was separated from the inner gallery by a large screen:

"Doddie!" he called out.

"Yes, papa?"

"Will you see that there are flowers in mamma's room to-morrow?"

"Very well, papa ... I'll see to it."

Van Oudijck became red and angry:

Next morning Theo went in the landau to fetch his step-mother from the station at half-past eleven.

"Remarkable, truly remarkable," the Vicar murmured to himself, fidgeting with the brass buttons of his waistcoat. "Never in all my years, never in all my wildest imaginings..." His voice trailed off, lost in the enormity of the situation. He was, after all, having a conversation with an Angel, a celestial being whose very existence had been relegated to the realm of sermons and Sunday hymns.

The Angel, propped against the ancient oak tree, regarded the Vicar with a mixture of curiosity and amusement. The pain in his wings, a searing, throbbing agony, was beginning to subside, replaced by a dull ache that pulsed in time with his ethereal heartbeat. He had never experienced pain before, not like this. It was, he decided, most unpleasant.

"Is this 'pain,' as you call it, common to all of your kind?" the Angel inquired, his voice a melodious chime that seemed to resonate with the rustling leaves overhead.

"Indeed," the Vicar replied, adjusting his spectacles and peering at the Angel with an air of scholarly interest. "Pain, my dear fellow, is an unfortunate but integral part of the human condition. It is, one might say, the price we pay for our mortal existence."

The Angel tilted his head, processing this new information. The concept of mortality was another strange and unsettling notion. In the Land of Dreams, from whence he hailed, life was a perpetual tapestry of ever-shifting colors and sounds, a symphony of existence without beginning or end.

"And what of these 'humans'?" the Angel asked, gesturing towards the distant village with a flick of his uninjured wing. "They are but figments, are they not? Whimsical creations of our angelic artists, given form and movement in this wondrous dreamscape?"

The Vicar, a man of profound faith and unwavering belief in the tangible world, found himself struggling to reconcile his understanding of reality with the Angel's ethereal perspective. He cleared his throat, adjusting his clerical collar as if it were a lifeline to normalcy.

"My dear Angel," the Vicar began, choosing his words with the utmost care. "I assure you, these humans are as real as you and I. They are not figments of imagination, but flesh and blood creatures with their own hopes, dreams, and, yes, even pains."

The Angel, however, remained unconvinced. He surveyed the world around him with an air of detached wonder. The vibrant hues of the wildflowers, the gentle swaying of the trees, the very air itself, all seemed imbued with a dreamlike quality. To his celestial senses, it was all so very... unreal.

"But look around you!" the Angel exclaimed, his voice echoing with a hint of amusement. "The very trees whisper secrets to the wind, the clouds dance like celestial ballerinas, and the sun, that glorious orb, paints the sky with strokes of pure artistry. Surely, this must be a realm of dreams, a masterpiece crafted by the divine hands of our celestial brethren."

The Vicar, his patience wearing thin, sighed deeply. How, he wondered, could he possibly convince this celestial being of the reality of the human world when the Angel himself seemed so utterly convinced of its illusory nature? It was, the Vicar mused, akin to explaining the concept of color to the blind or the beauty of music to the deaf.

"My dear Angel," the Vicar began, his voice laced with a mixture of exasperation and amusement. "I assure you, this world, with all its imperfections and complexities, is very much real. And as for humans being mythical creatures..." He paused, a twinkle in his eye. "Well, let us just say that some days, I'm rather inclined to agree with you."

The morning sun cast a golden glow over the expansive estate, and Claudia awoke with a sense of restless anticipation. The fresh air, the unfamiliar scent of pine and damp earth, and the distant chirping of birds conspired to awaken in her a curiosity she had not felt in some time. She dressed with dispatch, her mind already wandering to the possibilities the day might hold, and descended the stairs with a spring in her step.

Philippa was seated in the drawing room, a book in her lap, when Claudia entered. The older woman looked up, her sharp eyes taking in Claudia’s appearance with a critical gaze.

"You look as though you’ve been sprinkled with fairy dust," Philippa remarked drily.

Claudia coloured, though she could not suppress a smile. "I have never seen such a place. It is as though the very air here is alive."

Philippa closed her book with a snap. "Alive, indeed. I trust you slept well?"

"Very well, thank you," Claudia replied, her tone bright. "I found the room most comfortable, though I could have done with a little more light."

Philippa raised an eyebrow. "No doubt you will find a way to remedy that."

The two women exchanged a knowing glance, and Claudia felt a flicker of amusement. It was clear that Philippa had little patience for the fragilities of others, yet she carried an air of quiet authority that commanded respect.

As they took their places at the breakfast table, Claudia found herself drawn into conversation with Emily, the young woman who had accompanied them on their journey. Emily was fresh-faced and open-hearted, with a manner that was both engaging and disarmingly straightforward.

"You must tell me about the river," Claudia said, her eyes sparkling with excitement. "I saw it from my window, and it is simply… remarkable."

Emily’s face lit up. "It is, isn’t it? I have spent many a happy hour by its banks. The water is so clear you can see the fish swimming beneath the surface."

Claudia leaned forward, her elbows resting on the table. "Fish, you say? I have no interest in fishing, but the river itself… there is something almost magical about it. I can already see it being transformed, made into something… something beautiful."

Emily blinked, taken aback. "Transformed? I don’t understand."

Claudia waved a dismissive hand. "Nothing so drastic, I assure you. A few well-placed shrubs, perhaps, or a winding path along the bank. It would only enhance its natural beauty."

Emily’s expression softened, and she nodded. "I see. Well, I daresay you will find a way to do it."

As the breakfast table was cleared, Claudia found herself drawn outside, the crisp morning air invigorating her senses. She wandered away from the house, her boots crunching on the gravel path, until she came to a spot where the river came into full view. The water flowed gently, reflecting the sky like a mirror, and Claudia felt a surge of inspiration.

"Beautiful, isn’t it?" said a voice behind her.

Claudia turned to see Jane, the parlourmaid, standing at the edge of the woods, a basket of laundry in her hands.

"Yes," Claudia replied, her gaze still fixed on the river. "It is."

Jane smiled, a shy, almost secret smile. "I’ve lived here all my life, and I still find it stunning every time I see it."

Claudia turned to her, her expression thoughtful. "You must be proud to live in such a place."

Jane ducked her head, her cheeks flushing. "Well… yes, miss. It’s a good enough place."

Claudia studied her for a moment, then nodded. "I suppose it is."

As she walked back toward the house, Claudia’s mind was alive with ideas. She could see the potential for improvement everywhere—here a garden, there a gazebo, over there a bench for visitors to rest. The river itself, with its crystal-clear waters, could be the centrepiece of the entire estate.

Back in the house, she found Philippa in the parlour, engaged in conversation with Emily. The two women fell silent as Claudia entered, and she felt the weight of their combined scrutiny.

"Where have you been?" Philippa asked, her tone sharp.

"I went for a walk," Claudia replied, her voice calm. "The river is… fascinating."

Philippa arched an eyebrow. "Fascinating, is it?"

Claudia hesitated, then nodded. "Yes. There is much to be done here, Philippa. Much to be improved."

Philippa looked at her for a long moment, then turned to Emily. "See to the tea, will you?"

Emily bobbed a curtsy and hurried away, her steps light.

Philippa turned back to Claudia, her expression unreadable. "Improvements, Claudia? Do you have a particular vision in mind?"

Claudia’s heart raced, but she met Philippa’s gaze steadily. "I do. I have always had a… a way of seeing things. Of making things better."

Philippa smiled, a slow, calculating smile. "I see. Well, we shall see."

The two women remained in the parlour for some time, the air thick with unspoken words. When Emily returned with the tea, Claudia found herself drawn into conversation, her mind racing with ideas.

As the afternoon wore on, Claudia found herself in her new room, the one with the south-facing window. The light streamed in, casting patterns on the floor, and she felt a surge of excitement. This was where she would begin. She would transform this room, make it her own, and from there, she would begin to transform the entire estate.

Philippa had suggested she unpack on her own, and Claudia had agreed without hesitation. Now, as she looked around the room, she felt a sense ofOwnership, of purpose. She would make this her home, and from here, she would begin to shape the world around her.

She opened her notebook, the pages blank and waiting. With a confident hand, she began to sketch, her ideas spilling out onto the page as though they had been waiting for this moment. The river, the gardens, the house itself—all of it would be transformed, made into something beautiful, something lasting.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, Claudia continued to work, her mind alive with plans and possibilities. She was determined, and nothing would stand in her way.

Upon our arrival at the host's residence, the air was filled with the mingled scents of freshly pressed wool and the faint whiff of roasting meats, its promise as inviting as the day's noon sun. Conversation flowed effortlessly among the guests, like the bubbling brook that graced the courtyard's edge, each melody contributing to the symphony of social discourse.

"Pray, madam," ventured the gentleman, with an impish glint in his eye, "have you ever given thought to venturing into the realm of literature? Your keen observations and the vibrant portrait of society you paint in your discourse are most admirable."

Margaret, twirling a delicate silk handkerchief between her fingers, replied with unaffected grace, "Indeed, I have pondered the art of writing, yet I find myself more inclined to observe rather than articulate. A novelist's life, with its solitary evenings, may offer a respite from the buzz of the ballroom, but I am yet to conquer the quill with the finesse of a born author."

"A most prudent decision," commended the gentleman, "for the demands of the authoress's pen might well eclipse the beauty of a lady's social grace. It is much like selecting the finest produce at the market – one must discern which fruits of the mind are ripe for the picking."

Margaret's laughter echoed softly through the room, a delicate ripple upon the pond of chatter. "I must admit, my dear sir, your analogy is rather apt. Though, one could argue, the finest novelists are those who capture the fleeting moment with a brush so deft, it mimics the very pulse of society itself."

As if on cue, Lady Harriet, ever an eloquent hostess, seized the moment from its ebb. "Ah, but what of the novels which address the delicate matter of health? They are as useful as the knowledge of a judicious hostess, informing us of which foods to favor and which to avoid. I do say, in the name of good taste and digestion, one ought to beware of the sumptuous dessert tray which arrives after the main course."

The gentleman, ever quick with a jest, nodded sagely. "Most frugal advice, madam. Particularly when one's constitution is as sensitive as my own to the heavy sauces that accompany our host's generous table."

The hostess, ever aware of her duties, interrupted with a graceful bow. "Pray, allow me to recommend the light and flavorful dishes produced by the farm. Our produce is a testament to the skill of our farmer, whose carrots are as crisp and resplendent as the fields from which they were plucked."

The subject shifted, turning to lighter matters as the evening's entertainment commenced. A gentleman, animated by spirits, proposed a wager concerning a forthcoming hunt. "Miss Margaret, as a lady of such refined sensibilities, perhaps you would care to join us in a less, shall we say, strenuous activity?"

Margaret, ever polite yet firm, declined with the elegance of a well-spoken refusal. "Thank you for your kind invitation, but the company of books and the tranquil countryside are, for me, pursuits far more exhilarating than the chase."

"A spirited lady, yet one of intellect," mused the gentleman, unable to suppress a smile. "Do you not fear, my dear, that the constant pursuit of knowledge may become a burden to the mind? As I have found, abandoning the horseback and indulging in scholarly pursuits leaves one's intellect unscathed, if a tad unexercised."

"A jest, sir, but one might argue that it is the very balance of activity and repose which cultivates the mind," Margaret retorted, her eyes twinkling with the wisdom of playful repartee. "In the same vein, one does not confine a bird to its cage for fear of it taking flight."

The evening waned, as did the discussion, drawing to a close with the gentle suggestion of retiring for the night. As Margaret bid adieu to her companions, she reflected upon the delightful interchange of ideas and the shared amusement that had graced the evening. Each conversation, like the myriad notes in a composer's symphony, contributed to the rich tapestry of life, inviting one to partake in the grand performance of human interaction.

The unexpected carriage ride with the old Countess and her granddaughters left Mr. Titmarsh in a state of both excitement and confusion. As they journeyed through the bustling streets of London, he couldn't help but steal glances at the elegant Lady Jane and her charming sister, who seemed to be engaged in a spirited conversation about the latest fashion trends.

The Countess, sitting regally beside him, turned to Mr. Titmarsh with a mischievous twinkle in her eye. "My dear Mr. Titmarsh," she began, "I hope you don't mind our impromptu invitation. It's not every day that one comes across a gentleman with such impeccable manners and a quick wit."

Mr. Titmarsh, still trying to make sense of the situation, merely nodded in response. The rhythmic clatter of the carriage wheels against the cobblestones seemed to lull him into a state of dreamlike fascination, as if he had been transported to a different world altogether.

Lady Jane, who had been listening intently to her grandmother's words, suddenly spoke up. "Do you know, Mr. Titmarsh, I've always admired your writing. Your wit and humor in your stories never fail to entertain me."

Mr. Titmarsh blushed at the unexpected praise and cleared his throat before replying, "Thank you, Lady Jane. Your kind words are far too generous. I consider myself merely a humble scribe, attempting to capture the beauty and absurdity of the world around me."

The carriage turned a corner, and Mr. Titmarsh caught a glimpse of St. Paul's Cathedral towering majestically in the distance. It was a sight that never failed to fill him with awe and reverence, reminding him of the fleeting nature of time and the immensity of the universe.

As the conversation veered towards the topic of literature and art, Mr. Titmarsh found himself engaged in a lively debate with Lady Jane about the merits of romantic poetry versus satirical prose. The Countess, observing their animated discussion with amusement, interjected with her own witty observations, much to the delight of her granddaughters.

The carriage eventually came to a stop outside a grand townhouse that Mr. Titmarsh recognized as the Countess's residence. Servants rushed forward to assist the ladies out of the carriage, while the Countess turned to Mr. Titmarsh with a twinkle in her eye.

"Mr. Titmarsh, would you do an old lady the honor of joining us for tea? I must confess, I find your company quite delightful, and I would be remiss if I did not extend my hospitality to such a charming guest."

Mr. Titmarsh, caught off guard by the unexpected invitation, could only stammer his thanks before accepting graciously. As he was led into the opulent drawing room, he couldn't shake the feeling that this chance encounter with the Countess and her granddaughters would mark a turning point in his life, leading him down a path he had never dared to imagine.

He went to the cottage next day, between three and four upon a drowsy summer afternoon, and was so fortunate as to find Marian sitting under one of the walnut-trees at the end of the garden reading a novel, with her faithful Skye terrier in attendance. He seated himself on a low garden-chair by her side, and took the book gently from her hand.

"I have come to spoil your afternoon's amusement," he said. "I have not many days more to spend in Lidford, you know, and I want to make the most of a short time."

"Yes," she said, with a bright inquiring look in her eyes. "But what have I to do with that?"

"Everything. It is you who have made the little country village my paradise. O Marian, tell me that it has not been a fool's paradise! My darling, I love you with all my heart and soul, with an honest man's first and only love. Promise that you will be my wife."

He took the hand that lay loosely on her lap, and pressed it in both his own. She withdrew it gently, and sat looking at him with a face that had grown suddenly pale.

"You do not know what you are asking," she said; "you cannot know. Captain Sedgewick is not my uncle. He does not even know who my parents were. I am the most obscure creature in the world."

"Not one degree less dear to me because of that, Marian; only the dearer. Tell me, my darling, is there any hope for me?"

"I never thought----" she faltered; "I had no idea----"
