It is vivid in my memory still—the way the red flame-light flared over his big burly front, and sparkled on his beard, and made his face to shine like that of Moses.

But soon I learned that there were Abolitionists everywhere—Abolitionists right here in our own little farmland township of northern New York! The impression which this discovery made upon me was not unlike that produced on Robinson Crusoe by the immortal footprint. I could think of nothing else. Great events, which really covered a space of years, came and went as in a bunch together, while I was still pondering upon this. John Brown was hanged, Lincoln was elected, Sumter was fired on, the first regiment was raised and despatched from our rustic end of Dearborn County—and all the time it seems now as if my mind was concentrated upon the amazing fact that some of our neighbors were Abolitionists.

There was a certain dreamlike tricksiness of transformation in it all. At first there was only one Abolitionist, old “Jee” Hagadorn. Then, somehow, there came to be a number of them—and then, all at once, lo! everybody was an Abolitionist—that is to say, everybody but Abner Beech. The more general and enthusiastic the conversion of the others became, the more resolutely and doggedly he dug his heels into the ground, and braced his broad shoulders, and pulled in the opposite direction. The skies darkened, the wind rose, the storm of angry popular feeling burst swooping over the country-side, but Beech only stiffened his back and never budged an inch.

The curious manifestation of Archibald's malady had, by now, enthralled the entire household. While but recently his name would only be whispered in passing, it had now become the subject of animated debate—speculation born not from the wisdom of elders, but rather the mystique of the unknown. Archibald himself lay at the center of this maelitude, an enigma, surrounded by whispering nurses and solemn sages. What odd fate had befallen him, none could venture to assert with conviction, though theories, grand and small, abounded with reckless abandon. The hush that had once accompanied his slumber had given way to a tumult, as the very air seemed to hold its breath, yearning for the unraveling of the riddle that held Malmaison in thrall.

As Archibald stirred from his trance-like repose, it was as if a veil was lifted, though it revealed not answers but further questions. His eyes, once vacant pools of dreams, now flickered with a light at once innocent and bewildered. Yet, for all the alerted comprehension that seemingly dawned, his tongue took to dumb show, failing to free the words that ought to have accompanied such awakening. Instead, a fragile cooing, interspersed with incomprehensible tidbits, emerged—infantile almost, yet possessed by an uncanniness that unsettled more than soothed. In some, this inspired dread; in others, an amused affection, yet not one soul could claim indifference under such peculiar circumstances.

In the bewilderment, food, in its myriad forms, was presented as a litmus test of his cognitive faculties. Confections that might tempt the most aloof of children; hearty broth to comfort and restore what weakness might remain; crusty loaves rich with the scent of hearth and homemaker—each tried and were in their turns, scorned or ignored. Archibald did not repudiate these offerings out of spite, nor could it be said he maintained even a passive disinterest; there was, instead, a curious absence, a lacuna where pleasure or distaste might have dwelt. The simple act of sustenance had transformed into a conundrum, a dietary parable for all but the most discerning to unravel.

Thus it was, amid the chaos and consternation, that a most unexpected resolution presented itself: the wet-nurse, matronly and composed, stepped forward—her very presence a testament to the ancient bond infants hold to nurture and survival. Instinctively, as happens oft with the miraculous choreography of life, Archibald leaned forth, drawn to the promise of sustenance innate within her. The air, once tense, softened. In that moment, the assembled cast of observers—noblemen, maids, and doctors alike—saw a rekindling of the cord that links humanity to some primal inception. The realization was at once humbling and clarifying; the pattern, though altered, maintained its rhythm.

The wise eyes of Dr. Rollinson, gleaming with the zest of discovery, watched the proceedings with a curiosity unmarred by the certainty that ages lesser men. For him, Archibald was not merely an idiosyncrasy to be written off in the annals of medical oddity; he was, rather, a living journal, replete with the possibility of new understanding. Here was a man who grasped that illumination lay not in declamation but in listening to the silent lexicon of phenomena. He resolved, then and there, to delve deeper into the mysteries inherent in Archibald's reversion, to unearth whatever might lie beneath the veil of this singular condition, for it was his creed that truth, no matter cloaked, awaited its unmasking by those who dared to seek it.

In the quiet of the parlor, Mrs. Quimby's scathing regard was piercing as she surveyed the apartments, her disapproval evident even before she spoke. "Sir Montague," she pronounced, her voice crisp and uncompromising, "you did not ask Miss Albina's permission before taking a slice of the fruitcake. This behavior, I must say, is quite at odds with the genteel conduct I've come to associate with you."

Mr. Montague, however, seemed unmoved by her rebuke. He maintained his seat, his eyes shifting between the cake and Mrs. Quimby's disapproving countenance. "I thought, madam, that the cake was meant for our consumption. I assure you, it was not my intention to upset you or Miss Albina." His tone was smooth, but Mrs. Quimby was not mollified.

Mrs. Marsden, observing the scene from her seat by the window, interjected, "Now, Winslow, I'm sure there's no harm done. After all, the cake was left out for guests to enjoy." She paused, regarding her visitor's pressed magnificence. "I must admit, I've not seen a more dapper gentleman since Lord Westbrooke's last visit. I've heard tell that in England, one need not ask permission to partake in refreshments."

"Nonsense, Isadora," Mrs. Quimby retorted, her eyes narrowing. "This is America, not London. Here, courtesy and politeness are a gentleman's first defense. One does not trespass into another's hospitality without invitation."

Mrs. Marsden sighed, her gaze returning to the open window. "Yet, does not the Montagues' style reflect a certain ease of fashion, a gallantry born of English sophistication? Would it cause scandal if we embraced their freedom, Winslow?"

Mr. Montague, it seemed, was discomfited by this line of discussion. He shifted in his seat, a polite smile playing on his lips. "I assure you, Mrs. Quimby, our adherence to certain rules is not an indication of our dignity, but of our respect for your customs."

Mrs. Quimby's response was immediate. "Then perhaps, Mr. Montague, it is time that you acquainted yourself more closely with them. For my part, I cannot abide by such liberties taken with hospitality."

As the conversation continued, Albina entered, her eyes bright from recent tears. Her robe was elegant, a stark contrast to the morning's dishabille, but her cheeks bore the remnants of her distress. "You seem to have attracted quite a gathering," she remarked, her voice cool. "I trust my absence was no cause for undue consternation."

"Albina, dear," Mrs. Marsden exclaimed, "you are looking rather pale. Come, sit down. We were just about to eat." She patted the seat beside her, but Albina shook her head, keeping her distance.

"I am quite well, thank you. I believe I shall retire to my room to compose myself. You see, I must maintain a certain composure when hosting such celebrated guests." Her gaze fell on Mr. Montague, who met her stare with a small nod.

As Albina left the room, the Montagues watched her departing figure. Mr. Montague sighed, his eyes thoughtful. "I fear we have overstepped our bounds, Emily," he said softly. "Our arrival seems to be a source of distress, not the pleasure we intended."

Emily, however, was unperturbed. She leaned back in her seat, her eyes bright. "You must never apologize for being who you are, dear brother. This is a long way from London, but it is our home, too. We need not adhere to every trite rule of manner. We must impose our own grace."

Mrs. Quimby, however, seemed unmoved by this line of discussion. "In my opinion," she declared, her voice ringing with conviction, "our role is not to upend the delicate balance of society but to enhance it. And this is not a matter of simple courtesy, but of mutual respect and understanding."

As the room fell silent, the echoes of Albina's departure lingered in the air, a metaphorical echo of the discord that had settled over the apartment. The Montagues and the Quimbys, each with their own code of conduct, each with their own understanding of etiquette, stared at each other, waiting for the storm to abate and the dance of conversation to recommence.

"I am waiting for mamma," she said. "One of her pensioners is ill in that cottage. I was glad of the chance of bringing her out for a little air. We are with poor Carry, you know."

"How is Lady Caroline?" John asked.

"Oh, well enough, when one considers all things," said Edith, hastily; and to escape that subject, which was not to be entered on before strangers, she said, "You are going to Dunearn?"

"On painful business," he said. "I wonder if I may ask you one thing?" She looked up at him with a smile which said much--a smile of trust and belief, which might have encouraged any man to speak. Edith had no fear of what he might ask her. For John it was more difficult to command himself and his voice at that moment than at any previous one since his trial began. He cleared his throat with an effort, and his voice was husky. "You will hear things said of me--that may make you turn from--an old friend altogether. I want you not to believe them. And tell Lady Lindores. Do not believe them. It is not true."

"Mr Erskine, what is it--what is it? You may be sure I shall believe nothing against you--nor mamma either! Is it--is it----" her eyes fixed upon him anxiously and upon the stranger beside him, whose face was unknown to her, and who sat blank and passive like a servant, yet who was not a servant. Edith rose in the carriage in her great anxiety, and gazed as if she would have read a volume in John's face. What it cost him to look at her and to keep a kind of smile on his, it would be hard to tell.

"I cannot enter into explanations now. I may not be able to do so soon. Only--tell Lady Lindores."

She held out her hand to him, which he stooped to touch--it was all he could do--and once more gave him an anxious, tender smile. "You may trust both mamma and me," she said.

And in another moment, so it seemed, the dogcart stopped again. John went over the streets of Dunearn like a man in a dream--in a sort of exquisite anguish, a mingled sweetness and bitterness such as never went into words. Their looks seemed to cling together, as, with a start, the horse went on; and now they stopped again and got down--for a very different encounter. Even now, however, John's progress was to be interrupted. Some one called to him as he was about to go into the sheriff's court in the little Town-house of Dunearn. "Is that you, John Erskine? and what has brought you here?" in peremptory tones. He turned round quickly. It was Miss Barbara in her pony-carriage, which Nora was driving. The old lady leaned across the young one and beckoned to him with some impatience. "Come here. What are you doing in Dunearn without coming to me? It's true I'm out, and you would not have found me; but Janet would have understood to be prepared for your luncheon. And what's your business in the Town-house this fine morning, and with strange company?" Miss Barbara said. She cast a keen glance at the man, who stood aside respectfully enough, and yet, backed by his assistant, kept a watchful eye on John.

"I am afraid I cannot wait to tell you now. It is not pleasant business," John said.

"Come round here," said the old lady, imperiously; "can I keep on skreighing to you before all the town? Come round here." Her keen eyes took in the whole scene: John's glance at his grave companion, the most imperceptible gesture with which that person made way for him. Miss Barbara's perceptions were keen. She gripped her nephew by the arm. "John Erskine, have ye done anything to bring ye within the power of the law?"

"Shot?--what dost thou mean, Maggie? Surely, we haven't any such thing in the house!" Edward exclaimed, feigning surprise, though a glint in his eye betrayed his cunning.

"Yes, we have," Maggie replied, matter-of-factly. "Mother keeps it in the pantry, in that old earthenware jar, for the sparrows in the garden. I've seen her use it dozens o' times."

Edward's face clouded over. "The pantry! That's next to impossible. Thou knowest Mother is always fussin' about in there, measuring out flour and whatnot. I couldn't possibly go in there without her seein' me."

"But the boat will never float properly without it!" Maggie protested, her lower lip trembling slightly. "I should think you'd rather face mother's wrath than see your lovely boat sink to the bottom o' the pond."

Edward sighed dramatically. "It's easy for thee to say. Thou dost not have to face her scolding."

A moment of silence hung between them, broken only by the distant chirping of birds. Maggie looked from Edward's pleading face to the model boat, lying forlornly on the grass. A pang of guilt shot through her. It was she who had refused to fetch his paints just yesterday, leading to a small argument, one she now regretted.

"Oh, very well," she mumbled, finally relenting. "I'll get it, I suppose."

Edward's face brightened instantly. "Wilt thou really, Maggie? Oh, thank you! Thou art the best sister a fellow could ask for."

Maggie tried to hide her amusement. "Just don't expect me to carry it all the way to the pond. It's heavy, thou knowest."

She turned and headed towards the house, a sense of determination hardening her resolve. She would be quick, silent, and invisible. Or so she hoped.

As she crept along the hallway, she could hear the sound of Mrs. Grimshaw, the cook, bustling about in the kitchen, her voice booming above the clatter of pots and pans. Maggie held her breath and tiptoed past the door, her heart pounding in her chest.

The pantry was just around the corner. She reached the door and gently pushed it open, peering inside. It was dim and cool, filled with the mingled scents of dried herbs, pickled vegetables, and freshly baked bread. Thankfully, the pantry was deserted.

There, on the bottom shelf, was the earthenware jar she had described to Edward. It was larger than she remembered, its surface covered in a layer of dust. She lifted it carefully, surprised by its weight.

Suddenly, a voice startled her. "Maggie, is that thee? What art thou doing in the pantry?"

It was Mrs. Grimshaw, her round face peering around the door. Maggie froze, the jar clutched tightly in her arms.

"I... I was just looking for a piece of apple," she stammered, her cheeks flushing crimson. "I was feeling a bit peckish."

Mrs. Grimshaw narrowed her eyes. "An apple, eh? And what's that in thy hands? Looks suspiciously like mother's bird shot."

Maggie's mind raced. She had to think fast. "Oh, this?" she said, trying to sound nonchalant. "Mother asked me to bring it outside. She wants to scare away the blackbirds that are stealing her raspberries."

Mrs. Grimshaw looked skeptical. "Raspberries? But the raspberries haven't ripened yet."

Just then, a shrill voice rang out from upstairs. "Grimshaw! Grimshaw, where are you? I need you this instant!"

Mrs. Grimshaw sighed. "That's Mother. I'll deal with thee later, young lady. And don't go eating all the shot, mind!"

With a final glare, she bustled away, leaving Maggie alone in the pantry, weak with relief. She quickly grabbed a handful of shot and stuffed it into her pockets, then replaced the jar on the shelf.

As she turned to leave, she bumped into a stack of plates, sending them crashing to the floor. The sound echoed through the house, followed by a chorus of startled cries.

"Maggie!" Mrs. Buxton's voice rose above the din. "What in heavens art thou doing?"

The soft glow from Mrs. Franklin's quill illuminated the parlor, casting dancing shadows on the walls adorned with Dolly's renderings of dinosaurs. The house echoed with the gentle tap of her knitting needles, a rhythmic harmony to the ticking of the grandfather clock. Dolly, her face flushed with excitement, leaned forward in her wheelchair, her eyes sparkling like the pearls strung upon her necklace.

"You know, Billy," she began, her voice barely above a whisper, "I've been thinking about what mother said last evening. About the planchette."

Miss Wilhelmina Breeze, or Miss Billy as she was more often called, looked up from her embroidery, her fine eyebrows puckering in confusion. "What about it, Dolly? I thought she made her disapproval clear enough."

Dolly shrugged, a mischievous grin playing on her lips. "Perhaps, but I believe it's a means to an end. A doorway to the minds of the departed, Billy. If we cannot communicate with them directly, then we should find a way to listen to their whispered thoughts."

Miss Billy frowned, her needle pausing mid-stitch. "But Dolly, mother fears it's a deception, a pawn of the devil."

"Ah, mother fears many things, doesn't she?" Dolly laughed softly. "But tell me, Billy, don't you sometimes wonder about them? Don't you crave the certainty of their voices?"

Miss Billy looked down at her needlework, her fingers tightening around the pieces of cloth. "I suppose I do," she admitted.

Dolly clapped her hands together, the sound like tiny bells. "Then we must try! When mother is occupied with her preparations for Mr. Chase, and the servants are about the house, I shall bring out the planchette. It will be our secret."

Miss Billy glanced towards the balcony, where the soft murmurs of Mrs. Franklin's voice could be heard, discussing the menu for dinner. "I don't know, Dolly. Mr. Chase... Mother expects me to entertain him. I barely know him."

"Mr. Chase!" Dolly scoffed. "I've seen him, Billy. He's a confirmed skeptic, no different from mother. They will be absorbed in their doubts, leaving us unnoticed. Besides, think of the stories you could tell him. Our mind travels unending."

Miss Billy bit her lip, considering the idea. She wanted to believe in the power of the planchette, to hear the voices that hovered on the edge of her consciousness, urging her to listen. But the polite mask of her mother's expectations weighed heavily on her. She could not simply disregard them, especially with Mr. Chase in attendance.

Dolly, misreading her hesitation, leaned forward, her eyes beseeching. "Billy, please. For the love of our shared fascinations. I promise, we shall use it sparingly, and only when mother is too occupied to interfere."

Miss Billy sighed, her hands falling into her lap. "Very well. But we must be careful. Very careful."

The grandfather clock chimed the hour, its deep tones echoing throughout the house. Mrs. Franklin appeared in the doorway, her eyes sweeping the room, stopping briefly at Miss Billy's bowed head. "There you are, Wilhelmina. Please come and assist me in the drawing room. I am preparing a tray for Mr. Chase."

Miss Billy stood, her embroidery clutched in her hand like a lifeline. "Yes, Mother. I'll be right there."

Dolly, undeterred by her mother's arrival, bent back to her knitting, her voice barely audible as she whispered, "I won't rest until we've tried it, Billy."

Miss Billy screwed up her face in a tight smile, following her mother out the room. "Until this afternoon," she whispered, not turning back to look at Dolly.

The drawing room was bathed in the gentle light of the setting sun. Mr. Chase sat near the window, his face buried in a book. He looked up as Miss Billy entered, offering her a polite nod. "Miss Wilhelmina," he acknowledged.

"Mr. Chase," she replied, her voice barely above a whisper. She helped her mother arrange the tea things on the silver tray, her heart pounding in her chest. The planchette, hidden in her pocket, pulsed with an almost tangible energy.

Mrs. Franklin pointedly ignored the obvious nervousness of her daughter, her gaze flicking to Mr. Chase. "I trust you find the library to your liking, Mr. Chase?"

"Yes, indeed," he replied, closing his book. "Your collection is impressive."

Miss Billy, feeling her mother's stern gaze, took a deep breath. She knew she must engage Mr. Chase, to keep her mother from noticing Dolly's earlier conversation. "Miss Wilhelmina is not the only one who shares an interest in ancient creatures," Dolly had said earlier. "Mr. Chase is also a collector."

Miss Billy heightened her voice, injecting it with a level of excitement she barely felt. "Mr. Chase, have you ever seen a mastodon? I find them fascinating, with their long tusks and massive size."

Mr. Chase turned to her, his eyes twinkling with interest.

It was a place of contrasts, the theatre, where the world of make-believe and the world of men met and mingled, and where the crudest realities were cloaked in the softest silks and satins. I found myself lingering in the wings, as I often did, watching the strange, half-lit figures flit about like shadows on a wall, each one more fantastical than the last. The air was thick with the scent of paint and oil, and the click of heels on polished wood echoed through the narrow corridors, while somewhere in the distance, a piano tinkled, as though someone were practicing their scales, though it sounded more like a hesitant prayer than music.

The girls, as always, were the most striking. They moved with a curious grace, their bodies swaying under the weight of their elaborate costumes, their faces painted to resemble those of queens or courtesans—or sometimes, simply girls. I saw one young woman, her hair the color of chestnuts, leaning against a backdrop, her eyes fixed on the far wall as she sewed a rents in her skirt with needle and thread. Her movements were deliberate, her posture so absorbed in her task that she seemed unaware of the world around her. Yet when she looked up, the transformation was sudden and startling—her lips curved into a smile, and she called out to a nearby boy in a voice that was at once imperious and kind.

They were all so alive, these creatures of the stage. Their laughter rang out like music, and their quarrels, though sharp, were settled with a laugh or a touch of the hand. I envied them their ease, their capacity for such raw emotion, and yet I could not help but feel a kinship with them. For in their world of make-believe, I was just another shadow, a figure who moved through the wings unseen, unheard, yet never truly unobserved.

Lester, as usual, found me deep in these thoughts, his stocky figure appearing at my elbow like a wisp of smoke. “You should come,” he said, his voice low and urgent, as though imparting some great secret. “The children are set to perform in the second act. You’d never believe the way they carry themselves, as though they were born to this life. It’s enough to make a man believe in angels, I tell you.”

I hesitated, for such spectacles often left me with a strange, disquieting feeling, as though I were intruding upon something sacred. But Lester’s persistence was infectious, and before I knew it, I was following him through the labyrinth of corridors, the air growing warmer with each step. The backstage was alive with the hum of voices, the clatter of props, and the occasional shout from the stage manager. The actors, wrapped in their costumes, moved like dancers in a macabre ballet, their faces painted and their movements deliberate.

The anticipation was palpable as we approached the wings. I could feel the weight of the audience’s attention pressing against the wooden barriers, as though the very air itself were strained with expectation. Then, as the final notes of the act drew to a close, the house erupted into applause, and I saw the children emerge, their tiny figures dwarfed by the grandeur of the stage.

Among them was a girl, no older than ten, with hair the color of freshly turned soil and eyes as dark as midnight. She moved with a confidence that belied her age, her every gesture deliberate, her every smile a command. The audience, as Lester had predicted, was captivated. Their cheers swelled, drowning out the faint sound of the orchestra, and for a moment, it seemed as though the world had been reduced to that single, shining figure.

But as the performance progressed, I noticed something odd—a restlessness in the child’s movements, a tension that betrayed her youth. She stumbled once, her foot catching in the folds of her dress, and though she recovered quickly, there was a flicker of uncertainty in her eyes. Yet still, the audience roared, their cheers growing louder, more insistent.

When the act concluded, the room was alive with applause, and the backstage burst into a cacophony of shouts and laughter. The girl, however, stood apart, her face a study of quiet determination, as though she had just survived some great ordeal. I found myself drawn to her, not out of pity, but out of a strange, inexplicable curiosity.

“Amazing,” Lester said, his voice thick with admiration, as he clapped the child on the shoulder. “Simply amazing. You’ve got a gift, miss, mark my words.”

She nodded, her dark eyes meeting mine for a moment, before she turned and disappeared into the throng of actors and stagehands. For a moment, I was left with only the echo of her performance, the memory of her presence lingering in the air like the faintest whisper.

It was then that I realized—I had found another subject for my endless musings, another soul caught in the thrall of the theatre’s magic.

In the gentle warmth of a languid afternoon, the narrator found himself once more ensconced within the embrace of the ancient demolished abbey. The rays of the setting sun cast a golden hue upon the weathered stones, as if to remind him of the grandeur of yore. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming flowers that had taken root amidst the decaying remnants of the once mighty edifice. Mr. Malone, ever the stalwart companion, was by his side, his keen eyes scanning the debris-laden landscape with a gardener's interest.

"Pray, Mr. D.," he inquired, his voice barely above a whisper, "Do you recall the tale of our dear old lady, Queen Anne's Lace? I've always believed she is the spirit of the abbey, reigning over these ruins with her delicate charm." The narrator nodded, his gaze following the playful dance of the wind through the tufts of grass that waved among the crumbling columns.

As they traversed the path, their conversation turned towards the delicate threads of time and memory. "No doubt," Mr. Malone observed, "the search for Phoebus has taken ahold of your fancy, dear fellow, but remember, time tends to smooth the rough edges of our obsessions. It will not be long before the quest for this lost dahlia is but a faded memory, like the sweet Petrovaria that bloomed in the shade of the abbey's overgrown walls last season."

The narrator smiled at his friend's wisdom, allowing his thoughts to drift away from the all-consuming quest. Yet, as they paused to observe the vibrant flora that thrived in the decay, a sudden shift in the breeze brought a whiff of something unusual. Mr. Malone caught it too, his expression turning sharp. "What's this?" he murmured, bending down to sniff the fetid earth.

To the narrator's disbelief, his fingers brushed against something smooth and silken, hidden beneath the mounds of manure. There, in all its radiant splendor, was Phoebus, the most vibrant dahlia he had ever laid eyes upon. It seemed to bloom with a life of its own, defying the unspectacular surroundings that had harbored its secret growth. Surrounded by the ruins of time, the future's forgotten trend was revealed, and with it, the abbey's whispers echoed anew.

Great men are only nourished on the elements. Woman is an element, all the elements in one,--earth, air, fire, and water, met together in a rose. She is a spring among the rocks, and she comes up dimpling from the roots of the world. She is just as simple and just as strange. O! little shining spring of woman that is called Jenny, a great man must draw up through you the unfathomed, deep strengths of the old world. He bends above you and drinks, and as he drinks, his face is mirrored in yours.

"Jenny, I don't think I'd read 'Miss ----,' if I were you," would say the great man.

"No, dear?" So Jenny was presently reading Ruskin instead, and wondering how she could ever have read "Miss ----." And deep in her dear heart she was saying, "Of course not; great men's wives never read 'Miss ----.'"

And yet had the great man said, "Read Gaboriau instead,"--as a certain very great man does,--Jenny's heart would have said, "Of course, great men's wives always read Gaboriau."

No! great men's wives read "Sesame and Lilies," and "Sartor Resartus," and "Marius the Epicurean," and "Richard Feverel," and "Virginibus Puerisque,"--they even try to read Newman's "Apologia." Such were the books on the sunnier side of Theophilus Londonderry's little library in No. 3 Zion Place. In dark corners behind easy-chairs were the deep-sea pools of theology,--pools which had long since given up all the fish they had in them for their owner,--slabs of antique divinity, such as you would find likewise in the equally cherished library of Londonderry Senior.

Such were the fathers that slumbered on in a well-earned repose, and which, far from desiring new readers, were so old that they were glad to rest undisturbed,--being far too self-important to confuse a considerate regard for their repose with neglect. And many of them were really quite valuable as decoration, because of their fine old coats of gilded leather; and such were ranged in the more penetrable shadows or even in the lamp-light. Theophilus would point to them as to a portrait-gallery of dead ancestors. One might admire the quaint and distinguished cut of their clothes without dreaming of wearing the same,--and indeed old divinity, he used to say, was poor food for young divines.

His divinity indeed was fed on the technical side, it is to be feared, by the more destructive biblical criticism, like most destructive engines, coming all the way from Germany, and at its more vital centres by importations of strong meat from Russia and Scandinavia. Tolstoi and Ibsen were his archprophets.

There was likewise a great Paris moralist called Zola, and a strange old American father called Walt Whitman. And beauty, that can never be far away from strength, found many new and wonderful prophets in that little library,--poets and painters and musicians of whom hardly anyone else in Coalchester had yet heard, and certainly no one above the age of twenty-five.

Surely youth is in nothing more marvellous than in its mysterious power of attracting to itself into the most out-of-the-way places the sustenance and companionship it needs. In the unlikeliest wilderness inspired youth is never without the mysteriously-brought food and the company of angels. Powers of the air will sweep across continents to rescue it from prison, soft gales travel from south to north to sow seeds of beauty in its narrow ways, and little songs will flutter like butterflies for hundreds of miles to cheer its heart.

The Time-Spirit had given its angels charge concerning these young people, and, remote as they were from all the fiery centres of thought and the dreaming schools of art, Zion Place, no less than the Rue de Rivoli, took its thought of the newest and its beauty of the best.
