The sun had not yet fully risen when the Rectory's stained-glass windows cast their kaleidoscopic patterns on the polished marble floor, teasing the occupants with shards of light and shadow. Lilias, her face newly rosy from a hearty breakfast, lingered at the drawing-room window, hermind still admissible to the quiet of the churchyard. The morning had brought an unusually warm air, a gentle tease that promised the coming summer's respite. The cool, damp smell of the vicarage was slowly being displaced by the faint fragrance of blooming roses from the garden.

As the clatter of the carriage wheels announced the return of the Westerns from their morning ride, Lilias turned from her window, her curiosity piqued. The family retinue, led by her elder brother Basil, had traveled to the town's market square to procure provisions. Lilias, however, had found her own morning chores to be less taxing than the chase for the freshest fruits and meatiest cuts. As she descended the grand staircase, she was admonished by the scraping sound of her dress against the polished wood. Yet, she moved with a grace that belied her initial apprehension, her eyes glinting with an unshed excitement.

The day was shaping up to be a peculiar one. The family's new maid, Sarah, had dropped a tray of freshly baked bread mere minutes before, leaving a trail of half-smashed loaves and broken dreams. Lilias, with her usual charm, had coaxed the girl out of her fright, laughing along with her at the absurdity of the situation. It was not often that the Rectory's affairs offered such a mundane diversion.

But as the clock in the hallway struck ten, a sudden chill swept through the house, as if nature itself had sought to challenge the warmth of the day. The maids at their washstands paused, their hands hovering above the linens, ears perked for any hint of disturbance. A singular silence hung over the house, a hush that whispered of unspoken secrets and latent unease. Lilias, her hands tucked into the folds of her apron, felt the tension in the air. She knew something was troubling the house's equilibrium.

As she ascended the stairs, she noticed her younger brother George seated at the landing, his book forgotten on his lap. His eyes, wide and round as a frightened deer, stared into the distance. Lilias smiled, mirroring his expression, and sat down beside him, her knee gently touching his. "What ails you, dear brother?" she asked softly.

George looked at her, his voice barely above a whisper, "I believe we have visitors, Lilias."

Before Lilias could ask further, she heard the shuffling of footsteps and the rustle of silk. She turned towards the sound, her breath catching in her throat. Standing before them now was a figure that seemed to have stepped straight out of a tale of old. The woman wore a gown of deep, rich velvet, her hair adorned with garlands of spring flowers. Her eyes, a startling blue, met Lilias's gaze with a candor that left her slightly disconcerted. Behind the woman, a procession of servants, each proficient in their tasks, stood attention, waiting for their lady's command.

The woman, perceiving Lilias's confusion, offered a polite curtsy. "I do apologize for the intrusion, miss. I am Lady Edwina_vane. My carriage has been delayed, and I was directed to this address by a most kind and elderly individual. He assured me that this household would be hospitable to my companions and myself while we await our transport."

Lilias, recovering her composure, stood and extended her hand. "Indeed, madam. You are most welcome at the Rectory. We are always happy to offer aid to those in need. Permit me to introduce myself. I am Lilias Western, and this is my brother George."

At the sound of their names, George jumped to his feet, his book forgotten in his haste. "My lady, it is a pleasure to meet you. My mother will be most pleased to know of your arrival. She is the kindest of souls, our mother."

Lady Edwina smiled, her eyes crinkling at the corners. "I am delighted to hear it, young man. Your mother's reputation precedes her in these parts. I am most eager to make her acquaintance."

As they spoke, Mary, Lilias's younger sister, descended the stairs, her skirts swishing softly against the carpet. Her eyes met Lilias's, a silent communication passing between them. Mary's eyes darted to the visitors before returning to Lilias, a plea in their depths. Lilias nodded her agreement, understanding her sister's unspoken request.

"I am Mary," she said, curtsying to Lady Edwina. "We are at your service, madam. I believe Mother is preparing for your arrival in the drawing-room."

The poor, blubbering girl said, "Indeed, my lady, I wouldn't hurt a fly, much less a king, and I cannot abide the French, nor frogs neither, for that matter."

But my lady was inexorable, and took a girl who could neither read nor write, to make up for her alarm about the progress of education towards addition and subtraction; and afterwards, when the clergyman who was at Hanbury parish when I came there, had died, and the bishop had appointed another, and a younger man, in his stead, this was one of the points on which he and my lady did not agree. While good old deaf Mr. Mountford lived, it was my lady's custom, when indisposed for a sermon, to stand up at the door of her large square pew,--just opposite to the reading-desk,--and to say (at that part of the morning service where it is decreed that, in quires and places where they sing, here followeth the anthem): "Mr. Mountford, I will not trouble you for a discourse this morning." And we all knelt down to the Litany with great satisfaction; for Mr. Mountford, though he could not hear, had always his eyes open about this part of the service, for any of my lady's movements. But the new clergyman, Mr. Gray, was of a different stamp. He was very zealous in all his parish work; and my lady, who was just as good as she could be to the poor, was often crying him up as a godsend to the parish, and he never could send amiss to the Court when he wanted broth, or wine, or jelly, or sago for a sick person. But he needs must take up the new hobby of education; and I could see that this put my lady sadly about one Sunday, when she suspected, I know not how, that there was something to be said in his sermon about a Sunday-school which he was planning. She stood up, as she had not done since Mr. Mountford's death, two years and better before this time, and said--

"Mr. Gray, I will not trouble you for a discourse this morning."

But her voice was not well-assured and steady; and we knelt down with more of curiosity than satisfaction in our minds. Mr. Gray preached a very rousing sermon, on the necessity of establishing a Sabbath-school in the village. My lady shut her eyes, and seemed to go to sleep; but I don't believe she lost a word of it, though she said nothing about it that I heard until the next Saturday, when two of us, as was the custom, were riding out with her in her carriage, and we went to see a poor bedridden woman, who lived some miles away at the other end of the estate and of the parish: and as we came out of the cottage we met Mr. Gray walking up to it, in a great heat, and looking very tired. My lady beckoned him to her, and told him she should wait and take him home with her, adding that she wondered to see him there, so far from his home, for that it was beyond a Sabbath-day's journey, and, from what she had gathered from his sermon the last Sunday, he was all for Judaism against Christianity. He looked as if he did not understand what she meant; but the truth was that, besides the way in which he had spoken up for schools and schooling, he had kept calling Sunday the Sabbath: and, as her ladyship said, "The Sabbath is the Sabbath, and that's one thing--it is Saturday; and if I keep it, I'm a Jew, which I'm not. And Sunday is Sunday; and that's another thing; and if I keep it, I'm a Christian, which I humbly trust I am."

But when Mr. Gray got an inkling of her meaning in talking about a Sabbath-day's journey, he only took notice of a part of it: he smiled and bowed, and said no one knew better than her ladyship what were the duties that abrogated all inferior laws regarding the Sabbath; and that he must go in and read to old Betty Brown, so that he would not detain her ladyship.

I lay long awake, my thoughts in a sad turmoil. The visitant of the night, whether real or the figment of a fevered brain, haunted me with a persistence that bordered on torment. Who could it have been? And what motive could prompt such a strange and unsettling apparition? Was it a playful jest, cruelly executed? Or something far more sinister?

The monotonous tramping from the room above had ceased some hours since, yet the echo of it seemed to reverberate still within the confines of my skull. It was a sound that chilled me to the very marrow, devoid of any discernible rhythm or purpose, yet filled with an indefinable menace. I dared not conjecture what manner of creature, human or otherwise, could be responsible for such a dispiriting din.

At length, weary with speculation and worn down by the lack of sleep, I drifted into a troubled slumber, punctuated by fitful dreams wherein the kiss, both tender and unsettling, was re-enacted with an alarming regularity. Phantoms danced attendance in the shadows, their faces obscured, their intentions inscrutable. I awoke with a start as dawn threatened to break, my heart pounding, my brow slick with perspiration.

The first rays of the sun, pale and hesitant, filtered through the gaps in the heavy curtains, casting long, distorted shadows upon the walls. I rose from my bed, feeling strangely weak and disoriented, and proceeded to dress myself with a listlessness that belied my youth. The world beyond my window seemed cloaked in a somber gray, reflecting the mood that gripped my soul.

Having made such toilette as I could muster, I ventured forth from my chamber, intent upon seeking out Mrs. Dance and, if possible, extracting from her some morsel of information that might shed light upon the mysteries that enshrouded Dupley Walls. I descended the staircase with trepidation, each creak of the aged timbers seeming to amplify the silence that pervaded the house.

I found Mrs. Dance in the stillroom, busying herself amongst a profusion of herbs and spices, her face illuminated by the morning sun. She greeted me with a kindly smile, though I thought I detected a certain wariness in her gaze.

"Good morning, Miss Holme," she said. "Did you rest well?"

I hesitated, unsure of how to broach the subject that weighed so heavily upon my mind. "Not entirely," I replied, choosing my words with care. "I found the night somewhat… unsettling."

Mrs. Dance’s eyes narrowed slightly. "Unsettling, you say? In what way, pray?"

"There was a… noise," I began, "from the room above. A constant tramping that prevented me from sleeping."

"Ah, yes," she said, with a dismissive wave of her hand. "That would be Mr. Grimes. He is of a restless disposition, and often paces his chamber at odd hours."

"Mr. Grimes?" I echoed, my curiosity piqued. "And who, may I ask, is Mr. Grimes?"

A shadow seemed to cross Mrs. Dance’s face. "Mr. Grimes is… a guest of Lady Pollexfen," she said, her voice carefully neutral. "He has been residing here for some time."

"And what manner of man is he?" I pressed, unable to resist the urge to delve deeper into the mysteries of Dupley Walls.

Mrs. Dance sighed, a hint of exasperation in her eyes. "Miss Holme," she said, "I must implore you to curb your curiosity. Lady Pollexfen does not take kindly to being questioned, and it would be best for you to avoid arousing her displeasure."

"But surely," I protested, "I am entitled to know something of the circumstances that surround me. I have been brought here under the pretext of companionship, yet I am treated with suspicion and kept in the dark about everything."

"I understand your frustration," Mrs. Dance said, softening her tone. "But I am not at liberty to divulge any information that Lady Pollexfen deems confidential. Suffice it to say that there are forces at work here that are beyond your comprehension."

She paused, and regarded me with an expression of mingled pity and concern. "Believe me, Miss Holme," she added, "it is for your own good that you remain ignorant of these matters. The less you know, the safer you will be."

"But I cannot help but feel that I am in danger," I said, my voice trembling slightly. "The kiss, Mrs. Dance, during the night...!"

Mrs. Dance gasped and she placed a comforting hand upon my arm. "You cannot trust such fancies, Miss Holme, sometimes at night the mind may play tricks."

I might, indeed, have mistaken it for a picture; for it now reflected a half-length portrait of a singularly beautiful woman, seated in the very heart of a dimly-lit chamber. She was, as I had first observed, absorbed in the perusal of a letter, an expression of profound melancholy etching her refined features.

The glow from a single taper cast a delicate halo around her, accentuating the folds of her gown, which seemed to whisper of bygone eras. It was not merely her allure that captivated me, but the aura of quiet sorrow that enveloped her like a shroud, rendering her presence both haunting and entrancing.

As my eyes dared to lift and meet hers, I was confronted with a pair of eyes as striking as they were intense. They were the color of the twilight sky, possessing an inexplicable depth that betrayed a complexity beyond mere beauty. She regarded me with a haughty stare that was both disdainful and veiled by a hint of recognition. Her eyebrows, delicately arched, seemed to cast inscrutable shadows over her face.

In that instant, I was seized by an inexplicable sentiment, a tumult of emotions that I could not, nor indeed wished to, readily comprehend. My heart, hitherto immune to the vagaries of love, now beat wildly in a maelstrom of feelings, at once alluring and bewildering. It was an impulse, both curious and embarrassed, to have intruded upon her solitude, yet the privilege of beholding her presence rendered the impertinence of my presence tolerable.

Yet, to my astonishment, she was the first to break the silence weaving itself between us. Addressing me in a melodious voice that seemed to emanate from a distant land, she inquired in French, her words tinged with a subtle reproach, "Monsieur, may I ask what brings you into my sanctuary?"

Her question was as much a statement of her discomfiture as it was a reminder of the boundaries she had unwittingly allowed me to cross. I replied, attempting to match her poise, "Madame, I am but an inadvertent trespasser, seeking only the solace of your serene surroundings."

She regarded me again, her violet eyes assessing the sincerity of my words, before acquiescing with an air of reluctance, "Then, in the interest of our previous acquaintance, and given your assistance of which I am grateful, remain but a moment longer."

As she said this, a shadow flitted through her chamber, casting a fleeting, almost sinister silhouette against the wall. It was as if an unseen presence had marked the limits of her tolerance. Embarrassed anew by my intrusion, and with a lingering image of that fleeting shadow, I bowed respectfully and took my leave, feeling both flattered and slightly alarmed by our unique encounter.

As I departed, the chamber's walls seemed to close in behind me, as if sealing the memory of her gaze within the confines of my own heart. The night, ever thickening, enveloped me, and yet within its cloak, her image danced, an elusive enigma that I could not immediately exorcise.

Hours passed, veiled in the uncertainty of dreams, as I replayed our exchange in my mind. Her voice, like a distant melody, lingered in my thoughts, mingling with the echoes of my own inarticulate desires. I was left to ponder the mystery of her presence, the nature of her melancholy, and the truth behind the shadow that had darkened her chamber.

The next day, I found myself wandering the city streets, attempting to quell the questions that tormented my mind. Yet, it was as if the city itself conspired to obscure the truth, its labyrinthine paths leading me ever further from the sanctuary I had, however momentarily, envied.

It was upon my return to the quietude of my own abode that I encountered a letter, seemingly awaiting my arrival. The seal, ornate and familiar, bore the mark of the very lady who had so unexpectedly dominated my thoughts. My heart quickened, anticipation warring with incertitude, as I broke the seal and unfurled the parchment.

"Dear Monsieur," it began, in a script as elegant as the flow of her speech, "I have much to thank you for. Our paths may have crossed by chance, but I believe, as does my heart, that our connection shall endure."

My fingers trembled as they traced the familiar handwriting, each letter a testament to the lingering influence of her presence. As I read on, I was struck by a realization that our encounter, fleeting and fraught with quiet tension, had sparked the kindling of an affection that defied explanation.

In moments like these, I wished fervently for the ability to articulate the tumult of emotions that swirled within me. Yet, as I pondered her words, and the enigma that was her presence, I understood that love, when intertwined with mystery, often defies logic, remaining forever enigmatic, a riddle to be solved in the chambers of the heart.

That anxious summer, so heavily shadowed by cholera's darkly spreading wings, found me stubbornly keeping to my own humble rooms near Temple Bar, notwithstanding the advice of more cautious acquaintances who urged my swift retreat. George, encumbered as he was with wife and children, had wisely withdrawn to a breezy cottage in Kent, a pleasant situation which he assured me was tolerably safe from contagion, though none could say for certain how securely Providence had there drawn the intolerable circle of pestilence. Our correspondence took place regularly, bearing tidings more cheerfully inclined from him, yet tempered by earnest admonitions for my care. For myself, had I been governed merely by apprehension, no sooner would I have stayed near Fleet Street than would a sailor take to a leaking boat; but duty called me to remain, and moreover, my habits of handling poisons and chemicals in pursuit of scientific enquiries had lately inspired within me a curious calmness, bordering perhaps recklessly upon defiance. Only poor Mrs. Crumple, my dear landlady, gave rise to present disquietude, her pallid face and trembling hand betraying constant fears, and her ceaseless remedies, chiefly vinegar fumigations and aromatic herbs, making the premises so pungently disagreeable that even the cat retreated in disgust.

Under these circumstances it was an unforeseen event, during the height of that sweltering July, that would soon alter the quiet tenor of my days, and introduce an adventure both perilous and curious in its complexion. One sultry evening, while I sat absorbed in the perusal of a treatise recently printed by the Royal Society, a sharp knock sounded insistently upon my door. So rarely had guests sought my chambers recently that for a moment I scarcely recognized the signal, nor yet remembered the due civilities attached thereto; but hastening at length to open the door, curious as to who might thus intrude upon my solitude, I discovered upon my threshold a young gentleman of troubled countenance and haggard eye—one whose refined features belied the careworn negligence of his attire, and whose anxious bearing seemed tightly coiled, inspector-like in its intensity. He held something wrapped in a kerchief, cradled carefully in his arm, as though precious beyond ordinary estimations.

"Mr. Phillips, Sir?" he inquired gravely, bowing slightly and interposing with breathless haste. I gave my assent and invited him inside, wondering greatly at this unsought visitation. He entered swiftly, closing the door briskly and glancing apprehensively over his shoulder, as though pursued by unseen spectres. "Forgive me this intrusion," he began, his voice strained and proving the urgency behind his visit, "but word of your scientific reputation has spread wide enough to include even the distant corners of Yorkshire. In my possession, Sir, is an instrument—a watch whose operation both perplexes and troubles me with most awful presentiments. My own family physician assures me I suffer from mere superstition or nervous strain owing to the current public distress. But I swear, Mr. Phillips, upon my honour, that since coming into this accursed object's possession, I have been afflicted with the most frightful dreams, and have grown weak in both body and spirit till the sight of my own shadow has become hateful to me."

All this he narrated in hurried accents, uncovering meanwhile the object in question: a beautiful and substantial timepiece of solid gold, the very counterpart of the Barwise watches numbered 7777 and 7778 which George and I had chosen. The watch the stranger laid before me was indeed also of Barwise's exquisite workmanship, yet it was numbered 7776—thus falling immediately before our own cherished pair in that curious numerical sequence I had myself marked upon acquisition. Examining closely, I felt at once the astonishment of the coincidence and an inexpressible uneasiness at the singularity of its condition; for though seemingly perfect in appearance, the watch ticked irregularly, almost feverishly, and its hands continually faltered, hesitating slightly at certain intervals, as though desperately endeavouring yet failing to overcome some internal hindrance. The young man gazed upon me anxiously, hopeful yet apprehensive that from my presumed knowledge some easy solution might soon present itself to dispel his growing terror, though at the same moment a dreadful loudness of commotion sounded below-stairs, and Mrs. Crumple flew upward, crying out in sharp distress that the cholera had found its way into the very street, a proclamation fit to shake even the bravest spirit into dread.

Launcelot Linzie had his reasons (apparently) for declining to let his host offend him on any terms whatever.

"Thank you!" he rejoined, in a tone of satirical good humor. "It isn't easy to keep my place on board your vessel. I can't help presuming to enjoy myself as if I was the owner. The life is such a new on–o me! It's so delightfully easy, for instance, to wash yourself here. On shore it's a complicated question of jugs and basins and tubs; one is always in danger of breaking something, or spoiling something. Here you have only to jump out of bed, to run up on deck, and to do this!"

He turned, and scampered to the bows of the vessel. In one instant he was out of his night-gown, in another he was on the bulwark, in a third he was gamboling luxuriously in sixty fathoms of salt-water.

Turlington's eyes followed him with a reluctant, uneasy attention as he swam round the vessel, the only moving object in view. Turlington's mind, steady and slow in all its operations, set him a problem to be solved, on given conditions, as follows:

"Launcelot Linzie is fifteen years younger than I am. Add to that, Launcelot Linzie is Natalie Graybrooke's cousin. Given those two advantage–uery: Has he taken Natalie's fancy?"

Turning that question slowly over and over in his mind, Richard Turlington seated himself in a corner at the stern of the vessel. He was still at work on the problem, when the young surgeon returned to his cabin to put the finishing touches to his toilet. He had not reached the solution when the steward appeared an hour later and said, "Breakfast is ready, sir!"

They were a party of five round the cabin table.

First, Sir Joseph Graybrooke. Inheritor of a handsome fortune made by his father and his grandfather in trade. Mayor, twice elected, of a thriving provincial town. Officially privileged, while holding that dignity, to hand a silver trowel to a royal personage condescending to lay a first stone of a charitable edifice. Frank then relieved his sable friend of the wheel.

“We will assume the first watch,” he suggested.

“To be sho’,” assented Pomp. “Am yo’ satisfied wif her, Massa Frank?”

“Yes; the machine is certainly the greatest invention I have ever turned out. And she’s the simplest kind of an air-ship to work. It is only necessary to elevate the angle of the propeller plane, drive her faster, and ascend to any height. To go down, the impinging edge of the forward plane is simply depressed, and she descends. To remain at a fixed altitude we have only to keep the rudder perfectly horizontal.”

“No gas bags to bust wif dis high flyer.”

“And as long as our mechanism operates she’ll go ahead.”

“But s’posin’ de propellers done stop?”

“She would fall gently, as her planes would act on the wind like parachutes,” replied Frank, promptly.

“Dat make her safer yet, don’ it, chile?”

“Of course,” Frank assented, with a nod.

“Yo’ gwine straight to de Gulf of Mexico?”

“I am. In two or three days we’ll reach it, too.”

“Dat am if nuffin’ happen, sah.”

Frank nodded and smiled, and examined the electric motors to see that the current did not vary.

The dynamo was working under full load of five hundred volts, with an output of thirty kilowatts at the terminals, and as the gloom of night had fallen, Frank turned one of the switches.

It sent the electric current into the searchlight, and a brilliant flood of fifty thousand candle power light gushed out.

A funnel-shaped streak of white light was projected a mile ahead by the powerful lens, and the barometer showed the inventor that they had gone up to a height of nine hundred and sixty rods, or three miles.

People on the earth imagined the searchlight was a comet with an extremely long tail, when the clouds did not conceal its flight across the firmament.

Although the wind was dead ahead, and the strata they were in blew at the velocity of fifty miles an hour, the Jove was forging into it at the rate of forty miles an hour.

Frank depressed the rudder, and the machine slowly drifted downward, as she was then in an extremely cold region.

At two o’clock Zamora and Barney relieved the inventor and the coon, who thereupon turned in.

The airship traveled stiffly, steadily and well for two days, traversing the continent in a southerly direction and passing the most diversified scenery.

When night fell upon the scene again the sky had a dark, ominous appearance.

Indeed, Frank realized that as they were in the tropical cyclone region he had cause to fear a heavy storm, and for that reason he refused to retire.

Barney remained up with him that night.

Toward midnight the airship stood at an altitude of 5,280 feet in the air, when a jet-black cloud was encountered.

She was rushing toward it, and the cloud ran at her.

In a moment she was shot into the middle of it.

Her entrance into the cloud seemed to agitate it.

At first the motion was easy, but gradually it intensified, and began to shake and toss the Jove.

Then it began to whirl.

Soon this motion grew furious.

The airship was checked in its flight, and spun around with the gyrating cloud at an appalling speed.

“A cyclone!” gasped Frank, in alarm.

“Look out!” yelled Barney. “We’re upsettin’!”

The Jove was suddenly hurled high up into the air like a mere wisp of straw in the terrible blast.

It was then dashed downward by a reacting gust, and as it fell, it swung over upon its side and suddenly capsized.

A scene of terrible confusion followed.

In the solitary expanse of the Great Plains, where the wind howled like an unaware specter, stood a modest homestead, its walls weathered by the relentless sun and harsh winters. Mrs. Sellers sat on the front porch of her humble abode, her eyes scanning the horizon, and her mind drifting with the free-flowing thoughts that seemed to dance on the breeze. She had always been a woman of quiet strength, her spirit unbroken by the unyielding hardness of life on the frontier.

Colonel Sellers, her husband, was a man of mystique and contradiction. Some saw him as a failure, a shadow unfortunately attached to those he sought desperately to lift. Yet, he labored on, his heart as vast as the land he tried to tame, ever ready to lend a hand to the downtrodden and the desperate. His latest obsession, Washington Hawkins, had piqued his interest. The Colonel was convinced that Hawkins, despite his lack of official recognition or structure, possessed potential as vast as a desert that awaited the first rain.

"Mrs. Sellers, dear wife, I've been meaning to discuss a matter with you," Colonel Sellers began, his voice as amiable as a summer's evening. "I've hit upon an idea, an idea that could change the course of Hawkins' life and, by extension, our own."

Mrs. Sellers turned from her fantastical thoughts to her husband, her eyes reflecting the warmth of her regard. "Pray, tell me, Colonel," she coaxed, her voice gentle as a mother's lullaby.

Colonel Sellers expelled a breath, his eyes gleaming with the zeal of a true believer. "Hawkins, with his vast acres of presumably fertile land but lacking formal title, is a treasure waiting to be discovered. I see in him a man with a noble heart, enough charisma to sway the hearts of the two hundred souls who call the region home."

Mrs. Sellers chuckled, a sound as sweet as the dandelion blossoms that dotted their acreage. "But Colonel, the land is uncharted, the population insignificant. What influence could he hope to wield in the great political machine of this nation?"

"Ah, my dear," the Colonel replied, his eyes twinkling, "Influence is not merely about numbers or titles. It's about conviction, about the power of a good speech, about the ability to kindle the spark of possibility in the darkest corners of the soul. Hawkins, I believe, possesses all these qualities, though he may not yet see them for the assets they are."

"But Colonel," Mrs. Sellers protested, her expression one of amused exasperation, "What could you possibly do to help him? The government pays us no mind, the law recognizes us not. Hawkins is but a speck on the vast map of the nation."

Colonel Sellers, undeterred, threw up his hands in a grand gesture, his smile as broad as the sun. "Why, organize him, dear wife! Organize him up like a well-oiled machine. A populace that has never seen itself as a unit, unified under a banner of purpose and hope, can be a formidable force. We'll write to the government, ask for a territorial recognition, perhaps even a seat in the legislature. We'll show them what Hawkins and his people are capable of."

Mrs. Sellers raised an eyebrow, a hint of skepticism in her eyes. "An ambitious goal, Colonel. Yet, I fear the government's heart may not be so open to our cause."

The Colonel waved a hand dismissively, his faith in his vision undeterred. "Ah, you underestimate the power of a good speech, dear wife. Washington himself has risen from the most humble of beginnings, only to stand as the father of our nation. Hawkins, too, can rise if we but give him the stepping stone. I see in him a man whose heart beats with the rhythms of America, a man whose soul is intertwined with the great tapestry of this land."

As the Colonel's words floated in the air, Mrs. Sellers couldn't help but smile, her heart warming at his optimism. Despite the world's use and discard of him, he remained steadfast, his heart never deterred from the lofty ideals that burned within him. She remembered a time, long ago, when they had first met at a small gathering in the East, his eyes ablaze with the same passion that fueled him now. She had been drawn to him then, and that attraction had only deepened with time.

Colonel Sellers was a failure in the eyes of the world, yet she counted him among her most precious possessions. His unwavering belief in people, his boundless generosity, and his inherent kindness—all these qualities made him, to her, a true success. She loved him for his mistakes, his flaws, his enduring optimism, and his unyielding pursuit of the impossible.

"So, dear wife," he continued, his hands clasped behind his back, his eyes scanning the horizon, "what do you say to my plan?"

Mrs. Sellers sighed, her gaze falling on the wild, untended land that stretched out before them.

The town of Micklethwayte was rising and thriving. There were salubrious springs which an enterprising doctor had lately brought into notice. The firm of Greenleaf and Dutton manufactured umbrellas in large quantities, from the stout weather-proof family roof down to the daintiest fringed toy of a parasol. There were a Guild Hall and a handsome Corn Market. There was a Modern School for the boys, and a High School for the girls, and a School of Art, and a School of Cookery, and National Schools, and a British School, and a Board School, also churches of every height, chapels of every denomination, and iron mission rooms budding out in hopes to be replaced by churches.

Like one of the animals which zoologists call radiated, the town was constantly stretching out fresh arms along country roads, all living and working, and gradually absorbing the open spaces between. One of these arms was known as St. Ambrose's Road, in right of the church, an incomplete structure in yellow brick, consisting of a handsome chancel, the stump of a tower, and one aisle just weather-tight and usable, but, by its very aspect, begging for the completion of the beautiful design that was suspended above the alms-box.

It was the evening of a summer day which had been very hot. The choir practice was just over, and the boys came out trooping and chattering; very small ones they were; for as soon as they began to sing tolerably they were sure to try to get into the choir of the old church, which had a foundation that fed, clothed, taught, and finally apprenticed them. So, though the little fellows were clad in surplices and cassocks, and sat in the chancel for correctness sake, there was a space round the harmonium reserved for the more trustworthy band of girls and young women who came forth next, followed by four or five mechanics.

Behind came the nucleus of the choir--a slim, fair-haired youth of twenty; a neat, precise, well-trimmed man, closely shaven, with stooping shoulders, at least fifteen years older, with a black poodle at his heels, as well shorn as his master, newly risen from lying outside the church door; a gentle, somewhat drooping lady in black, not yet middle-aged and very pretty; a small eager, unformed, black-eyed girl, who could hardly keep back her words for the outside of the church door; a tall self-possessed handsome woman, with a fine classical cast of features; and lastly, a brown-faced, wiry hardworking clergyman, without an atom of superfluous flesh, but with an air of great energy.

'Oh! vicar, where are we to go?' was the question so eager to break forth.

'Not to the Crystal Palace, Nuttie. The funds won't bear it. Mr. Dutton says we must spend as little as possible on locomotion.'

'I'm sure I don't care for the Crystal Palace. A trumpery tinsel place, all shams.'

'Hush, hush, my dear, not so loud,' said the quiet lady; but Nuttie only wriggled her shoulders, though her voice was a trifle lowered. 'If it were the British Museum now, or Westminster Abbey.'

'Or the Alps,' chimed in a quieter voice, 'or the Ufizzi.'

'Now, Mr. Dutton, that's not what I want. Our people aren't ready for that, but what they have let it be real. Miss Mary, don't you see what I mean?'

'Rather better than Miss Egremont herself,' said Mr. Dutton.

'Well,' said the vicar, interposing in the wordy war, 'Mrs. Greenleaf's children have scarlatina, so we can't go to Horton Bishop. The choice seems to be between South Beach and Monks Horton.'

The weary voice quivered and failed here, and the man sank back in his chair with a bitter sigh.

The young girl, her own face now blanched to the hue of death, laid down her work, arose, and moved swiftly to her father's side, where she knelt by his chair.

"Papa, do not talk so. You must not leave me," she cried, in a voice of agony. "I cannot spare you. There must be something to help yo–o build up your strength. Let us go back home, where you can have the best medical advice."

The man sat up in his chair, stopping her with a gesture almost of despair.

"Home!" he cried, hoarsely. "Virgie, we have no home but this. You know that I am already the same as dead to every one but you; that even our real name is sunk in oblivion."

"But, papa, you must try to live for my sake," Virgie cried, clasping her trembling hands about his emaciated arm, and shuddering as she felt how frail it was. "If you will not go back, let me at least send for Dr. Truel. He is skillful. He was always our friend. He will cheer you and give you something to build you up, and he will keep our secret, too. Oh, you ought to have had advice long ago. What shall I do in this dreary place if you leave me alone?"

The sick man unclasped her clinging hands from his arm, and drew her slight form to him in a tender embrace.

"My darling," he said, fondly, "that is just what I wish to talk with you about; so calm yourself and listen to me. Neither Dr. Truel, nor any other doctor, can help me now; if I had called him a year ago he might have prolonged my life; but my pride would not let me face any one whom I had ever known. But I will not speak of the past; it is too familiar and painful to both of us. It is useless, however, for me to think for a moment of going back, even to die, in the home where we were once so happy, for only disgrace is connected with our nam–isgrace and wrong, all the more keenly felt because unmerited."

"Hush, Virgie!" he continued, as a shuddering sob burst from the breast pressed so closely to his, "you must not give way so. I did not mean to alarm you unnecessarily by what I have said; I may not leave you for some time yet. I may be spared for a few months, perhaps until autumn, but I feel that the time has come to arrange some definite plan for your future. I must, however, give up my work, for I have no longer strength to carry it on; but if there was only some one whom I could trust to take charge of my claim. I might even yet reap something of benefit from it to add to the hoard that I have been saving for you against this emergency."

"But, papa, I would much rather that you should spend every dollar that you have, if it would prolong your life; if I lose you, I have not a friend in the world."

The man heaved a heavy sigh, for too well he realized the truth of her words.

"My dear," he returned, with tender pathos, "if it were possible for me to regain my health, at any sacrifice, I would gladly make it for your sake. But I know that it cannot be, and my care now must be to make the best provision that I can for you."

"I have been very successful since coming here," he went on, speaking more cheerfully, "more so than I ever dared to hope, and the claim promises much for the future and ought to bring a good price if sold; so you will have quite a snug little fortune, my Virgie, and I trust that your lot in life will yet be happy, in spite of the dark cloud that has so shadowed it in the beginning. What say you to writing to my old friend, Laurence Bancroft, of New York, confiding you to his care after----"

"Yes," said my father, "there is no doubt about it; it is the best thing to do. So that is decided."

The "yes" was no expression of agreement with any one but himself. It was simply the emphatic reiteration of the decision he had already arrived at.

He folded up the letter he had been reading, and replaced it carefully and methodically in its envelope, then glanced round the breakfast-table with the slightly defiant, slightly deprecating, yet nevertheless wholly good-tempered air which we all knew well--so well that not one of us would have dreamt of wasting time or energy by beating his or her wings against the bars of the dear man's resolute determination.

Some faces fell a little, others expressed philosophic resignation, one or two, perhaps, a kind of subdued exhilaration; but no one said anything except mother, who replied quietly, as was her wont--

"Very well; I daresay you are right."

Then ensued a little talk as to the details of the proposal, or rather decision, just announced, and five minutes later the family group had dispersed.

The one face on which something more than resignation had been distinctly legible was that of my youngest brother, Moore.

He was only fourteen, an age at which--for boy nature especially--it does not take much provocation to get up one's spirits to some pitch of agreeable excitement and expectancy. He ran after me as I left the dining-room, and followed me down the long cold stone passage leading to what he and my other brothers and I myself considered our own quarters. Then, as he overtook me, he slipped his hand through my arm.

"Do you mind, Reggie?" he said in a tone of some deprecation of his own satisfaction. "I think you might be a little pleased--any way for my sake. It's awfully jolly for me."

"Then I will be pleased, really pleased, my poor old Othello," I replied, heartily, I think. For Moore was our baby and pet, and we thought him irresistible. He was so pretty--everybody said that he, and not I, should have been the girl, if only one girl there was to be among us. He was fair-haired and fair-complexioned, yet not insipid looking, for his eyes were deeply blue, or at least appeared so, thanks to their bordering of dark eyelashes. "Irish eyes," though in other respects Moore's beauty was decidedly of the Saxon type. He had a right to his Irish eyes, as the rest of us to our Irish locks and browner skin. For Irish we were, really so as to ancestry, and in many particulars as to inherited character, though none of us, not even my parents since their childhood, had ever been in Ireland.

Moore's face beamed, and lost its half-apologetic expression.

"Good old Reggie," he said. "Then I'll let myself be jolly right out, however Terry and Horry and Ger grumble at mother and you going away before the holidays are over," and he showed signs of whooping or hurrahing or something of the kind, which I hastened to nip in the bud.

"You had better be quiet about it, however you feel," I said warningly, "or father will begin to think you don't need change and rest, and all that kind of thing, after all."

"No, he won't," the boy replied confidently. "He never goes back once he's settled a thing. You know he never does, Reggie. Sometimes," and here certain reminiscences momentarily sobered his expression, "sometimes I wish he would--"

"And," I continued, "you'd better not let Terence and Gerald hear you talk of holidays. They don't own to anything but vacations now."

"That's just because they're not really grown-up," said Moore shrewdly; "at least not out in the world. Look at Jocelyn now--he might give himself airs. But he always talks of his holidays when he comes home. He very seldom even calls it `leave,' though he is--how old is he now, Rex? Twenty-five? Yes--eleven years older than I."

He sat for some time in Gumley’s trim little parlor, where everything bespoke the handy Jack Tar, chatting about sea life in general and the Ariadne in particular. Then the talk came round to Jack’s new vessel, the Fury, and brought up the question of smuggling.

"Mr. Gudgeon said that a good deal goes on about here," said Jack, "and by George! my cousin, Mr. Bastable, told me that the villains ran a cargo ashore only last night. I suppose he met the riding-officer as he went for his morning canter. Did you hear anything of it?"

"Not a word, sir. I keep myself to myself."

"Yes, Mr. Gudgeon said much the same thing, I remember. But I suppose you hear talk in the village sometimes?"

"Never bin into the village since I gave up fishing, sir. I get all my victuals from Wynport, and often don’t set eyes on the village folk from week-end to week-end, except at Church at Wickham Ferrers on Sunday."

"Why you’re quite a hermit—almost as bad as Congleton."

"True, sir, but I’ve never bin crossed in love, ’cos I never seed a maid I fancied afore I lost my leg, and there’s ne’er a maid would take a fancy to a poor chap with a stump like this. And I’m afeard of going like Congleton, sir."

"Yes, but, Gumley, never mind about that. Tell me straight out, man; are the people in Luscombe below there smugglers or not—the whole crew of ’em, I mean?"

"Well, since you put it plain, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of ’em think a sight more of French brandy than of Jamaica rum."

"That’s no answer, you old rascal. Well, I’m going down to the village to have a look round. I saw some neat little smacks at the jetty yesterday, and one of ’em put out pretty smartly, too: was uncommonly well handled."

"Well, sir, you be a fine, mettlesome young gentleman; but if so be as I might advise you, I’d say keep your weather-eye open. If so be they are a smuggling lot below—well, they won’t be exactly main pleased to see a king’s officer."

"Bless you, they won’t know me. I’m not in uniform, you see. Nobody knows who I am but my cousins and you and Mr. Gudgeon."

"True, sir; and me and Mr. Gudgeon keeps ourselves to ourselves, to be sure."
