The dahlias, in their vibrant splendor, were a testament to Mr. Cooper's artistry, but it was the memory of Copenhagen that lingered. For who could forget the sight of the Duke's own charger, grazing peacefully in the paddock, a living legend enjoying a well-deserved rest? Named after one of Mr. Cooper's most striking dahlias, a bloom of deepest crimson, Copenhagen carried the weight of history upon his broad back.

The late Duchess, a renowned horsewoman herself, had ensured Copenhagen's every comfort after his retirement from the battlefield. Oats of the finest quality, a rubdown with a silk cloth, and always, a kind word and a gentle pat - such was the life of the Duke's charger at Strathfield-saye. When his time came, it was a peaceful passing, a soldier laid to rest with honor amongst the whispering trees of the estate. Yet, even in death, Copenhagen’s fame proved a double-edged sword. A group of overzealous admirers, unable to contain their fervor, disturbed his final resting place, seeking a relic of the great horse, a piece of history to claim as their own. The incident caused quite a stir, a blemish on the legacy of the noble steed, a stark reminder that even the most hallowed ground is not immune to the trespasses of ill-judged enthusiasm. But Copenhagen's story, much like the ruins of Reading Abbey, was not defined by a single act, no matter how jarring. His image, captured in a portrait by young Master Edmund Havell, continued to grace the halls of Strathfield-saye.

The painting, commissioned by the late Duke himself, was a testament not only to Copenhagen's stature but also to the burgeoning talent of young Havell. The artist, barely a man when he received the commission, had poured his heart and soul into capturing the essence of the warhorse. The result was a masterpiece of light and shadow, of power restrained and dignity earned. The brushstrokes, confident yet delicate, breathed life into the canvas, making Copenhagen almost leap from the frame, a flicker of battle still burning in his eye. The painting hung in the main hall, a silent sentinel guarding the memories of a bygone era. The Duchess often remarked that the portrait captured not only Copenhagen's physical likeness but also the indomitable spirit that had carried the Duke to victory. Havell, with his keen eye and steady hand, had managed to immortalize not just a horse, but a symbol of courage and loyalty, qualities as timeless as the stones of Reading Abbey itself.

"You may laugh at your sister, little one; but it will not be long before you do the same!" said Don Mateo.

"I pray for a man! You are getting imbecile, señor."

"It won't be long before I hear of it," returned the old man, as he passed on to another box to greet the Señores de Maza.

At that moment Pablito joined his family, accompanied by his faithful friend, who merits special notice.

He was the son of the picador, the famous bull slayer, of the place, and the cast of the lad's features was such as would have been the delight of the spectators at a circus. His face would have required no addition in the way of powder, rouge, or dye to convert him into a clown. The nose, highly colored by nature, the narrow slits of eyes, the lack of any mustache or whiskers, the thick lips, the excessive width of his shoulders, the bow of his legs, and, above all, the facial contortions which accompanied every word he uttered, were provocative of mirth without the aid of paint or wig. Piscis, for so he was called, was aware of this peculiarity, and resented it so intensely that he resolved to counteract the ludicrous cast of his features by determining never to laugh, and he religiously kept to his decision. Moreover, he, for the same reason, interspersed his remarks with the sharpest, strongest interjections of the vernacular, varied by those of his own invention. But this, instead of producing the desired effect, only added to the amusement he provoked among his acquaintances.

The only person who ever took him seriously--up to a certain point--was Pablito. Piscis and Pablito were born to inspire each other with mutual love and admiration. The point of union between the two kindred spirits was "the cult of the horse-god." Piscis, through his father, was an adept in that line from a child; and as the best mount in Sarrio, he was the object of Pablito's warmest admiration, and the son of Don Rosendo being the richest young fellow of the place, there was, according to Piscis, no person in the world more deserving of respect and admiration.

Nobody knew when this friendship had begun; Pablito and Piscis had always been inseparable from the time they were children, and the difference of their social positions did not separate them as they grew up to manhood. Don Rosendo's stable was their constant place of meeting; from thence, after a long and erudite conference, partly theoretical, partly practical on the horses, they proceeded to betake their presence and their profound knowledge to the town, where they took a few turns, sometimes on high-spirited horses, and at other times in a smart trap, with Pablito driving, and Piscis absorbed in affectionate contemplation of the backs of the animals. On some occasions, however, they gave the town a lesson of humility by perambulating on their own legs. Pablito now came up to his family party convulsed with laughter.

"What has come over you?" asked Doña Paula, smiling in sympathy.

"We just followed Periquito to the gallery, and there we found him hand in hand with Ramona," whispered the young man into his sister Venturita's ear.

"Well, what did he say?" she asked with great curiosity.

"He said"--and here a burst of laughter interrupted him for some minutes--"he said, 'Ramona, I love you.'"

"Ave Maria! and an anchovy seller, too!" exclaimed the girl, joining in the laugh, and making the sign of the cross.

"If you could have heard the trembling voice in which he said it, and the way in which he turned up the whites of his eyes---- Ah! here is Piscis, who was also witness of it."

An observation, if one may be permitted to indulge in such an inclination, will reveal the palpable absurdity into which the genteel semblance of a dinner party often collapses. It is not merely the tedious recurrence of the ragout, the inexorable return of boiled potatoes—it is the very architecture of the event itself; a mausoleum of culinary predictability where every guest is enjoined to adopt a mask of delight, while beneath that fine facade, the truth is harboured in secret murmurs and suppressed yawns. As our eager host stands at the head of the table, brandishing his silver fork as though it were a knight's sword, we become acutely aware of the tiresome ritual that binds us—every course served with a flimsy politeness, every toast pronounced with pomp enough to rival a royal occasion, and every exchange of pleasantries positively laden with insincerity. In such a tempest of artifice, one might lose a sense of self, submerged beneath the elaborate drapery of etiquette.

It was during one such interminable supper, a gathering of local notables to which I had been all but condemned by circumstance, that I took distinct stock of my aversion towards the monotony of social discussions wrapped neatly in a bow of compliance. I sat, inconspicuous in my corner, awash in an ocean of genteel conversation; the progeny of physicians and bankers, insinuating their ambitions upon the tablecloth. As the courses paraded themselves—a mediocre consomme followed by a zesty fowl—the seeds of my discontent burgeoned into a full blooming resolve. Each forkful resonated with the hollow clangour of a bell tolling the death knell of my aspirations, and in that moment, fraught with gastronomical anguish, I resolved to sever my ties from the odious quagmire of medical profession to which I had adhered with a guileless fervor.

Thus I descended, as it were, from that lofty station of medical expertise to embrace a far humbler alternative—an artist’s vocation replete with the joys of anonymity. My talents, another consequence of my public schooling amidst a mine of stifling decorum, had flourished into a delightful dispensation of caricatures—vivid, oftentimes grotesque renderings of individuals whose grandeur was effaced in their representation. In secret corners, far from the prying eyes of my esteemed family, I invited the voyeurs of society into the ribs of my pencil and the ink of my wit. Each stroke of the quill was a form of liberation, each delineated figure a step away from the mundane expectations that had sought to ensnare my spirit within the cloister of conventionality.

Anonymity, my dearest friend, became vast as the expanse of the sea, yet brimming with the charge of possibility. I soon found myself in possession of considerable financial return, the fruits of my labor yet to be clutched by the hands of the family that reared me—a family entirely oblivious to my nocturnal pursuits. In the dark hours of the night, I sketched the likeness of well-known individuals, society’s darlings, their flaws magnified through the lens of jovial critique. Who could fault a man for serving art to a hungry audience that revelled in the nuances of human folly? Yet the irony of my situation layered itself atop my conscience like a rich cream upon stale bread; for while I danced through lanes of financial emancipation, I should have been donning the garb of propriety, prescribing remedies and sounding the heights of hospitals as an adroit physician.

Each caricature I drafted served as a mirror not merely to the subject’s visage but to the hollow precisions of societal propriety itself. Did I not wield a brush against the trivialities and fleeting vanities of our shared existence? Consequently, my evenings transformed from dull gastronomical banquets to vivid celebrations of absurdities. Should my esteemed family one day uncloak the truth of my sidelong enterprises, what grand ruckus would they stage? What conscientious collision between their aspirations and my newfound identity! Yet, even as folly danced through my mind, I could not help but smile at the very idea, all the while sharpening my pencils, preparing for the exhilarating journey ahead, unfettered by the weighty chains of convention and resplendent in my exploration of humanity’s follies.

"If you please, Mister, I was the first you know," said Clemency Newcome. "She was a walking out here, before sunrise, you remember. I was in the house."

"That's true! Clemency was the first," said Alfred. "So I defy you with Clemency."

"Ha, ha, ha!--for Self and Craggs," said Snitchey. "What a defiance!"

"Not so bad a one as it appears, may be," said Alfred, shaking hands heartily with the Doctor, and also with Snitchey and Craggs, and then looking round. "Where are the--Good Heavens!"

With a start, productive for the moment of a closer partnership between Jonathan Snitchey and Thomas Craggs than the subsisting articles of agreement in that wise contemplated, he hastily betook himself to where the sisters stood together, and--however, I needn't more particularly explain his manner of saluting Marion first, and Grace afterwards, than by hinting that Mr. Craggs may possibly have considered it "too easy."

Perhaps to change the subject, Doctor Jeddler made a hasty move towards the breakfast, and they all sat down at table. Grace presided; but so discreetly stationed herself, as to cut off her sister and Alfred from the rest of the company. Snitchey and Craggs sat at opposite corners, with the blue bag between them for safety; and the Doctor took his usual position, opposite to Grace. Clemency hovered galvanically about the table, as waitress; and the melancholy Britain, at another and a smaller board, acted as Grand Carver of a round of beef, and a ham.

"Meat?" said Britain, approaching Mr. Snitchey, with the carving knife and fork in his hands, and throwing the question at him like a missile.

"Certainly," returned the lawyer.

"Do you want any?" to Craggs.

"Lean, and well done," replied that gentleman.

Having executed these orders, and moderately supplied the Doctor (he seemed to know that nobody else wanted anything to eat), he lingered as near the Firm as he decently could, watching, with an austere eye, their disposition of the viands, and but once relaxing the severe expression of his face. This was on the occasion of Mr. Craggs, whose teeth were not of the best, partially choking, when he cried out with great animation, "I thought he was gone!"

"Now Alfred," said the Doctor, "for a word or two of business, while we are yet at breakfast."

"While we are yet at breakfast," said Snitchey and Craggs, who seemed to have no present idea of leaving off.

Although Alfred had not been breakfasting, and seemed to have quite enough business on his hands as it was, he respectfully answered:

"If you please, Sir."

"If anything could be serious," the Doctor began, "in such a--"

"Farce as this, Sir," hinted Alfred.

"In such a farce as this," observed the Doctor, "it might be this recurrence, on the eve of separation, of a double birth-day, which is connected with many associations pleasant to us four, and with the recollection of a long and amicable intercourse. That's not to the purpose."

"Ah! yes, yes, Doctor Jeddler," said the young man. "It is to the purpose. Much to the purpose, as my heart bears witness this morning; and as yours does too, I know, if you would let it speak. I leave your house to-day; I cease to be your ward to-day; we part with tender relations stretching far behind us, that never can be exactly renewed, and with others dawning yet before us," he looked down at Marion beside him, "fraught with such considerations as I must not trust myself to speak of now. Come, come!" he added, rallying his spirits and the Doctor at once, "there's a serious grain in this large foolish dust-heap, Doctor. Let us allow to-day, that there is One."

Crane, that singular fellow, had a way of wringing poetry from the very guts of despair, did he not? One feels it, reading his tales of men and their boats, the rasp of salt spray and the gnawing hunger born of shipwreck. He knew suffering, that much is plain. He saw it plain, too, and set it down with a starkness that could make your teeth ache. But what comes next is my own attempt to follow the spirit of his writings, to try and capture his poetic prose and relentless sense of motion.

The sun, a molten penny in the grimy sky, beat down upon the cobblestones of the Rue de la Poissonnerie. It was a day fit to fry eggs on paving stones, a day when even the gutters seemed to exhale heat like the breath of some colossal beast. Monsieur Dubois, a man whose trade involved gutting fish rather than catching them, stood before his stall, a tableau of damp aprons and shimmering scales. Usually, he reveled in the cacophony of the market, the haggling and the squawks of vendors, but today, the noise scraped against his nerves like a rusty knife. Trade was poor. The fish lay limp and unappealing on their beds of ice, mirroring, perhaps, the despair in Dubois's own heart. His wife, Marie, had fallen ill, a fever that clung to her like a persistent vine. The doctor, a pompous fellow with a waxed mustache and pronouncements that cost more than medicine, had spoken of leeches and tonics, of "rest and nourishment." Rest and nourishment! When the till was as barren as a winter field? Dubois sighed, a sound like air escaping a punctured bellows. He wiped his brow with a fishy hand, leaving a shimmering smear on his forehead.

Across the square, a commotion stirred. A gaggle of urchins, ragged and nimble as sparrows, clustered around a figure who stood by the fountain, declaiming to the pigeons. It was the poet, Monsieur Verlaine, easily identifiable by his rumpled suit, his perpetually bloodshot eyes, and the absinthe stain permanently etched upon his waistcoat. Verlaine, when sober, was a harmless sort, a dreamer who traded verses for bread. When drunk, however, he was a menace, a whirlwind of slurred pronouncements and unpredictable gestures. Today, he was clearly somewhere in between, swaying slightly as he recited his poems to the indifferent birds. A crowd began to gather, drawn by the spectacle of a poet making a fool of himself. Dubois watched with a mixture of amusement and pity. Verlaine, for all his failings, possessed a spark, a fire that flickered even in the depths of his drunken stupor. It was a spark that Dubois, in his own humdrum existence, could only envy.

Suddenly, Verlaine stopped mid-stanza, his gaze fixed on something beyond the fountain. He pointed a wavering finger, his voice rising in a drunken crescendo. "Thieves! Cutthroats! Bandits!" he bellowed, startling the pigeons into flight. The crowd turned to see what had captured his attention. Two men, burly and rough-looking, were hurrying away from the direction of Dubois's stall. One of them clutched a small, canvas bag in his hand. Dubois, his heart lurching with sudden fear, instinctively reached for the till. It was empty. The blood drained from his face, leaving him as pale and lifeless as the fish on his stall.

Dubois, forgetful of his dignity and his damp apron, charged after the fleeing figures. He was a fishmonger, not a policeman, but the thought of Marie, lying sick and helpless, fueled him with a desperate energy. He dodged baskets of vegetables, sidestepped a bewildered butcher, and cursed the paving stones beneath his feet. The two men, sensing his pursuit, began to run faster, weaving through the crowded streets. The chase was on, a desperate ballet of desperation and opportunism, played out against the backdrop of the bustling market.

The chase lead Dubois to a dark and filthy corner of the city, full of dark alleys and shadows that hid many secrets. And as he was catching up on the thieves, he noticed something even more strange than the men he was pursuing. It was a small, black rowboat, barely visible from the dark alleys. What was it doing there?

As the sun rose over the tranquil Seine, casting a golden glow upon the City of Light, the discreet whispers of the administrative labyrinth began to stir, like the gentle lapping of waves upon the river's banks. In the sanctum of the ministry, a subtle transformation was taking shape – a metamorphosis, wrought by the judicious hand of the Minister of Finance, M. Dreux. His lordship had long been an ardent advocate for a more streamlined and efficient administration, and now, under the watchful eye of their illustrious leader, the machinery of the state was adapting itself to his design. By a subtle synergy of ingenuity and reform, Dreux aimed to recast the fiscal apparatus, knitting together the loose threads of a byzantine tax system, hitherto rendered grotesque by an unwieldy multiplicity of indirect imposts.

Beneath the unassuming façade of a Bourbon Paris, where aristocratic privilege and corruption reigned supreme, Dreux labored tirelessly behind the scenes to distill a simpler, fairer tax code, founded upon the realities of a consumption-based taxation. His counsels, which at first found little echo in the hallowed halls of the École des Ponts et Chaussées, now gained traction as the rising tide of public opinion gradually shifted in his favor. As he navigated the treacherous waters of Ministerial politics, with its shoals of jealous rivalries and capricious alliances, Dreux displayed an unyielding will, ever guided by his clear vision of a France remade in the image of his ideal – a nation reborn through the thrifty management of its resources, and the decreasing burden of an unbearable fiscal weight. Yet, beneath his measured demeanor, a secret fire burned, driving this tireless reformer, now frame and determined as he waded, as ever, in the opaque waters of the human heart.

But I thought you said that the last time you saw her was at the old mansion, before it was sold to the wealthy merchant? The words hung in the air, like a challenge, as Emily gazed at her mother with a mixture of confusion and curiosity. Her mother, Mrs. Fanshawe, shifted uncomfortably in her seat, avoiding Emily's piercing stare. It was a chilly autumn evening, and the fire crackling in the hearth cast a warm glow over the room, but the atmosphere was tense, heavy with unspoken words and unresolved secrets.

As Emily waited for her mother's response, her mind wandered back to the events of the past few weeks. The sale of the old mansion had stirred up a flurry of emotions within her, and the revelation that her mother had been in contact with the new owner, Mr. Harrington, had come as a shock. Emily's mother had always spoken of Mr. Harrington with a mix of disdain and wariness, and yet, it seemed that she had been secretly meeting with him, discussing matters that Emily could hardly begin to imagine. The more she thought about it, the more Emily felt a sense of disquiet, a feeling that her mother was hiding something from her, something important.

Mrs. Fanshawe's eyes darted around the room, as if searching for an escape from the conversation, before finally coming to rest on Emily's face. Her expression was guarded, but Emily could see the faintest glimmer of sadness in her eyes, a hint of a deeper sorrow that she had never seen before. "I did see her, Emily," Mrs. Fanshawe said finally, her voice low and hesitant. "I saw her at the old mansion, just before it was sold. She came to me, out of the blue, with a proposal, of sorts." Emily's curiosity was piqued, and she leaned forward, her eyes fixed intently on her mother's face.

The clock on the mantelpiece ticked away, marking the passing of time, as Mrs. Fanshawe paused, collecting her thoughts before continuing. "It was a strange encounter, Emily. She seemed...different, somehow. Her manner was cold, calculating, and yet, there was something in her eyes, a spark of desperation, perhaps, that I had never seen before." Emily's mind was racing, trying to piece together the fragments of information, to understand the mysterious circumstances surrounding her mother's meeting with the woman in question. She felt a shiver run down her spine as she realized that her mother was speaking of Mrs. Blackwood, the infamous society hostess, rumored to be involved in all manner of scandalous activities.

As the fire crackled and spat, sending sparks flying up the chimney, Mrs. Fanshawe's eyes seemed to glaze over, lost in thought. Emily could see the tension in her mother's body, the rigid set of her shoulders, the tightness of her lips. It was as if she was reliving the encounter, replaying the events of that fateful day in her mind. "She proposed a partnership, of sorts," Mrs. Fanshawe continued, her voice barely above a whisper. "A partnership that would benefit us both, or so she claimed. But I knew, Emily, I knew that it was a trap, a cleverly laid snare, designed to entangle us in her web of deceit." Emily's eyes widened as she listened, her imagination running wild with possibilities.

The room seemed to grow darker, the shadows deepening, as Mrs. Fanshawe's words painted a picture of intrigue and deception. Emily felt a sense of trepidation, a feeling that her mother was being drawn into a world of danger and uncertainty. She reached out, taking her mother's hand in hers, trying to offer what comfort she could. "What did you do, Mother?" she asked, her voice soft and gentle. Mrs. Fanshawe's eyes focused on hers, and for a moment, Emily saw a glimmer of the woman she used to be, before the weight of secrets and scandals had taken its toll.

As the silence stretched out between them, Emily felt a sense of anticipation building, a sense that her mother was on the verge of revealing a long-hidden truth. The fire crackled and spat, sending a shower of sparks up the chimney, and in the sudden burst of light, Emily saw something in her mother's eyes, a flicker of determination, perhaps, or a hint of resolve. Whatever it was, it sent a shiver down her spine, a sense that their conversation was far from over, that the secrets and revelations were only just beginning to unfold.

The sun had not long descended beyond the horizon when, with eager hearts and curious spirits, Reuben, Jane, and Draxy ventured once more into the embrace of Captain Melville’s dwelling. The evening light filtered through the high, intricately carved windows, casting a warm glow upon the room, wherein shadows danced playfully upon the walls, as if joining in the wonderment that lay in every corner. Each glance exchanged among them bore the weight of unspoken gratitude, for they had found themselves embraced by a hospitality that seemed a peculiar blend of fortune and kindness.

Jane, with her delicate fingers brushing the smooth wood of a finely crafted tablet, marveled aloud, “I fear I shall never grow accustomed to this strangeness. How wonderful it is, and how very strange!” Her voice trailed off, wrapped in the softest echoes of awe, her eyes glancing upward to the soaring ceilings adorned with splendid carvings of ships battling titanic waves. Draxy, seated nearby, could not help but feel a wave of warmth surge through her as she recalled Aunt Emma’s words — spoken so earnestly just days before — concerning the many challenges that yet lay before Captain Melville and his dear wife.

“Do you think,” Draxy mused, her voice a gentle thread woven in with Jane’s own reverie, “that they need our assistance? Aunt Emma seemed troubled by their struggles.” The profound thought hung suspended between them, coloring their surroundings with a shade of melancholy as they took in the fine china displayed upon the shelves, the delicate floral patterns speaking of a grace that rose above mere appearances.

Before they could indulge in any further contemplation, Mrs. Carr, an ever-dutiful soul, entered the room, her arms cradling a tray that bore a steaming teapot alongside dainty cups that shone with the brilliance of porcelain. “Ah, my dears,” she proclaimed in a voice that resonated with a gentle authority, “it is time for our evening respite. You may find comfort in this brew; it has been prepared with care.” As she set the tray before them, the inviting aroma wafted through the air, mingling with the faint scent of varnished wood and the rich, earthy tones of dusk.

“Thank you, dear Mrs. Carr,” Jane replied, her countenance transforming into one of heartfelt appreciation. “We scarcely know how to express our gratitude for your generosity.” She took a cup, warmth enveloping her fingers as the tender steam kissed her face.

Just as they began to sip their tea, an enthusiastic voice burst through the doorway. “What ho! There you are!” Captain Melville strode into the room, splendidly attired in a crisp coat which bore the insignia of the sea upon its lapel, his eyes twinkling with the vibrant energy of one who had weathered both storms and calm. The very air shifted as he entered, filling the space with an unmistakable sense of vitality. “I hope all is well, for that which dwells within these walls belongs not only to my wife and me, but now to you, dear friends!”

His eyes alighted upon Draxy, catching her by surprise. A charming grin spread across his face, revealing an unstudied warmth that made her heart skip, the compliment lingering in the air as he added, “And beauty must dwell here, for it is the grace of a lady like you that lends character to a home!” Her cheeks flushed, not from self-consciousness but a sudden rush of unexpected joy, which combined with the aura of their surroundings, made her feel as if she belonged there.

“Truly, Captain,” Reuben interjected, a grateful tremor in his voice, “we are in your debt. This home—though grand—seems offered in earnest hospitality, a welcome we scarcely expected, considering the accounts of struggle we’ve heard.”

“Ah, but those accounts should ebb away like the tide!” The Captain waved his hand dismissively, a playful spirit twinkling in his eye. “Fear not of the toil that now seems distant; it is the heart that matters—yours and ours alike. Melville Harbor will embrace you as family, with laughter and love, and doubt not that we seek to share the warmth of friendship amid life's unpredictable currents.”

Draxy’s heart sang at his words, finding an unanticipated solace in the promise of camaraderie. The sound of the sea danced through her thoughts as she envisioned future evenings gathered around the fireplace, hearts entwining alongside flames, sharing stories that would age like fine wine, enriching their souls for years to come.

As the sun completely surrendered to the horizon’s edge, casting a deep blue cloak over the world, the three companions from the humble corners of the world looked around at their new home and welcomed its blossoming memories with open hearts.

The harsh glare of midday softened imperceptibly to a lingering intensity as the sun hovered reluctantly towards the western peaks above Devil's Ford. Across the steep and treeless slope, where each gray and dusty fissure seemed to gasp thirstily at the oppressive sky, faint shadows began at last to creep tentatively outward, offering scant relief from the relentless heat. Thompson's newly acquired establishment—formerly a place vibrant with rough revelries and sharp exchanges, now in readiness for more genteel occupants—stood silent and expectant, its uneven plank veranda absorbing every ray, and exhaling faint ripples of shimmering vapor that wavered unsteadily above the well-worn boards.

Down through the settlement a lethargy, born of scorching heat and protracted anticipation, claimed every miner. The afternoon labor, always precarious at best, now lay abandoned—shovels and picks reclining idly beside deserted shafts, sluice boxes dry and bleached white as bone in the fierce sunlight, while the men themselves, the erstwhile vigorous seekers of fortune, clustered languidly under lean-tos and awnings, drawing breath in shallow sighs and watching impassively for any movement along the winding road that twisted its dusty trail upward from the distant valley.

Even Fairfax, whose restless energy had rallied these rough pioneers into something resembling gentility—a procession of unfamiliar wardrobes laid ceremoniously out on cots, clean boots lining the wall as if in earnest expectation of a Sunday devotion—now paced nervously between the deserted workings and the shade of Thompson's porch. His face bore the strained expression of a man to whom tasks once achievable had suddenly become uncertain, and whose smile, beneath the careful composure, betrayed doubts that he had perhaps overestimated the ability of a rugged mining hamlet to transform overnight into something suitably gentle for feminine eyes.

Thus passed another hour; thus deepened the silence, interrupted briefly only by a tentative breeze sighing faintly through the parched golden grasses. Then—a murmur passed like wildfire from miner to miner, mouth to ear, eye to straining eye fixed down upon that distant bend—there came into view the dusty and uncertain outline of the stagecoach, a distant blur behind veils of pale dust which rose lazily in its wake, like reluctant ghosts startled forth by some impertinent intrusion. The watching group stirred with enthusiasm tempered by an anxious hesitation, withdrawing involuntarily steps backward into shadow while casting sharp glances toward Fairfax, whose posture straightened visibly in readiness.

When the vehicle rattled abruptly into the settlement, with a tentative jangling of harness and an abrupt halt in a choking, swirling cloud, the miners stood motionless—starkly silhouetted in groups—silent, awkward, expectant. Its driver, a man hardened by countless dusty journeys, glanced curiously upward beneath a broad-brimmed hat, and with a palpable restraint descended, opening the stagecoach door to reveal a figure whose fashionably attired outline drew an involuntary gasp from the rough assembly. Mr. Carrington, the engineer, emerged first, stepping firmly but warily onto the dusty ground, the brisk and confident lines of his clothing standing incongruously sharp against the crude backdrop. After a silent pause as Carrington surveyed his surroundings, two young women followed, their delicate forms appearing strangely luminous in garments whose soft fabric, stirring gently, seemed far more suited to parlors and shaded lawns than to this barren and harshly exposed terrain of stone and sun.

Fairfax moved forward at once, pushing aside his brief turmoil and uncertainty, offering a polite bow and greetings both reassuring and deliberately formal, which the strange surroundings seemed to demand. Mr. Carrington accepted this courtesy with measured gratitude; yet it was to the two daughters that all eyes covertly turned, their delicate presence—the fair lines of their faces flushed faintly beneath wide-brimmed hats; their eyes wide in curiosity and apprehension as they hesitantly glanced about at Devil's Ford—transforming instantly a rough mining encampment into something different, something softened by expectancy, hope, and uncertainty, something as yet unknown, but already touched by gentler promise.

When the warmth of the prevailing equinoctial gales had somewhat abated, and the westerly winds, though still able to howl and buffet with unimpaired vehemence, began to relent in their unremitting assault upon the sturdy gates of Cecilia's parents' house, it became possible to venture forth with some degree of comfort. Thus, as the days lengthened, and the trees, which a few weeks previously had stood bare and gaunt, burst forth in a riot of verdure, Cecilia and her mother, Mrs. Holt, would often stroll forth into the garden, now clothed in a soft and emerald verdure, which nearly rivalled the glory of its exquisite counterparts in the paintings of the great masters.

Cecilia, now fully twenty-two years of age, was rapidly approaching that period of life wherein the frivolous gabble of young ladies, the capricious fancies of their bosoms, and the impartial supremacy of their understanding seemed destined to surrender altogether to the sentimental melancholy of existence. Though not yet arrived at that moment, when the chilly dreaminess of knowledge, that peculiarity of the courtesan that abounds in encouragement, might gently usurp the ardent continuity of romantic enthusiasm, Cecilia's life in Exeter still abounded in cheerful scenes and society. Her daily routine was punctuated by the conventions of drawing-room meetings, the polite gossip of fashionable acquaintance, the leisurely promenades in the Exeter walks, and the Wednesday-evening assemblies at Dalkey Manor, which, as yet, did not seem too wearisome even to the most juvenile and frank spirits.

"But why must you always be reading, Edward?" asked Maggie, her voice tinged with a familiar note of exasperation. She stood in the doorway of the small parlour, her hands on her hips, her gaze fixed upon her brother, who sat comfortably ensconced in their father's old armchair.

Edward, for his part, did not even bother to lift his eyes from the pages of his Latin grammar. "Why must you always be bustling about, Maggie?" he countered, his tone a touch sharper than he perhaps intended. "Can a fellow not have a moment's peace in his own home?"

Maggie crossed the room, her footsteps muffled by the worn rug, and perched herself upon the edge of the settee opposite Edward. The silence stretched between them, punctuated only by the rustle of turning pages and the gentle ticking of the grandfather clock in the corner.

"It is not bustling, Edward," Maggie said at length, her voice quieter now. "It is called keeping a home." She gestured vaguely at the room around them, at the dust motes dancing in the afternoon sunbeams, at the stack of mending piled high upon the table. "These things do not see to themselves, you know."

Edward finally lowered his book, but his expression remained distant, his thoughts still seemingly lost in the intricacies of Latin declensions. "Yes, yes, I know," he murmured, a hint of impatience creeping into his voice. "But surely there is someone else who could attend to such matters. Mrs. Jenkins, perhaps?"

Maggie let out a small sigh. "Mrs. Jenkins has her own tasks to see to, Edward. Besides, it is not seemly for a young lady of good family to shirk her domestic duties."

"Seemly?" Edward scoffed, tossing his book onto the nearby table with a thud that made Maggie wince. "Since when have you cared about what is 'seemly', Maggie? You spend more time in the garden with your hands in the dirt than any lady I know."

Maggie's cheeks flushed pink at his words. It was true, she felt most at peace amongst the flowers and vegetables, her hands stained with earth, the sun warm upon her face. But Edward, with his books and his studies and his grand ambitions of becoming a clergyman, could not be expected to understand such simple pleasures.

"Gardening is honest work, Edward," she said quietly, picking at a loose thread on her skirt. "And someone must tend to the vegetables if we are to eat."

Edward sighed, his earlier impatience giving way to a weary sort of resignation. "You know I do not mean to be unkind, Maggie," he said, rising from his chair and crossing the room to stand by the window. "It is just that...well, I have my studies, my future to consider. A clergyman must be a scholar, a gentleman. He cannot be expected to concern himself with the mundane details of running a household."

"And what of a clergyman's wife, Edward?" Maggie challenged, her chin lifting a fraction. "Is she not also expected to be a lady? And yet, I wager she knows her way around a kitchen and a mending basket just as well as any housemaid."

Edward turned back to face her, a flicker of amusement dancing in his eyes. "Ah, so that is it, is it? You fancy yourself the future wife of a clergyman, do you?"

Maggie felt her cheeks flush even warmer now. "Do not be absurd, Edward," she retorted, though a small smile played at the corners of her lips. "I am merely pointing out that there is more to life than books and sermons."

Edward chuckled, the tension between them easing somewhat. "Perhaps you are right, little sister," he conceded, reaching out to ruffle her hair in a rare display of affection. "Perhaps you are right."

If one happened to pass through Atkinson Street on his way to the Athenaeum, he would notice a large, square, painted, brick house, in which lived a leading representative of old-fashioned coleopterous Calvinism, and from which emerged one of the liveliest of literary butterflies. The father was editor of the “Boston Recorder,” a very respectable, but very far from amusing paper, most largely patronized by that class of the community which spoke habitually of the first day of the week as “the Sahbuth.” The son was the editor of several different periodicals in succession, none of them over severe or serious, and of many pleasant books, filled with lively descriptions of society, which he studied on the outside with a quick eye for form and color, and with a certain amount of sentiment, not very deep, but real, though somewhat frothed over by his worldly experiences.

Nathaniel Parker Willis was in full bloom when I opened my first Portfolio. He had made himself known by his religious poetry, published in his father's paper, I think, and signed “Roy.” He had started the “American Magazine,” afterwards merged in the “New York Mirror.” He had then left off writing scripture pieces, and taken to lighter forms of verse. He had just written

“I'm twenty-two, I'm twenty-two, They idly give me joy, As if I should be glad to know That I was less a boy.”

He was young, therefore, and already famous. He came very near being very handsome. He was tall; his hair, of light brown color, waved in luxuriant abundance; his cheek was as rosy as if it had been painted to show behind the footlights; he dressed with artistic elegance. He was something between a remembrance of Count D'Orsay and an anticipation of Oscar Wilde. There used to be in the gallery of the Luxembourg a picture of Hippolytus and Phxdra, in which the beautiful young man, who had kindled a passion in the heart of his wicked step-mother, always reminded me of Willis, in spite of the shortcomings of the living face as compared with the ideal. The painted youth is still blooming on the canvas, but the fresh-cheeked, jaunty young author of the year 1830 has long faded out of human sight. I took the leaves which lie before me at this moment, as I write, from his coffin, as it lay just outside the door of Saint Paul's Church, on a sad, overclouded winter's day, in the year 1867. At that earlier time, Willis was by far the most prominent young American author. Cooper, Irving, Bryant, Dana, Halleck, Drake, had all done their best work. Longfellow was not yet conspicuous. Lowell was a school-boy. Emerson was unheard of. Whittier was beginning to make his way against the writers with better educational advantages whom he was destined to outdo and to outlive. Not one of the great histories, which have done honor to our literature, had appeared. Our school-books depended, so far as American authors were concerned, on extracts from the orations and speeches of Webster and Everett; on Bryant's Thanatopsis, his lines To a Waterfowl, and the Death of the Flowers, Halleck's Marco Bozzaris, Red Jacket, and Burns; on Drake's American Flag, and Percival's Coral Grove, and his Genius Sleeping and Genius Waking,--and not getting very wide awake, either. These could be depended upon. A few other copies of verses might be found, but Dwight's “Columbia, Columbia,” and Pierpont's Airs of Palestine, were already effaced, as many of the favorites of our own day and generation must soon be, by the great wave which the near future will pour over the sands in which they still are legible.

"The Elms" was a misnomer. It should have been called "The Shagbark" or "The Doodle Bug's Lair." It was supposed to mean a wide sweep of meadow, a vine covered lodge, a broad velvet lawn, and a carriage way, where the drowsy locust, in the sensuous shadow of magnanimous elms, gnawed a file at intervals through the day, while back of all this the mossy and gray-whiskered front and corrugated brow of the venerable architectural pile stood off and admired itself in the deep and glassy pool at its base.

In the first place none of the yeomanry for eight miles around knew that he called his old malarial tank "The Elms," so it was hard to find. But when I described the looks of the lord of The Elms they wink at each other and wagged their heads and said, "Oh, yes, we know him," also interjecting well known one syllable words that are not euphonious enough to print.

When I got there he was down cellar sprouting potatoes, and his wife was hanging out upon the clothes line a pair of gathered summer trousers that evidently were made for a man who had been badly mangled in a saw-mill.

The Elms was not even picturesque, and the preserves were out of order. I was received with the same cordiality which you detect on the face of any other kind of detected liar. He wanted to be regarded as a remarkable host and landed proprietor, without being really hospitable. I remained there at The Elms a few days, rubbing rock salt and Cayenne pepper into the wounds of my host, and suggesting different names for his home, such as "The Tom Tit's Eyrie," "The Weeping Willow," "The Crook Neck Squash" and "The Muskrat's Retreat." Then I came away. His old look of apprehensive cordiality did not leave him until he had seen me climb on a load of hay with my trunk and start for home.

During my brief sojourn I noticed that the surrounding country was full of people, and I presume there was a larger population of "boarders," as we were called indiscriminately, than ever before. The number of available points to which the victims of humidity and poor plumbing may retreat in summer time is constantly on the increase, while, so far as I know, all the private and public boarding places are filled to their utmost capacity. Everywhere, the gaudy boarder in flannels and ecru shoes looms upon the green lawn or the brown dirt road, or scales the mountain one day and stays in bed the following week, rubbing James B. Pond's Extract on his swollen joints.

I scaled Mount Utsa-yantha in company with others. We picked out a nice hot day, and, selecting the most erect wall of the mountain, facing west, we scaled it in such a way that it will not have to be done again till new scales grow on it.

Mount Utsa-yantha is 3,365 feet above sea level, and has a brow which reminds me of mine. It is broad, massive and bleak. The foot of the mountain is more massive, however. From the top of the mountain one gets, with a good glass, a view of six or seven states, I was told. Possibly there were that many in sight, though at that season of the year states look so much alike that it takes an expert to pick them out readily. When states are moulting, it is all I can do to tell Vermont from Massachusetts. On this mountain one gets a nice view and highly exhilarating birch beer.

Albany can be distinctly seen with a glass--a field glass, I mean, not a glass of birch beer. Some claim that the nub of a political boom may be seen protruding from the Capitol with the nude vision. Others say they can see the Green mountains, and as far south as the eye can reach. We took two hours and a half for the ascent of the mountain, and came down in about twenty minutes. We descended ungracefully--the way the Irishman claimed that the toad walked, viz.: "git up and sit down."

“That it is wrong to alter the good old course of things:”

“That there is nothing tolerable out of Vondervotteimittiss:” and--

“That we will stick by our clocks and our cabbages.”

Above the session-room of the Council is the steeple, and in the steeple is the belfry, where exists, and has existed time out of mind, the pride and wonder of the village--the great clock of the borough of Vondervotteimittiss. And this is the object to which the eyes of the old gentlemen are turned who sit in the leather-bottomed arm-chairs.

The great clock has seven faces--one in each of the seven sides of the steeple--so that it can be readily seen from all quarters. Its faces are large and white, and its hands heavy and black. There is a belfry-man whose sole duty is to attend to it; but this duty is the most perfect of sinecures--for the clock of Vondervotteimittis was never yet known to have anything the matter with it. Until lately, the bare supposition of such a thing was considered heretical. From the remotest period of antiquity to which the archives have reference, the hours have been regularly struck by the big bell. And, indeed the case was just the same with all the other clocks and watches in the borough. Never was such a place for keeping the true time. When the large clapper thought proper to say “Twelve o’clock!” all its obedient followers opened their throats simultaneously, and responded like a very echo. In short, the good burghers were fond of their sauer-kraut, but then they were proud of their clocks.

All people who hold sinecure offices are held in more or less respect, and as the belfry--man of Vondervotteimittiss has the most perfect of sinecures, he is the most perfectly respected of any man in the world. He is the chief dignitary of the borough, and the very pigs look up to him with a sentiment of reverence. His coat-tail is very far longer--his pipe, his shoe--buckles, his eyes, and his stomach, very far bigger--than those of any other old gentleman in the village; and as to his chin, it is not only double, but triple.

I have thus painted the happy estate of Vondervotteimittiss: alas, that so fair a picture should ever experience a reverse!

There has been long a saying among the wisest inhabitants, that “no good can come from over the hills”; and it really seemed that the words had in them something of the spirit of prophecy. It wanted five minutes of noon, on the day before yesterday, when there appeared a very odd-looking object on the summit of the ridge of the eastward. Such an occurrence, of course, attracted universal attention, and every little old gentleman who sat in a leather-bottomed arm-chair turned one of his eyes with a stare of dismay upon the phenomenon, still keeping the other upon the clock in the steeple.

By the time that it wanted only three minutes to noon, the droll object in question was perceived to be a very diminutive foreign-looking young man. He descended the hills at a great rate, so that every body had soon a good look at him. He was really the most finicky little personage that had ever been seen in Vondervotteimittiss. His countenance was of a dark snuff-color, and he had a long hooked nose, pea eyes, a wide mouth, and an excellent set of teeth, which latter he seemed anxious of displaying, as he was grinning from ear to ear. What with mustachios and whiskers, there was none of the rest of his face to be seen. His head was uncovered, and his hair neatly done up in papillotes. His dress was a tight-fitting swallow-tailed black coat (from one of whose pockets dangled a vast length of white handkerchief), black kerseymere knee-breeches, black stockings, and stumpy-looking pumps, with huge bunches of black satin ribbon for bows. Under one arm he carried a huge chapeau-de-bras, and under the other a fiddle nearly five times as big as himself. In his left hand was a gold snuff-box, from which, as he capered down the hill, cutting all manner of fantastic steps, he took snuff incessantly with an air of the greatest possible self-satisfaction. God bless me!--here was a sight for the honest burghers of Vondervotteimittiss!

"Father," whispered Ottilia, pulling at the speaker's coat, "surely the gentleman is ill."

"I beg your pardon," cried the farmer, re-waking to hospitable thoughts; "can I offer you anything?"

"I thank you. I am very weary," answered Otto. "I have presumed upon my strength. If you would show me to a bed, I should be grateful."

"Ottilia, a candle!" said the old man. "Indeed sir, you look paley. A little cordial water? No? Then follow me, I beseech you, and I will bring you to the stranger's bed. You are not the first by many who has slept well below my roof," continued the old gentleman, mounting the stairs before his guest; "for good food, honest wine, a grateful conscience, and a little pleasant chat before a man retires, are worth all the possets and apothecary's drugs. See, sir," and here he opened a door and ushered Otto into a little whitewashed sleeping-room, "here you are in port. It is small, but it is airy, and the sheets are clean and kept in lavender. The window, too, looks out above the river, and there's no music like a little river's. It plays the same tune (and that's the favourite) over and over again, and yet does not weary of it like men fiddlers. It takes the mind out of doors; and though we should be grateful for good houses, there is, after all, no house like God's out-of-doors. And lastly, sir, it quiets a man down like saying his prayers. So here, sir, I take my kind leave of you until to-morrow; and it is my prayerful wish that you may slumber like a prince."

And the old man, with the twentieth courteous inclination, left his guest alone.

IN WHICH THE PRINCE COMFORTS AGE AND BEAUTY AND DELIVERS A LECTURE ON DISCRETION IN LOVE

The Prince was early abroad: in the time of the first chorus of birds, of the pure and quiet air, of the slanting sunlight and the mile-long shadows. To one who had passed a miserable night, the freshness of that hour was tonic and reviving; to steal a march upon his slumbering fellows, to be the Adam of the coming day, composed and fortified his spirits; and the Prince, breathing deep and pausing as he went, walked in the wet fields beside his shadow, and was glad.

A trellised path led down into the valley of the brook, and he turned to follow it. The stream was a break-neck, bolling highland river. Hard by the farm, it leaped a little precipice in a thick grey-mare's tail of twisted filaments, and then lay and worked and bubbled in a lynn. Into the middle of this quaking pool a rock protruded, shelving to a cape; and thither Otto scrambled and sat down to ponder.

Soon the sun struck through the screen of branches and thin early leaves that made a hanging bower above the fall; and the golden lights and flitting shadows fell upon and marbled the surface of that seething pot; and rays plunged deep among the turning waters; and a spark, as bright as a diamond, lit upon the swaying eddy. It began to grow warm where Otto lingered, warm and heady; the lights swam, weaving their maze across the shaken pool; on the impending rock, reflections danced like butterflies; and the air was fanned by the waterfall as by a swinging curtain.

It was a misty morn at the manse, and a queer hush lay over every parlor and narrow passage.
Jess stood by the low window, peering out at the gloamin’ light that crept o’er the dew-damp garden.
“Aye, Leeby,” she began, “it seems that Wilkie’s lodgin’ has stirred a right jumbly notion amongst us, ken ye?”
Leeby, polishing a pewter mug, replied, “Ah, true enough, lass; the matter’s been a topic since last eve’s supper, an’ by my troth I scarce ken the proper turn it’ll take.”
The conversation turned to the tea-dinner for which an unexpected guest were to be lodged in the manse, as murmured by the servants.
“A minister’s sure to come,” Leeby added, “and with ’em, there’ll be words of praise—and not all silent, as some might wish.”
Jess’s eyes sparkled with anxious curiosity: “Do ye reckon Tibbie Mealmaker and her husband’ll be among the company this day?”
“Aye,” came a low voice from the hall. Hendry, clutching a crumpled note, stammered, “I—I forgot to mention that Tibbie’s visit was rightly promised some days past.”
A murmur of discontent followed his fumble, and the household tumbled into a flurry of scattered preparations and hurried commands.
Old Auntie McKendrick, with a frown carved upon her weathered face, tutted, “Hendry, ye daft fellow! How could ye have left out such an important matter?”
Hendry scratched his head in perplexity, “I was afeared I might add fuel to the fire, but now it seems I have indeed stirred the pot, by my soul.”
The clatter of pots and pans came as servants scrambled to tidy the cluttered parlour, for the house had not been readied for high company.
Leeby, ever the voice of calm amid chaos, said, “Now, now, we must be swift, for the minister’s tea-dinner awaits and Tibbie’s laugh is not one to be trifled with.”
Jess, rallying her spirit, gathered the scattered linens and chairs, “We must all pull together, lest we find ourselves in a state of proper disarray.”
Outside, the echo of carriage wheels signalled the approach of newcomers, and the entire household braced itself for a day of unaccustomed bustle.
In a hushed corner of the kitchen, a young maid whispered to her comrade, “They say Tibbie’s husband is as loud as a coup de vent and twice as wild!”
The hushed suspense only added to the murmurings about Wilkie’s future lodgings, with some betting he’d be left with the lawyer like a stray pup.
“And what of the lawyer himself?” inquired one, his tone laced with both jest and genuine concern.
“Ye ken he’s a stickler for order,” replied another, “and if the lad is placed with him, he might well learn the value o’ silence and propriety.”
Yet another voice in the back of the room speculated, “But Mistress Ogilvy would nae abide the lad lodging with any soul but her kin, pricking her nose at every unsuitable match.”
As the debate simmered, Hendry roamed the corridors in a fitful daze, his earlier error still a weight upon his brow.
“Sam, fetch me a candlestick, will ye?” he mumbled to a passing servant, his words trailing off as he vanished round a corner.
The household, though perturbed by the looming arrival of the minister and the unannounced Tibbie couple, strove to carry on in a semblance of order.
In the parlor, a quiet murmur arose: it was said that even the minister might arrive with unexpected tidings of a change to Wilkie’s dwelling.
“Ye ken,” whispered Leeby, “the very notion does pare our hearts, for change is oft as unpredictable as a summer storm in May.”
Jess, still bustling with the day’s demands, nodded, “Aye, but we must weather it—lest the entire cheer of our humble manse be spoiled by undue disquiet.”
Peals of laughter and the ruffling of skirts mingled with the sound of clanging utensils as every soul set about their errand with brisk determination.
The grand hall was transformed in haste; chairs aligned just so and a modest table set for tea-dinner, all under a sky of anxious expectation.
Every moment ticked by with measured suspense, and the air, thick with both apprehension and duty, was as charged as a storm on the high seas.
A sudden knock at the door sent a ripple through the assembled throng, and all hearts skipped as one in unison.
Hendry, still flustered and shy of a proper greeting, muttered as he opened the door, “Welfare to ye, Tibbie—an’ welcome to our broken manse upon this fine morn.”
As the visitors stepped inside, the household collectively exhaled a shuddering breath; the stage was set for an afternoon of unexpected turns and familial capers.

Before that pleasant day was over we had compared notes on almost every department of girl-life. I had confided to her my newly awakened feelings of dissatisfaction as to my want of feminine tastes and tendency to "tomboyishness," and she on her side had told me that she was often afraid of growing too prim or narrow-minded in the well-arranged regularity of her own home-life.

"That was why," she said, "I was so glad to travel a little. I feel as if I needed to rough it in some ways. Father is too careful of me, too unselfish. I am afraid I have always been a spoilt child, and having no brothers, you see, may make me selfish without knowing it!"

She looked up at me anxiously with her sweet brown eyes. What was it they reminded me of? I had already noticed that her people called her by some peculiar pet name; I had not caught it exactly.

"What is it that your sister and father call you sometimes?" I said. "Is it `Ella'?"

Isabel blushed a little.

"No," she said, "it is Zella. Rather a silly name, I am afraid. It came from a fancy of father's that my eyes were like a gazelle's."

"And so they are!" I exclaimed; "that is the look I have seen in them-- some dogs have it too! I don't think it is at all a silly name. Will you let me call you by it sometimes?" for of course under the circumstances there had been no question of anything but "Isabel" and "Regina" between us from the first.

"Of course you may, if you like," she said. "But--" and she hesitated.

"But what?" I asked.

Isabel smiled.

"You mustn't be vexed with me," she replied, "if I can't promise to call you `Reggie,' as your brother does. I don't like it--and Regina is such a pretty name and uncommon too."

"Mother never calls me anything else," I said, "but I am afraid I am half a boy. You must civilise me--mother will be eternally grateful to you if you do."

"I don't think you need civilising," said Isabel; "but perhaps in our different ways we may do each other good. I do hope your people will let you come to stay with us when we go home."

"I should love it of all things," I said. "I have scarcely ever paid any visits, and I have seen very little of England except quite near our own home. Is it very pretty where you live?"

"Not so much pretty as picturesque," Isabel replied. "To begin with, it is very, very out of the way; we are six miles from a railway station of any kind, and sixteen from an important one. But papa's people have lived there for so long, that it doesn't seem out of the way to us. It is a place that changes very little."

"Then it is to be hoped that you have some nice and interesting neighbours," I said. "Near us there are so few young people."

"And there are not many near Millflowers either," said Isabel; "at least not within a good long drive. I hope you would not find it dull. There are interesting walks, if you care for wild, rugged scenery. The village itself is quite tiny. There is only one house of any importance besides the vicarage and ours, and that is--no good," she added, rather abruptly.

"Why not?" I inquired. "Is it uninhabited?"

Isabel hesitated.

"No," she replied. "The same people have lived in it for a great many years. They were there before father came into possession, on my uncle's death. But--" and again she paused.

My curiosity was aroused.

"Do tell me about them," I said.

"Well, yes, I don't see why I shouldn't," answered Isabel. "Father always tells us not to gossip about the Grim House, but you are sure to notice it when you come, so I may as well prepare you beforehand."

The young officer's heart pounded in his chest as he followed the woman he loved into the dimly lit passageway. The flickering gas lamps cast eerie shadows on the ancient stone walls, creating a sense of mystery and anticipation. As he watched her graceful figure disappear into the darkness ahead, he couldn't help but feel a sense of longing and desire stirring within him.

Her movements were as fluid and elegant as a swan gliding on a tranquil pond, each step filled with purpose and determination. He marveled at the way she carried herself, her every gesture exuding a quiet strength and confidence that left him breathless. As she ascended the narrow stairway with an air of eagerness and anticipation, he couldn't help but be struck by her beauty and grace.

In that moment, the young officer felt as though he was witnessing a scene from a romantic novel, where love and fate intertwined in a dance as old as time itself. His love for this woman, this paragon of virtue and grace, burned within him like a fiery passion, consuming his every thought and desire. And as he stood there in the shadows, watching her disappear into the night, he knew that he would stop at nothing to win her heart and make her his own.

As the sun dipped low in the azure heavens, casting a golden hue upon the languid basin of the Kennett, I turned my thoughts towards the Loddon, that cherished stream to whose banks I had often wandered with delight. Its waters, crystalline and untainted, sang a melody of life, captivating even those birds of variegated plumage whose very names denote rarity and splendor. The kingfishers, those ethereal denizens of the air, found within its tranquil depths a realm where they could perform their aerial ballet with unconstrained joy.

In stark contrast, the Kennett, whose embrace once held promise of fecundity, now revealed a different visage, one marred by neglect and human endeavor. The meadows, once thriving with verdure and teeming with life, were reduced to an expanse of drained and dreary earth, a testament to the reach of our industrious hand. The water that traversed these lands had been channeled through intricate networks, its natural flow usurped by man's ambition for improvement. No longer did it mirror the radiant sky, nor did it cradle the silver-beaked swans in its placid bosom.

However, even within the desolation wrought by progress, there remained a vestige of untamed spirit, a whisper of the Kennett's former glory. As night enfolded the land, the moon rose and cast her silver glow upon the forlorn scene, lending an ethereal beauty to the water-meadows. The reeds swayed in silent mourning, their shadows dancing on the still surface, creating a mirage of tranquility amid the desolation. The stars, like faithful guardians, watched over the Kennett's forlorn passage, promising that even in the face of mankind's advancement, the natural world held secrets of resilience and renewal.

I found myself reflecting upon the duality of our existence, caught between the desire for progress and the yearning for the untouched beauty of nature. As the Kennett whispered its secrets to the nocturnal creatures, I was reminded of the Loddon's carefree flow, a reminder that amidst our ceaseless striving, there remained corners where time honored the earth with serene constancy. The Kennett, once vibrant and full of promise, now bore the marks of our intervention, yet it too, in its solitude, told a story—one of change, adaptation, and the enduring power of the natural world.

The lady of the house, in whose society Clara was then so much gratified, being the Dowager Lady Martindale, whose family had long been distinguished for the importance of their alliances, and the weight of their influence in circles, now found herself reaping the bitter fruits of that too tranquil and secluded life which she had for so many years adopted.

Her ladyship, in surrendering the reins of power to the dominant will of her family, had equally delegated to her the task of guarding her own heart, in abstaining from all those ties, the inevitable consequences of which she foresaw would interrupt her otherwise serene and peaceful existence; and, by her own volition, overseeing the withholding of her smiles, and heeding not the declarations of a certain Mr Entwhistle, a gentleman whose character, for all its unassuming gravity, never failed to awake a certain tremulous flutter in the breast of all those by whom he was esteemed.

And yet, that very consideration for her ladyship's settled tranquillity, so parsimoniously cherished by the peerage, had led, in the opinion of the world at large, to a life of solitary isolation; in which, now that age and reflection had gifted her with the stern face of necessity, she found herself pondering the venerable aesthete's eloquent pang of it 'Et verbis sapientia domus', for in veritable truth, her experience left her with the appearance of a thrice-folded door well worth trying; yet for the self-produced boon of her prior conduct never justified itself by the obligation to gratitude. But now to Mr Entwhistle we shall turn, the understanding of whose place in society was so far from local or uncertain; his favourite pursuit having furnished him, during the hectic, hot fibres of youth, a safe escape from serious revelations in the more intimate quarters of life.
