There, as you sat and watched, stretched out the plain in the moonlight, with its low, tomb-like bushes, its clear space of bare land, the archway rising behind it. But, on the spot of bare land, before the archway, would rise the Shadow; not looking as if it were a shadow cast on the ground, but a palpable fact: as if a bier, with its two bending mourners, actually stood there in the substance. I say that I cannot explain it, or attempt to explain it; but I do say that there it was to be seen. Not often: sometimes not for years together. It was called the Shadow of Ashlydyat: and superstition told that its appearance foreshadowed the approach of calamity, whether of death or other evil, to the Godolphins. The greater the evil that was coming upon them, the plainer and more distinct would be the appearance of the Shadow--the longer the space of time that it would be observed. Rumour went, that once, on the approach of some terrible misfortune, it had been seen for months and months before, whenever the moon was sufficiently bright. The Godolphins did not care to have the subject mentioned to them: in their scepticism, they (some of them, at least) treated it with ridicule, or else with silence. But, like disbelievers of a different sort, the scepticism was more in profession than in heart. The Godolphins, in their inmost soul, would cower at the appearance of that shadowed bier; as those others have been known to cower, in their anguish, at the approach of the shadow of death.

This was not all the superstition attaching to Ashlydyat: but you will probably deem this quite enough for the present. And we have to return to Mrs. Godolphin.

Five years before the present time, when pretty Cecilia was in her fifteenth year, and most needed the guidance of a mother, Mrs. Godolphin died. Her illness had been of a lingering nature; little hope in it, from the first. It was towards the latter period of her illness that what had been regarded by four-fifths of Prior's Ash as an absurd child's tale, a superstition unworthy the notice of the present-day men and women, grew to be talked of in whispers, as something "strange." For three months antecedent to the death of Mrs. Godolphin, the Shadow of Ashlydyat was to be seen every light night, and all Prior's Ash flocked up to look at it. That they went, is of no consequence: they had their walk and their gaze for their pains: but that Mrs. Godolphin should have been told of it, was. She was in the grounds alone one balmy moonlight night, later than she ought to have been, and she discerned people walking in them, making for the ash-trees.

The dawn broke with a pallid light over the Chequers, and though the inn’s walls were wrapped in stillness, the events of the previous night stirred many a thought in the minds of those who dwelt there. The memories of a brave soul risking all for the sake of others, even whilst captive, hovered like a fragile spirit over every heart present. Even the aged beams of the inn seemed to murmur in subdued awe.

Jesse lay upon a narrow cot in his modest chamber, his eyes tracing the feeble streaks of early light seeping through the boarded window. The chill of his confinement was momentarily forgotten as he recalled the desperate clamor of roaring flames and the thunderous crackle which had alarmed his guards merely minutes before, rousing them to an act of valor unknown to his captors. In that instant, though bound by circumstances, his noble spirit had soared above all human frailty.

It was whispered now in hushed tones among the servants that his alert had saved not one, but two lives; that in the raging inferno at Farmer Cobham’s, the very hand which had once been sorely rebuked for misdeeds had become an instrument of salvation. His feat had transformed him immeasurably in the eyes of Daniel and the venerable farmer, who had yet moments before given sin a harsh judgment. The accident of fire had bestowed upon him an almost saintly air—one that troubled the hearts of those who had long harboured a darker sentiment.

At the last vigil of that harrowing night, the old farmer, his eyes raw with remorse, implored, “Jesse, thou art a man of unforeseen virtue. God grant that our rashness may mend the wounding we have wrought upon thy spirit.” His words, though hesitant and laced with the bitterness of regret, carried a weight of sincerity that even the hardened Daniel found hard to ignore. Thus, the misfortune of flame had become a harbinger of unexpected redemption.

Meanwhile, in a quiet corner of the world not far distant, Phoebe had departed for the Moors—a realm of untamed beauty and gentle isolation—hoping to find solace from the tumult of recent days. Her countenance, once pale with distress, now shone with a delicate light of determination, as though the vast expanse of the moorland might bear witness to a rebirth of her anxieties into hope. In the soft, forgiving winds, she heard echoes of a better fate which might yet grace her tender existence.

Back at Chequers, Daniel conferred with the inn’s caretaker in the low tones of remorse. “There is a wisdom in the heated trial we have sustained tonight,” he murmured, "and though we once looked upon our captive with disdain, the providence of fire has taught us that even the least among us may possess a heart aflame with nobility." His voice, though tempered by remorse, bore an unmistakable note of admiration that whispered of lessons painfully learnt.

The night following the calamity was spent in thoughtful silence, with each character—whether bound by duty or by past prejudice—reflecting deeply upon the sudden, unforeseen reversal of fortunes. In murmured prayers and in solitary contemplations around the modest table, each soul sought to reckon with the mystery of goodness that had been so boldly revealed in Jesse’s actions.

Once the fervour of emergency had yielded to a gentler calm, the old farmer found himself again in conversation with Daniel near the inn’s narrow staircase. “Had I but seen sooner the kinship of courage and conscience within his breast, perhaps I might not now be so sorely contrite,” he intoned, his voice trembling like a leaf in a mild autumn gust. Such words, borne from a legacy of stubborn misjudgment, spoke of an earnest desire to reconcile past folly with present truth.

One evening, as light sank low in the sky, a kindly nurse came to tend for Jesse, who was now lodged within the household in a modest wing set apart from the common quarters. Her gentle care and timely ministrations spoke volumes of the change that had taken root among his former captors; for now he was looked on not as a criminal, but as an unexpected benefactor of circumstance and courage.

In a secluded room adorned modestly with the spoils of humble living, Jesse listened to his caretakers with the quiet resignation of a man who had known both misfortune and redemption. “If fate deems my days to differ henceforth,” he confided softly to a compassionate listener, “then let them be a measure of what grace there is, even in the bounds of captivity.” And so his voice, though low, carried the assurance of one who had been to the brink and returned, transformed.

Elsewhere, Phoebe’s letters from the moors arrived in time with the soft caress of spring winds. Each missive was suffused with the raw beauty of her new world—an untamed landscape where the wounds of sorrow might heal amidst the wild heather and the quiet majesty of rolling hills. There, amid the solitude, she envisioned a life unfettered by the strictures of her past.

Daniel, whose heart had grown ever more thoughtful since that night, now pondered the fickleness of man’s judgment. “How strange it is,” he observed to himself in silent wonder, “that a fire so cruel might yet serve to kindles better understanding.” His reflections filled the long hours before dusk, a contemplative interlude amid the routine of inn and farm.

In a final act of heartfelt contrition, the farmer sent for Jesse one crisp morning. “Let us walk together,” he implored, as though the act of ambling side by side might mend the rift wrought by earlier harshness. And so, with hesitant steps and eyes meeting in quiet reconciliation, they endeavoured to rediscover that long-lost fraternity of man.

The modest congregation at Chequers, though still wary of the caprices of fate, embraced the morning with a new spirit—a kinship forged in the crucible of dire crisis and tempered thereafter by unexpected grace. Each man and woman present now bore within their breast an inkling of humility, acknowledging that even in the direst of circumstances, valor might blossom anew.

Thus, under a sky that promised both renewal and lingering shadows, the lives of Phoebe, Jesse, and those who had once doubted him were irrevocably intertwined. Their fates, like the winding paths across the moors and fields, would continue to converge in events both mysterious and redemptive, each step a testament to the enduring strength of the human spirit.

Mr. Norman's visit left me in a state of agitation I could scarce conceal from my colleagues at the Exchange. The merest hint, the faintest glimmer of hope, was enough to set my mind ablaze with possibilities, each more improbable than the last. Could it be that Captain Burke and – and the ladies – were indeed, as Mr. Butcher had suggested, plucked from their perilous situation by some passing vessel? The vastness of the ocean, which had before seemed a monstrous maw swallowing my hopes whole, now transformed into a boundless expanse where miracles might yet occur.

I seized upon the South African newspaper with a trembling hand, my eyes scanning the columns for any mention, any whisper, of a rescue at sea. The date mentioned by Mr. Norman was weeks old; an eternity for a man whose heart beat in time with the waves that might have carried his beloved to safety or – the thought was unbearable – to an even crueller fate. I devoured every report of maritime activity, every mention of ships arriving from the South Atlantic, but to no avail. Each dead end amplified the hollow echo of despair within me.

The day dragged on with agonizing slowness. Each tick of the clock, each rustle of paper in the hands of my fellow clerks, grated on my raw nerves. My usual keen interest in the fluctuations of commerce had deserted me, replaced by a gnawing anxiety that threatened to consume me entirely. I was adrift in a sea of speculation, buffeted by conflicting currents of hope and despair.

Wall, bless his honest soul, remained a steadfast presence throughout the day. He insisted on accompanying me back to my lodgings, sensing, I believe, the turmoil raging within me. His presence was a strange comfort. Though he could offer no new insights into the mystery that plagued us, his unwavering loyalty and the depth of his own sorrow mirrored my own, providing a grim solace in shared grief.

That night, sleep offered no escape. Instead, I was tormented by vivid dreams, each more horrifying than the last. I saw the Albatross , her masts snapped like twigs, her once proud hull now a mangled wreck tossed upon a raging sea. The storm raged around her, a monstrous symphony of howling wind and crashing waves. And amidst the chaos, I saw her .

Marie, her face pale with terror, clung desperately to the shattered remnants of the deck. The wind tore at her clothing, her hair whipping around her face like living tendrils of fear. I tried to reach her, to pull her back from the brink, but an invisible barrier held me fast. I could only watch in helpless horror as the waves rose up to claim her, their icy fingers dragging her down into the black abyss.

I awoke with a gasp, my body slick with a cold sweat, the echo of the storm still ringing in my ears. The darkness of my room pressed in on me, suffocating, mirroring the despair that threatened to drown me. I knew then that I could bear this agonizing uncertainty no longer. I would set sail for myself, retrace the Albatross's ill-fated course, and scour the ocean until I found some trace of her, some answer, however painful, to the questions that tormented my soul.

Originally there had been a much older mansion, which, after having been partially destroyed by fire, had been razed to the ground, all of it save one sturdy fragment which, for some unknown reason, had been allowed to stand.

This relic of a state of things long vanished was an octagonal tower, about sixty feet in height, built of undressed blocks of grey stone, held together by a mortar as hard as themselves. The interior of the tower consisted of three small rooms, one above the other, with a leaded roof surmounted by a breast-high parapet. Each of the rooms was lighted by a couple of long narrow openings in the wall, which at one time might have been glazed, but were so no longer. Of these rooms the ground floor one alone was now put to any service, access to the others, owing to the rotten state of the woodwork, being deemed a risk not worth adventuring. The basement in question was used as a receptacle for gardeners' tools, and a general storage place for things horticultural, which had been allowed to accumulate there for years.

As already stated, the tower had formed a part of the older mansion of Withington Chase, although what the intention had been in building it, and to what special purposes it had been put, nobody nowadays seemed to know. There it was, however; and there--the elements being its only enemies--it was likely to remain for some centuries to come. It was about five or six hundred yards apart from the more modern mansion, the space between the two being occupied by the belt of timber before mentioned.

The main entrance to Withington Chase was approached by a broad carriage-drive, which swept with a graceful curve from the lodge some half a mile away. The park was well timbered, and contained a number of grand old trees said to have been planted before the present mansion was in existence. In front of the house, but intersected by the drive, was a spacious expanse of closely-shaven lawn, to the right of which was a small but choicely kept flower-garden, while on its left was a shrubbery of tall clipped hedges and thick clumps of evergreens, among the sheltered paths of which Sir Gilbert found it pleasant to take his constitutional when the weather was too cold and raw to allow of his walking elsewhere in the open air.

The master of Withington Chase was proud of his long descent, and that not without reason.

He could trace back his pedigree on the male side in unbroken sequence to the time of Henry IV. One head of the family had fought at Agincourt, another had distinguished himself at Malplaquet; while scions of the family, more than one could count on one's fingers, had fought and, in several cases, died for their king and country wherever the British flag had penetrated. Quite a number of Clares had been in Parliament from time to time, and if none of them had been noted for his eloquence, or had risen to office, they had all possessed the negative virtue of being staunch voters, men whose political opinions could be relied upon never to stray beyond the hard and fast lines laid down by their own party.

The present baronet had taken no share in public affairs, and had declined more than once to allow himself to be nominated for a seat in Parliament. An occasional appearance on the magisterial bench, which grew still more occasional with advancing years, just sufficed to remind his brother justices and the good folk of Mapleford, that Sir Gilbert Clare of Withington Chase had not yet been gathered to his ancestors in the family vault.

The Vicar assisted his victim to stand up. The Angel turned gravely and the Vicar, with numberless insignificant panting parentheses, carefully examined the injured wings. (They articulated, he observed with interest, to a kind of second glenoid on the outer and upper edge of the shoulder blade. The left wing had suffered little except the loss of some of the primary wing-quills, and a shot or so in the ala spuria, but the humerus bone of the right was evidently smashed.) The Vicar stanched the bleeding as well as he could and tied up the bone with his pocket handkerchief and the neck wrap his housekeeper made him carry in all weathers.

"I'm afraid you will not be able to fly for some time," said he, feeling the bone.

"I don't like this new sensation," said the Angel.

"The Pain when I feel your bone?"

"The what?" said the Angel.

"The Pain."

"'Pain'--you call it. No, I certainly don't like the Pain. Do you have much of this Pain in the Land of Dreams?"

"A very fair share," said the Vicar. "Is it new to you?"

"Quite," said the Angel. "I don't like it."

"How curious!" said the Vicar, and bit at the end of a strip of linen to tie a knot. "I think this bandaging must serve for the present," he said. "I've studied ambulance work before, but never the bandaging up of wing wounds. Is your Pain any better?"

"It glows now instead of flashing," said the Angel.

"I am afraid you will find it glow for some time," said the Vicar, still intent on the wound.

The Angel gave a shrug of the wing and turned round to look at the Vicar again. He had been trying to keep an eye on the Vicar over his shoulder during all their interview. He looked at him from top to toe with raised eyebrows and a growing smile on his beautiful soft-featured face. "It seems so odd," he said with a sweet little laugh, "to be talking to a Man!"

"Do you know," said the Vicar, "now that I come to think of it, it is equally odd to me that I should be talking to an Angel. I am a somewhat matter-of-fact person. A Vicar has to be. Angels I have always regarded as--artistic conceptions----"

"Exactly what we think of men."

"But surely you have seen so many men----"

"Never before to-day. In pictures and books, times enough of course. But I have seen several since the sunrise, solid real men, besides a horse or so--those Unicorn things you know, without horns--and quite a number of those grotesque knobby things called 'cows.' I was naturally a little frightened at so many mythical monsters, and came to hide here until it was dark. I suppose it will be dark again presently like it was at first. Phew! This Pain of yours is poor fun. I hope I shall wake up directly."

"I don't understand quite," said the Vicar, knitting his brows and tapping his forehead with his flat hand. "Mythical monster!" The worst thing he had been called for years hitherto was a 'mediaeval anachronism' (by an advocate of Disestablishment). "Do I understand that you consider me as--as something in a dream?"

"Of course," said the Angel smiling.

"And this world about me, these rugged trees and spreading fronds----"

"Is all so very dream like," said the Angel. "Just exactly what one dreams of--or artists imagine."

"You have artists then among the Angels?"

"All kinds of artists, Angels with wonderful imaginations, who invent men and cows and eagles and a thousand impossible creatures."

"Impossible creatures!" said the Vicar.

"Impossible creatures," said the Angel. "Myths."

"But I'm real!" said the Vicar. "I assure you I'm real."

The Angel shrugged his wings and winced and smiled. "I can always tell when I am dreaming," he said.

As they were turning the corner of a narrow street, their attention was suddenly excited by a sharp cry of blended surprise and fright.

"What is it, Jack?" asked Harry, grasping his companion by the arm.

He did not need to await a reply, for by the indistinct light he saw two men struggling a few rods further on. One appeared to be an old man, with white hair, the other was a man of middle age. Clearly it was a case of attempted robbery.

"Run, Jack, run!" said Harry, in excitement. "Let us help the old man!"

"I'm with you," answered the young sailor briefly.

Harry had in his hand a heavy cane--his only weapon--but he did not stop to consider the personal risk he was running. As he drew near, the old man, whose feeble strength was quite unequal to a conflict with a man so much younger, swayed and fell backward. His assailant bent over him, and despite his feeble resistance began to search his pockets, at the same time indulging in savage threats. The old man gave himself up for lost, but help was nearer than he anticipated.

So occupied was the villain with his disgraceful work that he did not hear the approaching footsteps.

His first intimation of them came in a sounding blow over his shoulders, given by Harry's stick, which was laid on with a good will.

He jumped to his feet with an oath, and darted a rapid glance at his two assailants. Then, much to the surprise of Harry, he turned and ran rapidly away. It was a piece of great good luck, Harry thought, for he was not at all sure that he and Jack combined would have been a match for the highwayman.

"Are you hurt, sir?" asked Harry, bending over the old man.

"Not seriously," was the reply. "Will you kindly help me up?"

With Jack's help Harry got the old man on his feet. He was a tall man, of splendid aspect, over sixty years of age. He looked like a gentleman of wealth and position.

"You have had a narrow escape, sir," said our hero.

"Yes, indeed," answered the old man, "thanks to your brave interference. It surprises me that my brutal assailant should have run away from two boys."

"I am surprised also, sir. I feared we should have a hard fight. I suppose his object was robbery."

"Yes, he must have heard in some way that I had a large sum of money about me. Thanks to you, it is safe."

"I am very glad, sir."

"Do you mind accompanying me to my house? This attack has made me timid."

"With pleasure, sir."

The old gentleman lived perhaps a quarter of a mile distant in a handsome house. He pressed the boys to enter, and they did so. He questioned them as to their plans, and then selecting two bank-notes of large denomination, urged the boys to accept them as a recognition of the help they had given him at a critical moment. The boys, however, declined positively to accept any compensation, but expressed their satisfaction at having been of service.

"At least," said the old gentleman, "you must promise to call on me when you return from the mines. There is my card."

"That we will do with pleasure, sir," answered Harry.

He looked at the card, and read the name of Henry A. Woolson.

"Harry," said Jack, as they resumed their walk, "do you know that robber had a look like Fletcher?"

"So I thought, Jack, but I had only a glimpse, and could not be sure. I wish he were not to be in our party."

"We must be on our guard; I don't fancy him much."

When the boys saw Fletcher in the morning he appeared as usual, and they were disposed to think they were mistaken. Yet the lurking suspicion occurred to them from time to time, and made them feel uneasy.

Balaam was in his young master’s room when the latter went in. He had unpacked the trunk and the valise and was placing the things in a clothes-press, meanwhile talking with himself, as most negroes will when left to themselves. Berrien entered, humming the tune of a college glee.

“I ’lowed you was at dinner, Marse Berry,” said Balaam.

“I have finished,” said young Cozart. “Have you had yours?”

“Lord! no, suh. Hit’ll be ’way yander todes night ’fo’ I kin git dese clo’es straightened out.”

“Well,” said the young man, “you go and get your dinner as soon as you can. This valise must be repacked. Before the sun goes down we must be away from here.”

“Good Lord, Marse Berry! I ain’t said howdy wid none er de folks yit. How come we got ter go right off?”

“You can stay, if you choose,” said Berrien. “I reckon you’d be a better negro if you had stayed at home all the time. Right now you ought to be picking your five hundred pounds of cotton every day.”

“Now, you know, Marse Berry, dat of you er gwine, I’m gwine too—you know dat p’intedly; but you come in on me so sudden-like dat you sorter git me flustrated.”

“Well,” said Berrien, seating himself on the side of the bed and running his fingers through his curling hair, “if you go with me this time you will be taking a big jump in the dark. There’s no telling where you’ll land. Pap has taken the studs, and I have made up my mind to leave here for good and all. You belong to me, but I’ll give you your choice; you can go with me, or you can stay. If you go, I’ll probably get into a tight place and sell you; if you stay, Pap will make a pet of you for my sake.”

Regarding this as a very good offhand joke, the young man laughed so loud that the sound of it penetrated to the dining-room, and, mellow and hearty as it was, it struck strangely on the ears of those still sitting at the table.

“I knowed in reason dat dey was gwine to be a rippit,” said Balaam; “kaze you know how you been gwine on up yander, Marse Berry. I tole an’ tole you ’bout it, an’ I dunno whar in de name er goodness you’d been ef I hadn’t been right dar fer ter look atter you.”

“Yes,” remarked Berrien, sarcastically, “you were just about drunk enough half the time to look after me like a Dutch uncle.”

Balaam held his head down and chuckled. “Yes, suh,” he said, “I tuck my dram, dey ain’t no ’sputin’ er dat; yit I never has tuck so much dat I ain’t keep my eye on you. But ’t ain’t do no good: you des went right ’long; an’ dar was ole Mistiss, which she done sick in bed, an’ Miss Sally Carter, which she’s yo’ born cousin—dar dey all was a-specktin’ you ter head de whole school gang. An’ you did head ’em, mon, but not in de books.”

“My fair Cousin Sarah!” exclaimed Berrien in a reminiscent way.

“Yes, suh,” said Balaam; “an’ dey tells me down in de kitchen dat she comin’ yere dis ve’y day.”

“Then,” said the young man, “it is time for me to be going. Get your dinner. If I am to have your company, you must be ready in an hour; if you want to stay, go to the overseer and tell him to put you to work.”

Laughing good-naturedly, Balaam slipped out. After a little while Berrien Cozart went down the stairway and into the room of his mother, who was an invalid. He sat at her bedside and talked a few moments. Then he straightened and smoothed her pillows, stroked her gray hair, gazed into her gentle eyes, and kissed her twice. These things the poor lady remembered long afterwards. Straying into the spacious parlor, the young man looked around on the familiar furniture and the walls covered with portraits. Prominent among these was the beautiful face of Sally Carter. The red curtains in the windows, swaying to and fro in the wind, so swiftly changed the light and shadow that the fair face in the heavy gilt frame seemed to be charged with life. The lustrous eyes seemed to dance and the saucy lips to smile. Berrien remembered his fair cousin with pleasure. She had been his playmate when he was younger, and the impression she made on him had been a lasting one. Beautiful as she was, there was no nonsense about her. She was high-spirited and jolly, and the young man smiled as he recalled some of their escapades together. He raised his hand to salute the portrait, and at that moment a peal of merry laughter greeted his ears. Turning, he saw framed in the doorway the rosy original of the portrait. Before he could recover from his astonishment the young lady had seized and kissed him. Then she held him off at arm’s length and looked at him.

“I really can’t say.”

“I can, sir. You’d have run away. She’ll run away. Don’t you worry your head about her--she’ll save you the trouble. I tell you again, she’ll run away.”

With those ominous words the housekeeper took up her basket, sighed heavily, and left me.

I sat down under a tree quite helpless. Here was the whole responsibility shifted upon my miserable shoulders. Not a lady in the neighborhood to whom I could apply for assistance, and the nearest shop eight miles distant from us. The toughest case I ever had to conduct, when I was at the Bar, was plain sailing compared with the difficulty of receiving our fair guest.

It was absolutely necessary, however, to decide at once where she was to sleep. All the rooms in the tower were of ston–ark, gloomy, and cold even in the summer-time. Impossible to put her in any one of them. The only other alternative was to lodge her in the little modern lean-to, which I have already described as being tacked on to the side of the old building. It contained three cottage-rooms, and they might be made barely habitable for a young lady. But then those rooms were occupied by Morgan. His books were in one, his bed was in another, his pipes and general lumber were in the third. Could I expect him, after the sour similitudes he had used in reference to our expected visitor, to turn out of his habitation and disarrange all his habits for her convenience? The bare idea of proposing the thing to him seemed ridiculous; and yet inexorable necessity left me no choice but to make the hopeless experiment. I walked back to the tower hastily and desperately, to face the worst that might happen before my courage cooled altogether.

On crossing the threshold of the hall door I was stopped, to my great amazement, by a procession of three of the farm-servants, followed by Morgan, all walking after each other, in Indian file, toward the spiral staircase that led to the top of the tower. The first of the servants carried the materials for making a fire; the second bore an inverted arm-chair on his head; the third tottered under a heavy load of books; while Morgan came last, with his canister of tobacco in his hand, his dressing-gown over his shoulders, and his whole collection of pipes hugged up together in a bundle under his arm.

“What on earth does this mean?” I inquired.

“It means taking Time by the forelock,” answered Morgan, looking at me with a smile of sour satisfaction. “I’ve got the start of your young woman, Griffith, and I’m making the most of it.”

“But where, in Heaven’s name, are you going?” I asked, as the head man of the procession disappeared with his firing up the staircase.

“How high is this tower?” retorted Morgan.

“Seven stories, to be sure,” I replied.

“Very good,” said my eccentric brother, setting his foot on the first stair, “I’m going up to the seventh.”

“You can’t,” I shouted.

“She can’t, you mean,” said Morgan, “and that’s exactly why I’m going there.”

“But the room is not furnished.”

“It’s out of her reach.”

“One of the windows has fallen to pieces.”

“It’s out of her reach.”

“There’s a crow’s nest in the corner.”

“It’s out of her reach.”

By the time this unanswerable argument had attained its third repetition, Morgan, in his turn, had disappeared up the winding stairs. I knew him too well to attempt any further protest.

Here was my first difficulty smoothed away most unexpectedly; for here were the rooms in the lean-to placed by their owner’s free act and deed at my disposal. I wrote on the spot to the one upholsterer of our distant county town to come immediately and survey the premises, and sent off a mounted messenger with the letter. This done, and the necessary order also dispatched to the carpenter and glazier to set them at work on Morgan’s sky-parlor in the seventh story, I began to feel, for the first time, as if my scattered wits were coming back to me. By the time the evening had closed in I had hit on no less than three excellent ideas, all providing for the future comfort and amusement of our fair guest. The first idea was to get her a Welsh pony; the second was to hire a piano from the county town; the third was to send for a boxful of novels from London. I must confess I thought these projects for pleasing her very happily conceived, and Owen agreed with me. Morgan, as usual, took the opposite view. He said she would yawn over the novels, turn up her nose at the piano, and fracture her skull with the pony. As for the housekeeper, she stuck to her text as stoutly in the evening as she had stuck to it in the morning. “Pianner or no pianner, story-book or no story-book, pony or no pony, you mark my words, si–hat young woman will run away.”

Well, it was a bitter pill to swallow, that the uncle had seen fit to leave his worldly possessions to a distant cousin, without so much as a thought for those nearest to him. Yet, perhaps it was to be expected, given the uncle's long-standing propensity for selfishness. To be sure, he had often been heard to express his disapproval of our family's modest circumstances, though his declarations of disdain had always been accompanied by a reticence to lend a helping hand.

As we sat within our humble abode, Mrs. Carter gazed out the window with a look of quiet resignation, her eyes clouded by the weight of our family's financial struggles. "If only he had left us something," she sighed, her voice barely above a whisper. "A small sum, indeed, but it would have been a blessing in disguise, for it would have alleviated some of life's pressing necessities."

"Ah, but mother," I exclaimed, "we must not set our hearts on what is not to be. The uncle's estate has gone to his chosen heir, and we must not harbor any expectations we know to be fruitless. It is a disappointment, I confess, but it is one we must bear with dignity." My words, meant to be consoling, seemed to fall flat, for my mother's countenance only deepened in its sorrow.

The reality was, our financial situation remained precarious. I had a natural aptitude for learning, and a desire to improve myself, but the means to do so were woefully lacking. My mother, a seamstress of some talent, struggled to eke out a meager living, her hands moving deftly as she worked to finish a patchwork coat for a customer. She had always desired more for me, to have me educated and trained in a trade, but such opportunities were far beyond our reach.

The days passed slowly, as they often did when one's prospects seemed uncertain. I prowled the field and woods surrounding our home, lost in thought, and often finding solace in the peace and beauty of nature. The thought of my uncle's funeral, however, cast a pall over these gentle joys. I knew, of course, that I should attend the service, as would be expected of me by the community. My mother would want me to honor his memory, though I must confess that I felt little genuine sorrow at his passing.

After some consideration, I arrived at a decision. I would travel to the distant town where my uncle lay buried, on foot. It would be a long and tiring journey, some twenty miles as the crow flies, but I felt it was essential to make the trip. A coach would be a luxury we could ill afford, and my pride would not permit me to burden my mother with the expense. I was confident in my ability to walk it, though the distance would certainly be a trial.

My mother's concerns, as I feared they would be, were numerous. "But Herbert, dear boy," she said, "you are so young, and the road can be treacherous, especially in this time of year. Are you certain you wish to undertake such a journey?" I nodded resolutely, and attempted to reassure her, though I could see the worry etched on her face.

The journey ahead would be long and arduous, but I steeled myself for the challenge. I remained conscious of the fact that only by such sacrifices might I carve out a better life for myself and my family. A parting thought, a whispered word of encouragement from my mother, and I set off on my way.

"Chester," said the minister, kindly, "how does it happen that you have an assistant to-day?"

"I am the assistant, Mr. Morris. Abel is Mr. Tripp's new boy."

"Indeed, I am surprised to hear that. When did you leave the store?"

"Last Saturday night."

"Have you another place?"

"Not yet."

"Are you at leisure this afternoon?"

"Yes, sir."

"Then perhaps you will walk around with my friend, Mr. Conrad, and show him the village. I was going with him, but I have some writing to do, and you will do just as well."

"I shall be very happy to go with Mr. Conrad," said Chester, politely.

"And I shall be very glad to have you," said the young man, with a pleasant smile.

"Come back to supper, Chester," said the minister; "that is, if your mother can spare you."

"Thank you, sir. I suppose you will be able to carry back the empty basket, Abel," added Chester, as his successor emerged from the side door, relieved of his burden.

"I guess so," answered Abel, with a grin.

"I was never in Wyncombe before," began Mr. Conrad, "though I am a second cousin of your minister, Mr. Morris. I have to go away to-morrow morning, and wish to see a little of the town while I am here."

"Where do you live, Mr. Conrad?"

"In the city of New York."

"Are you a minister, too?"

"Oh, no!" laughed the young man. "I am in a very different business. I am an artist--in a small way. I make sketches for books and magazines."

"And does that pay?"

"Fairly well. I earn a comfortable living."

"I didn't know one could get money for making pictures. I like to draw, myself."

"I will see what you can do this evening; that is, if you accept my cousin's invitation."

Before the walk was over Chester had become much interested in his new friend. He listened eagerly to his stories of the great city, and felt that life must be much better worth living there than in Wyncombe.

A NOTEWORTHY EVENING.

Chester enjoyed his supper. Mr. Morris, though a minister, had none of the starched dignity that many of his profession think it necessary to assume. He was kindly and genial, with a pleasant humor that made him agreeable company for the young as well as the old. Mr. Conrad spoke much of New York and his experiences there, and Chester listened to him eagerly.

"You have never been to New York, Chester?" said the young artist.

"No, sir, but I have read about it--and dreamed about it. Sometime I hope to go there."

"I think that is the dream of every country boy. Well, it is the country boys that make the most successful men."

"How do you account for that, Herbert?" asked the minister.

"Generally they have been brought up to work, and work more earnestly than the city boys."

When the supper table was cleared, Mr. Conrad took from his valise two or three of the latest issues of Puck, Judge and Life. He handed them to Chester, who looked over them eagerly.

"Do you ever contribute to these papers, Mr. Conrad?" he asked.

"Yes; here is a sketch in Judge, and another in Life, which I furnished."

"And do you get good pay for them?"

"I received ten dollars for each."

Chester's eyes opened with surprise.

"Why," he said, "they are small. It couldn't have taken you long to draw them."

"Probably half an hour for each one."

"And you received ten dollars each?"

"Yes, but don't gauge such work by the time it takes. It is the idea that is of value. The execution is a minor matter."

Chester looked thoughtful.

"I should like to be an artist," he said, after a pause.

"Won't you give me a specimen of your work? You have seen mine."

"I have not done any comic work, but I think I could."

“Pray don't disturb yourself,” said Mainwaring, rising hastily, but not quickly enough to prevent the young girl from slipping past him into the house, whence she rapidly returned with a decanter and glasses.

“Perhaps Mr. Mainwaring would prefer to go into Jim's room and wash his hands and put on a pair of slippers?” said Mrs. Bradley, with gentle concern.

“Thanks, no. I really am not tired. I sent some luggage yesterday by the coach to the Summit Hotel,” he said, observing the women's eyes still fixed upon his knapsack. “I dare say I can get them if I want them. I've got a change here,” he continued, lifting the knapsack as if with a sudden sense of its incongruity with its surroundings, and depositing it on the end of the veranda.

“Do let it remain where it is,” said Mrs. Bradley, greatly amused, “and pray sit still and take some refreshment. You'll make yourself ill after your exertions,” she added, with a charming assumption of matronly solicitude.

“But I'm not at all deserving of your sympathy,” said Mainwaring, with a laugh. “I'm awfully fond of walking, and my usual constitutional isn't much under this.”

“Perhaps you were stronger than you are now,” said Mrs. Bradley, gazing at him with a frank curiosity that, however, brought a faint deepening of color to his cheek.

“I dare say you're right,” he said suddenly, with an apologetic smile. “I quite forgot that I'm a sort of an invalid, you know, travelling for my health. I'm not very strong here,” he added, lightly tapping his chest, that now, relieved of the bands of his knapsack, appeared somewhat thin and hollow in spite of his broad shoulders. His voice, too, had become less clear and distinct.

Mrs. Bradley, who was still watching him, here rose potentially. “You ought to take more care of yourself,” she said. “You should begin by eating this biscuit, drinking that glass of whiskey, and making yourself more comfortable in Jim's room until we can get the spare room fixed a little.”

“But I am not to be sent to bed--am I?” asked Mainwaring, in half-real, half-amused consternation.

“I'm not so sure of that,” said Mrs. Bradley, with playful precision. “But for the present we'll let you off with a good wash and a nap afterwards in that rocking-chair, while my cousin and I make some little domestic preparations. You see,” she added with a certain proud humility, “we've got only one servant--a Chinaman, and there are many things we can't leave to him.”

The color again rose in Mainwaring's cheek, but he had tact enough to reflect that any protest or hesitation on his part at that moment would only increase the difficulties of his gentle entertainers. He allowed himself to be ushered into the house by Mrs. Bradley, and shown to her husband's room, without perceiving that Miss Macy had availed herself of his absence to run to the end of the veranda, mischievously try to lift the discarded knapsack to her own pretty shoulder, but, failing, heroically stagger with it into the passage and softly deposit it at his door. This done, she pantingly rejoined her cousin in the kitchen.

“Well,” said Mrs. Bradley, emphatically. “DID you ever? Walking fifteen miles for pleasure--and with such lungs!”

“And that knapsack!” added Louise Macy, pointing to the mark in her little palm where the strap had imbedded itself in the soft flesh.

“He's nice, though; isn't he?” said Mrs. Bradley, tentatively.

“Yes,” said Miss Macy, “he isn't, certainly, one of those provincial fine gentlemen you object to. But DID you see his shoes? I suppose they make the miles go quickly, or seem to measure less by comparison.”

And now, the timbers being stacked high, an admirable screen indeed against the curious gazes of Mrs. Abernathy, whose dwelling stood but a scant hundred feet from my own, I turned my mind to the matter of the framing. For it is one thing to possess the lumber, delivered by a seeming Providence, and quite another to assemble it into a structure fit to withstand the ravages of time, and the scorn of more accomplished builders.

I confess, a pang of conscience, sharp and unwelcome, did pierce my heart as I contemplated the deception I had wrought, small though it may seem. Yet, necessity, as they say, knows no law, and my need for a secluded retreat, a sanctuary from the ceaseless demands of my family and the stifling constraints of our household, far outweighed any minor transgression against the strict letter of honesty. Besides, I reasoned with myself, the lumber was surely of little consequence to Mr. Hawthorne, a man of such wealth and consequence that he scarce knew the amount of shillings in his own purse. To him, the loss of a few boards would be as inconsequential as the loss of a single leaf to a mighty oak.

And so, I cast aside such niggling doubts and plunged headlong into the task at hand. The mornings, as I have said, I devoted to the pretense of labor on Mr. Hawthorne’s uptown project, a charade that grew increasingly tiresome with each passing day. My mother, bless her trusting soul, remained blissfully unaware of my true activities, accepting my explanations with an unquestioning faith that both warmed and shamed me. Yet, I dared not reveal my secret, for fear of her disapproval, and perhaps even her interference in my grand design.

The afternoons, however, were mine to command. Under the guise of fetching tools or running errands for the uptown job, I would slip away to my hidden plot, armed with hammer, saw, and a fervent determination. There, amongst the sheltering timbers, I labored with a vigor born of both necessity and excitement. The frame began to take shape, slowly but surely, like the unfolding of a long-held dream. Each beam, each joist, each precisely measured cut brought me closer to the realization of my private haven.

The German, too, proved to be a most valuable asset. He, with his stolid nature and unwavering dedication to the task at hand, asked no questions and harbored no suspicions. He was content to follow my instructions, to lift and carry and hold, without inquiring as to the ultimate purpose of our endeavors. For this, I was eternally grateful, for his silence was as golden as the nails he drove with such methodical precision. His name, as I recall, was Herr Schmidt, a man of few words but boundless strength, and a simple kindness that belied his gruff exterior. To my great fortune, he possessed a smattering of carpentry skills, acquired, I believe, during his apprenticeship in the old country. He knew the difference between a tenon and a mortise, a plane and a chisel.

And so, the work progressed, each day bringing me closer to my goal. The frame rose higher and higher, like a skeletal promise against the afternoon sky. I found myself growing increasingly bolder, more confident in my ability to conceal my clandestine activities. Perhaps it was hubris, or perhaps it was simply the intoxicating allure of creation, but I began to take greater risks, spending longer hours at my secret work, pushing the boundaries of my deception to their very limits. Yet, fortune, it seemed, continued to favor me. No one questioned my absences, no one suspected my true purpose. The lumber remained undisturbed, the German remained unquestioning, and Mrs. Abernathy remained blissfully oblivious behind her rose-covered trellis. And I, for the time being, remained master of my own little domain, a secret architect of my own hidden sanctuary.

The air within the room seemed to hold a palpable tension, one which Mrs. Compton could feel weaving through each syllable that escaped her sister’s lips. She gazed around at the modest furniture, strained to discern the delicate ticking of the clock on the mantelpiece, and finally allowed her eyes to rest once more on Miss Betsy. Her sister was now gently stroking the arm of her chair with an abstracted air, lost in a reverie that appeared far from their pressing concerns.

“Indeed, it astonishes me, Betsy, how you can maintain such composure amid the tumult that surrounds us,” Mrs. Compton began, a tinge of exasperation threading her voice.

“Composure is but a balm for the soul, dear sister,” replied Miss Betsy, her tone flowing as smoothly as the stream by her garden where the bees buzzed in tranquil harmony. “Much the same as tending to my hives calms my mind, so does sitting quietly with a favorite book.”

“But the village whispers, Betsy—Josiah’s affairs—” ventured Mrs. Compton, her expression a mixture of imploring eagerness and weary familiarity.

“Ah, yes, the hum of bees is naught compared to the clamor of gossip, I suppose,” Miss Betsy mused aloud, her hands now resuming their rhythmic motion along the chair’s finely polished wood. “And yet, sister, sometimes it is best to let matters settle of their own accord.”

Mrs. Compton sighed, a sound both resigned and reflective, as she considered the unyielding calm of her sister, contrasted against her own anxious spirit. “If only matters would resolve themselves so easily, Betsy,” she murmured, more to herself than to the untroubled spinster.

Into this contemplative pause, Miss Sophy entered with a quick and lively step, cheeks flushed from the afternoon air. Her arrival was as a gust of fresh wind through a long-closed room. “Is it not a lovely day, Mama?” she exclaimed, with a brightness in her voice that seemed in stark contrast to the subdued atmosphere.

“It is indeed a fine day, Sophy,” Miss Betsy replied before Mrs. Compton could speak, rising slightly in her seat to acknowledge her niece. “Your presence never fails to remind me of the sun breaking through clouds.”

Sophy smiled with the innocent delight of youth unburdened, though she detected the undercurrent of her mother's distress. “Perhaps you could join us in the garden presently, Aunt Betsy. The roses have begun to bloom in such splendour.”

“You do know how to tempt me, my dear. A stroll among the roses at this hour might bring as much pleasure as an afternoon with my books,” Betsy allowed, her lips curving into a gentle smile that seemed to soften the very air about her.

Mrs. Compton watched this exchange with a mixture of relief and bemusement, grateful for her daughter's ability to draw warmth from even the most composed heart. “It does one good to forget, if only for a moment,” she reflected, her own spirits lifting slightly.

Sophy cast a sidelong glance at her mother, perceiving a lingering shadow upon her features. “The Colonel's gathering was delightful, Mama. We sang and danced, and all were in fine spirits.”

“Indeed, a successful evening, but such gaiety is fleeting,” Mrs. Compton replied, her words touched with the faint melancholy of experience.

“Even still, it's worth cherishing those happy hours. Aunt Betsy, would you not agree?” Sophy turned her bright eyes towards the spinster, eager for a second ally in her argument for joy amid concern.

“There is wisdom in what you say, child,” Betsy nodded slowly. “For a day filled with laughter holds a certain charm that even the bees cannot match.”

“And your ribbons, Sophy?” Mrs. Compton interjected, a note of practicality entering her tone. “Those new ribbons must be seen to before the next visit to the Colonel’s.”

“They are quite lovely, Mama, and Martha promised to help me with them tomorrow,” Sophy reassured, her voice harmonious with the cheer she brought into every room.

Mrs. Compton wondered privately at the mystery that her daughters never seemed to share in her own tired misgivings, yet she could not deny the youthful vigor they brought to her days. With a quieter resolve, she turned to her sister once more. “Then, Betsy, shall we? The roses await us outside, and surely it would do your soul good, as it would mine, to partake in such earthly delights.”

“To the garden, then,” agreed Miss Betsy, rising with an elegance any true lady of leisure would envy, thus setting aside, at least for the next act, the swirl of familial misgivings that neither books nor bees could fully quiet.

At daybreak the following morning, the village of Rockpier bustled with anticipation as the sun ascended, casting its warm glow upon the quaint cottages and the grand old rectory. The aroma of fresh bread wafted through the air, mingling with the sweet scent of blooming flowers that lined the cobblestone streets. The inhabitants of Rockpier, a mixture of farmers, tradesfolk, and the curious, gathered in knots to share tidings and gossip. The talk of the day was a resounding echo of the previous evening's events at the Hornblowers' lodgings. Frank, with his usual exhilaration, regaled his friends with tales of Herbert Bowater's installation, the temple of St. Chrysostom awash with the resplendent dresses of the Bowater family as they showered the new curate with praise and recognition.

As the church bell chimed the hour, a commotion in the crowd caught the attention of all present. A carriage, drawn by two matched grays, clattered over the cobblestones, and drawing to a halt outside the church door. From it emerged Mr. and Mrs. Duncombe, a couple of such unconventional disposition that their very arrival in Rockpier was enough to stir up a whirlwind of speculation. Mr. Duncombe, a tall man with a perpetual smirk and a penchant for sweeping yet uncouth phrases, was accompanied by his wife, a lady as bold as she was passionate, known to advocate for causes far removed from the polite society's norm. Behind them stepped their three daughters, each as unique as their parents, their laughter ringing out as they chatted animatedly.

The Duncombes, it was known, had been previously engaged in matters of high stakes betting, their house in London often the scene of extravagant gatherings. Yet their participation in the movement for women's rights had earned them a reputation amongst the reformers, and the conservative society in Rockpier had yet to reconcile these dual personae. As they stepped into the church, a hush fell over the crowd, the scent of their revolution mingling with the sweet incense and the familiar scent of beeswax candles.

News of the Duncombes' presence spread swiftly, reaching the ears of Julius, the curate's assistant, who had been engaged in the task of preparing the communion bread. His brow furrowed as he mixed the ingredients, the motion rhythmic and focused. He had heard much about the Duncombes, their unconventional views on marriage and finance, their willingness to challenge the status quo. He was unsure what to expect, and his uncertainty was etched onto his face as he made his way to the church.

Meanwhile, in the rectory, Lady Rosamond, wife of the late Mr. 뿁érichard Hornblower, sat by the window, her eyes reflecting the distant hills. She was a woman of quiet strength, her untraditional upbringing in the midst of a family she now called her own, her husband's death having left a void in their curved world. Her thoughts were interrupted by the sight of the Duncombes' carriage. She rose from her seat, her steps measured as she walked to the door, her mind racing with possibilities of what this newcomer might mean for Rockpier's Church.

In the midst of this turmoil, Mrs. Poynsett, the matriarch of the village, found herself drawn towards the church, as if pulled by an invisible thread. Her mind was filled with the images of her daughters, now married women, each a reflection of her own past. She had seen the good in them all, even Lady Rosamond, whose background in the art of lobbying had once caused her to blanche. Yet now, she found a strength in that background, a solidity in her resolve that made their marriage a partnership, not a merely a union. She was, she believed, a beacon of wisdom, a guiding light in a world that often veered from the safe path. As she approached the church, her steps steady and sure, she could not help but feel that the Duncombes' arrival was a test, a challenge to the very core of her convictions.

Inside the church, the whispers had grown into a hum as the Duncombes made their way to the front. Mr. Duncombe, with a flourish, took his seat in the pew, a self-satisfied smile on his face. His wife, with a nudge of her elbow, quieted him, her eyes scanning the congregation, taking in their expressions, their reservations. Their elder daughter, Miss Isabel, seated beside her father, looked around with a twinkle in her eye, a hint of mischief in her smile as she caught sight of Julius. Her eyes met his, a silent dialogue passed between them, a challenge, a promise, a spark of something more.

A subdued and ineffable charm, as if summoned by some clandestine hand, dwells amidst the annals of New Zion, where words that pass the tongue in the ephemeral fashion of oratory pale when compared to the perennial echoes of poetry. In this sacred assemblage, the clamor of fleeting speeches is but a transient glitter on the surface of existence, while the deeper reverberations of verse, wrought by the straining hearts and stuttering pens of human endeavor, endure as the true legacy of spirit. It is in such profound disparity that Reverend Theophilus Londonderry finds his daily consolation—not in the hollow gestures of his pulpit’s rambling diatribe but in the subtle art of discerning the inner music of his flock, that ineffably varied collection of souls whose frailties and light share a universe of intermingled dreams.

In the arduous task of tending to souls so intricate and imperfectly made, the minister is confronted with the inevitable challenge of mediocrity, and yet, with each stutter of the mundane, there arises a portrait of pathetic yet exquisite splendor. For every transient spark of rhetorical bravura given vent to by the congregation is met by a lingering afterglow, like the soft imprint of moonlight on the battered flags of some forgotten fortress. Thus, with the kindly assistance of Eli Moggridge—a man whose vitality compliments the Reverend’s study of human dissonance—the embattled spirit of New Zion is enlivened; the once dreary service becomes an intricate milieu in which every errant parable and half-whispered prayer attains a dignity of its own. In such company, the minister repudiates the notion that his religious labors are a sterile chore, instead embracing each anecdote and melancholy confession as a precious note within the broader canticle of communal life.

The Reverend, whose perceptive eyes trace the delicate nuances of human frailty in the lines etched upon every aged visage, discerns that the art of ministry is not so much the erudition of learned words but rather the compassionate attunement to each man’s own elegy of longing. He frequently muses that, in the tumultuous machinery of life whereby dreams are ground into the dust of daily toil, the surviving gleams of individual worth must be nurtured like rare blooms in an unforgiving winter’s garden. Consequently, Theophilus finds solace in the deliberate exercise of focusing on each individual’s singular impulse—the spark of intellect here, the touch of caritas there—thus fashioning from the rough and assorted materials of the human heart a portrait both tragic and exquisite. It is, perhaps, this gentle art of accentuating the little flecks of beauty amid the quotidian decay that renders his labors transcendent, repelling the dreariness of routine with bursts of charming novelty.

In the convivial yet pensive aftermath of each solemn service, as the twilight mingles with the dim lamplight of modest halls, the mind of the Reverend wanders to the broader vista of his endeavors. He contemplates the curious manner in which the fleeting murmurs of piety resound beyond the narrow confines of the chapel and extend into the vast, uncharted realms of human creativity. A sense of rapturously mournful gratitude fills him—a gratitude which, in its very essence, is indebted to the perennial verity that no man is condemned wholly by his faults but is instead replete with irregular flashes of sublimity. It is here, in the meeting of the ephemeral and the eternal, that the art of ministry, like that of a poet compelled by a lingering muse, balances on a narrow cusp between despair and exaltation. Within the communal dialogue that grows ever more animated under his gentle guidance, every discarded word gains a semblance of permanence, every neglected shortcoming finds its twin in an overlooked virtue.

And so, the New Zion community, vibrant with renewed purpose and emboldened by the synergy of its varied members, steps forward into a future as uncertain as it is promising. There is an ineffable beauty in observing how the modest hearts of humble parishioners, once resigned and dulled by the relentless grind of existence, now shimmer with the possibility of transcendence. With the unyielding commitment of Theophilus Londonderry, whose every interaction is a meticulous study in the transformative power of attentive care, and with the earnest assistance of his dutiful friend, Eli Moggridge, the spirit of New Zion finds itself buoyant and expanding. Amid the clamor of mortal mediocrity, the artful weaving together of diverse human threads now produces a vibrant tapestry—a living testament to the notion that while transient words may falter, the resonant music of the soul endures.

It was a sultry evening in late August, the sort of night when the very air seemed to vibrate with the languor of the languishing summer. The sun had set hours before, casting a golden glow over the verdant landscape of Cowles' Farms, but the heat still lingered, heavy and oppressive, like a wet blanket that one could not shake off. I stood on the veranda, gazing out into the darkness, my mind still reeling from the events of the day.

Mr. Orme had departed the hour before, a sense of gratitude etched upon his features, and a gentle smile upon his lips. I had watched him go with a feeling of relief, for though I had grown accustomed to our company, there were still times when I felt the need for solitude, for a respite from the gentle flow of conversation and the plodding familiarity of country life.

As I stood there, lost in thought, the back door of the house swung open, and a young planter, Harry Singleton, stumbled onto the veranda. He was a rough-hewn young man, with a coarse, unshaven face and a mop of unruly hair that threatened to spill over his brow at any moment. He was drunk, and I knew it, but what I did not know was why.

"By the Lord above, I'll never tire of the CSA!" Harry exclaimed, his voice rising to a shout, as he lurched from one foot to the other. "We'll rise again, we'll rise again, and the Yankees will be sent fleeing!" His words were slurred, but they were also laced with a fire that I had seen before in his eyes, a fire that spoke of passion and conviction.

I felt a flutter of unease as I watched him, for I knew that the subject of his peroration was best avoided, especially in his present state. But Harry seemed oblivious to everything around him, his words tumbling forth in a torrent, as he proclaimed his unwavering support for the Confederate States.

"And Miss Sheraton, bless her lovely soul!" he bellowed, his words echoing off the trees. "She'll be the first to stand by our side, come what may!" His eyes were wild, unfocused, and I knew that I had to act, for Harry's drunken ramblings were about to get him into trouble.

"Harry, my boy," I said, placing a gentle hand upon his shoulder, "perhaps you should not speak of...certain ladies in a public forum. It's not seemly, not here, where our company is scattered and tongues are loose."

Harry's face twisted in a snarl, and for a moment, I thought he might lash out at me. But then, his eyes seemed to focus, and he turned on me, his gaze cold and hard. "What business is it of yours?" he growled.

I took a step back, my heart racing, for I knew that Harry was not in control, and that his next words could prove disastrous. But I also knew that I could not let him continue, not here, not now. "It's where your manners are concerned, Harry," I said, trying to keep my voice even.

His face convulsed in a snarl, and before I could react, he launched himself at me, his fist flying in a wild arc. I sidestepped it with ease, but Harry's wild blow caught me off guard, and I stumbled backward, my hand flying up to deflect the blow.

As Harry lunged at me again, I saw a figure emerging from the darkness, a tall, imposing form that moved with a quiet purpose. It was Mr. Orme, and he strode forward, his eyes narrowed, his face tight with concern. "Hold him, man!" he exclaimed, his voice low and steady.

Without hesitation, I threw myself at Harry, my body enveloping his as we crashed to the floor. Harry struggled and kicked, but I held him fast, my strength unyielding, until at last he went limp, his struggle spent. As I rose to my feet, panting, I saw Mr. Orme's face, his eyes fixed upon me with a look of approbation.

"It's a good job you subdued him," he said, his voice full of praise. "A pity he was so taken with his liquor. Perhaps a night's rest will sober him."

As I stood there, gasping for breath, I felt a sense of pride, of dignity, and I knew that I had done what was necessary. And as I looked at Mr. Orme, I saw a glimmer of something more, something that went beyond mere approval, something that spoke of respect, of admiration.

But for now, I pushed the thought aside, for the night was still young, and there was still so much to do. I watched as Mr. Orme walked back into the darkness, his figure silhouetted against the starry sky, and I knew that I had a long night ahead of me.

The girls sat in the parlor, their conversation light and airy, yet beneath the surface, a subtle tension lingered. Agatha’s speech had left them thoughtful, and though they endeavored to appear as though it had not reached them, their heightened awareness of one another was difficult to conceal. They moved with an exaggerated care, as though each motion might betray the stirrings within. Magdalen, ever the observer, noted the shift in their manner, and though she said nothing, her eyes betrayed a mixture of amusement and concern.

The afternoon sun streamed through the tall windows, casting patterns of light and shadow across the room. Magdalen found herself drawn to the view beyond the glass—a stretch of lawn leading down to a small copse of trees. The world outside seemed to call to her, offering a respite from the quiet undercurrents of uncertainty that had settled over the group. She rose gracefully, herskirts rustling softly as she crossed the room, and with a nod to the others, stepped into the garden.

The fresh air enveloped her, and for a moment, she closed her eyes, letting its breeziness soothe her. The girls followed soon after, drawn by the quiet invitation of the outdoors. They strolled along the gravel path, their footsteps rhythmic against the stones. Magdalen led the way, her mind wandering to the plans she had made for the Sunday school. It was a cause close to her heart, and though she longed to speak of it, she held her tongue, knowing the time was not yet right.

As they walked, the conversation turned to the various churches in the vicinity. The girls exchanged light-hearted banter, poking fun at one another’s preferences with a playfulness that belied their earlier silence. Magdalen listened with a smile, her thoughts drifting to the chapel at Clipstone and the quiet comfort it offered. She had always found solace in its simplicity, but as the others laughed and jests were thrown about, she couldn’t help but feel a flicker of guilt for her own reticence. The girls were younger, their spirits brighter and less burdened, and she could not help but envy them their carefree nature.

Their path wound through the garden, leading them to a small meadow where wildflowers bloomed in abundance. The girls paused, their laughter dying away as they took in the vibrant display. Magdalen, ever the student of nature, began to name the flowers, her voice soft and deliberate. She spoke of the delicate patterns on the petals, the way the light caught the shimmer of the bees flitting between them. The girls listened, their earlier jests forgotten, their faces alight with wonder.

But as she continued, Magdalen noticed a growing look of confusion in their eyes. Their lack of knowledge on the subject Became evident, and though she tried to mask her amusement, a chuckle escaped her lips. The girls turned to her, their expressions a mixture of embarrassment and teasing. “Magdalen,” one of them said with mock severity, “you have become quite the expert on these matters.”

The interruption came suddenly, as a figure emerged from beyond the meadow—a farmer’s wife, her face weathered but kind, carrying a basket of eggs. She greeted the girls with a broad smile, her dialect thick with the local accent. “Good day, my dears,” she said, her eyes crinkling with warmth. “I was just out seein’ to the chickens when I heard your voices. Beautiful day for a walk, isn’t it?”

The girls exchanged glances, their earlier ease returning as they engaged with the woman. Magdalen stepped back, letting them take the lead in the conversation, her mind wandering once more. The farmer’s wife spoke of her chickens, her voice filled with pride, her hands gesturing animatedly as she described their antics. The girls listened, their laughter returning, blending with the woman’s hearty chuckles.

Magdalen watched, her thoughts turning inward. The scene before her was one of simple, unassuming joy—a moment of connection between people from different worlds. She felt a pang of envy, for though she loved her routine and her plans for the Sunday school, there was a part of her that longed for such ease, such freedom from the weight of expectations.

As the woman departed, her basket still heavy with eggs, the girls resumed their walk, their conversation lighter, their spirits lifted. Magdalen fell into step beside them, her earlier concerns pushed aside for the moment. The world around them seemed to breathe with life, and for a brief moment, she allowed herself to simply be, to enjoy the beauty of the day and the company of her friends.

Yet, as they turned back toward the house, a shadow of doubt crept back into her thoughts. She wondered if she had heard Agatha’s speech clearly, if her caution in responding had been wise. The girls, ever the youths, seemed untouched by such worries, their laughter echoing across the meadow as they disappeared into the distance.

Magdalen lingered for a moment, the weight of her thoughts settling upon her. She knew the path she had chosen, the responsibilities she had taken upon herself. It was a heavy burden, but one she bore with a quiet strength. She believed in her cause, in her ability to make a difference, and though the road ahead was uncertain, she pressed on, her resolve unbroken.

"What are you fellows joking about?" he asked, while he roared with laughter, as if with an anticipatory relish of the fun. "Some chaff at my expense, eh? Something about my not having made up my mind to do something or not; the usual nonsense, I suppose?"

"Not at all Geoff," said Tom Wrigley. "The question asked by Mr. Stompff here was--whether you wished to sell this picture, and what you asked for it."

"Ah!" said Geoffrey Ludlow, his lips closing and the fun dying out of his eyes. "Well, you see it's of course a compliment for you, Mr. Stompff, to ask the question; but I've scarcely made up my mind--whether--and indeed as to the price--"

"Stuff, Geoff! What rubbish you talk!" said Charley Potts, who had rejoined the group. "You know well enough that you painted the picture for sale. You know equally well that the price is two hundred guineas. Are you answered, Mr. Stump?"

Ludlow started forward with a look of annoyance, but Stompff merely grinned, and said quietly, "I take it at the price, and as many more as Mr. Ludlow will paint of the same sort; stock, lock, and barrel, I'll have the whole bilin'. Must change the title though, Ludlow, my boy. None of your Sic wos non thingummy; none of your Hebrew classics for the British public. 'The Vow,' or 'the Last Farewell,' or something in that line.--Very neatly done of you, Charley, my boy; very neat bit of dealing, I call it. I ought to deduct four-and-nine from the next fifteen shillin' commission you get; but I'll make it up to you this way,--you've evidently all the qualities of a salesman; come and be my clerk, and I'll stand thirty shillings a-week and a commission on the catalogues."

Charley Potts was too delighted at his friend's success to feel annoyance at these remarks; he merely shook his fist laughingly, and was passing on, with his arm through Ludlow's; but the vivacious dealer, who had rapidly calculated where he could plant his newly-acquired purchase, and what percentage he could make on it, was not to be thus balked.

"Look here!" said he; "a bargain's a bargain, ain't it? People say your word's as good as your bond, and all that. Pickles! You drop down to my office to-morrow, Ludlow, and there'll be an agreement for you to sign--all straight and reg'lar, you know. And come and cut your mutton with me and Mrs. S. at Velasquez Villa, Nottin' 'Ill, on Sunday, at six. No sayin' no, because I won't hear it. We'll wet our connection in a glass of Sham. And bring Charley with you, if his dress-coat ain't up! You know, Charley! Tar, Tar!" And highly delighted with himself, and with the full conviction that he had rendered himself thoroughly delightful to his hearers, the great man waddled off his brougham.

Meanwhile the news of the purchase had spread through the rooms, and men were hurrying up on all sides to congratulate Ludlow on his success. The fortunate man seemed, however, a little dazed with his triumph; he shook all the outstretched hands cordially, and said a few commonplaces of thanks, intermingled with doubts as to whether he had not been too well treated; but on the first convenient opportunity he slipped away, and sliding a shilling into the palm of Flexor the model, who, being by this time very drunk, had arranged his hair in a curl on his forehead, and was sitting on the bench in the hall after his famous rendering of George the Fourth of blessed memory, Geoff seized his hat and coat and let himself out. The fresh night-air revived him wonderfully, and he was about starting off at his usual headstrong pace, when he heard a low dismal moan, and looking round, he saw a female figure cowering in a doorway. The next instant he was kneeling by her side.

The meeting was opened with prayer. Deacon Bates remarked prefatorily that such would be the proper thing in a class composed of adults, and then he looked around hesitatingly for the proper man to make the first formal committal of the class into the hands of the Lord; but Squire Woodhouse saved him the trouble by springing to his feet and volunteering to Heaven an address so concise that there remained nothing unsaid. Then Bibles were distributed, and opened at the fifth chapter of Matthew's Gospel, and every one looked unspeakably profound, though Mr. Hopper had the presence of mind to place his hand beneath his coat-tails and take hold of the review containing the paper on "The True Location of the Holy Sepulchre," so as to be ready in case occasion offered.

"Let us begin with the beatitudes," said the leader. "'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' By the way, I would suggest that each member speaks in the order of his sitting. Mr. Lottson," continued Deacon Bates, addressing the insurance president, "whom do you suppose Jesus referred to as 'the poor in spirit'?"

"Before answering that question," said Mr. Lottson, "I think attention should be called to a passage in the opening of the chapter. It is said that 'When he was set, his disciples came unto him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying,' etc. Now, before we try to understand this beautiful succession of blessings, we should realize whom they were spoken to--to the disciples, who had left all and followed him, and therefore to a set of men to whom he could say things which it would be nonsensical for him to say to the common people and business men around him. The disciples were out of business, and lived on their friends--it was right enough for them to do so under the circumstances, but for this very reason Jesus told them the things which nobody else could understand. This sermon was preached to self-forgetting preachers, not to men who had to make their living and take the world as they found it; and I suppose the first beatitude meant to them just what it said. They were poor in spirit--any man has to be, if he be willing to go around without a cent in his pocket--but to pay them for it he gave them the kingdom of heaven, that is, the church of which Christ is prophet, priest, and king. It's the greatest charge in the world; all business enterprises are nothing in comparison with it; but Jesus showed his divine nature by giving them this, for while they managed it splendidly, it's the only great affair in the world that a lot of poor-spirited men could manage without running it into the ground."

"That depends upon what 'poor in spirit' means," remarked Squire Woodhouse. "President Lottson seems to think it's the same thing as mean-spirited, but if it is, I can tell him that there's more money for that kind of chaps in other businesses. Now I'm a farmer--my principal crop is hay, and when my barn burned down last winter with eleven tons loose and forty odd tons pressed, and I went to the insur----"

"The members will please speak as called upon," said the leader, whose watchful ear imagined it detected a personality in the immediate future of the Squire's address. Squire Woodhouse subsided after a soft whisper to his right-hand neighbor, which caused that gentleman to notice that President Lottson's face was flushing a little, and his lips touching each other more firmly than usual.

"It seems to me," said Mr. Radley, who was next called upon, "that the passage means just what it says. The kingdom of heaven means the place we all hope to get to some day, and the poor in spirit are the people who aren't touchy and don't put on airs Christ was a man of this kind himself, and he knew by experience what he was talking about."

Sir Francis Geraldine, with a slight arch of his brow and a manner both haughty and weary, broached the subject with a delicacy that belied his inner discontent. "My dear Cecilia," he began, his tone measured as if each syllable were weighed against a ledger of past wont, "I find that the proximity of these twenty-four hours has grown oppressive, and I must entreat some brief reprieve from our present arrangement." His eyes, warmed with a mixture of amusement and melancholy, searched her face as though seeking evidence of a similar sentiment.

Cecilia, who had her long practiced skill in concealing turbulent passions beneath a mask of genteel reserve, merely inclined her head as if to acknowledge a tacit understanding. Yet within her breast stirred a fierce deliberation, a silent verdict that the life to which she had so long aspired—the prestigious role of Lady Geraldine—now appeared as little more than a gilded shackle. Her thoughts, bordering on melancholy resolve, traversed the past and the volatile present, daring to defy convention by contemplating freedom over complacency.

At the hour when the drawing-room, adorned with the faint aroma of lavender and old parchment, should have witnessed the customary gaiety of a couple betrothed, a poignant distance had set in. Though Sir Francis’s hand found its way to Cecilia’s, as if to clasp a relic of comfort, it was received with a tender yet distant touch—a silent protest against further entanglement. The domestic scene, adorned by the soft clink of china and the distant murmurings of servants, became a stage for a conflict of hearts and wills.

Cecilia, her resolve firming with each measured beat of her heart, discreetly summoned her mother with a courteous yet feigned excuse. "Pray, Mother, might I impose upon you to entertain yourself in the solarium for a spell?" she had ventured, a request wrapped in the gentle tones of respect yet underlain by a secret urgency. And as her mother retired with a fond smile and murmured assurances, Cecilia felt the cloak of isolation descend—a setting in which truth, at last, could be confessed as neither pomp nor predestined roles nor sweet assurances could overcome the disquiet harboured within her spirit.

Now, within the quiet seclusion of a modest sitting chamber lit by the gentle glow of twilight, Cecilia allowed herself a moment of candour. The embers of hope for a different life, unmarred by expectations and true to her own aspirations, flickered in her breast.
