My dear Reverend,

Your kind words, like the gentle zephyrs of Spring, have wafted across the chasm that separates us – you, a shepherd tending to your flock amidst the verdant pastures of virtue, and I, a humble observer, peering at the human comedy from the gilded cages of our fair city. How apt your comparison of manners to the very air we breathe! Indeed, just as the atmosphere, imperceptible yet ever-present, shapes the landscape, so do manners mold the contours of society.

You, my dear Reverend, with your keen eye and discerning mind, have perceived the truth behind the glittering façade of Mrs. Potiphar and her ilk. Fear not, for she is but a fictional construct, a whimsical exaggeration intended to hold a mirror up to our follies, not a malicious caricature of any particular individual.

Let me assure you, my dear Reverend, that Mrs. Potiphar, for all her eccentricities and aspirations, is but a harmless butterfly, flitting from one gilded salon to another, pursuing the ephemeral pleasures of society's favor. She is, in a way, a tragic figure, mistaking the acquisition of material wealth and social standing for true happiness.

Ah, but you, with your profound understanding of the human heart, see through such superficiality. You recognize that true worth resides not in the ostentation of wealth or the allure of titles, but in the steadfast pursuit of virtue, in the unwavering commitment to one's fellow man. Your sermons, my dear Reverend, are a beacon of light amidst the fog of vanity that often engulfs our city.

You strike at the very heart of our societal pretensions, exposing the hollowness of chasing after empty grandeur, the futility of mimicking the customs of foreign courts. You remind us, with eloquence and wit, that true nobility lies not in lineage or riches, but in the inherent dignity of a life lived with integrity and purpose.

The upper echelons of our society, so eager to emulate the aristocratic airs of European courts, often resemble children playing dress-up, mimicking gestures and adopting accents that are as foreign to their nature as palm trees are to our wintry shores. They strive to outdo one another in the extravagance of their soirées, the lavishness of their gowns, and the sheer absurdity of their pronouncements on matters of art and culture – pronouncements delivered with an air of authority that belies their utter lack of genuine understanding.

They seem to believe that by importing Italian marble for their foyers and French chefs for their kitchens, they can somehow transplant the elegance and refinement of those cultures onto our own, forgetting that true refinement springs not from material possessions, but from the cultivation of the mind and spirit.

Yet, amidst this whirlwind of social climbing and conspicuous consumption, your voice rises above the din, a clarion call to reason and authenticity. You remind us that true happiness is not to be found in the glittering ballrooms of the elite, but in the quiet satisfaction of a life well-lived, in the pursuit of knowledge and beauty, and in the service of others.

And for that, my dear Reverend, I, for one, am eternally grateful.

The estate was abuzz with gentle excitement on that splendid autumn afternoon when Lady Lillycraft, the esteemed sister of the Squire, made her debut upon the old grounds. Horses trotted gracefully along the gravel drive, and the servants, long accustomed to the noble customs of the Hall, arranged themselves in a dignified array near the entrance. The Squire himself awaited her arrival with a subtle, affectionate anticipation, his countenance lighting up as the carriage came to a stately halt.

With a refined air that bespoke both delicacy and determination, Lady Lillycraft disembarked from the carriage, her gown rustling softly like silken leaves in the mellow breeze. A cadre of family members—each bearing the proud but unostentatious manner of generations past—rushed forth to receive her warmly. In a manner reminiscent of cherished familial reunion, the Squire’s gentle smile and soft words bespoke the deep-rooted affection held by all, and the hall seemed to resonate with the echoes of ancient, hallowed tradition.

Among the assembled company, Master Simon, a young man of keen intellect and attentive charm, stepped forward with the bearing of a true devotee of the country’s sporting glory. With a measured bow, he extolled the virtues of Lady Lillycraft’s country lands, emphasizing not only their splendid reputation for the pursuit of sport but also their indispensable role in ensuring the family’s long-enduring prosperity. His words, spoken with a mixture of admiration and dutiful respect, alluded to a rich tapestry of history and the inevitable confluence of honor and inheritance.

The estate itself, preserved with an almost pious fidelity to the customs of old English country gentlemanly decorum, impressed upon every visitor the timelessness of its character. Stately oak panels adorned the corridors, and within the great parlour, portraits of ancestors—rendered with careful detail in oil—observed the proceedings as silent sentinels of days long past. The unruffled airs maintained by those serving within these venerable walls only deepened the impression that tradition was not merely a relic of memory but a living, breathing force sustaining all present.

At the heart of this enduring tableau stood the housekeeper, a venerable woman whose life had been indelibly intertwined with the fortunes of the Hall. Raised amid these noble environs, she carried herself with an austere dignity and a steadfast devotion that had come to mark the very spirit of the household. Her eyes, reflecting both quiet wisdom and an unyielding resolve, surveyed the scene with a serenity that belied the transient innovations of a changing world, whilst her every motion evoked the grace of figures immortalized in the ancestral portraits.

Clad in attire that spoke of another era—with modest cut and sober hues—the housekeeper moved with an almost choreographic precision, guiding those in need whilst dispensing gentle remembrances of propriety and order. It was as if in her was embodied the continuous thread of heritage, linking the bygone days to the present. Her measured pace and deliberate words thus became an unspoken benediction, assuring both family and servant that the venerable customs of the Hall would endure despite the capricious winds of modern fortune.

In the wake of this grand reception, conversation mingled with the pleasant strains of the pianoforte, and the drawing room became a forum for both reminiscence and anticipation. Gentle laughter and modest exclamations of admiration then wove through the crowd, as guests, guided by the impeccable manners instilled in them, engaged in discourse on the merits of sport, estate, and the enduring values of refinement. There was a sense, too, that the airs of the past were softly whispering promises of yet more stirring chapters to come.

Thus, as twilight descended with its mellow purple hues upon the venerable estate, it became evident that tradition and modernity were not at odds but, indeed, in harmonious concurrence. Lady Lillycraft’s graceful arrival, Master Simon’s attentive charm, and the dignified oversight of the stalwart housekeeper converged to reinvigorate the lore of the Hall—a narrative as enduring and elegant as the very stone and timber from which it was built.

"And what happened to Tobias?" asked Barbel, who was listening with deep interest.

"Wait a moment, I am coming to that, but I cannot tell you everything at once," replied Dete. "Tobias was taught his trade in Mels, and when he had served his apprenticeship he came back to Dorfli and married my sister Adelaide. They had always been fond of one another, and they got on very well together after they were married. But their happiness did not last long. Her husband met with his death only two years after their marriage, a beam falling upon him as he was working, and killing him on the spot. They carried him home, and when Adelaide saw the poor disfigured body of her husband she was so overcome with horror and grief that she fell into a fever from which she never recovered. She had always been rather delicate and subject to curious attacks, during which no one knew whether she was awake or sleeping. And so two months after Tobias had been carried to the grave, his wife followed him. Their sad fate was the talk of everybody far and near, and both in private and public the general opinion was expressed that it was a punishment which Uncle had deserved for the godless life he had led. Some went so far even as to tell him so to his face. Our minister endeavored to awaken his conscience and exhorted him to repentance, but the old man grew only more wrathful and obdurate and would not speak to a soul, and every one did their best to keep out of his way. All at once we heard that he had gone to live up the Alm and did not intend ever to come down again, and since then he has led his solitary life on the mountain side at enmity with God and man. Mother and I took Adelaide's little one, then only a year old, into our care. When mother died last year, and I went down to the Baths to earn some money, I paid old Ursel, who lives in the village just above, to keep and look after the child. I stayed on at the Baths through the winter, for as I could sew and knit I had no difficulty in finding plenty of work, and early in the spring the same family I had waited on before returned from Frankfurt, and again asked me to go back with them. And so we leave the day after to-morrow, and I can assure you, it is an excellent place for me."

"And you are going to give the child over to the old man up there? It surprises me beyond words that you can think of doing such a thing, Dete," said Barbel, in a voice full of reproach.

"What do you mean?" retorted Dete. "I have done my duty by the child, and what would you have me do with it now? I cannot certainly take a child of five years old with me to Frankfurt. But where are you going to yourself, Barbel; we are now half way up the Alm?"

"We have just reached the place I wanted," answered Barbel. "I had something to say to the goatherd's wife, who does some spinning for me in the winter. So good-bye, Dete, and good luck to you!"

Dete shook hands with her friend and remained standing while Barbel went towards a small, dark brown hut, which stood a few steps away from the path in a hollow that afforded it some protection from the mountain wind. The hut was situated half way up the Alm, reckoning from Dorfli, and it was well that it was provided with some shelter, for it was so broken-down and dilapidated that even then it must have been very unsafe as a habitation, for when the stormy south wind came sweeping over the mountain, everything inside it, doors and windows, shook and rattled, and all the rotten old beams creaked and trembled. On such days as this, had the goatherd's dwelling been standing above on the exposed mountain side, it could not have escaped being blown straight down into the valley without a moment's warning.

In a cheerless alcove of the rambling farmhouse, sequestered from the general disarray, stood a battered secretary. Its once-gleaming mahogany surface was now dulled by layers of dust and neglect, yet within its recesses lay more of young Elara’s heart than the world suspected. Upon the top shelf rested a meager collection – relics salvaged from her father’s once-extensive library, dispersed to creditors years past. There was Plutarch’s Lives, its leather binding cracked and faded; a much-thumbed copy of The Canterbury Tales, bearing annotations in her father’s elegant script; and a volume of Shakespeare’s Sonnets, its pages softened with countless readings. Beside these literary companions sat a small, tarnished silver locket, containing a miniature portrait of her late mother. The delicate filigree frame was obscured by grime, but through its oval window, Elara could still discern the faint, wistful smile that haunted her memories. In the corner, atop a rickety pedestal, rested a celestial globe. It was a magnificent thing, though its painted constellations were chipped and peeling, its brass meridian tarnished with age.

Elara spent many hours in this sanctuary, seeking refuge from the daily trials that beset her. Her father, a man of profound intellect but little practical acumen, was perpetually engrossed in abstract pursuits, leaving the management of the farm to her weary shoulders. Her younger brother, Finnian, possessed a restless spirit and a penchant for mischief, requiring constant vigilance. Yet, it was the shadow of her aunt, Hester Grimshaw, that loomed largest in her life. A woman of rigid morality and boundless self-regard, Aunt Hester had descended upon the household after Elara's mother's passing, determined to instill order and piety into what she deemed a hopelessly dissolute family. Hester’s sharp tongue and censorious gaze followed Elara like a persistent draught. She found fault in Elara’s fondness for books, deeming them frivolous distractions from more practical concerns. She disapproved of Finnian’s boisterous games, labeling them unseemly for a boy of his age. And above all, she cast a perpetual pall over the memory of Elara’s mother, hinting at indiscretions and a life lived far from the path of righteousness. Elara had little memory of her mother beyond the portrait in the locket.

Despite her aunt's constant disapproval, Elara discovered solace in the dusty books and the quiet companionship of the alcove. She would lose herself in the ancient tales of heroism and tragedy, of love and loss, finding echoes of her own longings and fears within their pages. She read of valiant knights and virtuous ladies, of far-off lands and unimaginable adventures, and dreamed of a life beyond the confines of the farm. She imagined herself a scholar, poring over ancient texts in a grand library. She saw herself a traveler, exploring exotic locales and encountering fascinating people. Above all, she longed for a world where she could be free from the watchful gaze of her aunt and the endless drudgery of her daily chores. Elara’s only joy was on the occasions when Mr. Thornton, the village schoolmaster, came to call upon her father. He would often bring her books from his own library, works of poetry or essays that sparked her imagination and nourished her mind. He saw in her a rare intelligence and encouraged her to pursue her studies, promising to help her find a path towards a more fulfilling life. These visits were beacons of light in the otherwise dreary landscape of Elara’s existence, reminding her that there was still hope for a future beyond the confines of the farm.

‘At length and at last, the old gentleman’s legs appeared upon the steps leading through the roof, and he came slowly down: bringing along with him, the gifted Mooney. This Mooney, gentlemen, was even more scientific in appearance than his friend; and had, as Tom often declared upon his word and honour, the dirtiest face we can possibly know of, in this imperfect state of existence.

‘Gentlemen, you are all aware that if a scientific man isn’t absent in his mind, he’s of no good at all. Mr. Mooney was so absent, that when the old gentleman said to him, “Shake hands with Mr. Grig,” he put out his leg. “Here’s a mind, Mr. Grig!” cries the old gentleman in a rapture. “Here’s philosophy! Here’s rumination! Don’t disturb him,” he says, “for this is amazing!”

‘Tom had no wish to disturb him, having nothing particular to say; but he was so uncommonly amazing, that the old gentleman got impatient, and determined to give him an electric shock to bring him to—“for you must know, Mr. Grig,” he says, “that we always keep a strongly charged battery, ready for that purpose.” These means being resorted to, gentlemen, the gifted Mooney revived with a loud roar, and he no sooner came to himself than both he and the old gentleman looked at Tom with compassion, and shed tears abundantly.

‘“My dear friend,” says the old gentleman to the Gifted, “prepare him.”

‘“I say,” cries Tom, falling back, “none of that, you know. No preparing by Mr. Mooney if you please.”

‘“Alas!” replies the old gentleman, “you don’t understand us. My friend, inform him of his fate.—I can’t.”

‘The Gifted mustered up his voice, after many efforts, and informed Tom that his nativity had been carefully cast, and he would expire at exactly thirty-five minutes, twenty-seven seconds, and five-sixths of a second past nine o’clock, a.m., on that day two months.

‘Gentlemen, I leave you to judge what were Tom’s feelings at this announcement, on the eve of matrimony and endless riches. “I think,” he says in a trembling voice, “there must be a mistake in the working of that sum. Will you do me the favour to cast it up again?”—“There is no mistake,” replies the old gentleman, “it is confirmed by Francis Moore, Physician. Here is the prediction for to-morrow two months.” And he showed him the page, where sure enough were these words—“The decease of a great person may be looked for, about this time.”

‘“Which,” says the old gentleman, “is clearly you, Mr. Grig.”

‘“Too clearly,” cries Tom, sinking into a chair, and giving one hand to the old gentleman, and one to the Gifted. “The orb of day has set on Thomas Grig for ever!”

‘At this affecting remark, the Gifted shed tears again, and the other two mingled their tears with his, in a kind—if I may use the expression—of Mooney and Co.’s entire. But the old gentleman recovering first, observed that this was only a reason for hastening the marriage, in order that Tom’s distinguished race might be transmitted to posterity; and requesting the Gifted to console Mr. Grig during his temporary absence, he withdrew to settle the preliminaries with his niece immediately.

‘And now, gentlemen, a very extraordinary and remarkable occurrence took place; for as Tom sat in a melancholy way in one chair, and the Gifted sat in a melancholy way in another, a couple of doors were thrown violently open, the two young ladies rushed in, and one knelt down in a loving attitude at Tom’s feet, and the other at the Gifted’s. So far, perhaps, as Tom was concerned—as he used to say—you will say there was nothing strange in this: but you will be of a different opinion when you understand that Tom’s young lady was kneeling to the Gifted, and the Gifted’s young lady was kneeling to Tom.
