Evacuating or discharging these patients was not an option due to the severity of their conditions and other hospitals being filled with COVID patients.

The unprecedented combination of a catastrophic hurricane and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic placed immense mental stress on healthcare workers. Staff at Chabert Medical Center stood together, fearing the building might collapse, and sought solace in prayer for protection during the storm.

Terrebonne General Health System, another crucial healthcare facility in Houma, also bore the brunt of Ida, enduring severe damage including a collapsing roof and shattered windows. Both hospitals were forced to coordinate a massive evacuation in the aftermath of the hurricane's devastation.

Richard Zuschlag, Owner of Acadian Ambulance Service, expressed the challenges faced in evacuating over 100 patients, many with COVID, from Terrebonne General. He highlighted the difficulties and risks involved in moving critically ill patients to safety amidst the chaos.

Describing the concurrent impact of the hurricane and the COVID-19 surge, Dr. Chuck Burnell, Chief Medical Officer of Acadian Ambulance, referred to the situation as a "perfect twin-demic," emphasizing the unparalleled strain inflicted on the healthcare system in Houma by these dual disasters.

Celebrating Derek Chauvin’s conviction is not enough. We want to live | Derecka Purnell

A jury has found Derek Chauvin guilty of all charges against him for killing George Floyd, including unintentional second-degree murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter. A judge remanded Chauvin in custody after the verdict and a cop quickly cuffed the dazed defendant to carry him out of the courtroom. Chauvin will remain in jail until his sentencing hearing in two months.

Presidents did what presidents do after the criminal justice system seems to work for the people who it exploits, but this time with a twist. Neither Obama nor Biden considered the verdict justice, but rather accountability and “a step in the right direction”. Obama emphasized eliminating racial bias in policing and implementing concrete reforms for change; Biden explained that the verdict was a giant step forward towards justice in America.

There are two fatal flaws with these statements. The first is that reforms cannot fix racial bias in policing because police was formed as a system of racial and economic control, and remains so. As I’ve written before: if Derek Chauvin were the kindest cop in Minnesota and did not have a biased bone in his body, he still would have been able to arrest George Floyd for any number of alleged illegal acts. Because of capitalism, racism and ableism, the darkest and poorest peoples in the United States are relegated to live precarious lives where they do what they can to survive, sometimes including breaking the law. Rather than eliminating the unjust conditions, cities and the federal government send in police to manage the inequality.

Additionally, even if we could remove racial bias from police, this would not solve the underlying problems of inequality and exploitation. If it did, then there wouldn’t be so many poor, white people in prison. Last week, I watched a video of three cops arresting and slamming a 73-year-old white woman with dementia who was picking flowers on her way home. She’d forgotten to pay for her groceries at Walmart. Police dislocated her shoulder, and tied her hands and feet like a hog. She repeatedly cried that she wanted to go home and they chuckled at her. If removing racial bias in police is supposed to ensure that that Black people will be treated like white people under the law, then equal protection is completely insufficient for anyone’s freedom and safety.

Additionally, we cannot expect cop convictions to save anyone’s lives because prior cop convictions did not even save George Floyd’s life. Thousands of cops have killed more than 10,000 people of all races between 2005 and 2017; only 82 cops have been charged with murder or manslaughter. According to criminologist Phil Stinson, only 19 cops were convicted and mostly on lesser charges in that time period. A judge sentenced former South Carolina cop Michael Slaeger to 20 years in prison in 2017 for shooting Walter Scott several times in the back. A judge sentenced former Chicago PD officer Jason Van Dyke in 2019 to a little over six years in prison for fatally shooting Laquan McDonald 16 times. Despite the increasing convictions, the police nationwide still kill about three people a day. Just a few years ago, Minnesota convicted a cop for a murder while on duty for the first time. Minneapolis police officer Mohamed Noor was sentenced to about 12 years. Why didn’t all of these convictions save the thousands of people who were killed after them? Why didn’t Chauvin get the message?

The celebration of the conviction as “accountability” or “justice” that will send chills down the spines of police simply doesn’t comport with the law, which protects the police’s right not to think before they act. The US supreme court opined in Graham v Connor that cops “are often forced to make split-second judgments – in circumstances that are tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving – about the amount of force that is necessary in a particular situation”. This means that police currently have the constitutional authority to quickly decide when to use force. Every now and then, a conviction will slip through the cracks and people will celebrate, similar to how slave patrols were punished and sometimes sent to prison for their mistreatment of slaves. But, the underlying power to be violent will remain virtually unchanged and many more people will die because of it.

Even if we could remove racial bias from police, this would not solve the problems of inequality and exploitation

Tragically, we witnessed this on Tuesday. As the nation awaited the jury verdict’s reading against Chauvin, a white cop in Columbus, Ohio killed Ma’Khia Bryant, a 15-year-old Black girl. According to Bryant’s family, the teen reportedly called the police for help because older kids were trying to assault her. Police arrived during the altercation and shot Bryant four times.

There will be calls for justice for Ma’Khia, just as there were calls for justice in the recent police killings of Daunte Wright in Minnesota and 13-year-old Adam Toledo in Chicago. Clearly cops did not get the message about justice because all of these victims were killed in the course of the Chauvin trial. But we will never know what accountability or justice means for George, Daunte, Adam or Ma’Khia because justice requires the participation of the people impacted by it. The dead cannot participate. Convictions only provide relief for the living, and they surely do not save lives. The question is: do we want convictions or do we want to live?

If we want to live, then we must continue to join, support and create social movements and protests to end policing. Police abolition is not mere police absence. It is a political commitment and practice to recreate the society that thinks it needs police in the first place. People must avoid repeating the same tired reforms in the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act which does not undermine police power, and look to more transformational demands, such as those in the Breathe Act. We need abolition. Organizations like Critical Resistance, the Movement for Black Lives, Dream Defenders and various “defund the police” campaigns across the country are articulating ways to make change. We have to decide whether we have the will and imagination to join them.

El Paso Weathers Historic Winter Storm Unscathed: A Tale of Preparation and Grid Connections

El Paso, a border city in West Texas, experienced minimal disruptions during the historic winter storm that left much of the state in the dark. In stark contrast, other Texas cities grappled with severe power outages and a crippled energy grid.

Local resident Robert Gomez shared his observation, "I was shocked to find stores fully stocked and utilities functioning normally. It's a stark difference from what I've been hearing about the rest of Texas."

El Paso's preparedness for winter storms, following the devastating 2011 outages, and its connection to the Western Interconnection grid played pivotal roles in its ability to withstand the storm. Steve Buraczyk, Senior Vice President of Operations at El Paso Electric, emphasized the importance of these factors, stating, "Our experience in 2011 taught us valuable lessons, and we've been proactive in winterizing our facilities ever since."

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages about 90% of Texas's electric load, faced challenges during the storm. ERCOT couldn't draw power from other states due to the widespread power outages there. Buraczyk added, "Our connection to the Western Interconnection allowed us to sell excess energy out-of-state and purchase power from other regions when needed."

Many Texas power companies disregarded voluntary winterization guidelines issued by ERCOT following the 2011 outages. Ramanan Krishnamoorti, Chief Energy Officer at the University of Houston, commented on the situation, "The lack of action from some power companies to winterize their facilities was a major contributor to the widespread outages."

El Paso Electric spent millions on winterizing its facilities, including the construction of the Montana Power Station with dual-fuel capability. Carey King, Assistant Director at the University of Texas's Energy Institute, highlighted the significance of these investments, "El Paso Electric's commitment to winterization has paid off during this storm. Their resilience is a testament to the importance of preparing for extreme weather events."

Despite El Paso's success in weathering the storm, the widespread suffering in Texas has sparked calls for mandatory winterization. Responsibility for implementing these measures falls on state legislators and agencies. Krishnamoorti urged, "We need to address the systemic failures in policy and planning that led to these outages. Mandatory winterization may be a necessary step."

Experts are divided on the best approach to avoid future outages. Some suggest policy changes, while others recommend altering market rules. King offered his perspective, "We need a comprehensive approach that includes both policy changes and investment incentives for power companies to winterize their facilities."

The stark contrast between El Paso's resilience and the widespread suffering in Texas underscores the importance of preparation and grid connections. As the aftermath of the storm continues to unfold, the focus remains on finding long-term solutions to prevent future power outages.

The canal is a pivotal link, and its interruption can lead to delays and increased shipping costs. This assurance comes amid growing concern surrounding the wellbeing of those on board, as tensions mounted with the ever-increasing number of vessels waiting to navigate through the canal. Previously, there have been incidents in the canal that emphasize its challenging navigation. For instance, a Japanese ship ran aground in 2017, and another incident involved the CSCL Indian Ocean near Hamburg in 2016. The stakes are high, and the potential ripple effects from this incident could linger for months. As Jensen aptly pointed out, “Supply chains are already fragile due to the pandemic, and such blockages can easily exacerbate existing issues.”

While the ever-looming shadows of trade delays and shipping price hikes linger, there is hope that the operational efforts will be within reach of a successful conclusion.

Such lessons are essential not just for the ships that transit the canal but for the entire shipping industry navigating a post-pandemic world.

As observers await further updates on the ongoing operations, the focus will undoubtedly remain on ensuring that the Suez Canal’s vital role in international shipping is preserved. Armorer's Negligence, Cost-Cutting Measures Led to Fatal Shooting on 'Rust' Set

On the set of Alec Baldwin's film "Rust," 24-year-old armorer Hannah Gutierrez-Reed's carelessness with guns had been a concern prior to the fatal shooting that killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins and injured director Joel Souza. Gutierrez-Reed served as the head armorer on the set where Baldwin discharged a prop gun, resulting in the tragic accident.

Hannah Gutierrez-Reed, in a podcast interview earlier this year, admitted to feeling overwhelmed with her responsibilities on the set of "The Old Way," her first film as head armorer. "I was really nervous about it at first, and I almost didn't take the job because I wasn't sure if I was ready," Gutierrez-Reed said in the "Voices of the West" podcast.

Production sources on the set of "Rust" have cited the accident as a result of overall failings, including budget and safety measures. At least two prior incidents of accidental gun discharges occurred on the "Rust" set before the fatal shooting. Assistant director Dave Halls, who declared the gun "cold" before handing it to Baldwin, is now deemed partially responsible for not adequately checking the weapon. Halls previously had a gun mishandling incident on the set of "Fargo" in 2019.

Mamie Mitchell, the script supervisor on the "Rust" set, described the shooting as "negligent homicide." She revealed that there were complaints about safety practices and previous gun misfires made to the production team. "There were no safety meetings. There was no assurance that it wouldn't happen again. All they wanted to do was rush, rush, rush," Mitchell said.

Richard Howell, a film armorer with Foxtrot Productions, emphasized the armorer's responsibility for weapons safety on set. "The armorer is the last line of defense. They're the one that's responsible for making sure that the weapon is safe, that it's not loaded with live rounds," Howell explained.

The production company behind "Rust" is being criticized for cost-cutting measures that compromised safety on set. Gutierrez-Reed is described as inexperienced, with "Rust" being one of her first jobs as head armorer. Reportedly, she only had half a day of safety training prior to the start of filming.

Safety protocols dictate that the armorer should be present when a firearm is loaded or discharged, yet Gutierrez-Reed was not on set when the fatal shooting occurred. The prop gun that killed Hutchins and injured Souza was left unattended and unsecured on a cart.

A search warrant executed by the Santa Fe County Sheriff's Office revealed that Gutierrez-Reed had laid out three prop guns on a cart outside the set location. Halls grabbed the gun from the cart and brought it inside to Baldwin, bypassing Gutierrez-Reed.

As the investigation into the fatal shooting on the "Rust" set continues, concerns about safety protocols and the responsibility of the armorer and assistant director have come to light. The tragic incident underscores the importance of adhering to strict safety guidelines when working with firearms on film sets.

Deep freeze sends Texas electricity prices soaring 10,000%

Tonight: Global banks are, once again, learning about the dangers of excessive leverage; the Great Stuck may be unstuck, but the Suez saga isn’t over; and the housing market has truly gone bonkers. Let’s get into it.

FROZEN OVER

Unthinkably cold temperatures have knocked Texas’ energy facilities offline.

Electricity prices spiked more than 10,000% when the winter storm hit this week. There are blackouts across the state. More than 4 million Texans were without power early Tuesday.

POINTING FINGERS

Although some are attempting to pin the blame on one fuel source or another, the reality is that the Arctic temperatures are hobbling fossil fuels and renewable energy alike, my colleague Matt Egan explains.

It’s striking that these power outages are happening in mighty Texas, the energy powerhouse of America. A bit of context:

Texas produces more electricity than any other US state — generating almost twice as much as Florida, the next-closest, according to federal statistics.

Texas is the No. 1 state in both crude oil and natural gas.

Wind power is also booming in Texas, which produced about 28% of all the US wind-powered electricity in 2019.

WHAT HAPPENED?

So how did such a powerhouse get knocked so thoroughly offline?

We may not know the full definitive reason for a while, but a few things are clear:

Obviously, Texas winters ain’t usually this cold. The state’s infrastructure is simply not prepared for a deep freeze.

Critics of renewables will try to blame wind turbines, but experts note that wind makes up a small share of Texas’ energy consumption.

It’s also worth poinitng out that a lot of chillier places have wind turbines that don’t buckle in the cold — hello, Iowa; hej hej, Denmark — they just need to be winterized, a step experts said Texas has skipped.

The Lone Star State is … all alone. Texas made a conscious decision to isolate its energy grid from the rest of the country. That means that when things are running smoothly, it can’t export excess power to neighboring states. And in the current crisis, it can’t import power either.

In other words: “When it comes to electricity, what happens in Texas stays in Texas,” said Dan Cohan, associate professor of environmental engineering at Rice University. “That has really come back to bite us.”

Widening Of Suez Canal Is Lesson On Preventing The Repeat Of A Crisis

The latest lesson for business leaders from the recent Suez Canal crisis is to learn from a crisis and immediately take steps to help prevent it from happening again. That’s exactly what Suez Canal officials are doing in the aftermath of the giant container ship that blocked the international shipping lane for six days.

According to the Associated Press, Egypt “plans to widen and deepen the southern part of the Suez Canal where a hulking vessel ran aground and closed off the crucial waterway in March.” Business Insider reported that, “In a televised address on Tuesday the head of the Suez Canal Authority (SCA), Osama Rabie, said an 18.6 mile stretch of the waterway would be widened by about 131 feet (40 meters) and deepened by 32 feet (10 meters) to improve the movement of ships in the area.”

A Top Priority

When companies and organizations have recovered from a crisis, one of the first things they should do is to carefully review the cause of the crisis, then implement reforms or changes to help ensure the same situation is not repeated.

Starbucks apparently did the right thing in 2018 in the wake of a headline-making crisis. The manager of one of their cafes in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania had two black men arrested who were waiting for a colleague. A few weeks later, the company closed 8,000 restaurants in the U.S. for a day so that 175,000 employees could receive anti-bias training.

The U.S. Secret Service has been criticized over the years for the handling of their own crisis situations.

In a story yesterday on CBS’s Sunday Morning, correspondent Jim Axelrod reported on the publication of Zero Fail: The Rise and Fall of the Secret Service. The book by Pulitzer Prize-winning Washington Post reporter Carol Leonnig is critical of the agency and how it has responded to its crises.

In response to a request for comment for this story, the agency said, “The U.S. Secret Service is aware of an upcoming book which re-hashes past challenges the agency overcame and evolved from. Now and throughout its 156 year history, the agency’s skilled workforce is dedicated to the successful execution of its critical protective and investigative missions.”

Among those interviewed in the CBS story was former Agent Jonathan Wackrow, who was with the Secret Service for 14 years where he served on the details protecting President and Mrs. Obama. Axelrod said Wackrow’s experience, “... gives him insight into another problem plaguing the Secret Service that more money can't address: a culture lacking transparency and accountability.”

According to a transcript of the story, “On November 11, 2011, a man fired a rifle at the White House, striking the building seven times. The Obamas weren't home, but their daughters were. Despite agents reporting gunfire, Leonnig writes they were told by superiors to stand down. Secret Service leadership initially told no one – not their agents, not the public, not even President and Mrs. Obama.

"Thankfully, [it] didn't have a tragic outcome. But afterwards? Nothing," said Wackrow. "There was no, 'Hey, let's get everybody together and let's review what happened.’”

“Axelrod asked, "But how could there not be?"

"The Secret Service is the best organization in the world in crisis management. Yet, they can't manage themselves," Wackrow replied. "It was an embarrassment, but you have to learn from it."

Secret Service Responds

In response to a request to comment on the CBS story, the Secret Service provided a link to a report by the National Academy of Public Administration. The agency said in a statement that, “The Academy Panel determined that the U.S. Secret Service has taken significant, wide-ranging, and important actions.”

Substantial Changes Made

“Specifically, the agency has made a substantial number of organizational, policy, and process changes to transform the way it does business; professionalize administrative, technical, and management functions; and address numerous staffing and employee issues. Agency leadership has made these changes in a relatively short time, demonstrating a strong commitment to change.”

The agency also provided a link to a report by the inspector general of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security with this title: “The Secret Service Has Taken Action to Address the Recommendations of the Protective Mission Panel”.

An Independent Review

The CBS story included information about someone who jumped the fence at the White House several years ago. The Secret Service told me that, “Following the September 19, 2014 White House fence jumping incident, the Secretary of Homeland Security established the Protective Mission Panel (PMP) to undertake a broad independent review of the United States Secret Service’s protection of the White House Complex. The PMP made 19 recommendations in its December 2014 unclassified report.

“The Secret Service has clearly taken the PMP’s recommendations seriously, which it has demonstrated by making a number of significant changes. Specifically, it has improved communication within the workforce, better articulated its budget needs, increased hiring, and committed to more training. Using funding appropriated for PMP initiatives, the Secret Service has also begun enhancing security and refreshing technology at the White House Complex.”

Advice For Business Leaders

Unique Opportunity

“Every resolved crisis presents an opportunity to avoid future ones, by a thorough after action review, followed up by new policies and procedures to avoid a repeat of the same circumstance,” observed Brian Glicklich, CEO of public affairs firm Digital Strategies.

Writing in Risk Management magazine, Suzanne Folsom and Rob Garretson observed that, “Today, most organizations spend the majority of their planning and preparation resources on addressing current and potential operational challenges. Far too many neglect to take the critical next steps to learn from the organization’s successes and failures after a crisis. In doing so, they needlessly discard a valuable resource for continuous improvement.

“Moreover, even when an organization does perform a critical look back, it is often not used to maximum effect. The days and weeks after a crisis abates can provide leaders with a unique opportunity to identify the organization’s strengths that should be sustained or built upon and weaknesses that require improvement,” they said.

Debriefing Is A Challenge

The authors noted that, “Debriefing after a major crisis is a challenge. Critically, a senior leader like the CEO must clearly articulate the value of this effort, stressing what the process is meant to accomplish. Participants need to understand that the post-crisis review is not intended to critique or grade success or failure. Instead, the process is meant to be a candid discussion and analysis of the organization’s actual performance during the crisis, either in keeping with or differing from the established crisis plan.”

More than $889 million in total financial help and direct services to those who have necessary eligible expenses following the disaster and are unable to meet those needs through insurance or other means.

$492 million of that amount includes housing assistance to help homeowners repair or replace residential property damage from the disaster and/or for a safe place to stay while they recover.

$396 million is for Other Needs Assistance to cover necessary, disaster-related expenses such as medical bills, cleaning, repair or replacement of essential household items or vehicles and other non-housing needs.

More than $816 million approved in U.S. Small Business Administration loans, with more than $782 million for homeowners and renters and more than $34 million for businesses to repair, rebuild and replace damaged property and contents and for economic injury.

Rental assistance for more than 179,000 homeowners and renters.

"Effective communication and coordination are crucial in preventing widespread power outages," said Moura. "We urge all stakeholders to work together to ensure the reliability of the grid this winter."

In conclusion, Texas faces a high risk of widespread power outages this winter in case of extreme weather, according to NERC's report. The report highlights the need for power companies to be prepared for extreme weather events and for better communication and coordination between stakeholders to prevent widespread power outages. FDA Expands Use of COVID-19 Vaccine Booster Doses

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken action to expand the use of booster doses for COVID-19 vaccines in eligible populations. This action amends the emergency use authorizations (EUA) for COVID-19 vaccines, allowing for a single booster dose under the following circumstances:

Moderna COVID-19 Vaccine:

  • Individuals 65 years of age and older
  • Individuals 18 through 64 years of age at high risk of severe COVID-19
  • Individuals 18 through 64 years of age with frequent institutional or occupational exposure to SARS-CoV-2

Janssen (Johnson and Johnson) COVID-19 Vaccine:

  • Individuals 18 years of age and older

Heterologous (Mix and Match) Boosters:

  • Individuals who have completed their primary vaccination with a different COVID-19 vaccine can receive a booster dose from any of the available vaccines.

Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine:

  • Individuals 18 through 64 years of age with frequent institutional or occupational exposure to SARS-CoV-2

Rationale for Booster Doses:

The FDA's decision is based on data suggesting waning immunity in some fully vaccinated individuals. Booster doses are intended to provide continued protection against COVID-19, including severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

Data Supporting Authorization:

  • Moderna: Immune response data from clinical studies demonstrated a booster response in participants who received a booster dose at least six months after their second dose. Additionally, data suggest waning vaccine effectiveness over time.
  • Safety: Safety data from clinical trials showed that the most common side effects of booster doses were similar to those experienced after the primary vaccination series.

Next Steps:

The FDA will continue to monitor data on the safety and effectiveness of booster doses and will provide updates as needed.

Statement from Acting FDA Commissioner:

"Today’s actions demonstrate our commitment to public health in proactively fighting against the COVID-19 pandemic," said Acting FDA Commissioner Janet Woodcock, M.D. "Vaccination continues to be the safest and most effective way to prevent COVID-19."

Statement from Director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research:

"The amendments to the emergency use authorizations are based on available data and information and follow the input from our advisory committee," said Peter Marks, M.D., Ph.D. "We are also taking action today to include the use of mix and match boosters to address this public health need. We will work to accrue additional data as quickly as possible to further assess the benefits and risks of booster doses in additional populations and plan to update the healthcare community and public with our determination in the coming weeks."

DarkSide carefully selected its targets based on financial analysis and information gleaned from corporate emails. Michael Walshe Jr., Chair of the Management Committee at Stone Pigman Walther Wittmann, stated, "DarkSide's targeted approach to selecting victims demonstrates a high level of sophistication and planning."

Ballod noted, "Zero-day exploits give attackers a significant advantage, as they can bypass security measures that rely on known vulnerabilities."

Once inside a target's network, DarkSide moved swiftly to encrypt files and exfiltrate data. They also investigated victims' cyber insurance policies to tailor ransom demands effectively. Wittmann commented, "DarkSide's understanding of cyber insurance policies is a testament to their research capabilities and knowledge of the cyber threat landscape."

DarkSide's quick attack window and demands on the high end, typically $5 million or more, put pressure on organizations to respond rapidly. Ballod cautioned, "The window of opportunity for organizations to prevent a ransomware attack is shrinking, making it essential for them to invest in robust cybersecurity measures and incident response plans."

DarkSide threatened to share stolen information with short-sellers if publicly traded companies refused to pay the ransom. Wittmann warned, "The potential for public disclosure of sensitive information can lead to significant reputational damage and financial losses for organizations."

After DarkSide's shutdown by law enforcement, affiliates complained on a forum that they had not been paid their share of the ransoms. Walshe Jr. commented, "The lack of transparency in ransomware-as-a-service operations can lead to mistrust among affiliates and potential legal repercussions."

Seven of Tantleff's clients paid ransoms ranging from $1.25 million to $6 million after negotiations from higher initial demands. Press Release: President Biden's COVID-19 Strategy Leads to 300 Million Vaccine Doses Administered in 150 Days

This swift and effective vaccination campaign has played a crucial role in lowering COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths across the country.

When President Biden took office, only 5% of adult Americans were vaccinated, and the initial pace of vaccinations was slow. Now, more than 175 million Americans have received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, with 65% of adult Americans having received at least one shot and 55% fully vaccinated.

The Biden Administration's comprehensive efforts to combat the pandemic have included securing vaccine supply, increasing vaccination sites, and mobilizing federal personnel for vaccinations. Over 81,000 vaccination sites have been established, ensuring that Americans can easily access vaccines within 5 miles of their residences.

Furthermore, the federal pharmacy vaccination program has expanded to 42,000 local pharmacies, where over 82 million shots have been administered. Additionally, 39 federally-run, high-volume vaccination sites have been set up, with a particular focus on reaching vulnerable neighborhoods.

Community health centers have played a crucial role in ensuring vaccine access for underserved populations, including those living at or below the poverty line and racial/ethnic minorities. These centers have hosted almost 11,000 pop-up clinics, making vaccines more accessible to those who need them most.

The Biden Administration has made equity a top priority in its vaccination efforts, ensuring that a majority of federally-provided shots have gone to people of color. Moreover, the administration has supported over 20,000 community-based pop-up vaccination clinics, furthering its commitment to reaching all communities across the nation.

As a result of these concerted efforts, the United States is making significant progress in the fight against COVID-19, with vaccination rates steadily climbing and the number of cases, hospitalizations, and deaths on the decline. President Biden's steadfast leadership in this crisis has been instrumental in guiding the nation toward a safer and healthier future.

For more information on vaccination locations and eligibility criteria, please visit www.cdc.gov or contact your local health department.

New Coronavirus Variant B.1.1.529 Sparks Global Concern as South Africa Sees Rapid Spread

South Africa's Minister of Health, Joe Phaahla, has announced the discovery of a new and highly mutated coronavirus variant, B.1.1.529, which is spreading rapidly in parts of the country. The variant has also been detected in neighboring Botswana and in a traveler to Hong Kong from South Africa, sparking global concern over its potential impact on public health and vaccination efforts.

"The variant has an unusually high number of mutations, particularly in the spike protein, which is responsible for the virus's entry into human cells," said Tulio de Oliveira, director of South Africa's Center for Epidemic Response and Innovation. He warned that the variant, known as Omicron, is spreading at an alarming rate and could put significant pressure on the country's health system.

Scientists are worried that the variant's mutations may allow it to evade immune responses generated by vaccines or prior infection, as well as enhance its transmissibility. However, it is still too early to determine the precise impact on vaccine efficacy or the severity of illness caused by the new variant.

UK Health Minister Sajid Javid echoed these concerns, stating, "We are concerned that this new variant may be more transmissible and that it may reduce the protection of vaccines." In response, the UK has banned flights from South Africa, Namibia, Lesotho, Botswana, Eswatini, and Zimbabwe, adding them to the country's travel red list.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified B.1.1.529 as a 'variant under monitoring,' acknowledging the potential risks associated with the high number of mutations. The global health body is working with researchers in South Africa to better understand the variant's characteristics and implications.

South Africa, which is approaching a predicted fourth wave of infections, has been grappling with a slow vaccine rollout. Despite relatively low current infection rates, the emergence of the new variant underscores the importance of increasing vaccination coverage to mitigate the impact of new variants.

Phaahla emphasized the need for continued vigilance and adherence to public health measures, stating, "We urge all South Africans to continue wearing masks, washing their hands, and practicing social distancing. Vaccination remains our best defense against severe illness, hospitalization, and death."

As the world awaits more data on the Omicron variant, scientists and health officials are working diligently to evaluate its potential threat and determine the most effective strategies to combat its spread. The global response to this new variant serves as a reminder of the ongoing challenges posed by the ever-evolving nature of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Press Release: American Medical Association Urges Mandatory COVID-19 Vaccination for Health Care Workers

In a recent statement, Susan R. Bailey, M.D., Immediate Past President of the American Medical Association, emphasized the critical importance of COVID-19 vaccination for health care workers to ensure the safety of both patients and colleagues. Dr. Bailey highlighted that over 300 million doses have been administered in the United States alone, with nearly 4 billion doses administered worldwide, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of the vaccines.

Health care organizations across the country are now advocating for mandatory COVID-19 vaccinations for all health care and long-term care workers. The recent surge in COVID-19 cases, driven by highly contagious variants and pockets of unvaccinated populations, underscores the urgent need for widespread vaccination efforts.

Despite the availability of vaccines, many health care and long-term care workers remain unvaccinated, posing a significant risk to vulnerable populations they serve. In response to this concerning trend, the statement calls for all employers in the health care and long-term care sectors to mandate COVID-19 vaccinations for their employees to ensure the highest standards of safety and care.

Support for universal vaccination of health workers is gaining momentum among experts and institutions, with a growing recognition of the vital role that health care workers play in promoting community health and wellbeing. While some individuals may be exempt from vaccination mandates due to medical reasons, they represent a minority, and efforts should be made to address their concerns and ensure alternative safety measures are in place.

Historically, vaccine mandates have proven to be effective in bolstering overall vaccination rates and reducing the spread of infectious diseases. However, addressing longstanding mistrust in health care institutions and fostering open dialogue with workers are crucial steps in ensuring the success of these mandates.

The leadership shown by the health care community in implementing vaccine mandates sets a positive example for all employers to follow. By prioritizing the health and safety of both employees and those they serve, health care organizations can play a pivotal role in stemming the spread of COVID-19 and protecting vulnerable populations.

Vice President Harris Addresses U.N. on Pandemic Preparedness

WASHINGTON – In a virtual address to members of the United Nations on Thursday, Vice President Kamala Harris emphasized the urgent need for global leaders to collaborate in drafting comprehensive plans to tackle future pandemics. This marks Harris' second engagement with a U.N. body since her inauguration in January and comes at a crucial time as the United States makes significant strides in its vaccination efforts, while many countries around the world grapple with vaccine shortages.

Harris' speech, a shared effort with the U.N. permanent representatives of Argentina, Japan, Norway, and South Africa, underscored the essential focus areas for a global pandemic response plan that include enhancing the accessibility of health systems, investing in scientific research, bolstering healthcare workforces, and expanding manufacturing capabilities for vaccines and protective gear. “As we start to imagine what a post-COVID world looks like, it is crucial we lay the groundwork now for a robust, equitable response to future health crises,” Harris stated.

Amid the Biden administration's approach to its first 100 days in office, President Joe Biden is poised to review the administration's pandemic response victories in an upcoming address to Congress. The Vice President's speech precedes this milestone, serving as a critical reminder of the lessons learned from the ongoing pandemic and the unparalleled necessity for innovation in our approach to global health crises.

Echoing Harris’ call for heightened readiness was U.N. Ambassador Linda Thomas-Greenfield, who also took the virtual stage, stressing the need for establishing an effective “future pandemic preparedness architecture.” Thomas-Greenfield candidly expressed the global community's shortcoming, saying, "The world barely withstood this pandemic," to underscore the grave importance of being better equipped for similar challenges ahead.

As the United States continues with its vaccination campaign, Vice President Harris and U.N. Ambassador Thomas-Greenfield’s contributions to the global dialogue on pandemic preparedness highlight a proactive move towards fostering a unified and resilient international community ready to face any future health emergencies.

Tiger Woods Teaches Jada Pinkett Smith How to Golf in Miniseries Filmed Day Before His Rollover Car Crash

The first episode of the series Tiger Woods filmed the day before his rollover car crash in California earlier this year has been released.

Golf Digest's A Round with Tiger: Celebrity Lessons features Woods teaching other celebrities the game, including Jada Pinkett Smith, David Spade and Dwyane Wade. The entire four-part miniseries was filmed in February the day before Woods' accident in Rancho Palos Verdes, a message at the beginning of the premiere episode says.

"The content was captured in February, the day before Tiger had his unfortunate car accident, from which he is still recovering," the message says. "With this knowledge, the deep and poignant conversations will undoubtedly resonate even more strongly with viewers. The series is being released with the blessing of Tiger and his guests."

"Shooting this series was some of the most fun I've ever had filming on the golf course," Woods, 45, said in a statement. "Each guest brought a unique perspective on life, both professionally and personally. I'm always inspired by others who are considered the best at what they do and learning about how they made it to the top."

In the debut episode, the 82-time PGA Tour winner and Pinkett Smith reflect on aging and its effect on their bodies.

"I need to have a little bit of help," Woods said when Pinkett Smith brought up his family workouts with his daughter Sam Alexis Woods, 13, and son Charlie Axel Woods, 11.

He added, "Sucks getting older."

"I like the wisdom that comes with it," the actress said, to which Woods replied, "Yeah, but the body."

The three-time U.S. Open winner continued, "You're right, about the wisdom part of it, but the body. I've had 10 operations."

"Where do you think your resilience comes from, like building your body back, building your game back, building your life and the fact that you don't even recognize it?" Pinkett Smith asked Woods.

Jada Pinkett Smith and Tiger Woods. golf digest

"I'm always fighting, you know, and I'm always trying to get better," he said. "That's all I know. I feel like I'm never out of the fight, you know, in that regard, I'm always pushing."

While the actress commented that Woods' golf game has seemingly been unaffected by his multiple injuries, he admitted, "The body definitely knows it."

The conversation now marks an eerie precursor to Woods' Feb. 23 car accident — he struck a sign in the road's center divider and cut through a tree — that led to the golfer's 11th major surgery.

The vehicle sustained major damage, and Woods underwent emergency surgery for "significant orthopedic injuries to his right lower extremity." He did not return back home to Florida until mid-March.

Wade previously spoke about filming with Woods during an appearance on Inside the NBA on the day of the accident, saying "we're all shaken" by the news of the horrible crash.

"My prayers go out to him, and hopefully a speedy recovery for him, and hopefully he gets a chance to get back to doing what he loves to do, and that's playing the game of golf," he said.

In late May, Woods told Golf Digest that recovering from the crash has been "an entirely different animal" from his previous injuries.

"I understand more of the rehab processes because of my past injuries, but this was more painful than anything I have ever experienced," he shared. When asked by the outlet if he would be able to play golf again, the athlete declined to answer.

Ultimately, the Los Angeles County Sheriff found that speed was the primary cause of Woods' single-car rollover crash, but that there were "no signs of impairment" and that the pro golfer would not be cited for the accident.

After the sheriff's announcement, Woods issued a statement saying that he would "continue to focus on my recovery and family, and thank everyone for the overwhelming support and encouragement I've received throughout this very difficult time."

A Round with Tiger: Celebrity Playing Lessons airs Tuesdays on Golf Digest through August 10.

Hurricane Ida Slams into Louisiana: Governor Edwards Warns of Challenges Ahead

On Sunday, August 29, 2021, Hurricane Ida, a monstrous Category 4 storm with 150-mile-per-hour winds, made a devastating landfall in Port Fourchon, Louisiana, marking the anniversary of the disastrous Hurricane Katrina and just two days following the anniversary of Hurricane Laura. Governor John Bel Edwards spoke gravely of the "severe challenges" the state would confront in the days and weeks to follow in a sobering press conference.

"The impact of this storm is immense, and we should expect significant challenges in the coming days ahead," said Governor John Bel Edwards. He urged residents in southeastern Louisiana to hunker down and remain in place for the next 72 hours, until the storm has safely passed.

The arrival of Hurricane Ida on the Katrina and Laura anniversaries is no mere coincidence, as the Gulf of Mexico remains a hotbed for hurricane activity. In preparation, over 5,000 members of the Louisiana National Guard and additional personnel from 16 other states have been called to arms, ready to embark on search and rescue missions as soon as possible.

The hurricane left coastal towns in shambles, with more populous regions such as New Orleans and Baton Rouge bracing themselves for potentially catastrophic ramifications. Although mandatory evacuations were issued in numerous coastal parishes, the city of New Orleans decided not to follow suit due to the storm's rapid approach. Mayor LaToya Cantrell implored residents who had not evacuated to "stay put," emphasizing the importance of staying safe during and after the hurricane.

An unfortunate aspect of this storm is that it comes in the midst of a global pandemic. Governor John Bel Edwards acknowledged the immense strain on Louisiana hospitals, which have been dealing with capacity issues due to COVID-19. With hospitals having to prepare for power outages and evacuations, the situation is far from ideal. Governor Edwards noted, "We understand the complexities brought by this storm during a pandemic, but we are working diligently to ensure that our healthcare facilities are equipped to deal with these dual challenges."

Despite the ongoing pandemic, the state has been working tirelessly to provide public shelters and transportation for residents to safer areas. The National Guard has been tasked with the responsibility of making certain that social distancing measures are maintained, and personal protective equipment (PPE) is made available to mitigate COVID-19 risks.

Not one to ignore potential risks, Louisiana has taken considerable steps to improve its hurricane preparedness. In particular, a new protection system has been implemented around New Orleans in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. This multi-billion dollar system of floodgates, levees, and pumps is meant to provide an added layer of security for New Orleans, while acknowledging that "nothing is foolproof."

As Hurricane Ida moves further inland and residents begin to assess the damage caused by the hurricane, Governor John Bel Edwards and state officials are urging those affected to exercise caution. With countless trees downed, flooding in certain areas, and electrical wires strewn about, any exploration must be undertaken with care and diligence. Governor Edwards reassured residents who stayed behind that help was on the way, saying, "We will rebuild once more, and we will stand stronger than ever."

While Hurricane Ida has already proven itself to be a formidable force, those in its path can take solace in the knowledge that their fellow Louisianans are standing beside them, united in the face of adversity. In the coming days and weeks, the resilience of the state's communities will be put to the test, as they work to clean up, repair the damage, and heal in the wake of yet another powerful hurricane.

Broncos Fans Stuck Between a Rock and a Hard Place for Super Bowl LV

As Super Bowl LV approaches, Broncos fans find themselves facing an unenviable decision: root for the Kansas City Chiefs, their most despised AFC West adversary, or the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, led by their longtime arch-nemesis, Tom Brady. It's a conundrum that leaves fans grappling with a choice between, as some might say, the lesser of two evils.

For years, Broncos fans have nurtured an intense rivalry with the Kansas City Chiefs. Divisional games have consistently stoked emotions and fostered an unwavering sense of animosity. If there's any team that Broncos fans relish defeating, it's the Chiefs. And yet, here they are, watching them contend for a Super Bowl title, with the potential to eclipse the Broncos' historical success within the AFC West.

At the opposing end of the Super Bowl spectrum stands Tom Brady, a player who has haunted the Broncos' narrative for decades. Known for his incredible NFL career and numerous Super Bowl victories with the New England Patriots, Brady has been a formidable rival to the Broncos on many occasions. His startling move to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was an unwelcome surprise for many, further solidifying his status as a perennial antagonist to Broncos fans everywhere.

A recent Twitter poll revealed that about a third of Broncos fans adamantly refuse to root for either the Chiefs or Tom Brady in this year's Super Bowl, illustrating the deep-seated frustration that has taken hold. It paints a vivid picture of a fan base caught in a bind, unable to support either team and finding themselves wondering who, if anyone, they should lend their cheers to this weekend.

Julie Thuis, a diehard Broncos fan, echoes this widespread sentiment, "Honestly, this is a nightmare scenario. How am I supposed to choose between the Chiefs and Brady? It's like asking me to pick between two of my worst nightmares!" Her frustration unfurls a line shared by many fans who view both options with palpable disdain.

On the other hand, Christine Voss, another devoted fan of the Broncos, feels a sense of obligation to prioritize the divisional rivalry over personal dislike. When discussing her support for Tampa Bay, she exclaims, “Rooting for Brady over the Chiefs just makes more sense. I've despised the Chiefs since day one; I refuse to see them celebrate another win in our division.”

However, not every fan can overlook their animosity for the infamous quarterback. A good number of Broncos fans consider Tom Brady as the NFL's 'Voldemort,' the somber specter who has haunted their dreams too long to ignore. With his attempt to trademark 'Tompa Bay,' the moniker meant to meld his name with his current team’s, Brady managed to draw even more ire from Bronco country, confirming that some resentments run deeper.

While Dave DeNovellis, another staunch Broncos fan, admits he’s struggling with this year’s Super Bowl predicament, he proposes a little levity as a solution, "I just might root for the commercials this year. There's always some good ones to look forward to, and let's be honest, who doesn't appreciate a clever ad in the middle of the game?" It’s a sentiment shared by those yearning for a neutral option, an escape from the emotional turmoil of choosing what feels like an inevitable loss.

Former State Rep. Cole Wist expresses his perplexity, saying, "As a Broncos fan, there's no win here. I'll just have to flip a coin or watch the game for the love of football. It’s not the end of the world, but it sure feels like it." The reality of unprecedented times calls for unexpected choices, and humor often paves the way to easing the decision-making process for many fans who simply don't want to choose.

For fans feeling increasingly alienated from both Super Bowl contenders, contrasting criteria may open new avenues of support. Some fans may find it more favorable to lend their backing to teams with strong connections to Colorado, either through players, coaches, or even cities involved in historic games. Others might simply choose to support the team perceived as the underdog, hoping to witness an enthralling victory against all odds.

But at the heart of this complex decision lies a profound sense of alienation, deepened by the seasonal absence of the Denver Broncos from the championships, only to be further burdened by an unenviable choice. Fans are tossed into the choppy seas of choice, left with an ironic predicament that tests their fandom in new and bewildering ways.

Historical natural antagonism toward the Chiefs collides head-on with the long-standing personal grievance against Brady in a mashup that appears only when stars misalign in this unlucky scenario for Broncos fans. In essence, the Super Bowl LV contest invites Broncos supporters to ponder what it really means to be a fan amidst a thorny reality.

For those unable to root for the commercial breaks or split loyalties, look to the fundamental reasons that Broncos fans tune into football: thrill, unpredictability, and the love of the game. The very spirit of sport is illuminated in contests wrought with contention and invocations of biblical rivalries when unanticipated paths merge.

In conclusion, this Super Bowl LV serves as a stark reminder of football’s beautiful nature – messy rivalry, classic battles, and the possibilities that arise out of uncertainty. Broncos fans, meanwhile, find humor in their hiatus from cheerful support, arguing whether choosing between Brady and the Chiefs might just be the strongest indication yet of a world led astray.

While some have jokingly suggested questioning the existence of a higher power when faced with supporting their most loathed rivals, this predicament, though unwelcome, invites reflections on the core of sporting spirit. Broncos fans, remain heartened; football endures as a testament to resilience, proving that even the polarizing matchups, like choosing among Super Bowl LV's two unwanted contenders, urge us to treasure its dynamic unpredictability.

FBI Warned of Potential Violence Ahead of Capitol Riot, Officials Say

In the wake of the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol, questions have been raised about whether law enforcement agencies were adequately prepared for the violence that unfolded. While some officials initially claimed to be caught off guard, the FBI now insists that they had warned about the potential for extremist-driven violence leading up to the event.

FBI Shared Warning with Law Enforcement Agencies

According to U.S. officials, the FBI issued a report on January 5th from its field office in Norfolk, Virginia, detailing the possibility of "war" in Washington the following day. This information was then shared with other law enforcement agencies through the joint terrorism task force.

Assistant Director Steven D'Antuono, initially claimed that law enforcement had no indication of anything beyond First Amendment protected activity. However, he later clarified that the Norfolk warning was based on non-specific information and lacked individual leads to investigate.

Justice Department Considering Sedition Charges

In the aftermath of the riot, the Justice Department has vowed to aggressively pursue those responsible. Acting U.S. Attorney Michael Sherwin announced that they are considering bringing sedition charges against some of the rioters, which could carry up to 20 years in prison.

A specialized strike force has been created to investigate the possibility of sedition charges. Officials are utilizing techniques commonly used in international counterterrorism investigations, examining the financial transactions and movements of individuals leading up to the breach.

Questions Remain About Coordination and Communication

Despite the FBI's claims, questions remain about the level of coordination and communication between agencies in the lead-up to the riot. Some officials, including the Capitol Police Chief, have stated that they were unaware of any serious concerns and had only prepared for a peaceful protest.

Additionally, a U.S. defense official revealed that Army Secretary Ryan McCarthy was not notified about the FBI warning. It remains unclear whether other defense or military officials were informed.

The discrepancies in statements and the lack of clarity surrounding the communication of the FBI warning have raised concerns about the preparedness of law enforcement agencies for the January 6th attack. As the investigation continues, it is crucial to determine the extent of communication between agencies and identify any potential failures that may have contributed to the violence.

Renowned Author and Journalist Joan Didion Dies at 87

Renowned author and journalist Joan Didion passed away at her Manhattan home on Thursday, due to complications from Parkinson's disease. She was 87 years old.

Penguin Random House announced her passing, describing her as a trenchant writer and astute observer. Didion was a leading figure in the 'New Journalism' of the 1960s and had a widely acclaimed career.

Born in Sacramento in 1934, Didion started her career with a Vogue magazine essay contest win. She went on to become a prominent voice in American literature, known for her incisive and introspective writing style.

Didion's essay collections, 'Slouching Toward Bethlehem' and 'The White Album', are considered modern classics. Her work often explored the American experience, politics, and culture.

In 2005, Didion won the National Book Award for Non-Fiction for her memoir 'The Year of Magical Thinking', which chronicled the death of her husband John Gregory Dunne. The book was later adapted into a Broadway play starring Vanessa Redgrave.

Didion was also a screenwriter, collaborating with her husband on several screenplays, including 'Panic in Needle Park'. The couple's daughter, Quintana Roo Dunne, died in 2005 at the age of 39.

Maria Shriver, journalist and former California first lady, paid tribute to Didion on Twitter, saying, "Joan Didion was a brilliant writer, a fierce intellect, and a trailblazer for women in journalism. Her work will live on, but her presence will be deeply missed."

Actress Reese Witherspoon, a fan of Didion's work, also shared her condolences on social media, writing, "I'm so sad to hear about the passing of Joan Didion. Her writing was always so insightful and thought-provoking. She was a true legend in the literary world."

In 2013, Didion received the National Medal of Arts from President Barack Obama, who praised her for her "bold and insightful writing" that had "captured the American experience."

A documentary about her life, 'Joan Didion: The Center Will Not Hold', was released in 2017. The film featured interviews with Didion, her family, and colleagues, offering a glimpse into her life and career.

Didion's passing has sparked an outpouring of tributes from the literary and entertainment communities, with many praising her contributions to American literature and journalism.

In a statement, Penguin Random House said, "Joan Didion's writing has had a profound impact on American literature and culture. Her unwavering commitment to the truth, her keen eye for detail, and her ability to capture the essence of the human experience have made her a beloved and respected voice in our literary landscape."

Didion's legacy continues to inspire new generations of writers and journalists, and her work remains a testament to her remarkable talent and dedication to the craft.

In her essay 'Goodbye to All That', Didion famously wrote, "I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not." Her work continues to be a nod to the people she used to be, and the people she encountered along the way.

Rest in peace, Joan Didion. Your words will live on.

Analysis: How Much Will the $1,400 Stimulus Check Help Financially Vulnerable Americans?

The lack of data-driven debate regarding the third stimulus package reflects the scarcity of data on households’ finances. To date, the focus has been on how a stimulus package will impact consumer spending, but it is not clear how President Joe Biden’s proposed $1,400 stimulus check for eligible households will affect Americans’ ability to pay their bills.

Conventional economic data such as gross domestic product and high-frequency consumer spending data both measure economic output. Similarly, aggregate personal saving data offers no insight into the distribution of savings across the population. While these data sources offer important insight into the likely impact of fiscal spending on the economy, they only tell part of the story.

To assess the impact, amount and eligibility of a third stimulus package, Morning Consult analyzed its proprietary tracking data on household finances, which offers insight into the current condition of households’ balance sheets.

Using this data, this analysis argues that a third round of $1,400 stimulus checks more narrowly targeted to low-income adults and parents combined with enhancements to the country’s unemployment benefit system would prevent unnecessary financial hardship and mitigate future economic risks.

$1,400 would help many Americans avoid financial hardship through July

The purpose of fiscal spending during a recession is not only to boost short-term economic activity; it’s also to provide financially vulnerable households with enough money to avoid unnecessary financial harm. As a society, delinquencies and defaults are inefficient and costly uses of resources, and financial uncertainty prevents families from investing in their futures. During recessions, it’s cheaper for the country as a whole to keep people out of financial trouble than it is helping them fight their way back.

Despite the second round of stimulus checks in January, the number of adults who experienced financial hardship in January remained relatively unchanged from December. In January, 16 percent of survey respondents indicated that their expenses exceeded their incomes for the month, from 15 percent in December. This financial suffering was concentrated among low-income households ($50,000 or less in annual income), underscoring how severely pay losses have been concentrated among low-income adults during this recession.

As the dust settles from this incident, Anderson Cooper’s messages resonate with many in the industry. His reflections serve as a sobering reminder of the need for accountability in journalism, especially in times of crisis. Although he empathized with Cuomo during this tumultuous period, he reiterated the steadfast importance of ethical guidelines that journalists must uphold, regardless of their standing within an organization.

In a world where journalism faces increasing scrutiny, the events surrounding Chris Cuomo’s firing will likely prompt enduring conversations about responsibility, integrity, and the often murky waters of personal connections in a professional landscape that demands transparency. The consequences of his actions will weigh heavily, not only on him and his family but on CNN and the broader media ecosystem as it navigates these challenging times.

Delta plus: What we know about the latest coronavirus variant

Viruses like to reproduce, but they need hosts to do it. And with a significant percentage of the world's population not yet vaccinated against COVID, the coronavirus has a lot of room to infect people, mutate and, eventually, form new variants. The newest coronavirus variant that health officials are watching is "delta plus," a mutation of the now-dominant delta variant. The original delta is highly contagious, suspected to cause more-severe disease and, according to an estimate by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, responsible for about 93% of coronavirus cases in the US right now.

Though news of coronavirus variants (alpha, beta, delta, lambda and so on) can be overwhelming, not every variant is cause for more concern than the original coronavirus.

We'll break down what scientists know right now about delta plus, and how concerned we should be about it.

Delta vs. delta plus

In June, health officials in India called out delta plus as a "variant of concern" because it's thought to be better at binding to lung cells and could possibly evade treatments for COVID. Delta plus has been detected in several other regions, including the US, the United Kingdom, Portugal, Russia and China, the BBC reported. South Korea is the latest country to raise a red flag about delta plus, identifying the variant in a man with no recent travel records, according to Reuters.

The "plus" in delta plus refers to the newer variant's K417N spike protein mutation, The Washington Post noted. (Spike proteins are what allows COVID and other viruses to get into our cells.) This mutation, also found in the earlier beta variant, can make certain COVID-19 treatments less effective, according to the CDC, adding emphasis to the warning from India.

Will delta plus be worse than the already horrible delta? To survive well enough and become a dominant variant, a variant needs to infect a lot of people and prove to be more transmissible. So far, delta plus hasn't done that, but more research is needed.

Derek Chauvin Found Guilty of Murder and Manslaughter in George Floyd's Death

CNN – Minneapolis, Minnesota

In a landmark verdict that has captivated the nation and reverberated worldwide, a jury in Minneapolis has found former police officer Derek Chauvin guilty of second-degree murder, third-degree murder, and second-degree manslaughter in the death of George Floyd. The verdict, delivered after three weeks of a closely watched trial, brings a measure of justice to the Floyd family and ignites hope for meaningful police reform in the United States.

The Jury's Composition and Selection Process

The jury, composed of 12 individuals, reflected the diverse fabric of the community. Five men and seven women deliberated over Chauvin's fate, with a racial makeup of six White, four Black, and two multiracial jurors. Two alternate jurors, both White women, were dismissed before deliberations commenced.

The jury selection process, which spanned from March 9 to March 23 at the Hennepin County Government Center, was meticulous and exhaustive. Potential jurors were rigorously questioned about their backgrounds, beliefs, and potential biases to ensure a fair and impartial panel.

The Tragic Death of George Floyd

At the heart of this trial lies the tragic death of George Floyd, an unarmed Black man whose life was cut short on May 25, 2020, after Chauvin, a White former Minneapolis Police officer, kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds. Floyd's death, captured on a bystander's video, sparked outrage and ignited a global movement against racial injustice and police brutality.

Potential Sentences and Sentencing Date

Chauvin now faces a significant prison sentence for his actions. He could receive up to 40 years for second-degree murder, 25 years for third-degree murder, and 10 years for second-degree manslaughter. The sentencing, scheduled for eight weeks from the trial's conclusion, will be determined by Judge Peter Cahill.

Trial Highlights and Witness Testimony

The trial, which captivated the nation, featured testimony from 45 witnesses over approximately three weeks. Key witnesses included bystanders who witnessed Floyd's death, police officers who responded to the scene, medical experts, and use-of-force experts. Their testimonies provided crucial insights into the events leading up to Floyd's death and the actions of Chauvin and the other officers involved.

Co-Defendants and Future Trials

Chauvin was not the only officer charged in connection with Floyd's death. Three other former officers—Tou Thao, J. Alexander Kueng, and Thomas Lane—are charged with aiding and abetting in the case and are expected to stand trial later this year. Their trials will likely delve deeper into the complexities of police accountability and the systemic issues within law enforcement.

Jury Selection: Shaping the Panel

During jury selection, both the defense and prosecution strategically employed peremptory challenges to shape the jury based on their views on policing and the Black Lives Matter movement. These challenges, which allow lawyers to exclude potential jurors without providing a reason, sparked discussions about the fairness and potential biases in the jury selection process.

A Moment of Reckoning and Hope

The guilty verdict in the Derek Chauvin trial marks a pivotal moment in the fight for racial justice and police accountability. While it does not erase the pain and loss suffered by the Floyd family and countless others, it offers a glimmer of hope that the wheels of justice can turn and that meaningful change is possible. As the nation grapples with the legacy of systemic racism and police brutality, the Chauvin verdict stands as a reminder that progress, though incremental, can be achieved through collective action and unwavering commitment to justice.

Major US Pipeline Hit by Ransomware, Colonial Pays $5 Million in Ransom

DarkSide, which has gained notoriety for its so-called double-extortion tactic—where attackers both encrypt data and threaten to release it unless a ransom is paid—seems to have, for now, refrained from dumping Colonial Pipeline's data on their leak site. This restraint might be due to the potential "social" problems that could arise from such an action, given the critical nature of the pipeline's operations for US fuel supply.

As of May 11, there was no evidence that Colonial Pipeline's data had been posted on DarkSide's leak site. However, reports from Bloomberg on May 13 indicated that Colonial Pipeline had paid close to $5 million in ransom for a decryption key. This action highlights the severity of the situation and the desperate measures the company had to undertake to restore the vital service.

This incident is among the largest cyberattacks against US critical infrastructure, shedding light on systemic vulnerabilities. It's not the first time essential services have been targeted; previous cyberattacks include an attempt to poison a Florida city's drinking water and causing a power outage in Ukraine, both demonstrating the growing threat to public safety and national security.

The Colonial Pipeline attack underscores the urgent need for a comprehensive review and improvement of cybersecurity practices within the United States. Cybersecurity firm Bitdefender notes the increasing appeal of targeting critical infrastructure to ransomware operators. The firm points out vulnerabilities in remote maintenance systems as a significant risk factor.

In response to this growing threat, a new executive order has been issued emphasizing enhanced cybersecurity measures. These measures include the implementation of multi-factor authentication, data encryption, and adopting a zero-trust security model—where default trust is removed from all systems, requiring verification from everyone trying to access resources in a network.

Furthermore, a Cybersecurity Safety Review Board will be established to enforce and monitor the implementation of these new security protocols. This board will be tasked with ensuring that critical infrastructure sectors, and beyond, follow through with the mandated cybersecurity enhancements.

The recent attack on Colonial Pipeline serves as a stark reminder of the vulnerabilities that exist within the fabric of the US's critical infrastructure. It emphasizes the need for immediate action to bolster defenses against increasingly sophisticated and bold cybercriminals. The news was confirmed on Facebook Wednesday by his bandmates Billy Gibbons and Frank Beard, who said he passed away in his sleep in his Houston home.

“We, along with legions of ZZ Top fans around the world, will miss your steadfast presence, your good nature and enduring commitment to providing that monumental bottom to the ‘Top,'” the two wrote on Facebook.

Born Joe Michael Hill in Dallas, Dusty Hill headed to Houston in 1970 and joined ZZ Top, alongside guitarist Billy Gibbons and drummer Frank Beard. The band grew in popularity blending blues and rock and roll, and went on to release 15 albums in their roughly 50-year history.

Their 1984 album “Eliminator,” which featured the hits “Gimme All Your Lovin'”, “Sharp Dressed Man”, and “Legs,” sold more than 10 million copies and was certified Diamond by the Recording Industry Association of America. The band also had four Platinum records — with the 1985 album “Afterburner” going five-times Platinum — and four Gold records with Hill on bass and backing vocals.

Hill and his bandmates were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2003 by Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards.

While ZZ Top is among the most successful rock bands in history, they’re perhaps best known for the signature black sunglasses and long beards worn by Hill and Gibbons, which were introduced in the 1970s. According to the liner notes of their 2004 album "Rancho Texicano: The Very Best of ZZ Top,” detailed by Yahoo! Entertainment in 2012, the two returned from a vacation and realized they’d both grown out their facial hair. Rather than shave, the pair decided to keep it.

In 1984, razor company Gillette reportedly offered the duo $1 million to shave off their famous facial hair. They declined.
