Donald J. Trump: A Life in Business and Politics

Donald John Trump, born on June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, is a businessman and politician who served as the 45th President of the United States from 2017 to 2021.

Early Life and Business Career

Trump's father, Fred Trump, was a successful real estate developer. Following his education at the New York Military Academy and the Wharton School of Finance and Commerce at the University of Pennsylvania, Trump joined his father's company in 1971, later renaming it the Trump Organization. The company expanded into various real estate ventures, including hotels, resorts, residential and commercial buildings, casinos, and golf courses.

Literary and Television Ventures

Trump published his first book, "The Art of the Deal," in 1987. In 2004, he launched the reality television show "The Apprentice".

Personal Life

Trump has been married three times and has five children: Donald Jr., Ivanka, Eric, and Tiffany from his first two marriages, and Barron from his current marriage to Melania Knauss.

Political Career

With no prior political experience, Trump entered the 2016 presidential race as a Republican candidate. He defeated several rivals to win the nomination and went on to win the general election against Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton, despite losing the popular vote. His campaign slogan was "Make America Great Again".

Presidency

During his presidency, Trump implemented several key policies, including a major tax reform bill, a reduction of federal regulations, and protectionist trade policies. He also appointed two Supreme Court justices and numerous federal judges.

Foreign Policy

Trump's foreign policy was marked by several notable events, including the relocation of the U.S. Embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, brokering normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries, and holding a historic summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

Challenges and Controversies

Trump's presidency was also marked by controversy and challenges, including a partial government shutdown over border wall funding and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

Legacy

Donald Trump remains a highly polarizing figure in American politics. His legacy will continue to be debated and analyzed for years to come.

Stimulus Check Disbursement Sparks Debate Over Economic Equity and Effectiveness

As discussions heat up among policymakers regarding the next round of stimulus checks under the American Rescue Plan, a growing body of evidence suggests that targeted financial relief could yield more significant economic benefits. Recent analyses of consumer spending patterns reveal a stark contrast between low-income families and their higher-earning counterparts. Prior to the distribution of stimulus checks, both groups exhibited similar spending behaviors; however, following the issuance of $600 checks on January 4, 2021, low-income families dramatically increased their spending, while high-income households tended to save a majority of their payments. This trend points to a fundamental shift in consumption that raises questions about the efficacy of blanket stimulus payments across income brackets. Experts argue that continuing to provide substantial checks to higher-income individuals may not spur the same level of immediate economic activity, potentially undermining the intended goals of the stimulus initiative.

Emerging strategies advocate for the use of real-time economic data from credit card transactions and payroll systems to inform policymakers on where funds would most effectively be allocated. Historical data often fails to capture the nuances of how different income groups respond to financial assistance, especially during a recession that has disproportionately affected low- and middle-income families. The divergent saving patterns observed during the pandemic—where high-income individuals have tended to stash away more savings—underline the necessity of localized data analysis to better address the varying economic realities experienced throughout the nation. By adopting an evidence-based approach that leverages contemporary economic indicators, policymakers can more effectively support vulnerable households, ensuring that economic relief reaches those who need it most. Such measures could fortify local economies and promote a more equitable recovery as communities continue to grapple with the implications of an uneven economic landscape.

Update on Omicron

On 26 November 2021, WHO designated the variant B.1.1.529 a variant of concern, named Omicron, on the advice of WHO’s Technical Advisory Group on Virus Evolution (TAG-VE). This decision was based on the evidence presented to the TAG-VE that Omicron has several mutations that may have an impact on how it behaves, for example, on how easily it spreads or the severity of illness it causes. Here is a summary of what is currently known.

Current knowledge about Omicron

Researchers in South Africa and around the world are conducting studies to better understand many aspects of Omicron and will continue to share the findings of these studies as they become available.

Transmissibility: It is not yet clear whether Omicron is more transmissible (e.g., more easily spread from person to person) compared to other variants, including Delta. The number of people testing positive has risen in areas of South Africa affected by this variant, but epidemiologic studies are underway to understand if it is because of Omicron or other factors.

Severity of disease: It is not yet clear whether infection with Omicron causes more severe disease compared to infections with other variants, including Delta. Preliminary data suggests that there are increasing rates of hospitalization in South Africa, but this may be due to increasing overall numbers of people becoming infected, rather than a result of specific infection with Omicron. There is currently no information to suggest that symptoms associated with Omicron are different from those from other variants. Initial reported infections were among university students—younger individuals who tend to have more mild disease—but understanding the level of severity of the Omicron variant will take days to several weeks. All variants of COVID-19, including the Delta variant that is dominant worldwide, can cause severe disease or death, in particular for the most vulnerable people, and thus prevention is always key.

Effectiveness of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection

Preliminary evidence suggests there may be an increased risk of reinfection with Omicron (ie, people who have previously had COVID-19 could become reinfected more easily with Omicron), as compared to other variants of concern, but information is limited. More information on this will become available in the coming days and weeks.

Effectiveness of vaccines: WHO is working with technical partners to understand the potential impact of this variant on our existing countermeasures, including vaccines. Vaccines remain critical to reducing severe disease and death, including against the dominant circulating variant, Delta. Current vaccines remain effective against severe disease and death.

Effectiveness of current tests: The widely used PCR tests continue to detect infection, including infection with Omicron, as we have seen with other variants as well. Studies are ongoing to determine whether there is any impact on other types of tests, including rapid antigen detection tests.

Effectiveness of current treatments: Corticosteroids and IL6 Receptor Blockers will still be effective for managing patients with severe COVID-19. Other treatments will be assessed to see if they are still as effective given the changes to parts of the virus in the Omicron variant.

Studies underway

At the present time, WHO is coordinating with a large number of researchers around the world to better understand Omicron. Studies currently underway or underway shortly include assessments of transmissibility, severity of infection (including symptoms), performance of vaccines and diagnostic tests, and effectiveness of treatments.

WHO encourages countries to contribute the collection and sharing of hospitalized patient data through the WHO COVID-19 Clinical Data Platform to rapidly describe clinical characteristics and patient outcomes.

More information will emerge in the coming days and weeks. WHO’s TAG-VE will continue to monitor and evaluate the data as it becomes available and assess how mutations in Omicron alter the behaviour of the virus.

Recommended actions for countries

As Omicron has been designated a Variant of Concern, there are several actions WHO recommends countries to undertake, including enhancing surveillance and sequencing of cases; sharing genome sequences on publicly available databases, such as GISAID; reporting initial cases or clusters to WHO; performing field investigations and laboratory assessments to better understand if Omicron has different transmission or disease characteristics, or impacts effectiveness of vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics or public health and social measures. More detail in the announcement from 26 November.

Countries should continue to implement the effective public health measures to reduce COVID-19 circulation overall, using a risk analysis and science-based approach. They should increase some public health and medical capacities to manage an increase in cases. WHO is providing countries with support and guidance for both readiness and response.

In addition, it is vitally important that inequities in access to COVID-19 vaccines are urgently addressed to ensure that vulnerable groups everywhere, including health workers and older persons, receive their first and second doses, alongside equitable access to treatment and diagnostics.

Recommended actions for people

The most effective steps individuals can take to reduce the spread of the COVID-19 virus is to keep a physical distance of at least 1 metre from others; wear a well-fitting mask; open windows to improve ventilation; avoid poorly ventilated or crowded spaces; keep hands clean; cough or sneeze into a bent elbow or tissue; and get vaccinated when it’s their turn.

WHO will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available, including following meetings of the TAG-VE. In addition, information will be available on WHO’s digital and social media platforms.

Powell envisioned moving the GOP ‘close to the spirit of Lincoln.’ It embraced Trump’s view instead.

Colin L. Powell had kept the political world guessing: Was he a Democrat or a Republican? At a packed news conference in November 1995, dominated by speculation about a presidential bid for the trailblazing four-star general, Powell delivered the big reveal: He was a Republican. Wp Get the full experience. Choose your plan ArrowRight That announcement was overshadowed by his other news, that he wouldn’t seek the presidency, clearing the way for Sen. Bob Dole (Kan.) to seize the GOP nomination and removing a challenge to President Bill Clinton (D). But Powell used that very public moment to lay out his vision for the Republican Party and what the first Black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff hoped to accomplish.

“I believe I can help the party of Lincoln move once again close to the spirit of Lincoln,” Powell said in a tacit rebuke of GOP ideologues who opposed racial diversity and extending a welcoming hand to immigrants.

His vision for the Republican Party, however, never materialized. Instead, it swiftly and surely moved toward Donald Trump’s political worldview, a party warning of immigrants replacing White Americans, one wary and sometimes mocking of international engagement and willing to embrace a populism that has divided the nation. Powell, the hero of the 1991 Persian Gulf War who once was heralded as the next Dwight D. Eisenhower, became an outlier in the party.

In 2008, he endorsed Barack Obama, the first Black president, and later backed Democratic presidential candidates, soundly rejecting Trump. In January, after a pro-Trump mob stormed the U.S. Capitol, Powell said he could “no longer call himself a Republican.”

The divorce seemed inevitable for a never-Trumper often described as a RINO — Republican in name only — by the party faithful, some of whom had once promoted him as a possible presidential nominee, a Black Republican in a GOP struggling for diversity.

“He certainly is one of the greatest political what-ifs,” said Douglas Heye, a former Republican National Committee communications director who served as deputy chief of staff to former House majority leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.), referring to Powell’s potential as a leader of a modern GOP. “It highlights the fact that people like him were turning away in part because of some of that increased — especially racial — rhetoric that was acceptable in too many parts of the Republican Party.”

Powell, who died Monday at the age of 84 due to complications from covid-19, was widely praised by presidents, politicians and former colleagues. His death cast his complicated political legacy in sharp relief.

“Colin was, first and foremost, a military leader, probably one of the finest leaders in the post-World War II era,” former defense secretary Leon Panetta said in an interview with The Washington Post. “He was totally dedicated to the country, to our national security, to the truth, and always put country ahead of party. That’s who he was.”

Powell resisted entreaties to seek the presidency, saying that he was turning them down because he believed he lacked the “passion and commitment” needed for political life. Panetta agreed, saying he never thought Powell had the “fire in the belly to run for public office” because he never “felt comfortable having to play the political game.”

“I thought of him really more as just a straight public servant, and I think, because of that, he really believed in doing what was right for the country and adhering to the values that he thought were important to the country,” Panetta said. “When he sensed that the Republican Party was moving away from those values, it really meant for him that he had to stay true to who he was.”

Following the Jan. 6 insurrection, Powell disavowed his party. In an interview with CNN, he was asked if members of the GOP realized that they “encouraged at least this wildness to grow and grow,” referring to the Trump administration.

“They didn’t, and that’s why I can no longer call myself a fellow Republican,” Powell replied.

“I’m not a fellow of anything right now,” he added. “I’m just a citizen who has voted Republican, voted Democrat, throughout my entire career, and right now I’m just watching my country and not concerned with parties.”

President Biden and former presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama paid tribute to Powell Monday. Former president Donald Trump was silent until Tuesday morning, when, in a statement, he called Powell a “classic RINO” who was always “the first to attack other Republicans.” “He made plenty of mistakes, but anyway, may he rest in peace,” Trump said.

“He’s a rare breed,” Ari Fleischer, George W. Bush’s former White House press secretary, told The Washington Post about Powell. “He’s done the opposite of what a lot of people both sides do today, which is appeal to their base and ignore the middle. Powell built a huge middle and ignored both bases.”

Fleischer said that, had Powell run in 1996, he would have created a “very exciting, different political dynamic about the center.” He now hopes that, someday, someone will successfully replicate Powell’s political ways.

“Eventually, our polarization is going to get pierced by someone who runs up the middle and unites people,” Fleischer said. “A Powell-like person might be the right one to do it. I don’t know who that person is, but it intrigues me.”

As he stood before the cameras to say he would not run for the White House in 1995, Powell took a moment to recognize the fact that a Black man was being seriously considered as a presidential candidate.

“That’s the realization of a great dream, even though I may not be the one to fill it,” he said, a line others would later cite to explain why he endorsed Obama instead of Sen. John McCain (Ariz.), the 2008 Republican presidential nominee who, like Powell, was a Vietnam War veteran.

His backing of Obama “wasn’t some kind of radical shift,” said Anthony Cordesman, who served as national security adviser to McCain on the Senate Armed Services Committee and is the emeritus strategy chair of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“It was dictated more by the character of what was a candidate on the Republican side he respected a great deal more than perhaps a preceding president, but that was replaced by a figure who, for obvious reasons, was a symbol of many of the other causes and issues that he supported,” Cordesman said Monday.

Former secretary of state Madeleine Albright, who preceded Powell, said his support for Obama was “clearly a difficult decision. I obviously think it was a very good one, but it was because of the way that he approached issues in terms of seeing beyond party.”

Powell’s warnings against Trump, Heye said, may have come at a time when not many in the GOP were listening to him anymore, given that he had chosen to endorse Obama over McCain.

“Since he essentially had left the party in 2008 and had warned — in a lot of cases, perhaps presciently so — of more extreme elements in the party, by the time we get to an actual Trump presidency, much less January 6, Powell had largely left that conversation,” Heye said.

In their tributes to Powell, Republicans focused on his pioneer status and years of service.

“It is hard to imagine a more quintessentially American story: A son of Jamaican immigrants who learned Yiddish from his boyhood neighbors in the Bronx becomes a four-star General in the United States Army and serves four presidential administrations, including as National Security Advisor, the youngest-ever Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the first Black Secretary of State,” said Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) in a statement.

Democrats, most notably Obama, highlighted the times Powell broke with the GOP.

“At a time when conspiracy theories were swirling, with some questioning my faith, General Powell took the opportunity to get to the heart of the matter in a way only he could,” Obama said in a statement.

“The correct answer is, he is not a Muslim; he’s a Christian,” Powell said of Obama in 2008. “But the really right answer is, ‘What if he is?’ Is there something wrong with being a Muslim in this country? The answer’s no, that’s not America. Is there something wrong with some 7-year-old Muslim American kid believing that he or she could be president?”

“That’s who Colin Powell was,” Obama said. “He understood what was best in this country, and tried to bring his own life, career, and public statements in line with that ideal.”

House Majority Leader Steny H. Hoyer (D-Md.) recognized the significance of Powell’s move to endorse Obama, saying “it meant something to the many Republicans and Democrats who had hoped they might cast such a vote for him years earlier.”

Texas Plunges into Icy Emergency, Leaving Millions Without Power

A brutal winter storm has plunged Texas into an unprecedented icy emergency, leaving over 2 million people without power and disrupting essential services. The storm, which brought snow, sleet, and freezing rain to the southern Plains, has also caused treacherous road conditions and forced the closure of grocery stores and vaccination sites.

Temperatures have plummeted to single digits as far south as San Antonio, leaving homes without heat or light for extended periods. The state's overwhelmed power grid has been forced to implement rolling blackouts, typically seen only during scorching summer months.

"We're living through a really historic event," said Jason Furtado, a meteorology professor at the University of Oklahoma. The widespread winter storm warning and the extent of the freezing temperatures are unprecedented for Texas.

In Houston, where officials warned of potential hurricane-level disruption, one electric provider estimates that some homes may remain without power until Tuesday.

"This weather event is truly unprecedented," said Dan Woodfin, senior director of system operations at the Electric Reliability Council of Texas. He defended preparations made by grid operators but acknowledged that the demand on the system is record-breaking.

"This event was well beyond the design parameters for a typical, or even an extreme, Texas winter," Woodfin said. "And so that is really the result that we're seeing."

The storm has also disrupted the distribution of COVID-19 vaccines, with some providers scrambling to find takers for doses nearing expiration. The largest grocery store chain in Texas, H-E-B, has closed locations in Austin and San Antonio, further complicating the situation.

The slow thaw and continued frigid temperatures are expected to prolong the challenges faced by Texans. As the state grapples with the aftermath of this historic winter storm, concerns remain about the impact on infrastructure, essential services, and public health.

The review of their roles had been conducted in the year following their departure, and discussions included the impossibility of continuing with public service responsibilities.

Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Harry engaged in a frank conversation surrounding the couple’s intentions. "Both sides recognize the realities of their situation, and they understand the importance of defining their roles clearly," said Angela Levin, a biographer of Prince Harry. "It is undoubtedly a bittersweet moment, but it reflects how things have changed over the past couple of years."

As a result of this decision, Meghan will also lose her esteemed patronages, which include organizations such as Britain's National Theatre and the Association of Commonwealth Universities. While these affiliations were vital aspects of her work, palace officials highlighted that they remain committed to serving their chosen causes in different capacities moving forward.

Despite this formal separation from royal duties, the couple continues to be regarded as cherished members of the royal family. A spokesperson for Harry and Meghan reiterated their ongoing commitment to duty and service, emphasizing that their dedication to charitable initiatives will persist outside the confines of royal duties.

Harry and Meghan's departure stems from their move to North America, driven by a desire to escape relentless media intrusions and the horrific racist attitudes highlighted in some media narratives. The couple sought not only privacy but a space to cultivate their family away from the spotlight of public scrutiny.

Even as they retain their Duke and Duchess titles, the couple will no longer use the style of 'royal highness' or receive public funding related to royal engagements. "This is an opportunity for them to forge their own paths," Levin noted. "They have navigated a difficult road, and this decision reflects the need for autonomy in an evolving landscape."

Moving ahead, they plan to focus on a range of charitable endeavors, media projects, and philanthropic initiatives that were not possible whilst serving as working royals.

As the couple moves forward, their journey serves as a stark reminder of the complex relationship between modernity and tradition within the British monarchy. The decision, while laden with emotional ramifications, ultimately allows both Harry and Meghan to contribute to society on their own terms.

Palace insiders suggest that this finalization of roles signals a new era for the Sussexes, one where they can engage in initiatives that resonate deeply with their values. The royal family must now regroup and redefine the future of their monarchy in a world increasingly scrutinizing its relevance and practices.

Moving forward, all eyes will undoubtedly remain on the couple as they navigate their life beyond royal duties and carve out their identities as private citizens committed to service in today's global context.

The Ever Given Debacle: A Multimillion-Dollar Mishap in the Suez Canal and the Maritime World's Reckoning

The Suez Canal, a critical artery for global trade, was brought to a grinding halt in late March 2021 when the colossal Ever Given cargo ship, longer than the height of the Eiffel Tower, became lodged in the canal's eastern bank. The incident, which unfolded over six days, sent shockwaves through the maritime industry and beyond, as the global supply chain faced unprecedented disruptions.

François Mayor, Director of Port Revel, a maritime research and training center in France, explained the gravity of the situation, stating, "The Ever Given incident highlighted the vulnerability of these vital shipping lanes and the far-reaching consequences of even a temporary closure."

Initial reports attributed the mishap to the ship's aggressive maneuvers in response to strong winds and the Suez Canal's shallow and narrow passageways. However, the Egyptian authorities, who oversee the canal, blamed the Ever Given's captain for disregarding their instructions and sailing too quickly, leading to the grounding. Bruno Mercier, a former Marseille pilot with extensive experience navigating large ships through the Suez Canal, refuted these claims, asserting, "The Suez Canal pilots have full control over a vessel's speed as it transits the canal."

As the world waited with bated breath for the Ever Given to be refloated, marine engineer Julianne Cona documented the incident from her vantage point, snapping a series of photographs that would later go viral on social media. Her images, depicting the behemoth Ever Given wedged between the canal's banks, offered a stark reminder of the precarious balance between man, machine, and nature.

The Egyptian government's initial response to the incident was to demand a staggering $916.5 million in damages from the Ever Given's owners, Shoei Kisen Kaisha Ltd. Martin Davies, Head of Tulane University's Maritime Law Center, expressed skepticism over the claim, stating, "The damages being demanded by Egypt are highly unusual and could set a dangerous precedent in maritime law."

The incident brought renewed attention to the training and handling challenges of large ships in narrow canals. Port Revel, with its state-of-the-art simulation facilities, played a crucial role in shedding light on the factors contributing to the Ever Given's grounding. François Mayor explained, "Our simulations demonstrated the impact of speed on ship control and the effectiveness of tugboats in managing navigation under strong winds and currents."

The Ever Given's crew, stranded aboard their vessel for an extended period, faced uncertainty and the possibility of charges. Abdulgani Serang, General Secretary of the National Union of Seafarers of India, emphasized the importance of ensuring the welfare of seafarers in such situations, stating, "Seafarers are often the forgotten heroes in the maritime industry. Their well-being must be prioritized during crises such as these."

Negotiations between Egypt and the Ever Given's owners reached a resolution in June 2021, with Egypt reducing its demand to $550 million and an undisclosed settlement being reached after three months. Mercier offered his perspective on the outcome, stating, "This incident serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of maritime legal disputes and the importance of effective communication and cooperation between all parties involved."

The Ever Given debacle underscored the need for better handling techniques in canals and the complexities of maritime legal disputes. As Mayor reflected, "The Ever Given incident was a wake-up call for the maritime community. It highlighted the importance of investing in research, training, and innovation to ensure the safety and efficiency of global shipping."

As the maritime industry continues to grapple with the challenges posed by the Ever Given debacle, experts and stakeholders remain committed to learning from the incident and implementing the necessary changes to prevent similar occurrences in the future. In the words of Davies, "The Ever Given incident may have been a costly and disruptive lesson, but it also presents an opportunity for the maritime community to come together and improve the way we navigate the world's waterways."

Capitol Riot: A Culmination of Hateful Rhetoric and Online Extremism

COLLEGE PARK, Md. (AP) – The violent insurrection at the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday was a culmination of years of hateful rhetoric, fueled by disinformation and conspiracy theories that have proliferated online, experts say.

Far-right extremist groups, including the Proud Boys and white supremacist organizations, played a significant role in the riot, which left five people dead, including a Capitol Police officer.

"This is the natural outcome of the violence and extremism that has been promoted online for years," said Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL). "It's a dark day for democracy."

Online forums used by Trump supporters celebrated the chaos at the Capitol, with some users calling for further violence. The riot also included figures and groups known for spreading conspiracy theories, such as QAnon.

"The Capitol riot was the logical conclusion to extremism and hate going unchecked," said Oren Segal, Vice President of the ADL's Center on Extremism. "We've seen a surge in online threats and calls for violence in recent months, and this is the result."

Social media platforms were working to remove threats and calls for violence following the event. Twitter suspended President Trump's account, citing "the risk of further incitement of violence."

"This is a necessary step to prevent further harm," said Amy Spitalnick, Executive Director of Integrity First for America. "Social media companies have a responsibility to protect their users from hate speech and violence."

According to Zignal Labs, a media intelligence firm, the phrase "civil war" surged in online mentions in the days leading up to the riot. The phrase "storm the capitol" also spiked in popularity.

"This is a wake-up call for all of us," said Greenblatt. "We need to address the root causes of extremism and hate, both online and offline."

Proud Boys leader Henry "Enrique" Tarrio was arrested prior to the riot and ordered to stay out of Washington. However, many members of the group participated in the violence.

"The Proud Boys are a violent extremist group that has been involved in numerous acts of violence," said Segal. "Their presence at the Capitol riot is not surprising."

The ADL called for Trump to be removed from office immediately.

"This is a dangerous man who has incited violence and hatred," said Greenblatt. "He must be held accountable for his actions."

The Capitol riot has sent shockwaves through the nation and raised concerns about the future of American democracy.

"This is a dark day for our country," said Spitalnick. "We must come together to reject extremism and hate, and to build a more just and equitable society."

In the aftermath of the riot, law enforcement agencies are investigating the involvement of far-right extremist groups and individuals. The FBI is asking for the public's help in identifying those who participated in the violence.

"We will not tolerate violence and extremism in our country," said FBI Director Christopher Wray. "We will bring those responsible for this attack to justice."

Bucs' Initial 2021 53-Man Roster Includes Just 10 Newcomers

Head Coach Bruce Arians hinted during the last week of training camp that his team would carry either 10 linebackers (outside and inside) or 10 defensive backs (cornerback and safety). At the moment, the extra spot goes to the linebackers, with outside linebacker Cam Gill and rookie inside linebackers K.J. Britt and Grant Stuard all making it.

The Buccaneers retained six of their seven 2021 draft picks, with the exception being seventh-round cornerback Chris Wilcox. The only undrafted rookie still on the roster after Tuesday's cuts is kicker Jose Borregales, who handled the placekicking duties in the preseason finale at Houston with Succop unavailable.

Listed below is how the initial 53-man roster breaks down, with the players listed alphabetically at each position (rookies marked with an asterisk). We've also included the four players currently on the reserve/COVID-19 list, some or all of whom could be activated to the 53-man roster in the coming week.

Quarterbacks (3): Tom Brady, Blaine Gabbert, Kyle Trask*

The Buccaneers kept Trask, a second-round draft pick and possibly an eventual successor to Brady, over long-tenured but little-used veteran Ryan Griffin. Gabbert is likely to be the primary reserve for Brady in 2021, however.

Running Backs (4): Giovani Bernard, Leonard Fournette, Ronald Jones, Ke'Shawn Vaughn

One of the few new veterans on the roster, Bernard appears to have carved out a significant role as a third-down back, while Fournette and Jones remain essentially co-starters. Vaughn, the 2020 third-round pick, helped his cause for the fourth spot in the backfield by finding a role on special teams as a gunner.

Wide Receivers (6): Antonio Brown, Jaelon Darden*, Mike Evans, Chris Godwin, Tyler Johnson, Scotty Miller

There was little surprise in the top five receivers retained with the starting trio of Evans, Godwin and Brown backed up by promising young players Johnson and Miller. Darden appears to have beaten out Jaydon Mickens for the return job, thus securing the sixth spot. The Bucs cut Mickens, Cyril Grayson and Travis Jonsen to get down to six and any or all of those three could be top candidates for the practice squad.

Tight Ends (3): Cameron Brate, Rob Gronkowski, O.J. Howard

Neither Hudson nor McElroy apparently offered enough as a blocker or a special teams player to prompt the Bucs to keep a fourth tight end, though both are strong pass-catchers and could stick around on the practice squad. With both Howard and Brate coming off injuries and Gronkowski coming off his first-ever 20-game season, the Bucs will likely keep some depth on that secondary unit.

Offensive Linemen (9): Alex Cappa, Robert Hainsey*, Ryan Jensen, Ali Marpet, John Molchon, Donovan Smith, Aaron Stinnie, Josh Wells, Tristan Wirfs, (Nick Leverett and Earl Watford – COVID list)

There is likely room for some post-Tuesday-cuts maneuvering with this group. Molchon was injured at the end of the preseason and could be a candidate for injured reserve. Also, Leverett was a favorite of the coaching staff during camp thanks to his versatility and could join this group after coming off the COVID list.

Defensive Linemen (6): Khalil Davis, Will Gholston, Steve McLendon, Rakeem Nunez-Roches, Patrick O'Connor, Vita Vea, (Ndamukong Suh – COVID list)

This group will swell to seven players after Suh's expected activation from the COVID list, and it may have been difficult even to get to that number. Defensive line was one of the deepest spots on the training camp roster and the Bucs have shown interest since last season or earlier in cut players Jeremiah Ledbetter, Benning Potoa'e and Kobe Smith.

Outside Linebackers (5): Shaquil Barrett, Cam Gill, Anthony Nelson, Jason Pierre-Paul, Joe Tryon-Shoyinka*

The Bucs managed to keep five edge rushers on Tuesday, as Outside Linebacker Coach Larry Foote had lobbied for earlier in camp, but this might also be a fluid situation depending on how seriously Gill has injured. The second-year pro who got half of a sack in Super Bowl LV missed the majority of training camp with a lower-leg injury. Whether the Bucs end up with four or five OLBs, Tryon-Shoyinka, the team's first-round pick in April, makes the edge rotation much deeper in 2021.

Inside Linebackers (5): K.J. Britt, Lavonte David, Kevin Minter, Grant Stuard, Devin White

Britt and Stuard, fifth and seventh-round draft picks respectively, were selected in part due to their special teams abilities, and both apparently did enough in that department to make the 53-man roster. Britt was the more impressive player on defense during training camp. The Buccaneers made it through their Super Bowl season with very little depth at this spot but look better in that regard after the 2021 draft.

Cornerbacks (5): Ross Cockrell, Carlton Davis, Jamel Dean, Dee Delaney, Sean Murphy-Bunting,

Cockrell essentially gives the team a balanced secondary of 4.5 cornerbacks and 4.5 safeties after learning the latter position in training camp and quickly showing affinity for it. The Buccaneers are confident in him as a backup at outside corner, slot corner and free safety. Delaney came on strong in the preseason, both on defense and on special teams, and won a crowded competition for a fifth spot over Wilcox, Antonio Hamilton and Herb Miller.

Safeties (4): Chris Cooper, Mike Edwards, Jordan Whitehead, Antoine Winfield

Cooper is probably the most surprising player remaining after Tuesday's cuts given that he only arrived in Tampa on the day training camp began. He impressed on special teams during the preseason, which was emphasized by Arians in regard to the competition for the last five or six spots on the roster. Whitehead missed significant time in training camp due to COVID and injury but Arians is hopeful the incumbent starter will be ready by the regular-season opener.

Specialists (3): Jose Borregales*, Bradley Pinion, Zach Triner, (Ryan Succop – COVID list)

The Buccaneers would have a rookie handling the kicking job if they had a game to play on Wednesday, but Succop will soon be eligible to return from the COVID list, so there could be further movement here. Succop made 37 of his 40 field goal attempts for the Buccaneers last season, including the postseason, and then got a sizeable new contract to remain with team in 2021. Pinion and Triner had no competition in camp.

Lone Survivor in Rittenhouse Trial Admits Pointing Gun at Shooter Before Being Shot

KENOSHA – Gaige Grosskreutz, the lone survivor among those shot by Kyle Rittenhouse during the Kenosha protests last year, testified on Wednesday that he had unholstered his gun and pointed it at Rittenhouse before being shot. Grosskreutz, a trained paramedic, insisted that he did not intend to kill Rittenhouse but was trying to preserve his own life.

Grosskreutz's testimony appeared to bolster Rittenhouse's self-defense claim, as he acknowledged that he believed Rittenhouse was being chased with the intent to harm. The defense argued that Rittenhouse acted in self-defense when he shot and killed two men and wounded Grosskreutz during the tumultuous protests.

Grosskreutz organized a medical corps at the protests and was carrying a gun and providing first aid during the unrest. Unlike Rittenhouse, who obtained his firearm illegally and was not certified as an emergency medical technician (EMT), Grosskreutz obtained his firearm through proper channels and was certified as an EMT.

Grosskreutz testified that he did not consider himself to be participating in the protests but was there in a medical and protective capacity. However, he did accuse Rittenhouse of "murdering" another individual, Anthony Huber, during the encounter. The judge instructed the jury to disregard the comment.

Grosskreutz's testimony revealed that he might have unintentionally pointed his gun at Rittenhouse before being shot. According to him, he raised his gun in the direction of Rittenhouse after seeing him being chased by a group of people.

After being shot, Grosskreutz underwent several surgeries, losing sensation below the elbow of the injured arm. He is now suing Kenosha law enforcement for $10 million, claiming they shared blame for Rittenhouse's actions.

The shooting took place on August 25, 2020, during protests over the police shooting of Jacob Blake, a Black man, in Kenosha. Rittenhouse, who was then 17, traveled from his home in Antioch, Illinois, to Kenosha with an AR-15-style rifle, claiming he wanted to protect property and provide medical aid.

The trial, which is being held in Kenosha County Circuit Court, is being closely watched as it could set a precedent for the use of deadly force during protests. Rittenhouse is charged with first-degree reckless homicide, first-degree intentional homicide, and attempted first-degree intentional homicide in the shootings of Huber, Grosskreutz, and Joseph Rosenbaum.

Grosskreutz's testimony marked the second day of the trial, where the defense and prosecution presented their cases to the jury. Rittenhouse himself took the stand on Tuesday, tearfully recounting the events of that fateful night.

The trial is expected to continue for several more days, with testimony from other witnesses and closing arguments scheduled for later in the week. The jury is expected to begin deliberations on Friday.

In the meantime, tensions remain high in Kenosha, with both sides of the political divide expressing strong opinions about the case. Some supporters of Rittenhouse view him as a hero who acted in self-defense, while others see him as a vigilante who escalated the situation with his presence and use of deadly force.

As the trial progresses, it is likely that more revelations will come to light, shedding new light on the events of that night and the wider context of the protests in Kenosha and beyond. For now, the focus remains on the testimony of the witnesses and the legal arguments being made by the defense and prosecution.

Tragedy Strikes Again: Utah Football Mourns the Loss of Aaron Lowe

Salt Lake City, UT — In a devastating turn of events, the University of Utah football community is mourning the loss of one of its own. Aaron Lowe, a young and promising player for the Utah Utes, was fatally shot early Sunday morning in Salt Lake City. This tragic incident occurred less than a year after the accidental shooting death of Lowe’s close friend and teammate, Ty Jordan.

Utah Head Coach Kyle Whittingham expressed his heartbreak over the loss, stating, “We are devastated to hear about Aaron’s passing. Aaron was a beloved member of our team, and his loss is felt deeply by all who knew and admired him. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.”

The incident unfolded at a house party where, according to police reports, a second victim, an unidentified woman, was also shot and is currently in critical condition. The Salt Lake City police responded to calls regarding a noise complaint and a fight involving a weapon at the location of the party. Despite their efforts, no arrests have been made in connection with the shooting.

Athletic Director Mark Harlan spoke on behalf of the university, praising Lowe’s character and leadership. “Aaron was a shining example of what it means to be a Utah Ute,” Harlan said. “His dedication on the field and in our community was exemplary. We stand with Aaron’s family, friends, and all who are grieving this unimaginable loss.”

In his third season at Utah, Lowe had made a significant impact both on and off the field. Recently, he was honored as the first recipient of the Ty Jordan Memorial Scholarship, a tribute to his late friend and teammate, which makes this loss even more poignant for those connected to the program.

Salt Lake City Police Chief Mike Brown shared his condolences with Lowe’s family and the university community, emphasizing the ongoing investigation. “Our hearts go out to Aaron’s family and to the University of Utah community,” said Chief Brown. “We are working diligently to bring justice to Aaron’s loved ones and are calling on anyone with information to come forward.”

Utah Governor Spencer Cox also weighed in, offering his sympathies and support. “Abby and I are heartbroken over the loss of Aaron Lowe,” Governor Cox remarked. “This senseless act of violence has no place in our communities, and we are committed to ensuring that those responsible are held accountable.”

Detectives are urgently working to identify any suspects involved in the shooting as the university and its football program grapple with this tragic loss. While the investigation continues, the Utah community comes together once again to remember a life taken too soon, advocating for peace and justice in the wake of another young athlete's untimely death.

Family Blames Trump for Woman's Death in Capitol Riot

WASHINGTON (Reuters) – In the wake of the violent siege on the U.S. Capitol that shocked the nation and the world, the family of Rosanne Boyland, a Georgia woman who died during the chaos, is pointing the finger of blame squarely at President Donald Trump for inciting the riot and, by extension, her tragic death.

Boyland, a fervent supporter of Trump, traveled to Washington D.C. on January 6th, drawn by the president's calls to his followers to gather and "fight" as Congress was set to certify the election results in favor of President-elect Joe Biden. The events that unfolded turned deadly as Boyland lost her life amidst the turmoil, her cause of death not officially disclosed. Yet, according to a friend who was with her, Boyland was tragically trampled in the frenzied crowd.

Speaking out in the aftermath, Justin Cave, Boyland's brother-in-law, did not mince words in assigning blame. "I hold Donald Trump personally responsible for the death of my sister-in-law," he stated, reflecting the anger and grief felt by Boyland's family.

The tragedy has led Cave to further criticize the president's role in the events of January 6th, supporting the rallying call among many for Trump's immediate removal from office. "It is my firm belief that the president's rhetoric and actions have gone too far," Cave said, expressing his support for invoking the 25th Amendment as a means to remove Trump from office.

As the family mourns, a White House spokesman has declined to comment on Boyland's death specifically, amid mounting outcry over the president's incitement and the violent actions of his supporters.

The riot at the Capitol, fueled by Trump's unfounded claims of election fraud and his encouragement of confrontation, has led to widespread condemnation and calls for accountability. Democratic leaders, alongside some Republicans, are advocating for Trump's removal, whether through the 25th Amendment or impeachment proceedings.

Boyland was among four civilians who lost their lives during the chaotic scenes in and around the Capitol. Ashli Babbitt, another ardent Trump supporter, was fatally shot by Capitol Police as she attempted to breach a barricaded door inside the building. Two men also died from medical emergencies during the riot, their names and details of their deaths providing a grim tally of the day's fallout.

The violence also claimed the life of Capitol Police officer Brian Sicknick, who succumbed to injuries sustained while clashing with the insurrectionists, adding to the day's grim legacy.

Justin Winchell, a friend who witnessed Boyland's distressing final moments, recounted their experience amidst the chaos. "We were there to support our president, and it turned into a day of horror," he said. Winchell's account underlines the stark reality that the day’s events, driven by unfounded claims and vitriolic rhetoric, resulted in unnecessary loss of life and lasting trauma for many involved.

As the nation reckons with the fallout of the Capitol siege, the voices of Boyland's family and friends add to the growing chorus of those seeking accountability and change in the wake of such an unprecedented assault on democracy.

Congressmen Meijer and Moulton Defend Surprise Kabul Trip Amidst Criticisms

Amidst mounting security concerns and a rapidly evolving situation in Afghanistan, Congressmen Peter Meijer (Michigan Republican) and Seth Moulton (Massachusetts Democrat) have gone public with details of their surprise trip to Kabul, which they describe as an exercise in conducting essential oversight on the evacuation operation during the U.S. military withdrawal and the subsequent Taliban takeover.

Both Meijer and Moulton, who are Iraq War veterans, have characterized their actions as being aimed towards minimizing risk and disruption. "We wanted to ascertain the state of evacuation operations, to understand the ground reality, and to ensure that every American, both military and civilian, was able to return home safely," Meijer elaborated.

Their visit to Kabul, however, has received significant criticism from various quarters. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, for instance, has criticized the trip as a dangerous 'freelance' journey, liable to divert valuable resources from ongoing emergency evacuation operations.

In response, Congressman Moulton has pointed out the emotional strain on personnel at Kabul airport, emphasizing that "the lack of leadership from President Biden was evident in his plans for evacuations and the execution of those plans."

The White House, while not directly commenting on the criticism levelled at the congressmen, maintains that over 100,000 people have been safely evacuated from Kabul in recent days. According to a White House spokesperson, "the President is committed to bringing back every American who wants to return home, and has taken concrete steps to facilitate that process."

Regarding the criticism of potentially diverting resources, Moulton has stated that the lawmakers in question paid 'out of pocket' for their commercial flights to the United Arab Emirates, and then took military flights to and from Kabul, thereby ensuring minimal impact on ongoing operations.

The political undertones of the visit have also emerged as a focal point for debate, with Meijer stating that "the urgency of the situation demanded bipartisan action, as opposed to political point-scoring."

Although the visit was not pre-announced to minimize the potential risk to operations and people on the ground, Moulton has emphasized that a thorough understanding of the ground reality was necessary, in order to facilitate effective decision-making and oversight.

"The American people deserve a frank assessment of the situation on the ground, as well as a clearer understanding of the decisions being taken by their elected representatives and government officials," Moulton added.

Pelosi, in her capacity as House Speaker, has indicated her opposition to the unsanctioned nature of the trip, stating that "the deployment of military resources to support such a visit could potentially have diverted attention from more critical priorities in the region."

The two congressmen have also publicly stated their opposition to President Biden's August 31 deadline for troop withdrawal. The Biden administration has maintained that this deadline is crucial for the safe and orderly conclusion of the evacuation operation.

Meijer, in this context, has highlighted that "the situation remains fluid, and the U.S. must be prepared to extend the deadline, if necessary, in order to bring every American citizen and NATO ally home safely."

As the situation in Afghanistan continues to unfold, Congressmen Meijer and Moulton's visit to Kabul has emerged as a microcosm of the broader political debate surrounding the U.S. military withdrawal, the evacuation operation, and the ramifications of these actions for the future of U.S.-Afghan relations.

Moulton, in summarizing the need for the visit, stated that "the American people deserve a transparent explanation of the situation, and as veterans, we felt a duty to see the evacuation operation for ourselves, and to share our findings with our constituents and fellow lawmakers."

The coming days and weeks are likely to reveal further information regarding the visit, and the implications of the findings from Kabul for the ongoing political and military strategies in Afghanistan. In the meantime, Congressmen Meijer and Moulton will continue their work in Washington, advocating for a measured, inclusive, and bipartisan approach to Afghanistan-related issues.

Colonial restarts pipeline amid debate over federal role

The Colonial Pipeline, which had been offline since late last week due to a cyberattack that sparked worries of fuel shortages, started coming back online Wednesday evening, its operator said.

The restart began around 5 p.m. EDT, though the process to return the pipeline to normal operations will take “several days,” the company said.

Closure of full use of the pipeline touched off debates in Congress over cybersecurity and led to confusion over which federal agency is primarily responsible to address hacks against public works projects like pipelines. Biden administration officials used the breach as an example of the need to shore up defenses against the hacking of energy hardware.

“It certainly is a reminder that we need to take a hard look at how we need to harden our necessary infrastructure, and that includes cyber threats,” Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm said Tuesday.

President Joe Biden issued an executive order Wednesday to update the federal government’s approach to cybersecurity. Among several steps, the order directs the heads of federal agencies to develop plans for cloud computing, calls for an assessment of federal information technology-contracting policies and moves to establish a “cyber safety” review board at the Department of Homeland Security.

Before Colonial announced the restart, Reps. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J., and Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-Wash., the chairman and ranking member of the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over pipelines, said Deputy Energy Secretary David Turk had briefed committee members on the hack.

“DOE is the right agency to be coordinating this government-wide effort,” they said in a joint statement, encouraging support of a bipartisan bill from Reps. Fred Upton, R-Mich., and Bobby L. Rush, D-Ill., to defend against cyberattacks.

“It would directly help DOE respond to physical and cyber threats to our pipeline and LNG facilities, like in the case of Colonial,” their statement about the bill said. “This attack and ongoing outage simply underscore the vulnerabilities we have highlighted, and how crucial it is that Congress act to enhance DOE’s cybersecurity authorities so that an incident like this does not happen again.”

Colonial first reported the hack to the FBI rather than the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency that is charged with guarding against cyberattacks on equipment like pipelines, the head of the agency told the Senate on Tuesday. The FBI then notified CISA.

The FBI said a crime organization called DarkSide carried out the attack. Colonial shut down full operations Friday after learning of the attack, it announced Saturday. Arteries and offshoots of the main pipeline have remained running.

Buttigieg pitch

Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Wednesday characterized fuel shortages caused by the ransomware attack on the Colonial Pipeline system as evidence of the need for aggressive investment in the nation’s infrastructure.

Buttigieg said the attack was “a wake-up call” for the country to get serious about the systems that keep it running.

“We’ve now had, you could argue, two major wake-up call experiences, one in Texas, and now one here, each with a different cause but both reminding us about the work that we have to do as a country,” Buttigieg said, referring to power outages caused by unusually cold weather and haphazard preparation by electrical utilities triggered in Texas in February.

“The reality is that investing in world-class, modern and resilient infrastructure has always been central to ensuring our country’s economic security, our national security and as we’re seeing right now, that includes cybersecurity,” he said. “This is not an extra, this is not a luxury, this is not an option.”

Buttigieg made his comments at a White House briefing, appearing with EPA Administrator Michael Regan to emphasize administration moves to help states in areas the hack affected.

The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration this week issued an emergency declaration giving truck drivers making emergency fuel deliveries in affected areas relief from federal hours of service limits and certain other safety regulations.

Buttigieg said his department is also considering temporarily waiving the Jones Act, a law forbidding foreign-owned, operated or built ships from carrying goods between U.S. ports.

The waiver would apply to the shipping of transport fuel. The DOT’s Maritime Administration has initiated a survey of Jones Act-qualified vessels to determine which ships could carry petroleum products within the Gulf up the Eastern Seaboard to determine if a waiver is warranted.

The Federal Railroad Administration, meanwhile, is reaching out to rail operators to see if they can help transport fuel from ports inland.

Buttigieg, who has emerged as one of the top salesmen for Biden’s $2 trillion-plus infrastructure proposal, has been diverted from that role this week as his agency turned its focus to the fuel crisis. But speaking to reporters Wednesday, he made it clear that he views the two issues as linked.

“This is part of what we have in mind when we talk about resilience,” he said. “We need to make sure our infrastructure is resilient to climate security issues caused by the increased frequency and severity of weather events, but we also need to be sure that we are resilient in the face of cyber threats, and certainly the kinds of things that the [Biden infrastructure plan] will be funding and supporting.”

Ever Given Standoff Continues: Cargo Caught in Compensation Crossfire

The Ever Given, a colossal container ship of 20,124 teu capacity, remains anchored in the Suez Canal's Great Bitter Lakes area, marking two and a half months since its high-profile refloating. The vessel, which captured global attention following its grounding in March, continues to be embroiled in a protracted legal and financial standoff that has left its cargo in limbo.

At the heart of the dispute is a compensation claim by the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) against the ship's Japanese owners. Initially demanding a staggering $916 million for damages and losses incurred during the blockage, the SCA has since moderated its claim to $550 million. This figure is still far above the $150 million offered by the shipowner, resulting in the Ever Given and its 18,000 teu of cargo being held under arrest.

The situation has led to growing frustration among North European importers who have goods stuck onboard. Faced with prolonged delays, some are even contemplating abandoning their cargo, reflecting the dire straits in which numerous businesses find themselves.

Mathu Jagannath, director of logistics consultancy NAU Pte, expressed concern over the stalemate, stressing the need for a swift resolution. "The impasse not only strains the parties involved directly but also significantly impacts supply chains globally," Jagannath said. "I urge the SCA and the shipowner to find a quick resolution to minimize further losses and disruptions."

The cause of the Ever Given's grounding has been a point of contention. The SCA insists the accident resulted from "excessive speed" on part of the vessel. In contrast, the ship’s protection and indemnity (P&I) club has criticized the canal authority’s navigation directives. This disagreement further complicates the ongoing negotiations for compensation.

Another layer of complexity is the declaration of General Average, necessitating all cargo owners to contribute to the salvage costs. However, contributions cannot be processed until the vessel is released, leaving cargo owners in a precarious position.

Despite its current predicament, the value of the Ever Given has risen to $183 million, a $13 million increase since its grounding. This appreciation highlights the ongoing demand and shortage in the containership capacity market, a situation exacerbated by the vessel's inactivity.

Questions also remain over whether Evergreen, the Taiwanese operator that leases the Ever Given, continues to pay for its daily hire while it remains detained. Securing the quick release of the Ever Given is a priority for Evergreen, given the acute shortage and high demand for containership capacity. The company is keen to return the vessel to service, alleviating some pressure on global shipping routes.

The ongoing detention of the Ever Given serves as a stark reminder of the complex interplay between international maritime law, global shipping logistics, and the vulnerabilities of supply chains. As parties work towards a resolution, the world watches, hoping for a swift end to a saga that has disrupted global trade and highlighted the fragility of international shipping lanes. The resolution of this dispute will undoubtedly serve as a precedent for future maritime incidents, emphasizing the need for clearer regulations and more efficient mechanisms for conflict resolution in the global shipping industry.

Vice President Harris Launches Nationwide Call to Action to Improve Maternal Health

In an unprecedented move to combat the growing crisis of maternal mortality and morbidity in the United States, Vice President Kamala Harris has announced a nationwide Call to Action, seeking united efforts from all states and stakeholders to improve maternal health outcomes. Addressing a persistent and alarming issue, the Vice President's announcement comes in alignment with the broader agenda of the Biden-Harris Administration to prioritize maternal health as a critical component of public health policy. This initiative is part of the White House's commitment to reverse the troubling statistics that have placed the U.S. as having the highest maternal mortality rate among affluent nations.

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has projected that, if all states opt to extend Medicaid postpartum coverage, an additional 720,000 individuals could benefit from this crucial support. Currently, the limited Medicaid coverage of just 60 days postpartum fails to adequately support many new mothers, leaving them vulnerable to health complications. Extensive research and recent reports from HHS highlight the positive impact of prolonging this coverage to 12 months, which is a pivotal recommendation in the current Call to Action.

In alignment with these efforts, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) unveiled their proposal for a "Birthing-Friendly" hospital designation. This new initiative aims to set higher standards for care facilities, ensuring they meet criteria that improve maternal health outcomes and provide safer birthing environments. In addition, CMS has issued updated guidance to promote seamless, year-long Medicaid postpartum coverage, designed to stabilize the recovery and well-being of new mothers.

The Biden-Harris Administration underscores maternal health as a significant priority, especially in light of the disproportionately higher rates of maternal mortality among Black women and Native American women. The statistics are sobering, with these groups experiencing maternal mortality rates three times higher than their white counterparts. The Administration's strategy emphasizes closing this gap, ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare, and addressing underlying social determinants that contribute to these disparities.

Marking the first-ever White House Maternal Health Day of Action, the Administration reaffirms its commitment through new initiatives fortified by the Build Back Better Act. This legislation, currently under consideration, proposes an ambitious $3 billion investment into maternal health reform. This transformative effort focuses not only on the enhancement of the healthcare workforce and improvement of data collection but also targets broader societal factors such as substance abuse, access to research, and better coordination of care delivery.

The Biden-Harris Administration is urging states to adopt policies that expand Medicaid coverage for postpartum care to one year, citing the substantial body of evidence supporting this extension. By doing so, it provides a comprehensive window during which new mothers can access healthcare, thereby reducing the risk of life-threatening complications and fostering healthier family dynamics.

A newly released report from HHS provides compelling evidence of the benefits associated with extending Medicaid postpartum coverage to a full year. Such expansion is linked to decreased maternal mortality and improved maternal and infant health outcomes. The findings further underscore the necessity of federal and state collaboration in adopting these policies to safeguard new mothers and their infants.

The maternal health crisis in the United States requires urgent attention, having worsened significantly over the past two decades, notably for Black and Native American women. Vice President Harris, through her legislative efforts with the Maternal CARE Act and the Black Maternal Health Momnibus Act, has long championed the cause of maternal health, advocating for systemic reforms that provide equitable healthcare solutions for all women, regardless of race or socioeconomic status.

The White House continues to call upon healthcare providers, community organizations, and policymakers to act decisively, responding to the Vice President’s Call to Action with measures that ensure safety, support, and dignity for every mother. By fostering an environment of innovation and accountability, the Administration hopes to transform maternal health care into a model of excellence that reflects America's commitment to the wellbeing of its citizens.

This nationwide Call to Action heralds a new chapter in maternal healthcare, one where collaborative commitment can save lives and create healthier communities. As the United States seeks solutions to this critical issue, the Biden-Harris Administration remains steadfast in its mission to pave the way for a future where maternal mortality and morbidity no longer cast a shadow over the nation’s healthcare landscape.

EVER ACE, the World's Largest Container Ship, Navigates the Suez Canal on Maiden Voyage

The world's largest container ship, EVER ACE, successfully completed its maiden voyage through the Suez Canal on August 25, 2022. Built by Samsung Heavy Industries for Evergreen Marine Corporation, this monumental vessel marks a significant milestone in maritime transportation.

The EVER ACE is the first of a series of 12 container ships ordered by Evergreen. With a carrying capacity of 23,992 TEU (Twenty-foot Equivalent Units), it surpasses the HMM Algeciras as the largest container ship in the world. Measuring 400 meters in length, 61.53 meters in width, and weighing approximately 235,000 tons, the EVER ACE is a colossal engineering feat.

The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) provided navigation support to ensure the safe passage of the EVER ACE through the canal. In March 2021, Evergreen-owned Ever Given caused global trade disruptions when it became lodged in the Suez Canal, blocking traffic for six days. The successful transit of the EVER ACE is a testament to the Suez Canal's capacity to accommodate giant container ships.

The EVER ACE embarked on its maiden voyage from the Port of Taipei, Taiwan, and is scheduled to reach Rotterdam, Netherlands, on September 4, 2022. The journey spans over 7,000 nautical miles, making it an impressive feat for the shipping industry.

The EVER ACE's successful transit through the Suez Canal signifies a new era in maritime transportation, with larger container ships increasingly dominating global trade. This trend reflects the growing demand for more efficient and cost-effective shipping solutions.

Evergreen Marine Corporation, the owner of the EVER ACE, is no stranger to record-breaking container ships. In addition to the EVER ACE and the Ever Given, the company also operates the Ever Largest, which previously held the title of the world's largest container ship, before being surpassed by the EVER ACE. The ongoing expansion of Evergreen's fleet underscores its commitment to staying at the forefront of the container shipping industry.

FACT SHEET: President Biden's Global COVID-19 Summit: Ending the Pandemic and Building Back Better

A Call to Action for Global Collaboration

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, President Biden convened the Global COVID-19 Summit: Ending the Pandemic and Building Back Better. This virtual summit brought together heads of state, leaders from international organizations, the private sector, philanthropies, NGOs, and other partners to tackle the ongoing pandemic and build a more resilient future.

The Urgency of Ending the Pandemic

President Biden emphasized the need to accelerate global efforts to end the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in light of emerging variants that threaten progress. He called on world leaders to embrace a set of ambitious global targets across four key themes:

  • Vaccinate the World: Ensuring equitable access to vaccines and increasing vaccination rates globally.
  • Save Lives Now: Addressing the oxygen crisis and ensuring widespread availability of tests, therapeutics, and personal protective equipment (PPE).
  • Build Back Better: Preparing all countries for future pandemics by establishing a sustainable health security financing mechanism and demonstrating political leadership.
  • Calling the World to Account: Aligning around common global targets, tracking progress, and holding each other accountable for fulfilling commitments.

Bold U.S. Commitments

President Biden has consistently prioritized ending the pandemic, launching the National Strategy on COVID-19 Response and Pandemic Preparedness and elevating pandemic preparedness as a top national security priority. The United States has already donated more vaccines than any other country and launched a comprehensive U.S. COVID-19 Global Response and Recovery Framework.

During the summit, President Biden announced several new U.S. commitments to accelerate progress towards the global targets:

  • Vaccinating the World:
    • Donating an Additional Half-Billion Pfizer Vaccines: The U.S. will donate an additional 500 million Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines to low and lower-middle income countries, starting in January 2022. This brings the total U.S. vaccine donations to over 1.1 billion doses, including the 500 million Pfizer doses purchased earlier this year. With this commitment, the U.S. will have donated three doses to the world for every one administered domestically.
    • Shipping Millions More Vaccines: The U.S. has already shipped nearly 160 million doses to 100 countries, donating more than any other nation. Millions more doses are shipped daily, all free of charge and with no strings attached.
  • Saving Lives Now:
    • Addressing the Oxygen Crisis: The U.S. is working with partners to increase oxygen production and distribution in countries facing shortages.
    • Expanding Access to Tests, Therapeutics, and PPE: The U.S. is supporting efforts to make tests, therapeutics, and PPE widely available globally.
  • Building Back Better:
    • Supporting a Sustainable Health Security Financing Mechanism: The U.S. is committed to working with partners to establish a sustainable financing mechanism for global health security.
    • Demonstrating Leadership on Emerging Threats: The U.S. will continue to provide leadership in addressing emerging threats and preparing for future pandemics.

A Collective Effort for a Healthier Future

The Global COVID-19 Summit underscored the need for continued global collaboration to end the pandemic and build a more resilient future. By working together, we can overcome this challenge and ensure a healthier future for all.
