Norsk Hydro's Defiant Stand Against Ransomware: A Case Study in Cyber Resilience

Oslo, Norway – In a bold display of resilience against cyber threats, Norsk Hydro, a prominent Norwegian renewable energy and aluminum manufacturing company, refused to bow to the demands of hackers who launched a crippling ransomware attack on the company in 2019. The incident, which occurred on the same day Hilde Merete Aasheim assumed the role of CEO, serves as a compelling case study in the importance of robust cybersecurity measures and unwavering leadership in the face of adversity.

A Crippling Blow to Norsk Hydro's Digital Infrastructure

The ransomware attack, launched on March 19, 2019, unleashed a wave of disruption across Norsk Hydro's digital infrastructure. Over 3,000 servers and thousands of PCs were locked out, with key areas of the IT network encrypted, effectively paralyzing the company's operations.

"It was a very sophisticated attack," Hilde Merete Aasheim, CEO of Norsk Hydro, recalled in an interview with TIME. "We were completely taken by surprise."

The attack's impact was immediate and severe. Production facilities ground to a halt, communication systems were disrupted, and employees were left scrambling to maintain operations amidst the chaos.

Refusing to Pay the Ransom: A Principled Stand

Despite the severity of the attack and the pressure to restore operations swiftly, Norsk Hydro made a resolute decision: they would not pay the ransom demanded by the hackers.

"We had a very clear policy against paying ransoms," Jo De Vliegher, CIO of Norsk Hydro, explained. "We didn't want to encourage this type of criminal behavior."

This principled stance, while admirable, came with significant challenges. Without a quick fix, Norsk Hydro faced the daunting task of manually restoring its operations, a process that would require weeks of painstaking effort.

A Herculean Effort: Manual Operations and Cybersecurity Collaboration

Undeterred by the magnitude of the task, Norsk Hydro embarked on a herculean effort to manually handle operations. Production lines were kept running through pen-and-paper processes, while IT teams worked tirelessly to decrypt the affected systems.

"It was like going back in time," Aasheim remarked. "But we were determined to keep our operations going, no matter what."

To bolster their efforts, Norsk Hydro enlisted the expertise of cybersecurity experts and forged collaborations with Microsoft and the Norwegian National Cyber Security Centre. This collective effort proved instrumental in accelerating the recovery process.

Counting the Costs: Financial Losses and Lessons Learned

The ransomware attack exacted a heavy toll on Norsk Hydro's operations. The company incurred significant financial losses, estimated to be around $70 million. Production disruptions, reputational damage, and the costs associated with recovery efforts all contributed to this substantial setback.

However, the incident also served as a catalyst for change. Norsk Hydro underwent a comprehensive reevaluation of its cybersecurity measures, prioritizing investments in preventive technologies and employee training.

"We learned a lot from this attack," Aasheim reflected. "We've made significant improvements to our cybersecurity posture, and we're now better prepared to face future threats."

A Cautionary Tale: The Perils of Ransom Payments

Norsk Hydro's experience aligns with the advice of cybersecurity experts who strongly discourage organizations from paying ransoms to hackers.

"Paying ransoms only fuels the criminal economy and encourages further attacks," warned Eric Goldstein, an official at the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). "Organizations should focus on prevention and response strategies to mitigate the impact of ransomware attacks."

A Legacy of Resilience: Norsk Hydro's Triumph Over Adversity

Norsk Hydro's unwavering stance against paying ransoms and its successful recovery from the ransomware attack stand as a testament to the company's resilience and commitment to cybersecurity. Under the leadership of Hilde Merete Aasheim and Jo De Vliegher, Norsk Hydro emerged from this crisis stronger and more determined to safeguard its operations against future cyber threats.

Their story serves as an inspiration to organizations worldwide, demonstrating the importance of robust cybersecurity measures, unwavering leadership, and a collective commitment to combating cybercrime.

Impeachment After Office: Lessons from History and the Case of William Blount

The debate surrounding the impeachment of federal officials after their terms end has gained renewed attention in light of the discussions surrounding former President Donald Trump. Historical precedents, including the impeachment of U.S. Senator William Blount of Tennessee, provide insight into the complexities and implications of such actions.

William Blount was a U.S. senator who became the first-ever federal official impeached by the House and tried by the Senate. His case arose after he was expelled from the Senate in 1797, with charges revolving around a plan to attack Spanish territories to benefit Great Britain. This early instance of impeachment serves as a critical reference point in contemporary discussions around Trump’s potential trial post-presidency.

“Historically, the impeachment process has always been about holding officials accountable, regardless of their current status,” stated Jonathan Turley, a law professor at George Washington University. “Blount’s case demonstrates that impeachment was not simply a tool for removing sitting officials— it has legal merit even after someone has left office.”

Blount was initially impeached by the House, making him the first senator to face such a consequence, after which he was expelled from the Senate. His offenses, deemed severe at the time, included plotting with a foreign power. Interestingly, the Senate later dismissed his case on jurisdictional grounds, and Blount did not attend his trial, another crucial detail in understanding the complexities of impeachment.

As discussions about Trump’s impeachment linger, legal experts like Stewart Harris emphasize the flexibility the Senate holds in these matters. “The Senate has the discretion to conduct an impeachment trial whenever it chooses,” Harris, a constitutional law professor and board member of the Blount Mansion in Knoxville, said. This flexibility may alter how gatherings around impeachment potential unfold in the future.

Chris’s viewpoint highlights that impeached officials may still engage in public service after an impeachment and trial. In fact, Blount’s political career continued in Tennessee, indicating that an impeachment does not necessarily signal the end of a political figure's journey in public office. “Impeachment is arguably about accountability, but it does not terminate the political careers of some individuals,” Harris continued.

Dr. Gregory Ablavsky, a history professor at Stanford University, noted that historical instances should frame the current political landscape. “Looking back to Blount and others, we see that impeachment acts as a significant process for setting standards of conduct rather than simply as a punitive measure.”

Despite the theoretical foundations suggesting that Trump could lose political influence post-impeachment, Blount’s experience tells a different story. Obtaining substantial support in Tennessee politics suggests that public opinion and political reappointment can recover from such judicial challenges.

Moreover, the case of Secretary of War William Belknap also provides precedent. Impeached in 1876 after resigning amidst bribery allegations, Belknap's case further underscores that officials can face impeachment after they have vacated their offices.

Turley posited, “It’s crucial to recognize that the impeachment framework was designed to enforce checks on power, not to extinguish the political ambition of every official who missteps.” The lesson from history is clear; even when impeached, individuals can return to political life, often depending on their constituent support.

Legal experts remind us that the mere act of impeachment does not dictate a politician's fate. Blount's ultimate re-entry into Tennessee politics reveals a narrative where impeachment brought him neither disgrace nor obscurity.

Additionally, amid claims from supporters of Trump that impeachment could rob him of future political opportunities, Blount’s enduring political influence counters this argument. “Many impeached officials continue to engage politically and, in fact, thrive afterward,” Harris noted.

Historically, impeachments are less about the removal from power and more about the accountability mechanism they represent. For instance, after the dismissal of Blount's impeachment case, he remained an influential figure, serving as a member of the Tennessee House of Representatives for several terms.

The Blount case, along with others throughout history, indicates that impeachment has a dual role— remedying accountability violations while giving space for continued political engagement.

As conversations around Trump's impeachment trial evolve, the historical precedents serve as reminders that the implications of such political actions can be unpredictable and can yield unforeseen opportunities. History demonstrates that an impeachment does not merely erase a political narrative; sometimes, it becomes a stepping stone.

In reflecting on the nature of impeachment, one can’t overlook its potency in shaping not just political careers, but American governance itself. The story of William Blount and those who followed him illustrates that the complexities of impeachment will continue to unfold, affecting not only the individuals in question but the political landscape at large.

Facebook Cracks Down on Israeli ‘Surveillance for Hire’ Operations

Leaders of the Israeli cyber intelligence firm Cognyte this February celebrated their first day of trading on Nasdaq by ringing the stock exchange’s opening bell. In remarks beamed across a giant screen in New York’s Times Square, CEO Elad Sharon celebrated his company’s success, including nearly half a billion dollars in annual revenues, 2,000 employees around the world, and 1,000 clients in 100 countries — including the U.S. Department of Justice. Sharon also touted Cognyte’s virtue, claiming it provided governments and businesses the tools they need to fight terrorism and stop crime. “Our analytics software empowers our customers to save lives,” Sharon said.

But on Thursday, banned Cognyte from its platform as it released the results of a six-month investigation by the social media giant’s security researchers. According to the report, Cognyte’s customers have targeted journalists and politicians around the world. Some of those clients were located in countries with dubious records on human rights such as Colombia, Kenya, Mexico, Thailand, and Indonesia. Also Thursday, Facebook took down about 100 Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to Cognyte.

Beyond Cognyte, the Facebook report took aim at five other firms and one unnamed Chinese entity that are part of what social media giant calls the “surveillance for hire” industry. Israel, where four of the six named companies were founded, appears to be a hub of the global industry.

According to Facebook, the firms abuse social media platforms to collect intelligence, including by manipulating people into revealing information and compromising their devices. Targets included journalists, dissidents, critics of authoritarian regimes, families of opposition members, human rights activists, celebrities, and even ordinary people. In total, the company says it took down approximately 1,500 accounts that it says were part of surveillance for hire operations. The social media company also notified about 50,000 people in 100 countries that their Facebook and Instagram accounts were targets of malicious activities by the seven entities identified in the report released Thursday.

Editor’s picks

Facebook outlined a three-step process that explained how the surveillance-for-hire industry operates. In the reconnaissance phase, the companies typically scrape information about a target from across the Internet, often using fake accounts to view social media profiles, friends, and likes. Next, the fake accounts built up trust by, for example, feigning a shared interest on a Facebook group and connecting with the target in seemingly innocuous ways. Some companies stopped there, but others abused this trust to hack the target. The most sophisticated actors may send veiled hacking tools that give them instant access to all the personal information stored on a cellphone or computer.

“Companies engage in this kind of thing because they think there’s a viable business model behind it,” Nathaniel Gleicher, Facebook’s head of security policy, told Rolling Stone. “A key part of our goal is demonstrating that, at least on our platforms, there isn’t.”

In addition to Cognyte, Facebook’s investigation names Cobwebs Technologies, Black Cube, and Bluehawk CI–all based in Israel. Also named in the report were BellTroX, a “hacking-for-hire” firm based in India, and Cytrox, a North Macdeonian company. A Chinese entity was surveilling minority groups in China’s Xingjian region, home to the country’s mostly Muslim Uighur minority, but Facebook was unable to identify the group. The Chinese entity made few mistakes and revealed little about itself. In one case, the Chinese entity’s online surveillance was paired with facial-recognition software which could allow for real-word tracking of a targets’ movements.

Broadly, the report paints a picture of companies that have developed a powerful set of tools and techniques for extracting information from individuals, including sensitive data they wouldn’t otherwise be inclined to hand over. The companies often emphasize that they are trying to stop would-be criminals or terrorists, but the Facebook report says they are also be used by bad actors — including repressive regimes — to target vulnerable people and marginalize dissent.

Cobwebs Technologies, another Israeli surveillance-for-hire firm singled out by Facebook, has a growing U.S. business. Customers include the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Internal Revenue Service, according to a government spending database, as well as the Hartford, Connecticut police department. The company has also reportedly been making inroads into the U.S. intelligence community. In addition to work related to law enforcement activities, Facebook found Cobwebs often targeted activists, opposition politicians, and government officials in Hong Kong and Mexico.

Related Stories

A separate investigation by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz found Cognyte targeted members of the LGBTQ community in Indonesia and Azerbaijan, where an employee said he was asked how to use Facebook to check someone’s sexual inclinations.

Perhaps the best-known company in the Facebook report is Black Cube, the Israeli private intelligence firm that lawyers for movie producer Harvey Weinstein hired to suppress news stories exposing his predatory behavior toward women. Facebook said it was banning 300 Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to employees of Black Cube who used them to pose as graduate students, NGO and human rights workers, and film and TV producers. Facebook found a wide range of Black Cube customers — private individuals, businesses, and law firms around the world that it declined to name. Targets included Palestinian activists and real estate development and media in Russia.

In a statement, Black Cube said it does not undertake any phishing or hacking and does not operate in the cyber world. A representative said the company works with the world’s leading law firms on cases involving bribery, corruption, and stolen assets. “Black Cube obtains legal advice in every jurisdiction in which we operate in order to ensure that all our agents’ activities are fully compliant with local law,” the company said.

The other companies named in the Facebook report were not immediately available for comment.

Another company banned by Facebook, Cytrox, was the subject of a separate but related report issued Thursday by the Canadian research group, Citizen Lab. Security researchers at Citizen Lab concluded with a high degree of confidence that Cytrox was behind a new, previously-unknown form of cellphone spyware called Predator.

Predator can quietly hoover up emails, texts, and photos and turn a cellphone into a personal monitoring device by remotely turning on a user’s microphone and record any call.

It was discovered on the iPhone of one of Egypt’s most prominent politicians in exile, Ayman Nour, a one-time presidential candidate who was jailed for years for daring to challenge the leadership’s stranglehold on power. Not only was Nour’s fully up-to-date and patched iPhone infected with Predator, but it had also been simultaneously infected with Pegasus, an even more sophisticated phone spyware made by the Israeli firm NSO Group. “It’s another reminder how dangerous the mercenary spyware industry is,” Citizen Lab’s Bill Marczak, who discovered Predator earlier this year, tells Rolling Stone.

Pegasus and Predator were unrelated, Citizen Lab found, and were being operated by two different nation-state clients. The Egyptian government was likely behind the Predator attack on Nour’s iPhone, in part because the spyware had been inserted by a message sent from an Egyptian number on WhatsApp. Egypt, however, is not a client of Pegasus, and it’s not clear who was behind that exploit, Marczak says.

Security investigators often struggle to pinpoint who is financing and directing the hacking and surveillance, but they have an easier time exposing the mercenaries doing the work. That trail frequently leads to Israel, where four of the six named companies were based. Cytrox, based in North Macedonia, was acquired by a retired Israeli colonel, Tal Dillian. The iPhone payload inside Cytrox’s Predator was referred to as “Nahum,” a minor prophet in the Hebrew Bible.

Israel is also home to NSO Group, the maker of Pegasus phone spyware, one of the most aggressive and sophisticated products on the open market. Pegasus has been so misused by its customers like Saudi Arabia and Mexico that NSO has become the target of widespread global opprobrium and is reportedly considering selling off its Pegasus spyware unit. Facebook was one of the first big tech firms to take action against NSO. It sued NSO in 2019 for using its WhatsApp servers to infect 1,400 phones belonging to attorneys, journalists, human rights activists, political dissidents, diplomats, and other senior foreign government officials. Apple sued NSO last month.

Facebook’s bans on what it called “security mercenaries” come as the social media giant is still dealing with the fallout from its own past failures to protect its users’ privacy. The company was fined a record $5 billion in 2019 by the Federal Trade Commission for deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their personal data.

Josephine Wolff, a professor of cybertechnology at Tufts University in Boston, acknowledged that Facebook has been entangled in privacy-related controversies, but she said the harms caused by the surveillance-for-hire firms were of a different order of magnitude. “To my mind, the harm that Facebook has done and the mistakes they have made have not constituted anything close to the same kind of threats to life and liberty that NSO Group or other spyware companies have enabled by helping authoritarian governments conduct surveillance on journalists, activists and human rights advocates,” Wolff said.

While other countries carefully restrict exports of cyber exploits, the Israeli government has allowed its booming tech sector to sell offensive technologies to repressive regimes. Part of the reason is that selling the technology gives Israel insight into other countries’ security needs and capabilities. “My take on it is that the Israeli government says, ‘They’re going to get it anyway, so it might as well be us,’” says Ian Amit, an Israeli security executive.

Israel also views sales of hacking tools as a way of fostering relations with some of its neighbors. The Israeli government encouraged NSO Group to continue working with Saudi Arabia even after the international condemnation that followed the brutal murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, The New York Times reported. Finally, there’s also a financial incentive for companies to sell to repressive regimes: It’s good for business. “The shadier countries pay more because they are unable to develop these tools themselves,” Amit said.

Israel’s booming tech sector can draw from a deep pool of homegrown talent versed in intelligence and cyberweapons. The largest unit in the Israel Defense Forces or IDF is Unit 8200, the equivalent of the U.S. National Security Agency. All Israelis serve in the military, and experience in “special IDF units” becomes a selling point later on in business, as it did for the founders of Cobwebs Technologies. Bluehawk CI’s founder, Guy Kleizman, was a senior IDF intelligence officer whose online bio claims he played a role in the 2007 operation that destroyed a nuclear reactor in Syria. Black Cube is known to employ former officers of Mossad, Israel’s intelligence service.

“Mercenary surveillance companies are casting a cloud over Israel’s vibrant tech and cybersecurity sector in the eyes of the world right now,” said Citizen Lab’s John Scott-Railton. “Imagine being a legitimate Israeli cybersecurity company and having to deal with this damage when you talk to potential customers or investors?”

Pressure has been mounting on Israel to close Pandora’s box and rein in its surveillance industry. In surprise move, the Biden administration last month blacklisted NSO Group for facilitating “transnational repression.” At a democracy summit hosted earlier this month by President Biden, the governments of the United States, Australia, Denmark, and Norway, joined by others, pledged to create nonbinding guidelines to prevent the spread of technologies used to enable human rights abuses. On Tuesday, a group of Democratic congressmen, including Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Adam Schiff, signed a letter calling on the Treasury Department to sanction NSO Group.

Facebook said part of its goal was to drive the conversation to cover the broader surveillance industry. Exploits like NSO’s Pegasus command attention but they are built upon the earlier, more mundane, but still critical work of reconnaissance and engagement. “If we as a society are going to put pressure on this industry, we’ve got to open the aperture to cover the whole surveillance attack chain,” said Gleicher.

Colin Powell: A Legacy of Service and Leadership

Colin Powell, the first Black U.S. Secretary of State and a two-time Presidential Medal of Freedom recipient, passed away on October 18, 2021, at the age of 84 due to complications from COVID-19. His net worth at the time of his death was estimated at $60 million.

Powell's distinguished career spanned decades of dedicated service. He served as National Security Advisor in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff during the Gulf War. He retired from the Army as a four-star general in 1993.

Beyond his military and political roles, Powell was a renowned author and sought-after public speaker. His autobiography, "My American Journey," earned him a $6 million advance in 1995. He also commanded significant fees for speaking engagements, reportedly earning as much as $100,000 per appearance.

Powell's early career began with a White House Fellowship under President Richard Nixon in 1972. His military service continued under various presidents, culminating in his retirement as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff under President George W. Bush.

"He was a great public servant, starting with his time as a soldier during Vietnam," President Bush said in a statement. "He was such a favorite of presidents that he earned the Presidential Medal of Freedom — twice."

Following his retirement, Powell remained active in both the business and philanthropic spheres. He served as a strategic partner for the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins and held board positions with organizations like Revolution Health.

In 1997, Powell founded America's Promise Alliance, a non-profit dedicated to improving the lives of young people. He also established the Colin L. Powell Center for Leadership and Service at the City College of New York, aiming to cultivate leaders from underrepresented groups while serving the community.

Congressman Jamaal Bowman, representing New York's 16th Congressional District, expressed the profound impact Powell had on him via Twitter: "He was a giant who dedicated his life to service and leadership. His legacy will continue to inspire generations to come."

Colin Powell's life and career represent an exemplary dedication to service and leadership. His legacy will undoubtedly continue to inspire future generations.

The Unintended Consequences of Banning Trump from Social Media

In the wake of the violent breach of the Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. by a mob incited by President Donald Trump, social media giants Facebook and Twitter took a drastic step by banning the president from their platforms. Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg even went a step further by extending Trump's ban at least until January 20, post his term's end. These unprecedented bans were a direct response to Trump's relentless promotion of baseless claims about election fraud and the theft of the election, which he continued to propagate on social media and during a rally.

Gianluca Stringhini, an Assistant Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Boston University, supports the ban on Trump's accounts but also warns of potential unforeseen consequences. In his research, Stringhini found that bans on platforms like Reddit resulted in a reduction in posting activity but also led to increased toxicity and radicalization among migrated users. Online communities have a significant role in spreading conspiracy theories and disinformation, often transitioning from fringe platforms to mainstream social media.

Stringhini believes that while Trump's ban may temporarily reduce the spread of conspiracy theories, it may also have the unintended effect of making his supporters feel censored and further disenfranchised. The president's amplification of conspiracies from polarized online communities has played a significant role in disseminating false information and sowing distrust in democratic institutions.

Research on banned online communities has shown a nuanced effect of platform moderation – while fewer users may be exposed to toxic content, those who are may become more extreme in their beliefs. Stringhini cautions that Trump's ban from mainstream social media may drive him and his supporters towards alternative platforms where they can freely spread misinformation without oversight.

If Trump does transition to an alternative platform, Stringhini predicts that many of his supporters will likely follow him, creating an echo chamber where conspiracy theories can flourish unchecked. The challenge then becomes how to combat misinformation and radicalization in these alternative spaces without outright bans that could further fragment an already polarized society.

As social media companies grapple with how to balance free speech with the responsibility to combat misinformation, Stringhini's research highlights the complex nature of platform moderation. While the ban on Trump's accounts may seem like a straightforward solution to curbing the spread of falsehoods, the unintended consequences on his supporters and the broader online ecosystem cannot be overlooked. Balancing the need for accountability with the protection of democratic values remains a pressing challenge in the digital age.

What is ISIS-K? The Group Responsible for the Kabul Airport Attack and Rival of the Taliban

On August 26, 2021, a bombing and shooting outside Kabul's Hamid Karzai International Airport killed 13 U.S. service members and over 150 Afghan civilians. The attack was claimed by the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISIS-K), a regional affiliate of the Islamic State and a significant threat in the region.

This event occurred just one day before the U.S. withdrawal deadline from Afghanistan, marking the end of a 20-year war. The chaotic evacuation of Americans and Afghan refugees was partly spurred by intelligence suggesting planned attacks on U.S. troops by ISIS-K.

Understanding ISIS-K:

  • Branch of Islamic State: ISIS-K is officially recognized by the Islamic State leadership, making it a branch of the extremist group that attempted to establish a caliphate in parts of Iraq and Syria before being defeated by U.S.-led forces.

  • Emergence and Goals: The group emerged in 2014 and seeks to establish a caliphate in the historical region of Khorasan, encompassing parts of Afghanistan, Pakistan, Iran, and Central Asia.

  • Composition: ISIS-K is comprised of former members of the Pakistani Taliban, the Afghan Taliban, the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan, and other militant and terrorist groups.

Rivalry with the Taliban:

Despite both groups opposing the U.S. presence in Afghanistan, ISIS-K is considered an enemy of the Taliban. ISIS-K holds even more extreme views on women and ethnic minorities than the Taliban, leading to a split within the groups.

This rivalry was evident in several attacks:

  • May 2021: A bombing at a girls' school attended by Hazara students killed over 85 children.

  • June 2021: Masked gunmen, believed to be ISIS-K members, killed 10 Hazara mine-clearers in Baghlan province.

  • August 2021: The Kabul airport attack, targeting U.S. troops and Afghan civilians.

The Taliban condemned the Kabul airport attack and denied involvement in the Baghlan attack. Experts believe this rivalry makes it unlikely for the Taliban to offer safe haven to ISIS-K members in Afghanistan.

Conclusion:

ISIS-K remains a significant threat in the region. Their extreme ideology and violent tactics pose a danger to civilians and stability in Afghanistan and neighboring countries. Understanding the group's origins, goals, and rivalry with the Taliban is crucial for assessing the evolving security landscape in the region.

Kamala Harris Sworn In As Vice President

Vice President-elect Kamala Harris and husband Doug Emhoff arrive to the inauguration on the West Front of the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday.

Kamala Harris has been sworn in as vice president of the United States, becoming the first woman, first Black person and first Asian American to hold the office. She is also the first graduate of a historically Black college and the first member of a Black sorority to do so.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor administered the oath. Sotomayor, the first woman of color to serve on the Supreme Court, previously administered the vice presidential oath to Biden in 2013.

Harris used two Bibles in the ceremony. The first belonged to Regina Shelton, a family friend whom Harris viewed as a surrogate mother. Harris has used this Bible before, when she took the oath of office as both California attorney general and U.S. senator. The second Bible was previously owned by the late Justice Thurgood Marshall, the first Black member of the Supreme Court and Harris’ lifelong political role model.

In a recent interview with NPR’s Scott Detrow, Harris reflected on the moment that she would take the oath of office as vice president. “I will be thinking about my mother, who’s looking down from heaven. I will be thinking of all the people who are counting on us to lead,” she said.

Harris often quotes her mother, Shyamala Gopalan Harris, in speeches. A popular refrain she attributes to her mother: “You may be the first to do many things, but make sure you are not the last.”

At the start of the ceremony, Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar said of Harris, “When she takes the oath of office, little girls and boys across the world will know that anything and everything is possible. And in the end, that is America.”

The vice president’s oath is slightly different than the presidential oath, matching the oath taken by members of Congress:

“I , _________, do solemnly swear [or affirm] that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion; and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter: So help me God.”

Storm Aftermath: Texas Winter Crisis Exposes Systemic Inequalities

AUSTIN -- – Maria Benitez and her family huddled together in their darkened Austin home, the cold winter air seeping through the walls. With no power or water for several days during Texas's recent winter storm, the already struggling family faced devastating financial hardships. “We had no choice but to throw out all the food in the fridge. It’s just not a situation anyone should have to go through, especially not in this country,” Benitez lamented.

The severe winter storm that swept across Texas in February had a far-reaching impact; however, it disproportionately affected Black and Latino communities. The stress of the storm was compounded by the existing economic and social disparities these communities often face. “This storm highlighted the vulnerabilities that have long been present in the system,” said Chauncia Willis, Chief Executive of the Institute for Diversity and Inclusion in Emergency Management.

Experts assert that the path to recovery will be challenging for these vulnerable communities due to prolonged power outages and burst pipes that have damaged homes and infrastructure. João Paulo Connolly, Director of Housing and Community Development at the Austin Justice Coalition, emphasized this point, noting that “the recovery process is not going to be equitable unless we actively work towards it.”

As the storm subsided, the power outages in Texas diminished significantly, from a staggering four million to about 139,000. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is now providing emergency relief to affected areas, but questions remain about the efficacy and reach of these programs. “The recovery from such disasters is often slow, and those who need help the most are frequently left behind,” explained Varun Rai, Director of the University of Texas-Austin's Energy Institute.

Indeed, the aftermath of the storm has revealed stark inequalities in disaster relief and utility management. In Houston, the city faced a severe water crisis, with County Commissioner Rodney Ellis advocating for "an equitable disaster response that ensures all communities, especially marginalized ones, are prioritized."

Ellis's concerns underscore a broader pattern observed throughout the crisis: utility companies prioritized restoring power to critical services in affluent neighborhoods, inadvertently neglecting lower-income families who were left more vulnerable. “It is unacceptable that in times of crisis, resources are allocated based on zip codes rather than need,” noted Junia Howell, an Assistant Professor at the University of Pittsburgh.

As some Texas residents begin to recover from the physical impacts of the storm, many face a new wave of financial strain. The demand for electricity surged during the storm, leading to significant damages to the water infrastructure. Utility companies are now warning consumers to brace for higher bills as they attempt to recover the costs associated with the unprecedented utility demands during the disaster.

The call for equitable disaster relief is just beginning, with many community organizations stepping in to fill the gaps left by government aid. The Austin Justice Coalition reported that they have assisted over 40 families, primarily from Black and Latino backgrounds, by providing much-needed food donations during the crisis. “Our community often comes together in times of need. It shows the resilience and solidarity that exists within us,” Connolly remarked.

At the same time, the federal response to disaster assistance has come under scrutiny following the storm. Studies show that federal aid is often distributed unevenly, with white communities receiving a disproportionate amount of reinvestment post-disaster. This disparity only serves to deepen the chasm of inequality, leaving marginalized communities to fend for themselves when they need help the most.

Since the winter storm, conversations around systemic bias and racism have moved center stage in discussions about disaster management. Experts like Chauncia Willis have emphasized that addressing these ingrained biases is crucial in formulating a response that ensures all communities receive fair treatment. “Acknowledging that these disparities exist and actively working against them is the first step towards a better system,” she stated.

As families like the Benitez clan work to rebuild their lives, they are left to grapple with an uncertain future. “It’s frustrating to think about the money we’ll need to spend just to get back to where we were; it feels like we’re being punished for something we couldn’t control,” Benitez shared, reflecting on the challenges faced by those living on the edge of economic stability.

In the wake of the storms, many advocacy groups are pushing for better infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and equitable policies to ensure that those most affected are given priority in future aid discussions. Rai believes that the lessons learned from this crisis must propel policy changes. “If there is one silver lining to this disaster, it’s the opportunity to rethink how we approach energy and water management across the state,” he said.

Despite these efforts, the road to recovery remains fraught with difficulties. “There needs to be intentionality in how we rebuild,” Howell stated, pointing to the need for more inclusive approaches in disaster planning that consider the specific needs of marginalized communities.

As Texas faces the long-term effects of the winter storm, residents brace themselves for the long recovery. “Surviving this storm was just the beginning; now we have to figure out how we’re going to thrive,” Benitez concluded, echoing the sentiments of many who find themselves navigating the complexities of a system that has, for too long, overlooked the vulnerable.

Sean Payton's Optimism Hints at Jameis Winston's Bright Future as New Orleans Saints' Starting Quarterback

As the NFL offseason unfolds, all eyes will be on Brees and his decision regarding his football future. If Brees decides to retire, Winston's opportunity to lead the Saints will come into sharp focus.

With Sean Payton's endorsement and the potential to learn from one of the all-time greats in Drew Brees, Jameis Winston is poised to make the most of his opportunity and potentially revitalize his career in New Orleans.

Colonial Pipeline Cyberattack Halts Operations, Efforts Underway for Restoration

Colonial Pipeline, a critical fuel delivery system spanning 5,500 miles from the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast, has been halted due to a cyberattack that struck on May 7. As of May 10, the main lines remain non-operational, exacerbating concerns over fuel transportation in the southeastern United States amidst rising demand. While the company has made progress with smaller lines that are currently functioning, the impact of this major disruption has already begun to ripple through the economy, highlighting the essential role of the pipeline in transporting key fuels such as gasoline, diesel, heating oil, and jet fuel.

In an effort to mitigate the effects of the outage, Colonial Pipeline has announced plans to restore service by the end of the week. However, officials caution that even once service resumes, pipeline flow may be slow, leading some areas to rely on existing inventories for days as they await the return to normalcy. This situation is particularly critical for the Southeast, where fuel supplies are already strained.

To ensure that consumers have access to fuel during this challenging time, the Southeast will depend on inventory levels and alternative sources such as the 720,000 barrels per day Products (SE) Pipeline. Additionally, markets along the Atlantic Coast will have the option to import fuel and utilize marine shipments to supplement supplies, while the Central Atlantic and Northeast regions are looking towards importing fuel from Europe and Canada or tapping into in-region refineries. These strategies may help alleviate some pressure on regional fuel supplies as Colonial Pipeline works diligently to restore its main operations.

In response to the crisis, regulatory waivers have been issued to ease trucking restrictions for petroleum product deliveries across 17 states and the District of Columbia. This regulatory relief is expected to expedite fuel distribution and help stabilize supplies throughout the affected regions. As the situation unfolds, authorities are closely monitoring developments while reinforcing the need for robust cybersecurity measures in critical infrastructure sectors.

After 'Rust' Tragedy, Hollywood Reevaluates Its Relationship with Guns on Set

The 1903 silent film 'The Great Train Robbery' is often credited with kickstarting Hollywood's love affair with guns on screen, but the recent accidental shooting on the set of 'Rust' that resulted in the death of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins has sparked a heated debate about the use of firearms in film production. As the industry mourns the loss, key figures are calling for change, with some advocating for the outright elimination of live fire and a shift towards technological alternatives.

Rachel Morrison, the acclaimed cinematographer known for her work on 'Black Panther,' has been vocal about her stance. "We need to prioritize safety on set, and that means getting rid of live weapons," she says. "With the technology available today, there's no reason we can't achieve the same level of realism without the risk."

In the aftermath of the 'Rust' tragedy, some productions have already started adopting safer practices. 'The Rookie,' an ABC police drama, has decided to eliminate the use of live weapons, according to showrunner Alexi Hawley. "Our top priority is the safety of our cast and crew, and this decision reflects that commitment," Hawley explains.

California State Senator Dave Cortese has gone a step further, announcing plans to introduce legislation that would ban live ammunition and firearms on movie and theatrical production sets. "We need to ensure that what happened on the set of 'Rust' never happens again," Cortese says.

The International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE), currently in contract negotiations with studios, is also pushing for improved safety measures. This renewed focus on safety follows a series of high-profile incidents that have put the spotlight on working conditions in the industry.

While many support the ban on live ammunition, some argue that guns capable of firing blanks should still have a place on sets if strict safety protocols are followed. Dan Frenkel, a cinematographer and armorer, says, "It's about competence and adherence to established safety guidelines, not about banning all guns outright."

Armorer and weapons master Gary Truers, who worked on 'Jurassic World,' echoes this sentiment, emphasizing the importance of experienced professionals handling weapons. "Proper training and responsible use are key," he asserts. "Blank-firing guns have been used safely in the industry for decades."

However, proponents of using computer-generated imagery (CGI) for gun effects, like airsoft guns and digital enhancements, contend that it not only enhances safety but also aligns with contemporary audience expectations. Joe Henderson, co-showrunner of 'Lucifer,' notes, "As technology advances, it allows us to create more realistic and immersive experiences without compromising safety."

Vice President Harris Announces $1.5 Billion Investment to Strengthen and Diversify the U.S. Health Care Workforce

Washington, D.C. – Vice President Kamala Harris today announced a significant $1.5 billion investment to bolster and diversify the nation's health care workforce. This investment, made possible through the American Rescue Plan, underscores the Biden-Harris Administration's commitment to addressing health care disparities and ensuring equitable access to quality care for all Americans.

"A strong and diverse health care workforce is essential to ensuring the well-being of our nation," said Vice President Harris. "This $1.5 billion investment will help us grow and diversify the health care workforce, so that all Americans have access to the high-quality care they deserve, no matter their background or where they live."

The funding will be distributed across several critical programs, including the National Health Service Corps (NHSC), Nurse Corps, and Substance Use Disorder Treatment and Recovery programs. These programs provide financial support and educational opportunities to individuals pursuing careers in primary care, mental health, and substance use disorder treatment.

Thanks to the American Rescue Plan, this initiative is expected to support over 22,700 health care providers, including doctors, nurses, dentists, and mental health professionals. These providers will serve in underserved communities across the country, providing care to more than 23.6 million patients.

In addition to addressing immediate workforce needs, the investment aims to tackle the root causes of racial and ethnic disparities in health care professions and outcomes. By increasing the diversity of the health care workforce, the initiative seeks to improve cultural competency, reduce implicit bias, and enhance patient-provider communication.

Recognizing the projected shortage of up to 60,000 primary care doctors, dentists, and psychiatrists over the next decade, the federal government plans to award an additional $330 million in funding for primary care education. This funding will support the training of new primary care providers and help ensure that communities have access to the essential care they need.

The investments announced today align with the recommendations of the Presidential COVID-19 Health Equity Task Force, which highlighted the urgent need to address health disparities exacerbated by the pandemic. As part of the Biden-Harris Administration's broader efforts to center equity in the COVID-19 response, $785 million was previously announced for equity-focused programs and initiatives.

"This investment is a critical step towards building a more equitable and resilient health care system," said Vice President Harris. "By investing in our health care workforce, we are investing in the health and well-being of all Americans."

The Biden-Harris Administration remains committed to addressing health disparities and ensuring that all Americans have access to quality, affordable health care. This $1.5 billion investment represents a significant step towards achieving these goals and building a healthier future for the nation.

Kamala Harris Still Living Out of Suitcases at Blair House Amidst Prolonged Renovations

Chris Cuomo's Return to CNN Amid Ethical Concerns: Blurred Lines and Calls for Accountability

CNN – Vice President Kamala Harris has taken on a central role in the Biden administration's efforts to address the root causes of migration from Central America, rather than directly managing the United States' southern border. President Joe Biden has tasked Harris with leading diplomatic efforts with Mexico and the Northern Triangle countries – Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador – in an attempt to stem the flow of migrants to the US.

Harris and her team are acutely aware of the potential political pitfalls associated with being linked to the contentious border situation. They fear that any missteps could damage her reputation and the administration's agenda. However, critics, particularly from the Republican Party and some media outlets, have portrayed Harris' role as a direct border assignment, a characterization that her team has sought to refute.

In anticipation of her upcoming trip to Guatemala and Mexico, Harris is preparing to delve into the complex issues driving Central Americans to leave their homes in search of a better life in the US. A key aspect of her mission is to secure commitments from private companies to invest in the Northern Triangle countries, fostering economic growth and stability as a means to reduce migration.

Administration officials and migration experts emphasize that addressing the root causes of migration cannot be decoupled from the situation at the US-Mexico border. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and the resulting economic downturn have exacerbated the challenges faced by many in Latin America, contributing to a surge in migration to the United States.

As a prominent figure within the Democratic Party, Harris' performance in this role is being closely watched, particularly in the context of the 2024 presidential race. Recognizing the significance of her assignment, the Vice President has been actively engaging with immigration advocates and regional experts to gather diverse perspectives and develop a comprehensive approach to tackling the migration crisis.

In recent meetings, Harris has sought to understand the economic, social, and political factors that push people to leave their homes, including poverty, violence, corruption, and natural disasters. She has also emphasized the importance of addressing climate change, which has led to crop failures and environmental displacement in the region.

To bolster her diplomatic efforts, Harris has reached out to leaders in the private sector, encouraging them to invest in the Northern Triangle countries and create job opportunities. By fostering economic development, the administration hopes to provide alternatives for individuals and families who might otherwise be compelled to migrate.

In addition to economic incentives, Harris is also expected to discuss governance and anti-corruption measures during her visits to Guatemala and Mexico. Strengthening democratic institutions and fighting corruption are seen as crucial in creating a more stable environment that can retain its citizens.

The Vice President's team acknowledges that solving the migration issue will not happen overnight and will require sustained commitment from the US and its regional partners. They argue that investing in Central America is not only a humanitarian endeavor but also a strategic investment in regional stability and US national security.

Critics, however, argue that the Biden administration should focus more on securing the US border and enforcing existing immigration laws. They contend that addressing the root causes of migration should not come at the expense of border security.

As Harris embarks on her diplomatic journey, she faces the challenge of balancing short-term crisis management with long-term solutions. Her ability to navigate this complex issue will likely have a significant impact on her political future and the fate of the Biden administration's immigration policy.

Impeachment and the First Amendment: Why Trump's Speech Doesn't Protect Him

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long been a champion of free speech rights, and in the current impeachment proceedings against President Trump, the organization has taken a clear stance: impeachment does not conflict with the First Amendment. In a unanimous resolution, the ACLU board called for Trump's impeachment, citing his efforts to subvert the 2020 election results as part of a pattern of behavior that justifies his removal from office.

Some have argued that impeachment proceedings against Trump would violate his First Amendment rights, but the ACLU disagrees. Impeachment is a political remedy, not a criminal proceeding, aimed at removing an executive official for abuse of office. The First Amendment does not protect public employees, including the president, from sanctions related to speech in their official capacity. In fact, the Supreme Court has established that public employees do not have a First Amendment right to engage in political speech while on the job.

The ACLU's support for impeachment is not about silencing Trump's speech, but about holding him accountable for his actions. Trump's Jan. 6 speech, in which he urged his supporters to "fight like hell" against the election results, is part of a pattern of behavior that has undermined the democratic process and threatened the rule of law. Impeachment is a way to ensure that public officials are held accountable for such actions, regardless of their political popularity.

The ACLU has a long history of defending free speech rights, regardless of the popularity of the speech. In landmark cases like Brandenburg v. Ohio, the Supreme Court has established that the First Amendment protects even hate speech, as long as it does not rise to the level of inciting imminent violence. However, this does not mean that public officials are immune from accountability for their actions. Impeachment does not require conviction of a crime but a determination of abuse of office warranting removal.

Trump's legacy may include sparking a resistance movement focused on social justice and constitutional norms. His presidency has ignited passionate debates about race, rights, and freedoms, and the ACLU believes that these debates are essential to a healthy democracy. As society grapples with complex issues, the ACLU will continue to defend the First Amendment rights of all individuals, while also advocating for accountability and transparency in government.

In conclusion, the ACLU's support for Trump's impeachment does not conflict with their commitment to free speech rights. Impeachment is a political remedy aimed at removing an executive official who has abused their office, and the First Amendment does not protect public employees from accountability for their actions. The ACLU will continue to defend the rights of all individuals, while also advocating for accountability and transparency in government.

Hurricane Ida wreaked havoc on electricity services, causing service outages for up to 1.2 million customers across eight states. The impact of the storm extended beyond the initial states, reaching as far as five northeastern states, including Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts by September 1.

Fortunately, most affected customers in the northeastern states had their power restored within 24 hours of the outages. Mississippi saw significant progress with almost complete power restoration by September 7. However, the recovery process was slower in Louisiana, where approximately 500,000 customers were still without power as of September 7. It wasn't until September 13 that 85% of Louisiana customers had their power restored.

Entergy, a major utility provider in the region, estimated that Hurricane Ida caused substantial damage, with around 30,000 utility poles affected – a number nearly equivalent to the combined impact of Hurricanes Katrina and Laura in previous years. The challenges are evident as power restoration efforts continue, particularly in some southeastern Louisiana parishes where the process may extend until the end of September according to Entergy. Trump accounts on Twitter, Facebook and Instagram frozen after storming of U.S. Capitol

It took a violent insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, fuelled by years of false statements, conspiracy theories and violent rhetoric, for social media giants Twitter and Facebook to bar President Donald Trump from addressing his vast audiences on their platforms.

On Wednesday, in an unprecedented step, the two companies temporarily suspended Trump from posting to their platforms after a mob of his supporters stormed the house of Congress.

It was the most aggressive action either company has yet taken against Trump, who more than a decade ago embraced the immediacy and scale of Twitter to rally loyalists, castigate enemies and spread false rumours.

Twitter locked Trump out of his account for 12 hours and said that future violations could result in a permanent suspension. The company required the removal of three of Trump's tweets, including a short video in which he urged those supporters to "go home" while also repeating falsehoods about the integrity of the presidential election. Trump's account deleted those posts, Twitter said; had they remained, Twitter had threatened to extend his suspension.

If the Tweets are not removed, the account will remain locked. —@TwitterSafety Our public interest policy — which has guided our enforcement action in this area for years — ends where we believe the risk of harm is higher and/or more severe. —@TwitterSafety

Facebook and Instagram, which Facebook owns, followed up in the evening, announcing that Trump wouldn't be able to post for 24 hours following two violations of its policies. The White House did not immediately offer a response to the actions.

While some cheered the platforms' response, experts noted that these actions follow years of hemming and hawing regarding Trump and his supporters spreading dangerous misinformation and encouraging violence that contributed to Wednesday's events.

Jennifer Grygiel, a Syracuse University communications professor and an expert on social media, said what happened in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday is a direct result of Trump's use of social media to spread propaganda and disinformation, and that the platforms should bear some responsibility for their previous inaction.

"This is what happens," Grygiel said. "We didn't just see a breach at the Capitol. Social media platforms have been breached by the president repeatedly. This is disinformation. This was a coup attempt in the United States."

Grygiel said the platform's decision to remove the video — and Twitter's suspension — are too little, too late.

"They're creeping along towards firmer action," Grygiel said, calling Trump "Exhibit A" for the need for greater regulation of social media. "Social media is complicit in this because he has repeatedly used social media to incite violence. It's a culmination of years of propaganda and abuse of media by the president of the United States."

Trump posted the video more than two hours after protesters entered the Capitol, interrupting lawmakers meeting in a joint session to confirm the electoral college results and president-elect Joe Biden's victory.

Too little, too late?

Guy Rosen, Facebook's vice-president of integrity, said on Twitter Wednesday that the video was removed because it "contributes to rather than diminishes the risk of ongoing violence."

"This is an emergency situation and we are taking appropriate emergency measures, including removing President Trump's video," Rosen said.

This is an emergency situation and we are taking appropriate emergency measures, including removing President Trump's video. We removed it because on balance we believe it contributes to rather than diminishes the risk of ongoing violence. —@guyro

Twitter initially left the video up but blocked people from being able to retweet it or comment on it. Only later in the day did the platform delete it entirely.

Trump opened his video saying, "I know your pain. I know your hurt. But you have to go home now."

After repeating false claims about voter fraud affecting the election, Trump went on to say: "We can't play into the hands of these people. We have to have peace. So go home. We love you. You're very special."

Republican lawmakers and previous administration officials had begged Trump to give a statement to his supporters to quell the violence. He posted his video as authorities struggled to take control of a chaotic situation at the Capitol that led to the evacuation of lawmakers and the death of at least one person.

Trump has harnessed social media — especially Twitter — as a potent tool for spreading misinformation about the election. Wednesday's riot only increased calls to ban Trump from the platform.

"The President has promoted sedition and incited violence," said Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive officer of the Anti-Defamation League, in a statement. "More than anything, what is happening right now at the Capitol is a direct result of the fear and disinformation that has been spewed consistently from the Oval Office."

In a statement Thursday morning, Trump said there would be an "orderly transition on January 20th" and acknowledged defeat in the election for the first time. His aides posted the statement on Twitter because his account remained suspended.

Texas wind farms sue Citigroup over charges from winter storm

April 21 (Reuters) - A Canadian renewable energy firm on Wednesday sued Citigroup Inc for rejecting force majeure declarations during a February winter storm and billing it over $100 million for replacement power, according to lawsuits filed in a Texas state court.

Shannon Wind and Flat Top Wind, subsidiaries of Innergex Renewable Energy Inc (INE.TO) operate North Texas wind farms that halted their wind turbines during an arctic deep freeze. Both had agreements to physically deliver power to Citi Energy, a unit of Citigroup Inc (C.N) at fixed prices.

Unusually frigid temperatures knocked out nearly half of the state's power plants in mid-February, leaving 4.5 million people without heat or light for days and bankrupting at least three companies due to high wholesale power prices.

The wind firms, partly owned by Starwood Energy Group Global and a fund run by BlackRock Inc (BLK.N) respectively, declared force majeure after their turbines froze. But, their lawsuits in a Texas court claimed Citi ignored the declarations and invoiced them for electricity it bought at inflated prices.

BlackRock declined to comment and Starwood did not have an immediate comment. Innergex did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Citi said the contracts require the disputes to be resolved by courts in New York and applying to New York law.

"We are unaware of any legitimate basis for these cases to be filed in Texas," Citi said in a statement.

Citi billed Shannon Wind for $39.5 million for four days of electricity, and billed Flat Top Wind for $79.3 million for seven days of electricity, according to the suits filed in Harris County District Court, Houston.

The invoices represent more than their projected revenues for the entire year, the lawsuits said, claiming Citi Energy "improperly defaulted" them and is poised to foreclose on both projects.

The lawsuits asked the court to prevent Citi Group from taking further action after the wind companies were advised that they have until Friday to pay their invoices.

Citi billed for replacement power at $9,000 per megawatt hour, versus the roughly $22 to $26 per megawatt hour under their contracts.

Fact Check: Colonial Pipeline Hack and Election Fraud Claims Don't Mix

In recent days, social media users have been misleadingly connecting the Colonial Pipeline hack to unfounded claims of election fraud in the 2020 presidential election. However, a fact check reveals that these claims are misleading and baseless.

On May 7, the Colonial Pipeline, which transports gasoline, diesel fuel, and jet fuel from the Gulf Coast to the East Coast, was hit by a ransomware attack that affected its IT systems and halted operations. The FBI identified the software used in the attack as coming from the cybercrime group DarkSide.

Kevin Feeney, a spokesperson for Colonial Pipeline, highlighted the company's stringent IT and operational technology segmentation policies, which helped prevent the attack from spreading to the company's operational systems.

However, some social media users have been connecting the pipeline hack to unfounded claims of election fraud in the 2020 election. Will Adler, a senior technologist for elections and democracy at the Center for Democracy & Technology, stated that the comparison is misleading and that U.S. voting systems are not vulnerable on a large scale.

"The Colonial Pipeline attack and the 2020 election have nothing to do with each other," Adler said. "Voting systems in the United States are decentralized and secure, and there is no evidence to suggest that they were hacked or compromised in any way."

Dominion Voting Systems and other authorities have consistently refuted claims of election infrastructure hacking in the 2020 election. In fact, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the FBI have both stated that the 2020 election was one of the most secure in U.S. history.

While ransomware attacks like the one on the Colonial Pipeline are a serious concern, they are not a threat to U.S. election systems. The decentralized nature of U.S. elections and the numerous security measures in place to protect voting systems make it highly unlikely that a cyberattack could impact election outcomes.

In conclusion, the comparison between the Colonial Pipeline hack and unfounded claims of election fraud is misleading and baseless. U.S. voting systems are secure and reliable, and there is no evidence to suggest that they were compromised in the 2020 election.

Norsk Hydro's Cyber Resilience: A Year After the Ransomware Attack

In March 2019, Norsk Hydro, the Norwegian renewable energy and aluminum manufacturing giant, found itself on the front lines of the cybersecurity battle when a ransomware attack crippled its operational network. On the day that Hilde Merete Aasheim was appointed as CEO — a moment often marked by hope and ambition — the company faced one of its most significant challenges in its history.

The ransomware infiltrated Norsk Hydro's systems, locking out users from over 3,000 servers and thousands of personal computers, effectively encrypting key areas of the IT network. The incident thrust the company into a state of disarray. Employees faced hurdles accessing critical files, as they were locked out from their own infrastructure, drastically affecting productivity and daily operations.

Despite the chaos, Aasheim and her team made a resolute decision: they would not concede to the hackers’ demands. "Paying the ransom would have meant giving in to criminal behavior," Aasheim stated, emphasizing the company’s commitment to uphold its integrity. "We chose to fight back and take control of the situation, even when it was incredibly challenging."

The immediate aftermath of the attack resulted in substantial operational disruptions. Norsk Hydro experienced an estimated loss of $70 million as production slowed, and its entire operational framework was forced to pivot. In an extraordinary move, employees reverted to manual processes that involved pen and paper for about three weeks, showcasing their resilience and adaptability in times of crisis.

Jo De Vliegher, the Chief Information Officer at Norsk Hydro, described the situation as "quite surreal." He reflected on the climate within the company following the attack: "We had to rapidly reassess our capabilities. The entire organization rallied together, but we had to think outside the box to maintain our production.” With the challenge at hand, De Vliegher spearheaded decentralization efforts, allowing the divisions to operate somewhat independently and effectively, despite the limitations.

Norsk Hydro opted to work with cybersecurity experts and refrained from paying the ransom. This decision proved to be a turning point in the company’s approach to cybersecurity. Aasheim remarked, "We were fortunate to work with experts who guided us through the recovery process, allowing us to regain our autonomy and confidence."

Support came from notable partners, including Microsoft and the Norwegian National Cyber Security Centre. Together, they provided essential resources and guidance, enabling Norsk Hydro to navigate through the complexities of the digital crisis. "The collaboration underscored the importance of collective security measures and cross-industry support," Aasheim added.

As the weeks progressed, the recovery took shape, and operations resumed to a more regular rhythm. De Vliegher noted that ultimately, the ordeal laid bare the vulnerabilities within their infrastructure, leading to a comprehensive reevaluation of Norsk Hydro's cybersecurity measures and priorities. "The attack became a catalyst for us to rethink our digital landscapes, implement stronger security protocols, and enhance our overall resilience," he stated.

This dramatic incident also drew the attention of organizations beyond Norway's borders. Eric Goldstein, an official at the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), emphasizes the dire consequences of paying ransoms. "Not only does paying ransom fail to guarantee a solution, but it contributes to the ongoing cycle of cybercrime," Goldstein stated, reinforcing the belief shared by many in the cybersecurity community that organizations should strengthen their defenses rather than comply with attackers' demands.

In the months following the attack, Norsk Hydro adopted a more robust cybersecurity strategy, incorporating lessons learned from the incident. The commitment to not pay the ransom served as a model for other firms grappling with similar threats. Aasheim expressed pride in the company’s response, stating, “This experience brought out the best of our people, their resilience, and their dedication to upholding the same values we strive for every day.”

The cyber resilience demonstrated by Norsk Hydro in the wake of the attack has positioned the company to face future challenges more effectively. Aasheim and De Vliegher remain committed to restoring full functionality while ensuring that such a situation would not compromise their operational integrity again. "We will continue to invest in our cybersecurity measures to shield our organization from future threats," De Vliegher assured.

As companies globally grapple with the pervasive risks of cybercrime, Norsk Hydro’s experience stands as an example of defiance against the unjust pressures exerted by malicious actors in the digital age. The balance between operational dependency and security resilience remains an ongoing conversation, and Norsk Hydro is now better equipped to navigate that terrain, holding true to their principles of sustainability and innovation.

Some disabled Californians feel abandoned by Newsom’s Golden State Stimulus

A $600 check would go a long way for Janet Clendenin.

The costs of the sugar-free foods she buys to manage her diabetes have risen sharply in South Lake Tahoe during the pandemic, Clendenin said. She usually has to criss-cross the picturesque region by bus to find discounts at Dollar Tree, Grocery Outlet and Walmart.

So when she learned about Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to send $600 payments to the lowest income Californians in February, Clendenin felt relief.

Then came frustration.

Clendenin scoured the news for details on eligibility. She learned that she could have qualified if she worked in 2020. But a constellation of diabetes, arthritis, migraines, back injuries and nerve pain made work impossible about six years ago. Given her disabilities, she could also have qualified if only she received Supplemental Security Income, a federal safety-net program for elderly, blind and disabled people with limited income.

But nowhere could Clendenin find mention of Social Security Disability Insurance, the other main federal program for people with disabilities, which sends her $1,056 a month.

“I couldn’t believe that we were left out,” said Clendenin. “How unfair is that?”

It’s a sentiment shared by many Californians on federal disability insurance, who have asked why Newsom’s stimulus payments skipped them over.

While California lawmakers automatically sent checks to 1.2 million people who receive SSI, the 1.2 million Californians on SSDI only qualify if they had income from work in 2020. But that’s rare — research shows that fewer than one in five SSDI recipients work during a typical year, often because they are limited by their disabilities or risk losing their benefits if they work too much.

Disability advocates say it’s the latest example of the state abandoning some of its most vulnerable residents during the pandemic, after having directed medical health providers to ration COVID-19 care to elderly and less healthy people last spring and deprioritize people with disabilities for vaccines earlier this year — both policies that were reversed after considerable outcry.

“Overall the state has been uneven in how it’s helped people with disabilities navigate the pandemic,” said Andrew Imparato, executive director of Disability Rights California. “A lot of people with disabilities have had to fend for themselves.”

Department of Finance spokesperson H.D. Palmer cites logistical challenges. California maintains an up-to-date list of residents who get SSI because the state supplements the federal benefit by a few hundred dollars, but doesn’t have access to the same information for SSDI.

“Trying to include SSDI… would be a time-consuming and laborious process with the feds that doesn’t line up with the intent of (the Golden State Stimulus) — to get immediate relief to Californians with whom we have an existing relationship,” Palmer wrote in an email.

‘Make hard decisions quickly’

The Newsom administration may have also based the decision on a consideration of need.

California’s SSI recipients live in poverty by definition. Elderly, blind and disabled people can only qualify if they have extremely low income and wealth, and they typically receive just $954.72 per month.

On the other hand, people with sufficient work history can qualify for monthly SSDI payments based on their former wages, with the average national benefit at $1,280 per month.

Still, California’s SSDI recipients often face steep financial challenges. They are more than twice as likely to live in poverty compared to the rest of the population, according to calculations by Andrew Houtenville, an economist at the Institute on Disability at the University of New Hampshire. And people with disabilities often have to cover expensive medical equipment, appointments with specialists and drugs out-of-pocket.

Imparato acknowledged that the state was “trying to make hard decisions quickly” but “including everyone on SSDI probably would have been a more equitable thing to do than excluding them because you don’t have access to their program or because it’s not a means-tested program.”

There are some signs that lawmakers could still include SSDI recipients. Newsom’s proposed expansion of the Golden State Stimulus still requires approval from state legislators. Though they passed a placeholder budget to meet a June 15 deadline, state lawmakers continue to disagree with Newsom over how much surplus money the state has at its disposal and how to spend it.

According to a legislative staffer familiar with ongoing budget negotiations, some members of the Legislature are pushing the Newsom administration to expand eligibility for the Golden State Stimulus payments to Californians on SSDI, among other groups.

The evolution of the Golden State Stimulus

Eligibility for Newsom’s Golden State Stimulus has gone through several twists and turns. In January, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a $2.4 billion plan to send $600 Golden State Stimulus checks to approximately 4 million low-income workers.

By February, with the state’s revenue estimates swelling, the Legislature negotiated and approved an even more generous $3.8 billion stimulus payment plan that included extra aid for undocumented workers.

Under this plan, the state also sent $600 payments to certain Californians living in poverty — regardless of whether they work. That included very low-income families with children enrolled in CalWorks, as well as recipients of SSI or the state’s alternative for some immigrant groups, known as the Cash Assistance Program for Immigrants.

It took Charis Hill several days of searching online and contacting their state assemblymember to discover that they did not automatically qualify. A Sacramento-based disability activist who lives on $1,027 per month from SSDI, Hill eventually deduced that they could qualify not because they were disabled, but rather because they had done freelance writing and speaking last year.

Charis Hill, a disability activist based in Sacramento, was able to get the Golden State Stimulus because they did some freelance work in 2020. But Hill says that it’s unfair that most Californians receiving federal disability insurance don’t currently qualify. Photo by Salgu Wissmath for CalMatters

Hill would have to file taxes, something they hadn’t done in years because their earned income is far below the filing requirement. They decided it was worth it. Their expenses have jumped during the pandemic, especially as they’ve opted for grocery deliveries instead of shopping in stores because they are immunocompromised.

Hill said that, unlike many disabled people, they were fortunate to have internet access and a friend who could help them file their taxes. They were lucky to be able to work last year despite experiencing constant pain and fatigue from an inflammatory condition called axial spondyloarthritis. But, they said, it’s wrong that the Golden State Stimulus program is “basing a disabled person’s value on their ability to work.”

When Newsom proposed a second round of Golden State stimulus payments aimed at California’s middle class in May, Hill was hopeful that other SSDI recipients would finally be able to benefit, too. However, as the details of Newsom’s plan emerged, there was still no mention of SSDI recipients.

“It’s really hard to see and read coverage of Newsom touting how great this is for middle-class people,” said Hill, when people with disabilities are “some of the most impoverished people in the whole country.”

Financial burden can fall to caretakers

Sydney Chandler manages the finances and healthcare of her cousin, Chris Batiste, who is paralyzed. Batiste breathes through an apparatus and communicates with Chandler through a laptop, blinks and head movements.

Chandler, who is a Los Angeles-based writer, said she was livid to learn that SSDI recipients were left out of the state stimulus. To her, it was just another obstacle in the arbitrary and bureaucratic maze that people with disabilities face in trying to attain a liveable income.

Caretakers often carry a significant financial burden. Batiste receives $975 per month in SSDI, and Chandler said she contributes over $1,000 more each month to help cover his rent and full-time nursing.

“If it wasn’t for me, he would be one of the homeless,” Chandler said, “and you’re telling me that you couldn’t set up a portal for SSDI (recipients) to input their information?”

This article is part of the California Divide, a collaboration among newsrooms examining income inequality and economic survival in California.
