Millions of people rely on Facebook to get online. The outage left them stranded.

But this crucial question would go unanswered for hours, after all Facebook’s services—including Facebook.com, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram—suddenly became unavailable from around 11:40 a.m. US Eastern time. The outage was due to changes to Facebook’s backbone routers, the firm said in a blog post. Those changes meant that traffic was not being handled properly by the Domain Name System (DNS), a tool that directs traffic and tracks addresses across the internet. In total, Facebook’s apps and sites were down for almost six hours.

For many internet users in the United States, the outage was a minor annoyance. But for the millions of people around the world who rely on Facebook’s products to access the internet, including Afghans that already feel abandoned by the international community's withdrawal in mid-August, the sudden downtime was far more serious.

For much of the world, Facebook has become “synonymous with the internet,” says Sarah Aoun, vice president for security at the Open Technology Fund, a US nonprofit that supports technology projects like the private browser Tor and encrypted message service Signal. That made the outage the equivalent of nothing less than “a big infrastructure collapse,” she says.

The outage also came at an inauspicious time for Facebook. On Sunday, just hours before the outage, the CBS television program 60 Minutes aired a highly anticipated interview with a Facebook whistleblower, Frances Haugen, who has leaked a number of documents suggesting the firm knew that its products were bad for teen girls, among other revelations. She is due to testify before the US Senate later today. Facebook is also fighting an antitrust investigation in the US that could force it to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

Facebook’s internet

More than 3.5 billion people around the world use Facebook’s suite of social networks and apps, including Facebook.com, Messenger app, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among others. The country with the largest population of Facebook users is India, with an estimated 340 million users. (The United States, by contrast, has an estimated 200 million users.)

This was by design. For years, Facebook has been working to expand internet access in the developing world—which would also expand its own user base. The company has explored the use of satellites, drones, and radio-linked wireless networks. It has partnered with local telecommunication firms to improve physical internet infrastructure.

In 2013 Facebook launched Internet.org, an initiative that allowed users to access Facebook, and certain other websites, without incurring any data charges. This was part of Mark Zuckerberg’s grand plan to get the world online by providing internet access to the 85% of the world (at the time) that had access to cellular data.

Ever Given crew smile for group snap after mega container ship caused global trade chaos by blocking Suez Canal

CALAMITY CREW Ever Given crew smile for group snap after mega container ship caused global trade chaos by blocking Suez Canal

THE crew of the container vessel Ever Given smile in their first picture since the ship brought world trade almost to its knees by blocking the Suez Canal.

The 25 Indian sailors have been onboard the 1,312ft megaship for two months and have no immediate prospect of going home after Egypt demanded $1billion in compensation.

Trade was brought to a halt when after the Ever Given - which has almost 20,000 containers onboard - jackknifed across the Suez Canal last month.

It blocking the vital trade waterway for six days before she was straightened with the help of diggers and a flotilla of tug boats.

The canal is a vital through route for ships coming from Asia and heading to Europe and avoids the long trip around Africa.

Experts say the blockage cost world trade an eye watering £7billion a day as more than 400 ships were held up during the massive operation to free her.

Egypt says it lost $15million in transit fees for each one and is refusing to let the Ever Given continue its voyage.

She is currently at anchor on the Great Bitter Lake midway along the Suez Canal after she was seized by Egypt last week as part of a court order.

Our exclusive picture shows Egyptian reps from the International Transport Workers Federation (ITF) onboard while the compensation row is thrashed out.

The crew are pictured smiling for the camera, but secretly union officials in their home country of India fear they will be kept hostage for weeks until the compensation is paid by the ship's owners.

No identities were revealed. The only person wearing merchant navy epaulettes is on the far left with insignia identifying him as a fourth engineer.

Two of the crew have been allowed to leave the Ever Given and are being replaced while a second master (captain) has flown out from India to join the ship.

She should have arrived at her destination in Hamburg earlier this month after stopping at Felixstowe, Suffolk.

Today Abdulgani Serang of the National Union of Seafarers of India told The Sun: "The visit was primarily a welfare one - we wanted to make sure the crew were all safe and well and not suffering.

"It was important to show solidarity with our fellow countrymen and seafarers, they should not be held to ransom and should be allowed to leave the ship.

"We want to make sure they are not victims of any injustice.

"I have personally spoken to the master (captain) twice and he has assured me everyone on board is well.

"Two seafarers were given permission to leave because of personal family matters at home in India.

''The ITF representatives spent several hours onboard and passed on our good wishes and solidarity to the crew.

"The message from us is that they are not alone and they have our support and the support everybody locally, nationally and internationally.

"The Captain and the crew onboard stated that there were no problem regarding wages, food or provisions. They fully understand the situation.

"The crew are keen to resume sailing soon. The ITF team also delivered internet devices to all the crew."

$1BN COMPO BATTLE

The ship’s insurer for third-party losses, the U.K. P&I Club, said in a statement that it received a claim for $916million, the size of which is “largely unsupported”.

It said it was disappointed that the vessel was seized last week.

The U.K. P&I Club said the claim included a $300million salvage bonus and another $300million for loss of reputation, but not the professional salvor’s claim for its services.

It said a generous offer was made to settle the claim and that negotiations will continue.

It added: "When the grounding occurred, the vessel was fully operational with no defects in her machinery and/or equipment and she was fully manned by a competent and professional Master and crew.

"Navigation was being conducted under the supervision of two Suez Canal Authority pilots, in accordance with the Suez Canal Rules of Navigation.

"The UK Club is working with all parties involved. Our priority is the fair and swift resolution of this claim to ensure the release of the vessel and cargo and, more importantly, her crew of 25 who remain on board."

The Sun can also reveal that three weeks ago in London's High Court the owners also filed a limited liability suit for $114million for the owners of containers on the Ever Given which are thought to contain aircraft spares. washing machines and other electrical goods.

It is expected either Japanese company Shoei Kisen Kaisha, which owns the Panama-flagged Ever Given, or the Taiwanese firm Evergreen Marine Corp, which had charted the ship, will be liable for the compensation.

The ship was initially said to have got into difficulty after high winds and a sand storm hit but officials in Egypt said they had not yet ruled out human or mechanical error.

The ACLU, often seen as a bastion of staunch support for the First Amendment, has faced backlash from some civil libertarians for endorsing the impeachment of Donald Trump. Critics argue the organization should defend Trump's free speech rights. However, the ACLU contends that free speech does not provide immunity from accountability, especially in the case of efforts to undermine the outcome of a legitimate election.

The ACLU's board, a diverse group of top-tier lawyers and activists from across the United States and the District of Columbia, engaged in a rigorous analysis over two consecutive days. Their unanimous decision to call for Trump's impeachment reflects a deep commitment to civil liberties, coupled with an understanding that actions threatening the democratic process must be addressed.

In their deliberations, they carefully considered the implications of impeachment for free speech. They determined Trump's January 6 remarks were part of a broader attempt to contest an election defeat. This pattern of behavior—spreading falsehoods, exerting illegal political pressure, and inciting violence—clearly constitutes an abuse of power that merits impeachment.

This stance does not conflict with the First Amendment. The impeachment resolution emphasizes Trump's actions on January 6 within a wider context of efforts to derail the certification of the 2020 election results. This included exerting undue pressure on Georgia's Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to manipulate the vote count, actions which go beyond what the First Amendment protects.

The ACLU posits that a president may be impeached for actions that would not lead to prosecution were he a private citizen. Impeachment, fundamentally a political process aimed at removing an official from office, differs from criminal proceedings. The premise is that a president, through their actions, may forfeit the protections normally afforded to free speech under the First Amendment, particularly when their conduct undermines democracy itself.

Public employees, including the president, do not enjoy unlimited free speech rights when acting in an official capacity. Their roles endow their words with significant authority, necessitating a higher level of responsibility. As such, Trump's actions on and leading up to January 6, which sought to subvert electoral integrity, cannot be shielded by claims to free speech rights.

In essence, the First Amendment does not extend to the right of a president to engage in speech aimed at unlawfully overturning election results. Therefore, the ACLU's support for impeachment underscores a principled stance that accountability, especially at the highest levels of government, is imperative to safeguarding democratic principles.

Former U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld Dies at 88

Former U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld has died at the age of 88 due to complications from multiple myeloma. Throughout his long and notable career, Rumsfeld was known for his involvement in the George W. Bush administration, particularly during the Middle East wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. In addition to his service under Bush, Rumsfeld also served as the U.S. Secretary of Defense twice before, first under President Gerald Ford and later under Bush in 2001.

During his tenure in the Bush administration, Rumsfeld played a crucial role in managing the post-9/11 military conflicts. The administration's response to the attacks on September 11, 2001, was marked by contentious policies and strategies in the Middle East, with Rumsfeld at the helm of military operations.

The management of these military conflicts, however, was not without controversy. Rumsfeld faced criticism over the handling of the conflicts, particularly regarding the search for weapons of mass destruction and reports of detainee abuses.

Despite the controversy, Rumsfeld remained steadfast in his belief that removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq was justified, even admitting faulty intelligence later. In a 2011 interview with CBS News, Rumsfeld said, "It was a situation that required action, and it was the right decision. We gave the Iraqi people a chance at a better future."

Following his departure from politics, Rumsfeld focused on various projects, including writing a memoir titled "Known and Unknown: A Memoir," participating in a documentary titled "The Unknown Known" directed by Errol Morris, and launching a mobile game called "Churchill Solitaire."

Errol Morris, who spent 33 hours interviewing Rumsfeld for his documentary, described the former Secretary of Defense as somewhat "clueless" during the interview process. According to Morris, Rumsfeld was not fully aware of the consequences of his decisions in the Middle East.

Despite the controversy, Rumsfeld remained a dedicated public servant throughout his career. In a statement following Rumsfeld's death, President George W. Bush paid tribute to his former Secretary of Defense, remembering him for his service and dedication in the aftermath of the attacks on September 11, 2001.

The Rumsfeld family issued a statement following the former Secretary of Defense's death, highlighting his love for his wife, family, and friends, as well as his dedication to public service. The statement read, "He was a true American patriot who served his country with distinction and honor."

In conclusion, the passing of Donald Rumsfeld marks the end of a remarkable career in public service. Although his tenure as Secretary of Defense was marked by controversy, Rumsfeld's dedication to his country and his commitment to public service cannot be denied. He will be remembered for his contributions to the country and his leadership during a critical time in American history.

In the aftermath of 9/11, former President George W. Bush spoke highly of Rumsfeld, stating, "At the Department of Defense, Donald Rumsfeld led our nation after the attacks on September 11, 2001, and demonstrated the leadership and resolve necessary to win the global war on terror."

Similarly, Errol Morris, who spent extensive time with Rumsfeld, noted, "He was a man who was both fascinating and frustrating, intelligent and at times elusive. He was someone who had a profound impact on the world, and his legacy will be debated for years to come."

The Rumsfeld family remembered the former Secretary of Defense as a loving husband, father, and grandfather, stating, "He was a true patriot who loved his country and served it with distinction for many years."

Rumsfeld's career in public service was marked by both controversy and achievement. Despite the criticism he faced, he remained committed to his country and his duty as a public servant. His legacy will continue to be a topic of debate, but one thing is certain: Donald Rumsfeld will be remembered as a significant figure in American history.

WHO Validates Sinovac-CoronaVac COVID-19 Vaccine for Emergency Use, Boosting Global Access Efforts

Geneva, Switzerland – The World Health Organization (WHO) has granted Emergency Use Listing (EUL) to the Sinovac-CoronaVac COVID-19 vaccine, marking a significant milestone in the global fight against the pandemic. This validation confirms that the vaccine meets international standards for safety, efficacy, and manufacturing.

Dr. Mariângela Simão, Assistant-Director General for Access to Health Products at the WHO, emphasized the importance of this development, stating, "The addition of this vaccine has the potential to rapidly accelerate COVID-19 vaccine access for countries globally." She further highlighted the need for a diverse portfolio of vaccines to address the global access inequity, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

The EUL is a prerequisite for vaccines to be included in the COVAX Facility, a global initiative aimed at equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines. With the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine now on the list, it will be available for procurement by countries and international organizations, contributing to the global vaccination campaign.

As part of the rigorous assessment process, the WHO conducted on-site inspections of Sinovac's production facilities, ensuring compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP). The vaccine's ease of storage, requiring standard refrigeration temperatures, makes it particularly suitable for low-resource settings.

According to the WHO, the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine is recommended for individuals aged 18 years and older, with a two-dose schedule. Clinical trial data revealed that the vaccine was 51% effective in preventing symptomatic disease and demonstrated 100% efficacy against severe COVID-19 and hospitalization in the studied population.

Addressing concerns about the vaccine's efficacy in older adults, Dr. Simão noted, "While the efficacy in those over 60 years could not be estimated from the trials, there is no reason to believe that the vaccine would behave differently in this population." Based on supportive data, the WHO does not set an upper age limit for the vaccine's use.

The EUL process is a vital tool employed by the WHO during public health emergencies, enabling the rapid assessment of novel health products while maintaining a stringent focus on safety, efficacy, and quality. Dr. Simão concluded, "This Emergency Use Listing is a testament to the power of solidarity and the tireless work of researchers, manufacturers, and regulatory authorities working together to respond to this global health crisis."

With the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine now part of the global arsenal against COVID-19, the hope is that it will contribute to curbing the pandemic's spread and reducing the disparities in vaccine access worldwide.

Judge: Kenosha shooter can’t associate with supremacists

KENOSHA, Wis. (AP) — An 18-year-old Illinois teen charged with fatally shooting two people during a protest in southeastern Wisconsin last year is prohibited from associating with known white supremacists under a judge’s recently modified bail conditions.

Kyle Rittenhouse was 17 during the Aug. 25 demonstration in Kenosha, Wisconsin, as hundreds were protesting the police shooting of Jacob Blake, a Black man. Rittenhouse has been charged with multiple counts, including reckless and intentional homicide, endangerment and being a minor in possession of a firearm.

Prosecutors allege Rittenhouse, who is white, left his home in Antioch, Illinois, and traveled to Kenosha to answer a call for militia to protect businesses. Kenosha was in the throes of several nights of chaotic street demonstrations after a white officer shot Blake in the back during a domestic disturbance, leaving Blake paralyzed.

Rittenhouse opened fire with an assault-style rifle during the protest, killing Joseph Rosenbaum and Anthony Huber and wounding Gaige Grosskreutz, authorities said. Rittenhouse has pleaded not guilty to all counts and argued he fired in self-defense. Conservatives have rallied around him, generating enough money to make his $2 million cash bail.

According to online court records, a Wisconsin judge modified Rittenhouse’s conditions of release on Friday to note Rittenhouse “shall not knowingly have conduct with any person or group of persons known to harm, threaten, harass or menace others on the basis of their race, beliefs on the subject of religion, color, national origin, or gender.”

He is also barred from possessing and consuming alcohol and from having firearms.

Prosecutors had requested the modifications after Rittenhouse was seen drinking at a bar in the southeastern Wisconsin city of Mount Pleasant, about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south of Milwaukee, earlier this month. The legal drinking age is 21, but in Wisconsin, Rittenhouse could legally drink alcohol because he was with his mother.

According to WMTV, prosecutors wrote in their request that Rittenhouse also posed for a photo outside Pudgy’s Pub with two men as they made the “OK” sign with their hands, a symbol used by white supremacists. Prosecutors also alleged five men at the tavern serenaded Rittenhouse with a song that has become the anthem of the Proud Boys, a neo-fascist group.

No Plans for a Fourth Stimulus Check, Focus Shifts Elsewhere

Moreover, some families are poised to benefit from advanced payments of an expanded child tax credit. Despite several states prematurely halting federal unemployment benefit supplements to encourage workforce re-entry, some individuals continue to benefit from this federal enhancement.

Updates on Stimulus Payment Adjustments

The majority of the third batch of stimulus payments has been dispatched, though funds are still being allocated to individuals whose 2020 income losses make them eligible for additional "plus-up" payments. This adjustment particularly benefits those whose 2019 tax returns did not fully reflect their qualification for the stimulus, with over 8 million people already receiving these supplementary funds this year.

Additionally, payments are being processed for individuals who the IRS lacked sufficient information on but who have filed recent tax returns. This group largely comprises low-income individuals not typically required to file tax returns due to their income levels. Filing this year enables them to claim the stimulus funds for which they qualify.

Enhanced Child Tax Credit Payments Imminent

The March pandemic relief legislation also amplified the child tax credit, with distributions set to commence on July 15. An estimated 36 million families stand to gain from this initiative, with most not needing to take any actions to receive these funds, which are based on 2020 or 2019 tax returns.

Using newly introduced IRS tools, parents can verify their eligibility and choose between monthly payments or a lump sum credit on next year's tax return. Low-income families not required to file taxes can also register for these payments online.

Eligible families will receive an advanced tax credit of $3,600 for each child under 6 and $3,000 for each child under 18, a significant increase from the previous maximum of $2,000 per child under 17. At least half of this amount will be distributed over the summer, with the balance included in the following year's tax refund. Juror Journee Howard Sheds Light on Key Factors in Derek Chauvin Trial

Portland, OR - The trial of Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer convicted of murdering George Floyd, captivated the nation and sparked important conversations about race relations and police brutality. Now, one of the jurors in the high-profile case is speaking out about the critical evidence and testimonies that influenced their decision.

Journee Howard, a Minneapolis resident and juror in the Chauvin trial, recently shared her insights on the pivotal moments during the proceedings. Among the most compelling pieces of evidence, Howard highlighted the bodycam footage captured by former officer Tou Thao, which provided a crucial perspective of the incident.

"The bodycam footage was very important," Howard stated. "It showed exactly what happened, and it was very difficult to watch. It was very clear that Chauvin was on Floyd's neck for an extended period of time, and that he did not let up even when Floyd was clearly in distress."

The prosecution also presented expert testimony from Dr. Martin Tobin, a renowned lung specialist, who testified that Floyd died from asphyxiation caused by Chauvin's knee on his neck. Howard found Dr. Tobin's testimony particularly impactful, especially considering that he offered his expertise without any financial compensation.

"Dr. Tobin's testimony was very important because he was a lung specialist and he was able to explain exactly how Floyd died," Howard explained. "The fact that he did not receive any payment for his testimony made it even more credible."

Another significant moment in the trial, according to Howard, was the testimony of Minneapolis Police Chief Medaria Arradondo, who criticized Chauvin's tactics and stated that they violated department policy.

"Chief Arradondo's testimony was very important because he is the head of the Minneapolis Police Department and he was saying that Chauvin's actions were wrong," Howard said. "It was very powerful to hear that from someone in his position."

However, Howard also expressed criticism towards the defense's strategy, particularly their treatment of witness Donald Williams III, a bystander who recorded the incident on his phone.

"I thought the defense did a poor job of cross-examining Mr. Williams," Howard stated. "They were very aggressive and they tried to discredit him, but I didn't think they were successful."

Regarding Chauvin's decision not to testify, Howard believed it had little impact on the outcome of the trial.

"I don't think it would have made a difference if he had testified," Howard said. "The evidence against him was very strong, and I don't think anything he could have said would have changed the outcome."

Another juror in the trial, Brandon Mitchell, previously made headlines when he stated that convicting Chauvin was an easy decision. Mitchell faced criticism for attending a protest in support of George Floyd, but he defended his impartiality.

"I understand why people were critical of me for attending the protest, but I want to make it clear that I did not let that influence my decision in the trial," Mitchell said. "I was able to separate my personal feelings from my role as a juror, and I based my decision solely on the evidence presented in court."

George Floyd's death sparked widespread protests and discussions on race relations and police brutality across the United States. The Chauvin trial brought these issues to the forefront once again, and the outcome has been seen as a step towards accountability and justice.

As the nation continues to grapple with these complex issues, the insights provided by jurors like Journee Howard and Brandon Mitchell offer a deeper understanding of the factors that led to Chauvin's conviction and the ongoing pursuit of meaningful change.

Donald J. Trump

The biography for President Trump and past presidents is courtesy of the White House Historical Association.

Donald John Trump was born in Queens, New York, on June 14, 1946. His father, Fred Trump was a successful real estate developer. Trump was educated at the New York Military Academy and the Wharton School of Finance and Commerce at the University of Pennsylvania.

In 1971, he took over his father’s real estate company, renaming it the Trump Organization. The business soon became involved in variety of projects, including hotels, resorts, residential and commercial building, casinos, and golf courses. His first of many books was The Art of the Deal, published in 1987. In 2004, he launched the reality television show The Apprentice.

In 2005, Donald Trump married Melania Knauss. They have one son, Barron. Trump also has four adult children from previous marriages: Donald Jr., Ivanka, Eric, and Tiffany.

During the 2016 primary, Trump defeated more than a dozen rivals to win the Republican nomination. While he lost the popular vote, Trump defeated former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in the general election by winning a majority of Electoral College votes. His campaign slogan was “Make America Great Again.”

Without previous elected political experience, President Trump used unconventional methods to communicate his priorities. Most notably, he used the social media platform Twitter as a primary mechanism for direct communication with the American public, other politicians, and the press corps.

As president, he signed a major tax reform bill into law and oversaw a reduction of federal regulations. His protectionist trade policies included tariffs in foreign aluminum, steel, and other products. The Trump administration also renegotiated trade agreements with Mexico, Canada, China, Japan, and South Korea. Other domestic priorities included Supreme Court and federal judiciary appointments, increased military budgets, aggressive border and immigration control, criminal justice reform, and the reduction of prescription drug prices.

In foreign policy, the Trump administration moved the U.S. Embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem and brokered normalization agreements between Israel and a number of countries. In 2018, President Trump attended a summit with Kim Jong Un, marking the first time a sitting president met with a North Korean leader.

In 2018, there was a partial government shutdown as Trump disagreed with Congress over funding for a border wall between the United States and Mexico. The funding lapse lasted thirty-five days before it was resolved.

In 2019, a federal whistleblower filed a complaint that Trump had pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to investigate former Vice President Joe Biden’s son Hunter, who had served on the board of Bursima Holdings, a natural gas company in Ukraine. Later that year, the House of Representatives impeached President Trump based upon allegations of obstruction of Congress and abuse of power. In 2020, the Senate acquitted Trump on both articles of impeachment.

The first confirmed case of COVID-19 was reported in the United States on January 20, 2020. The remainder of Trump’s presidency was consumed with the coronavirus pandemic. Critics argued that Trump’s response to the pandemic was delayed and did not sufficiently encourage public health practices to reduce the spread of the virus. However, the Trump administration’s program “Operation Warp Speed” assisted in the private sector development of two approved vaccines. Nonetheless, by the time Trump left office, more than 400,000 Americans had died of COVID-19.

Trump lost reelection to Democratic candidate Joe Biden, but publicly claimed widespread voter fraud had affected the outcome. Supporters of President Trump traveled to Washington, D.C. for a “Save America” rally on January 6, 2021. Trump spoke to the large crowd on the Ellipse near the White House and encouraged attendees to protest the counting of the Electoral College votes in Congress. The rally turned violent when the president’s supporters overwhelmed law enforcement, breaching the United States Capitol and disrupting the vote count. Five people died as a result of the violence, and the Capitol complex suffered millions of dollars in damage.

On January 13, 2021, Trump’s actions resulted in the House of Representatives approving another article of impeachment: the incitement of insurrection. He is the only president in American history to be impeached twice by Congress.

Ever Given Freed from Suez Canal After Six-Day Blockage

Cairo, Egypt - The colossal container ship Ever Given, which had been wedged in the Suez Canal for six days, was successfully freed on Monday, March 29, after a complex and arduous operation. The ship's liberation from the vital waterway has been hailed as a significant victory for global trade.

A Global Effort to Dislodge a Maritime Leviathan

The Ever Given, one of the world's largest container ships, became wedged in the canal on March 23 due to poor visibility and high winds. The ship's massive size and weight, coupled with the narrowness of the canal, created an unprecedented challenge for maritime authorities.

"It was like an enormous beached whale," said Gregory Tylawsky, a licensed shipmaster and founder of the Maritime Expert Group. "The sheer scale of the ship made it incredibly difficult to move."

Dredging, Tugboats, and High Tides

A global effort was swiftly assembled to dislodge the Ever Given. Dredgers and more than 10 tugboats worked round the clock, removing sand, mud, and water from around the vessel. The 10th of Ramadan and the Mashhour, two heavy-duty dredgers, played significant roles in the dredging process.

To aid in refloating the ship, 9,000 tons of the Ever Given's ballast water were released. This reduced the ship's weight and draft, making it easier to move.

The ship was fully dislodged on March 29, following efforts that coincided with high tide conditions due to a full moon. The high tide provided additional buoyancy, helping to lift the ship free.

"It was a combination of dredging, tugboat maneuvering, and taking advantage of high tides that ultimately freed the ship," said Peter Berdowski, CEO of Dutch dredging company Boskalis.

A Vital Artery for Global Trade

The Suez Canal is a crucial waterway for global trade, with about 15% of all shipping passing through it. The blockage caused significant disruptions to global supply chains, with hundreds of ships waiting to transit the canal.

"The Suez Canal is the lifeline of global trade," said Ragui Assaad, a professor at the University of Minnesota and research fellow at the Economic Research Forum in Cairo. "Its blockage had a major impact on the global economy."

Implications for Global Trade

The successful freeing of the Ever Given has been celebrated by workers and has significant implications for global trade. The resumption of traffic through the canal will help to alleviate supply chain disruptions and stabilize global markets.

"The freeing of the Ever Given is a major victory for global trade," said Gary Cordes, a retired shipmaster and senior adviser at the Maritime Expert Group. "It will help to get the global economy back on track."

A Testament to Human Ingenuity

The successful operation to free the Ever Given is a testament to human ingenuity and the power of collaboration. It demonstrates the ability of nations to come together to solve complex challenges and ensure the smooth flow of global trade.

2 dead in fire as heating safety warnings, emergency calls linked to winter storm continue

Two people were killed and others were injured in an East Austin fire Wednesday morning as authorities continue to warn people who remain without power amid gelid temperatures not to endanger themselves when trying to stay warm.

Austin firefighters responded to a single-family home in the 2900 block of East 12th Street, west of Airport Boulevard, after receiving a call from a passerby at 10:48 a.m., said Austin fire Division Chief Stephen Truesdell. The caller reported seeing flames coming out of a window.

When firefighters arrived, at least one of the home's occupants had made it outside, Truesdell said. That person told firefighters that five people were still inside.

Two people were reported dead at the scene, and one person was taken to a hospital with critical, possibly life-threatening injuries. Three others were injured in the fire, medics said.

The home is considered a total loss and investigators are still working to determine the fire's cause, Truesdell said.

Many fires in Austin and Travis County were reported this week as residents tried to heat their homes with propane, charcoal and other methods. Some fires were also started by fireplaces or faulty heating units.

Firefighters and medics on Wednesday urged Travis County residents to avoid trying to heat their homes with methods that could lead to poisonings and death.

Starting a fire by bringing a charcoal barbecue pit inside or using a gas grill inside could lead to a structure fire or carbon monoxide poisoning.

If people go to sleep with fires from items like a barbecue pit or gas grill, the danger is they won't wake up, officials have said.

"Once the fire starts, they don't have the wherewithal to wake up," Truesdell said.

Austin-Travis County EMS Captain Darren Noak on Wednesday said medics and firefighters have worked around the clock to respond to thousands of emergencies in Travis County since the severe winter weather began.

Dozens of those calls were from Austin-Travis County residents who were injured after slipping on icy pavement, while many others included such emergencies as carbon monoxide poisoning, vehicle crashes and fires.

Medics say a person died from a cardiac arrest Monday afternoon at the camp that Gov. Greg Abbott set up for people experiencing homelessness near U.S. 183 and Texas 71. It is unclear whether the death was related to the cold weather, they said.

Noak said if bodies are located in homes or outside in the Austin area, first responders can't immediately link those deaths to cold weather. It's the job of local medical examiners to determine how a person died, which is a process that could take weeks.

Austin firefighters and medics said Wednesday there didn't appear to be more calls about fatalities than normal.

More than two dozen people across the country have died in the extreme weather this week, some while struggling to find warmth inside their homes.

In the Houston area, one family succumbed to carbon monoxide from car exhaust in their garage. Another perished as they used a fireplace to keep warm. On Monday, law enforcement reported two men were found dead along Houston-area roads. Their causes of death were pending, but officials said the subfreezing temperatures were likely to blame.

Just before noon Wednesday, nearly 183,000 Austin Energy customers were without power and continued to suffer in the cold without any clear answers as to when their electricity would be restored. Some of those residents have been without power for days.

Austin and Travis County leaders on Wednesday opened more locations for cold weather shelters. Noak said residents who are most vulnerable to the cold, or those who have no home and normally camp on the streets, appear to be using those shelters in large numbers.

Ever Given refloated and freed! How did they get the ship out of the Suez Canal?

Salvage crews relied on powerful tugboats, large-capacity dredgers and high tides to pull the stranded container ship Ever Given from the banks of the Suez Canal on Monday.

Six days after wedging itself sideways into a single-lane section of the canal, the 220,000-ton ship was freed by around-the-clock digging and tugs that pushed and pulled it into the center of the waterway.

Workers removed 30,000 cubic meters of sand, enough to fill about a dozen Olympic-sized swimming pools, USA TODAY reported Monday.

The ship is as long as a skyscraper is tall. At 1,312 feet, it is comparable to the Empire State Building, which is 1,454 feet tall, including its spire and antenna. Here it is compared with Manhattan's Central Park:

A composited 3D illustration shows how the Ever Given would look in Central Park. Photo illustration by Stephen J. Beard; Getty Image

The Suez Canal Authority said canal traffic would resume by evening. It's not known how long it will take to clear the backlog of more than 300 ships waiting to enter the canal.

A canal official said it would take three days while data company Refinitiv estimated it could be 10 days or more.

The disruption costs the canal as much as $15 billion per day, according to Suez Canal Authority chairman Osama Rabie, the BBC reported.

How they got the ship out of the Suez Canal:

The ship's stern was freed first Sunday, and the bow was removed from the canal bank Monday. The canal authority said the ship "came out intact and it has no problems."

As conventional earthmoving equipment worked on shore, tugboats and dredgers were busy in the water.

Dredgers clawed away underwater sand

Dredgers are ships equipped with machines to remove underwater sand and sediment. Material can be lifted to the surface with bucket-like devices or vacuumed up by hydraulic pumps.

Two dredgers played an important role in refloating the container ship: the 10th of Ramadan and the Mashhour, both owned by the Suez Canal Authority.

The Mashhour is reported to be the largest and most powerful cutter suction dredger in the world. It was used to widen and deepen sections of the Suez Canal in previous operations.

Tugboats pushed, pulled ship free

Tugboats are powerful, specialized craft that essentially help ships “park” in ports and assist larger ships in moving in and out of berths. They can push or rotate ships by direct contact or pull them with heavy cables called tow lines.

Large ships, such as the Ever Given, have reinforced hull areas designed for tugboat pushing.

Tugboats are used in ports because large ships can’t precisely maneuver in tight spots at low speeds. They can guide ships safely through narrow passages.

About 14 tugboats of varying sizes were used to free the Ever Given, the BBC reported.

High tides made a critical difference in freeing the ship

Salvagers were aided by a full moon and high tides within the canal. The full moon offers spring tides, or king tides, which are higher and lower than average, The Associated Press reported.

Gravity has a greater effect on tides during the straight-line alignment of the Earth, the moon and the sun.

The spring high tides added a few inches of water inside the canal, making removal easier.

How many ships are waiting?

Satellite imagery shows ships jammed up around the Suez Canal. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

Charlotte Cook, head trade analyst at VesselsValue, said there were more than 300 ships waiting in and around the Suez Canal. "This means that despite a successful operation to move the grounded vessel, we could still be looking at a possible five- to seven-day wait for the buildup to clear," she said.

And there are even more ships on the way.

Data from VesselsValue shows 130 vessels en route to the canal, including 18 with an ETA on or before March 30, 26 vessels before March 31 and 44 arriving before April 1.

Motion seeks evidence of past violence at Kyle Rittenhouse trial

KENOSHA, Wis. — Prosecutors in Wisconsin want a judge to allow evidence at Kyle Rittenhouse’s trial that shows he had a previous violent encounter in Kenosha before he fatally shot two men and injured another during a police brutality protest last year.

The state’s motion filed Thursday in Kenosha County Circuit Court also seeks to show Rittenhouse, of Antioch, was associated with the far-right Proud Boys, a group linked to political violence.

Rittenhouse, 18, is charged with killing Joseph Rosenbaum, 36, and Anthony Huber, 26, and wounding Gaige Grosskreutz, 26, on Aug. 25 during protests in Kenosha over the police shooting two days earlier of Jacob Blake, a Black man who was left paralyzed when he was shot by a white police officer.

Prosecutors want to introduce a video from July 1, 2020, which they say shows Rittenhouse striking a teenage girl in the back at Kenosha’s lakefront.

“In both the July 1, 2020 incident and the August 25, 2020 incident, the defendant, an Illinois resident, willingly and intentionally put himself in violent situations in Wisconsin that do not involve him in order to commit further acts of violence,” the motion states.

Prosecutors also said Rittenhouse’s association with the Proud Boys should be considered at the trial because it shows that he takes pride in violence.

Photos taken in January show Rittenhouse drinking inside a Mount Pleasant bar and gesturing with what appeared to be a white power symbol. The motion states that prosecutors have since learned that the people with Rittenhouse at the bar included the leader of the Wisconsin Proud Boys chapter and several of its highest-ranking members.

Prosecutors allege Rittenhouse, who is white, left his home and traveled to Kenosha to answer a call for paramilitary groups to protect businesses during the protest.

Rittenhouse faces multiple charges, including two homicide counts. He has argued he fired in self-defense after protesters attacked him.

Black Lives Matter supporters have painted him as a trigger-happy white supremacist, but some conservatives see him as a symbol for gun rights and have rallied around him, generating $2 million for his bail in November.

Rittenhouse’s defense attorney did not immediately respond to a message and email seeking comment on prosecutors’ latest motion.

Rittenhouse’s trial is scheduled to start Nov. 1.

The upcoming distribution of the expanded federal Child Tax Credit, carrying approximately $15 billion in aid, is poised to assist around 61 million children across families eligible for the benefit. These payments, initiated by the American Rescue Plan in March, aim to support families by partial monthly payments now through the end of this year, with the remainder to be settled during the 2022 tax filing period.

Scheduled for direct deposit on August 15, the forthcoming payment requires additional mailing time for recipients receiving physical checks. Marking the third of six planned disbursements, the IRS aims to administer the first-half through these monthly checks. Eligibility for the July and August payments extends to this round, benefiting families with at least one child under the age of 18. Specifically, those with children under 6 receive $300 per child, and $250 per child is allocated to families with children aged 6 to 17.

However, eligibility hinges on certain income thresholds. The Child Tax Credit commences phase-out at a Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) exceeding $150,000 for jointly filing couples or qualifying widows/widowers, $112,500 for heads of households, and $75,000 for single or separately filing married individuals. This phase-out reduces the credit by $50 for each $1,000 exceeding these thresholds.

Additionally, a notification from the IRS indicated a previous direct deposit issue affecting roughly 15% of July's recipients, expected to be resolved in this month's payment. It's also important for families to retain the IRS's year-end letter summarizing the received credit amounts, as it is essential for accurate tax filing in 2022.

Disparities within countries are exacerbated by unequal access to healthcare services, which has resulted in the most deprived communities being disproportionately affected.

These disparities have underscored the urgent need for equitable vaccine distribution and more robust global cooperation. Wealthier nations have been called upon to not only support international supply chains but also to address inequities within their borders.

The pandemic's impact transcends statistics, affecting individuals and families worldwide. Each story reveals the profound emotional and societal ripple effects of COVID-19. From losing loved ones prematurely to grappling with the long-term implications of the virus, personal stories mirror the broader narrative of a world straining under the pandemic's weight.

Despite vaccination efforts, the world remains vulnerable to new variants and further waves of infection. As the death toll continues to climb, the message from global health leaders is clear: the fight against COVID-19 requires a committed, united effort across geographic and societal lines.

Dr. Ko concluded poignantly, "The journey ahead is long and unpredictable, but with solidarity and commitment, we can make strides towards a future where such staggering losses are a dark chapter of the past."

White House Unveils $1.5 Billion Investment to Strengthen and Diversify U.S. Healthcare Workforce

Despite the complexity of the password, the lack of a second verification step like a text message allowed hackers easy access.

Suez Canal Blockage: A Wake-Up Call for Supply Chain Resilience

The recent blockage of the Suez Canal by the 1,300-foot-long container ship Ever Given has sent shockwaves through the global economy, highlighting the fragility of interconnected supply chains and the urgent need for businesses to bolster their crisis management strategies. The incident has caused significant disruptions to global trade, with far-reaching implications for various industries and economies worldwide.

The Fragility of Global Supply Chains

The Suez Canal, a vital artery for global trade, handles approximately 12% of the world's trade volume, connecting Europe and Asia. The blockage has brought into sharp focus the vulnerabilities of global supply chains, which are often built on complex and interdependent structures. As Chris Nicholson, CEO of Pathmind, aptly puts it, "The Suez Canal blockage is a stark reminder that even a single event can have a profound impact on the global economy."

Immediate Industry Crises

The blockage has triggered immediate crises for several industries. Oil prices have jumped as concerns mount over potential disruptions to crude shipments from the Middle East to Europe. The automotive industry, already grappling with a semiconductor shortage, now faces further setbacks as the blockage hampers the transportation of essential components. Lukas Kinigadner, CEO and co-founder of Anyline, emphasizes the urgency of the situation, stating, "The Suez Canal blockage is exacerbating the global chip shortage, which could have severe consequences for industries heavily reliant on electronics."

Trade Credit Insurance: A Lifeline for Businesses

In the face of such disruptions, trade credit insurance emerges as a crucial tool for businesses to mitigate risks and protect against potential losses. David Macknin, principal of risk assessment and management firm ChicagoRisk, explains, "Trade credit insurance provides a safety net for businesses, ensuring they are compensated in case their customers fail to pay due to supply chain disruptions or other unforeseen events."

Supply Chain Visibility and Agility

Experts stress the importance of supply chain visibility and agility in navigating disruptions effectively. Paul Hong, Distinguished University Professor of global supply chain management and Asian studies at The University of Toledo's College of Business and Innovation, advises leaders to "invest in real-time tracking technologies and scenario planning to ensure they can respond swiftly to unexpected challenges."

Decision-Making Agility and Team Involvement

David Paulson, global vice president of Avnet, underscores the significance of decision-making agility and team involvement during crises. He says, "Leaders must empower their teams to make quick decisions and foster a culture of collaboration to find creative solutions in the face of adversity."

Onshoring and Nearshoring: Reducing Supply Chain Complexity

The Suez Canal crisis may prompt companies to reconsider their global supply chain strategies. Brett Rose, national retail expert and founder and CEO of United National Consumer Suppliers, suggests, "Companies may explore onshoring and nearshoring to reduce supply chain complexity and risks, although this may come at the expense of cost-effectiveness."

Potential Shortages and Shipping Container Deficiencies

A prolonged blockage of the Suez Canal could lead to shortages of finished goods in Europe, particularly those reliant on just-in-time manufacturing. Additionally, the incident is likely to exacerbate the ongoing shipping container shortage, further straining global supply chains.

Conclusion

The Suez Canal blockage serves as a stark reminder of the fragility of global supply chains and the urgent need for businesses to enhance their resilience. By investing in supply chain visibility, agility, and crisis management strategies, companies can better navigate disruptions and mitigate their impact on operations and profitability. As Pierre Subeh, business expert and chief operating officer of marketing technology firm X Network, concludes, "The Suez Canal crisis is a wake-up call for businesses to reassess their supply chain strategies and ensure they are prepared for the unexpected."

Rory McIlroy on a Tiger Woods comeback: 'Golf is so far from the equation right now'

BRADENTON, Fla. – Rory McIlroy always speaks his mind.

Sometimes to his detriment, but mostly, he gives thoughtful, wise response and never sounds like his answers are washed through a P.R. machine. He doesn’t shy from any question nor does he hide from any answer given.

He’s an emotional sort, too, so it wasn’t surprising McIlroy became a tad irritated during his conference call with reporters Wednesday ahead of the World Golf Championships-Workday Championship at The Concession Golf Club when a couple questions irked him.

“He’s not Superman,” McIlroy said when asked if Woods was the guy who can come back from his horrific car crash that left him with multiple, serious injuries to his right leg, ankle and foot.

“He’s a human being at the end of the day,” McIlroy continued. “And he’s already been through so much. At this stage I think everyone should just be grateful that he’s here, that he’s alive, that his kids haven’t lost their dad.

“That’s the most important thing. Golf is so far from the equation right now, it’s not even on the map at this point.”

Woods, 45, was involved in a single-car rollover crash early Tuesday morning in the Los Angeles area. He was awake and responsive after surgeons at the Harbor-UCLA Medical Center operated on his right leg; he shattered the tibia and fibula and suffered significant injuries to his right foot and ankle. A rod was inserted to stabilize his tibia and a combination of screws and pins were used to stabilize the ankle and foot.

McIlroy, 31, also was miffed about a query wondering if there was any talk about paying tribute to Woods during the tournament.

Gallery Photos: Tiger Woods through the years View 32 photos

“Like you say ‘pay tribute to him.’ He’s not gone,” McIlroy said. “He’s been in a very bad accident. We’re very lucky that he’s still here. I feel like we should pay tribute to him every day for being on the PGA Tour and what he’s done for golf.

“It’s always great when he plays at a tournament or is out here because it gives that tournament an extra dimension that it usually doesn’t have. We’re all sort of heading towards that day that Tiger wasn’t going to be a part of the game. I’m not saying that that was soon. Before this accident, he was rehabbing a back injury and hopefully going to come back and play this year. It’s inevitable that one day he won’t be a part of it, and that’s going to be just something that the game of golf and the Tour is going to have to deal with and adapt to.

“Obviously, hopefully, he comes back and is able to play, but if he’s not, I think he’ll still be a part of the game in some way, whether it’s obviously his design business and his foundation and hosting golf tournaments. It may be the end of seeing the genius at work with a club in his hand, but there’s still a lot of other ways that he can affect the game in a great way.”

As for his own game, McIlroy, the former world No. 1 and four-time major champion, hasn’t won since the fall of 2019 and is coming off a missed cut in last week’s Genesis Invitational at Riviera Country Club north of Los Angeles. But in his next start after missing his last five cuts, McIlroy has two wins, a second, a fourth and a tie for 12th.

“It’s funny, it’s going to sound really weird, I worked so hard the week before Riviera in that week off, but I felt so unprepared to play, if that makes sense,” he said. “I stood on the range for hours a day hitting golf balls and working on my swing but didn’t play golf. Didn’t chip, didn’t putt, didn’t do any of the things that you need to do to shoot scores.

“So even though I worked hard and worked on some stuff, I feel like it’s sort of like clockwork. I have these weeks where I want to work on some things and fix some things and I try to cram everything in in the space of a week when it’s probably something that should take two or three months to iron out.

“I went to Riviera after feeling like I worked hard but was completely unprepared because I had sort of neglected sort of all other aspects of the game. I think I learned a couple of things last week. I was thinking way too much about the golf swing last week, even when I was out on the course.

“So I need to play with more freedom and I need to be able to swing away.”

Biden’s Virtual Inauguration: A Historic Event Amid a Pandemic

US President-elect Joe Biden will be inaugurated in a mostly virtual ceremony, marking a historic shift in tradition aimed at keeping Americans safe amidst the COVID-19 pandemic. In stark contrast to past inaugural gatherings, Biden's event will significantly reduce crowd sizes as efforts to curb the virus continue.

The Biden administration’s decision comes as a clear departure from President Donald Trump's 2017 inauguration, where he notably claimed the attendance to be "the largest audience to ever witness an inauguration," despite evidence suggesting otherwise. Trump's inauguration saw an estimated 500,000 people, far fewer than Barack Obama's 2009 inauguration, which unofficially drew a crowd of 1.8 million, the largest in history.

In an effort to maintain safety protocols, Biden's inaugural celebrations will include a reimagined parade and only around 1,000 people will witness the swearing-in ceremony in person, a stark reduction from the tens of thousands typically expected. Missouri Senator Roy Blunt, chairman of the Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies (JCCIC), emphasized this adapted approach, stating, “Our goal is to create an inauguration that keeps people safe and respects the traditions while showcasing a dynamic program that will inspire Americans.”

Additionally, the traditional Inaugural Luncheon will not take place, as the pandemic dictates significant changes to the customary program. "The health and safety of everyone involved is a top priority," said Paige Waltz, the JCCIC Communications Director.

The scaling down of events has drawn some parallels with Ronald Reagan's second inauguration in 1985, which also underwent adjustments, albeit due to severe weather conditions. In a move to avoid further inaccuracies and controversy, the federal government has stopped providing official estimates of crowd sizes for large gatherings in Washington.

Former White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer once insisted on Trump's record-breaking claim, stating, “This was the largest audience to ever witness an inauguration. Period.” Yet, it is increasingly clear that Biden’s ceremony will not be measured by crowd size but by its unique adaptation to challenging times.

Marked in history with an asterisk owing to its pandemic-induced circumstances, Biden's inauguration serves as a reminder of how traditional ceremonies evolve to respond to contemporary challenges while still sparking hope and unity among citizens.

Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene has found herself at the center of a social media storm after her Twitter account was temporarily suspended for violating the platform's integrity policy. Colin Powell's Path from Assistant to Consequence: Unveiling Layers at City College

Before ascending to the pivotal role of National Security Advisor during Ronald Reagan's presidency, Colin Powell was instrumental as an assistant to Reagan's Secretary of Defense, Caspar Weinberger. In an era still reeling from the shadows of Vietnam, Weinberger, with Powell's aid, undertook the task of reigniting a sense of fear and hostility in the American public. This effort was part of a broader initiative to promote a new, diverse image of American military interventionism, leading the charge in the controversial conflicts in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua. It was here that Powell began to leave a marked imprint on Defense Department policies, most notably with the development of the Powell-Weinberger Doctrine. This doctrine argued for the use of "overwhelming force" by the military, when diplomatic channels have been exhausted, underlining the need for clear objectives, exit strategies, and the safeguarding of national security interests.

Upon George H.W. Bush assuming the presidency, Powell was elevated to the position of Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, where he found the opportunity to apply his doctrine firsthand during the U.S. invasion of Panama. The aftermath of this invasion was recounted by Clarence Lusane, a Howard University professor, on Democracy Now!, highlighting the devastating impact on poorer neighborhoods while wealthier areas remained untouched. “It was a horrific invasion. And Powell said nothing about it,” Lusane noted, pointing out the disproportionate suffering inflicted on Afro-Panamanians and contradicting the doctrine's supposed adherence to diplomacy and minimal harm.

Powell's tenure continued to draw criticism, most notably for his role in propagating false intelligence about Saddam Hussein's weapons of mass destruction, which led to the invasion of Iraq. This action starkly deviated from Powell's own principles, lacking both clear objectives and an exit strategy, resulting in a conflict that caused the death of hundreds of thousands of civilians. This episode arguably forms the crux of Powell's legacy, where the massive loss of life, facilitated by deceit, starkly contrasts with the ideals he was supposed to uphold. Despite late apologies and explanations citing misinformation from intelligence sources, Powell's responsibility in catalyzing the illegal invasion stands as a grim chapter, irreconcilable with international humanitarian laws.

Colin Powell's story, intertwined with his responsibilities and the outcomes of his actions, particularly in Iraq, leaves a complex legacy. Despite his peaceful later years, admired for philanthropy, the devastation experienced by the Iraqi people, facilitated by his actions, cannot be overlooked or forgiven.

Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s words resonate in this context: “A nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense than on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death.” This sentiment captures the essence of the dichotomy in Powell's legacy between military action and the true costs of such endeavors on human lives and dignity.

Frustration Mounts as Louisiana Grapples with Power Outages Post-Ida

LaPLACE, La. – Tens of thousands of Louisiana residents remain in the dark as the state continues to grapple with the aftermath of Hurricane Ida, which hit the state over a week ago. More than nine days after the devastating storm, power restoration efforts continue, with a glaring disparity in progress between New Orleans and other heavily affected communities.

Frustration has been mounting among residents who feel neglected in the state's restoration priorities. "It seems like some areas are getting power back quickly while others are being left behind," said State Rep. Tanner Magee, expressing the concerns of residents who are fed up with the delays in returning to normal life.

Entergy Louisiana, the state's largest electric utility, has been striving to speed up the restoration process. "While we are making significant progress, it's likely some areas will not have power until the end of September," said Phillip May, Entergy Louisiana President and CEO. More than 159,000 household applications for disaster assistance have been approved by FEMA, highlighting the widespread need for support across the state.

In a tragic development, the state has revoked the licenses of seven nursing homes after seven residents died in post-Ida conditions. Warner Thomas, President and CEO of Ochsner Health, emphasized the strain on healthcare facilities, noting how Ochsner Health's two hospitals in the hardest-hit parishes are operating emergency rooms but are not fully open due to the extensive damage. "We've faced enormous challenges in keeping our facilities operational in these conditions," Thomas said.

In an effort to aid recovery efforts, the Carnival Glory has docked in New Orleans to temporarily house first responders assisting with the relief efforts. The state, however, is struggling with widespread fuel shortages, water service intermittency, and countless homes left uninhabitable by the storm.

Many residents are still seeking shelter, with about 3,200 people staying in mass shelters and around 25,000 in FEMA hotel rooms for transitional accommodation. "It’s difficult not knowing when we’ll be able to go back to living safely at home," said Kim Bass, a resident of St. John the Baptist Parish. According to the latest reports, the death toll from Ida has risen to 15 in Louisiana, with additional fatalities attributed to storm-related injuries and a lack of oxygen during power outages.

For Michael Lathers, a resident of LaPlace, coping with the slow pace of recovery adds to the burden. "The waiting game feels endless," he remarked. The road to recovery appears lengthy as the community braves the hardships left in Ida’s wake, yearning for a semblance of normalcy.

The state and utility companies are called to address the immediate needs of all affected regions equitably while also planning for long-term resilience in the face of future storms. For now, the priority remains restoring power and essential services to the hundreds of thousands still waiting for relief.

US Recovers Most of Colonial Pipeline Ransom in Historic Seizure

The Justice Department has successfully recovered the majority of the multimillion-dollar ransom paid to hackers following the cyberattack on Colonial Pipeline last month. This operation marks a significant victory in the fight against ransomware, representing the first successful seizure of its kind by the Biden administration's specialized ransomware task force.

"By targeting the entire ecosystem that fuels ransomware and digital extortion attacks, including criminal proceeds in the form of digital currency, we will continue to use all of our resources to increase the cost and consequences of ransomware and other cyber-based attacks," stated Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco during a press conference announcing the operation.

The attack, which utilized the DarkSide ransomware variant, forced Colonial Pipeline, responsible for supplying roughly half the fuel consumed on the East Coast, to temporarily shut down its operations on May 7th. The company subsequently paid a ransom of 75 bitcoin, then valued at approximately $4.4 million, in an attempt to quickly restore its systems.

In a statement, Colonial Pipeline President and CEO Joseph Blount expressed gratitude for the FBI's efforts, emphasizing that holding hackers accountable and disrupting their activities is crucial for deterring future attacks. He further stressed the importance of the private sector taking cyber threats seriously and investing in robust defenses.

The FBI, through its investigation of DarkSide since last year, closely monitors over 100 ransomware variants. In this case, the agency was able to identify a virtual currency wallet used by the hackers and successfully recover the stolen funds. While details regarding the acquisition of the bitcoin address key remain undisclosed, the Justice Department confirmed that law enforcement tracked multiple cryptocurrency transfers.

This successful operation demonstrates the growing resolve of US authorities to combat the escalating threat of ransomware attacks targeting critical infrastructure worldwide. The recovered funds serve as a powerful message to cybercriminals, highlighting the potential consequences of their actions and the increasing sophistication of law enforcement efforts.

Fact Check: Will Millions of Illegal Immigrants Get Stimulus Checks, as Ted Cruz Says?

Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) proposed an amendment to the American Rescue Plan that would bar illegal immigrants from access to the $1,400 stimulus checks.

His amendment was voted down after Senator Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) criticized Cruz for trying to "rile people up over something that is not true."

The Claim

Cruz claimed on Twitter that illegal immigrants would be eligible for the $1,400 stimulus checks included in the American Rescue Plan.

On March 6, Cruz tweeted, "When the checks go out, millions of illegal immigrants WILL GET $1400 checks."

He wrote that many people considered illegal immigrants are those who have overstayed their visas, and therefore have Social Security numbers.

Cruz argued that the possession of Social Security numbers will allow unlawfully present individuals to obtain the stimulus money.

The Facts

Anyone who pays taxes in the United States as a resident is eligible for a stimulus payment under the American Rescue Plan. That includes non-citizens.

For example, a citizen of Canada who is living and working full time in the U.S. would have a Social Security number and would be eligible for a stimulus payment.

The United States Department of Homeland Security website describes unauthorized immigrants as foreign-born non-citizens who live in the United States without legal residence.

Individuals who overstay their visas but pay tax in the United States using a Social Security number can be eligible for stimulus payments. The most recent available data for the number of visa overstays in the United States is from 2019, released by the Department of Homeland Security. It said that 1.21 percent of visas in that year were overstayed, or 676,422 overstays. In 2019, student visas (1.52 percent) had a higher overstay rate than those from Canada and Mexico (.75 percent, 1.27 percent, respectively).

Illegal immigrants would not be eligible to receive a check if they do not have a Social Security number.

Immigrants who overstay their visas no longer are lawfully in the country but retain their Social Security numbers and therefore are eligible to receive a check.

"Technically, if they have overstayed their visa, they are here illegally," a spokeswoman for U.S. Customs and Border Protection told Newsweek. "If a visitor has not been granted an extension of status by USCIS [United States Citizenship and Immigration Services], then they are considered to be overstays and subject to deportable status under 237 of the Immigration and Nationality Act."

But Durbin is not convinced that the number of overstays with Social Security cards is as high as Cruz said.

A Durbin aide released a statement that said, in part:

"CBP's limited data sample of overstays and other estimates of visa overstay numbers do not contain the numbers of tax filers with SSNs who overstayed visas. It is simply false to assume that each visa overstayer has a social security number, for which the person must have been work-authorized to qualify for a SSN in the first place. By far the largest visa category of visas issued/visas overstayed each year (tourist/business B visas) according to DHS data do not qualify noncitizens to get a SSN.

"Generalized visa overstay estimates do not reveal how many individuals have overstayed visas who were a) authorized to work, b) provided the documentation necessary to get a Social Security Number, c) did not subsequently get a green card or otherwise obtain a lawful immigration status, d) overstayed their visa, but e) continued filing tax returns with the IRS such that they now qualify for stimulus checks.

"Additionally, a claim based on incomplete visa overstay data about the American Rescue Plan stimulus checks must also acknowledge that this hypothetical scenario (of stimulus checks going to visa overstayers with SSNs) would have applied just the same to the CARES Act and the December 2020 stimulus package, and is not a new or unique feature of the American Rescue Plan."

People who qualify as legal residents include those who have passed the green card test (permanent legal residents) or those who pass the substantial presence test. That test requires taxpayers to be physically present in the United States for 31 days of the current year and 183 days for the past three years."

Anyone who has a green card is considered a legal permanent resident, and would be eligible for the stimulus payment.

The Ruling

True.

Cruz's claim that millions of illegal immigrants would receive stimulus payments is true, given the amount of people who have overstayed their visas over the years. Once they overstay, they technically are considered "illegal."

FDA Expands Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Booster Eligibility to 16- and 17-Year-Olds

This authorization comes after a thorough review of safety and effectiveness data, further reinforcing the agency's commitment to combatting the ongoing pandemic.

Acting FDA Commissioner Janet Woodcock, M.D., emphasized the significance of this decision, stating, "As we move forward in our fight against COVID-19, we continue to prioritize the health and safety of all Americans, including our younger population. Today's action allows for 16- and 17-year-olds to receive a booster dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine at least six months after their primary series, providing added protection against the virus."

This expansion follows the FDA's authorization on November 19, which allowed booster doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for individuals 18 years and older. It is important to note that the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine, also known as Comirnaty, is the only vaccine authorized for use in the 16- and 17-year-old age group.

Dr. Peter Marks, M.D., Ph.D., the director of the FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, explained the rationale behind the decision, saying, "We have observed waning immunity over time following the primary vaccination series, particularly in certain populations. The available data support the benefits of a single booster dose in this age group, helping to maintain a high level of protection against the virus."

The FDA's analysis has shown that a booster dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine elicits a robust immune response in both adults and youth, supporting its effectiveness in preventing severe COVID-19, hospitalization, and death. In making this decision, the agency carefully assessed the potential risks, including myocarditis and pericarditis, which have been reported in a small number of adolescents and young adults following vaccination.

Dr. Woodcock addressed these concerns, stating, "We have determined that the known and potential benefits of a booster dose in 16- and 17-year-olds outweigh the known and potential risks, including the risk of myocarditis. We will continue to closely monitor the safety of the vaccine, and Pfizer is conducting studies to better understand the risk of myocarditis and pericarditis."

The FDA did not convene the Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee for this decision, as it was based on a comprehensive review of existing data and information. The agency collaborated with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to evaluate the need for boosters in this age group, and the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) is expected to meet soon to discuss recommendations for the use of the booster dose in 16- and 17-year-olds.

Suez Ship’s Owner Braces for ‘Thousands’ of Legal Claims

The owner of the Ever Given, the cargo ship that blocked the Suez Canal for almost a week, hampering global trade and roiling markets, expects to be hit with “many hundreds or thousands” of legal claims.

The scale of future litigation against the vessel’s owners was laid bare at a London court hearing Tuesday where lawyers won a court order to put any potential claims on hold for two months. Two subsidiaries of Shoei Kisen Kaisha Ltd., the container vessels’ owner, and Evergreen Group, a Taiwanese conglomerate that operated it under a long-term charter, had asked a London judge for the stay.

Earlier this year, they obtained another order limiting some claims against the ship to 84 million pounds ($116 million).

The 400-meter-long Ever Given grounded in the Suez canal for several days in March, blocking the route in both directions and disrupting global trade. Last week, it began its voyage out of the canal and left Egyptian waters on Wednesday.

The owners expect to be sued by Evergreen and foresee potentially thousands more legal claims lodged by individual cargo owners against individual ship owners, their court lawyer Stewart Buckingham said at the London hearing.

The stay in proceedings will allow similar and overlapping claims to potentially be grouped together, limiting legal costs and court time, he said.

A further court hearing will be held in two months, when the owners will be equipped with more information as to any claims filed against it, allowing them to “see the lay of the land,” Buckingham said.

“The owners’ position is that they are not liable for the grounding incident or its consequences,” he said in a court filing. When the ship became stuck, it was being led by a Suez Canal pilot, who had earlier taken over from the harbor pilot who had driven the ship from the Suez anchorage into the canal, he said.

While there was some damage to the bow of the ship as a result of the incident, no injuries, deaths or pollution are understood to have occurred and the death of a canal worker involved in the re-floating is thought to be unrelated, he said.

Lawyers for the owner didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. A lawyer for Evergreen declined to comment.

Any claims filed in the U.K. will likely take years before reaching a resolution. Some may be resolved by arbitration, an alternative and generally private alternative to long and costly court battles.

"White Vigilantism on Trial: Rittenhouse and Arbery Cases Highlight Racial Injustice"
