Saints Stifle Buccaneers 9-0, Stall Division Title Celebration

TAMPA, Fla. (AP) – In a commanding display of defensive prowess, the New Orleans Saints halted the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' march toward a division title with a 9-0 victory. The game, overshadowed by the absence of Saints' head coach Sean Payton due to COVID-19, saw the Saints' defense, under the stewardship of defensive coordinator and acting head coach Dennis Allen, shut down the Buccaneers' formidable offense.

Cameron Jordan led the defensive effort, with the Saints leveling Tampa Bay's high-powered offensive lineup. Buccaneers quarterback Tom Brady expressed the team's collective frustration, stressing the lack of execution. "We just didn't execute well enough across the board," said Brady. "It's a tough game, and we have to do better."

Despite Payton's absence, the Saints managed to extend their regular-season winning streak against the Buccaneers to seven games, a testament to their defensive strategy and resilience. This victory not only prevented the Buccaneers from clinifying their first division crown since 2007 but also propelled the Saints into playoff contention, securing the conference's final wild card spot.

Saints quarterback Taysom Hill spoke to the team's mindset, stating, "We knew what was at stake, and we just stuck to our plan. It's a big win for us." Meanwhile, Acting Head Coach Dennis Allen praised his team's performance, particularly the defense. "I couldn't be prouder of this group. They stepped up, knowing the challenge that was ahead," Allen remarked.

Cameron Jordan, whose standout performance included two sacks and surpassing 100 career sacks, highlighted the team's collective effort. "It's about the collective over the individual. We knew if we kept applying pressure, good things would happen," said Jordan.

Buccaneers coach Bruce Arians reflected on the game's outcome and the missed opportunity. "This was a game we expected to win, and to not score a single point is disappointing. We have to regroup and focus on the next game," Arians noted.

In an unprecedented event for his illustrious career, Brady's team was shut out for the first time in 255 starts, including the playoffs. Despite the setback, the Buccaneers remain comfortably ahead in the division with three weeks left in the regular season.

As both teams look ahead, the Saints leave Tampa with not only a victory but a statement win that shakes up the playoff picture. The Buccaneers, while still in a commanding division lead, must recalibrate to secure their path forward. The NFL season continues to be unpredictable, and each game is a crucial step toward the postseason.

House Judiciary Chairman Calls for DOJ Review of Rittenhouse Acquittal Amidst Ongoing Debates

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jerry Nadler is urging the Department of Justice (DOJ) to review the controversial acquittal of Kyle Rittenhouse, who was found not guilty on all charges related to the fatal shooting of two men during protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin, in 2020. Rittenhouse, who was 17 years old at the time of the incident, claimed self-defense in the shootings that took place amid escalating unrest following the police shooting of Jacob Blake.

“This case has raised significant questions about the intersection of race, self-defense laws, and vigilantism in America,” Nadler, a Democratic representative from New York, said in a statement. His call for a federal review highlights the deep public concern over Rittenhouse's actions and the implications of the trial's outcome.

During the trial, Rittenhouse, who took an AR-15-style rifle to the protests, asserted that he traveled to Kenosha to protect property from looting. His defense argued he acted in self-defense when confronted by individuals they claimed posed an imminent threat. This narrative of "protection" has become central to the broader discussions around gun rights and vigilantism.

Prosecutors depicted Rittenhouse as a "wannabe soldier," suggesting he was seeking to play the role of an armed protector rather than simply defending himself in a chaotic situation. The narrative established by the prosecution, however, did little to sway the jury, which ultimately found Rittenhouse not guilty on all charges, including first-degree homicide.

Judge Bruce Schroeder, who presided over the case, was a focal point of attention throughout the trial. His decisions, including the controversial dismissal of a firearm possession charge against Rittenhouse, sparked debates over judicial interpretations of the law. “I have to abide by the laws of the state,” Judge Schroeder stated during the proceedings, underscoring his judicial philosophy in navigating the case.

The dismissal of the weapon charge was based on the length of the rifle's barrel, which defense attorneys argued was legally compliant under Wisconsin law. This decision has prompted discussions about critical legal distinctions and their ramifications for self-defense claims. Kenosha-based defense attorney Michael Cicchini reflected on the unique circumstances surrounding the case, saying, "The law can be complex, and in Rittenhouse’s situation, it became a matter of understanding those nuances."

Despite calls for a federal review, analysts assert that bringing new charges against Rittenhouse at the federal level is highly unlikely. Federal charges typically involve specific violations of federal statutes, none of which Rittenhouse faces. Experts note that the case has underscored significant regional and national divides, particularly concerning one's rights to carry firearms and self-defense in volatile situations.

The trial and its outcome have reignited conversations about racial justice, as Rittenhouse is a white male who engaged with predominantly Black protesters, highlighting stark racial disparities in how the justice system handles such cases. The discussions surrounding guns, vigilantism, and racial equity continue to reverberate beyond the courtroom.

Rittenhouse’s case has emerged as a flashpoint in America’s struggle to reconcile its laws with the realities of social unrest and how individuals perceive their right to protect themselves and their property. As communities engage in critical dialogue, the implications of this case will likely persist in the public consciousness as a symbol of broader societal challenges.

In this tense climate, Nadler's call for a DOJ review may further fuel the fire of an ongoing national debate that has yet to find resolution.

Mark Zuckerberg should quit Facebook, says Frances Haugen

Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen has delivered her strongest call yet for Mark Zuckerberg to step down as chief executive of his social media empire, saying the business will be better off with a leader who focuses on user safety.

Frances Haugen said Facebook’s parent company, rebranded Meta last week, is unlikely to change if its founder remains in charge. Speaking at the Web Summit in Lisbon, the former Facebook employee, who has leaked tens of thousands of internal documents detailing the company’s struggles with user safety and misinformation, also criticised Zuckerberg’s “unconscionable” decision to invest in its metaverse concept instead of focusing on fixing its current problems.

Asked if Zuckerberg should step down, Haugen said: “I think Facebook will be stronger with someone who is willing to focus on safety, so yes.”

However, Haugen acknowledged that Zuckerberg’s control of Meta was an issue for any independent shareholders who might wish for a change at the top. Zuckerberg controls decision-making at the company through his majority ownership of the voting shares in Meta, which makes his position unassailable.

“Mark holds 54% of the voting shares in Facebook. He is the chairman and the CEO and I think that at a minimum the shareholders have the right to actually choose their CEO. And so I think it is unlikely the company will change if he remains the CEO,” said Haugen.

“And I hope that he can see that there is so much good he could do in the world, and maybe it’s a chance for someone else to maybe take the reins.”

Haugen also criticised the strategic shift behind the company’s surprise rebranding last week, with Zuckerberg committing the business to a major investment in the metaverse, a space where digital representations of people – avatars – interact at work and play, meeting in their office, going to concerts and even trying on clothes.

Haugen said the documents she had released to Congress, regulators and the press made clear that the company needed to spend more on basic safety systems and not an expansion into virtual reality.

The documents released by Haugen have revealed that Meta was aware its Instagram photo-sharing app has been accused of exacerbating mental health problems for teenage girls, that its own workers were dismayed by a failure to stem misinformation spreading in the run-up to the 6 January riot in Washington, and that Facebook was helping to fan ethnic violence in Ethiopia.

“I think there is a meta problem at Facebook which is that over and over again Facebook chooses expansion in new areas over sticking the landing on what they have already done and I find it unconscionable that, as you read through the documents, it states very clearly there needs to be more resources on very basic safety systems,” she said.

Haugen added that her actions were driven by a belief that Facebook needed to change in order to save lives. “I genuinely believe that there are a million, or maybe 10 million lives on the line in the next 20 years, and compared to that nothing really feels like a real consequence.”

Haugen’s appearance at the Web Summit follows her testimonies at the US Congress and in Westminster last month. In London she told MPs and peers that urgent external regulation was needed to rein in the tech company’s management. Haugen was speaking at a joint committee scrutinising the draft online safety bill, which imposes a duty of care on social media companies to protect users from harmful content. Meta’s apps, including Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, are used daily by 2.8 billion people.

Responding to Haugen’s comments, a Meta spokesperson said: “The argument that we deliberately push content that makes people angry for profit is deeply illogical. We are on track to spend more than $5bn on safety and security in 2021 – more than any other tech company – and have 40,000 people to do one job: keep people safe on our apps.”

The spokeperson added that Meta was able to invest in expansion and safety at the same time. “Obviously, we can and must do both of these things at the same time – and we are.”

FDA Authorizes New Over-the-Counter COVID-19 Tests for Asymptomatic Screening

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken a significant step forward in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic by authorizing several tests for over-the-counter (OTC) use without a prescription. These tests are specifically designed for serial screening of individuals who do not show symptoms of COVID-19. This authorization is a critical development in enabling more widespread screening in various settings, including schools, workplaces, and communities at large.

In addition to the OTC authorizations, the FDA has also expanded access to COVID-19 testing in point-of-care (POC) settings. One of the newly authorized tests can be used without a prescription for serial screening, while another requires a prescription. These flexible options are intended to help communities and organizations implement COVID-19 screening programs more effectively and tailor them to their specific needs.

Dr. Jeff Shuren, M.D., J.D., director of the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health, emphasized the significance of these authorizations. "Screening testing, especially with the over-the-counter and POC tests authorized today, is an important part of the country’s pandemic response—many schools, workplaces, and communities are setting up testing programs to quickly screen for COVID-19. With today’s authorization, we are providing more options for accurate and reliable serial screening tests that can be conducted in the comfort of people’s homes or in point-of-care settings, enhancing our efforts to find and contain outbreaks of the virus." Shuren reassured the public that these tests meet the FDA's scientific standards for emergency use authorization, reflecting the agency's commitment to supporting the nation's ongoing response to the pandemic.

Throughout the pandemic, the FDA has undertaken numerous steps to facilitate the development and authorization of COVID-19 tests. By working closely with test developers and streamlining regulatory processes, the agency has significantly expanded the arsenal of diagnostic tools available to fight the spread of the virus.

Three tests, in particular, have been highlighted for their authorization for serial screening claims: the Quidel QuickVue test, the Abbott BinaxNOW test (available in multiple configurations), and the BD Veritor System for Rapid Detection of SARS-CoV-2. These tests had previously been authorized for use in individuals showing symptoms of COVID-19. However, with the new authorization, their use has been extended to include asymptomatic individuals in serial testing programs.

This expansion of testing options is part of the FDA’s broader initiative to increase consumer access to COVID-19 testing. By supporting the establishment of comprehensive screening programs, the FDA aims to play a pivotal role in controlling the spread of the virus.

The FDA's actions throughout this public health crisis underscore its broader mandate to safeguard public health by regulating not just drugs and medical devices, but also the nation’s food supply and other critical areas. By offering several options for accurate and reliable screening tests, the FDA continues to support public health measures designed to control the spread of COVID-19 and protect communities across the United States.

Hurricane Ida's Remnants Unleash Devastating Floods, Tornadoes Across East Coast, Killing at Least 46

NEW YORK (AP) – The remnants of Hurricane Ida unleashed devastating floods and tornado damage across the U.S. East Coast, leaving a trail of destruction and claiming the lives of at least 46 people.

New Jersey bore the brunt of the storm's fury, with at least 23 fatalities reported. Governor Phil Murphy described the situation as "heartbreaking," saying, "We're praying for the families who've lost loved ones."

New York City also suffered significant losses, with 13 people killed, 11 of whom perished in flooded basement apartments. Mayor Bill de Blasio lamented, "This is a tragedy for our city. We're doing everything we can to help those affected."

Flooding and damage were widespread across multiple states, including Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. In Elizabeth, New Jersey, Mayor J. Christian Bollwage said, "We've never seen anything like this before. The water rose so quickly, people couldn't escape."

Sophy Liu, a survivor from Elizabeth, recounted her harrowing experience: "The water came in so fast, I had to climb onto my kitchen counter. I was trapped for hours, waiting for help."

Deborah Torres, another survivor from New York City, described the terrifying moment when her basement apartment flooded: "I heard a loud noise, and then the water just started gushing in. I grabbed my children and ran for our lives."

Experts attributed the storm's devastating impact to climate change. "Warmer air can hold more rain, and urban settings like New York City exacerbate flooding due to extensive pavement," explained Jeanine Zubrzycki, a resident of Mullica Hill, New Jersey.

Despite warnings from the National Hurricane Center about potential flash flooding, officials in New York expressed surprise at the storm's ferocity. "We knew there was a risk of flooding, but we didn't anticipate it would be this severe," said Governor Kathy Hochul.

The storm's aftermath left a chaotic scene in New York City. Nearly 500 vehicles were abandoned on flooded highways, and subway service was disrupted due to water entering the tunnels. Chief of Department Rodney Harrison said, "We've never had to deal with this volume of water in the subway system before."

President Joe Biden responded to the crisis, declaring a state of emergency in New Jersey and New York. "We're going to do everything we can to help these communities recover and rebuild," he said.

Federal first responders have been deployed to assist in cleanup efforts. Greg Turner, whose father was killed in the flooding in New Jersey, expressed gratitude for the support: "We're devastated, but we're also grateful for the help we're receiving."

The storm also spawned at least 10 tornadoes across the region, causing additional damage. This disaster follows just days after Ida made landfall in Louisiana as the fifth-strongest storm ever to hit the U.S.

As the cleanup and recovery efforts continue, officials are urging residents to stay vigilant and follow safety guidelines. "This storm has shown us the importance of being prepared for extreme weather events," said Mayor de Blasio. "We need to learn from this and take steps to mitigate the risks in the future."

FDA Amends EUAs for Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 Vaccines for Additional Dose for Certain Immunocompromised Individuals

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken a crucial step to protect a vulnerable segment of the population by amending the Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA) for the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines. This amendment allows for an additional dose of these vaccines for certain immunocompromised individuals, including solid organ transplant recipients or those with equivalent levels of immunocompromise.

"Today's action allows for a third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna COVID-19 vaccines for a specific group of immunocompromised individuals who may not have had a sufficient immune response to the standard two-dose regimen," said Acting FDA Commissioner Janet Woodcock, MD. "This is an important step in ensuring we're doing everything we can to protect those who are most vulnerable to COVID-19 during this pandemic wave."

Immunocompromised individuals, due to their reduced ability to fight infections, are at a higher risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. The additional dose is intended to increase their protection against the virus, but the FDA emphasizes that physical precautions, such as wearing masks and social distancing, should still be followed.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices is scheduled to convene to discuss further recommendations for this specific group. The third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine is authorized for individuals aged 12 and older, while the Moderna vaccine is authorized for those aged 18 and older. Both vaccines require an initial two-dose regimen, with the third dose to be administered at least 28 days after the second shot.

Dr. Woodcock highlighted the importance of healthcare providers playing a critical role in guiding their immunocompromised patients. "We encourage these individuals to have a conversation with their healthcare provider about their individual circumstances and whether an additional dose may be appropriate for them," she said.

In addition to the additional vaccine dose, the FDA also advises immunocompromised individuals to discuss monoclonal antibody treatment options with their healthcare providers in case they contract COVID-19. The EUA amendments have been issued to Pfizer Inc. and ModernaTX Inc. for their respective vaccines.

This amendment underscores the FDA's commitment to adapting its response to the evolving COVID-19 landscape and ensuring the safety and efficacy of vaccines for all Americans, particularly those most at risk.

Post-'Rust' Shooting: Hollywood Reevaluates Use of Real Firearms on Sets as Safety Concerns Surge

In the wake of the tragic shooting on the set of "Rust" that claimed the life of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins, the film industry finds itself at a crossroads, reevaluating the use of real firearms on sets and grappling with concerns over safety.

Actor Leslie Grossman, known for her roles in "American Horror Story," shared her experiences working with rubber or air guns in place of real firearms for shooting scenes. "Safety should always be our top priority," she stated emphatically. "I've never used a real gun on set, and I don't think it's necessary for authenticity."

The incident on "Rust" has led several productions to follow suit in banning real firearms. Among them are "The Rookie" and "The Boys." Eric Kripke, showrunner for "The Boys," shared, "There's no reason for us to risk the safety of our cast and crew for the sake of authenticity."

A petition initiated by filmmaker Bandar Albuliwi on Change.org has garnered nearly 70,000 signatures, advocating for a ban on real guns and live ammo on film and TV sets. Albuliwi stated, "We can no longer ignore the potential consequences of using real firearms on sets. It's time for a change."

California State Senator Dave Cortese and New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham are pushing for legislative action. Cortese declared, "We need stronger regulations to protect the lives of those working behind the scenes." Lujan Grisham added, "New Mexico has a rich film industry, but safety must be our top priority."

Filmmaker and activist Cameron Kasky, a survivor of the Parkland shooting, weighed in on the issue. "The film industry needs to take a hard look at its safety standards," he urged. "We've seen the devastating consequences of complacency."

Advances in visual effects technology have made it increasingly unnecessary to use real firearms for authenticity in production. Visual effects artists can easily create gun effects like muzzle flashes in post-production. Leslie Grossman echoed this sentiment, stating, "There's no need to put lives at risk for a visual effect that can be achieved in post."

However, concerns have been raised about on-set safety standards and oversight, particularly outside Los Angeles where many productions are filmed. Grossman highlighted a culture that often silences safety concerns, stressing, "No story is worth risking lives for."

As the film industry grapples with this issue, it remains to be seen what measures will be taken to ensure the safety of cast and crew members. One thing is clear: the tragic events on the set of "Rust" have shone a spotlight on the need for change.

Eric Kripke weighed in on the issue, expressing his belief that "the film industry can and should do better when it comes to safety. We owe it to our cast and crew to make sure they're working in a safe environment."

California State Senator Dave Cortese added, "We cannot afford to wait for another tragedy to occur. It's time for action."

As the debate continues, the film industry faces a pivotal moment in its history. Will it choose to prioritize safety and adapt to technological advancements, or cling to outdated practices that put lives at risk? The answer will undoubtedly shape the future of film and television production.

Michelle Lujan Grisham emphasized, "We cannot allow the pursuit of authenticity to overshadow the importance of safety. Lives are at stake."

Bandar Albuliwi, the filmmaker behind the Change.org petition, summed up the sentiment of many when he stated, "It's time for the film industry to evolve and prioritize safety over authenticity. We owe it to the memory of Halyna Hutchins and to all those who work behind the scenes."

Colin L. Powell, Trailblazing Military Leader and Diplomat, Leaves Behind Complex Political Legacy

Colin L. Powell, the first Black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and a former secretary of state, died on October 25 at the age of 84 due to complications from Covid-19. Powell's passing has sparked widespread tributes from both Republicans and Democrats, highlighting his service, his breaking of barriers as a Jamaican-American, and his moral stances. However, his political legacy is more complex, as he navigated a changing Republican Party and ultimately distanced himself from it.

In November 1995, Powell announced that he was a Republican, but he never sought the presidency. According to Douglas Heye, former Republican National Committee communications director, Powell aimed to move the Republican Party closer to the spirit of Lincoln, promoting racial diversity and welcoming immigrants. However, Powell's vision contrasted sharply with the direction the GOP took under Donald Trump, emphasizing anti-immigrant rhetoric and populism.

Powell endorsed Barack Obama in 2008 and later Democratic candidates, distancing himself from the GOP, especially after the January 6 insurrection. He was criticized by some in the GOP as a "RINO" (Republican in Name Only) and diverged from the party due to its shift towards Trump's ideology.

Leon Panetta, former defense secretary, remembered Powell as a dedicated public servant who put country ahead of party. Powell's centrist approach to politics could eventually unify the increasingly polarized U.S. political landscape, according to Ari Fleischer, George W. Bush's former White House press secretary.

Anthony Cordesman, national security adviser to McCain and emeritus strategy chair at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that Powell's legacy is not just about his military or diplomatic service but also about his commitment to bipartisanship and civility in politics.

Madeleine Albright, former secretary of state, praised Powell's commitment to public service and his ability to bridge partisan divides. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) also paid tribute to Powell's service, acknowledging his contributions to the country's national security and diplomacy.

Donald Trump, however, criticized Powell as a "classic RINO" and for attacking Republicans. Powell's death has sparked a renewed debate about the future of the Republican Party and the role of moderate voices within it.

In conclusion, Colin L. Powell's political legacy is complex and multifaceted, reflecting his commitment to public service, his moral compass, and his efforts to promote bipartisanship and civility in politics. His passing is a reminder of the importance of dedicated public servants who put country ahead of party and of the need for a more centrist approach to politics in an increasingly polarized landscape.

Climate Change: A Preview of What's to Come?

Hurricane Ida, a Category 4 storm that devastated Louisiana, serves as a chilling reminder of the intensifying impact of climate change. While the exact frequency of future hurricanes remains uncertain, one thing is clear: a warming planet fuels stronger and more destructive storms.

"Climate change was once seen as a future problem," says Andrew Dessler, a professor at Texas A&M University. "But we are the future, and it's here now."

From Hurricane Ida to California's wildfires, climate change amplifies disasters, making them costlier and more impactful for humans. The UN's recent climate report confirms human influence on global warming, leading to extreme weather events worldwide.

Rising sea levels exacerbate storm surges, while hotter temperatures increase atmospheric water vapor, resulting in heavier rainfall. Warmer waters also fuel stronger winds, creating a perfect storm for destruction, as seen with Ida.

Recent hurricanes like Laura, Michael, and Harvey demonstrate the increasing intensity of these events. Harvey's record-breaking rainfall was once unimaginable, and scientists predict even more rapid intensification in the future.

"These storms look weak offshore and then turn into monsters in 24 to 48 hours," Dessler explains. This rapid intensification leaves local authorities with limited time to evacuate residents and deploy emergency services.

With hundreds of thousands in Louisiana still without power, concerns about another disaster in the form of a heat wave loom large. Dessler emphasizes the need for proactive measures: "We need to start preparing for these rapid intensification events now."

Hurricane Ida serves as a stark warning. As climate change continues, we must be ready to face more frequent and devastating extreme weather events.

Facebook Outage Exposes Risks of Over-Reliance on Single Platform

On October 4, 2021, Facebook and its subsidiaries Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Oculus experienced a six-hour outage that disrupted communication and business operations worldwide. The incident highlighted the perils of over-relying on a single platform for essential services.

"This outage is a wake-up call for businesses and organizations that have become overly dependent on Facebook for their communication and business operations," said John Guilfoil, Principal of John Guilfoil Public Relations LLC.

Many brands and organizations rely heavily on Facebook for advertising, retail outreach, virtual events, and customer service. The outage left these entities scrambling to find alternative ways to reach their audiences and conduct business.

"It's a dangerous game to put all your eggs in one basket," Guilfoil warned. "Diversifying your communication methods is crucial to ensure that you can still reach your target audience, even when one platform goes down."

Guilfoil noted that some entities, including town fire chiefs, have become overly reliant on Facebook, neglecting to create and maintain their own websites. "While social media can be a valuable tool, it should never be your primary means of communication," he said.

The outage resulted in significant communication disruptions for those who solely relied on Facebook. News archives disappeared, leaving journalists and researchers without access to vital information.

"This outage has shown us that we need to be prepared for anything," Guilfoil said. "Having backup systems and contingency plans in place is essential to ensure that you can continue to operate, even when the unexpected happens."

Guilfoil emphasized the importance of websites and diversified communication strategies, even in the era of dominant social media platforms. "A website is your own digital home, where you have complete control over your content and communication," he said.

During the outage, advised clients were able to maintain communication through other platforms like Twitter, LinkedIn, and email. "Having multiple channels of communication allows you to reach your audience, no matter what," Guilfoil said.

The Facebook outage serves as a stark reminder of the importance of having backup systems and contingency plans in place. It also underscores the need for businesses and organizations to diversify their communication strategies and invest in their own websites.

"The days of relying solely on social media are over," Guilfoil concluded. "It's time to adopt a 'web first' approach and ensure that you have a strong online presence that is independent of any one platform."

A timeline of what Donald Trump said before the Capitol riot

In the weeks leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol, President Donald Trump repeatedly said he wanted his supporters to fight Congress on accepting the electoral college results that showed Joe Biden won.

“We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators, and congressmen and women,” Trump told his supporters shortly before the Capitol assault. “We’re probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them because you’ll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong.”

His supporters listened. Thousands of Trump supporters, waving Trump or Confederate flags and wearing MAGA gear, descended upon the Capitol. They overwhelmed law enforcement, pushed past police barricades, and temporarily stopped Congress from counting electoral votes.

Trump’s supporters had gathered earlier in the day for the “Save America” rally organized by a group called “Women for America First.” Trump allies, including former campaign staffers, helped promote the event, ABC News reported. Trump’s White House schedule showed he was to speak at the rally that day.

Some of Trump’s fiercest allies also made incendiary statements at the rally. “Let’s have trial by combat,” said Trump’s lawyer Rudy Giuliani, warming up the crowd for Trump.

We looked closely at the words Trump used to urge his supporters to show up and “fight” on his behalf Jan. 6. With Trump’s Twitter account permanently suspended, we used archives of his tweets by Factba.se and the Trump Twitter archive.

We contacted spokespersons for Trump and did not get a response.

What Trump said before Jan. 6

For months before Election Day, Trump repeatedly told his supporters falsehoods about voting, including that Democrats had “rigged” the election. Trump ramped up the rhetoric after he lost the election, filing court challenges in battleground states trying to get judges to reverse the outcome. After he racked up defeats in court, Trump’s tactics turned toward ordering senators to “fight” for him.

“.@senatemajldr and Republican Senators have to get tougher, or you won’t have a Republican Party anymore. We won the Presidential Election, by a lot. FIGHT FOR IT. Don’t let them take it away!” he tweeted Dec. 18.

In December, Trump also issued a battle cry to his supporters broadly, encouraging them to gather on his behalf Jan. 6.

Dec. 12: On the day of pro-Trump rallies in Washington, D.C., Trump tweeted “Wow! Thousands of people forming in Washington (D.C.) for Stop the Steal. Didn’t know about this, but I’ll be seeing them! #MAGA.”

Dec. 12: “WE HAVE JUST BEGUN TO FIGHT!!!” Trump said in another tweet.

Dec. 19: Trump tweeted his praise for a report by his adviser Peter Navarro alleging election fraud: “A great report by Peter. Statistically impossible to have lost the 2020 Election. Big protest in D.C. on January 6th. Be there, will be wild!”

Dec. 26: Trump tweeted: “The ‘Justice’ Department and the FBI have done nothing about the 2020 Presidential Election Voter Fraud, the biggest SCAM in our nation’s history, despite overwhelming evidence. They should be ashamed. History will remember. Never give up. See everyone in D.C. on January 6th.”

Dec. 27: “See you in Washington, DC, on January 6th. Don’t miss it. Information to follow!” Trump tweeted.

Jan. 1: “The BIG Protest Rally in Washington, D.C., will take place at 11.00 A.M. on January 6th. Locational details to follow. StopTheSteal!” Trump tweeted.

Jan. 1: “January 6th. See you in D.C.” Trump tweeted.

Jan. 3: Trump retweeted @JenLawrence21, an organizer of a March for Trump bus tour: “Now we will bring it to DC on Jan 6 and PROUDLY stand beside you!”

Jan. 3: Trump retweeted Amy Kremer, another promoter of the march who said, “We are excited to announce the site of our January 6th event will be The Ellipse in the President’s Park, just steps from the White House!”

Jan. 3: Trump retweeted @CodeMonkeyZ: “If you are planning to attend peaceful protests in DC on the 6th, i recommend wearing a body camera. The more video angles of that day the better.”

Jan. 4: At a rally in Georgia the day before the Senate runoffs, Trump repeated his grievances about his own election. He spoke about a continued fight, both for himself and the Senate.

“If the liberal Democrats take the Senate and the White House — and they’re not taking this White House — we’re going to fight like hell, I’ll tell you right now,” Trump said.

“We’re going to take it back,” Trump said.

What Trump said before the riot

Trump’s final direction to supporters came during his “Save America” rally around noon Jan. 6, when he repeated his Pants on Fire claim that he won.

“Our country has had enough,” Trump told his supporters. “We will not take it anymore and that’s what this is all about. To use a favorite term that all of you people really came up with, we will stop the steal.”

The crowd later chanted: “Fight for Trump! Fight for Trump! Fight for Trump!” Trump thanked them.

Trump praised the crowd for traveling from across the nation and for “the extraordinary love.”

“We’re gathered together in the heart of our nation’s capital for one very, very basic and simple reason: to save our democracy,” Trump said.

Trump repeatedly said there was a need to “fight.” After he bashed “weak” Republicans and Biden, he said: “Unbelievable, what we have to go through, what we have to go through and you have to get your people to fight. If they don’t fight, we have to primary the hell out of the ones that don’t fight. You primary them. We’re going to let you know who they are, I can already tell you, frankly.”

He continued with the fighting metaphors: “Republicans are constantly fighting like a boxer with his hands tied behind his back. It’s like a boxer, and we want to be so nice. We want to be so respectful of everybody, including bad people. We’re going to have to fight much harder, and Mike Pence is going to have to come through for us. And if he doesn’t, that will be a sad day for our country because you’re sworn to uphold our constitution. Now it is up to Congress to confront this egregious assault on our democracy.”

Trump then invited the crowd to go to the Capitol.

“And after this, we’re going to walk down, and I’ll be there with you. We’re going to walk down. We’re going to walk down any one you want, but I think right here. We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators, and congressmen and women. We’re probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you’ll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong.”

Trump used the word “peacefully” once at his rally:

“We have come to demand that Congress do the right thing and only count the electors who have been lawfully slated, lawfully slated. I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard. Today we will see whether Republicans stand strong for integrity of our elections, but whether or not they stand strong for our country, our country. Our country has been under siege for a long time, far longer than this four-year period.”

What Trump said during and after the riot

By the time Trump finished his speech, crowds had already started to gather outside the Capitol.

Trump never joined them, but did tweet during the afternoon and night and released a video statement.

“Please support our Capitol Police and Law Enforcement. They are truly on the side of our Country. Stay peaceful!” he tweeted at 2:38 p.m. By that point, the mob had already shattered windows as they pushed inside the building.

His video statement repeated false claims about the fraudulent election and said, “We have to have peace. So go home. We love you. You’re very special.”

He rehashed those themes in his final tweet of the night. It ended with these words: “Remember this day forever!”

Investigational AstraZeneca vaccine prevents COVID-19

Results from a large clinical trial in the United States and South America indicate that AstraZeneca’s COVID-19 vaccine, AZD1222, is well-tolerated and protects against symptomatic COVID-19 disease, including severe disease or hospitalization. The independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) overseeing the trial identified no safety concerns related to the vaccine. The United Kingdom-based global biopharmaceutical company AstraZeneca developed the vaccine and led the trial as regulatory sponsor.

The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the National Institutes of Health, and the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response, provided funding support for the trial through the federal COVID-19 response.

The placebo-controlled trial began in August 2020. The analysis is based on results from 32,449 adult volunteer participants enrolled across 88 sites in the United States, Chile and Peru. One participant received a placebo for every two participants who received AZD1222, resulting in approximately 20,000 people receiving the investigational vaccine. The vaccine was administered as two doses of 5 x1010 viral particles four weeks apart.

AZD1222 demonstrated statistically significant vaccine efficacy of 78.9% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 and 100% efficacy in preventing severe or critical disease and hospitalization. In participants 65 years and older, who comprised 20% of the trial population, vaccine efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 was 79.9%.

The DSMB conducted a review of thrombotic events (blood clots) and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) among participants and found no increased risk of these conditions in vaccinated participants.

Approximately 79% of participants were white, 22% were Hispanic, 8% were Black or African American, 4% were Native American, including American Indian/Alaska Native participants residing in the U.S., and 4% were Asian. Vaccine efficacy was consistent across ethnicity. Approximately 60% of participants of any age had underlying health conditions associated with an increased risk of developing severe COVID-19, such as diabetes, severe obesity or cardiac disease.

Authorization and guidelines for use of the vaccine in the United States will be determined by the Food and Drug Administration and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention after thorough review of the data by independent advisory committees. Today’s results build on data from multiple clinical trials of AZD1222 conducted worldwide. The World Health Organization has recommended use of the vaccine for prevention of COVID-19 in adults and it is currently available for use in more than 70 countries. The European Commission has granted a conditional marketing authorization for the vaccine in the European Union.

The current trial defined symptomatic COVID-19 as having SARS-CoV-2 infection and at least one respiratory symptom (pneumonia, shortness of breath or low oxygen requiring supplemental oxygen) or at least two of the following symptoms: fever, new or worsening cough, muscle pain, fatigue, vomiting and/or diarrhea, and loss of smell and/or loss of taste. Severe or critical COVID-19 was defined as having SARS-CoV-2 infection and any of the following: clinical signs of severe systemic illness, respiratory failure (defined as needing high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, known as ECMO), evidence of shock, significant acute renal, hepatic or neurologic dysfunction, or admission to an intensive care unit or death.

AZD1222 was developed by Oxford University’s Jenner Institute and Oxford Vaccine Group and then licensed to AstraZeneca for further development. It is a viral vector-based vaccine that uses a safe, non-replicating chimpanzee adenovirus to deliver the genetic code of a protein found on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 (called the spike protein) to human cells so that the cells can make the protein. Adenoviruses can cause the common cold in humans, but the virus has been modified so that it cannot replicate and cause disease. The technology is based on a vaccine that Oxford previously was developing for Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV). AZD1222 can be stored, transported and handled at 36 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit (normal refrigeration temperatures) for at least six months.

A DSMB formed by NIH monitored the trial to ensure participant safety and the validity and integrity of the data. The same DSMB is overseeing other ongoing Phase 3 vaccine clinical trials as part of the federal COVID-19 response effort. Representatives from AstraZeneca, NIAID and BARDA receive recommendations from the DSMB.

Sites that are part of the COVID-19 Prevention Network (CoVPN) enrolled volunteers in the clinical trial. The CoVPN is composed of existing NIAID-supported clinical research networks with infectious disease expertise and was designed for efficient and thorough evaluation of vaccine candidates and monoclonal antibodies for the prevention of COVID-19. CoVPN investigators Ann R. Falsey, M.D., professor of medicine, University of Rochester School of Medicine in New York, and Magdalena E. Sobieszczyk, M.D., associate professor of medicine at Columbia University Medical Center in New York, are coordinating investigators for the trial.

Participants will continue to be followed as part of the trial for approximately two years following their second injection. More details about the trial are available at PreventCovid.org and at clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT04516746.

About the COVID-19 Prevention Network: The COVID-19 Prevention Network (CoVPN) was formed by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health to respond to the global pandemic. Through the CoVPN, NIAID is leveraging the infectious disease expertise of its existing research networks and global partners to address the pressing need for vaccines and antibodies against SARS-CoV-2. CoVPN will work to develop and conduct studies to ensure rapid and thorough evaluation of vaccines and antibodies for the prevention of COVID-19. The CoVPN is headquartered at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center. For more information about the CoVPN, visit: PreventCovid.org.

About HHS, ASPR, and BARDA: HHS works to enhance and protect the health and well-being of all Americans, providing for effective health and human services and fostering advances in medicine, public health, and social services. The mission of ASPR is to save lives and protect Americans from 21st century health security threats. Within ASPR, BARDA invests in the innovation, advanced research and development, acquisition, and manufacturing of medical countermeasures – vaccines, drugs, therapeutics, diagnostic tools, and non-pharmaceutical products needed to combat health security threats. To date, BARDA-supported products have achieved 59 FDA approvals, licensures or clearances. To learn more about the nationwide COVID-19 response, visit https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus.

About the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases: NIAID conducts and supports research — at NIH, throughout the United States, and worldwide — to study the causes of infectious and immune-mediated diseases, and to develop better means of preventing, diagnosing and treating these illnesses. News releases, fact sheets and other NIAID-related materials are available on the NIAID website.

Twin Blasts in Kabul: ISIS-K Attack Exposes Lingering Terror Threat Amid Taliban Rule

In the aftermath of devastating twin blasts outside Kabul's airport, which left scores dead and injured, U.S. officials have placed the blame on the Islamic State affiliate in Afghanistan, ISIS-K. The group, known for its ruthless tactics, has vowed more attacks, setting the stage for potential retaliation from the United States.

President Joe Biden, in a statement, vowed to hunt down the perpetrators, saying, "We will not forgive. We will not forget. We will hunt you down and make you pay." He defended the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, emphasizing that the original mission was to neutralize al-Qaeda following the 9/11 attacks.

The attack underscores the continuing terrorism threat in Afghanistan, with both ISIS-K and al-Qaeda posing challenges despite the Taliban's takeover. Fawaz Gerges, a professor at the London School of Economics, explains, "The Taliban's return to power does not mean the end of terrorism in Afghanistan. Both al-Qaeda and ISIS-K have shown resilience."

Taliban spokesman Mohammad Naeem has assured the international community that the group will not allow Afghanistan to be used as a base for terrorism. However, doubts persist about the Taliban's ability or willingness to sever ties with al-Qaeda. Abdul Sayed, an Afghanistan analyst, notes, "The Taliban and al-Qaeda share a common history and ideology, which makes it hard to believe they will completely part ways."

Al-Qaeda, while significantly weakened, still maintains a presence in the country, with estimates of its membership ranging from a few dozen to 500. Secretary of State Antony Blinken acknowledged this, stating, "We remain vigilant about the threat posed by al-Qaeda and other terrorist groups."

A recent U.N. report indicates that al-Qaeda and the Taliban maintain close ties, sharing an ideological alignment and personal relationships. Nathan Sales, a former senior counterterrorism official, warns, "The Taliban's relationship with al-Qaeda is one of convenience and mutual interest. It's not something that can be easily dissolved."

On the other hand, ISIS-K, which emerged in 2015, operates independently from the Taliban and al-Qaeda, focusing on territorial control within Afghanistan. The group has been responsible for numerous attacks on civilians and minorities. Michael Kugelman, the deputy director of the Asia Program at the Wilson Center, says, "ISIS-K is more of a domestic threat, but its presence in Afghanistan raises concerns for neighboring countries."

While al-Qaeda may currently lack the capacity for immediate threats against the United States, experts caution that its resurgence under Taliban rule remains a possibility. The situation on the ground in Afghanistan, with multiple extremist factions vying for influence, complicates the international community's efforts to ensure the country does not once again become a breeding ground for terrorism.

Hurricane Ida Leaves Devastation and Oil Slicks in Wake

Hurricane Ida, which recently tore through Louisiana and made its way up the Eastern Seaboard, leaving destruction and despair in its path, has also resulted in significant environmental damage. Federal and state agencies, along with private companies, are now investigating oil slicks that have appeared in the Gulf of Mexico following the storm.

The U.S. Coast Guard has so far assessed over 1,500 reports of pollution, with nearly 350 incidents prioritized for further investigation. Collaborative efforts among the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the state of Louisiana, and the National Ocean Service (NOS) aim to address the escalating environmental concerns.

Landsat 8 satellite imagery has revealed oil slicks off Louisiana's coast near Port Fourchon, suggesting potential pipeline damage. With 90 to 95 percent of the region's oil and gas production disrupted, the Gulf of Mexico may be facing a substantial oil spill, the extent of which remains uncertain.

Near Port Fourchon, the surface oil slicks might originate from up to three damaged or ruptured submarine pipelines. Several factors could contribute to pipeline failures during hurricanes, such as corrosion, aging, or direct physical damage from floating debris.

The Gulf of Mexico's seafloor contains an extensive network of oil and gas infrastructure, raising concerns about its vulnerability to powerful storms like Ida. A U.S. Government Accountability Office report revealed that a staggering 97 percent of decommissioned pipelines were left on the seafloor, increasing the potential for environmental harm during future hurricanes.

The damage caused by Hurricane Ida not only highlights the importance of addressing the vulnerabilities of offshore infrastructure but also emphasizes the need for improved decommissioning practices. As response teams work diligently to restore the affected areas and investigate the extent of the oil spill, it is crucial to reflect on the lessons learned and develop strategies to mitigate similar environmental disasters in the future.

Chauvin Trial Nears End as Defense Rests, Leaving Jury to Decide George Floyd's Fate

The trial of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin, charged with the murder of George Floyd, is nearing its conclusion. After two weeks of prosecution testimony, the defense rested its case after only two days, with Chauvin choosing not to take the stand.

Closing arguments are scheduled for Monday, followed by jury deliberations in a city on edge. The recent fatal police shooting of a young Black man in a Minneapolis suburb has heightened tensions, leading to Minneapolis public schools switching to distance learning in anticipation of the verdict.

Before the jury's return on Thursday, Chauvin, without his mask, invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to testify, ending weeks of speculation. Judge Peter Cahill reminded jurors of their upcoming sequestration, advising them to "plan for long and hope for short."

Chauvin, 45, faces charges of murder and manslaughter in the death of Floyd, a 46-year-old Black man arrested on suspicion of using a counterfeit $20 bill. Bystander video of Floyd's death, where he repeatedly states he can't breathe while pinned under Chauvin's knee, sparked global protests and ignited a critical discussion on racism and policing in the U.S.

The most serious charge against Chauvin, second-degree murder, carries a potential sentence of 40 years, though state guidelines suggest a sentence around 12 years.

Prosecutors argue that Floyd died due to Chauvin's knee compressing his neck for over 9 minutes while he lay on his stomach, handcuffed and face-down. Testimony from law enforcement veterans, both within and outside the Minneapolis department, supported the prosecution's claim of excessive force and violation of training protocols. Medical experts further confirmed Floyd's death by asphyxiation due to restricted breathing.

Chauvin's defense countered with testimony from a police use-of-force expert and a forensic pathologist. They argued that Chauvin acted appropriately against a resisting suspect and that Floyd's death resulted from a combination of underlying heart conditions, illegal drug use, and high blood pressure.

The only public defense from Chauvin himself came from body-camera footage played for the jury. After Floyd was taken away by ambulance, Chauvin is heard saying, "We gotta control this guy 'cause he's a sizable guy... and it looks like he's probably on something."

The decision of whether to testify was a calculated risk for Chauvin. Taking the stand could have allowed him to directly address the jury and explain his actions, but it also opened him up to cross-examination and potential inconsistencies with previous statements.

With closing arguments and jury deliberations imminent, the eyes of the nation are on Minneapolis as the Chauvin trial reaches its climax. The verdict will not only determine the fate of the former officer but also potentially impact the ongoing conversation about racial justice and police accountability in the United States.

Discussions are ongoing between the Taliban, Qatar, and Turkey regarding the management of Kabul's airport following the withdrawal of US forces, which has left the airport without air traffic control services. These talks aim to facilitate the secure operation of the airport, enabling commercial flights for individuals seeking to leave Afghanistan, as stated by French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian.

Le Drian emphasized the importance of implementing the Security Council resolution concerning airport security and highlighted ongoing negotiations with Qatar and Turkey about its management. He stressed the necessity for safe access to the airport during an interview on France 2 television.

The departure of American forces has led to the prohibition of American civil aircraft from flying over Afghanistan without specific authorization, according to the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The FAA cited the absence of air traffic services and a functional civil aviation authority in Afghanistan, along with persistent security concerns, as reasons for this prohibition. However, they mentioned that US civil aircraft could use a high-altitude jet route along the country's far eastern border for overflights, subject to prior authorization from the FAA.

The US military had previously taken over air traffic control duties in Kabul earlier in the month to aid in evacuating tens of thousands from Afghanistan. While US air carriers and civilian pilots were allowed to fly into Kabul for evacuation or relief efforts with the US Defense Department's approval, all flights were required to receive prior authorization from the FAA. How Climate Change Made Hurricane Ida More Destructive

Hurricane Ida provided a stark illustration of how human-caused climate change is intensifying hurricanes, making them more dangerous and destructive. Warmer ocean temperatures fueled Ida's rapid intensification, leading to record-breaking rainfall and devastating storm surges.

Intensifying Storms:

  • Warmer oceans provide more "fuel" for hurricanes, leading to increased intensity and rapid intensification like Ida's 65 mph wind increase in just 24 hours.
  • The proportion of Category 3-5 hurricanes has risen in recent decades due to warming oceans.
  • For every degree Celsius of warming, intense rainfall events are projected to increase by 7%.

Increased Rainfall:

  • Warmer air holds more moisture, leading to heavier rainfall. Ida dumped over 15 inches of rain on parts of Louisiana, exacerbating existing flooding issues.
  • The remnants of Ida are expected to bring another 3-7 inches of rain to 12 states, including areas already hit by severe flooding.

Slower-Moving Storms:

  • Satellite data shows hurricanes are moving slower, particularly after landfall. This allows them to cover a larger area and dump more rain.
  • A 2020 study found storms are staying stronger further inland due to warmer sea surface temperatures, leading to "slower decay" and prolonged impacts.

Higher Storm Surge:

  • Sea level rise caused by climate change worsens storm surge, inundating larger areas with ocean water.
  • Storm surge from a hurricane of the same intensity today would be more extensive than 50 or 100 years ago.

The Future of Hurricanes:

  • As the planet continues to warm, scientists expect hurricanes to become even more intense, bringing heavier rainfall, slower movement, and higher storm surges.
  • These changes pose significant risks to coastal communities and infrastructure, highlighting the urgency of addressing climate change.

Key Takeaways:

  • Climate change is making hurricanes more dangerous.
  • Ida is a prime example of these changes, with record-breaking rainfall and storm surge.
  • We can expect more frequent and intense hurricanes in the future.
  • Addressing climate change is crucial to mitigate these risks.

Engineering Ingenuity: Expanding and Deepening for Safety

The SCA's expansion plans involve widening the canal by 40 meters and deepening it by two meters. These enhancements will enable the passage of larger vessels, reducing the risk of groundings and enhancing the canal's overall efficiency.
